text: Molecular equations of state (EoSs) represent an alternative route for predicting the thermodynamic properties of complex mixtures, including polymer systems. The statistical associating fluid theory (SAFT), first developed in the late 1980s, 55,56 has been widely used to model and predict the thermodynamic behavior of complex fluids. 57,58 It has a rigorous statistical mechanical foundation based on Wertheim's perturbation theory 59 -62 and considers the effects of molecular size, shape, and distinct intermolecular interactions, such as hydrogen bonding. The use of the equation of state to model the amorphous polymer as liquid-like has been shown to provide a complete description of the phase behavior of polymer + solvent mixtures, by considering vapor -liquid equilibrium (VLE), liquid -liquid equilibrium (LLE) 63 -65 as well as SLE 66 when crystalline polymer is present. Ghosh and Chapman 67 employed the original SAFT model to predict the SLE of 13.6 g/mol PE in degraded PE, paraffin wax, cetene, and n -heptane with good agreement with experimental data. The perturbedchain statistical associating fluid theory (PC-SAFT) EoS, 68 in which the original SAFT equation is modified by applying the perturbation theory of Barker and Henderson 69 to a hard-chain reference fluid, has also been used to study polymer + solvent mixtures. Arndt et al. 30 applied PC-SAFT to predict the solubility of 133 kg/mol PE in n -hexane and cyclohexane, finding close agreement to experimental data. Xiong et al. 65 compared the predictive performance of the original SAFT version with the Sanchez-Lacombe theory in predicting the LCST LLE curves of various PE samples in high-pressure n -butane and n -pentane. They found that SAFT yielded lower deviations from experimental data. Paricaud et al. 64 applied the SAFT-VR SW 70 (square well) version of the equation of state to predict the sorption of n -pentane in amorphous PE, via VLE and LLE calculations. They also examined the influence of polymer molecular weight on the cloud curves, reporting good overall agreement with experimental observations. In terms of SLE of polymer + solvent mixtures, Pan and Radosz 71 studied the phase behavior of semicrystalline polymers with the copolymer SAFT approach. 72 In this method, segment interactions are described through a Lennard-Jones potential, similar to the original SAFT equation. However, unlike the original SAFT, the copolymer approach incorporates heteronuclear segments to account for copolymers and introduces bond fractions to capture polymer branching density. They employed sensitivity analysis to verify the effects of crystallinity, fusion temperature, molecular weight, and pressure on the phase behavior (SLE and LLE) of mixtures of PE and propane, m -xylene and amyl acetate.

text: In the SAFT variants discussed so far, except for the copolymer SAFT model, which extends the theory to copolymers and branched polymers, the molecular segments are treated as homonuclear. This assumption limits the model's transferability to systems involving chemically diverse solvent molecules, particularly when experimental data are scarce and parametrization becomes time-consuming. text: The SAFTγ Mie EoS 73 -75 is such an approach, with molecules described as comprising distinct functional groups based on a fused heteronuclear model, with interactions between segments characterized through Mie potentials. 73 Employing a third-order perturbation expansion for the monomeric term using the Mie potential in the SAFTγ Mie equation has been shown to deliver accurate thermodynamic properties of complex fluids, including derivative properties. 75 -77 The key strength of the GC method is its ability to predict properties based on known functional group contributions, so that the behavior of any pure component or mixture containing the known functional groups can be predicted. The GC method allows for the description of compounds for which experimental data were not included in parameter development, increasing the transferability of the EoS.

Here, we examine the applicability of the SAFTγ Mie approach to different PE samples in various solvents that are relevant to solvent-based plastic recycling applications. We compare the calculations to measurements of the temperaturedependent solubility of PE in various solvents obtained using the polythermal method. Four PE samples with varying molecular weight, density, and fusion properties are investigated in solvents selected based on several properties that are relevant to plastic recycling. The results of the current study will deepen the understanding of the dissolution of PE, offering valuable insights for future solvent selection and process design in the solvent-based recycling of PE.

Here, we examine the applicability of the SAFTγ Mie approach to different PE samples in various solvents that are relevant to solvent-based plastic recycling applications. We compare the calculations to measurements of the temperaturedependent solubility of PE in various solvents obtained using the polythermal method. Four PE samples with varying molecular weight, density, and fusion properties are investigated in solvents selected based on several properties that are relevant to plastic recycling. The results of the current study will deepen the understanding of the dissolution of PE, offering valuable insights for future solvent selection and process design in the solvent-based recycling of PE.

Fusion Property Measurements

text:
Fusion properties of the PE samples were determined using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The instrument used was a NETZSCH 200 F3 thermal analyzer. The calibration was done with six standard samples (adamantane, bismuth, cesium chloride, indium, tin, and zinc) at a heating/cooling rate of 5 K/min. For each measurement, a weighed amount of polymer powder or pellets was sealed in an aluminum crucible, which was then placed alongside a reference in the measurement chamber. Nitrogen gas was purged through the chamber throughout the experiment to maintain an inert atmosphere.

The temperature program consisted of the following steps: initially, the temperature was raised from 298 to 423 K to fully melt the PE sample, removing any thermal history resulting from prior manufacturing processes. The temperature was then decreased to 273 K to ensure complete solidification. Finally, the sample was reheated to 423 K to measure the temperature of fusion T fus and the specific enthalpy of fusion Δ h fus . All heating and cooling rates in this thermal cycle were fixed at 5 K/min, consistent with the calibration conditions.

The temperature of fusion T fus was taken as the onset temperature of the endothermal peak, while Δ h fus was calculated as the area under the endothermal peak, divided by the mass of the PE sample.

text: The polythermal solubility measurements were conducted using an automated multireactor crystallizer, Crystal 16, from Technobis Crystallization Systems. It is equipped with 16 separate reactors, divided into 4 blocks. In each block, an individual temperature profile can be set. Temperature ramping can be realized in increments of 0.1 K/min with a detection accuracy of 0.5 K. Each reactor is equipped with magnetic stirring and an individual turbidity sensor with a red LED light source, which has a peak output at 645 nm.

text: The experimental procedure for polythermal solubility measurements was conducted as follows: a precisely weighed amount of PE sample and solvent was loaded into a 1.5 mL glass HPLC vial equipped with either a magnetic stir bar or an overhead stirrer, depending on the anticipated viscosity of the solution. The vial was sealed and placed in the reactor, which was then rapidly heated (heating rate of 20 K/min) to 5 K below the temperature of fusion of the respective PE sample (375.2 -399.5 K) to facilitate rapid dissolution while ensuring that a solid polymer phase may, in principle, be stable. This temperature was held until complete dissolution, which was confirmed by visual inspection. This initial dissolution step was intended to eliminate kinetic limitations arising from polymer morphology and thermal history, ensuring reproducible acquisition of the thermodynamic clear point in subsequent cycles. At this stage, the transmissivity was calibrated to 100%, thus setting the fully dissolved solution as a reference. This calibration accounted for possible optical variations such as diffraction, absorption, and refraction caused by the polymer, solvent, and the measurement vial. By setting this baseline of 100%, the clear point in the following thermal cycles could be consistently identified as the temperature at which the transmissivity returned to this calibrated value, indicating complete dissolution.

text:
Before starting the measurement cycles, a prerun cycle was conducted to set the temperature range of the cycles as follows: the temperature was decreased at a cooling rate of 3 K/min until the transmissivity dropped from 100%, i.e., the cloud point was reached. Phase separation was confirmed visually. The temperature was then increased at a heating rate of 3 K/min until the transmissivity returned to 100%, i.e., the clear point was reached. Visual confirmation of the complete dissolution was conducted again.

Subsequently, measurement cycles were undertaken: the temperature was decreased to 2 K below the cloud point (minimum temperature of the cycle) and then raised to 2 K above the clear point (maximum temperature of the cycle), as approximately determined by the prerun cycle. This thermal cycle was repeated at least three times. The average of the measured clear points of the first three cycles was taken as the representative value of the SLE temperature.

The key properties of the four PE samples used in our work are summarized in Table 1. The PE samples vary in density (from low-density to medium-density), molecular weight, polydispersity index, temperature, and enthalpy of fusion. As the molecular weight and melting properties were not provided by the manufacturer for most samples, they were measured as part of the current work. The temperature and enthalpy of fusion were measured by DSC. As can be seen in Table 1, the measured temperatures of fusion T fus lie between 375.2 and 399.5 K, while the measured enthalpies of fusion Δ h fus lie between 89.3 and 201.5 J/g. The molecular weights of the PE samples were measured by high-temperature gel permeation chromatography (HT-GPC). The number-averaged molecular weights Mn , of the PE samples range between 1.5 and 22 kg/ mol, while the weight-averaged molecular weights Mw , range between 4.9 and 105 kg/mol. n CH2 values for the PE samples were calculated from the measured Mw using eq 18.

Solvent Selection

The selection of solvents was performed following the systematic procedure shown in Figure 3 and involved four criteria:

text:
1 HSP criterion. The RED value must be less than one, when calculated using LDPE as the solute, for which the parameter values were taken from Hansen's original database: δ d = 15.9, δ p = 4.9, δ h = 1.5, and the interaction radius R 0 = 8.0. 82

2 Boiling-point criterion. The normal boiling temperature of the solvent must be sufficiently high for operational purposes, because the dissolution of PE is usually slow and occurs at elevated temperatures. A value of 338 K (the boiling point of THF) was set as the minimum normal boiling point criterion.

3 Hazard criterion. Solvents that are commonly known to raise toxicity/or environmental concerns should be excluded, as using harmful solvents would contradict the aims of sustainable polymer recycling.

SI Table S1) was chosen from commonly used organic solvents, bio-derived solvents, and solvents previously reported in the literature for PE. 12 -19,21 The HSP values were calculated, and it was found that 33 solvents had a RED value lower than one. These 33 solvents were further reduced down to 23 following the boiling-point criterion and 16 following the hazard criterion. For example, low-boiling-point solvents (e.g., acetone, dichloromethane) were excluded due to criterion 1, and solvents that are known to be particularly hazardous (e.g., benzene, chlorinated hydrocarbons such as trichlorobenzene and chloroform) were excluded due to criterion 2.

After the solubility criterion was applied, 10 solvents were selected and used to measure and model the solubility of PE. They are n -dodecane, decalin, dibutoxymethane, p -cymene, limonene, mesitylene, cyclohexanone, α -pinene, p -xylene, and toluene. The structure and properties of the selected solvents, their RED values, and the SAFTγ Mie groups used to model them, are listed in Table 2. For solvents with stereochemistry, racemic mixtures were used in the experiments, as they are considerably less expensive and are expected to show minimal differences in dissolution performance compared to pure enantiomers.

text: It is known that the dissolution of polymers can occur at an extremely low rate. 92 Thus, the effect of the heating rate was investigated first to ensure the consistency and reliability of clear-point acquisition. For this purpose, each of the four PE samples was prepared in decalin and n -dodecane at polymer weight fractions of 0.02 and 0.15 g/g, respectively. These two solvents were selected based on preliminary experiments, which identified decalin mixtures as having the lowest SLE temperature at a given weight fraction, indicating the highest PE solubility, while PE + n -dodecane exhibited the highest SLE temperature, reflecting the lowest solubility. Experiments were conducted with a fixed cooling rate (0.3 K/min) and a varying heating rate across a minimum of three repeating cycles (from 0.1 to 0.5 K/min). The stirring rate was set to 700 rpm to ensure uniform mixing and rapid heat transfer. It was observed that heating rates below 0.5 K/min produced consistent clearpoint results, indicating that equilibrium was reached under this condition. Higher heating rates were observed to cause shifts of the clear point to higher temperatures due to delayed equilibration. Based on this, a heating rate of 0.1 -0.2 K/min was chosen throughout the measurements to ensure data reliability.

text: Comparing LDPE-1 and LDPE-2, it can be seen in Table 1 that they have similar densities (0.92 vs 0.925 g/cm 3 ) but differ significantly in molecular weight (4.9 vs 105 kg/mol) and present small differences in the temperature and specific enthalpy of fusion (375.2 K, 89.3 J/g vs 379.9 K, 123.0 J/g). Comparison of their SLE temperatures in the various solvents (Figures 4 and 5) reveals a 10 K difference at a given weight fraction for all solvents. When comparing the properties of LDPE-2 and MDPE, we find that their melting properties are in a similar range (379.9 K, 123.0 J/g vs 378.5 K, 114.7 J/g), but they differ in molecular weight (105 vs 7.6 kg/mol) and density (0.92 vs 0.94 g/cm 3 ). Despite these differences, the measured solubility temperatures of LDPE-2 and MDPE are found to be close in value at a given weight fraction. These observations suggest that the temperature and enthalpy of fusion of PE have a greater influence on the solubility of PE than molecular weight and density. This conclusion is further supported by the significantly higher SLE temperatures observed in the mixtures with LDPE-3 compared to those with other PE samples. Across all solvents, LDPE-3 exhibits SLE temperatures approximately 10 -20 K higher than those of other PE samples at a given weight fraction, consistent with the higher temperature of fusion of LDPE-3 (cf. Table 1).

SLE temperatures corresponding to weight fractions of 0.05, 0.15, and 0.25 g/g are determined by interpolating linearly from the two nearest experimental data points. The resulting temperatures for a given PE sample at a given weight fraction are then normalized based on the maximum and minimum values across all solvents, and a graded color scheme in 10 intervals is applied to emphasize visually the differences in SLE temperatures for different solvents.

An analysis of the heat-map uncovers a pattern of solvent performance in the four PE samples. First, the ranking of the solvents remains largely consistent for various PE samples. Decalin, a bicyclic molecule, is found to be the best solvent, with the lowest SLE temperature recorded for any given composition. Aromatic solvents such as toluene and p -xylene, two widely reported solvents for PE dissolution, 14,17,93 along with their structural analogue mesitylene, consistently exhibit an SLE temperature slightly above that of decalin.

Interestingly, the three reported bioderived solvents for PE 21  limonene, p -cymene, and α -pinene  exhibit only slightly higher SLE temperatures than toluene and p -xylene, suggesting their potential as alternatives with comparable solubility performance. n -Dodecane, despite its structural similarity to PE, performs less effectively in dissolving all of the PE samples. Finally, dibutoxymethane and cyclohexanone, though having low RED values, exhibit the poorest solubility performance. Notably, they fail to dissolve LDPE-2 and MDPE at higher weight fractions.

SAFTγ Mie Modeling

We start by evaluating the effects of temperature of fusion and specific enthalpy of fusion, crystallinity and molecular weight of PE, on the SAFTγ Mie-predicted SLE of PE in selected solvents. We then analyze the predictive capability of SAFTγ Mie for different solvent types and PE samples. LDPE-1 and LDPE-2 are chosen as representative polymer samples for detailed investigation, as they have the lowest and highest Mw values, respectively (cf. Table 1). The SAFTγ Mie predictions for MDPE and LDPE-3 are included in the SI (cf. Figures S4 -S8). The modeling section concludes with an assessment of the accuracy of the SAFTγ Mie model by comparing the predictions to the solubility data measured in the current work and to data available in the literature.

text: LDPE-2 is chosen as the first sample polymer, and four values of the temperature of fusion are considered: that of the fully crystalline polyethylene, reported as T 414.6K LDPE,c fus = 94 for 1.4 × 10 7 g/mol PE, our measured value of T 379.9K LDPE 2,1 fus = (cf. Table 1), the value specified by the manufacturer 90 of T 389.0K LDPE 2,2 fus = , and the average of our measured value and that reported by the manufacturer, T 384.2K LDPE 2,3 fus = . In Figure 7, we present SAFTγ Mie predictions of the orthobaric P P ( ) sol vap = solubility of LDPE-2 in toluene using these four T fus values and setting h 293.0J/g LDPE,c fus = , chosen to be consistent with previous modeling of PE + solvent mixtures with SAFTγ Mie. 79 The ∼ 35 K range of values results in a very wide variation of predicted solubility values. The SAFTγ Mie predictions are found to be in excellent agreement with our solubility data when using the manufacturer's specified temperature of fusion, T 389.0K LDPE 2,2 fus = ; this value is used throughout for sample LDPE-2. It is important to note that deviations in the predicted solubility when using our measured value do not necessarily indicate an inaccuracy in the measurement of T LDPE 2 fus itself. The predicted solubilities also depend on the value of h i fus , and importantly, on the SAFTγ Mie interaction parameters used to predict the activity coefficient (cf. Equation15), which we use in an entirely transferable manner as part of the group-contribution methodology, and which have not been refined to polymer data. It is worth noting that the use of a T LDPE 2 fus value lower than 414.6 K is justified by the semicrystalline nature of the PE samples analyzed in this study. The presence of amorphous regions leads to thinner lamellar crystals and lower T LDPE 2 fus values compared to a fully crystalline PE structure. This relationship is explained by the Thomson -Gibbs equation. 95

text: The impact of the value of Δ h fus is studied by comparing the calculated solubility of LDPE-2 in toluene using values of the enthalpy of fusion measured in the current work h ( 123.6J/g) LDPE 2,1 fus = , the reported enthalpy of fusion of fully crystalline polyethylene ( h 293.0J/g) LDPE,c fus = , and the average of t h e t w o , h 208.3J/g LDPE 2,2 fus = , using T 389.0K LDPE 2,2 fus = . Although this corresponds to a very wide range of possible enthalpy of fusion values, the impact on the predicted solubility is not as pronounced as that of the variation in the temperature of fusion. As previously, we observe significantly better agreement between the SAFTγ Mie predictions and our experimental data when the largest value of the enthalpy of fusion is used, corresponding to the fully crystalline polymer. This value of the enthalpy of fusion is chosen for all subsequent PE solubility predictions in all solvents. As discussed in the previous section, the SAFTγ Mie parameters were transferred from smaller molecules; our investigation indicates that selecting the enthalpy of fusion of fully crystalline PE h ( 293.0J/g) LDPE,c fus = is an effective way to correct for small errors introduced by the parameter transfer and improve the accuracy of our solubility predictions, even though the PE sample is not fully crystalline.

text: We analyze the impact of the PE molecular weight on the PE solubility predictions in several solvents, using the same solids t a t e p r o p e r t i e s , T T 389.0K LDPE fus LDPE 2,2 fus = = a n d h h 293.0J/g LDPE fus LDPE,c fus = = , regardless of molecular weight. To ensure broad applicability, we carry out calculations over 1000 Mw values ranging from 4 to 270 kg/mol, encompassing both the PE samples studied here and other commercially relevant PEs. Our calculations in toluene and decalin, shown in Figure 8, and similar results in dibutoxymethane and dodecane (cf. Figure S1 in the SI), indicate that, overall, the molecular weight of PE has a minimal effect on solubility at a given temperature. The solubility exhibits a moderate sensitivity to molecular weight at low temperatures and at low PE molecular weights (<13 000 g/mol), 1 although with some sensitivity also dependent on the solvent. For molecular weights greater than the (solvent-dependent) plateau, the solubility is seen to be independent of molecular weight. This suggests that polydispersity is likely not to significantly influence the calculated solubility curves of LDPE2 ( Mw = 105 kg/mol), but may impact the predictions for LDPE-1 ( Mw = 4.9 kg/mol). This can be contrasted with what was observed by Paricaud et al., 96 who reported a strong influence of polymer molecular weight and polydispersity on SAFT (Wertheim TPT1) LLE predictions. Although they did not explicitly model polyethylene, increasing the chain length significantly broadened the LLE region of the model polymer + solvent mixture, suggesting a stronger molecular weight dependence in LLE than in SLE boundaries. This in turn led to a strong dependence of the predicted LLE behavior on the degree of polydispersity.

text: We validate further the selected value of the enthalpy of fusion by comparing SLE calculations carried out with different values of h LDPE fus with SLE data from the literature. 97 In Figure 9, we present calculations of the isobaric SLE of 17 kg/mol PE n ( 1210) CH2 = + m -xylene at 1 atm, using T fus = 389.0 K 97 and four crystalline fractions ( c ) to calculate h LDPE fus through eq 17. We calculate h LDPE fus as it was not measured in the experimental study. 97 In agreement with the conclusions for the PE + toluene mixture (cf. Figure 7b), we observe that using the enthalpy of fusion of fully crystalline PE, corresponding to c = 1, gives the best agreement between the SAFTγ Mie predictions and the experimental data. 97 In the calculation of Figure 9, the experimental value of T fus reported in Richards et al. 97 was used. The PE solubility calculated assuming the PE + m -xylene mixture behaves ideally, that is, with the activity coefficient of the polymer in solution of γ PE = 1, is also presented in the figure for comparison and, as expected, can be seen to lead to poor agreement with the reported experimental solubilities, highlighting the highly nonideal nature of PE + solvent mixtures.

text: In Figure 15, we present parity plots with the predicted and the experimental SLE temperatures for LDPE-1 and LDPE-2 in the solvents studied at the same w PE . As can be seen, the SAFTγ Mie calculations are found to be within 20 K of the measurements, a satisfactory level of agreement in the context of fully predictive thermodynamic models, given the uncertainty in the solid-state properties of the polymer samples. 99 It is noteworthy that the agreement is best for LDPE-2, the PE sample with a higher temperature of fusion and molecular weight, for all solvents except n -dodecane. As the SAFTγ Mie group interaction parameters are fitted to small molecule fluid-phase behavior, one may have expected larger deviations for larger polymers (which contain more repetitions of given groups; e.g., CH2 here). We find this, however, not to be the case. As discussed previously, the solubility predictions for lower molecular weight LDPE-1 are likely influenced by the sample's polydispersity. Furthermore, low-density PE is known to exhibit significant branching, 54 but this factor has not been explored in our work. An experimental investigation of the degree of branching and the development of polymer-specific groups to account for branching may enhance the agreement with the experimental data further.

text: We provide a quantitative analysis of the accuracy of the SAFTγ Mie predictions in Table 4, reporting the %AAD and AAD of the equilibrium temperature for each PE (LDPE-1, MDPE, LDPE-2, LDPE-3 and 17 kg/mol PE) + solvent combination considered in this section (cf. eqs 19 and 20, respectively). These deviations were evaluated using the T SLE and, in the case of LDPE-1 + cyclohexanone, the T SLLE predicted with SAFTγ Mie, with the corresponding experimental weight fraction employed as input to the calculations. For each system and property, we indicate the number of experimental points used in the evaluation together with the thermodynamic conditions employed. We have conducted a systematic investigation of the temperature dependence of polyethylene solubility in various solvents, including both conventional and bioderived candidates featuring different functional groups. From an initial pool of 61 solvents, 33 were shortlisted based on low RED values, as derived from Hansen solubility parameter calculations, and further refined by considering their normal boiling points and toxicity. A preliminary screening at a PE weight fraction of 0.01 g/g identified 10 solvents capable of dissolving PE: decalin, toluene, p -xylene, limonene, p -cymene, α -pinene, mesitylene, n -dodecane, cyclohexanone, and dibutoxymethane.

We performed solubility measurements for four PE samples differing in molecular weight, density, and solid-state properties (temperature and specific enthalpy of fusion) in the 10

text: selected solvents. Our results show that melting properties  specifically temperature and enthalpy of fusion, which are related to the crystallinity of the PE sample  dominate solubility, outweighing the effects of molecular weight and density in low to medium polymer densities. This is exemplified by MDPE and LDPE-2, which, despite differing in Mw by more than an order of magnitude and differing densities, exhibit nearly identical solubility profiles due to their similar melting properties. Notably, the ranking of solvent + PE SLE temperatures remains largely consistent across PE grades, with the traditional solvents decalin, toluene, and p -xylene outperforming the other solvents. Encouragingly, the bioderived solvents limonene, p -cymene, and α -pinene, were found to exhibit comparable SLE temperatures to these traditional solvents, offering promising potential as sustainably sourced alternatives.

text: We carried out fully predictive SAFTγ Mie calculations of the SLE of PE + n -dodecane, decalin, toluene, pxylene, m -xylene, mesitylene, p -cymene, and dibutoxymethane binary mixtures as well as for the SLLE of PE + cyclohexanone binary mixtures. We observed that the melting properties -enthalpy and temperature of fusion -have a significant impact on the SLE predictions, consistent with experimental observations. We found that using the PE sample-specific temperature of fusion and the enthalpy of fusion of fully crystalline PE for the SAFTγ Mie calculations offers the best agreement with experimental data. Furthermore, we observed that the polymer molecular weight affects solubility predictions only at low Mw values and temperatures. This work has allowed us to assess the transferability of the existing database of SAFTγ Mie parameters, relevant to n -alkanes, ethers, cyclic, and aromatic solvents, using both our experimental data and data from the literature. Across all systems, the model delivers satisfactory accuracy, with %AAD and AAD not exceeding 5.17% and 18.4 K (observed for MDPE + mesitylene), respectively. Parity plots and PE + solvent phase diagrams confirmed the reliability of the SAFTγ Mie group-contribution approach, which has been applied here in a fully predictive manner, providing a robust foundation for integrated molecular and process design frameworks. In practice, this predictive framework can provide key thermodynamic inputs for process simulation, enabling the design of plastic recycling processes, even for mixed waste streams of unknown composition, by evaluating a range of polymer properties. 100 Further refinement of group interactions with polymer data and accounting for branching in LDPE may improve the accuracy of the model.

We carried out fully predictive SAFTγ Mie calculations of the SLE of PE + n -dodecane, decalin, toluene, pxylene, m -xylene, mesitylene, p -cymene, and dibutoxymethane binary mixtures as well as for the SLLE of PE + cyclohexanone binary mixtures. We observed that the melting properties -enthalpy and temperature of fusion -have a significant impact on the SLE predictions, consistent with experimental observations. We found that using the PE sample-specific temperature of fusion and the enthalpy of fusion of fully crystalline PE for the SAFTγ Mie calculations offers the best agreement with experimental data. Furthermore, we observed that the polymer molecular weight affects solubility predictions only at low Mw values and temperatures. This work has allowed us to assess the transferability of the existing database of SAFTγ Mie parameters, relevant to n -alkanes, ethers, cyclic, and aromatic solvents, using both our experimental data and data from the literature. Across all systems, the model delivers satisfactory accuracy, with %AAD and AAD not exceeding 5.17% and 18.4 K (observed for MDPE + mesitylene), respectively. Parity plots and PE + solvent phase diagrams confirmed the reliability of the SAFTγ Mie group-contribution approach, which has been applied here in a fully predictive manner, providing a robust foundation for integrated molecular and process design frameworks. In practice, this predictive framework can provide key thermodynamic inputs for process simulation, enabling the design of plastic recycling processes, even for mixed waste streams of unknown composition, by evaluating a range of polymer properties. 100 Further refinement of group interactions with polymer data and accounting for branching in LDPE may improve the accuracy of the model.

text:
These findings offer practical insights for optimizing the solvent-based recycling, contributing to more sustainable PE recycling practices. Future research could focus on extending the solvent range to additional environmentally benign solvents, exploring other polyolefin types, such as polypropylene (PP) and high-density polyethylene (HDPE), potentially mixed with common additives. This would allow for further investigation of the thermodynamics of solvent-based recycling, especially for complex waste streams such as multilayer and contaminated plastics. 101,102

1. Introduction

text:
Multilayer (ML) plastic films have been pivotal in promoting product safety, security, and handling (Alias et al., 2022; Anukiruthika et al., 2020; Ashok et al., 2016; Matthews et al., 2021). However, their predominant disposal in landfills or the environment at their endof-life raises significant environmental concerns (Bauer et al., 2021; Horodytska et al., 2018; Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2018). ML films can be composed of different polymers (e.g., PE, EVOH, PET) and up to hundreds of layers that serve diverse functions in prolonging the shelf life of products (Morris, 2022; Niaounakis, 2019). Unfortunately, the intricate combination of polymer layers complicates the recycling process; only 5% of ML plastic films are currently recycled in the United States (the rest are diverted to incineration facilities or landfills) (Hutchings et al., 2021; Milbrandt et al., 2022).

ML films can be composed of different polymers (e.g., PE, EVOH, PET) and up to hundreds of layers that serve diverse functions in prolonging the shelf life of products (Morris, 2022; Niaounakis, 2019). A B S T R A C T

text: Multilayer (ML) plastic films are essential packaging materials that help protect products from diverse external factors; however, only 5% of all ML films are recycled in the United States. Solvent-based technologies are a promising alternative for recycling ML films because they enable recovery of constituent polymer resins. For example, the Solvent Targeted Recovery and Precipitation (STRAP TM ) process sequentially dissolves and separates polymer components using a series of targeted solvent washes. A crucial design aspect of this process is the impact of selected solvents on human health and on the environment. This work introduces a computational framework that integrates molecular modeling, process modeling, techno-economic analysis (TEA), and life-cycle analysis (LCA) to quickly screen green solvents for solvent-based ML recycling processes. Initial screening for solvents based on selectivity is performed by estimating temperature-dependent solubilities using molecular-scale models. Subsequent screening uses basic estimates of energy use and octanol-water partition coefficients (logP) as key measures of health, safety, and environmental hazards. Detailed process modeling, TEA, and LCA are used on a reduced set of promising solvents identified in early screening steps to more accurately determine how solvent selection and associated operating conditions impact overall economics and environmental impacts. The framework is used for the identification of green solvents (from a database of 1,000 solvents) that separate an industrial ML film composed of polyethylene (PE), ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH), and polyethylene terephthalate (PET). Our analysis shows the effectiveness of the framework and reveals fundamental trade-offs between solvent greenness, solubility, and economics. Our work emphasizes the importance of taking a holistic systems view during solvent design and aims to inform the development of new processes for ML film recycling and the identification of new ML films that are easier to recycle.

text:
Several technologies are currently being explored for recycling plastic waste (Li et al., 2022), including thermochemical processes such as pyrolysis (Li et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023) and thermal oxodegradation (Olafasakin et al., 2023), physicochemical processes such as supercritical fluid separation (Anouar et al., 2015), and mechanical processes (Jeswani et al., 2021; Suzuki et al., 2022). The selection of a recycling technology significantly hinges on the intended final product, which influences process design, economics, safety, and environmental impact. For instance, pyrolysis of plastic waste primarily targets the production of pyrolysis oil, which can be processed into high-value chemicals, thus altering the original polymer structure. Mechanical recycling preserves the polymer structure and is scalable but cannot be used for complex materials that involve multiple polymers, such as ML films (Lisiecki et al., 2024; Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2023).

text: , Reid Solvent-based separation technologies have recently emerged as an alternative for recovering resins with near-virgin properties from ML plastic films (Zhao et al., 2018). An illustrative embodiment of this methodology is the Solvent-Targeted Recovery and Precipitation (STRAP ™ ) process introduced by Walker et al. (2020), see Fig. 1. This approach systematically separates the polymer constituents of ML plastic films through dissolution and precipitation by employing selective solvents and by exploiting temperature-dependent solubility of polymers in solvents (Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2021). A critical step in designing this process is solvent selection/design, which serves as the linchpin of the entire approach and which requires the prediction of temperature-dependent polymer solubilities in many possible solvents. To address this need, molecular-scale models have been used to predict the solubilities of various plastic components, including but not limited to PE, EVOH, and PET, in over 1000 solvents (Zhou et al., 2023; Munguía-López et al., 2024). These predictions are made by modeling polymers as short oligomers and then employing molecular dynamics simulations and the COnductor-like Screening MOdel for Real Solvents (COSMO-RS) to predict thermodynamic quantities that dictate solubility.

text: Solvent-based separation technologies have demonstrated their efficacy in handling diverse plastic waste feedstocks such as face masks (Yu et al., 2023) and reverse-printed films (Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2023); however, environmental and health concerns associated with using solvents to upcycle certain materials (e.g., food-contact materials) place limitations on such technologies. In addition, when addressing ML plastic recycling challenges by deploying solvent-based approaches, it is imperative to mitigate the emergence of new toxic wastestreams from harmful solvents to avoid burden-shifting (Algunaibet and GuillénGosálbez, 2019). Although high solvent recycling rates are ensured in the solvent-based recycling process, small quantities of these solvents potentially escape into the environment or are deliberately disposed of after several uses. The ecological impact of such waste streams can be substantial when the solvents in use possess toxic attributes. Moreover, using toxic solvents may pose risks to the safety of operation personnel. Similarly, the choice of solvent impacts the process economics as the use of different solvents will impact energy requirements (e.g., due to changes in temperature-dependent solubilities). Therefore, it is crucial to incorporate toxicity considerations in selecting solvents and understand their influence on process design, economics, and environmental impacts in a holistic manner (Hessel et al., 2022; Winterton, 2021).

text: Previous work has sought to define what a ''green solvent'' is by using green chemistry principles. Saleh and Koller (2018) characterize green solvents as those possessing low reactivity and flammability, exemplified by ionic liquids. Choi et al. (2011) initially identified natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES) and deemed them green due to their derivation from plant sources. A review by Janicka et al. (2022) classifies supercritical fluids as green solvents, as they can dissolve materials at temperatures and pressures exceeding their critical points without necessitating purification during recovery or reuse. Knez et al. (2014) examined industrial applications of supercritical fluids and delineated the associated risks of high-pressure processes and elevated operational costs.

Saleh and Koller (2018) characterize green solvents as those possessing low reactivity and flammability, exemplified by ionic liquids. Choi et al. (2011) initially identified natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES) and deemed them green due to their derivation from plant sources. A review by Janicka et al. (2022) classifies supercritical fluids as green solvents, as they can dissolve materials at temperatures and pressures exceeding their critical points without necessitating purification during recovery or reuse. text: Considering these perspectives, the greenness of solvents can be broadly quantified using the following criteria: (1) whether they are derived from a renewable source, (2) their usage efficiency, (3) health, safety, and environmental hazards, (4) recyclability, and (5) biodegradability. The ideal green solvent, designed to harmonize sustainability and technical efficiency, should ideally originate from a renewable source (e.g., plant-derived solvents) and maintain cost-effectiveness as a fundamental criterion. It should also have benign health, safety, and environmental characteristics throughout its life-cycle. In addition, it should be easily recyclable or biodegradable after disposal. It is important to highlight that the utility of the green solvent in the actual process is of particular importance (e.g., high solubility and reduced energy consumption), as this impacts the overall process efficiency and greenness of the entire process. Although it is desirable to find an ideal solvent that satisfies all these greenness criteria, it is difficult (if not impossible) to simultaneously achieve all these goals simultaneously.

text:
Several studies have sought to identify and design green solvents, but, to the best of our knowledge, no existing study has developed a holistic framework to evaluate and select green solvents within the context of a solvent-based plastic recycling process (Ikegwu et al., 2024). Therefore, in this study, we aim to develop a green solvent screening framework for separating ML plastic films into their polymer constituents. This computational framework is holistic and considers polymer solubility, various solvent greenness metrics, and the impact of solvent selection on the overall process design and economics. Although this framework was developed in the context of ML plastic film separation, it can be adapted for any solvent-based process. This work can also guide the design of new green solvents with relevant properties for ML plastic film separation and inform the design of easy-to-recycle ML plastic films.

The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 details the computational framework and its various elements. Section 3 present an application of the framework to a practical case study involving the separation of an industrial ML plastic film, illustrating the utility of the framework and highlighting how green solvent selection informs process design. Finally, Section 4 offers our concluding remarks on this study and identifies potential avenues for further studies.

2.1. Polymer solubility prediction and selective dissolution

The framework begins by predicting polymer solubilities in over 1000 solvents at a standard temperature of 120 °C ( Step 1 ). This temperature is chosen to prevent thermal degradation of the polymers (Pielichowski et al., 2022) while providing adequate temperature leeway to achieve desired solubilities, as discussed by Zhou and coworkers (Zhou et al., 2023). The target polymers were modeled as short oligomers in reference solvents using molecular dynamics simulations to obtain different conformations from corresponding simulation trajectories. These conformations are then optimized and serve as inputs into COnductor-like Screening MOdel for Real-Solvents (COSMORS) (Zhou et al., 2021) to predict temperature-dependent solubilities at the infinite dilution limit. This molecular simulation approach has been previously shown to predict temperature-dependent polymer solubilities in reasonable agreement with experimental measurements (Zhou et al., 2023).

text:
To ensure solvent selectivity in Step 2 , the solubility difference between the target polymer and other polymers in the ML films should be greater than 10 wt.% (Zhou et al., 2023). In addition, the solvents with boiling points lower than room temperature (RT) are removed in Step 3 ; this rule only applies to processes that wish to operate at standard atmospheric pressure and is intended to avoid high solvent volatilization and extremely low operating temperatures. Similarly, the highest operating temperature (Th) is set to 1 °C less than the solvent boiling point in Step 3 to maintain this operating condition. Solvents with at least 15 wt.% solubility for the target polymer at Th are then selected in Step 4 . This solubility range has been identified to be reasonable for ML plastic film separation (Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2023). To recover the dissolved layer after filtering the solution to remove residual solids (i.e., undissolved polymers) at the high operating temperature, solvents with a low solubility of the target polymer at room temperature are selected in Step 5 to ensure easy precipitation after cooling the polymer solution (Walker et al., 2020). Although Steps 2-5 pertain specifically to selective procedures conducted at standard atmospheric pressure, other aspects of this framework are generalizable to solvent-based processes.

In Step 6 , we assess the environmental impact of the selected solvents from a process perspective by using the minimum energy required by each solvent. This is done by using a simple energy balance 𝑄 = 𝑚𝐶𝑝 𝛥𝑇 . Here, 𝑄 is the total energy intensity (in J ), 𝑚 (in grams) is the mass of the solvent, 𝐶𝑝 (in J g -1 K -1 ) is the heat capacity of the solvent assuming temperature-independence, and 𝛥𝑇 (in K ) is the temperature difference between RT and Th (this difference capture the operating range of the solvent in the process). The measure 𝑄 is simple but comprehensive; this captures the overall carbon intensity originating from employing a solvent within the process, as it captures the total energy required to adjust the solvent temperature across the entire operating range in the process. Upon calculation of 𝑄 , the solvents are ranked using these estimated minimum energy requirements from lowest to highest.

2.3. Octanol-water partition coefficient (logP) prediction

text:
The octanol-water partition coefficient (logP) is a fundamental molecular property that provides information about the tendency of a solvent to bioaccumulate in living organisms. Several regulations around the world, including the United States, have emphasized estimating the solvent logP prior to their usage (Renner, 2002). This quantity is often described as the equilibrium ratio of concentrations of a chemical in a mixture of octanol (hydrophobic or non-polar phase) and water (hydrophilic or polar phase) (Cevc, 2015). Several empirical and physics models have been developed to predict compound partition coefficients, including quantitative structure-retention relationship (QSRR) models (Qiao et al., 2023), solvation models based on electronic density (SMD) and COSMO-RS methods (Van der Spoel et al., 2019), and physics-informed machine learning models (Zhu et al., 2022). Van der Spoel et al. (2019) showed that the COSMO-RS model performs well compared to other models and values from the PubChem public database.

In Step 7 of our framework, we use the COSMO-RS model to calculate logP values of all solvents, where logP for solvent 𝑖 is computed using Eq. (1).

We use the notation logP for solvent 𝑖 as shorthand for log 10 ( 𝑃 𝑖 ) . The chemical potentials 𝜇 𝑖 (1) and 𝜇 𝑖 (2) of all solvents 𝑖 in infinite dilution in pure octanol (phase 1) and water (phase 2) are automatically computed, respectively. The quantity 𝑉 𝑞 is the volume quotient between octanol and water, estimated from their densities. Solvents with logP > 0 are considered lipophilic and thus have higher bioaccumulation tendencies; solvents with logP < 0 are considered hydrophilic, indicating lower bioaccumulation tendencies. Although solvents with logP > 0 are generally not regarded as green, there are no clear indications on what the acceptable logP threshold is for food packaging applications. Hence, we consider only solvents with logP ≤ 3 as an initial screening process in Step 7 of our framework. We use this to assess the trade-offs among the different selected solvents.

Solvent toxicity is a crucial aspect to consider in the design and operation of any chemical process (Diorazio et al., 2016). This has inspired the development of quantitative toxicity metrics for common solvents that are used for guiding solvent selection. These guides mostly involve environmental implications of each solvent usage. Some of these include industrial guidelines developed by GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) (Henderson et al., 2011), the American Chemical Society (ACS) Green Chemistry Institute Pharmaceutical Roundtable (ACS GCI-PR) (Prat et al., 2014), and AstraZeneca (AZ) (Diorazio et al., 2016).

text: The GSK guideline categorized 111 solvents with over 10 primary functional groups under 6 headings. These categories include waste, environmental impact, health, flammability, reactivity, and life cycle. Scores between 1 and 10 were assigned to each solvent on the GSK guideline, with 1 indicating the solvents with the most concern and 10 indicating the solvents with the least concern. A couple of extra categories were included to classify solvents based on legislation and restriction bans placed by the Environmental Health Services (EHS). Conversely, AZ and ACS GCI-PR guidelines categorized 46 and 63 solvents, respectively, with a score of 10 indicating the solvent with the most concern and 1 with the least concern. Although these guidelines contain different metric categories, they all seek to rate solvents based on the Health, Safety, and Environment (HSE) metrics.

Scores between 1 and 10 were assigned to each solvent on the GSK guideline, with 1 indicating the solvents with the most concern and 10 indicating the solvents with the least concern. Conversely, AZ and ACS GCI-PR guidelines categorized 46 and 63 solvents, respectively, with a score of 10 indicating the solvent with the most concern and 1 with the least concern. text:
This study employs only the GSK solvent guideline. This guideline contains the most solvents, covers the HSE metrics, and includes the legislation and regulatory ban information about some solvents. Although the GSK guideline can be used with other guidelines, the difference in the meaning of the rank assigned to each solvent makes it more difficult. Moreover, using these guides is not the sole greenness check in this framework, as these guidelines do not contain information about most of the solvents in our database. Hence, other solvent regulatory standards such as the Registration, Evaluation, Authorization, and Restriction of Chemical Regulation (REACH) initiative and the Toxic Release Inventory (TRI) were adopted to discard solvents of concern. At the time of this study, benzene, toluene, formamide, and fluorinated solvents were included on the list of restricted substances (https://echa.europa.eu/substances-restricted-under-reach, Byrne et al., 2016, https://www.epa.gov/toxics-release-inventory-triprogram/tri-listed-chemicals). These solvents were subsequently removed from our dataset in Step 7.

This study employs only the GSK solvent guideline. This guideline contains the most solvents, covers the HSE metrics, and includes the legislation and regulatory ban information about some solvents. Although the GSK guideline can be used with other guidelines, the difference in the meaning of the rank assigned to each solvent makes it more difficult. Moreover, using these guides is not the sole greenness check in this framework, as these guidelines do not contain information about most of the solvents in our database. Hence, other solvent regulatory standards such as the Registration, Evaluation, Authorization, and Restriction of Chemical Regulation (REACH) initiative and the Toxic Release Inventory (TRI) were adopted to discard solvents of concern. At the time of this study, benzene, toluene, formamide, and fluorinated solvents were included on the list of restricted substances (https://echa.europa.eu/substances-restricted-under-reach, Byrne et al., 2016, https://www.epa.gov/toxics-release-inventory-triprogram/tri-listed-chemicals). These solvents were subsequently removed from our dataset in Step 7.

2.5. Process simulation and techno-economic analysis (TEA)

text:
The overall recycling process cost is an important economic factor when selecting solvents. While the cost of a solvent directly impacts total process cost, other process costs associated with using a specific solvent (such as energy costs affected by operating conditions) need to be accounted for. Hence, it is necessary to simulate the recycling process, conduct detailed material and energy balances, and carry out a detailed TEA that provides a more holistic cost evaluation. Our analysis captures total cost using the minimum selling price (MSP) of the recovered polymer resin; this is the price needed to reach a net present value of zero for the process over a specified period. The process simulation and TEA ( Step 8 of our framework) are performed using BioSTEAM, an open-source Python process simulator that has been benchmarked against proprietary software such as Aspen Plus (Cortes-Pena et al., 2020).

2.6. Life cycle assessment (LCA)

text:
LCA is a well-developed methodology for estimating the environmental impact of processes such as solvent-based plastic recycling (del Carmen Munguía-López et al., 2023). In addition to solvent screening using the solvent toxicity database and regulatory framework earlier mentioned, an LCA is performed to estimate the impacts of using each solvent within the process. These impacts include the human toxicity impact in cancer/non-cancer Comparative Toxic Units for humans (CTUh), the freshwater ecotoxicity in Comparative Toxic Units for aquatic ecotoxicity (CTUe), and the climate change impact in kg CO2 eq. units. OpenLCA and BioSTEAM are used to perform this assessment in Step 8 of our framework. The impact of producing 1 kg of virgin resins is estimated using Eq. (2).

𝐼 𝑖 = ∑ 𝑢 𝐼𝐹 𝑖,𝑢 × ̇ 𝑚𝑢 (2)

where 𝑖 denotes the impact categories and 𝑢 represents the utilities (electricity (MJ), steam (MJ), and cooling water (m 3 )). Therefore, the impact factor of a category ( 𝐼 𝑖 ) is the sum of the product of the impact factor of producing each utility ( 𝐼𝐹 𝑖,𝑢 ) and the flow rate of each utility ( ̇ 𝑚𝑢 ) required to produce 1 kg of virgin resins via the STRAP ™ process. The environmental footprint (mid-point indicator) method from the OpenLCA 2.0 environmental footprint database is employed for this study.

It is important to highlight that conducting detailed process modeling, TEA, and LCA is time-consuming and should thus be conducted only on a selected number of solvents. This is why it is critical to develop fast screening tools in earlier steps of the framework.

3. Case studies

We demonstrate the use of our framework using a case study in which we use STRAP ™ for separating an industrial ML film with 3 polymer components, see Fig. 1. The ML film is produced by the Amcor company and consists of 6.2 wt.% PE, 3.6 wt.% EVOH, and 90.2 wt.% PET (del Carmen Munguía-López et al., 2023). Our study delineates a couple of distinct scenarios originating from a systematic, bottom-up approach. The first scenario focuses on the identification of a green solvent to separate a 2-component film (EVOH-PET), which corresponds to selecting Solvent B for the process depicted in Fig. 1. The second scenario pertains to the identification of green solvents for separating PE from a three-component film (PE-EVOH-PET), which corresponds to selecting Solvent A for the process depicted in Fig. 1.

text: As depicted in Fig. 2, Step 1 of the framework involves screening for solvents that meet the solubility criteria for recovering all polymers within the ML plastic film. By adopting the solubility prediction framework introduced by Zhou et al. (2023), the solubilities of PE, EVOH, and PET in 1000 solvents were predicted at different temperatures ranging from 30 °C to 120 °C to obtain a solubility database. Fig. 3 provides a visualization of the solubility predictions in this set of solvents for these 3 polymers at each solvent's respective high operating temperature (Th), which is either a degree less than its boiling point or a maximum of 120 °C. The set of solvents are split into distinct classes based on their functional groups, to convey the breadth and diversity of the solvent space considered in this study. The illustration also shows the difficulty in finding solvents that can dissolve PET, as indicated by the small size of its node and the number of connecting edges. This difficulty compounds when trying to selectively dissolve PET while leaving the other two polymers undissolved because no solvent class node connects only to PET. The visualization shows that PE has more solvents that can be used to selectively dissolve it. For example, solvents with alkane, alkene, and alkyl groups preferentially dissolve PE. The color gradient within the solvent class nodes reflects the greenness ratings of each solvent within a class, according to GSK solvent selection guidelines (Henderson et al., 2011); green indicates the least hazardous concerns and red indicating the most hazardous concerns. While it is observed that red dominates the set of solvents under study (e.g., indicating that organic solvents are not the preferred choice of solvent), there is a need to examine the trade-offs due to the potential process efficiencies offered by organic solvents (e.g., high solubility and less energy usage) (Jimenez-Gonzalez, 2019). In addition, there is a need to more rigorously quantify the greenness of solvents, beyond what is recommended by the GSK guideline.

3.1. EVOH-PET separation

text: In alignment with the separation sequence outlined by SánchezRivera et al. (2021), our objective is to identify green solvents suitable for the selective dissolution of EVOH from an EVOH-PET polymer blend. A flowchart showing how solvents are screened out at each step of our framework for this case study is shown in Fig. 4. Although these steps are not necessarily hierarchical, this sequence was adopted for simplification. To ensure the selective dissolution of EVOH, solvents exhibiting a minimum of 10 wt.% difference in solubility between EVOH and PET at 120 °C were retained. This initial screening resulted in the identification of 116 potential solvents from a the entire set of 1000 solvents available. Subsequently, only solvents amenable to operation at ambient pressure (i.e., those possessing boiling points above room temperature), were selected. This criterion led to the further exclusion of 19 solvents, resulting in a remaining set of 97 solvents. The high temperatures (Th) for each of these solvents were further determined, and solvents exhibiting a minimum 15 wt.% solubility at Th were selected to ensure the solubility of EVOH. This refinement further reduced the solvent list to 56 candidates. To facilitate subsequent precipitation processes, our selection was refined by retaining only those solvents with less than 2 wt.% solubility of EVOH at room temperature (RT). Consequently, the number of viable solvents was reduced to 45.

text: The next step in the framework requires assessing solvent greenness. As high energy requirements equate to high carbon emissions, the minimum energy requirements for each of the 45 selected solvents were estimated using the simple energy balance. This calculation only accounts for the minimum energy required to raise the temperature of each solvent to the specified dissolution temperature, which is a function of the specific heat capacity of the solvent and Th. Although the energy required is a function of the required solvent mass which is a function of solvent-polymer solubility, the energy per mass (J/g) was calculated instead, because the solvent-to-plastic film feed ratio is typically fixed in the STRAP ™ process. The temperature-dependent specific heat capacities for the solvents were estimated using the BioSTEAM simulator (which uses a QSPR model). Next, logP of each solvent was estimated and screened to remove solvents with logP greater than 3, although it was found that none of the 45 solvents exceeded this threshold.

text: The estimated solvent energy requirements, logP, and EVOH polymer solubility are presented in Fig. 5. One of the highlighted data points ( i.e. , solvent) indicated by an arrow in Fig. 5 is dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO) with an EVOH solubility of 35 wt.% and PET solubility of 8 wt.%, fulfilling the selective solubility criteria for this separation process. This result agrees with the observations made by Walker et al. (2020) and Zhou et al. (2023), without necessarily considering its greenness. However, as depicted in Fig. 5, there are other factors to consider and a need for trade-off analysis. Some other solvents are also highlighted in the point cloud as shown in Fig. 5. To select a green solvent, we aim to locate solvents at the bottom left corner of Fig. 5, which is indicative of their low energy requirements and negative logP values. Moreover, choosing solvents with high solubility, while beneficial for selective dissolution, poses challenges in recovering foodgrade ML plastic films due to stringent solvent retention concentration requirements (Heckman, 2005). This elevated solubility can complicate or increase the energy demands for producing resins containing very low solvent concentrations embedded in the polymer matrix. For example, formic acid, with a lower but sufficient EVOH solubility of 19 wt.%, lower energy requirement of 120 J/g, and a negative logP of -0.6, could be a better alternative to DMSO as seen in Fig. 5. However, the corrosive nature of formic acid makes it less desirable for recovering food contact materials. Therefore, this begs the need for further qualitative solvent greenness assessment.

text:
Fig. 4. Green solvent selection flowchart for case-study one (EVOH-PET). This depicts how solvents are sequentially screened out when selecting green solvents to selectively dissolve and precipitate EVOH from an EVOH-PET plastic. Following the framework depicted in Fig. 2, this approach reduces the set of solvents from 1000 to 45. Note that no solvents are eliminated when considering the criteria in Steps 6 and 7.

The GSK solvent guidelines, the PubChem public database, the REACH initiative, and the Toxic Release Inventory (TRI) databases were used to evaluate the selected solvents qualitatively. Fig. 6 presents a heat map depicting some important solvent greenness metrics for 40 solvents for the selective dissolution and precipitation of EVOH. The full solvent list, labels, and properties are reported in the Extended Supplementary Information (ESI) . As seen in Fig. 6, using some solvents may be restricted or not depending on their associated hazards. For instance, solvents like ethylene glycol monomethyl ether, N-methyl formamide, dimethyl formamide (DMF), N,N-dimethyl acetamide, and N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), all have restrictions placed on their usage (Henderson et al., 2011).

text: When selecting a green solvent, the boiling point is crucial. Solvents with high boiling points require significant energy for separation via distillation, especially when dealing with solvent mixtures (del Carmen Munguía-López et al., 2023). Conversely, solvents with low boiling points should generally be avoided due to their volatility at ambient temperatures, posing health risks and requiring substantial energy for condensation. For instance, formic acid, with a boiling point of 101 °C, considerably away from ambient temperature, would be a preferred solvent. In contrast, N-(2-hydroxyethyl)-2-pyrrolidone with a high boiling point of 295 °C is less desirable, as indicated by the red color on the heat map. Furthermore, as previously mentioned, solvents with high logP are considered toxic. For instance, 4-ethyl phenol has a high logP of 2.3, making it not desirable, as marked red in Fig. 6.

In conclusion, a solvent may appear green based on one metric but may not satisfy other green criteria. Also, it is critical to note that the choice of which greenness metric to prioritize depends on the specific application of the solvent. Solvents like acetic acid, DMSO, epsilon-caprolactam, and bromoacetic acid are some recommended solvents for EVOH selective dissolution. Acetic acid appears to be a promising solvent for the selective dissolution of EVOH because it has the lowest logP value and a good LCA metric score of 8 out of 10 based on the GSK solvent screening guide. DMSO also appears to be a promising solvent for this process due to its negative logP and high solubility. Epsilon-caprolactam is another promising solvent for this process due to its negative logP and because it can be derived from biomass sources (Buntara et al., 2011). Lastly, based on the energy requirements, bromoacetic acid appears to be a good solvent.

text:
In the previous section, we applied our green solvent selection framework to the selective dissolution of EVOH from an EVOH-PET polymer blend. In this scenario, we will consider screening for green solvents to selectively dissolve PE from a PE-EVOH-PET polymer blend, as this is a common selection for typical ML plastic films (del Carmen Munguía-López et al., 2023; Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2023). Selectively dissolving PE instead of EVOH will lead to a different set of possible solvents due to their interactions with PE and because of the need to avoid dissolving EVOH and PET.

After the first screening step, 576 solvents were found to selectively dissolve PE at 120 °C. This large number of solvents is due to the fact that most organic solvents in the database are nonpolar, as is PE, and results from the heuristic principle of like-dissolves-like. Subsequently, only 456 solvents were amenable to operation at ambient pressure. The solubility of PE at the selected solvent high temperatures (Th) was determined, and 263 solvents exhibited a minimum of 15 wt.% solubility. Finally, to facilitate precipitation at room temperature, we retained only those solvents with less than 2 wt.% solubility of PE at room temperature (RT). This screening step further reduced the candidate solvents to 151.

text: Using the simple energy balance equation, the energy requirement of each solvent was estimated. The logP for each of the selected solvents was also screened, although all 151 solvents had logP values greater than 0. Fig. 7 shows the predicted energy requirement, PE polymer solubility, and logP for the 151 selected solvents. One of the highlighted data points (solvent) indicated by an arrow in Fig. 7 is toluene, because it was employed by Walker et al. (2020) for a similar separation process. Toluene was previously chosen because it has a predicted PE solubility of 20 wt.%, EVOH solubility of 0 wt.%, and PET solubility of 2 wt.%, which fulfill the selective solubility criteria for this separation process. However, its logP value ( + 2.5) is relatively high, making it a less desirable solvent for recovering food-grade ML plastic film. As seen in Fig. 7, all the selected solvents have positive logP, indicating a high bioaccumulation tendency. This observation highlights the difficulty in efficiently recovering PE from an ML plastic film using organic solvents while considering solvent greenness. Some other solvents are also highlighted in the point cloud as shown in Fig. 7. As previously noted, solvents at the bottom left are more desirable. For instance, this framework, as shown in Fig. 7 suggests that a solvent such as cyclopentanone with a logP value of 0.5, good solubility of 30 wt.%, and energy requirement of 200 J/g, could be a more desirable solvent for recovering PE compared to toluene.

text: It is also crucial to screen solvents based on their application. In this case, these solvents are applied to ML plastic films used in the food packaging industry. Hence, it is important to remove solvents that pose any form of health hazard (Mehrabani et al., 2022). For example, public solvent databases like PubChem show that toluene, naphthalene, MIBK, and indene all pose serious health hazards. The ether, ester, and ketone solvent classes were predominantly found for PE selective dissolution upon applying this green solvent selection framework, aligning with the GSK solvent guidelines, which categorize these classes as the greenest solvents (Henderson et al., 2011). Summarily, solvents like tetramethylene sulfide, cyclopentanone, o-xylene, and 𝛼 -chloro methyl acrylate are some recommended solvents for PE selective dissolution. Tetramethylene sulfide is a good candidate solvent for this separation process due to its high solubility for PE and relatively low energy requirements and logP values. As indicated earlier, cyclopentanone also proves to be a good solvent for recovering PE from this ML plastic film. Other solvents such as o-xylene and 𝛼 -chloro methyl acrylate also appear to be good solvents because they can be derived from biomass and have low energy requirements.

3.3. Process modeling and techno-economic analysis

Following the framework developed in this study, we model the entire separation process (Fig. 1) using the selected solvent pairs presented in Table 1 and estimate the MSP of the recovered polymer resins via techno-economic analyses. A similar process flow diagram, as well as process assumptions as presented by Sánchez-Rivera et al. (2021), were adopted for this study to provide a basis for comparison. Previous research indicates that a solvent recovery rate of ≥ 99.9% is necessary for the economic viability of ML plastic film separation via solventbased processes (Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2021, 2023). However, the anti-solvent STRAP ™ variant is characterized by lower recovery rates due to azeotrope formation during distillation. To avoid this challenge, the temperature-dependent STRAP ™ variant was adopted in this study.

text: The impact categories in this study include climate change impact (kg CO2 eq.), human toxicity cancer (CTUh), human toxicity non-cancer (CTUh), and freshwater ecotoxicity (CTUe). Climate change impact measures the global warming potential of greenhouse gases such as CO2 , NOx , SO2 , N2 O, CH4 , and particulate matter. Human toxicity (cancer and non-cancer) indicates the disease rate increase in the human population due to exposure to chemicals. Freshwater ecotoxicity measures the impact of exposure to harmful chemicals on aquatic life in freshwater. As indicated in the LCA system boundary (Fig. 10), it is critical to note that this study does not include the impacts of producing each of the solvents used in this case study. However, this approach can be adapted to this framework in future studies. The factors of the environmental impacts for each category were obtained using the environmental footprint (mid-point indicator) method from the OpenLCA 2.0 environmental footprint database. The necessary utility flow rates were obtained from the process simulation on BioSTEAM. All impact category factors were based on the European data to ensure fair comparison across the different processes (i.e., solvent pairs). This was due to the unavailability of virgin polymer resin impact factors based on the United States data.

text: The results from the LCA study for process I through process VII, as labeled in Table 2, are presented in Fig. 11. Fig. 11(a) shows the climate change impacts (CCI) for each process employing different solvent pairs. The average CCI for the different processes using various solvents was observed to be 1.0 kg CO2 eq./kg of ML film. This value differs slightly from the CCI of 0.5 kg CO2 eq./kg of ML film reported by del Carmen Munguía-López et al. (2023) for a similar ML film separation process using the same STRAP ™ process variant. This discrepancy is primarily due to differences in the databases used for impact factor calculations and the use of data obtained from a different process simulator (Aspen), despite both studies reporting a similar process energy use of 10 MJ/kg of film. It was also observed that Process VI, using 𝛼 -chloro methyl acrylate and bromoacetic acid, achieved the lowest CCI of 0.8 kg CO2 eq./kg of film. This solvent pair was originally chosen because they had the lowest solvent energy requirement. This observation hints at the fact that the solvent energy requirement, estimated from its heat capacity, is a major driver of the CCI of a process, except if the energy is sourced from renewables (del Carmen Munguía-López et al., 2023).

A score of 5 indicates the most green solvent pair, while 1 indicates the least green solvent pair. In summary, we seek to find a solvent-pair that covers the most area on the radar plot. As shown in Fig. 12, no solvent pair, and thus no solvent, performs perfectly in all greenness metrics. Process VI ( 𝛼 -chloro methyl acrylate & bromoacetic acid) ranks best in MSP, FE, HTN, HTC, CCI, and TSE metrics. However, it has the lowest average solubility (17.33 wt.%) and a relatively high (positive) average logP (0.90). This compromise, necessary to meet other greenness metrics, is referred to as the ''cost of greenness''. When we compare Table 1 with Fig. 12, we see that prioritizing solubility, Process II (Tetramethylene sulfide & DMSO), also ranks best under the logP metric, however, it performs lower than Process I (Toluene & DMSO) and Process VI under some other solvent greenness metrics.

text: Furthermore, we see that although the GSK solvent guideline identifies cyclohexanol and acetic acid (Process V) as having the best LCA metrics based on their study (Henderson et al., 2011), our study finds these to be the least green solvents compared to the other evaluated solvents (considering climate change impact, human toxicity and ecotoxicity as metrics). It is important to note that the GSK life cycle score evaluates the environmental impacts of solvent production and their environmental fate and effects. In contrast, our study assesses the life cycle and environmental impacts of using solvents in an ML plastic film separation via a solvent-based process. This discrepancy underscores the importance of considering both production and usage impacts within our frameworks when relevant data are available. Fig. 12 also reveals the relationship between the total solvent energy required and the LCA impact categories. We observe that the TSE and the LCA impact categories are highly correlated. This observation agrees with the correlation analysis on all eight solvent greenness metrics presented in the ESI. This suggests that designing solvents with lower heat capacities that exhibit high selective solubility at mild temperatures should be considered to improve the LCA impacts. Also, prioritizing logP (i.e., Process III), a toxicity measurement, did not result in a good score on other metrics. This observation indicates that the logP of solvents does not correlate with other solvent greenness metrics, as shown in the correlation matrix in the ESI.

text:
Based on the results obtained in this study, solvents used in Processes I, II, and VI exhibit the best greenness metrics. However, it is crucial to qualitatively assess the hazards of these solvents. For example, bromoacetic acid is corrosive, acutely toxic, and exhibits serious environmental hazards. Similarly, 𝛼 -chloro methyl acrylate is flammable, acutely toxic, and corrosive. Toluene presents significant health risks and is unsuitable for recovering food contact materials; it is also listed as a restricted substance under the REACH initiative. Both tetramethylene sulfide and DMSO are only classified as irritants. Therefore, Process II offers the least qualitative hazards and a high greenness ranking. Additionally, the bio-based solvents used in Process IV (o-xylene and epsilon-caprolactam) may benefit the LCA impact categories. Similarly, Cyrene ™ , an aprotic dipolar solvent derived from waste biomass (Camp et al., 2020), has been recommended as a green alternative to DMSO with similar functionalities. However, the selective solubility of EVOH in Cyrene ™ is yet to be determined. In conclusion, this framework effectively identifies green solvents and highlights trade-offs between solvent greenness metrics in ML plastic film separation via a solvent-based process.

text:
The design of a process often takes precedence before an LCA and TEA are carried out to evaluate and improve the environmental impact and feasibility of the process. In this section, we illustrate the use of our framework to guide the design of a sustainable process for ML plastic film separation using the same STRAP ™ case study by assessing green solvents and possible separation sequences. This approach sought to integrate sustainability considerations from the outset to guide the process design. Also, having identified the trade-offs from the case studies considered in the previous sections, we observe that selecting a green solvent for ML plastic film separation requires a multiobjective approach to avoid burden-shifting (Algunaibet and Guillén-Gosálbez, 2019). Therefore, designing a process to minimize the risk of burden-shifting in ML film separation is required from the outset.

text: To achieve a more sustainable process design for the case study considered in this work, our framework will be applied to the six possible sequences for separating the PE-EVOH-PET ML plastic film. It is critical to note that this study only sought to select the most sustainable separation sequence without optimizing the energy requirements or design of unit operations in the detailed process design. As we can observe, these possible sequences can quickly scale up as the number of polymer components ( 𝑛 ) increases by 𝑛 -factorial. Fig. 13 shows the separation sequences that can be adopted for a 3-component ML plastic film separation. ''P'' corresponds to the polymer components, and the six different separation sequences are PE-EVOH-PET, PET-EVOHPE, EVOH-PE-PET, PE-PET-EVOH, PET-PE-EVOH, and EVOH-PET-PE. Prior to the development of this framework, previous studies adopted the PE-EVOH-PET sequence as depicted in Fig. 1 because of its ease of operation. However, considering the ease of operation as well as the environmental impact of the different separation designs will be beneficial.
