Secondly, the selected solvents were further screened following the qualitative section of our framework. This screening includes assessing solvents based on their qualitative hazards. For instance, about half the solvents identified to achieve EVOH-PE-PET design are acids, making them unfit for recovering food-grade materials. Therefore, this section aimed to select solvent pairs with the least hazards for each sequence to conduct trade-off analyses using the eight solvent greenness metrics introduced in Fig. 12.

Table 5 presents the selected solvent pairs. First, we observe that the solvent space for the selective dissolution of PE is relatively large. We also observe that similar solvents in the reverse order can achieve both PE-EVOH-PET and EVOH-PE-PET designs. This is because tetramethylene sulfide is selective to PE, while DMSO is selective to EVOH. Furthermore, we also observe that while four solvents can selectively dissolve PET from a 2-component system, only one solvent is worth evaluating. Other solvents include 1,2-ethane dithiol, ethyl isothiocyanate, and methyl isothiocyanate, which possess severe environmental hazards, health hazards, corrosive nature, and are acutely toxic. This qualitative hazard further reduces the solvent space.

text: Having highlighted the advantages of organic solvents in selectively targeting polymer components in multilayer plastics for effective separation, this study identifies their significant health and environmental concerns. Some key properties for an optimal solvent include high selective solubility of target polymers at mild temperatures, low energy requirements, a high boiling point (except in the case of solvent mixtures), negative octanol-water partition coefficients (LogP), and biomass-derived origins. However, applying this framework could potentially lead to not finding solvents with satisfactory performance. Hence, computer-aided molecular design (CAMD) can be adapted to expand this framework. This can be achieved via two approaches, namely: computer-aided solvent design and computer-aided multilayer plastic design.

However, applying this framework could potentially lead to not finding solvents with satisfactory performance. Hence, computer-aided molecular design (CAMD) can be adapted to expand this framework. text: The first approach involves the use of traditional physics-based models and CAMD approaches to design and identify better solvents for specific applications. For instance, Struebing et al. (2013) combine quantum mechanics (QM) studies with CAMD approaches to design solvents to accelerate the reaction kinetics and study solvents effects in reactions. More recently, model-based design of experiments was integrated with a QM-CAMD framework to reduce the computational cost associated with designing and identifying solvents via traditional QM methods (Gui et al., 2023). CAMD methods have also found applications in designing solvent mixtures for dissolving additives in paints (Gani, 2007). Molecular-scale studies have also been combined with data-centric models to quickly design and predict glycerol-based solvents that can be synthesized from biomass and deep-eutectic solvents with favorable properties for polymer dissolution (Soyemi and Szilvási, 2023; Christodoulou et al., 2024). Given the preferred properties of a green solvent for multilayer plastic separation as identified by our framework, these tools can be adopted to design solvents with satisfactory performance.

Given the challenge of separating PET in recycling processes as highlighted in this study, the second approach involves integrating molecular-scale polymer studies with data-driven predictions to inform the optimal design of easily recyclable ML plastics that is fit for purpose. For instance, Munguía-López et al. (2024) developed a computational framework to quickly identify problematic ML plastic compositions and propose alternatives that reduce environmental impact and cost. The optimal design of recyclable polymers to fit specific applications have been explored in the literature. For instance, Rorrer et al. (2019) studied the combination of PET waste with bio-based monomers and observed both an improvement in its properties and its recyclability. Similarly, Shi et al. (2021) discussed in detail, the principles for designing next-generation intrinsically circular polymers with properties tunable for different applications. This design strategy follows the plastic redesign concept called recyclable-by-design (RBD) , ensuring easy recyclability of these plastics at their end-of-life. This approach enables the redesign of polymers compatible with green solvents, reducing reliance on screening organic solvents to dissolve legacy polymers.

This study presents a green solvent selection framework for multilayer (ML) plastic film separation via solvent-based processes. The framework addresses potential environmental risks, focusing on mitigating new toxic waste generation. A case study on PE-EVOH-PET ML plastic film separation using a temperature-dependent STRAP ™ process demonstrates the framework's effectiveness.

text: The eight-step framework begins by predicting temperaturedependent polymer solubilities in 1000 solvents. Solvents are screened based on their ability to selectively dissolve and precipitate individual polymers at ambient pressure. Solvent greenness is assessed using both quantitative and qualitative methods. Quantitatively, the solvents' logP and GSK solvent guide scores were used for rapid green solvent screening, while environmental impacts, including climate change, human toxicity (cancer & non-cancer), and freshwater ecotoxicity, were evaluated via LCA. Qualitatively, solvent hazards were reviewed from public databases and regulatory frameworks such as REACH and EPA. Process costs associated with each solvent choice are evaluated and assessed via a TEA. This framework was applied to a 3-component ML plastic film, resulting in two separation processes: selective dissolution of EVOH from EVOH-PET and PE from PE-EVOH-PET. The framework also guided process design by evaluating all possible separation sequence designs.

text: For the binary ML system involving selective dissolution of EVOH from an EVOH-PET film, we identified 45 out of 1000 solvents that met both selective dissolution and logP criteria. DMSO, previously used in the STRAP ™ process, outperformed most solvents in terms of energy requirement, solubility, and logP. Although formic acid showed lower energy requirements and logP, its corrosiveness makes it less suitable for recovering food contact materials. In the 3-component system involving selective dissolution of PE from a PE-EVOH-PET polymer mix, 151 out of 1000 solvents met the selective dissolution and logP criteria. Toluene, despite being flagged as a chemical of concern in the GSK solvent guidelines, also performed poorly in terms of energy requirements and logP. Solvent boiling points were found to significantly affect recovery rates, influencing the economics and sustainability of solventbased processes. High boiling point solvents should be avoided due to energy-intensive separation, while low boiling point solvents may hinder recovery rates. At high solvent recovery rates of ≥ 99.90%, the choice of solvent had a negligible effect on the MSP of recovered resins. However, below 99.90% recovery, the solvent contribution to the variable cost became significant. The LCA metrics indicated that a solvent's minimum energy requirement, which is a function of its specific heat capacity, is strongly correlated with environmental impact. A trade-off analysis showed that, while no significant improvements were observed in MSP and LCA metrics, tetramethylene sulfide emerged as a potential replacement for toluene based on qualitative hazard assessment. We further demonstrated how this framework can support more sustainable process design for ML plastic film separation by evaluating different separation sequences. PET presented the greatest challenge in selective dissolution, remaining undissolved at the final separation stage. Screening for green solvents further reduced the solvent space for separation, highlighting the complexity of selecting a green solvent for ML plastic film separation as a multiobjective problem.

text: Future work could investigate methods to combine our solubility database, this framework, and BioSTEAM, a process simulator, to rapidly screen for green solvents for separating ML plastic films with more polymer components while also considering potential contaminants including the intentionally and non-intentionally added substance (Tumu et al., 2024). Although this study applies our green solvent selection framework to an ML plastic comprising of three polymers, this framework can be applied to ML plastics comprising of up to 10 polymers studied by Sánchez-Rivera et al. (2025) as their temperature-dependent solubilities currently exist in our database. However, in the case where these temperature-dependent solubilities do not exist, our database can be extended to more polymers, employing similar physics-based solubility prediction workflow described by Zhou et al. (2023). One limitation encountered in this study was the insufficient quantitative approach to rapidly screen green solvents. There are potential opportunities to employ data science techniques to expand the GSK solvent screening guide to the 1000 solvents in our database. These quantitative metrics will aid the development and solving of multiobjective optimization models for green solvent selection in solvent-based processes. As mentioned earlier, this study employs a temperature-dependent solvent-based ML plastic separation process, avoiding the cost and environmental impacts associated with separating solvents via a distillation process and azeotrope formation. However, in the case where anti-solvents are employed, we recommend employing computational methods to quickly predict azeotrope mixtures and implementing a constraint to avoid such solvent combinations during the solvent selection process. As part of future work, we also are interested in using this framework to identify easy-to-recycle ML plastic films from a technical and sustainability standpoint. This will guide the design of more sustainable products and food packaging materials.

ABSTRACT: This study demonstrates the recycling of single-use technology (SUT) plastics for biomanufacturing by solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP), which recovers polymer resins by selective dissolution and precipitation. Polyethylene (PE) and ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) were extracted from the films of unused biocontainer bags. text: Single-use technologies (SUTs) have revolutionized the biopharmaceutical industry compared to traditional stainlesssteel technologies. SUTs are presterilized disposable components (bags, filters, tubing, mixers, storage bags) used in biomanufacturing. SUTs provide increased flexibility and productivity, faster time to market, decreased utility consumption, and reduced costs compared to traditional stainlesssteel equipment. SUTs reduce the risk of cross-contamination, thereby enhancing sterility. 1 Closed system processing also lowers facility sterilization requirements, thereby reducing the facility's energy consumption. SUTs are typically composed of multilayer polymer films, tubing, bioreactor bags, magnets, filters, sensors, and other disposable components. Despite the sustainability benefits of SUTs, the use of SUTs generates large amounts of waste. Millipore Sigma estimates that the biopharma industry disposes of 94,000 -200,000 tons of plastics every year, 2 including 30,000 tons of plastics from SUTs. 3,4 Due to stringent regulations in the biopharma industry, plastics in SUTs are high-purity, containing very few contaminants and additives. Used SUTs are commonly treated as hazardous waste and perceived as difficult to recycle. 5 Consequently, SUTs are typically incinerated or landfilled after a single use, contributing to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, 6 which motivates recycling efforts.

text: This paper will discuss the recycling of multilayer films from SUTs using solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP). 9 -17 STRAP is a solvent-based recycling method that uses solvents to selectively dissolve and precipitate a specific polymer from polymer mixtures without dissolving other polymers. 13 This method has been demonstrated with multilayer plastic films under relatively mild conditions. 11,13,18 Solvent-based recycling methods like STRAP can be applied to a variety of different feedstocks, such as printed multilayer films and agriculture films, and have been shown to produce higher-quality recycled polymers compared to mechanical recycling. 11,20 Solvent-based recycling is advantageous compared to mechanical recycling because it can remove the additives, inorganic and organic, including halogens, sulfurcontaining compounds, and antioxidants, as well as inks. 21 -24 Solvent-based recycling is also a viable method to remove individual plastics from complex composite materials and mixed waste streams. 25 -30 In comparison, mechanical recycling is challenging for contaminated and mixed plastics, and it can cause thermo-mechanical degradation. 31 Recycling plastics using pyrolysis is being used commercially for polyolefin-rich feedstocks at large scales (above 30 kton/year) when integrated with a steam cracker or other petrochemical complex. 32 This paper presents the results of STRAP technology applied to the recycling of unused SUT multilayer plastic bags. We show that STRAP yields a clear, high-quality PE film without any visible yellow color. We also assess the economic and environmental impacts of using STRAP to recycle SUT materials.

Materials. Unused 'single-use biocontainer systems' were collected from Cytiva. As shown in Figure 1, each system had three components: films (made of PE and EVOH), connectors, and fittings. The films contain approximately 90% PE and 8% EVOH. Each component was shredded to 3 mm in size through a 1/8 in. cross-cut shredder (Make: Allegheny 16 -75 CX) at Michigan Technological University. For this study, we only used films as feedstocks for STRAP because they were the major component by mass. Connectors and fittings will be analyzed in later studies. Virgin pellets of LDPE (Westlake EG412), mLLDPE (ExxonMobil Exact 3139), and EVOH (SoarnoL DC3203RB) were provided by Amcor. Dodecane, a mixture of isomers, was received from Thermo Scientific Chemicals. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (ACS reagent, ≥ 99.5%) was received from SigmaAldrich. Heptane, toluene, and xylenes were received from VWR Chemicals.

text: Computational Modeling. Solvent screening for the selective dissolution and recovery of PE and EVOH was accomplished following the approach developed in our previous work. 11,15 Polymer solubilities in various solvents were predicted using the conductor-like screening model for realistic solvents (COSMO-RS), a combined quantum chemical and statistical mechanical approach to calculate temperature-dependent polymer solubilities in various solvent systems. 15,33 -35 As shown in Figure S1, the COSMO-RS represents each molecule based on the screening charge density, obtained from density functional theory calculations in our previous work, that arises at molecular surfaces due to polarization of the surrounding medium. We approximated the screening charge densities of polymer molecules by modeling oligomer structures with deactivated terminal groups. COSMO-RS solubility calculations were performed using COSMOtherm 19 with the BP_TZVP_19 parametrization. The workflow established in our previous work can be adapted by using different reference inputs so that resin-specific polymer properties can be addressed with a minimum number of calculations, but resin information was not available for this commercial feedstock. Therefore, LDPE calculations relied on our previous PE molecular model with a reference melting temperature of 113 °C and reference solubility of 23.1 wt % at 110 °C in toluene, and with 31 conformers of a 6-mer structure for molecular modeling. Similarly, the EVOH calculations used previous experimental values with a reference melting temperature of 177.47 °C and a reference solubility of 19.4 wt % in DMSO at 95 °C, with 24 conformers of a 6-mer (4VA:2E) random copolymer structure for molecular modeling. The feedstock also contained a small percentage of a grafting layer, which consists of LDPE covalently bound to EVOH through a ring-opened maleic anhydride constituent. Solvent screening for the selective dissolution and recovery of PE and EVOH was accomplished following the approach developed in our previous work. 11,15 Polymer solubilities in various solvents were predicted using the conductor-like screening model for realistic solvents (COSMO-RS), a combined quantum chemical and statistical mechanical approach to calculate temperature-dependent polymer solubilities in various solvent systems. 15,33 -35 As shown in Figure S1, the COSMO-RS represents each molecule based on the screening charge density, obtained from density functional theory calculations in our previous work, that arises at molecular surfaces due to polarization of the surrounding medium. We approximated the screening charge densities of polymer molecules by modeling oligomer structures with deactivated terminal groups. COSMO-RS solubility calculations were performed using COSMOtherm 19 with the BP_TZVP_19 parametrization. The workflow established in our previous work can be adapted by using different reference inputs so that resin-specific polymer properties can be addressed with a minimum number of calculations, but resin information was not available for this commercial feedstock. Therefore, LDPE calculations relied on our previous PE molecular model with a reference melting temperature of 113 °C and reference solubility of 23.1 wt % at 110 °C in toluene, and with 31 conformers of a 6-mer structure for molecular modeling. Similarly, the EVOH calculations used previous experimental values with a reference melting temperature of 177.47 °C and a reference solubility of 19.4 wt % in DMSO at 95 °C, with 24 conformers of a 6-mer (4VA:2E) random copolymer structure for molecular modeling. The feedstock also contained a small percentage of a grafting layer, which consists of LDPE covalently bound to EVOH through a ring-opened maleic anhydride constituent. text: Small-Scale STRAP Setup. Figure 2a shows the overall experimental process for the recovery of PE and EVOH. The setup shown in Figure 2b involves five steps to recover the PE and residual film components. In step 1, 5 g of shredded films is dissolved in 100 g of dodecane (feed-to-solvent ratio of 1:20) at 110 °C. The solution is stirred in a silicone oil bath with a magnetic stirrer for 90 min to maximize PE dissolution. In step 2, the hot solution is filtered out to separate dissolved PE from other components using a stainless-steel wire mesh filter with an opening size of 0.0277 in. and an open area of 44.2%. In step 3, the dodecane -PE solution is cooled at room temperature for 30 min, allowing the PE to precipitate. In step 4, the cooled solution is mechanically filtered under vacuum to recover the precipitated PE. Finally, in step 5, the recovered PE and undissolved residual flakes are dried in a vacuum oven at 100 °C for 2 h. This process yielded 4 g of PE and 1 g of residual flakes for further analysis.

text: Jacketed Dissolution Vessel STRAP Setup. A 4 L jacketed dissolution vessel was used to perform experiments at larger scale and produce resins for mechanical testing. The vessel is heated by a continuous flow of silicone oil through the jacket. The undissolved fractions were collected in a filter mesh made up of steel with a 1000 μ m pore size. A total volume of 3.1 L ( ∼ 2120 g) of heptane was preheated to 95 °C in the vessel before 155 g of shredded film was added, maintaining a feed-to-solvent ratio of 1:13.6. This feed-tosolvent ratio was achieved after averaging 7 -8 runs. A feed-to-solvent ratio of 1:12 resulted in a low PE yield (70%) and undissolved flakes (20%) that were contaminated with PE. Undissolved flakes, presumed to be EVOH, were separated using an internal filter mesh and retained for subsequent analysis, as detailed later in this study. To generate sufficient STRAP PE for a cast film, the experiment was performed in ten iterations, with the average batch material balance illustrated in Figure 3.

Characterization. FTIR. Attenuated total reflectance Fouriertransform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectra were acquired with a Bruker Vertex 70 FTIR spectrometer equipped with a liquid-nitrogen-cooled mercury cadmium -telluride (MCT) detector (Bruker Corporation, Billerica, Massachusetts, USA). An average of 16 scans was collected in the range of 4000 -600 cm -1 with a resolution of 4 cm -1 . Each spectrum was scanned with an air background.

TGA. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was conducted on a TGA Q500 analyzer (TA Instruments, New Castle, Delaware, USA) from 40 to 550 °C for PE with a ramping rate of 15 °C min -1 under a nitrogen flow rate of 50.0 mL min -1 . For EVOH, TGA was conducted on the same machine from 40 to 220 °C with a ramping rate of 15 °C min -1 and held at 220 °C for 10 min.

DSC. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) was used to estimate the melting temperature ( T m) and crystallization temperature ( T c) on a DSC Q100 calorimeter equipped with a Refrigerated Cooling System 90 (TA Instruments, New Castle, Delaware, USA). Samples were encapsulated in standard aluminum pans, heated from -20 to 220 °C with a ramping rate of 15 °C min -1 and cooled from 220 to -20 °C at the same ramping rate. The heating/cooling process was looped twice at a 50.0 mL min -1 nitrogen flow rate.

Characterization of the PE Cast Film. Tensile properties of the films were measured using an Instron testing machine following ASTM Standard D882-1. 36 The thermal properties of the films were analyzed with a NETZSCH TGA 209F1Libra. The analysis compared the dynamic cooling and the second heating of the films, from -20 to 250 °C, at rate of 10 K/min. Final color of the cast films was quantified with a spectrophotometer and measurements were converted to CIELAB color space values, L * (lightness), a * (redgreen color component) and b * (blue-yellow color component), and YI (yellowness index). 37 Optical properties were analyzed following the ASTM standard D1003-21 for haze and luminous transmittance of transparent plastics. 38 The defect analysis for determining the number of impurities in the cast films was performed with an Amcor internal method.

The process model was developed in BioSTEAM, an opensource platform in Python for the design, simulation, and evaluation (via TEA and LCA) of chemical processes. 39,40 The model is based on data from laboratory experiments, the construction of a 25 kg/h STRAP pilot plant at Michigan Technological University, 41 and builds upon past TEA/LCA studies on STRAP. 13,17

text: The plastic feedstock is fed into a dissolution vessel and is mixed with the solvent to dissolve the target polymer (Figure 4). The effluent is sent through a series of filters to separate the solids (i.e., insoluble plastics and biogenic material) from the solution. A vacuum twin-screw drier recovers >99.9% of the solvent retained on the undissolved plastic. The undissolved plastic can be landfilled or further processed to remove another resin layer. The dissolved resin is then precipitated by cooling within a jacketed precipitation and filtration module. After precipitation, a melt devolatilizer removes the solvent down to <1 wt %, and an outgassing extruder recovers the last solvent fraction, leaving low concentrations (<10 ppm) in the resin. Plastic additives, inks, and any soluble biogenic material which may accumulate in the solvent are removed by adsorption with granulated activated carbon. The design of the adsorption module follows the procedure outlined by Gabelman. 42 The solute capacity was estimated using the fitted Freundlich isotherm of Yellow 12 dye (commonly found in plastics) with activated carbon. 43 The length of the unused bed was estimated through numerical mass transfer modeling. After adsorption, the cold solvent is reheated and returned to the dissolution tank. To improve energy efficiency and economics, a heat exchanger was added between the hot and cold solvent streams.

Techno-Economic Analysis. Cost estimates for solvent removal equipment were provided by Amcor. Cost estimates for specialized STRAP equipment (e.g., dissolution and precipitation vessels) were provided by industry vendors. The 6/10th rule for economies of scale was used to formulate capital cost correlations for the specialized modules in STRAP. 44 The cost of the adsorption columns was estimated as pressure vessels using ASME guidelines to vessel thickness. 44 All other equipment cost correlations originate from various public sources, 44,45 as detailed by Cortes-Pena and coworkers. 39 The chemical engineering plant cost index (used to account for the increasing cost of equipment due to inflation) was assumed to be 816.0. text: Development of STRAP Processing Steps. The general steps for the development and assessment of a new STRAP process for a multilayer film include identifying the polymer components of the film, choosing solvents and operating temperatures suitable for selectively dissolving each polymer component, performing STRAP at a small scale to assess recovered resin yields and properties, and then repeating STRAP at a larger scale to evaluate the properties, of films created from STRAP resins. We first acquired the FTIR spectra of the shredded films to verify the composition of polymers in the film. The FTIR spectra of the Cytiva film and virgin LDPE (Figure S2) were compared and display identical spectral bands with no bands belonging to other resins. This comparison confirmed that the films mainly consisted of PE, with EVOH expected as a minority component, as will be discussed later in the paper.

text: To choose STRAP solvents and operating temperatures, we leveraged our computational modeling approach to identify solvents with high predicted solubility for the target polymer (PE or EVOH) at an elevated temperature and negligible solubility for the other polymer. Additionally, ideal solvents have a low solubility for both polymers at room temperature, allowing for temperature-based precipitation. Figure S1c lists example solvents that are selective for each polymer, along with predicted solubilities. Based on these criteria, xylene, dodecane, toluene, and heptane were identified as potential selective solvents for LDPE dissolution. Similarly, DMSO, ethylene glycol, and propylene glycol were identified as potential selective solvents for EVOH dissolution. These solvents are commonly available and were selected from a larger database of 1000+ solvents. For initial small-scale experiments, we selected dodecane as the selective solvent for PE because of its low volatility, thereby decreasing unintentional solvent loss in this laboratory setup, and DMSO as a selective solvent for EVOH because it is easy to work with due to its low viscosity and has been used to dissolve EVOH in previous work. 13 -15

The recovered fractions were analyzed with FTIR to confirm polymer identity and assess purity after each step, as shown in Table 1. Figure 5 shows the FTIR scan of the Cytiva film, the extracted PE (referred to as STRAP PE), the extracted EVOH (referred to as STRAP EVOH), and the remaining DMSO undissolved fraction as well as comparisons to virgin resins. The FTIR results (Figure 5a) show that STRAP PE is comparable to virgin LDPE. Spectra of STRAP EVOH and virgin EVOH (Figure 5b) displayed identical spectral bands without traces of other resins, confirming that the purity of STRAP EVOH is comparable to virgin EVOH. The DMSO undissolved fraction (Figure 5c), after PE dissolution and before EVOH dissolution, showed the presence of PE and EVOH, which will be discussed in later sections.

Further characterization of STRAP PE and STRAP EVOH was done by using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to thoroughly analyze the purity of recovered polymers. Comparative TGA, shown in Figure 6, revealed that STRAP PE and virgin LDPE exhibit comparable thermal stability and decomposition behavior. The main decomposition ranges were similar, from 400 to 520 °C.

text: The DSC curves in Figure 7a and 7b reveal two melting point peaks for Cytiva film around 95 and 113 °C, corresponding to melting points of mLLDPE (98 °C) and virgin LDPE (113 °C), respectively. This indicates that Cytiva films are made up of two different types of polyethylene. The DSC results of the STRAP PE align with those of mLLDPE/ LDPE blends (Liu et al. 48 ), indicating that STRAP PE is a blend of mLLDPE and LDPE originating from the Cytiva film. Figure S3 and the heat of fusion values in Table S1 estimate the composition of STRAP PE as approximately 20/80 wt % LDPE/mLLDPE. Virgin LDPE exhibits the highest crystallinity, evidenced by its elevated fusion ( Δ H f ), while the lower Δ H f values for STRAP PE and Cytiva film are attributed to mLLDPE. mLLDPE is classified as plastomers with inherently lower heat of fusion. 49 The STRAP PE melting point range lies between the melting point ranges of Cytiva film component peaks (95 and 113 °C). This suggests that the extracted material is morphologically different from that of the film. The peak at 193 °C represents the melting peak of EVOH in the film, with a detailed discussion provided in later sections.

The DSC results of the STRAP PE cast film and virgin LDPE cast film are shown in Figure S4 and Table S1. Table S1 shows that the STRAP PE cast film has low heat of fusion ( Δ H f ) which is similar to STRAP PE. This shows the cast film is likely made up of mainly mLLDPE (plastomers) and making cast film did not change thermal properties. Table 2 shows tensile properties of the three films made from STRAP PE, STRAP virgin LDPE, and virgin LDPE. The LDPE control and STRAP virgin LDPE cast films have similar mechanical properties. The STRAP PE film was more flexible than the other two cast films due to its lower Young's modulus, which is likely caused by the presence of mLLDPE in the original feedstock (Figure 7). 50,51 The low heat of fusion, i.e., low crystallinity, is a characteristic of a plastomer and is responsible for the higher elongation at break and lower Young's Modulus. 49 It is also possible that some PE oligomers (C10 -C15) were permanently removed during STRAP.

text: We tested four solvents, heptane, dodecane, toluene, and xylenes, to get high-quality residual flakes comparable to virgin EVOH by dissolving only the PE. Dissolution with heptane was performed at 95 °C, whereas dissolution with dodecane, toluene, and xylenes was performed at 110 °C, all with a consistent feed-to-solvent ratio equal to 1:20. Heptane was heated to 95 °C, slightly below its boiling point ( ∼ 100 °C), to minimize vapor pressure buildup and to remain within safe operating limits, considering its low flash point ( -7 °C). Higher temperatures could impair solvent recovery and require design modifications to handle increased pressure in the STRAP systems. Table 3 summarizes these experiments and residual flake recoveries, while Figure 11 compares the FTIR spectra of the residual flakes to virgin EVOH for each of these solvents. Based on FTIR results, there was no noticeable difference in the quality of the EVOH recovered by each solvent. All solvents tested yielded EVOH with minimal contamination visible on FTIR. Additionally, Figure S5 shows the FTIR spectra of residual flakes recovered from varied feedto-solvent ratios. In the cases where less solvent was used, the FTIR spectra also indicated higher PE contamination. These findings provide evidence that the feed-to-solvent ratio can greatly impact the quality of the remaining undissolved polymer, and solvent amount may be more impactful than the type of solvent used.

text: The variability in the residual flakes after single-solvent washing was assessed by using FTIR, as shown in Figure 12. Each spectrum represents the analysis of 10 -15 residual flake samples. Table S2 shows characteristic peaks for PE and EVOH for a better understanding of FTIR spectra of residual flakes. However, variability in the OH stretching intensity ( ∼ 3300 cm -1 ) suggests the potential presence of PE adhering to residual flakes, which the solvents failed to remove during the previous step. This may be due to the presence of a coextruded adhesive layer positioned adjacent to the EVOH layer, typically PE grafted with maleic anhydride. The maleic anhydride reacts with EVOH hydroxyl groups to form interfacial covalent bonds. 54 The maleic anhydride content of a polyolefin tie layer can be 0.15 -0.30 wt.% for EVOH adhesion. 55 However, the maleic anhydride or any other grafting material was not detected with the characterization method used, but it is possible that the quality of residual flakes is affected by it and it is rigorous to detect the anhydride content. 54

text: Techno-Economic Analysis (TEA). The following analysis compares three commercial-scale scenarios for a STRAP plant that processes SUT film waste composed of PE and EVOH as depicted in Figure 14. Additional results are included in workbooks Supporting Information W1, W2, and W3. The SUT waste is received as whole films or bags, and shredding and preprocessing are included in the model. In scenario 1, only PE is recovered and all undissolved components are landfilled after drying. Scenario 2 is similar but assumes that the undissolved fraction is purified EVOH that can be sold. It uses a single PE-selective solvent, with increased solvent volume compared to scenario 1 to improve residual flake quality, and is best suited for minimally contaminated postindustrial waste. In scenario 3, the undissolved fraction is further processed with an EVOH-selective solvent to purify EVOH. Any remaining solid waste in scenarios 1 or 3 is landfilled at the average California tipping fee of $72/ton. 56 Base case parameters for each scenario are listed in Table S3.

Scenario 1 has the lowest capital cost but without the added revenue from EVOH, it is the least profitable option. Scenario 2 requires more capital due to increased solvent volume and equipment size but has the lowest UOC. The recovered EVOH contributes over 40% of scenario 2's revenue, making it the most profitable at 5 kton/year. This scenario depends on a clean, two-polymer feed  likely a well-sorted postindustrial waste  to ensure high-quality EVOH residue. Scenario 3 is the most capital-intensive option and has the highest UOC. However, the purified EVOH product makes this scenario more profitable than scenario 1. Scenario 3 has the potential to produce the highest-quality EVOH, but the economics may suffer if the feedstock regularly contains less than 8% EVOH.

Single-point sensitivity analysis was performed on selected variables to identify the key drivers of economics and environmental impact. All variables, along with their bounds and justifications, can be found in Table S3. Figure 16 displays the most impactful variables on minimum selling price (MSP), for scenarios 1 -3. MSP is defined as the minimum product sale price for a plant to be economically viable, covering all costs and the required return on investment over the plant lifetime. MSP was chosen for the sensitivity analysis because it reflects changes in both capital and operating expenses.

Figure 16. Single-point sensitivity of the most impactful variables on STRAP resin MSP. Variables are defined as the variable name (lower bound, base case, upper bound).

The most important economic driver is processing scale because plant capacity directly affects capital expenses which see benefits from economies of scale. Similarly, dissolved polymer concentration (dissolved solvent capacity) affects required solvent volume and equipment size, directly influencing capital expenses. In scenarios 1 and 3, the target polymer mass fraction in the feedstock strongly influences the economic performance, highlighting the need for careful feedstock selection. In contrast, scenario 2 benefits from a lower target polymer fraction  when two products are recovered with one solvent, less dissolved polymer reduces solvent and equipment requirements. This advantage, however, depends on sourcing clean feedstock that can be separated into two useable products; otherwise, contaminants will be mixed with the undissolved stream. Clean SUT waste and other twocomponent postindustrial streams are ideal candidates for this scenario.

Additionally, if solvent loss can be limited to 1% or less, it is only the fourth or fifth most impactful variable considered. The plant design includes solvent recovery from the waste and product streams as well as solvent cleaning/regeneration with adsorbents before each recycling step; therefore, maintaining solvent losses below 1% is reasonable.

Ultimately, the commercial design of a STRAP plant that processes SUT waste should be based on the quantity and quality of feedstock available. If sufficiently clean, twocomponent feed is available, then scenario 2 is a good design. However, further studies are needed to verify if there is a difference in EVOH quality between scenarios 2 and 3 and how that difference may impact the economics. In contrast, scenarios 1 and 3 are more robust options for varied feedstock and are also economically viable above 9 and 4 kton/year, respectively.

The GWP impacts were also analyzed with a single-point sensitivity analysis (Figure S8). The top four most sensitive variables are in descending order: target polymer mass fraction, feedstock distance, solvent loss, and dissolved polymer concentration. While GWP is not a comprehensive indicator, it effectively highlights relative environmental impact and trends. In all cases, scenario 3 EVOH produces higher impacts than scenario 2, due to the high processing requirements for relatively little product. This, again, emphasizes the importance of scale and feedstock selection.

■ CONCLUSIONS

STRAP successfully extracted high-quality polyethylene (PE) and ethylene-vinyl alcohol (EVOH) from single-use technology (SUT) biocontainer films. The resulting STRAP PE cast film exhibited comparable color and mechanical properties to those of a virgin low-density polyethylene (LDPE) cast film. However, the STRAP PE cast film displayed a lower Young's modulus, mainly attributed to the presence of mLLDPE plastomer in the Cytiva films. The STRAP PE was mainly composed of mLLDPE. STRAP also yielded high-quality residual EVOH flakes in a single PE-solvent wash. The quality of the residual EVOH flakes increased with increasing solvent amounts.

text: The techno-economic analysis shows that capital expenses and feedstock composition and quality are major drivers of the profitability of a commercial STRAP plant that processes SUT waste. Recovering EVOH can increase the revenue of a plant by nearly 40%. However, the capital cost of a plant that recovers EVOH is higher, which introduces risk if a consistent feedstock is not available. Additionally, life cycle analysis shows that most configurations of a STRAP plant processing SUT waste have similar environmental impacts while reducing GHG emissions and fossil fuel consumption by 50%. Electricity and heat are the main contributors to STRAP environmental impacts, and these are most influenced by variables such as feedstock composition and solvent loss. Future studies such as oxygen barrier tests on STRAP EVOH and extractable and leachable tests on STRAP resins could provide clearer insights into the value of STRAP-recovered resins. More bioprocess SUTs should be investigated as well to develop a clearer understanding of potential feedstock types and scales.

text:
Our results show that STRAP is a viable recycling method for SUTs that balances economic and ecological sustainability while producing high-quality recovered materials with mechanical, optical, and thermal properties similar to those of virgin resins. However, complex waste streams can contain more than two polymers, requiring further analysis to determine feasible scales for systems with three or more solvents. 57 As waste complexity increases, a combined approach of mechanical and solvent-based recycling can be a more effective approach to increase recycling rates. 58 Additionally, pretreatment and sorting require further investigation, as their importance varies with the SUT compositional complexity. Future work will involve comparing thermograms of STRAP solvent blends and melt blends of LDPE and mLLDPE to better interpret the DSC profile of STRAP PE. Further investigation will also determine if the initial application of STRAP to SUTs can facilitate the recovery of additional polymers and valuable materials, like neodymium magnets, PP fittings, filters, and silicone tubing, from other SUT components. While this study focused on postindustrial biopharma plastic waste, future research should assess postconsumer biopharma waste, evaluating its recyclability, quality, and pretreatment requirements compared to postindustrial waste.

While this study focused on postindustrial biopharma plastic waste, future research should assess postconsumer biopharma waste, evaluating its recyclability, quality, and pretreatment requirements compared to postindustrial waste.

text:
ABSTRACT: This study evaluated the thermal, morphological, chemical, and mechanical properties of virgin and recycled polystyrene. The recycling process was carried out by dissolution of polystyrene (extruded and crystal) in ethyl acetate, followed by two processes for solvent removal: vaporization by direct contact with water at 85 8 C in a tubular evaporator and vaporization during the extrusion process. For the samples produced by solvent evaporation in the tubular evaporator, there was practically no degradation on polymer chain, neither reduction in glass transition temperature. For the samples produced by solvent evaporation during the extrusion, a polymer chain degradation was noted by reduction in molar weight and in glass transition temperature. The FTIR evaluation suggests that polymer oxidative degradation, in both samples, was more pronounced in the extruded sample. The removal of plasticizing additives could be evidenced by the glass transition temperature increase in the recycled samples produced in the tubular evaporator. V C 2018 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. J. Appl. Polym. Sci. 2018 , 135 , 46208.

KEYWORDS: degradation; polystyrene; recycling; thermoplastics

text:
Polystyrene (PS) is a versatile polymer and it is used in rigid and foamed materials. The disposal of this material creates environmental problems because of its long degradation time in nature (hundreds of years). 1 Increasing landfill costs and decreasing landfill space are forcing consideration of alternative options for the disposal of PS materials. These problems are worse for the expanded form, because the low density of PS foams, which increases costs in transportation and disposal. Nowadays, there are four main approaches for polymer recycling: direct recovery without polymer modification (primary and secondary recycling), tertiary, or chemical recycling which plastic returns into a petrochemical product or monomer and energy recovery (also known as quaternary recycling). Environmental argumentations such as toxic emissions are building up a public resistance against incineration. Dissolution processes include different stages to manage plastic waste with solvents. Initially, the polymeric materials are dissolved, and then different processes are applied to recover the polymer and the solvent. The use of solvents as a method to recycle foamed polymers offers some advantages. Any

text:
In this study, two techniques for PS recycling by dissolution in ethyl acetate were used that are different in the way solvent evaporates. The reasons for choosing this solvent were its low toxicity compared to most organic solvents that also dissolve PS (benzene, toluene, chloroform, among others), its significantly lower saturation temperature in relation to other low toxicity solvents (77 8 C vs 176 8 C for D-limonene) and also its lower cost (1/10 of the price of D-limonene). The first process was based on the solvent vaporization by direct contact with water at 85 8 C in a tubular evaporator, and the second process was based on the solvent evaporation during the extrusion process of the polymer (which uses temperature up to 200 8 C). The aim of this study was to determinate the effect of the proposed recycling processes on thermal, morphological, chemical, and mechanical properties of virgin and recycled PS.

EXPERIMENTAL

Materials

The solvent used for dissolution was ethyl acetate, supplied by Butilamil (S ~ ao Paulo, Brazil), and had a purity higher than 99%. Ethyl acetate has a vaporization temperature of 77 8 C.

Extruded polystyrene (XPS) was obtained from food packages, supplied by Fibraform (S ~ ao Paulo, Brazil), and a weight-average molecular weight ( Mw ) of 244 kDa and a polydispersity index (PI) of 2.0.

Recycling Processes

The samples were dissolved in the solvent at concentrations of 27 and 35 wt % in a closed glass vessel, to avoid solvent evaporation. The solutions were used only after at least 24 h, to ensure complete dissolution. The polymeric solution was stirred by mechanical stirrer (300 rpm) for 3 min before the start of each solvent evaporation process. Relatively close concentrations of dissolved sample were used because of the pumping capacity and it is expected that the solution will contain a concentration of polymer to require less ethyl acetate, so reducing the concentration of polymer is not interest to the process.

text:
Solvent Evaporation in the Tubular Evaporator. The vertical tubular evaporator has an internal diameter of 95 mm and height of 700 mm and has no stirring system. The evaporator has a vessel, filled with 5 L of water at 85 8 C, maintained through a temperature monitoring and control system, performed with an Arduino microcontroller, with temperature measurement via thermocouple (type J) and 600 W electrical resistance controlled by an electronic dimmer. The electrical resistance is located at the bottom, near the place where the solution is fed. Molecular Weight Measurement

text:
The Mw and PI were performed by gel permeation chromatography (GPC) on a Shimadzu High Performance Liquid Chromatograph (HPLC model LC 20-A, supplied by Shimadzu Scientific Instruments, Japan) equipped with three Shim Pack GPC 800 Series columns (GPC 801, GPC 804, and GPC 807). The mobile phase was tetrahydrofuran (THF, Merck, Germany) at a flow rate of 1 mL min 2 1 at 40 8 C. Polymer was dissolved in THF at concentration of 5 mg mL 2 1 and filtered through 0.45 l m filter before analysis. The system was calibrated with narrow disperse PS standards and molecular weights are reported as PS equivalents supplied by Merck, Germany. The molecular weight ( Mw ) averages and the distribution of molecular weights are determined in accordance with ASTM D5296 standard. 16

Differential Scanning Calorimetry

A Perkin-Elmer model Jade differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, Waltham, MA, USA) calorimeter was used to obtain thermograms of the virgin material and the recycled samples. The measurements were carried out between 20 and 150 8 C in a nitrogen atmosphere and using an empty capsule as reference. Sample weights varied from 2.0 to 12.5 mg and the heating rate was fixed at 10 8 C min 2 1 .The glass transition temperature was measured by the half-extrapolated heat capacity temperature, in accordance with ASTM D3418 and ASTM E1356 standards. 17,18

Dynamic Mechanical Properties

text:
Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) is useful for the evaluation of viscoelastic properties of a polymer. When an oscillating sinusoidal load is applied to a specimen at a particular frequency, the strain will lag somewhat behind the stress because of the viscoelastic nature. The data of the storage modulus, loss modulus, and loss tangent are obtained through DMA. 19

A Netzsch model DMA 242-E Artemis (Selb, Germany) was used in this work. The mode chosen was single cantilever and the sample size was about 36 3 12 3 3 mm. The samples were produced by thermal press (5 min at 180 8 C and 65 MPa). Measurement was performed from 40 to 130 8 C, heating rate of 3 8 C min 2 1 and frequency of 1 Hz. DMA standard data analysis software was used to evaluate viscoelastic properties of the samples. The glass transition temperature was determined as the loss peak observed in dynamic mechanical test (tan( d ) has an accuracy of 0.00005 N/N), in accordance with ASTM D4065 and ASTM D4092 standards. 20,21

text:
Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) analysis was performed on CPS, before and after the recycling, with a FTIR Shimadzu model IR Prestige 21 (Shimadzu Scientific Instruments, Maryland, USA). The samples were films produced in a thermal press (1 min at 180 8 C and 5 MPa). The IR spectra (4000-400 cm 2 1 ) were measured with an average of 20 and a resolution of 4 cm 2 1 .

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Volatile Compounds Content

The results for the drying processes of the samples produced by solvent evaporation in the tubular evaporator are summarized in Table II.

The results show that there was no uniformity in the initial volatile compounds content. This is due to that the samples are removed from the tubular evaporator in the form of wires of different sizes. The high content of initial volatile compounds is largely due to the presence of water in the samples, caused by the characteristic of the proposed solvent evaporation method, which happens by direct contact of the polymer solution with hot water. The water is removed from the samples at the initial instants, while the solvent remains solubilized in the PS, and will be evaporated at a lower drying rate, controlled by diffusion.

For XPS sample recycled once in the tubular evaporator, a reduction of 0.2 8 C in Tg was observed. However, for the CPS recycled samples by the same process, there was an increase of 2.6-3.0 8 C in Tg . This increase in glass transition temperature can be explained by the removal of plasticizing additives, commonly used in CPS for lowering the processing temperature. 22

Dynamic Mechanical Properties

The DMA results are presented in Figure 5 and Table V. As reported in comparative studies, the value of Tg determined by DMA is higher than the value determined by DSC. 23 It was observed an increase in Tg of 3.4 8 C for the sample produced in tubular evaporator, and a reduction of 2.4 8 C in Tg for the extruded sample. The results corroborate the degradation observed in the extruded sample and the removal of plasticizing additives from CPS in the sample produced in the tubular evaporator.

CONCLUSIONS

text:
For the samples produced by solvent evaporation by direct contact with hot water in the tubular evaporator, there was practically no degradation of the polymer chain, neither significant change in the glass transition temperature of the polymer. In the evaluation of three consecutive recycling processes by this method, no changes were observed. However, the samples recycled by this method showed a volatile compound content, with values between 26.7 and 43.9 wt % for the samples before drying, values between 0.9 and 1.9 wt % for the dried samples for 60 h at 60 8 C, and between 0, 3, and 0.5 wt % for the dried samples for 200 h at the same temperature. In the initial measurements, the most part of the volatile compound content is water, due to the method of evaporation by direct contact with water.

The increase in the glass transition temperature observed in the CPS recycled sample by solvent evaporation in the tubular evaporator, in comparison to the virgin PS, indicates the removal of plasticizing additives from the CPS.

text:
For the samples produced by solvent evaporation during the polymer extrusion process was noted a degradation of the polymer chain, measured by Mw reduction. Degradation can also be observed in the reduction of the glass transition temperature, both in DSC and DMA. For the three times recycled sample, a higher degradation was observed in the molar weight, but without additional change in the glass transition temperature. The evaluation of the FTIR spectra in the region that indicates the polymer degradation suggests that thermal and oxidative degradation was more pronounced in the samples produced by this method compared to the samples produced in the tubular evaporator. A negative point observed in the process for this recycling method was the significant reduction in the processing capacity of the extruder. Under similar operating conditions, but using virgin PS pellets, the same extruder should operate with a production about three times higher.

A B S T R A C T

text: Material Recovery Facilities (MRFs) are crucial players in achieving a circular economy. MRFs receive complex waste  streams  and  separate  valuable  recyclables  from  these  mixtures.  This  study  conducts  techno-economic analysis (TEA) to estimate the net present value (NPV) and life cycle assessment (LCA) to estimate different environmental impacts of a commercial scale standalone, single-stream MRF to assess the economic feasibility and environmental impacts of recovering valuable recyclables from an MRF processing 120,000 tonnes per year (t/y). The TEA employs a discounted cash flow rate of return (DCFROR) analysis over a 20-year facility lifetime, along with a sensitivity analysis on the impact of different operating and economic parameters. Results show that the total fixed cost of building the MRF facility is $23 MM, and the operating cost is $45.48/tonne. The NPV of the MRF can vary from $3.57 MM to $60 MM, while 100-year global warming potential can range from 5.98 to 8.53 kg carbon dioxide equivalents (CO2-eq) per tonne of MSW. We have also found that MSW composition (arising from regional effects) significantly impacts costs, 100-year global warming potential, and other impact categories such as acidification potential, eutrophication potential, ecotoxicity, ozone depletion, photochemical oxidation, carcinogenic effects, and non-carcinogenic effects. Sensitivity and uncertainty analysis indicate that waste composition and market prices significantly impact the profitability of the MRF, and the waste composition mostly impacts global warming potential. Our analysis also indicates that facility capacity, fixed capital cost, and waste tipping fees are vital parameters that affect the economic viability of MRF operations.

MRFs are sophisticated industrial facilities that separate marketable recyclables from different waste streams and resell the recovered ma terials  to  secondary  recyclers.  MRFs  are  classified  into  four  primary types based on the input waste streams they process (Combs, 2011): single-stream, dual-stream, mixed-stream, and presorted MRFs. Mixedstream  MRFs  receive  and  process  all  kinds  of  MSW.  Single-stream MRFs  only  process  recyclable  materials  collected  in  dedicated  bins from households, and commercial organizations. Dual-stream and pre sorted MRFs receive and process waste streams that have been presorted and are almost ready to be repurposed. text: Recent studies  have  modeled the operations of  MRFs considering more  automated  separation  and  recovery  equipment  (Combs,  2011; Pressley et al., 2015). Combs (2011) analyzed material recovery pro cesses to characterize the relationship between crucial MRF parameters, processing cost, and resulting emission. Combs (2011) reported costs of $15.16, $9.72, $11.06, and $7.77 to process 1 tonne (t) of waste in single-stream,  dual-stream,  mixed-stream,  and  presorted  recyclables MRFs, respectively.  The  author  highlighted  that  a ± 25% change in equipment efficiencies and diesel cost could result in a 10% to 5% change in total cost. This same paper also reported a global warming potential (GWP) of 14.94, 14.94, 11.40, and 3.62 kg CO2-eq /t for singlestream,  dual-stream,  mixed-stream,  and  presorted  recyclables  MRFs, respectively. Moreover, this study also showed through sensitivity and uncertainty analysis that a ± 25% change in diesel combustion from rolling stock used to haul materials around the MRF results in a ± 20% change in CO2  emissions.  In  addition,  the  study  reported  that  waste composition is the most influential factor in the profitability of MRFs (Combs, 2011). Pressley et al. (2015) built on Comb ' s (2011) work and developed a process model to evaluate the MRFs ' cost and energy use. Their model allows for estimating the labor and energy requirements, cost, and mass transfers, given the MRF configuration and the type of waste to be processed. For example, this study reported that the elec tricity needs of MRFs can range from 4.7 to 7.8. kWh/t of waste pro cessed, and the amortized cost can vary from $19.8 to $24.9/t of waste processed (Pressley et al., 2015). The model developed by the authors is flexible and can be modified to analyze the four primary types of MRFs (Pressley et al., 2015). Although the study presented models to estimate the cost and emissions associated with a specific MRF configuration, the study did not consider market prices of recyclables to evaluate their return on investment (Pressley et al., 2015).

text: Other  studies  have  conducted  life  cycle  assessments  (LCA)  on standalone MRFs to estimate the environmental impacts associated with such  facilities.  Fitzgerald  (2012)  analyzed  and  compared  the  GHG emissions of dual-stream and single-stream MRFs. The study assessed the GHG emissions benefit or penalty associated with transitioning from dual-stream  to  single-stream  MRFs.  The  author  reported  that  singlestream  MRFs  could  recover  50%  more  recyclables  than  dual-stream MRFs.  Single-stream  MRFs  have  significantly  lower  emissions  than dual-stream  MRFs,  and  for  both  MRF  types,  avoided  emissions  from recyclables are significantly higher than emissions of MRF operations. However, this study did not report the impact of waste composition on emissions. Smith et al. (2022) evaluated the total emissions associated with an MRF as part of an analysis focusing on recycling polyethylene terephthalate (PET). The study reported that MRFs emit 8.58 kg CO2-eq /t of waste processed in the MRF. The study allocated 0.429 kg CO2-eq of the total GHG emissions to separate PET from the waste stream (Smith et al., 2022). Based on the literature review, no study has conducted TEA and LCA of a standalone single-stream MRF that considers the impacts of waste composition and market prices on net revenues while including multiple mid-point environmental impact categories. By addressing this gap, we aim to identify opportunities to improve the profitability and environmental sustainability of material recovery in MRFs.

This study investigates the economic feasibility and environmental impacts of a standalone MRF. We build upon the Pressley et al. (2015) process model that simulates a single-stream MRF and utilizes the mass and energy balance from the process model to conduct a TEA and LCA. This  study  also  investigates  the  effect  of  waste  composition  sampled from four U.S. regions on the economics and environmental impacts associated with the single-stream MRF.

2. Methodology

The TEA and LCA performance of a single-stream MRF that processes 120,000 t/y of waste obtained from four different U.S. locations are investigated. The analysis employs a process model that provides mass and energy flow data of a commercial-scale MRF. The MRF receives waste streams of various compositions and separates them into various post-consumer recovered materials (PCRM). Based on the waste stream, the  net  present  value  (NPV)  and  mid-point  category  environmental impacts of recovering recyclables are estimated. The analysis employs sensitivity  and  uncertainty  analysis  to  evaluate  the  effect  of  critical parameters, such as the waste stream ' s composition, capital cost, and tipping fees, on the economic and environmental impacts of recovering the recyclables.

text: The  baseline  analysis  employs  the  U.S.  national  average  waste composition reported in the U.S. EPA Waste Characterization Report (US EPA, 2010). The U.S. EPA waste composition was selected because it includes all the materials that can be recovered in the MRF. The mate rials  include  various  grades  of  plastics  (high-density  polyethylene (HDPE), PET, plastic film, and mixed plastics), iron, aluminum, glass, old-corrugated containers (OCC), and non-OCC. OCC is used in boxes, containers,  or  other  packaging  materials  consisting  of  three  or  more layers of kraft paper. Non-OCC materials are all other fiber materials that are not classified as OCC materials. PET is typically used in pack aging food and beverages, while HDPE is used in packaging bottles, milk jugs, bags, containers, and toys. Plastic films include trash bags, plastic labels, videotape, grocery bags, storage bags, sheet film plastic, etc. Most MRFs do not accept plastic films because it clogs process equipment. Our analysis  assumes  that  the  MRF  we  model  has  sufficient  capacity  to accept the plastic film. Mixed plastics consist of all other plastic grades that are not PET, HDPE, and plastic films.

2.2. MRF process model

This study assumes that garbage trucks collect waste from curbside recycling bins and transport it to the MRF. The trucks deliver the waste to the MRF tipping area, which can accommodate up to three days of stock, ensuring a steady supply of waste.

text: Fig. 2 shows the process flow of the MRF. The recovery process be gins with floor sorting, where sorters remove large materials from the waste stream. Rolling stock pushes the material to a drum feeder that distributes the commodities to a belt conveyor at a constant rate. The belt  conveyor  moves  the  waste  to  a  presort  location  where  sorters identify and remove large and bulky recyclables that can clog, jam, or damage the recovery equipment. Sorters remove the plastic films in the stream and direct the plastic films to vacuum, and recovered plastic films  are  sent  to  the  two-way  baler,  where  it  is  packaged.  The  pre liminary results of a national-level MRF survey show that approximately 8 out of 58 respondent MRFs keep track of the plastic films they sort in their  facility,  with  most  MRFs  sending  the  plastic  films  to  landfills (Personal communication with survey team, 2022). The rest of the waste stream go through a series of screens,  where  OCC and non-OCC are recovered. The rest of the materials in the stream (mostly packaging containers) fall through and go to the glass breaker screen, where the glass in the stream is broken into cutlets and recovered with other fines in the stream. The mix of broken glass and fines goes through an air knife which separates the fines and other light materials from the glass. The glass  is  further  separated  based  on  color  by  an  optical  sorter.  The separated glass is subjected to manual sorting to remove ceramics in the mix. The rest of the waste is then sent to optical sorters that recover the PET and another optical sorter that separates high-density polyethylene (HDPE) based on color. The remaining materials in the stream are sent to a  magnet  and  eddy  current  separator  to  recover  the  ferrous  and aluminum  materials,  respectively.  The  remaining  stream  is  sent  for manual sorting, where pickers recover other valuable commodities in the stream. The residuals, which represent a mix of all the materials that cannot be separated, are sent to a landfill.

The material and energy balance of the MRF is modeled based on the design described in Pressley et al.(2015). The mass of the recovered material is calculated by multiplying the mass of the waste material by the recovery equipment ' s  accuracy, shown in table S1 in the SI. The model estimates the electricity consumption of each piece of equipment based on its motor rating and maximum throughput using Eq (1).

Ej = e MaxMotor j * f MC j m MTP j * f MTP j (1)

Where:

Ej  is the electricity consumption of equipment j in kWh/t of waste input.

ej MaxMotor is the rated motor capacity,

f j MC is the fraction of motor capacity utilized,

mj MTP is the maximum throughput of equipment j, and.

f j MTP is the fraction of the equipment capacity used.

The electricity model assumes a linear relationship between the mass of the waste stream processed through each piece of equipment and the electricity  consumption.  The  limitation  of  this  assumption  is  that  it generalizes that all equipment ' s efficiency is constant across all loads; electricity consumption is directly proportional to load. However, some studies have shown that motor efficiencies vary with load (Burt et al., 2008; Li et al., 2015). Therefore, some equipment ' s  electricity  usage does  not  have  a  linear  relationship  with  the  mass  of  materials  they process.

In this work, we use NPV as our primary economic indicator, which is estimated based on discounted cash flows of the MRF throughout its lifetime. We derive NPV as the difference between the present value of cash inflow and the facility ' s cash outflow over its lifetime ( ˇ Zi ˇ zlavský, 2014). NPV is a common metric used in evaluating the profitability of an investment. This study employs NPV because it facilitates comparisons across  multiple  products,  unlike  the  minimum  product  selling  price (MPSP), and over a broader range of profitability measures than the return on investment (ROI), which is challenging to interpret when the NPV is negative.

text: The TEA employs n th plant assumptions (Meyer et al., 2020; Olafa sakin et al., 2021). The n th plant assumption assumes that the technology is mature, well-understood, and similar facilities have been built and are operating. It also implies that all technological breakthroughs needed for reliable and seamless facility operations have been accomplished. This is a realistic assumption as more than 335 MRFs are operating in the U.S. with similar equipment used in this analysis (Partnership, 2022). The study assumes that the cost of the MRF is financed through 40% equity and a 60% loan with a ten-year debt financing term at a 10% interest rate. The TEA estimates the NPV of the MRF, assuming a 10% internal rate of return (IRR) over 20-year plant life. The planning and construction period is assumed to be three years, and the start-up time is six months. All the financial assumptions we made for conducting the TEA are shown in Table 1.

text: LCA is a practical and widely accepted methodology for estimating the  health  and  environmental  impact  of  a  product  system  from  raw material  extraction  through  production,  consumption,  and  disposal/ recycling of the final product(s) (Finkbeiner et al., 2006). This study uses the LCA method, following the ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 framework (Finkbeiner et al., 2006), to assess the health and environmental impacts of processing one t of waste as delivered to the MRF, which is defined as the functional unit. The system boundaries are from cradle-to-gate. The system includes all activities within the MRF, and impacts related to upstream  energy  production  and  material  inputs  used  at  the  MRF (Fig.  3).  The  study  assumed  a  zero-burden  approach  for  the  waste received at the MRF, meaning that the environmental burdens associ ated with the production and use of the recovered waste materials before collection and transportation to the MRF are excluded. The zero-burden approach is a standard practice in solid waste management LCA (Voss et al., 2021). The cradle-to-gate scope covers all processes such as waste collection  and  transportation,  equipment  and  office  electricity  con sumption, rolling stock and conveyor diesel consumption, and waste residue disposal.

LCA is a practical and widely accepted methodology for estimating the  health  and  environmental  impact  of  a  product  system  from  raw material  extraction  through  production,  consumption,  and  disposal/ recycling of the final product(s) (Finkbeiner et al., 2006). This study uses the LCA method, following the ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 framework (Finkbeiner et al., 2006), to assess the health and environmental impacts of processing one t of waste as delivered to the MRF, which is defined as the functional unit. The system boundaries are from cradle-to-gate. The system includes all activities within the MRF, and impacts related to upstream  energy  production  and  material  inputs  used  at  the  MRF (Fig.  3).  The  study  assumed  a  zero-burden  approach  for  the  waste received at the MRF, meaning that the environmental burdens associ ated with the production and use of the recovered waste materials before collection and transportation to the MRF are excluded. The zero-burden approach is a standard practice in solid waste management LCA (Voss et al., 2021). The cradle-to-gate scope covers all processes such as waste collection  and  transportation,  equipment  and  office  electricity  con sumption, rolling stock and conveyor diesel consumption, and waste residue disposal.

text: MRF will be repurposed and used in place of virgin materials. Avoided emissions  account  for  the  impacts  of  displacing  materials  by  MRF products in the market. This LCA approach is also known as the system expansion  or  substitution  method.  The  study  employs  the  OpenLCA (OpenLCA,  2022)  software  to  analyze  the  inventory  data  using  the United States Life Cycle Inventory Database (USLCI) (NREL, 2012). The study did not include the embodied emissions and decommissioning of the facility. McKinsey and Company reported that 24% of emissions of a process come from embodied emissions in the building, while 76% come from energy used for cooling and heating. In an industrial facility, where electricity for heating and cooling represents a small amount of the total energy needed, embodied emissions are significantly smaller than 24%. They can be negligible compared to total emissions. Table S5 in the SI shows the life cycle inventory data as collected from OpenLCA.

text: Environmental and health impacts can be evaluated at the midpoint or  endpoint  level  using  various  life  cycle  impact  assessment  (LCIA) methods. Commonly used LCIA methods include ReCiPe, CML 2002, and eco-indicators (Al-Salem et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2019; Gu et al., 2017). This  analysis  employs  the  Tool  for  Reduction  and  Assessment  of Chemicals  and  Other  Environmental  Impacts  (TRACI)  impact  assess ment  method  at  the  midpoint  impact  assessment  level.  The  TRACI method is representative of U.S. conditions, and it groups the impact categories into environmental and human health impacts. The evaluated environmental impacts with TRACI include 100-year global warming potential (GWP) in kg CO2-eq, acidification potential (AP) in H + -eq, eutrophication potential (EP) in kg N, ecotoxicity (ETP) in kg 2,4-D-eq, ozone depletion (ODP) in CFC-11-eq, and photochemical oxidation (PO) in kg NOx-eq. The human health impacts include carcinogenic (Ca) in kg benzene eq and non-carcinogenic (NCa) in kg toluene eq. Table S4 in SI shows the emission factors used in this study.

text: Sensitivity analysis is a methodology employed to assess the vari ability of a model ' s output to critical model input parameters when each parameter is altered, and other variables are kept constant. Sensitivity analysis is used in this study to identify the parameters (changed by ± 30%) that most influence NPV and LCA impact assessment categories. For NPV, the changed variables are operating hours, waste tipping fee, total fixed capital investment cost, diesel consumption, residue disposal cost, and electricity consumption. Due to the high variability of waste composition and PCRM market prices, the study evaluates the NPV ' s sensitivity to variation in waste composition and recovered materials selling prices. The critical parameters varied for LCA impact categories include  diesel,  electricity,  baling  wire,  transportation,  and  waste composition. Table S5 in SI shows the sensitivity analysis variables for the base, optimistic, and lower cases.

text: The cost  for  a  120,000  t/y  single-stream  MRF  is  estimated  to  be $23.13 MM. This capital cost is in the range of $22.4 MM -$29.4 MM reported  in  the  literature  (Cimpan  et  al.,  2016;  Logan  City  Council, 2018; Pressley et al., 2015). An MRF feasibility report carried out by the Logan city council, Iowa, estimated the capital cost of a 60,000 t MRF which  services  about  93,000  households  as  $29.4  MM  (Logan  City Council, 2018), while Cimpan et al. (2016) estimated the capital cost of building an MRF could range from $7.42 MM for a 25,000 t/y facility to $22.4 MM for a 100,000 t/y MRF (Cimpan et al., 2016). The capital cost recorded in this study is similar to the values recorded by Cimpan et al. (2016). The slight difference could be attributed to the difference in facility size. Logan city MRF and the MRF modeled in this study have similar operating capacities per hour, the main difference being that the Logan city facility only operates one shift daily. However, the significant $6 MM difference in the capital cost is found to be attributed to the disparity in the equipment cost reported in this study and the Logan MRF report (Logan City Council, 2018). The Logan MRF report did not break down the equipment cost to allow for further investigation.

text:
The operating cost, capital cost, and revenue were used in a DCFROR analysis to estimate the NPV of the facility across the 20 years lifetime. Fig. 4a shows the NPV for the four waste streams. The NPV recorded for the U.S. EPA average waste stream showed a net present value of $59 MM. The TEA model resulted in an NPV value of $3.57 MM, $30.54 MM, and $43.39 MM for Seattle, Oregon, and Pennsylvania ' s waste compo sitions. The difference in NPV is because of the revenue generated from the different waste streams. Fig. 4b shows that the U.S. EPA, Oregon, and Pennsylvania  composition  generates  more  revenue  than  the  Seattle waste stream. Seattle generates the lowest revenue because the waste composition has high glass, OCC, and non-OCC fibers, which sell for lower  prices.  Whereas  the  other  waste  streams  have  more  valuable materials like aluminum and plastics. Glass increases the operating cost because of the high electricity required for sorting glass but contributes less  to  the  revenue,  hence,  reducing  the  NPV  of  the  system.  Plastics improve the MRF ' s economic viability but are a small component of the waste  streams  recovered  in  the  MRFs.  However,  the  NPV  (Fig.  4a) showed that the MRF is profitable for the four waste streams considered in this study.

text: The LCA shows that the 100-year global warming potential (GWP) for processing the various waste streams ranges from 5.98 to 8.53 kg CO2-eq /t of waste, with the Pennsylvania waste stream yielding the highest and Oregon the lowest emissions. Processing the U.S. EPA waste stream through the MRF resulted in 7.20 kg CO2-eq /t of waste emis sions. These  values are  smaller  than  those  recorded  when the waste streams ' GWP was evaluated using the average U.S. electricity mix. For Oregon and Seattle, hydroelectricity forms a significant per centage of the energy sources, reducing its GWP emission factors to 0.15 and 0.10 kg CO2-eq/ kWh, respectively. The range of emissions reported in this study is lower when compared to landfilling emissions of 15.02 kg CO2-eq/t of mixed plastic waste and 1552.6 kg CO2-eq/t of mixed paper waste reported in (Demetrious & Crossin, 2019).

text: The  range  of  the  GWP  recorded  both  by  using  the  average  U.S. electricity mix, and individual state ' s electricity mix is similar to the one recorded by Smith et al., (2022) where they reported a GWP of 8.58 kg CO2-eq/t of waste. They used average values from various studies for electricity, diesel, and baling wire requirements to arrive at the emission value (Smith et al., 2022). Fitzgerald et al. (2012) reported emissions of 11.07 kg CO2-eq /t of waste processed. The difference in these reported emissions  and  those  of  Fitzgerald  et  al.  (2012)  can  be  attributed  to assuming  that  more  energy-efficient lighting  and  equipment  are employed in the facilities. In rare scenarios where the PCRM from an MRF can replace virgin materials in the economy without secondary processing, the potential environmental savings are shown in Fig. 5 and Table S10, with GWP ranging from 1388 to 1809 kg CO2 eq. However, when  secondary  processing  of  the  PCRM  is  considered,  the  savings ranged from 656 kg CO2 eq for U.S. EPA stream to 1,040 kg CO2 eq for the Pennsylvania waste stream. Compared to emissions reported for alternative waste management strategies such as waste-to-energy (-36 to 40 kg CO2-eq /M.T. of waste), recovering waste in the MRF is a more environmentally friendly approach from a GWP perspective. In-depth analysis of secondary processing is beyond the scope of this study but discussions on substitution ratios and GWP data can be found in section 3.2 in SI. Also, information on the contributions of electricity, diesel, baling wire, and collection and transportation to all impact categories can be found in section 3.2 in SI.

text: U.S. EPA waste stream to key parameters, waste composition, and postconsumer  recovered  material  prices.  The  plant  capacity,  total  fixed capital cost, and waste tipping fee had the most impact on the NPV of the MRF. A 30% increase in the plant capacity can increase the NPV from $58.95 MM to $90 MM, while a 30% decrease in plant capacity can result in an NPV lower than $30 MM. Baling wire, diesel, waste disposal, and electricity costs show little effect on the NPV. Figure S6 in the S.I. shows the sensitivity analysis results for Oregon, Seattle, and Pennsyl vania ' s  waste  streams  to  key  parameters.  The  figures  show  similar sensitivity results to the U.S. EPA waste composition. However, the NPV in  Seattle ' s  waste  stream  resulted  in  a  negative  NPV  with  a  30% reduction in the most impactful parameters. This is due to the revenue generated from the Seattle waste stream being smaller than the other waste  streams.  Other  parameters  that  can  largely  influence  the  NPV include total fixed capital cost and waste tipping fees. A ± 30% change in the selling prices of OCC and Non-OCC fiber can result in a large change in the NPV in the U.S. EPA waste stream scenario because OCC and  Non-OCC  represent  about  70%  of  the  total  waste  composition. Aluminum represents about 2.6% of the U.S. EPA waste, but due to its high selling price, the NPV is very sensitive to variation in its compo sition and prices. Figure S7 and figure S8 in SI show the NPV sensitivity to  waste  composition and market price analysis results for the other waste streams considered in this study. The results show similar trends, with materials dominating the waste composition and materials with high selling prices significantly affecting the NPV.
