We then sampled representative oligomer structures (referred to as conformers) from the MD trajectories based on two structural parameters: the radius of gyration ( R g) and the solvent-accessible surface area (SASA). Sampling conformers that cover a range values of these two parameters can provide reliable input for COSMO-RS solubility estimations. 33,39 We thus selected conformers by superimposing a square grid over the two-dimensional R g-SASA scatter plot and choosing conformers closest to grid intersections following our previous work. 33 The number of sampled conformers for each polymer is listed in Table 1. The selected conformers were input to density functional theory (DFT) calculations to obtain screening charge densities (COSMO files). The DFT calculations included a geometry optimization in implicit water using the conductor-like polarizable continuum model and a singlepoint calculation in the infinite dielectric constant limit. These DFT calculations were performed with Gaussian 16 at the BVP86/TZVP/DGA1 level of theory. 40 Precalculated COSMO files for the solvents were obtained from the database COSMObase-1901-BP-TZVP.

COSMO files from the DFT calculations were input to COSMO-RS for solubility calculations. COSMO-RS predicts the thermodynamic properties of multicomponent systems based on quantum mechanical calculations and statistical thermodynamics methods. 41,42 The chemical properties of each molecule are represented by the probability distribution of the screening charge densities (called the σ -profile). σ -Profiles of all oligomer conformations with deactivated terminal groups were used to approximate the σ -profile of the corresponding polymer. 43 The σ -profiles were then used to calculate the chemical potential of the polymer to enable predictions of solubility via a solid -liquid equilibrium calculation. 44 This calculation requires the polymer melting temperature and an experimentally measured solubility as reference input. Table 1 shows the reference experimental solubilities used in this work (measured following the methods described below). Melting temperatures were taken from literature sources. 45,46 All COSMO-RS calculations were performed using the COSMOtherm 19 software with the BP_TZVP_19 parameterization. 47 -49

text: Experimental solubility measurements for all eight polymers in multiple solvents were performed to calibrate and validate the computational solubility predictions. PP (isotactic, weightaverage molecular weight ∼ 12 000, number-average molecular weight ∼ 5000) and PVC (high molecular weight) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St Louis, Missouri, USA). PS was purchased from Goodfellow Cambridge Ltd (Huntingdon, UK). Low density PE (DOW ™ 608A), EVOH (32 mol% ethylene content, CCP EV3251), PET (DAK Americas Laser+® C 9921), nylon 6 (BASF Ultramid® B36), and nylon 66 (DuPont Zytel® FG42A) resins were purchased and provided by Amcor Flexibles. These resins were selected because they are used commonly in industry and by major manufacturers. 11,22 Consequently, we expect their solubilities to be representative of the solubilities of components of common commercial plastic materials. Each polymer was separately dissolved in a reference solvent to support the creation of the computational solubility database. To validate computational predictions, each polymer was also dissolved in predicted good and nonsolvents.

Experiments to measure individual polymer solubilities were performed in a three-necked 100 mL round bottom flask which was equipped with a reflux condenser, a thermometer, and a glass stopper. Approximately 40 g solvent and a magnetic stir bar were put into the flask, which was then immersed in a 1000 mL silicon oil bath with continuous agitation and heated to the target temperature. When the target temperature was reached, 1 wt% (with respect to the solvent mass) of polymer resin was added into the heated solvent and the solvent and polymer were stirred for 0.5 h to permit dissolution. If the polymer resin dissolved completely, another 1 wt% of polymer resin was added, and the above process was repeated until no further resin could be dissolved after 0.5 h mixing. The undissolved resin was filtered from the solvent, washed with DI water, dried in a vacuum oven at 100 °C for 3 h, and weighed to determine its mass after drying. The solubility was then computed as shown in eqn (1).

Solubility wt % ð Þ ¼ Addedpolymermass � undissolved polymer mass massof solution -100 % ð 1 Þ

It should be noted that for some polymer resins, the solubility is regarded as a lower limit because the high viscosity of the solution at the measured value inhibited further dissolution. More details regarding experimental procedures are available in the ESI. †

Physical mixtures of polymers were experimentally separated by sequential dissolution to show the feasibility of our polymer separation strategies. Three polymer mixtures were studied, including a PE/PS mixture, PET/PVC mixture, and PP/EVOH/PET mixture. Around 3 g of the desired mixtures (with a 1 : 1 mass ratio for the 2-component mixtures and 1 : 1 : 1 mass ratio for the 3-component mixture) were added into ∼ 30 g of the selected solvents in a round bottom flask and heated to the desired temperature under stirring using a 1000 mL silicon oil bath. After 1 h dissolution, the flask was removed from the oil bath and emptied into a 250 mL beaker using a hot stainless wire cloth as the filter. The undissolved polymer was collected from the surface of stainless wire cloth and washed with DI water. A same amount of the non-solvent (if applicable) was added into the beaker to precipitate the dissolved polymer. The precipitated polymer was filtered with a Büchner funnel. Both dissolved and undissolved polymers were dried at 100 °C for 3 h in a vacuum oven. The mass balance was calculated based on the mass of dried polymers. For the 3-component mixture, the aforementioned dissolution step was repeated twice with di ff erent solvents.

Creation of the polymer solubility database

text: We developed a database of computationally predicted polymer solubilities following the approach detailed in the Methods section. We modeled polymers as short oligomers, performed MD simulations of these oligomers in dilute solution to obtain various chain configurations, selected 20 -31 conformers from the MD trajectories for each polymer (Table 1), and calculated screening charges for each of these conformers. 33 Fig. 2 shows some example conformers sampled from the MD simulations following this approach and their corresponding screening charge densities. Screening charge densities serve as the input to solid -liquid equilibrium calculations using COSMO-RS to evaluate polymer solubilities in various solvents. Solubilities were calculated for each polymer -solvent system at room temperature (RT) and a higher temperature (Th) because solubilities generally increase with temperature. The higher temperature is determined by the boiling point of the solvent: if the boiling point is greater than 120 °C, Th = 120 °C; otherwise, Th was selected as the temperature 1 °C lower than the boiling point. The upper bound on temperature enables calculations of polymer solubility at elevated temperatures while avoiding temperatures that are too high, which may lead to melting or thermal degradation and thereby influence the properties of the recovered materials. 45,50 Using this approach, we performed large-scale solubility predictions for 8 polymers and 1007 solvents at both temperatures, establishing a solubility database with over 16 000 data points. Table 2 shows some selected results from these solubility predictions for 25 common polymer -solvent systems. The complete database is available in the ESI. †

text: Table 3 summarizes the polymer -solvent systems and compares solubilities measured experimentally and predicted computationally. There are 2 experiments (nylon 6 and nylon 66 in DMF) for which accurate solubilities could not be measured due to the retention of the (good) solvent in the polymer. These values thus qualitatively support the prediction of high solubility, but numerical solubilities are not provided in the table. Among the 14 systems that have available experimental data points, 11 of them demonstrate good agreement between computations and experiments with the average absolute di ff erence between predicted and experimental solubilities equal to 1.3 wt%. Two systems (PP in THP and PS in THF) have acceptable accuracy, as the computational predictions correctly identify good/non-solvents but exhibit some deviations from experimental data. Only 1 system (PET in DMF) has a computational result that is qualitatively inconsistent with the experiment. In this system, DMF was predicted to be a good solvent for PET but proved to be a non-solvent experimentally. However, we note that PET is known to be challenging to dissolve and that it is possible that kinetic e ff ects associated with a slow rate of dissolution could inhibit accurate solubility measurements. 51,52 Overall, the experimental verification of the database identified 11/14 good, 2/14 acceptable, and 1/14 incorrect predictions. This overall good agreement between computational and experimental solubilities validates the suitability of the solubility database for further investigation.

text: Based on the large-scale solubility prediction results, we next analyzed the complete set of solvents to identify sets of good and non-solvents for each polymer by rank-ordering predicted solubilities. To provide heuristics regarding the feasibility of dissolving di ff erent polymers, we first defined a set of ' top ' solvents for each polymer. Here, we define the top solvents as the top 5% of all solvents ranked by solubility. The statistics of these solvents gives a general idea of the di ffi culty to dissolve each polymer. Fig. 3 shows the distributions of polymer solubilities in their top solvents at room temperature and at elevated temperatures. As expected, polymer solubilities are mostly low at room temperature and increase at higher temperatures. Accordingly, dissolution-based recycling processes typically dissolve the resins in a heated solvent and precipitate in a cooled system. 22 For example, Fig. 3 indicates that there are very few good solvents for PE at room temperature but such solvents are easy to identify at higher temperatures. As a comparison, PET, nylon 6 and nylon 66 have relatively low solubilities even in their high-temperature top solvents. This comparison indicates that the dissolution of PET and nylons can be challenging in general, and if possible, dissolution-based recycling processes should be designed to avoid dissolving these components. Indeed, we have recently developed STRAP processes for multilayer plastic films containing PET which was often the last in the separation sequence and thus was recovered as a residual solid without being dissolved. 11,22

text: The solubility database can also provide chemical heuristics on polymer dissolution. To study the general relationship between the molecular structures of polymers and solvents, we analyzed the occurrence of di ff erent functional groups in the top solvents of each polymer. For this comparison, we define the top solvents of a polymer as those within the top 10% of all solvents ranked by solubility while also having a minimum solubility of 5 wt% at any temperature. The 5 wt% threshold is to guarantee that the set of top solvents only includes solvents with appreciable solubility values. We then performed functional group analysis for these solvents based on their molecular structures and assign each solvent to one or more classes based on their functional groups. For example, toluene is considered to be part of the ' aromatic ' class and glycol is considered part of the ' alcohol ' class. This analysis was performed with SMILES string representation of molecules and SMARTS substructure matching syntax via RDKit. 53 -55

These solvent class rankings provide a general solvent selection guide for polymer dissolution and can also serve to guide the selection or design of new solvent systems with tuned chemical moieties. However, we note that these ranking results do not assert any absolute conclusion such as which class is always better for dissolution, since ranking classes by what percentage of the top solvents are in each class is not su ffi ciently comprehensive. For example, the aromatic class ranks quite high for multiple polymers, which can be partially attributed to the fact that it is the most common class (23%) in the solvent library.

text: A typical STRAP process employs a sequential series of solvent washes with each solvent selected to selectively dissolve a target polymer from the mixture. An important consideration in designing such a process is the sequence in which polymers are dissolved and separated because di ff erent separation sequences for the same mixture of polymers lead to di ff erent requirements for selectivity. For example, a STRAP process involving sequential dissolution of each component of mixed plastic waste containing 3 polymers can have 6 possible sequences. As noted above, each sequence can impact the selection of solvents ( e.g. , by leading to a small number of possible options for sequences that target hard-to-dissolve polymers first) and similarly influence process economics and life cycle metrics.

text: To guide the design of dissolution-based plastic recycling processes and automate solvent screening, we developed a tool to generate all possible sequence and screen suitable solvents for each solvent based on the computational solubility predictions. Fig. 4 shows an example of generating separation sequences for a polymer mixture containing PE, EVOH and PET, which are the constituents of a multilayer plastic packaging film studied in our previous work. 11 The tool first generates all 6 possible separation sequences for the polymer mixture under the assumption that only one polymer is to be selectively dissolved in each step. It then provides ranked lists of solvent candidates for all steps in all separation sequences. For example, in the first separation sequence, EVOH is the first polymer to be dissolved, PE is the second, and PET is then recovered as a residual component that is not dissolved because solvents for its dissolution are rare (Fig. 3). Step 1 of this sequence requires a solvent that selectively dissolves EVOH but not PE or PET and Step 2 requires a solvent that dissolves PE but not PET. A few top-ranked solvents for each of these steps are shown in Fig. 4 as an example. This ranking is based on the solubility di ff erence between the target polymer and other polymers; detailed criteria are available in the ESI. † Each separation sequence has its own selectivity requirements and therefore leads to di ff erent sets of eligible solvents. Some separation sequences will have a wide range of solvent candidates, while some sequences have few possible solvents ( e.g. , when a rarely soluble polymer like PET is the first in the sequence). Our program can thus provide results as input for process simulation and technoeconomic analysis to compare and determine suitable separation sequences and selective solvents. Below, we further demonstrate the applicability of this tool in several experimental case studies.

text:
Experimental case studies: separation of binary polymer mixtures

To demonstrate the applicability of our computational approaches in dissolution-based polymer recycling, we perform case studies on the experimental separation of several physical mixtures of polymers. These mixtures include PE/PS, PVC/PET and a 3-component mixture of EVOH/PP/PET which are representative of common real-world plastic products or application scenarios. For example, PE/PS is the composition of a commercial laminated plastic sheet, 56 the PVC/PET mixture represents a typical separation challenge in water bottle recycling processes where PVC is often a contaminant in PET, 57,58 and EVOH/PP/PET can be made into a food packaging material. 59 We use physical mixtures for these case studies to ensure that the system composition is controlled. Our past studies of multilayer plastic packaging materials have demonstrated that computational tools for solubility prediction can be applied to more realistic plastic materials. 11,22,23 We note that the time required for the dissolution of physical mixtures may di ff er from that of manufactured plastic materials ( e.g. , multilayer films) that may have components in nanoscale contact, but we focus only on solubility as opposed to dissolution kinetics in this work.

Fig. 4 An example of generating separation sequences for polymer mixtures.

text: In these case studies, we first select solvents and dissolution temperatures for di ff erent mixtures and separation sequences based on computational solubility predictions. To achieve selective dissolution, solvents are selected to have a high solubility for the target polymer and a low solubility for the other polymers in the mixture. As in the prior validation experiments, we preferentially select common laboratory solvents (even if they are not optimal according to computational predictions) to avoid concerns with toxicity. We then conduct experiments to perform the separation of polymers. The separation result is evaluated by the yield and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) of virgin and recovered resins to confirm resin purity.

text: The PE/PS mixture is separated in two di ff erent sequences. In the first sequence (PE → PS), dodecane at 120 °C is used to selectively dissolve PE but not PS. After 1 h of dissolution, the solid PS is separated by filtering it from the liquid solution of PE. Isopropyl alcohol is then added as a non-solvent ( i.e. , a solvent with low predicted solubility for the target polymer) to precipitate the PE. Fig. 5 shows photos and FTIR spectra of the virgin and recovered resins. The physical morphologies of the recovered resins change due to the dissolution and precipitation processes, as shown in the photos; the PE resin changes from pellets to flakes while the PS resin changes from a powder to a chunk. However, the FTIR spectra of the recovered resins are highly consistent with the virgin ones, indicating that the chemical structures of the polymers remain una ff ected and that the recovered resins each contain a single polymer component as expected. The yields of the recovered PE and PS are 99.18% and 99.96%, respectively. In the other separation sequence, ethyl acetate is used to selectively dissolve PS, and isopropyl alcohol is used for precipitation. Changing the order of dissolution leads to di ff erent yields of 100.21% of PE and 93.84% of PS (Table 5). FTIR analysis further indicates that the recovered resins are similar to the virgin resins (ESI Fig. S3 † ). This example shows how separation sequence impacts the performance of the dissolution-based recycling process.

Experimental case study: separation of ternary polymer mixtures

text: For the 3-component mixture (EVOH/PP/PET), we first study the separation sequence EVOH → PP → PET, in which ethylene glycol (EG) is used as an EVOH-selective solvent in the first step, then tetrahydropyran (THP) is used as the PP-selective solvent in the second step. With this sequence, it was found that the yield of PP is low (78.3%) and we observe an undissolved solid which clearly di ff ers from the PET resin. Photos and FTIR spectra of the undissolved solid are included in the ESI. † The FTIR spectra suggest that the undissolved solid is a mixture of PP and EVOH. We speculate that some EVOH and PP agglomerate in the presence of EG at the first step and remain undissolved throughout the remaining selective dissolution process. Therefore, a di ff erent separation sequence (PP → EVOH → PET) was tested with the same solvents and temperatures. In this sequence, PP is the first to be separated to avoid its contact with EG. With this sequence, we observe no undissolved solid and the yields for all three polymers are excellent (>94%, Table 5). This example shows how unexpected e ff ects can arise during selective dissolution processes to further demonstrate the value of assessing alternative separation sequences.

text: There are multiple other possible separation sequences for this 3-polymer mixture EVOH/PP/PET. We did not test all sequences experimentally, but instead propose some applicable solvent selections here. Table 6 presents four more separation strategies for this polymer mixture. In these strategies, we specifically focus on enabling temperature-controlled precipitation, in which a target polymer is dissolved at a high temperature and precipitated at a low temperature (as opposed to being precipitated through addition of a non-solvent). Temperature-controlled precipitation has been shown to be preferred in STRAP processes based on prior technoeconomic analysis. 17,22 We selected solvents from those that satisfy the following rules: the predicted solubility of the polymer to be dissolved must be greater than 5 wt% while the solubility of other polymers must be lower than 3 wt%, the di ff erence in the predicted solubilities must be greater than 5 wt% to achieve selectivity, and the predicted solubility of the dissolved polymer at room temperature must be 80% lower than its solubility at high temperature to assure the feasibility of temperature-controlled precipitation. Fig. 6 provides an illustrative example of the workflow of the first proposed separation strategy, in which EVOH is first dissolved in resorcinol and PET is then dissolved in pyrrole. These examples demonstrate the capability of the computational methods to rapidly generate potential separation sequences for further evaluation experimentally or as input for further technoeconomic/life cycle analysis.

Conclusions

text: In this work, we established a computational workflow for guiding the design of dissolution-based polymer recycling processes using large-scale, temperature-dependent polymer solubility predictions. Our method integrates MD simulations, conformational sampling, COSMO-RS calculations, as well as experimental calibration. Using MD simulations, we modeled polymers as oligomers in dilute solution and selected representative conformers from the resulting MD trajectories. These conformers, along with an experimentally measured solubility in a reference solvent, were input to COSMO-RS solid -liquid equilibrium calculations to predict polymer solubilities in numerous solvents. We established a solubility database for 8 polymers and 1007 solvents at multiple temperatures and experimentally verified computational predictions for a selected subset of systems. Based on the database, we studied the relationship between polymers and their top solvents via functional group analysis of solvent molecular structures. We further developed a computational tool to automatically select suitable solvents for sequential selective dissolution-based plastic recycling processes (like the STRAP process) while evaluating all possible separation sequences. We demonstrated the applicability of the method using multiple experimental case studies in which physical mixtures of polymers were successfully separated via sequential selective dissolution. This computational approach thus has promise for guiding the design of STRAP processes for multicomponent plastic waste, and could further be used to optimize existing STRAP processes by selecting alternative solvents ( e.g. , green solvents).

text:
While the approach in this work was demonstrated for sequential selective dissolution processes in which only one polymer was dissolved at each step, future work will continue to develop a combinatorial optimization model that allows for the dissolution of multiple polymers at a time in order to search for the best separation sequence of a STRAP process. The model will also account for factors such as the densities of solvents and the percentage of each polymer in the waste stream when considering challenges that may be faced while scaling up dissolution-based processes. We will further combine these models with technoeconomic analysis and lifecycle assessment tools to evaluate the comprehensive impact of solvents and identify tradeo ff s between possible separation sequences, which will facilitate the design of economically feasible and environmentally friendly STRAP processes. Finally, we envision further expanding the database to consider new classes of green or designer solvents with potential value in polymer dissolution, such as ionic liquids or deep eutectic solvents. 62,63

ABSTRACT: Disposal of textile waste is a growing concern in terms of environmental pollution. Especially, blends of different fibers such as polycotton render recycling of textile wastes difficult, which contributes to low recycling rates in the textile industry. The separation of polycotton into polyester and cotton can enable the recycling of these blended textiles. The selective dissolution of cotton using a switchable solvent system consisting of 1,8 -diazabicyclo [5.4.0]undec -7 -ene (DBU), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and carbon dioxide is investigated. After the separation of cellulose from polyester, upon addition of ethanol, cotton precipitates, which allows for facile Supporting Information

removal from the solvent system. Extraction at 40 °C and 5 bar CO2 is feasible for full separation of the constituents of polycotton without degradation of the polyester component, as identified by thermal gravimetric analyses, infrared spectroscopy, size-exclusion chromatography, and scanning electron microscopy of the extracted textiles.

■ INTRODUCTION

In the last 20 years, the production of clothing and textiles has risen sharply and will continue to grow. In addition, the average duration of time a piece of clothing is worn by the customer is decreasing. 1 -3 Both aspects are inevitably associated with a growing amount of textile waste. Around 73% of the waste is incinerated or landfilled instead of being recycled, which poses particularly severe problems in urban environments, where landfilling space is limited. 1,4 Moreover, less than 1% of textile waste is recycled with the aim of producing new clothes. 1,3 In addition, textile waste is often a heterogeneous and complex waste stream, consisting of different types of textile materials and many additives, such as coatings, prints, and processing chemicals like dyes and finishes. 5 The most widely used textiles worldwide are polyesters and cotton, with market shares of more than 50% and of 22%, respectively. Polyesters mostly consist of poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET). Frequently, polyesters and cotton are used as interwoven blends, so-called polycotton. 1,5 In order to enable efficient recycling and reuse, separation of polyester and cotton is advisable.

text:
Several strategies for the recycling of textiles in general were reported, which encompass mechanical, thermomechanical, thermochemical, chemical, and biochemical processes at different technical readiness levels. For the separation of polycotton, chemical recycling was suggested to be superior to mechanical recycling. 5 -8 Examples were provided for the removal of one type of fiber due to degradation, whereas the other component remains unchanged. Kirstein et al. reported the separation of polycotton through alkaline hydrolysis of PET using sodium hydroxide. 9 The cotton component obtained is not degraded and can be recycled afterward. 9,10

An alternative approach comprises degradation of cotton and subsequent recovery of the residual polyester. 11 To avoid degradation of one of the components and to allow for the reuse of both components, special solvent systems selectively dissolving one of the components are needed to separate PET and cotton. Since PET is inert to the majority of organic solvents, its dissolution requires harsh conditions or toxic solvents such as N -methyl -2 -pyrrolidone or phenols. 12,13

As an alternative, the use of a so-called switchable solvent system under mild process conditions is attractive. A switchable solvent allows for a facile change of the solvent properties due to the addition or removal of one component. A classical system reported by Jessop et al. is a mixture of hexanol and 1,8 -diazabicyclo [5.4.0]undec -7 -ene. The polarity can be switched through the addition CO2. The change is reverted by purging with nitrogen and, thus, replacing CO 2 . 17,18

With respect to cellulose, a system consisting of a strong base such as 1,8 -diazabicyclo [5.4.0]undec -7 -ene (DBU), DMSO, and CO2 was applied for dissolution, processing, and modification of cellulose. 7,8,19 -32 Typically, the dissolution of cellulose in the switchable solvent affords 40 to 60 °C and 1 h compared to 90 °C and 8 h in conventional ionic liquids. 19

The resulting cellulose -carbonate complex is soluble in DMSO. 22 -25,28 In the nonderivative approach (not shown), an alcohol such as ethylene glycol is carboxylated with CO2. The carbonate complex dissolves cellulose in the presence of DMSO and, upon removing CO2, cellulose is precipitated. 21,25,26 Alternately, the cellulose is precipitated by adding the cellulose solution to a precipitation bath of water or alcohols. 27,29 So far, this solvent system has mainly been used to modify the cellulose or to prepare films, membranes, fibers, or aerogels from regenerated cellulose. 7,8,19 -32 The recovery of the precipitant, DMSO, and DBU was proven feasible by Wolfs and Meier. 23

So far, the DBU/CO2/DMSO system has not been applied for the separation of cellulose from textile blends. Here, the feasibility of the solvent system for the selective extraction of cotton from polycotton in batch mode is reported. Compared to conventional ILs, it is expected that lower temperatures and shorter times are required. 20

text: Extraction Procedure. Extractions were carried out in a 100 mL pressure reactor from Bu chi, which was heated to 40 °C using a Julabo thermostat. The textile was cut into pieces with edge lengths of approximately 2.5 cm × 3 cm. In a typical extraction, a textile fraction of 1 wt % with respect to DMSO was used. Thirty milliliters (33 g) of DMSO and the required amount of DBU were added into the reactor under a nitrogen atmosphere using syringes to limit contact with air, since DBU and DMSO are hygroscopic. The composition of each extraction mixture and the corresponding extraction times are given in Table S1 of the Supporting Information. The weight percentage of DBU is given with respect to DMSO, which is also used in the remainder of the text. The textile samples were placed in the reactor, twice flushed with 5 bar CO 2 , and thereafter, a pressure of 5 bar CO 2 was applied for extraction. Upon starting the stirrer, the extraction time was measured. A stirring rate of 100 rounds per minute (rpm) was used. After the selected extraction time, the stirrer was stopped and the pressure was slowly released. The reactor was opened, and the content was poured through a sieve with a mesh size of 1 mm into 250 mL of ethanol serving as a precipitation bath. The recovered textile pieces were washed with 10 mL of DMSO. Then, the residual textile was extracted for a second time under identical conditions. Fresh DMSO and DBU were used. After the second extraction, the residual textile sample was filtered off and returned into the reactor with 30 mL DMSO. At 40 °C and 5 bar CO2 pressure, the mixture was stirred for 30 min to rinse off the remaining solubilized cellulose. Then, the textiles were filtered off through the sieve and subsequently washed with ethanol several times. After air-drying, the composition of the residual textile was determined using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The cellulose from the precipitation bath was filtered off the next day and washed 3 times with 100 mL of ethanol each time. Thus, in total, a volume of 300 mL of ethanol was used. Then, the cellulose was air-dried for several days.

Analytical Methods. Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA). A TGA 2 instrument from Mettler Toledo was used. Nitrogen atmosphere was applied for analysis in the temperature range from 25 -800 °C. Around 100 mg of the substance was analyzed in a 900 μ L Al2O3 crucible.

ATR -FTIR. Infrared spectra were recorded using a Bruker α -T ATR -IR spectrometer in the wavenumber range from 400 to 4000 cm -1 with a resolution of 2 cm -1 . The measured spectra were baseline corrected by using OPUS 7.8 software from Bruker.

The compositions of the residual textile samples were derived from TGA analysis. For reference, the virgin material was analyzed, too. The upper part of Figure 3 presents the TGA results. For virgin polycotton, a small decrease in mass at around 100 °C is observed, which is due to the evaporation of water contained in the fabric. Further, two distinct decomposition stages are observed at 355 and 430 °C, assigned to the thermal decomposition of cellulose and PET, respectively. 28,33 -36 Figure 3A indicates that the intensity of the first step at 355 °C becomes less pronounced upon increase of the DBU content to 10 wt %. Further increase in DBU content up to 20 wt % is associated with slightly increasing intensity of the decomposition stage at 355 °C, indicating that the dissolution of cellulose is less efficient. The differentials of the TGA curves are provided for easy assessment of the decomposition stages in Figure S1 of the Supporting Information.

To quantitatively compare the different extraction results, the composition of the samples was determined from the TGA results. The weight fractions of PET and cotton in the samples were calculated according to eq 1 and 2, respectively, with the mass loss due to decomposition of cellulose ( m d,cell) and PET ( m d,PET ).

text: The resulting compositions of the residual textile samples are given in the lower part of Figure 3. A composition of 48% cotton and 52% PET was determined for the virgin material, which is in close agreement with the information provided by the supplier, stating a composition of 50% cotton and 50% PET. Extraction with 5 wt % DBU reduced the fraction of cellulose to less than 30 wt %. By increasing the DBU content, initially, the amount of cellulose extracted was enhanced, and with 10 wt % DBU, the cellulose was completely extracted. Further increase in DBU content resulted in a lowering of cellulose extraction, e.g., with 20 wt % DBU, fabrics with 19% residual cellulose were obtained. The observed decline in cellulose extraction yield for DBU contents higher than 10 wt % is in agreement with data reported by Wang et al. 24 Similar findings for 1,5-diazabicyclo(4.3.0)non-5-ene used as organic base were reported by Zhang et al. 21 It is suggested that the decrease in extraction yield is related to the organic base primarily serving as a reactant rather than a solvent. Higher DBU amounts are associated with lower fractions of the solvent DMSO, which is suggested to lead to a decrease in cellulose solubility.

Previous studies into the modification of cellulose showed that 3 mol equivalents of the organic base with respect to the repeat units of cellulose were sufficient to achieve complete dissolution of the cellulose. 23 The much higher amounts of base required for dissolution of cellulose contained in polycotton suggest that PET hinders mass transfer to the surface of the cotton fibers and may also be involved in intermolecular interactions. Thus, less base is available to carboxylate cellulose, as shown in Figure 1, which in turn is compensated for by higher DBU contents.

text: To obtain information about the composition of the residual textile samples and to verify the results of the TGA analyses, IR spectra of the extracted textiles were measured. A detailed discussion of all peaks is beyond the scope of this manuscript and is already given in, e.g., refs 25,37 -41. Figure 4 shows two sections of the spectra, with peaks being characteristic of PET and cellulose. For comparison, the spectrum of virgin PC, PET, and cellulose is also included. Figure 4A indicates that peaks at 3314 and 2886 cm -1 assigned to cellulose have noticeably lower intensities for the samples after extraction. These peaks are no longer visible in the spectrum of sample # 3, which was extracted with 10 wt % DBU. The spectra of samples # 1 to # 6 also show very weak peaks at 2986 and 2902 cm -1 being representative of PET, which are not detectable in the spectrum of the virgin PC. These findings indicate the removal of cellulose from the textile. 10 wt % DBU being most effective is in excellent agreement with the TGA results shown in Figure 3.

text: Variation of Process Conditions. With the best DBU content of 10 wt %, the influence of extraction time was investigated. For this purpose, 1 wt % polycotton was extracted in two steps, with extraction times ranging from two times 1 h to 2 times 6 h, as indicated in Table S1 (samples # 3 and # 7 to # 13). The compositions of the residual textile derived from thermogravimetric analyses are depicted in Figure S3 of the Supporting Information. Applying 2 × 1 h and 2 × 2 h resulted in a substantial decrease of the initial cellulose content to 30 and 20%, respectively. Further decrease in cellulose content was obtained with 2 × 3 h. To obtain first information on the reproducibility, the extraction was carried out 4 times under ostensibly identical conditions ( # 3 and # 9 to # 11). While in two cases, the cellulose is completely removed, in two cases, a residual cellulose fraction of around 7% is found. The differences are suggested to be due to deviating amounts of atmospheric water dissolved in DMSO, since the experiments resulting in the full removal of cellulose were carried out at roughly the same time, whereas the two experiments resulting in 7% of residual cellulose were carried out at a later time. In addition, contributions from nonperfect mixing and mass transfer limitations in the small volume of the extraction vessel cannot be excluded.

text: Investigations into the reactions of CO2 and DBU with alcohols showed that the stirring rate has a strong influence on the CO2 uptake. 42 The findings were suggested to be due to the limited mass transfer of CO2 from the gas phase into the solution. It appeared interesting to study whether the stirring rate has an influence on the system consisting of DBU, DMSO, CO2, and polycotton as well. For this purpose, experiments were carried out with 2 wt % polycotton because transfer limitations were expected to be more prominent for a higher polycotton loading. Moreover, different amounts of DBU were used, and the extraction time was 2 × 3 h. Stirring rates of 100 and 300 rpm were applied. The results of the thermogravimetric analyses given in Figure 5 indicate that the stirring rate has no substantial influence on the amount of residual cellulose in the extracted samples for all DBU contents. This finding suggests that neither the mass transfer in the system containing a solid substrate nor the accessibility of the OH groups of the cellulose fibers contained in the polycotton fiber is noticeably varied due to the modest variation in stirring rate.

If the extraction times are increased, full separation will be possible, as indicated in Figure S4. An increase in PC loading to 4 wt % led to the full removal of the cellulose under the same conditions (samples # 25 and # 26 in Table S1). text: Molar Mass Distributions of PET. Since PET dissolves readily in HFIP, the residual textile samples were analyzed with an SEC instrument using HFIP as the eluent to determine the PET molar mass distributions (MMDs). SEC analyses of cellulose were not feasible since cellulose was not soluble in either HFIP or the other solvents available as SEC eluents (tetrahydrofuran and DMAc with traces of LiBr). Therefore, the residual textile samples and the virgin material exposed to HFIP were filtered to separate the nondissolved cellulose before injection. The resulting MMDs are shown in Figures 6 and S6 -S8 of the Supporting Information. Regardless of the DBU and polycotton contents and the extraction parameters, very similar MMDs of PET were obtained in all cases. The finding indicates that a noticeable degradation of PET does not occur under the selected extraction conditions.

text: SEM Analysis of Extracted Textiles. Virgin polycotton and some residual textile samples were examined by SEM. The original polycotton material shown in Figure 7A,7B is a homogeneous fabric with individual threads consisting of intertwined fibers. Higher magnification reveals that the threads consist of a mixture of two different fibers. One type of fiber is very smooth and homogeneous, while the second is inhomogeneous and has a rougher surface. The first type of fiber is assigned to PET, as this synthetic fiber is often produced using the melt -spin process, where molten PET is pressed through a nozzle to produce the fiber. 43 The second type of fiber is classified as cotton or cellulose. Cotton, as a natural product, results in an inhomogeneous unicellular fiber, which is composed of many cellulose microfibrils. The arrangement of the microfibrils creates a fiber structure characteristic of cotton with a corresponding surface structure. 44,45 During the production of blends such as polycotton, the polyester and cotton fibers are often mixed first and then spun into a yarn, which explains the fiber structure observed in the SEM images. 46 Intertwining of the individual fibers creates a mass transport limitation for the dissolution of cellulose. The inner cotton fibers can be dissolved only after the overlying cotton fibers have been dissolved. The polyester fibers cannot be dissolved, which limits the accessibility of the surface of the cotton fibers even further.

text:
In view of the circular economy and resource efficiency, recycling of textiles is mandatory. Particularly challenging are blended textiles consisting of two different fiber materials being interwoven. For these materials, chemical recycling was reported to be superior to mechanical recycling. 5 A prominent example for blended textiles is polycotton, which consists of cotton and PET. Mainly, recycling approaches for polycotton consist of degradation of one type of the fiber, whereas the second fiber requires the use of harsh solvent. 5,12 -17 On the contrary, the DBU/DMSO/CO2 solvent system applied here allows for the selective dissolution and extraction of cellulose from polycotton without degradation of PET. Moreover, as pointed out by McNeice and Feringa, traditional harsh conditions associated with large amounts of waste are avoided. 19

text: The feasibility study on the extraction of cellulose from polycotton was carried out at 40 °C in batches. The amount of base DBU strongly influences the extraction yield strongly. The best results were obtained with 10 wt % DBU. SEM images of the virgin polycotton revealed that the material consists of intertwined PET and cotton fibers. The extracted textile samples indicate the presence of gaps between the residual fibers. The latter are suggested to consist of PET, whereas the gaps are due to the absence of cellulose after dissolution. Following the extraction process, DMSO can be purified by distillation and used again. The results indicate that dry DMSO favors effective dissolution. As a result of the new approach, both polymers persist and the reuse of both of them is suggested to be feasible. Thus, chemical degradation of the polymers to the monomer units and subsequent polymerization are avoided. In addition, this solvent system is suitable for follow-up processing or the modification of cellulose.

The feasibility study on the extraction of cellulose from polycotton was carried out at 40 °C in batches. The amount of base DBU strongly influences the extraction yield strongly. The best results were obtained with 10 wt % DBU. SEM images of the virgin polycotton revealed that the material consists of intertwined PET and cotton fibers. The extracted textile samples indicate the presence of gaps between the residual fibers. The latter are suggested to consist of PET, whereas the gaps are due to the absence of cellulose after dissolution. Following the extraction process, DMSO can be purified by distillation and used again. The results indicate that dry DMSO favors effective dissolution. As a result of the new approach, both polymers persist and the reuse of both of them is suggested to be feasible. Thus, chemical degradation of the polymers to the monomer units and subsequent polymerization are avoided. In addition, this solvent system is suitable for follow-up processing or the modification of cellulose.

text:
With respect to industrial application, several aspects have to be addressed in the future. These comprise efficient recycling strategies for DMSO and DBU, replacement of the toxic base by a less harmful base, and the mode of operation. N -methylimidazole was suggested as an alternative base because, in addition to being nontoxic, its lower boiling point would facilitate distillation. 19 A semibatch or continuous extraction process with the circulation of the fresh or cleaned solvent system is expected to reduce the extraction time considerably. The extraction parameters need to be optimized with respect to, e.g., temperature, CO2 pressure, and the purity of the reused chemicals. In addition, the influence of impurities introduced by textile waste on the extraction process must be addressed. With respect to a highly sustainable process, the amount of chemicals required for dissolution and precipitation must be minimized. In the long run, the use of biobased alternatives for DMSO and the base is advised.

text:
Afterlife  textiles  have  been  a  major  environmental  concern.  The fashion industry accounts for a fifth of the 300 million tons of plastic produced each year globally  (Kasavan et  al.,  2021).  Garments  made from  polyester  and  other  synthetic  fibers  are  a  prime  source  of  the microplastic  pollutant,  which  is  especially  harmful  to  marine  life (Acharya  et  al.,  2021).  The  toxicity  of  synthetic  dyes  is  well  known today. Some cotton dyes raised both ecological and toxicological con cerns. Polyester dyes could lead to dermatitis due to their high degree of migration(Clement and Clement, 2011). Azo dyes may also lead to an increased risk of cancer (1999). Garments from fast-fashion brands such as Zara and Esprit were found toxic (2015). Furthermore, the scale of the textile fashion industry is still expanding rapidly (Peters et al., 2021). The  fashion  industry,  already  posing  substantial  threats  to  the  envi ronment and human health, consumes a tremendous amount of valuable resources such as crude oil, water, coal, and fertilizers (Mu and Yang, 2023). To solve the problems brought by afterlife textiles, large-scale recycling of waste textiles must be established globally.

text: The lack of economic dye-polymer and fiber-fiber separations for blended textiles prevents large-scale textile recycling. We focus on a clean, cost-effective, and destruction-minimized fiber-to-fiber recycling, suitable for polyester/cotton blended textiles. Here, dyed polyester was dissolved and separated from the blend, followed by controllable polyester precipitation to retain its dyes separately in the solution. The remaining-colored cotton was swollen to remove its dyes after cleavage of dye-cellulose bonds. Colorless polyester and cotton were re generated  into  fibers  with  similar  and  60  %  higher  tenacity  than  those  before  the  recycling,  respectively. Recycled fibers also had desirable dyeability, including dye exhaustion and colorfastness, after being dyed with the dyes extracted from the polyester/cotton blends, via our newly developed solvent dyeing system. More than 99 % of the solvent used in the recycling was recycled. Our recycling had a cost and energy consumption of less than 20 % of the production of virgin materials.

text: The circular economy plays a pivotal role in reshaping the textile industry into a more sustainable and socially responsible sector. Beyond its positive impact on environmental challenges, the circular economy brings forth economic advantages and societal benefits, establishing it self  as  the  foundation of textile recycling and a driving force behind sustainability practices within the industry (Jia et al., 2020). text: The current textile recycling mainly contains textile-to-non-textile, fabric-to-fabric,  yarn-to-yarn,  fiber-to-fiber,  and  polymer-to-polymer recycling  (Zhang  et  al.,  2022).  In  recent  years,  several  companies worldwide have initiated textile recycling based on the above recycling technology (Craig Bettenhausen, 2022; Mu  et al., 2023d). The textile-to-non-textile recycling refers to transforming waste textiles into non-textile  products  such  as  rags  and  insulation  materials  (Schmidt, 2016). In fabric-to-fabric  recycling,  sorted  waste  garments  are  trans formed into fabrics that are remade into new  garments in a labor-intensive manner (Johnson et al., 2020). In yarn-to-yarn recycling, waste garments are color sorted or discolored via oxidation/reduction and mechanically disintegrated to make yarns (Biesinger et al., 2011; Esteve-Turrillas and de La Guardia, 2017; Liu et al., 2011). Fiber-to-fiber recycling regenerates waste textiles into new textile fibers via melt or wet spinnings after textile discoloration or color sorting (Kwon et al., 1998; Ma et al., 2019). Polymer-to-polymer recycling refers to a polymer regeneration  process  containing  depolymerization  of  waste  textile polymers, distillation to the separation of impurities, and repolymeri zation (Kurian, 2005; Scott, 2022). However, due to either low-valued end products or unaffordable costs,  achieving  profitable  recycling  of waste  textiles  based  on  the  above  technologies  is  still  very  difficult (Elander and Ljungkvist, 2016; Lu et al., 2022; ¨ Ostlund et al., 2015). Till now, textile reuse has been much more popular than textile recycling. Less than 0.5 % of used clothes were recycled into new clothes in 2021 (Scott, 2022). About 7 -10 % of waste textiles in Europe were reused mainly via export to developing countries. Nevertheless, reuse cannot fully  solve  the  environmental  and  health  issues  waste  textiles  bring (Sandin and Peters, 2018).

text: Many recycled products from textile-to-non-textile, fabric-to-fabric, and yarn-to-yarn recycling have less-than-expected quality and values. For the textile-to-non-textile recycling, many non-textile products have lower  values  than  original  textile  products.  Apparels  from  fabric-tofabric  recycling  have  poor  quality  due  to  impairment  from  use.  In addition, the recycled garments faced style limitations (Johnson et al., 2020). For yarn-to-yarn recycling, mechanical disintegration of fabrics causes damage to the recycled fibers, mainly fiber breakage, fiber sur face cracking, and loss of strength (Araújo et al., 2017; Wanassi et al., 2016). As a result, those recycled cotton fibers have to be blended with virgin cotton fibers. Even so, the tensile strength of blended yarns was only 75 % of pure virgin cotton yarns (Yilmaz et al., 2017; Zeidman and Sawhney, 2002).

text: Non-destructive and sustainable separation of polymers, dyes, and other impurities from waste textiles are the most challengeable steps in fiber-to-fiber recycling (Mu et al., 2023a, 2023c). For example, vat dyes and  many  reactive  dyes  substantially  reduced  or  even  eliminate  the spinnability of cellulose solution (Haslinger et al., 2019b). Melt spinning of dyed polyester led to unsatisfactory color quality and serious envi ronmental  and  health  issues(Singha  et  al.,  2021).  To  recycle  textile polymers into fibers, impurities, especially dyes, have to be separated. However,  non-destructive  and  environmentally  responsible  technolo gies for dye-polymer separation have yet to be developed. Bleaching is the most common method to destroy dyes on textile fibers (Haslinger et  al.,  2019a;  Kwon et  al.,  1998; Yousef  et al.,  2019).  However, dye removal  via  time-consuming  bleaching  generates  large  quantities  of wastewater, and deteriorates the properties of recycled polymers (Lu et al., 2022).

text: Unaffordable polymer-to-polymer recycling cannot be applied to all textile forms and is unable to retain dye structures. Though polymer-topolymer  recycling  was  applied  to  polyester  recycling  in  the  1960s (Kurian, 2005; Scott, 2022), such recycling is still not widely used due to the  unaffordable  costs  of  depolymerization  and  repolymerization. Furthermore, the technology cannot be applied to recycling of synthetic fibers via addition polymerization, natural fibers, such as cotton, wool, and silk, and regenerated fibers from natural polymers, such as rayon and acetates. text: Here  we  have  developed  a  cost-effective,  and  destruction-anddischarge-minimized  fiber-to-fiber  recycling  technology  for  blended textiles,  the  dominant  textile  form  in  the  world  (Wang  and  Salmon, 2022; Zhang et al., 2022). For the first time, each polymer and dye is completely separated from polyester/cotton blended textiles via poly mer dissolution, polymer swelling, and polymer precipitation without chemical degradation or color destruction. Our recycling can overcome significant  obstacles  of  the  lack  of  cost-effective  and  non-destructive technologies  enabling  efficient  dye  removal  from  textiles.  As  our fiber-to-fiber  recycling  has  affordable  costs,  satisfactory  properties  of recycled products, and minimized discharge of pollutants, the portion of recycled textiles can be substantially improved. The high recyclability retention of chemical structures of textile after wearing and laundering indicates  the  feasibility  of  fiber-to-fiber  recycling.  The  polyester  is highly resistant to various environmental factors(Panowicz et al., 2021). The molecular weight of polyester did not change statistically even after 14,000  h  of  natural  weathering  (Al-Azzawi,  2015).  The  molecular weight of cotton after 50 laundering times was still higher than wood pulp (Palme et al., 2014), indicating that lyocell fibers from recycled cotton still have a high quality. Via the technology, textile fibers from fiber-to-fiber recycling have very high property retention. The regen erated fibers demonstrated similar or even higher mechanical properties and dyeability to those before the recycling. The process, eliminating costly depolymerization and repolymerization processes necessary for polymer-to-polymer recycling, enables profitable recycling of all textile wastes, including but not limited to polyethylene terephthalate (poly ester),  cotton,  and  their  blends  and  their  dyes.  Besides,  minimized discharge with 99.17 % recycling rate of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) has been achieved in the fiber-to-fiber recycling technology.

The  molecular weight of cotton after 50 laundering times was still higher than wood pulp (Palme et al., 2014), indicating that lyocell fibers from recycled cotton still have a high quality. Via the technology, textile fibers from fiber-to-fiber recycling have very high property retention. The regen erated fibers demonstrated similar or even higher mechanical properties and dyeability to those before the recycling. The process, eliminating costly depolymerization and repolymerization processes necessary for polymer-to-polymer recycling, enables profitable recycling of all textile wastes, including but not limited to polyethylene terephthalate (poly ester),  cotton,  and  their  blends  and  their  dyes.  Besides,  minimized discharge with 99.17 % recycling rate of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) has been achieved in the fiber-to-fiber recycling technology.

2.2.2. Controllable polyester precipitation for disperse dye-polyester separation

Since DMSO only dissolves polyester at temperatures higher than 150 °C, dissolved polyester can be precipitated to control the polymer morphologies via control of temperatures. As shown in Fig. 1, recycled polyester and disperse dyes in DMSO were cooled down, so that the precipitated polyester was completely amorphous. Dispersed dyes were separated from completely amorphous polyester via rinsing polyester with  a  small  amount  of  hot  DMSO.  After  the  disperse  dye-polyester separation,  colorless  polyester  was  washed  to  remove  DMSO  and dried.  DMSO  was  reused  by  water-DMSO  separation  driven  by distillation.

text:
Since recycled reactive dyes had their functional groups hydrolyzed, the reactive dyes cannot be reused to dye cotton. However, according to the previous research, such dyes can be used as acid dyes to dye poly mers such as nylon and wool (Yang and Xu, 1996). Here, we used the recycled Reactive Blue 19 to dye nylon 66 fabrics. About 2 % owf (on the weight of fibers) of recycled Reactive Blue 19 was used to dye nylon fabric. Different amount of water was added to the reactive-dye-stripping solutions to adjust solubility and charged groups of recycled dyes. The dyeing took place at 90 °C for 1 h. The pH of the dyeing medium was set to 3 using acetic acid. To compare the dyeability of recycled Reactive Blue 19, Acid Blue 25, with the same chromogenic structure as Reactive Blue 19, was used to dye nylon under an aqueous dyeing system. The dyeing temperature was 90 °C while the pH of the dyeing medium was set to 3 using acetic acid.

2.2.8. Conversion of spent dye bath into dye-stripping solutions for zeropollutant-discharge

After  dyeings,  water  was  removed  from  the  spent  dye  bath  via distillation to produce pure DMSO solvent. The recovered DMSO can be used to recycle polymers and dyes from waste polyester/cotton blends again.

text:
Polymer densities under different temperatures were determined by BIOVIA  Materials  Studio  2018  (18.1.0.2017).  The  software  module utilized the Amorphous Cell Calculation to generate an amorphous unit cell. This cell consisted of a unit volume containing 5 polyester mole cules with 15 repeating units and 200 DMSO molecules. The energy of the cells was minimized until convergence, with a convergence criterion set at a 0.001 kJ/mol difference between successive minimizations. To accomplish this, the Smart algorithm was employed with a maximum of 5000 iterations. The temperature range for the calculations was set be tween 313 K and 403 K. Following the construction of the amorphous cell, a Forcite calculation was applied to optimize the polymer-solvent interactions through a geometry optimization process. Multiple simu lations were conducted to ensure that the simulated structures ' confor mations were energy minimized to the extent that the energy differences between them did not change by more than 5 % after repeated simula tions. Finally, after the energy minimization, the densities of the poly mers were determined.

text: Figs. 2a-c discuss how to obtain colorless polyester from the blends. DMSO was found to fast dissolve polyester at 150 °C while precipitate polyester below 150 °C. According to Fig. 2a, the density of polyester can be adjusted by controlling the temperatures of DMSO in polyester precipitation. Previous study showed the decrease in polymer density led to a sharp decline in the van der Waals interactions between dyes and polymers and, thus, a substantial increase in the chemical potentials of dyes on polymers (Mu and Yang, 2022). When the chemical potential of the disperse dye at any position in the polymer was greater than the chemical  potential  of  the  dye  in  the  solvent,  the  disperse  dye  was completely separated from the polymer. Fig. 2a shows that as the tem perature increased, the density of the polyester decreased from nearly 0.8 g/cm 3 at 40 °C to less than 0.2 g/cm 3 at 130 °C. The sharp drop in the density of polyester substantially eliminated physical interactions be tween disperse dyes and polyester. Fig. 2b shows the separation ratios of disperse dyes from polyester at different temperatures in the process of polyester precipitation. The results show that almost all disperse dyes were separated from polyester polymer when controllable precipitation of polyester occurred at temperatures between 120 and 150 °C. As the temperature  continued  to  decrease,  the  proportion  of  disperse  dyes separated from polyester amorphous gels, resulting from controllable precipitation,  gradually  reduced  due  to  the  increase  in  the  polymer density (Mu et al., 2023b). The chemical potential of disperse dyes on polyester gels decreased with the increased in polymer density in the gel. The difference in chemical potential of the disperse dye between poly mer gel and polyester dissolution solvents determined the separation ratios  of  disperse  dyes  from  the  polymer. text: The remaining-colored cotton was swollen to remove the reactive dyes as shown in Figs. 2d-f. Fig. 2d shows that reactive dyes bonded with cotton  in  polyester/cotton  blends  can  be  completely  separated  by eliminating  dye-polymer  interactions  via  substantial  cotton  swelling. The  separation  process  maximized  retention  of  the  degrees  of  poly merization (DP) of cellulose. Before completely separating reactive dyes from cotton, the covalent bonds between reactive dyes and cellulose have to be cleaved without substantial damage to the dyes and cellulose. Reactive dyes are the dominant cotton-used dyes. An alkaline treatment was used to cleave the dye-cellulose bonds since alkalinity can retain the chemical  structures  of  cellulose  and  chromogenic  structures  of  dyes. Fig. 2d shows that only a low concentration of NaOH in a dye-stripping solvent, as low as 0.3 %, was strong enough to break all dye-cellulose bonds.  Without  covalent  bonds  with  cellulose,  reactive  dyes  were completely separated from cellulose under solvents with solubility pa rameters close to cellulose, as shown in Fig. 2e. When the solubility parameter of dye-stripping solutions is close to cellulose, the solution maximizes the swelling degrees of cotton. In Fig. 2e, by adjusting the parameters of the dye-stripping solution, two rinsing cycles realized a 99.9 % separation of the Reactive Blue 19 from cotton at 90 °C. The DMSO/water solvent, reactive-dye-stripping solvent, also greatly simplified  the  process  of  recycling  polyester/cotton  blended  textiles because the DMSO, used to separate polymers and recycle polyester as well  as  disperse  dyes,  was  not  necessary  to  be  removed  from  cotton before recycling of cellulose and reactive dyes. Fig. 2f shows that the process of separating polyester, disperse dyes, and reactive dyes did not change the chemical structure of cellulose except for a 6 % reduction in the molecular weight of cellulose. The FTIR of the cellulose before and after the separation process was the same. The DP of cellulose decreased from 2368, before the separation process, to 2223. Such a reduction resulted from the alkaline treatment for cleavage of dye-cellulose bonds. With such a decrease in the DP of cellulose, fibers from cotton recycling should have a desirable property. As shown in Fig. 1, colorless polyester and cotton were separated from 50/50 polyester/cotton blends. About 99.8 % of polyester was recovered after the recycling process while 99.9 % of disperse dyes were separated from polyester. Also, 99.2 % of cotton was also recovered. Up to 99.9 % of reactive dyes were separated from the  remaining-colored  cotton.  Next,  processibility  of  converting  the recycled polymers into textile fibers will be studied.

text: Figs.  3c  and  d  compare  the  morphology,  XRD  and  mechanical properties of lyocell fibers from recycled cotton to those of cotton fibers. The results indicated that complete cellulose recycling was realized by non-destructive dye-cellulose separation technology. Fig. 3c shows that the crystal structures of cellulose changed after regeneration in ionic liquid, from the original Cellulose I to Cellulose II. For example, new crystals formed at 2 θ = 20.1 (110) and 2 θ = 21.53 (200). Cellulose, found in its natural state, is referred to as cellulose I. In cellulose I, the individual cellulose strands are oriented in a parallel manner, and there is no hydrogen bonding between the strands. On the other hand, cellu lose  II  is  thermodynamically  more  stable  and  consists  of  cellulose strands  arranged  in  an  antiparallel  fashion,  with  hydrogen  bonding occurring between adjacent strands (Jacob John and Thomas, 2010). Even with changes in crystal structures, the degree of crystallinity of lyocell  fibers  was  not  significantly  different  from that  of  cotton.  The degrees of crystallinity of virgin cotton fibers and recycled lyocell fibers were 65.49 ± 4.65 % and 63.83 ± 4.23 %, respectively. Compared to the traditional wood-pulp-derived lyocell with a DP of about 1000, the DP of recycled cotton was higher than 2000. The higher DP did not affect the spinnability of cellulose in N-methylmorpholine N-oxide (NMMO). As shown in Fig. 3c, lyocell fiber had a desirable fineness. The diameter of  lyocell  fiber,  regenerated  from  recycled cotton, was about 11 µ m, much lower than that of regular cotton fibers, 20 -25 µ m. Fig. 3d com pares the mechanical properties of cotton-derived lyocell fiber and other cellulosic fibers. The results show that, like wood-pulp-derived lyocell fibers, cotton-derived lyocell fibers had higher tenacity than cotton and viscose fibers in both dry and wet states. The tenacity resulted from stronger  interactions  between  cellulose  molecules  in  lyocell  fibers. Compared to wood pulp, the cotton-derived lyocell fibers had an even higher tenacity due to the higher DP of cotton. In addition, recycling cotton into lyocell fibers not only reserves a lot of resources, including wood, but also eliminates various wood pre-treatment processes such as de-barking, chipping, defibration, bleaching, and washing. Therefore, recycling cotton into lyocell fibers is a green, sustainable, and environ mentally responsible process. Next, we will study recycling of dyes and dyeability of recycled fibers.

On the other hand, cellu lose  II  is  thermodynamically  more  stable  and  consists  of  cellulose strands  arranged  in  an  antiparallel  fashion,  with  hydrogen  bonding occurring between adjacent strands (Jacob John and Thomas, 2010). Even with changes in crystal structures, the degree of crystallinity of lyocell  fibers  was  not  significantly  different  from that  of  cotton.  The degrees of crystallinity of virgin cotton fibers and recycled lyocell fibers were 65.49 ± 4.65 % and 63.83 ± 4.23 %, respectively. Compared to the traditional wood-pulp-derived lyocell with a DP of about 1000, the DP of recycled cotton was higher than 2000. The higher DP did not affect the spinnability of cellulose in N-methylmorpholine N-oxide (NMMO). As shown in Fig. 3c, lyocell fiber had a desirable fineness. The diameter of  lyocell  fiber,  regenerated  from  recycled cotton, was about 11 µ m, much lower than that of regular cotton fibers, 20 -25 µ m. Fig. 3d com pares the mechanical properties of cotton-derived lyocell fiber and other cellulosic fibers. The results show that, like wood-pulp-derived lyocell fibers, cotton-derived lyocell fibers had higher tenacity than cotton and viscose fibers in both dry and wet states. The tenacity resulted from stronger  interactions  between  cellulose  molecules  in  lyocell  fibers. Compared to wood pulp, the cotton-derived lyocell fibers had an even higher tenacity due to the higher DP of cotton. In addition, recycling cotton into lyocell fibers not only reserves a lot of resources, including wood, but also eliminates various wood pre-treatment processes such as de-barking, chipping, defibration, bleaching, and washing. Therefore, recycling cotton into lyocell fibers is a green, sustainable, and environ mentally responsible process. Next, we will study recycling of dyes and dyeability of recycled fibers.

text: Figs. 4a -c show the recycling of disperse dyes via dyeing the recycled disperse  dyes  onto  recycled  polyester  fibers.  Fig.  4a  shows  that  the chromogenic structure of the Disperse Blue 56 remained intact after the dissolution  of  polyester,  formation  of  amorphous  polyester  gels,  and dye-polymer separation. Via visible wavelength scanning, there were no changes for Disperse Blue 56 before and after the separation process. Fig. 4b shows structures of the DMSO solvent, determined by 1 H NMR, involved in the separation process. The results showed that the structure of DMSO did not change after the separation process, given the stable structures of DMSO and short separation durations. In the separation, polyester and disperse dyes were fully dissolved in DMSO within 5 min at 150 °C and dye-polymer separation completed for another 5 min at 120 °C.  DMSO  is  highly  stable  at  temperatures  below  150 °C.  For example, DMSO was expected to lose 0.1 to 1 % of its weight at 150 °C for 24 h (Tudino et al., 2020). In 1 H NMR, no new impurity peaks except methyl hydrogen atoms attributed to DMSO appeared. The undamaged DMSO can be used to develop a new dyeing system to recycle dyes so that  recycled  dyes  in  the  dye-stripping  solutions  did  not  need  to  be extracted before the recycling. Fig. 4c shows that adding an appropriate proportion of water to the DMSO to adjust the solubility and chemical potentials of disperse dyes achieved similar dyeing results on polyester fibers compared to that in traditional aqueous dyeings. The dyeing result also indicated recycled polyester fibers had good dyeability. In addition, because of the better swelling properties of DMSO on polyester mole cules, the dyeing temperature could be 20 °C lower than that of tradi tional  aqueous  dyeing  to  achieve  a  similar  dye  uptake.  Dyeing temperatures for DMSO-involved dyeing and traditional aqueous dyeing were 95 °C and 115 °C, respectively. Reduced dyeing temperature saved substantial energy in the dyeing process.

text: Figs. 4d-f show the recycling of reactive dyes via dyeing the recycled reactive  dyes  onto  nylon  fabrics.  For  reactive  dyes,  their  functional groups  after  dye-cellulose  separation  were  hydrolyzed.  Therefore, recycled reactive dyes can no longer be used as reactive dyes to dye recycled cellulose fibers. However, given the undamaged chromogenic structures after dye-cellulose separation, recycled reactive dyes can be used as acid dyes for ionic fibers such as nylon, wool, and silk according to previous research (Yang and Xu, 1996). Fig. 4d compares the chro mogenic  structures  of  reactive  dyes  before  and  after  the  separation process. The results show separation process did not change the chro mogenic structures of reactive dyes given the same scanning curve in the visible wavelength range. For a fair comparison, functional groups of Reactive Blue 19 before recycling reacted with water before the visible wavelength scan. The solvent was 70 %DMSO/30 %water. Fig. 4e shows that DMSO was very stable during the dye-cellulose separation. 1 H NMR did not show any additional impurity peaks. Fig. 4f shows that slight increase in the water portion in reactive-dye-stripping solution trans formed the dye-stripping system into dyeing system, which provided the similar dye uptake as traditional aqueous system. The increase in water portion  helped  recycled  reactive  dyes  negatively  charged.  Therefore, dyes can be easily sorbed by nylon. The recycled reactive dyes, with hydrolyzed functional groups, were used as acid dyes to dye nylon. To compare the properties of recycled dyes, Acid Blue 25, with the same chromogenic structure as Reactive Blue 19, was used to dye nylon under an aqueous dyeing system. The dyeing temperature was 90 °C while the pH of the dyeing medium was set to 3. 2 % owf (on the weight of fibers) of recycled Reactive Blue 19 was used. Via water distillation, the solvent dyeing systems for disperse dyeing and reactive dyeing can be turned into fiber-to-fiber recycling system again.

3.4. Cost-effective fiber-to-fiber recycling

text: Supplementary Table 1 shows that fiber-to-fiber recycling is not only cost-effective but also energy-conservative. The fiber-to-fiber recycling only  needs  two  major  steps,  polymer  dissolution,  and  controllable polymer  precipitation,  to  obtain  colorless  polymer  materials  in  a destruction-minimized manner. The cost of the two steps is much less than that of depolymerization and polymerization, used in polymer-topolymer recycling to separate impurities. The recycled dyes can also be redyed onto recycled fibers. In addition, the fiber-to-fiber recycling realizes the recycling of not only synthetic fibers but also natural fibers and  recycled  fibers  from  natural  polymers.  Since  the  fiber-to-fiber recycling technology used the same spinning method to produce poly mer fibers as the other polymer-to-polymer recycling and traditional virgin fiber production, the cost calculation only covers the process of conversion of waste textiles to recycled polymers and dye recycling. For polyester, the calculation covered the process of conversion of waste polyester fabrics to polyester pellets while for cellulose, the calculation covered the process of conversion of waste cotton fabrics to cotton linter pulp. Based on calculations, recycling 1 ton of textile fibers, including polyester  and  cellulose,  potentially  adds  at  least  $  1600  values.  The added  values  were  calculated  based  on  the  difference  between  the market prices and the total production costs of materials and energy. The energy consumed by the recycling technology are also calculated. The recycling of 1 ton of polyester consumed about 830 kwh of energy while recycling of 1 ton of cotton consumed about 330 kwh of energy. The energy consumed by the recycling was substantially lower than that by producing virgin polymer materials.

Supplementary Table 1 shows that fiber-to-fiber recycling is not only cost-effective but also energy-conservative. The fiber-to-fiber recycling only  needs  two  major  steps,  polymer  dissolution,  and  controllable polymer  precipitation,  to  obtain  colorless  polymer  materials  in  a destruction-minimized manner. The cost of the two steps is much less than that of depolymerization and polymerization, used in polymer-topolymer recycling to separate impurities. The recycled dyes can also be redyed onto recycled fibers. In addition, the fiber-to-fiber recycling realizes the recycling of not only synthetic fibers but also natural fibers and  recycled  fibers  from  natural  polymers.  Since  the  fiber-to-fiber recycling technology used the same spinning method to produce poly mer fibers as the other polymer-to-polymer recycling and traditional virgin fiber production, the cost calculation only covers the process of conversion of waste textiles to recycled polymers and dye recycling. For polyester, the calculation covered the process of conversion of waste polyester fabrics to polyester pellets while for cellulose, the calculation covered the process of conversion of waste cotton fabrics to cotton linter pulp. Based on calculations, recycling 1 ton of textile fibers, including polyester  and  cellulose,  potentially  adds  at  least  $  1600  values.  The added  values  were  calculated  based  on  the  difference  between  the market prices and the total production costs of materials and energy. The energy consumed by the recycling technology are also calculated. The recycling of 1 ton of polyester consumed about 830 kwh of energy while recycling of 1 ton of cotton consumed about 330 kwh of energy. The energy consumed by the recycling was substantially lower than that by producing virgin polymer materials.

4. Conclusions

text: This novel, clean, and cost-effective fiber-to-fiber recycling, regen erating waste textiles into new textile fibers via spinning, completely separated dyes from polymers and retained the chemical structures of polymers  and  chromogenic  structures  of  dyes.  The  recycling  process maximized the retention of chemical structures of polymers. The recy cled  polyester  fibers  from  waste  polyester  had  similar  fineness  and mechanical properties compared to virgin fibers. The lyocell fibers from recycled cotton had much better fineness and strength than virgin cotton fibers. The recycled fibers also demonstrated desirable dyeabilities. The chromogenic structures of recycled dyes have not been damaged and can be further used as textile dyes without discharge. 99.17 % of DMSO used in  the  recycling  was  recycled.  The  recycling  is  techno-economically viable and energy conservative given that the cost, including material and  energy,  and  energy  consumption  for  the  recycling  process  were 6 -12% of the sale prices of raw polymers and 5 -20 % of the production of virgin materials, respectively. The fiber-to-fiber recycling promotes the establishment of a large-scale recycling industry with an emphasis on  environmental  sustainability,  resource  conservation,  waste  reduc tion, and fashion industry transformation. Besides, the technology can be fit for future regulatory changes, which mandate the textile recycling.

text: Abstract: Polyvinyl(butyral) (PVB) post-production waste collected from the windshields of endof-life vehicles and post-consumer building laminated glass are valuable polymeric materials that can be reused. Every year, large amounts of PVB waste are still being buried in landfills owing to a lack of appropriate recycling techniques. Before reuse, PVB should be thoroughly cleaned of solid contaminants such as glass dust, fused heating wires, and other waste polymers, metals, and ceramics. This can be done by polymer dissolution and filtration. In this study, we propose the purification of PVB from contamination by dissolving the post-consumer polymeric materials into single and binary organic solvents. As part of the experimental work, measurements and optimization of the dissolution time of PVB were performed. PVB dissolves faster when a binary solvent (2-propanol + ethyl acetate) than pure 2-propanol is used. From the point of view of the practical application of PVB solutions, measurements of density and dynamic viscosity as a function of PVB concentration and temperature were performed. The PVB solutions obtained in this work can be widely used as glues for glass, ceramics, metal, impregnating, and insulating materials or as paint additives that are entirely transparent for visible light and to block UV rays.

As part of the experimental work, measurements and optimization of the dissolution time of PVB were performed.
