text: Thermal Properties. Thermal analyses of recovered EVOH (Figure 7) provide further insight into its thermomechanical history. Table 4 summarizes the glass transition ( T g ), melting ( T m), and crystallization ( T c ) temperatures, as well as the corresponding melting and crystallization enthalpies of both virgin and recovered EVOH determined from the second heating cycle. The results indicate that the recovered EVOH samples exhibit T g values of 35 °C (rEVOH-frommultilayer) and 42 °C (rEVOH-from-Multilayer-R3), both significantly lower than that of virgin EVOH (57 °C). The observed decrease in T g can be attributed to residual DMSO, which acts as a plasticizer, 47 enhancing chain mobility and promoting structural reorganization. 48 -51 A similar behavior was reported by Cecon et al. 48 for PET recovered from PE/ EVOH/PET multilayer packaging films via a solvent-targeted dissolution -precipitation approach, where the reduction in T g was attributed to the presence of solvent within the polymer matrix. According to these authors, DMSO entrapped within the PET matrix contributes to the lowering of the glass transition temperature. To mitigate this effect, the samples were dried at 180 °C for 8 h prior to DSC measurements, using a hermetically sealed aluminum DSC pan. In the present work, the samples were dried at 80 °C for 48 h prior to analysis, and hermetically sealed aluminum DSC pans were also employed. Therefore, heating to 230 °C will not necessarily lead to volatilization of DMSO.

Rheological Properties

The rheological behavior of virgin and recovered EVOH was investigated by monitoring the evolution of complex viscosity as a function of the angular frequency at 210 °C (Figure 9a). The results reveal a clear decrease in complex viscosity for the recovered EVOH samples compared to the virgin material. This reduction is particularly pronounced for the rEVOHfrom-Multilayer-R3, derived from a multilayer film subjected to three successive thermomechanical recycling cycles. The observed decrease in viscosity can be attributed to reduced molar mass resulting from polymer dissolution and, in the case of rEVOH-from-Multilayer-R3, additional thermo-oxidative degradation.

text: Similar trends are observed for polypropylene (PP). A marked decrease in complex viscosity is detected for recovered PP obtained via dissolution -precipitation compared to virgin PP (Figure 9c). This pronounced reduction can be attributed to the partial dissolution of the interface/interphase region along with EVOH. As the region may include PP chains, its removal likely leads to a decrease in the molar mass of PP, and consequently, a reduction in viscosity. Thermal stability analysis (Figure 9d) corroborates this significant drop in complex viscosity. However, recovered PP samples exhibit improved thermal stability compared to virgin PP, as evidenced by the more stable evolution of complex viscosity over time at 210 °C. When comparing the rheological behavior of the three times thermomechanically reprocessed PP (PP-R3) with rPPfrom-multilayer-R3, PP-R3 exhibits a higher complex viscosity (Figure S8, Supporting Information). The presence of PPg -MA acting as a compatibilizer plays a key role in the behavior: maleic anhydride groups can react with hydroxyl groups of EVOH, resulting in the chemically bonded and morphologically cohesive PP/EVOH interfacial region. Consequently, separation is more challenging than that in simple immiscible polymer systems. During the selective dissolution, a part of this interface/interphase region could be dissolved with EVOH, which explains the lower viscosity of the recovery rPP. These findings are supported by SEC results, which show that the number-average molar masses of recovered rPP are lower than those of virgin PP.

Figure 10 illustrates the molecular weight distribution of virgin PP and EVOH, as well as their recycled counterparts. The number-average and weight-average molar masses, along with the polydispersity index, are presented in Table 7. Size exclusion chromatography (SEC) analyses show that virgin PP has a weight-average molar mass nearly twice as high as that of the recycled PP samples, as well as a slightly higher numberaverage molecular weight (results confirmed by morphological analysis). Regarding EVOH, the number-average and weight-average molecular weights of rEVOH-from-multilayer are slightly higher than those of virgin EVOH, suggesting the possible coprecipitation of a fraction of the copolymer present at the interphase (EVOH/PP-g-MA) with EVOH. This section compares MR by thermomechanical reprocessing with the SDP process. Both technologies are used for the valorization of the multilayer films. This study focuses on the applicability of the two processes, although they lead to products of a different nature and are generally intended for different markets. Two additional criteria, namely, environmental impact and economic aspects, are also addressed; however, the comparison for these criteria relies mainly on data from the literature. These aspects are currently being studied within the framework of this project.

text: MR is currently the most widely implemented industrial route due to its operational simplicity, low cost, and relatively low energy consumption. However, its main limitation lies in the immiscibility of most base polymers, which results in phase separation and poor interfacial adhesion in mixed plastic streams. Consequently, recycled materials often exhibit reduced mechanical performance, mainly due to thermal and mechanical degradation during processing. For instance, thermomechanical treatment of a multilayer film based on PP, PP-g-MA, and EVOH over several recycling cycles leads to multiple reaction mechanisms, including PP β -scission, EVOH cross-linking, and copolymer formation resulting from interactions between EVOH and PP-g-MA. These mechanisms affect the mechanical and rheological properties of the material. As a result, mechanical recycling of the PP/PP-gMA/EVOH/PP-g-MA/PP multilayer film remains promising up to the third cycle; beyond this point, rheological and mechanical properties deteriorate. 9,54,55 In terms of environmental impact, despite differing opinions in the literature, most studies consider MR to have a lower environmental impact than other methods (physical recycling and chemical recycling). 9,54,55 Furthermore, Faraca et al. 56 quantified the costs associated with mechanical and chemical recycling in Denmark and demonstrated that advanced MR is the only scenario generating net financial savings. Other studies also support the economic viability of mechanical recycling. 57,58

text: In contrast, the SDP process relies on differences in the polymer solubility to achieve separation and purification. This approach enables the recovery of high-purity polymers while preserving their molecular structure, thereby maintaining properties close to those of virgin materials. It is particularly advantageous for processing complex or multilayer plastic waste that cannot be efficiently treated by mechanical routes. In this study, the method was applied to two systems: a PP/ PP-g-MA/EVOH/PP-g-MA/PP multilayer film and the same multilayer film after three thermomechanical recycling cycles. The results show that the PP and EVOH fractions are well separated. However, their thermal and rheological properties are modified, likely due to solvent use at an elevated temperature.

In contrast, the SDP process relies on differences in the polymer solubility to achieve separation and purification. This approach enables the recovery of high-purity polymers while preserving their molecular structure, thereby maintaining properties close to those of virgin materials. It is particularly advantageous for processing complex or multilayer plastic waste that cannot be efficiently treated by mechanical routes. In this study, the method was applied to two systems: a PP/ PP-g-MA/EVOH/PP-g-MA/PP multilayer film and the same multilayer film after three thermomechanical recycling cycles. The results show that the PP and EVOH fractions are well separated. However, their thermal and rheological properties are modified, likely due to solvent use at an elevated temperature.

text:
Moreover, this process is more complex than MR because it involves several steps, namely, shredding, solvent selection, temperature adjustment, filtration, followed by washing and drying. Solvent selection is critical since a specific solvent must be used for each layer. The choice of the temperature and dissolution time is also important to ensure effective dissolution. Washing and drying are essential to separate the recovered products from the solvent. Within the scope of this project, the total time required to separate PP and EVOH is 60 h, including 12 h for dissolution and 48 h for washing and drying. In contrast, applying five recycling cycles to the multilayer film by MR required only 6 h.

From an environmental perspective, this process is more energy-intensive than MR due to heating and solvent evaporation steps. It also uses antisolvents, which require additional distillation stages to separate solvents from antisolvents, thereby increasing environmental impact. 59 Several studies emphasize the need to reduce antisolvent use and optimize solvent recovery loops. 25,37,60 Finally, the process is costly due to the use of solvents and antisolvents, as well as the required equipment, notably reactors and distillation/ evaporation units. 22,61

text:
This work presents a comparative assessment of two recycling technologies, MR and the SDP process, based on process robustness and product quality, as well as environmental and economic considerations. These approaches yield materials of a different nature and are therefore likely to target distinct market applications. The study focuses on multilayer films composed of PP, PP-g-MA, and EVOH.

MR was performed through thermomechanical processing over five successive recycling cycles. The results indicate that this approach remains effective up to the third cycle; beyond this point, both rheological and mechanical properties deteriorate due to reaction mechanisms occurring during processing. These include β -scission of PP chains, cross-linking of EVOH, and esterification reactions between EVOH and PP. According to literature data, MR exhibits a relatively low environmental impact and remains economically favorable.

This work presents a comparative assessment of two recycling technologies, MR and the SDP process, based on process robustness and product quality, as well as environmental and economic considerations. These approaches yield materials of a different nature and are therefore likely to target distinct market applications. The study focuses on multilayer films composed of PP, PP-g-MA, and EVOH.

MR was performed through thermomechanical processing over five successive recycling cycles. The results indicate that this approach remains effective up to the third cycle; beyond this point, both rheological and mechanical properties deteriorate due to reaction mechanisms occurring during processing. These include β -scission of PP chains, cross-linking of EVOH, and esterification reactions between EVOH and PP. According to literature data, MR exhibits a relatively low environmental impact and remains economically favorable.

text:
In contrast, the SDP approach relies on differences in the polymer solubility to achieve selective separation and purification. In the present study, SDP was applied to separate EVOH from PP in both a multilayer film and a Multilayer-R3 material composed of PP, PP-g-MA, and EVOH. The results demonstrate separation between PP and EVOH; however, alterations in thermal and rheological properties were observed. These changes may be attributed to residual solvent retained within the samples as well as to partial dissolution of interfacial regions. From an environmental perspective, the SDP process is more energy-intensive and exhibits a higher environmental footprint than that of mechanical recycling. The use of solvents and antisolvents necessitates additional processing steps, such as distillation, for their separation and recovery. Economically, beyond the capital investment required for reactors, heating, and evaporation systems, the cost of solvents and antisolvents may further increase the overall process cost.

So fi a C. Aparício, a Pedro M. Castro, b Bernardo D. Ribeiro c and Isabel M. Marrucho * a

text: Polyole fi ns comprise some of the most abundant plastics, but their recycling faces several di ffi culties. This work focuses on the recycling of high-density polyethylene (HDPE) through the dissolution -precipitation method. Although few works have been published on this topic, this is an extremely promising plastic recycling strategy. However, for this kind of process to become a viable alternative, the replacement of conventional solvents by green solvents and the minimization of energy usage need to be implemented. In this work, several natural terpenes were screened based on COSMO-SAC predictions for HDPE solubility, and three were tested: limonene, α -pinene, and p -cymene. These solvents showed a good capability of dissolving HDPE, con fi rming the computational predictions. The dissolution and precipitation conditions were optimized based on the results for limonene, with the optimal values being 3 wt% initial concentration of the polymer in the solvent, a dissolution period of 10 min at a temperature of 110 °C, and an antisolvent/solvent ratio of 2/1. Comparing both HDPE and solvent recoveries for the three selected solvents, the best results were obtained for α -pinene as the solvent and ethanol as the antisolvent. The recovered HDPE samples were analyzed by TGA, FTIR, and DSC, showing little modi fi cation between the recycled and pristine materials. Scaling up of the process and solvent reuse were also investigated. Through process simulation, it was concluded that solvent recovery and reuse is a crucial step for economic viability. HDPE dissolution -precipitation with α -pinene was found to be a sustainable process from preliminary sustainability analysis, and the separation of HDPE and PET (polyethylene terephthalate) was successfully carried out.

text: In 2019, polyolefins (PP, HDPE (high-density polyethylene), LDPE (low-density polyethylene) and LLDPE (linear low-density polyethylene)) accounted for nearly 40% of the global plastic use. 4 These polymers are commonly used in packaging applications. In particular, HDPE can be found in beverage bottles, sti ff bottles and as flexible films, but it is also typically used in rigid toys and outdoor products. 5,6 Polyolefins are also ideal constituents of multilayer films, commonly in combination with di ff erent polyolefins or PET, 7 where they can have sealing and structural functions. 8 Although these plastics can be individually recycled, they are often present in complex waste streams that cannot be e ffi ciently sorted, as is the case of multilayer films, or contain various additives that preclude the use of mechanical recycling processes. 7 -10 It is estimated that the total percentage of HDPE that followed recycling pathways between 1950 and 2016, in Europe, was 12%, while more than half ended up in landfills, 11 as shown in Fig. 1. This low recycling rate is clear evidence that the recycling processes implemented so far still lack e ffi ciency for post-consumer products. Although landfilling and incineration reduce the existing volume of plastic waste and minimize water and soil contamination, they come with few other benefits, as they do not reduce the need for primary polymer production. This is very important because polyolefins are usually obtained from the steam cracking of naphtha, a product of crude oil refining, 12,13 a fossil fuel whose consumption needs to be minimized.

The recycling routes for plastic materials include mechanical, chemical, and physical recycling. In spite of being most widely implemented, mechanical recycling faces various challenges regarding the quality of the recycled plastics, whose properties greatly depend on the uniformity of the input materials. 14 -19 Chemical recycling is also a limited approach in the case of HDPE, as its complete depolymerization to monomers has not been achieved so far. Instead, pyrolysis and gasification are the common approaches converting plastics to hydrocarbons that can be used as chemical feedstock, after further purification and separation treatments. 13,14,16,20 -23 On the other hand, physical recycling is better suited for complex plastic mixtures than mechanical recycling, yielding simpler processes. 14,24

text:
Physical recycling, and dissolution -precipitation in particular, makes use of solvents to recover the polymers without degradation or structural modifications, resulting in a recycled plastic with similar properties to the pristine material. 14,24 Dissolution -precipitation processes rely on the selective dissolution of a target polymer from a mixture of plastics. When this polymer is dissolved, the solution can be filtered, thus separating it from the other polymers. The dissolved polymer can then be recovered by precipitation, converting it back to a solid plastic, through the addition of an antisolvent or by lowering the temperature of the system. Physical recycling, and dissolution -precipitation in particular, makes use of solvents to recover the polymers without degradation or structural modifications, resulting in a recycled plastic with similar properties to the pristine material. 14,24 Dissolution -precipitation processes rely on the selective dissolution of a target polymer from a mixture of plastics. When this polymer is dissolved, the solution can be filtered, thus separating it from the other polymers. The dissolved polymer can then be recovered by precipitation, converting it back to a solid plastic, through the addition of an antisolvent or by lowering the temperature of the system. Additives and impurities can also be removed in the process, either through the solubil-

|

text: ization of the polymer (the additives and other polymers remain solid and are removed by filtration), or through the solubilization of both the polymer and the additive, and the use of an antisolvent causes the precipitation of the pure polymer. 13,14,25 The possibility of tuning the solvents to selectively dissolve a targeted polymer in a mixture opens up the way for the treatment of mixed plastic streams, such as multilayer films, where typical sorting is not possible. 8 This technology has already been successfully employed to separate mixtures of plastics at the laboratory scale: Kannan et al. 26 separated LDPE, HDPE, PS (polystyrene) and PET, Walker et al. 27 used dissolution -precipitation to separate a mixture of HDPE, EVOH (ethylene vinyl alcohol) and PET, and Cécon et al. and Sánchez-Rivera et al. 28,29 separated HDPE, EVOH, EVA (ethylene-vinyl acetate), PET and PETG (polyethylene terephthalate glycol). It was also implemented in some pilot-scale plants, using the CreaSolv process by Creacycle GmbH, namely for separating PE, PP, PA (polyamide) and PET, 30 and PE and PP. 31 HDPE, the focus of the present study, was the subject of various physical recycling studies using dissolution and precipitation, mostly using toluene, 27,29,32 -35 xylene 26,33,34 or petroleum ether-based solvents. 36 -38 Only in 2022, Ferreira et al. 39 proposed the use of D-limonene, a biobased solvent, for the dissolution of HDPE. However, the objective of that work was the recovery of dyes from the plastic, and plastic recovery itself was not considered in detail. In another study, p -cymene was found to be a good solvent for LDPE and PP, but HDPE dissolution was not studied. 40 Acetone, 26 -29,32,40 2-propanol 26 or n -hexane 33,34,36 -38 are the usual choices for antisolvents.

text: Although the dissolution -precipitation technology seems to be a promising option for recycling polyolefins, there are some bottlenecks that need to be addressed to guarantee its future applicability. First, the most commonly used solvents, toluene and xylene, are dangerous air pollutants 41 and pose serious hazards to aquatic and human life. 44,45 Toluene is even suspected to be a carcinogenic agent and harmful for the reproductive system. 42,43 The environmental, health and social impacts associated with the production and use of these solvents are extremely concerning, and current solvent selection metrics identify them as problematic. 44 Several legal measures have restricted their usage, both in Europe and the U.S.A. 45 -47 Thus, it is urgent to replace them by greener, natural, and less hazardous solvents in the dissolution of HDPE. Acetone, one of the most common antisolvents, should also be replaced by other less problematic compounds, such as alcohols. 44 Furthermore, from the economic point of view, this technology is currently limited, since the high amounts of energy required for the separation of the solvent and antisolvent drive the minimum selling price to a higher value than that of the virgin polymer. 48 Greenhouse gas emissions are also mostly related to the recovery of the solvent. 30,48 Thus, the present work aims to develop a novel circular approach for the dissolution -precipitation of HDPE using natural solvents and finding antisolvent combinations that allow a simple, coste ffi cient recovery of the solvent while recovering the polymer with its pristine quality.

2. Materials and methods

2.1 Materials

HDPE was used in the form of commercial clear fruit bags, obtained from Continente supermarkets. PET was used in the form of clear water bottles from Luso.

Limonene rich extract was graciously provided by SumolCompal, as a subproduct of mechanical processing of orange peels. It was then purified through steam distillation, followed by fractioned distillation. The remaining solvents and antisolvents used were purchased in the desired grade, according to the respective purities and suppliers described in Table S1 in the ESI. † For the separation of HDPE and PET, PET was dissolved with a thymol : carvacrol natural deep eutectic solvent (NaDES), whose characteristics are also presented in Table S1. † Bi-distilled water was used for solvent recovery, from the BioSan Labaqua Trace purification system, with a conductivity of 0.055 μ S cm -1 .

text:
HDPE dissolution was carried out by heating the polymer and solvent mixture in an oil bath at a controlled temperature, and a stirring speed of 400 rpm. After complete dissolution, the antisolvent was added, promoting the precipitation of the polymer. The obtained mixture was then filtered under vacuum, and the resulting polymer flakes were dried in an oven at 80 °C for 48 hours. The dry HDPE was then ground using liquid nitrogen, washed with ethanol, and dried for another 48 hours. The percentage recovery of HDPE was determined through gravimetric measurements.

For the solvent ' s recovery, water was added to promote phase separation between the solvent and the antisolvent, according to the liquid -liquid equilibrium diagrams calculated using COSMO-SAC. The resulting mixtures were centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 20 minutes, using a VWR CompactStar CS 4 centrifuge, and solvent recovery was evaluated by gravimetry.

2.2.2 HDPE and PET selective dissolution and recovery. The separation of HDPE and PET was performed from a solid mixture containing equal masses of both polymers shredded. HDPE was selectively dissolved first, at the optimized conditions studied in this work, following the procedure described above in section 2.2.1. The mixture was then filtered using a 2 mm mesh filter, retaining the solid PET, and allowing the solubilized HDPE to pass. Afterwards, the anti-solvent was used to precipitate and recover HDPE.

After filtration, PET was washed and dried at 40 °C and then dissolved and recovered following the procedure described by Pestana et al. 49 The solvent, a natural deep eutectic solvent (NaDES) composed of thymol and carvacrol (1 : 1), was prepared by heating the mixture of the two compounds up to 80 °C for around 1 hour, after which the obtained clear solution was slowly cooled. The PET dissolution, in the polymer to solvent ratio of 1/10, was carried out at 150 °C for 7 minutes, and a mixture of ethanol (60 v/v%) and water was used as the antisolvent to precipitate it, in the proportion of 50 mL of antisolvent for 1 g of PET.

2.2.3 Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy. Attenuated total reflectance-Fourier transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy was used to evaluate the integrity of the recovered polymer and solvents, in comparison with the virgin materials. A PerkinElmer UATR Two spectrometer with a diamond crystal was used, and the analysis was carried out in the range between 4000 and 400 cm -1 , based on the accumulation of 8 scans with a resolution of 4 cm -1 .

2.2.4 Di ff erential scanning calorimetry. Samples of the recovered HDPE were analyzed by di ff erential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to assess the changes in the main thermal properties of the polymer due to the dissolution and precipitation process. The equipment used was a DSC 200 F3 from NETZSCH, in which two sequential heating -cooling cycles were performed, between 20 and 250 °C, at a heating/cooling rate of 10 °C min -1 , and with a nitrogen flow rate of 50 mL min -1 . The melting and crystallization temperatures and the enthalpy of fusion were determined based on the second cycle. This value was used to estimate the percentage of crystallinity of the polymers, taken as the quotient of the enthalpies of fusion calculated from DSC data and that of the completely crystalline polymer. The values were 293 J g -1 for PE and 140 J g -1 for PET. 50

2.3.1 Thermodynamic estimations: COSMO-SAC solvent screening. HDPE molecules were simulated based on the charge density screening of the representative monomer, taken as the most central monomer of a trimer, thus minimizing the end groups ' influence on the density functional-theory (DFT) calculations, performed in an AMSinput 2023.101 interface, with the parameterization GGA:BP86/TZP86, using a pre-optimized molecular geometry with the Universal Force Field (UFF) package. The same parametrization was used to optimize the molecules of the solvents not included in the COSMO-SAC database, such as 3-carene and β -caryophyllene. After geometry optimization, the compounds were added to the COSMO-SAC calculation environment.

All calculations were performed with the activity coe ffi cient model COSMO-SAC, particularly with the parameter package DHB, determined as the most adequate for the systems under study. To improve the accuracy of the calculations, some properties, such as melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, and density at 25 °C, were manually introduced. Table S2 in the ESI † summarizes all the properties for the pure compounds used in this work. For HDPE, the properties of the completely crystalline polymer were used: T m = 141.4 °C, Δ H f = 293 J g -1 , 50 and ρ C = 1.00 g cm -3 . 51 The considered molecular weight was the COSMO-SAC default.

2.3.2 Process simulation: economic and sustainability evaluation. The proposed dissolution -precipitation process was simulated with the Aspen Plus V11 software to estimate energy requirements and the cost associated with each step.

The HDPE polymer was defined as an oligomer using C2H4R as the repeating segment. The polymer molecular weight is a required input parameter, which was fixed at a value of 100 kg mol -1 . The necessary phase equilibrium properties for the process simulation were estimated using the POLYUF method, which is a modification of the activity coe ffi cient ' s group contribution method UNIFAC, specifically improved for polymers. The distillation column used to separate water and ethanol, with residual amounts of α -pinene was also simulated using the UNIFAC method. Group contribution methods were used due to the lack of adequate data in the available Aspen databases for α -pinene.

The required utilities were defined according to the Aspen templates and attributed to each equipment so that the minimum temperature di ff erence of 10 °C between streams is respected. 52 Considering a pessimistic estimation of the process costs, no heat integration was performed. The utilities used were heated air, low pressure steam, cooling water and refrigerated water. Table S3 in the ESI † shows the properties of each utility.

From the analysis of HDPE ' s σ -profile and σ -potential, it is clear that no polar interactions are favored by the polymer ' s completely apolar structure. At this temperature, the experimental solubility limit has only been reported in toluene being between 14.56 wt% 28,35 and 23.1 wt%. 59 The di ff erence between the experimental and the COSMO-SAC predicted solubility can possibly be explained by the use of the properties of completely crystalline HDPE in the COSMO-SAC calculations, while commonly available samples have lower degrees of crystallinity. At 120 °C, the solubility predicted for HDPE in toluene and xylene is of 12 wt% and 1 wt%, respectively. The only green solvent studied that shows some HDPE solubility at this temperature is α -pinene (1 wt%). Nevertheless, at 130 °C, COSMO-SAC predicts that HDPE is soluble in all the screened solvents: β -caryophyllene is estimated to dissolve HDPE up to 32 wt%, while the predictions for all the other terpenes lay between 50 and 60 wt%.

The solvents D-limonene, α -pinene, and p -cymene were selected to proceed with the experimental study based on their promising predicted capability to dissolve HDPE and on their wide availability, namely as waste byproducts of existing industries, such as paper pulping and fruit processing. 60,61 It was also taken into account that these compounds have similar properties to those of toluene and p -xylene, such as melting and boiling points, density and viscosity. 62

text: 3.2.1 Optimization of the dissolution conditions. The dissolution of HDPE in limonene has been reported by Ferreira et al. , 39 with HDPE solubility values up to 2 wt%, but only at 110 °C and a minimum dissolution time of 30 minutes. Consequently, the dissolution conditions regarding limonene ought to be optimized. Thus, in this work, the dissolution time and the recovery yields of both HDPE and limonene were studied at temperatures between 100 °C and 120 °C, starting from di ff erent initial HDPE solid contents, up to 5 wt%. The precipitation of the polymer was carried out using ethanol as the antisolvent, in an antisolvent/solvent mass ratio of 2/1.

The dissolution of HDPE in limonene has been reported by Ferreira et al. , 39 with HDPE solubility values up to 2 wt%, but only at 110 °C and a minimum dissolution time of 30 minutes. Consequently, the dissolution conditions regarding limonene ought to be optimized. Thus, in this work, the dissolution time and the recovery yields of both HDPE and limonene were studied at temperatures between 100 °C and 120 °C, starting from di ff erent initial HDPE solid contents, up to 5 wt%. text: Regarding the required dissolution time, corresponding to the moment when a completely clear homogeneous solution was attained, it was observed that it does not depend on the initial solid polymer content within the range studied, implying that the solutions are not close to saturation. No experiments were conducted with larger HDPE initial solid contents due to the enormous increase in the viscosity of the polymer solutions, which causes di ffi culties in the subsequent recovery operations, ultimately compromising the reliability of the obtained results. The dissolution time decreases for high temperatures, although in all samples, HDPE was dissolved in less than 10 minutes (around 7 min at 100 °C, 4 min at 110 °C and 3 min at 120 °C). These dissolution times are significantly smaller than those commonly found in the literature for similar HDPE processes using the same polymer initial concentration range. 26 -29,33,34,36,39,57,59

text: Fig. 4 (and Table S5 in the ESI † ) shows the recovery of HDPE and limonene at di ff erent temperatures and initial solid polymer contents. It was observed that conducting the HDPE dissolution at the temperature of 110 °C yielded the best solvent recoveries, when solutions of 2 -5 wt% HDPE content are used. Up to 3 wt%, this is also the temperature at which most polymer was recovered. Above this polymer content, the HDPE recovery increased at 120 °C but yielded a significantly lower amount of recovered limonene. Taking this into consideration and also the increased handling di ffi culty of the samples containing 4 and 5 wt% HDPE, 3 wt% was established as the higher limit of the HDPE initial concentration. Polymer recovery is significantly reduced below 3 wt%, therefore this content was chosen for further experiments, together with the temperature of 110 °C, due to the increased solvent recovery. Under these conditions, 80.5 wt% HDPE and 47.3 wt% limonene are recovered.

3.2.2 Antisolvent study. The influence of the antisolvent used and the antisolvent/solvent ratio was studied at the aforementioned HDPE dissolution conditions: 110 °C, 3 wt% HDPE in limonene and dissolution time of 10 min. Several alcohols were selected for this antisolvent study, with varying alkyl chain length, number of OH groups and position of these groups in the molecule. Water was also added to the antisolvent screening.

Fig. 4 Recovery yield (wt%) of HDPE (A) and limonene (B) as a function of the concentration of HDPE in limonene solution.

The recovery of the solvent was achieved by adding water to the solvent -antisolvent mixture, which in most cases allows for the nearly complete recovery of limonene with high purity, with the antisolvent rich phase containing less than 2 wt% limonene, according to the ternary liquid -liquid diagrams calculated by COSMO-SAC and provided in the ESI (Fig. S3 -S11 † ). Two exceptions are the systems composed of 2-propanol and 1-butanol, in which the limonene-rich phase is not of high purity. Limonene is not soluble in water, so no further purification step was needed for its recovery.

However, di ff erent antisolvents lead to significantly di ff erent results, which can be further understood by analyzing the solubility of limonene in each one of these compounds, estimated at 25 °C using COSMO-SAC and listed in Table 1. In fact, the highest limonene recovery, above 50 wt%, was obtained using ethanol as the antisolvent, in which limonene is very soluble. Although TGA showed no traces of solvent residues, FTIR spectroscopy was performed to assess if the process had led to any modifications in the structure of the polymer. The FTIR spectra of both pristine and recovered HDPE, in Fig. 6, show the characteristic bands of PE (listed in Table S11 † ). For the α -pinene/ethanol system, the recovered polymer ' s spectrum di ff ers from that of the pristine only in the region between 800 and 1200 cm -1 , although these additional bands do not show clear correspondence with either the solvents or the antisolvents, and are not associated with any weight loss, as TGA had confirmed.

Furthermore, DSC allows comparison of the thermal properties of the pristine and recovered polymer, in particular the melting and crystallization temperatures and enthalpy of fusion, which are directly correlated with the crystallinity of the polymer. No significant changes were observed in any of the aforementioned properties, as shown in Table 3.

It can, thus, be concluded that the polymer was not degraded nor did it undergo significant modifications throughout the dissolution process, and that the removal of the solvent and drying step were e ffi cient, as no traces of α -pinene nor ethanol were identified in the recovered polymer.

3.7 Scaling up and solvent reuse

text:
The viability of scaling up the process of HDPE recovery using the α -pinene/ethanol solvent/antisolvent system was assessed by increasing the initial amount of polymer to be dissolved by 5 times, from 50 to 250 mg. All the ratios between the components were maintained at the optimal values, as well as the temperature (110 °C) and dissolution time (10 min). The results obtained are shown in Fig. 7, and in Table S13 in the ESI. † The possibility of improving the total solvent recovery was also assessed, by adding water and centrifuging the washing solution.

The recovery of HDPE increased nearly 10 wt% by scalingup the process. The most probable cause is that eventual losses related to the experimental procedure become less significant. On the other hand, the increase in scale did not lead to significant changes in the recovery of the solvent. From the washing step mixture, it was possible to recover roughly an additional 17 wt% α -pinene in both cases, resulting a total α -pinene recovery of 73 wt% at the larger scale, similarly to the small scale.

3.8 Process simulation: economic and sustainability analysis

The dissolution -precipitation process of HDPE was simulated as a continuous process, in order to assess the relative impact of each step in its economic performance. For this purpose, a calculation base of 1 kg HDPE per h was used, and the flowsheet representing the simulated process is shown in Fig. 9.

The simulation was performed based on the assumption that the polymer was completely dissolved and precipitated. Mimicking the experimental results attained for α -pinene, a 70% recovery and recycling percentage was considered, and ethanol and water were recycled through distillation and recycled back to the respective operations. Further information on the simulation details can be found in section 2.9 in the ESI. †

The required make-up of each solvent was determined as shown in Table 4, as well as the respective costs. It is clear that the cost associated with ethanol and water is negligible in comparison with that of α -pinene. On the one hand, the unitary cost of this last compound is one order of magnitude above the remaining compounds, but on the other hand, its cost is mostly caused by the incomplete e ffi ciency of its recovery.

The dissolution -precipitation process of HDPE was simulated as a continuous process, in order to assess the relative impact of each step in its economic performance. For this purpose, a calculation base of 1 kg HDPE per h was used, and the flowsheet representing the simulated process is shown in Fig. 9.

The simulation was performed based on the assumption that the polymer was completely dissolved and precipitated. Mimicking the experimental results attained for α -pinene, a 70% recovery and recycling percentage was considered, and ethanol and water were recycled through distillation and recycled back to the respective operations. Further information on the simulation details can be found in section 2.9 in the ESI. †

The required make-up of each solvent was determined as shown in Table 4, as well as the respective costs. It is clear that the cost associated with ethanol and water is negligible in comparison with that of α -pinene. On the one hand, the unitary cost of this last compound is one order of magnitude above the remaining compounds, but on the other hand, its cost is mostly caused by the incomplete e ffi ciency of its recovery.

A more detailed economic evaluation would require further optimization of the energy expenditure, namely by performing heat integration where possible. Nevertheless, even with the suboptimal implemented configuration, the total estimated cost of utilities is 6.9 € per h, compared to 628.3 € per h for raw materials, which represents 99% of the operating costs estimated. Thus, it is evident that α -pinene is the major driver for the economic performance of the process, and therefore solvent recovery is the step of the process that will need the most profound improvements to make this process attractive for industrial implementation. Possible influential factors that could not be optimized at the laboratory scale are the agitation parameters during the precipitation step, the control of the particle dimensions after this step, and the possibility of recovering the solvent evaporated during the drying step.

text: In addition, the process was evaluated from the sustainability perspective, through the EcoScale methodology. 56 α -Pinene recovery is the step with the lowest yield, and thus its value, 70 wt%, was considered representative, corresponding to 15 penalty points. The solvents used do not correspond to any penalty from the price and safety criteria. The unitary operations are conventional, thus not requiring any penalty for the technical setup. The dissolution temperature is associated to 2 penalty points, and the separation and purification operations (filtration, distillation, and washing) account for 6 penalty points. The combined total is 77%, a value that results in a score ' excellent ' of the EcoScale. In spite of the great result, the greatest share of penalty points is associated with the solvent ' s recovery yield, thus reinforcing the need for improvement in this sense.

Both preliminary economic and sustainability analysis reached the conclusion that α -pinene recovery is the main bottleneck of the HDPE dissolution -precipitation process. Despite α -pinene current price, which limits the economic attractiveness of the process, its use should be preferred to that of conventional solvents since it is associated with much less safety and health hazards. 65 The health safety shall also be an important driver to facilitate the licensing of recovered polymers for use in consumer goods such as food packaging. Furthermore, the demand for this solvent has been growing for multiple applications, and its global market size is expected to continue increasing in the next years. 66 This trend has also been a driving force for the search for novel extraction and production methods, which may play an important role in the future price decrease of this compound. 61

The remaining procedure was carried out as usual, with HDPE being recovered as described in section 2.2.1, using ethanol as the antisolvent in the antisolvent/solvent ratio of 2/1, while PET was dissolved and recovered as described in section 2.2.2, dissolved in NaDES at 150 °C and precipitated with a mixture of ethanol and water. text: 80 wt% HDPE was recovered, a value which agrees with the previous results obtained for the single polymer. The average recovery of α -pinene was 55 wt%, although the replicates are less coherent than in previous studies. This value is significantly lower than that observed for the individual studies, suggesting that the additional intermediate filtration step may lead to di ffi culties in the solvent removal during the precipitation step. In fact, it was observed that in general, HDPE solutions start to solidify as soon as the heat source is removed, and the intermediate filtration step to recover solid PET implies a larger amount of time spent between the end of the dissolution step and the addition of the antisolvent, which was not possible to mitigate with the laboratorial set-up used. In this way, it is possible that more solvent was entrapped in the polymer during precipitation, but the drying steps before and after grinding were still e ffi cient, as the FTIR analysis showed similar results to that of the individually dissolved samples (Fig. S27 † ).

80 wt% HDPE was recovered, a value which agrees with the previous results obtained for the single polymer. The average recovery of α -pinene was 55 wt%, although the replicates are less coherent than in previous studies. This value is significantly lower than that observed for the individual studies, suggesting that the additional intermediate filtration step may lead to di ffi culties in the solvent removal during the precipitation step. In fact, it was observed that in general, HDPE solutions start to solidify as soon as the heat source is removed, and the intermediate filtration step to recover solid PET implies a larger amount of time spent between the end of the dissolution step and the addition of the antisolvent, which was not possible to mitigate with the laboratorial set-up used. In this way, it is possible that more solvent was entrapped in the polymer during precipitation, but the drying steps before and after grinding were still e ffi cient, as the FTIR analysis showed similar results to that of the individually dissolved samples (Fig. S27 † ).

text:
Regarding PET, it was possible to recover 84 wt% from the initial amount of polymer, as well as 68 wt% DES. TGA analysis showed a weight loss of PET around 1%, peaking at 150 °C, and the polymer content was 98.4 wt%, according to the thermogram in Fig. S28. † Both the recovered PET and thymol : carvacrol NaDES were evaluated by FTIR analysis (in Fig. S29 and S30, † respectively), showing a complete correspondence with the spectra of the pristine materials.

The melting point of PET, evaluated by DSC, showed a small deviation between the virgin and the recovered samples. The crystallization point, on the other hand, increased around 10 °C. The estimated crystallinity was reduced around 7% with the recovery process, which might be caused by the quick crystallization during precipitation. These values are described in Table 6.

In conclusion, it was possible to selectively dissolve each polymer, e ffi ciently separate and recover both of them while maintaining their integrity and without causing significant changes to the pristine materials.

4. Conclusions

text: In this work, several natural solvents were screened for the dissolution of HDPE using the COSMO-SAC calculation model. The experiments performed on a selection of these solvents, limonene, α -pinene, and p -cymene, showed good qualitative agreement with the predictions for dissolving HDPE. The influence of the experimental dissolution conditions (temperature and polymer content) was observed to influence the quantitative recovery of both the polymer and limonene, the solvent for which these were optimized. The a ffi nity between the antisolvent and the solvent was also determined to be an important factor for the adequate recovery of the system ' s constituents.

In this work, several natural solvents were screened for the dissolution of HDPE using the COSMO-SAC calculation model. The experiments performed on a selection of these solvents, limonene, α -pinene, and p -cymene, showed good qualitative agreement with the predictions for dissolving HDPE. The influence of the experimental dissolution conditions (temperature and polymer content) was observed to influence the quantitative recovery of both the polymer and limonene, the solvent for which these were optimized. The a ffi nity between the antisolvent and the solvent was also determined to be an important factor for the adequate recovery of the system ' s constituents.

text:
The solvent/antisolvent system α -pinene/ethanol was considered to be the most promising, as it allows simultaneously high polymer and solvent recovery with high purity while maintaining their integrity in comparison with the pristine materials. Besides the fact that α -pinene is, by itself, a better option than most common solvents used for these processes, regarding its greener origin and low hazard, the studies conducted also point to the suitability of this system for largescale implementation, as scale-up and solvent reuse experiments were successful. Within the presented sustainability metrics, the proposed process scores as ' excellent ' , but from an economic point of view, the critical aspect of process feasibility will be the recovery of the solvent, which still needs improvement.

The same system was successfully applied to selectively dissolve HDPE from a mixture containing PET, and both polymers and solvents were recovered with good yield and quality, thus indicating the suitability of this dissolution -precipitation process to handle complex waste streams that most recycling processes fail to address.

Received 26 August 1996; received in revised form 16 December 1996; accepted 27 December 1996

Abstract

text:
The dissolution/reprecipitation technique is proposed here for the recycling of polypropylene (PP). It comprises dissolution of the plastic in an appropriate solvent, reprecipitation by using a non-solvent, thorough washing of the material obtained and drying. Furthermore, the solvent mixtures involved are separated by fractional distillation for reuse. In this paper model experiments on virgin material, either in the form of pellets or of commercial pipes for hot water piping applications, are presented. Xylene/acetone proved to be a particularly effective solvent/non-solvent system. Further investigation was focused on the effect of sample history through successive recycling cycles. The recycled grades were evaluated in terms of the following properties: melt flow index (MFI), crystallinity, mechanical performance in tensile and impact mode and grain size analysis. The properties of the recycled grades proved to have no substantial difference from the starting material. © 1997 Elsevier Science B.V.

2.1. Quaternary recycling

text:
According to the first option, the recovery of the locked-in' energy (Quaternary Recycling) is aimed by direct incineration and combustion or conversion to the so called Refuse Derived Fuel [5,6]. This recycling option is currently the most effective way to reduce the volume of organic material which, due to a lack of other recycling possibilities, may then be ended in landfilling disposal. Quaternary recycling has been widely accused as ecologically unacceptable due to the health risk from airborne toxics. Nevertheless, especially polypropylene is an easily burning hydrocarbon product, free from chlorine, sulphur, heavy metals. Combustion by-products are only water, CO2 and negligible quantities of ashes. So when compared to the usual sulphur-containing fuel oils, PP can be considered a pollution-free white coal' [7].

text:
Chemical recycling (Tertiary Recycling) includes pyrolysis, glycolysis, alcoholysis and hydrolysis. In principle, cleavage of the polymer chains results in chemical products of lower molecular weight distribution or even in the original intermediates (monomers) which can be used for another complete cycle of polymerization. In the literature results are referred on the glycolysis of poly(ethylene terephthalate), alcoholysis of polyurethanes, hydrolysis of nylon 6 and pyrolysis of polypropylene [2,8-10]. However, both incineration and chemical recycling are characterized by the fact that the value added during polymerization is lost. At current polymer prices this comprises a major disadvantage [11].

2.3. Primary recycling

text:
In terms of direct recovery (Primary Recycling), reprocessing in the melt phase remains the most popular recycling technique. It ensures simplicity and low cost, especially when done in-plant' and feeding with clean, uncontaminated, single-type plastic scrap of controlled history [12]. Nevertheless, this route often leads to degraded products, because during processing or in-service use a plastic may undergo chemical reactions that can affect its physical properties. If these properties are affected to any marked extent the plastic may become unsuitable for its original use. Screw extrusion is the most damaging procedure that polymers could be subjected to. It involves the mechanical scission of the polymer chain in its viscous environment in the polymer melt. This produces highly reactive macroradicals at the ends of the chain which, in the presence of the small amounts of oxygen dissolved in the polymer, cannot recombine but form peroxyl radicals and hydroperoxides [13].

In our laboratory a dissolution/reprecipitation technique has been studied, aiming to obtain recycled thermoplastics of the highest possible quality. The technique proposed consists of the following stages: (a) cutting the wastes into smaller pieces and washing with water if necessary; (b) dissolution to the highest possible concentration; (c) filtration of the solution under pressure to separate any insoluble ingredients, (d) precipitation of the polymer still in solution by means of non-solvents and (e) filtration, washing the polymer obtained and drying. Furthermore, the solvent/non-solvent mixtures involved are separated by fractional distillation for reuse.

Results published so far include recycling of rigid poly(vinyl chloride) bottles [23,24], polystyrene waste foam [25,26], poly(methyl methacrylate) decorative sheets [27,28], low density polyethylene film for greenhouses [29,30] and high density polyethylene bottles for agrochemicals packaging [31].

text:
Technologies that impart above-average heat deflection temperature, stiffness, hardness, clarity, gloss and barrier to grades establish polypropylene into uses held by higher-priced plastics and traditional materials [32]. Moreover, recycling of polypropylene has a profound environmental impact since it is one major component of the municipal solid waste plastic frame. In 1994 polypropylene constituted about 20% (5 m tonnes) of the total plastics consumption in Western Europe (25.5 m tonnes) [33].

In this paper, the dissolution/reprecipitation technique is applied for the recycling of PP and the combination of xylene/acetone is evaluated under the following criteria: (i) precipitation of the polymer in an acceptable form (granules), (ii) total recovery of the polymer, (iii) total recovery of the solvents employed, (iv) limited quantities, as much as possible, of the solvent and non-solvent employed. Xylene is an effective solvent of PP [17] while acetone is very successful as a non-solvent because the polymer can be precipitated in the form of powder without the formation of gelling lumps. This quenching/precipitating role of acetone to yield a flaky brittle product has been dealt in detail when the dissolution/reprecipitation of polyolefins was studied [29].

Furthermore, it seemed worthwhile to prove that the dissolution/reprecipitation process can be safely applied in successive cycles, since it is carried out at very mild temperatures, in contrast with melt recycling. 4.2. Melt flow index (MFI)

With regard to the melt flow index of virgin and recycled materials (Table 2), increased values for the recycled grades are observed. This behavior could be possibly related with some degradation occurring during the MFI measurement itself because of not adding any antioxidant in the recycled polymer mass. It should be pointed out that in polypropylene degradation is manifested either by reaction with oxygen at elevated temperatures or by chain scission, causing an increase in melt flow (thermal/oxidative degradation) [13,34].

It is worthwhile to mention here that a direct comparison between virgin material and its recycled grades is undoubtedly meaningful, but this is not necessarily the case between the latter and the material recycled from waste pipes. This is because the pipes manufacture process implies completely different history of the material in terms of both processing and additives employed.

The data also suggest that sample history has no practical effect on the mechanical properties of the recycled grades.

4.5. Grain size analysis

According to the grain size analysis (Table 5), over 87% of the recycled polymer mass has a grain size smaller than 1 mm, suitable for feeding polypropylene processing units.

5. Conclusions

The dissolution/reprecipitation technique is studied to recycle polypropylene based waste. Model experiments were run first on virgin pellets and then on polypropylene pipes for hot water piping applications. Concentrated solutions in xylene were employed (0.15 kg·1– ') and the polymer was precipitated, in the form of small grains, through the addition of acetone. Excellent recoveries in polymer and solvents are achieved, while all properties tested remained practically intact. An evaluation of the effect of the sample history on the properties of the recycled product has been also accomplished, but no considerable differences were monitored. Larger scale experiments are expected to result in even higher concentration levels and better recovery values for the solvents used. In accordance with previous studies, the information established provide fundamental input for the development of a selective dissolution process dealing with mixtures of waste plastics.

The composite packaging of liquid food, commonly known as Tetra Pak ® , was an idea of Erik Wallenberg, patented by Ruben Rausing and introduced into the market in 1952 (Rausing, 1969; Tetra Pak Interna tional, 2020a). text: Tetra  Pak  cartons,  i.e.  multilayer  packaging  consisting  of  paper,  low  density  polyethylene  (LDPE)  and aluminium, are widely used as aseptic packages in the food and beverage industry. Paper can be easily recovered from this type of post-consumer beverage cartons (PCBCs) by the pulp industry. The remaining LDPE/aluminium by-product, however, cannot be easily separated to its constituents so currently it is mostly downcycled or used for energy recovery. The aim of this work is to develop an effective process that separates and recovers LDPE and aluminium of high purity and good quality from Tetra Pak cartons. To this purpose, following paper recovery by hydropulping, LDPE and aluminium are separated using a selective dissolution-precipitation (SDP) process. The recovered LDPE is characterized by FTIR spectroscopy, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), differential scanning (DSC) and melt flow rate (MFR) measurements. The findings reveal that the SDP separation process is an effective method to recover LDPE and aluminium from PCBCs.

text: On the other hand, Al and PE can be also recovered from the Al-PE laminates  by  breaking  the  mechanical  bonds  that  keep  the  layers together.  Zhang  et  al.  (2009)  achieved  Al-PE  delamination  using aqueous solutions of organic acids. Al partially dissolved in the solution, so  both  Al  and  acid  were  consumed  to  some  extent.  Reaction  time, temperature, solid size and the type of acid affected separation time and Al loss, which for the optimum conditions was 4.7%. Delamination using mixed  organic  solvents  has  been  also  investigated  by  Zhang  et  al. (2014). In this case delamination occurred due to the swelling of PE. Some  material  loss  was  observed,  lower  that  the  one  obtained  with separation with organic acids. Concerning the efficiency of the separa tion, SEM images of the PE and Al surfaces indicated molecular structure consisting of C, O and Al (Zhang et al., 2015). Al-PE delamination has also found industrial application in China. (Zawadiak et al., 2017).

text: Finally, solvent-based PE extraction methods have been studied for the  separation  of  Al-PE  laminates  coming  from  PCBCs,  where  PE  is dissolved in an organic solvent and separated from the undissolved Al (Kaiser et al., 2018; Lindner, 2011; APK AG). This type of processes, referred to as Selective Dissolution-Precipitation (SDP), is grounded on controlling  and  adjusting  polymer ' s  solubility  by  changing  solvent and/or dissolution conditions and can be effective either for separating mixtures of plastics or for removing impurities/additives from post used plastics. The basic steps of SDP for recovering a certain polymer with high purity involve dissolution of the polymer of interest in properly selected solvent (S) and conditions, removal of the non-dissolved ma terial through filtration and addition of a non-solvent or anti-solvent (AS) so that the polymer precipitates again (Zhao et al., 2018). Start ing from four decades ago, SDP has been extensively studied and suc cessful experimental work has been carried out for recycling a variety of high quality polymers from post-used plastics, such as PVC (Achilias et  al.,  2009b;  Kampouris  et  al.,  1986;  Papaspyrides  and  Diakoulaki, 1986), PS (Achilias et al., 2009a, 2009b; Kampouris et al., 1987;1988; Schlummer et al., 2017), LDPE (Achilias et al., 2009b; Achilias et al., 2007; Papaspyrides et al., 1994), HDPE (Achilias et al., 2007; Poulakis

text: Interest on SDP has gradually faded, mainly because of the low cost of polymers, but lately it has boosted again, since the need to obtain high purity  recyclates  from  plastic  waste  is  recognized  (Sherwood,  2019; Ügdüler et al., 2020). Introduction of a variety of chemical additives into polymers to improve their performance depending on the application, as well as development of composite materials with specific characteristics have resulted to plastic waste of complex composition, which cannot be effectively sorted by mechanical methods and still end up in landfill or are recycled into poor quality plastics (Wagner and Schlummer, 2020). SDP  offers  the  ability  to  remove  additives  (Schlummer  and  M ¨ aurer, 2006) and reinforcements from polymers (Cousins et al., 2019; Knap pich et al., 2019; Tapper et al., 2019) and recycle polymers with quality that meets that of their virgin counterparts, broadening the closed-loop recycling options.

text:
This work aims to the effective separation of PCBCs to their con stituents.  To  this  purpose  hydropulping is  applied for  paper  removal followed  by  SDP  to  separate  the  Al-PE  laminate.  Hydropulping  is  a simple,  well-known  and  widely  applied  technique,  also  for  paper removal from PCBCs, so in this study it is used to provide the Al-PE input material  for  SDP  and  is  examined  only  in  terms  of  the  recoveries  it yields. On the other hand, with regards to SDP, this paper aims to prove its technological feasibility for the separation of Al-PE to recyclates of high quality with high recovery ratios. In this context, the purity of the separated Al and LDPE are examined while for LDPE several properties related to its quality and reprocessability are also investigated.

2. Experimental

2.1. Chemicals and materials

For hydropulping, deionized tap water was used. For SDP, analytical grade xylene and isopropanol obtained from Fisher Scientific were used. Regarding the Tetra Pak ® packages, typical post-used milk and juice containers  were  utilized.  The  lids  were  removed  and  packages  were washed, dried, flattened and stored.

Hydropulping  is  a simple,  well-known  and  widely  applied  technique,  also  for  paper removal from PCBCs, so in this study it is used to provide the Al-PE input material  for  SDP  and  is  examined  only  in  terms  of  the  recoveries  it yields. In this context, the purity of the separated Al and LDPE are examined while for LDPE several properties related to its quality and reprocessability are also investigated.

2. Experimental

2.1. Chemicals and materials

For hydropulping, deionized tap water was used. For SDP, analytical grade xylene and isopropanol obtained from Fisher Scientific were used. Regarding the Tetra Pak ® packages, typical post-used milk and juice containers  were  utilized.  The  lids  were  removed  and  packages  were washed, dried, flattened and stored.

2.2.1. Hydropulping process

text:
PCBCs were cut and mixed with water at a ratio of 1:25 (g/L). The mixture was stirred at 400 rpm for 2 h at ambient temperature until paper swelled and PCBC was split to outer LDPE/paper and inner LDPE/ Al/paper parts. Stirring continued for 3 more hours at 700 rpm to further remove paper fibers from the plastic surfaces. During stirring, water was absorbed by cellulosic fibers forming paper pulp, while the centrifugal forces of stirring contributed to the separation of the pulp from LDPE and aluminium. When hydropulping was completed, the mixture was filtered in order to remove paper pulp from the Al-PE laminate and outer LDPE layer, which were then subjected to an additional hydropulping cycle for 1 h at 700 rpm, in order to remove as much residual paper as possible. Finally, the obtained pulp was filtered for water removal and then  compressed and dried in a Gallenkamp OVA031.XX1.5 vacuum oven at 100 mbar and 40 °C until weight stabilization was observed, resulting to stiff paper. The process flowsheet is shown in Fig. 2.

text: In the first case, Al-PE laminate pieces and xylene, were fed at a ratio of 1:15 (g/mL) into a jacketed, vessel. The mixture was heated to 85 °C and stirred at 300 rpm for 2 h. A condenser was connected to the top of the vessel to minimize solvent losses. The hot solution was filtered to remove insoluble materials (aluminium and paper fibre residuals). The filtrate  was  led  to  another  jacketed  and  stirred  vessel,  where  roomtemperature isopropanol was added drop by drop up to a final ratio of 1.8 AS/S, causing precipitation of the plastic in fine granules, stirring conditions  similar  to  those  of  dissolution.  During  precipitation,  the temperature of the solution was kept at 85 °C by hot-oil circulation in the vessel ' s jacket. Then, heating was interrupted and the mixture was stirred until it reached ambient temperature, then filtered through filter paper and finally compressed to further reduce the remaining S/AS. In order  to  increase  LDPE  recovery  as  well  as  to  further  purify  Al,  the insoluble  material  of  the  first  filtration  was  subjected  to  two  more similar SDP cycles. After the 3rd dissolution the hot solution was first coarse-filtered for Al recovery and then fine-filtered for paper removal. The process flowsheet is shown in Fig. 3.

text:
In order to check the melt reprocessability of the recovered material the  MFR  of  LDPE  was  measured  according  to  procedure  A  of  ASTM D1238, 2013. The temperature was fixed at 190 °C and a capillary die, with length of 8 mm and diameter of 2.095 mm along with a driving weight  of  2.16  kg  were  used  for  the  measurements.  The  procedure involved cutting off the extrudate at specific time intervals as it exited the rheometer, weighing the pieces to determine the average mass and extrapolating to the mass extruded in 10 min by using the equation:

MFR = 600 t ⋅ w (2)

where, t ( sec ) is the time interval and w (g) is the weight of the extrudate material.

2.3.4. Fourier transform infrared spectrometers (FTIR)

FTIR analysis was conducted using a JASCO FT/IR-4200 spectrom eter, performing a total of 32 scans in the range 4000 -400 cm 1 at room temperature, displayed as absorbence vs. wavenumber. A background spectrum was subtracted before sample analysis. Sample was in the form of powder dispersion in a KBr tablet. The spectrum of the examined PE was compared with literature data (Asensio et al., 2009; Gardette et al., 2013; Jung et al., 2018; Noda et al., 2007) for material identification and observation of degradation signs.

Concerning the outer LDPE layer, 7.09 g were dissolved for 2 h in 141 mL S and LDPE precipitated with the addition of 263 mL AS. In this case, recycled LDPE was received as light-coloured agglomerates (Fig. 5 (c)) which indicates the presence of impurities.

3.1.3. Effect of solvent purity on dissolution

4.1 g of recycled LDPE powder were dissolved in 50 mL xylene (S). When dissolution was completed AS was gradually added at a rate of 1 mL/min.  After  the  addition  of  each  mL,  the  mixture  was  left  under stirring for 1 min, and then to rest for another 2 min. At the addition of 13 mL of AS, precipitation was observed and the procedure ended. The final concentration of LDPE in the xylene/isopropanol was calculated equal to 65.1 g/L. Based on the above, it was concluded that presence of isopropanol  up  to  20.6%  v/v  does  not  affect  dissolution  of  LDPE  in xylene, at least not at concentrations like those employed in this work for Al-PE. This suggests that it is not necessary to separate the S/AS mixture to high purity streams for reuse, since recycled xylene with less than ~20% v/v isopropanol is acceptable for mixture concentration up to 65.1 g/L. This is expected to have a positive effect on the distillation

cost especially for large scale application.

3.1.4. Discussion on the sdp solvent requirements

text:
The advantage of SDP to produce recycled plastics of high quality and in proper form for further processing is somewhat countervailed by the large solvent requirements. The dissolved plastic concentration that can be achieved is usually bounded by the solution viscosity, which affects stirring, filtration, etc., especially in a lab-scale apparatus. In this work, polymer solutions up to 50 g/L were obtained, so that they could be  easily  manageable  with  the  available  lab-scale  equipment.  This resulted to a ratio of 133 kg solvents per kg recycled LDPE, which is high both from a technological and an economic point of view and needs to be optimized for scale-up. There is, however, the possibility to use more concentrated solutions as pointed out by Papaspyrides et al., (1994) who applied SDP for LDPE recycling, using LDPE solutions up to 300 g/L in toluene and up to 200 g/L in xylene. Reducing the amount of solvent leads also to the reduction of antisolvent quantities. This suggests that there  is  a  large  margin  for  solvents  saving  and  consequently  lower distillation cost by using more effective equipment.

TGA curves of the inner and outer LDPE samples coming from the SDP process were also obtained and are presented in Fig. 6 (c) and (d). An important conclusion from the TG analysis was that LDPE ' s weight loss, for both inner and outer LDPE, in recycling process temperatures ( ∼ 85 °C) is insignificant. The weight loss of the second sample (outer) was also related to LDPE degradation around 482 °C ( T d), with an onset of degradation at 435 °C (Td, 5%) and char residue at 2 wt% after the temperature of almost 450 °C which indicates presence  of  impurities  such  as  printing  inks. MFR can provide an indication for the recycled plastic processability. The MFR of the recovered inner LDPE was measured equal to 4 ± 0.1 g/ 10 min, lying in the range of melt viscosities for polyethylene grades designated  for  film  production.  Indicatively,  commercial  LDPE  film grades from Polymerc GmbH, Repsol S.A and Sasol Chemicals USA LLC have MFR values from 0.2 to 9 g/10 min (Polymerc GmbH; Repsol S.A; Sasol Chemicals USA LLC). 3.2.3. Chemical structure

FTIR spectrum (Fig. 8 (a)) of the recovered inner LDPE showed the characteristic IR bands of polyethylene (Asensio et al., 2009; Gardette

0,7

et al., 2013; Jung et al., 2018; Noda et al., 2007): the stretching vibration of  carbon-hydrogen  (C -H)  group  of  the  main  polymeric  chain  at 2850 -2918 cm 1 , the wagging vibration of the methylene group (CH2) at 1466 cm 1 and the rocking vibration of CH2 at 719 cm 1 . These two last  bands  present  shoulders  at  1444  cm 1 and at  around 729 cm 1 respectively, which are attributed to the branched character of LDPE, and cannot be found in linear  structures  like  HDPE  (Martínez-Romo et al., 2015). The bending vibration of the methyl group (CH3) at 1377 cm 1 can also be seen and its intensity is proportional to branched chain ends (Jung et al., 2018).

Specific regions of the spectrum were observed to investigate any degradation of the material attributed to the herein applied separation process. The main degradation products of the polyolefins are hydroxyl (-OH)  (3200  -  3650  cm 1 ),  carbonyl  (C = O )  (1630  -  1850  cm 1 ), methylene ( = CH2) (1620 - 1680 cm 1 )  and vinyl (-CH --CH2) (800 1000 cm 1 )  groups  (Moldovan  et  al.,  2012).  Zero  absorbence  in  the region of 900 cm 1 (Fig. 8 (b)) proved the absence of -CH --CH2 groups. However, the appearance of a weak peak at 1701 cm 1 (Fig.  8  (c)) indicated the presence of C = O and the carbonyl index of the recycled LDPE was calculated 0.17. This value is considered low compared to aged LDPE samples after 500 h UV exposure (Luyt et al., 2020) and after 800  h  UV  exposure  (Gulmine  et  al.,  (2003)  that  present  CI > 1. Comparing the results with infrared spectrums of pure LDPE and Al/PE composite obtained from post-consumer aseptic packaging (Lopes and Felisberti,  2006),  it  was  concluded  that  the  polymer  degradation possibly takes place due to processing of LDPE films (Andersson and Wesslén, 2003), production of the multilayer composite or even envi ronmental factors, rather than SDP itself.

text: In  the  present  study,  post-consumer  Tetra  Pak ® PCBCs,  were processed by hydropulping followed by Selective DissolutionPrecipitation (SDP), leading to high recovery of paper, aluminium and LDPE.  The  identified  losses  are  related  to  paper  fibers  and  can  be managed with proper design and technical improvement of the process. LDPE coming from the inner layers was recovered as white powder of high  purity  with  thermal  properties  similar  to  those  of  pure  LDPE. Thermal  analysis  showed  only  some  restricted  degradation,  possibly originated from the virgin LDPE processing rather than the laminate recycling with SDP. On the other hand, LDPE from the outer plastic layer still contained impurities, such as printing inks, suggesting that further purification may be needed depending on the application it is destined for. It was also shown that the presence of AS in the S up to a certain content  does  not  affect  its  dissolution  ability  and  consequently  the effectiveness of the process. This can lead to a reduction of the energy requirements of the process coming from the Solvent/Antisolvent (S/ AS) separation for large scale applications. It, however, increases the time needed for dissolution. In conclusion, the combination of hydro pulping for paper recovery with Selective Dissolution-Precipitation for Al-PE separation is a very promising approach which recovers all the valuable materials that compose Tetra Pak ® cartons.

ABSTRACT: Direct mechanical recycling of multilayer plastic packaging (MPP) leads to downcycling, as the costly barrier layer loses economic value and often degrades the quality of the recycled blend. In this study, a five-layer MPP film consisting of low-density polyethylene (LDPE) structural layers, maleic anhydride-grafted linear LDPE (MAg -LLDPE) tie layers, and an ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) barrier layer was treated with formic acid to selectively extract the EVOH. The effects of the solvent concentration, temperature, sample size, and solvent-to-sample ratio on dissolution efficiency were evaluated, and optimal conditions were identified and scaled in a pilot setup. The polyolefins reclaimed after EVOH extraction were reprocessed into a blend through a conventional mechanical recycling process.

Article Recommendations

text:
Mechanical testing showed that the reclaimed polyolefin blend exhibited enhanced performance compared to the MPP film blend obtained via direct mechanical recycling and demonstrated properties comparable to those of virgin LDPE. Analysis of the chemical structure and rheological behavior revealed that chemical changes of the MAg -LLDPE tie layer via hydrolysis and ring-opening reactions played a key role in affecting intermolecular interactions and consequently the mechanical performance of the reclaimed polyolefin blend. Moreover, the thermal properties of the reclaimed polyolefin blend remained largely consistent with those of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend without dissolution treatment. These findings demonstrate that solvent-based selective dissolution is a practical and scalable method for extracting EVOH and reclaiming polyolefins, enabling subsequent mechanical recycling with satisfactory results.

1. INTRODUCTION

text: As plastic production continues to rise and less than 10% of plastic waste is recycled globally, the environmental and health concerns associated with plastic pollution have driven longstanding efforts to develop effective recycling strategies. 1,2 Among all plastic applications, packaging is the most prevalent, accounting for 40%, with a considerable portion being multilayer plastic packaging (MPP), widely used for food packaging. 3 -6 MPP refers to packaging materials composed of multiple layers of different polymers, each designed to provide specific functional properties and laminated together using tie layers between the polymer layers. 7,8 In MPP used in the food industry, polyolefins such as polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE) are commonly used as structural layers to provide the functions of mechanical strength, moisture resistance, and sealability, while ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) or nylon serves as the oxygen barrier layer, and maleic anhydride (MA)-grafted PP or PE is employed as the tie layer. 3,9 -11

text: Moreover, the presence of EVOH generally has a negative impact on the mechanical properties of the blend because it is incompatible with polyolefins and highly prone to thermooxidative degradation under high temperatures and oxygen atmosphere resulting in cross-linked structures, which are typically encountered during mechanical recycling processes. 18,25 For example, Briassoulis et al. 10 investigated the effect of EVOH on the mechanical properties of an MPP composed of low-density PE (LDPE) and linear LDPE (LLDPE) structural layers, along with a MA-grafted LLDPE (MAg -LLDPE) tie layer. They found that the presence of an EVOH barrier layer resulted in lower tensile strength and elongation at break compared to MPP without EVOH. A systematic study on the changes in the mechanical performance of MPP blends during mechanical recycling was also reported in our previous work. 26 It was observed that the mechanical performance of the MPP blend increased at the initial stage, as the MAg -LLDPE tie layer acted as a coupling agent providing good compatibility between LDPE and EVOH. However, the performance declined significantly after several recycling cycles due to EVOH gelation, which led to severe phase separation between the constituent polymers. Additionally, the color of the MPP blend progressively darkened with increasing cycles due to thermo-oxidative degradation which affects its aesthetics in other applications. Therefore, both economic and performance considerations establish the necessity of extracting the EVOH prior to mechanical recycling. Effective extraction of EVOH for potential reutilization not only saves the economic cost of producing virgin EVOH but also avoids the detrimental effect of the degraded EVOH on the properties of the mechanically recycled MPP.

́

istics and thermal properties comparable to those of virgin EVOH. 27 -30 Notably, Walker et al. 27 developed a solventtargeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP) process to deconstruct MPP into its constituent polymers. This method employed a series of solvent washes to selectively dissolve individual polymer layers, such as PE and EVOH, from MPP. The STRAP process enables the recovery of these polymers with high purity and efficiency, yielding materials that are chemically comparable to their virgin counterparts. Furthermore, Sa nchez-Rivera et al. 29 introduced a temperaturecontrolled polymer dissolution and precipitation approach to improve the STRAP process. By achieving polymer precipitation through controlled cooling, the modified process reduces reliance on antisolvents, thereby lowering operation costs and improving the potential for scalability.
