text: Solvent-based dissolution -precipitation is promising in terms of recycling rate and the quality of recovered materials, and efforts have been made to reduce costs by optimizing the precipitation process. However, as highlighted in recent studies, 18,31,32 there are still significant concerns regarding solvent costs and process complexity, which limit its scalability for commercial applications. Most reported approaches are designed to dissolve MPP layer by layer, starting from the outer structural layers and progressing to the inner ones. Each layer requires a specific solvent, a defined dissolution time, and a corresponding antisolvent to recover the dissolved polymers, which increases the complexity of the recycling process, energy consumption, and overall cost. For relatively inexpensive polyolefin layers, mechanical recycling may be the most widely adopted method, offering advantages such as cost-effectiveness, extensive existing infrastructure, and mature technology. 18,33,34 Additionally, many solvents and antisolvents used in the process are flammable, toxic, or volatile, raising operational safety and environmental concerns. 32 Simplifying or reducing the number of dissolution and precipitation steps could enhance the overall feasibility of the operation.

text: In a recently published work by Tushar et al., 35 both PE and EVOH components were recycled via the STRAP process, which employs cooling for the precipitation steps to eliminate the use of antisolvents. However, two separate dissolution steps were still required to sequentially dissolve the outer PE layer and inner EVOH layer. A combined strategy that applies only a single solvent-based dissolution to selectively extract the EVOH oxygen barrier layer, rather than dissolving each layer sequentially, followed by mechanical recycling of the remaining polyolefins, may provide a more practical, cost-effective, and environmentally friendly solution. This approach avoids handling large quantities of polyolefins, through solvent treatment and reduces the precipitation steps required for their recovery. It enables the recovery of high-value EVOH through dissolution -precipitation for reuse, preserving its high economic value, while allowing polyolefins to be mechanically recycled without the negative impact of EVOH on blend properties. Meadows et al. 30 recently demonstrated the potential of using selective dissolution to remove EVOH from coffee K-cups. However, the potential impact of the selective dissolution process on the structural and mechanical properties of the remaining polyolefin layers remains underexplored. Although the solvent is not intended to dissolve polyolefins, exposure to elevated temperatures and solvent contact may still cause property changes or degradation. Herein this work, we seek to explore this gap in this aspect of this approach.

text: 2.2.1. Lab-Scale Experiment. The lab-scale dissolution experiments were conducted in a 250 mL three-neck flask equipped with a condenser, with nitrogen continuously flowing through the flask to a bubbler to maintain an inert atmosphere. A magnetic hot plate stirrer was used to control both temperature and stirring speed. Formic acid served as the solvent to dissolve the EVOH from the MPP film, while deionized water was used to adjust the solvent concentration as needed. The stirring speed was maintained at 300 rpm, and the solvent volume was fixed at 50 mL for all experiments. The temperature of the dissolution system was controlled in a water bath with the hot plate supplying the heat. The effects of solvent concentration and temperature were investigated by monitoring the mass change of the MPP film samples over time, with formic acid concentrations of 88, 50, and 20% and temperatures of 75, 50, and 25 °C. Five circular samples (25.4 mm in diameter) were cut from the multilayer film and used for each experiment. After the solvent was heated and stabilized at the target temperature, the samples were introduced into the flask containing excess solvent at a ratio of approximately 200 mL/g. Samples were taken out every 30 min to record mass changes until no further change was observed, indicating complete EVOH dissolution. When the film samples were taken out of the reactor at various times, consistent cleaning and drying procedures were applied to each sample. All the samples were cleaned using Kim-wipes and dried at room temperature under the hood.

2.2.2. Pilot-Scale Experiment. The pilot-scale dissolution was carried out under the optimized conditions identified from the labscale experiments, using a 5 L single-jacketed glass reactor (Model JR5L, USA Lab) equipped with a heating circulation bath with silicone oil as the heat transfer fluid. The MPP film was cut into circular samples with a diameter of 16 mm. A total of 120 g of film samples in circular shape was placed into the 5 L glass reactor along with 4.2 L of 88% formic acid, achieving a solvent-to-sample ratio of 35 mL/g. The dissolution was carried out at 75 °C for 1 h with continuous stirring provided by a Teflon mechanical agitator operating at 200 rpm. After dissolution, the formic acid solution containing the dissolved EVOH was collected from the draining port and stored separately. Subsequently, 4.2 L of deionized water was added to the reactor to wash the remaining polyolefins with stirring at 200 rpm for 2 min. This washing step was repeated twice to thoroughly remove any residual solvent. The remaining polyolefins were then collected and dried in an oven at 80 °C overnight. The pilot-scale dissolution experiment was performed twice to collect an adequate amount of LDPE for further mechanical recycling studies.

text:
2.3.1. Thermal Compounding. A 200 g sample of reclaimed polyolefins from the pilot-scale experiment was compounded into a blend using an internal bowl mixer (Model 2128, C.W. Brabender Instruments, Inc.) equipped with two counter-rotating roller blades. Compounding was performed at 200 °C for 5 min at a speed of 60 rpm. After compounding, the molten polyolefin blend was scraped from the mixer using a scraper and allowed to solidify at room temperature.

2.3.2. Grinding. After solidification, the reclaimed polyolefin blend was ground into particles using a low-speed granulator (Model SG-2042NH, Shini Plastic Technologies, Inc.) equipped with a 3 mm sieve. The particles were then dried in an oven at 80 °C overnight to remove moisture prior to injection molding.

2.3.3. Injection Molding. Particles of the reclaimed polyolefin blend were manufactured into test samples using a benchtop injection molding machine (Proto-Ject 150 HP, Manning Innovations, Inc.) and three customized aluminum molds. Tensile testing samples were processed using a preheated mold (180 °C, 10 min) with dimensions of 102 mm × 20 mm × 0.98 mm at 235 °C under a pressure of 57 MPa. Samples for the essential work of fracture (EWF) test and rheological measurement were produced using molds with dimensions of 64 mm × 13 mm × 3.2 mm and 102 mm × 20 mm × 1.5 mm, respectively, at 200 °C under a pressure of 51 MPa.

The EWF concept was first proposed by Broberg 36 in 1968 and has been revived in recent years as a reliable method to evaluate the toughness of materials, particularly ductile polymers. 37 -42 In this concept, the total work of fracture ( W f) includes two components: the EWF ( W e ), which occurs within the inner process zone where crack initiation and propagation take place, and the non-EWF ( W p ), which is related to the outer plastic zone and accounts for energy dissipation through plastic deformation. The EWF is proportional to the ligament area, and the non-EWF is proportional to the volume of the plastic zone. The relationships among W f , W e , and W p are described in eq 1: 43

text: The dissolution kinetics of the MPP film at 50% concentration and 75 °C are shown in Figure 3b. Initially, the weight of the MPP film increased as the film was swollen by solvent penetration in the EVOH layer, which was also found by a measurable increase in film thickness. As the dissolution time progressed, the weight of the film sample began to decrease, reaching approximately 85 wt % of the initial sample weight after 2 h. The weight of the samples remained unchanged thereafter, indicating the complete EVOH dissolution and no more film mass change occurred. Notably, delamination of the outer layers was observed after the inner layer was completely dissolved. However, some of the delaminated films adhered together again after drying due to the presence of tie layers. The dissolution kinetics of the films at different solvent concentrations and temperatures were recorded and summarized in Table 1. Both solvent concentration and temperature significantly influenced dissolution efficiency. A notable improvement in dissolution efficiency was observed with increasing solvent concentration and temperature. Under the condition of 88% concentration and 75 °C, nearly complete EVOH dissolution was achieved within 0.5 h. The complete dissolution was also confirmed using FTIR and DSC in this study, as discussed in later sections.

text: 3.2.1. Tensile Properties. The tensile stress -strain curves of the polyolefin samples from the pilot-scale experiment after one-time mechanical recycling operation are shown in Figure 4a. Virgin LDPE exhibited typical yielding behavior, which was attributed to its inherent high flexibility that allowed easy chain slippage once the critical stress was reached at 10 MPa. A similar yielding behavior was observed for the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, however, the blend displayed a greater strain at break, likely due to improved intermolecular interactions introduced by the MA groups, which enhanced the blend's ductility. In contrast, the multilayer film blend showed no yielding behavior and a smaller strain at break, which was caused by the presence of EVOH. EVOH is inherently rigid and prone to gelling during the thermal compounding process. 10,26 The rigidity and gelling of EVOH restricted chain mobility and prevented easy chain slippage, making the blend stiffer and more brittle, and causing it to deform less and fracture earlier.

text: However, at higher frequencies above 10 rad/s, the complex viscosity of the reclaimed polyolefin blend was slightly lower than that of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend. This difference can be attributed to the reactive MA groups in the virgin LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, which likely formed strong covalent bonds with LDPE radicals generated during hightemperature compounding. In contrast, the MA groups in the reclaimed blend were chemically modified during the dissolution process, diminishing their ability to establish covalent interactions with LDPE. Although hydrogen bonds may still be present, rheological testing at higher frequencies probes smaller structural scales and shorter time scales, which may not be sensitive enough to detect the contribution of the transient hydrogen-bonded network. Interestingly, despite differences in complex viscosity across frequencies, both the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend and the reclaimed polyolefin blend exhibited good compatibility, as evidenced by the near-ideal semicircular arcs in the Cole -Cole plots (Figure 7b). 62 The reclaimed blend displayed a larger arc radius, suggesting a longer relaxation process, while the slight upward tendency observed at the low-frequency region is likely associated with the hydrogen-bonding network. Phase separation was also not observed in the multilayer film blend between LDPE and EVOH, as the MAg -LLDPE tie layer functioned as an effective coupling agent.

text: Similarly, the storage modulus (Figure 7c) and loss modulus (Figure 7d) of the reclaimed polyolefin blend were higher at low frequencies compared to the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend. The elevated moduli at low frequencies are attributed to the formation of intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which enhanced the capability to store and dissipate energy over long time scales. At the crossover point ( G ′ = G ″ ), the frequency for the reclaimed blend (10 rad/s) was lower than that of the virgin blend (25 rad/s), indicating a longer relaxation time resulting from increased intermolecular interactions via hydrogen bonding. This observation is consistent with the larger arc diameter observed for the reclaimed polyolefin blend in the Cole -Cole plot (Figure 7b). The crossover storage modulus of the reclaimed polyolefin blend was around 21,000 Pa, lower than that of the virgin LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend (around 37,000 Pa). This can be interpreted as the result of chemical modifications of MA, which likely disrupted interfacial bonding and uniform chain interactions in the reclaimed blend, leading to increased polydispersity. Notably, compared to the powerlaw dependencies observed in the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend ( G ′ ∼ ω 1.21 and G ″ ∼ ω 0.78 ) in the terminal region, the reclaimed blend ( G ′ ∼ ω 0.81 and G ″ ∼ ω 0.61 ) exhibited greater deviations from the ideal terminal behavior of a viscoelastic polymer melt ( G ′ ∼ ω 2 , G ″ ∼ ω 1 ). 63 These deviations confirm that hydrogen bonding disrupted the reptation process and hindered complete chain relaxation in the reclaimed blend.

text: 3.2.4.2. Time Sweep. Time sweeps were conducted to assess thermal stability, as shown in Figure 7f. Both the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend and virgin LDPE maintained relatively stable storage moduli during the first 25 min, after which the moduli began to increase due to radical-induced cross-linking during thermal aging under high-temperature conditions. 64 The storage modulus of the reclaimed polyolefin blend was comparable to that of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend during the initial 15 min but gradually increased thereafter. Although the reclaimed polyolefin blend exhibited lower thermal stability than virgin LDPE and the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, it was significantly more stable than the multilayer film blend, which showed a rapid and continuous increase in storage modulus from the beginning of the test. This behavior was ascribed to the presence of highly susceptible EVOH, which readily underwent cross-linking reactions under thermal conditions, as reported in our previous studies. 25,26

text: 3.2.5. Thermal Properties. 3.2.5.1. DSC. The melting and crystallization behaviors are presented in Figure 8a,b, respectively. The multilayer film blend exhibited two melting peak temperatures at 112.2 and 180.4 °C, and two crystallization peak temperatures at 102.5 and 159.8 °C, corresponding to LDPE and EVOH, respectively. However, in the reclaimed polyolefin blend, both the EVOH melting and crystallization peaks disappeared, indicating that EVOH was completely extracted after the selective dissolution process. The melting and crystallization peak temperatures of the reclaimed polyolefin blend (112.6 and 101.8 °C) were comparable to those of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend (112.7 and 101.5 °C), suggesting that the selective dissolution process had no significant effect on the melting and crystallization peak temperatures of the reclaimed polyolefin blend. Additionally, the melting and crystallization onset temperatures, as well as the degree of crystallinity, remained largely unchanged in the reclaimed polyolefin blend compared to the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, as shown in Table 2.

3.2.5.2. TGA. The TGA and DTA curves are shown in Figure 8c,d. EVOH exhibited a two-step thermal degradation behavior, with the first mass loss starting around 290 °C, attributed to the dehydration of vinyl alcohol units, and the second beginning near 430 °C, corresponding to the thermal degradation of ethylene segments. 65 LDPE and the LDPE/ MAg -LLDPE blend exhibited a single-step degradation profile, where thermal decomposition was primarily governed by random chain scission of their PE backbone, with the LDPE/ MAg -LLDPE blend showing a higher decomposition onset temperature around 410 °C. 66 The slightly lower decomposition onset temperature of the reclaimed polyolefin blend, compared to the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend, was likely originated from chemical changes of MAg -LLDPE during the dissolution process, which introduced polar groups and reduced its compatibilization effect, thereby weakening the structural stability of the reclaimed blend. However, it remained more thermally stable than the virgin LDPE and the multilayer film blend. DTG results showed that all samples exhibited similar thermal stability in terms of their decomposition temperatures at maximum weight loss rates, except for the multilayer film blend, which displayed an earlier decomposition peak at 390 °C due to the presence of EVOH.

text:
Against the backdrop of the increasingly stringent environmental policies around the world that aim to address plastic pollution (e.g., China's and other developing countries' waste import ban or restriction since 2018), the technology presented in the current study regarding MPP recycling has profound environmental and economic implications.

Due to existing technical barriers of recycling, only 9% of plastic waste is recycled annually, while the majority is landfilled (50%), incinerated for energy recovery (19%), or discarded as litter in the environment (22%). 67 Landfilling occupies valuable land resources and generates microplastics, while incineration releases greenhouse gases and toxic pollutants, such as carbon dioxide, methane, and aromatic hydrocarbons, both posing significant threats to the environment and human health. 68 -70 More than 100 million tons of MPP are produced globally each year, representing a substantial portion of the plastic waste that is landfilled or incinerated. 27 The presented recycling technology has the potential to significantly reduce the quantity of MPP landfilled, incinerated, or littered, thereby reshaping the landscape of MPP waste management and delivering notable environmental benefits.

Furthermore, from an economic perspective, the solventbased dissolution process has been reported to be cost-effective for recycling MPP via layer-by-layer recovery. 28,71 Meanwhile, mechanical recycling is one of the most economical methods for LDPE, with an estimated processing cost of approximately $0.38/kg compared to $1.00/kg for virgin LDPE produced from crude oil. 72,73 The presented recycling method involves applying solvent-based dissolution to remove the EVOH layer, while using mechanical recycling for the remaining LDPE. This combined approach may offer economic potential if the removed EVOH is also recovered. However, further investigation is required to perform a practical economic analysis to provide solid evidence. In future work, a comprehensive assessment could be conducted considering greenhouse gas emissions, toxic pollutants, recovered material selling price, solvent and equipment costs, labor, and other operational factors.

text: A solvent-based selective dissolution approach was applied to a five-layer MPP film for the extraction of the EVOH barrier layer and the separation of the remaining polyolefin layers. Key processing parameters, including solvent concentration, temperature, sample size, and solvent-to-sample ratio, were evaluated for their effects on dissolution efficiency. A condition of 88% formic acid at 75 °C, with a 3.6 mm 2 EVOH exposure area and a solvent-to-sample ratio of 35 mL/g, was identified as an effective condition for dissolving EVOH and reclaiming polyolefins at a 5L reactor. The reclaimed polyolefins, consisting of the LDPE layer and the MAg -LLDPE tie layer, were mechanically recycled through thermal compounding, grinding, and injection molding. The resulting polyolefin blend exhibited higher tensile strain at break and toughness compared to the MPP film blend produced via direct mechanical recycling and demonstrated mechanical properties mostly comparable to those of virgin LDPE, although with reduced tensile strain at break. FTIR analysis revealed that the MAg -LLDPE tie layer underwent chemical reactions, primarily through hydrolysis and nucleophilic ring-opening reactions with the existence of water and formic acid, contributing to the observed changes in material properties. Rheological data indicated that the resulting carboxylic acid and ester groups facilitated hydrogen bonding, enhancing intermolecular interactions within the blend. The thermal behavior of the reclaimed polyolefin blend closely resembled that of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend.

A solvent-based selective dissolution approach was applied to a five-layer MPP film for the extraction of the EVOH barrier layer and the separation of the remaining polyolefin layers. Key processing parameters, including solvent concentration, temperature, sample size, and solvent-to-sample ratio, were evaluated for their effects on dissolution efficiency. A condition of 88% formic acid at 75 °C, with a 3.6 mm 2 EVOH exposure area and a solvent-to-sample ratio of 35 mL/g, was identified as an effective condition for dissolving EVOH and reclaiming polyolefins at a 5L reactor. The reclaimed polyolefins, consisting of the LDPE layer and the MAg -LLDPE tie layer, were mechanically recycled through thermal compounding, grinding, and injection molding. The resulting polyolefin blend exhibited higher tensile strain at break and toughness compared to the MPP film blend produced via direct mechanical recycling and demonstrated mechanical properties mostly comparable to those of virgin LDPE, although with reduced tensile strain at break. FTIR analysis revealed that the MAg -LLDPE tie layer underwent chemical reactions, primarily through hydrolysis and nucleophilic ring-opening reactions with the existence of water and formic acid, contributing to the observed changes in material properties. Rheological data indicated that the resulting carboxylic acid and ester groups facilitated hydrogen bonding, enhancing intermolecular interactions within the blend. The thermal behavior of the reclaimed polyolefin blend closely resembled that of the LDPE/MAg -LLDPE blend.

text:
Overall, this study demonstrates the effectiveness and scalability of solvent-based selective dissolution for EVOH extraction and polyolefin reclamation from MPP. The reclaimed polyolefins can be mechanically recycled into a polyolefin blend with satisfactory performance and may serve as a potential replacement for virgin LDPE in similar applications, as it exhibits comparable properties and, in some cases, such as tensile strength and fracture toughness, even better performance. Future research can focus on EVOH recovery and property characterization, as well as a more comprehensive evaluation of this method's practical environmental and economic feasibility.

text: Efficient recycling of polypropylene (PP) from complex waste streams remains a significant challenge, particu larly for multilayer non-woven materials. Here, we report a rapid dissolution -reprecipitation process for poly propylene recovery using a tailored ionic liquid formed from tris(2-ethylhexyl)amine and 3,3-dimethylbutyric acid.  The  process  operates  at  160 °C under ambient pressure, achieving up to 99% polymer recovery, with complete dissolution occurring in less than one minute. An integrated hot filtration step simultaneously removes pigments and additives, eliminating the need for additional purification stages. The recovered polymer exhibits thermal, structural, and mechanical properties comparable to virgin polypropylene, confirming preservation of polymer integrity. Quasi-elastic neutron scattering (QENS) provides molecular-level insight into the dissolution mechanism, revealing enhanced polymer mobility and plasticisation induced by the ionic liquid. Complementary spectroscopic and chromatographic analyses confirm the chemical stability of the solvent across the investigated temperature range, supporting its potential for reuse. This work establishes a mechanistically informed, solventbased strategy for polypropylene recycling, offering a scalable pathway for recovering polyolefins from complex waste streams.

text: Conventional plastic recycling generally follows two main routes: mechanical  recycling  and  chemical  recycling.  [10] Mechanical  recy cling,  the  most  widely  implemented  approach,  involves  collecting, sorting,  cleaning,  shredding,  and  reprocessing  plastic  waste  through melting and re-moulding or re-extrusion. While this method is relatively straightforward and economically viable, repeated thermal -mechanical processing  often  leads  to  polymer  degradation,  resulting  in  reduced molecular weight, deterioration of mechanical properties, and limited applications for the recycled material. Conventional plastic recycling generally follows two main routes: mechanical  recycling  and  chemical  recycling.  [10] Mechanical  recy cling,  the  most  widely  implemented  approach,  involves  collecting, sorting,  cleaning,  shredding,  and  reprocessing  plastic  waste  through melting and re-moulding or re-extrusion. While this method is relatively straightforward and economically viable, repeated thermal -mechanical processing  often  leads  to  polymer  degradation,  resulting  in  reduced molecular weight, deterioration of mechanical properties, and limited applications for the recycled material. The presence of additives, dyes, and contaminants in the polypropylene waste further complicates me chanical  recycling,  affecting  the  quality  and  consistency  of  the  final product.

Chemical recycling offers several advantages over mechanical recy cling,  particularly  the  potential  to  recover  higher-purity,  virgin-like polymers,  through  the  removal  of  impurities.  [10] Various  chemical recycling approaches have been explored, including pyrolysis, super critical fluid extraction, and dissolution -reprecipitation processes. Py rolysis  and  supercritical  fluid  extraction  are  attractive  due  to  their ability to generate high-value chemicals from plastic waste; however, they typically require high operating temperatures (~400 °C) and spe cialised  equipment,  which  increases  process  complexity  and  cost.  In contrast, dissolution -reprecipitation methods generally operate at lower temperatures  and  require  less  complex  equipment,  making  them promising strategies for the selective recovery of polymers from mixed waste streams. [2]

Most approaches to polypropylene dissolution rely on aromatic hy drocarbons such as benzene and its derivatives, including toluene and xylene, which have demonstrated the ability to dissolve PP at concen trations of ~10% wt/v. [11,12] However, these conventional solvents present drawbacks including high volatility, toxicity, flammability, and their derivation from non-renewable fossil resources.

text: Ionic liquids (ILs) represent a promising yet underexplored alterna tive for PP dissolution and recovery. ILs are salts with melting points below  100 °C,  that  often  exist  as  liquids  at  room  temperature,  and consist of organic cations paired with various anions. [13,14] Unlike conventional  molecular  solvents,  ILs  exhibit  unique  physicochemical properties including negligible vapour pressure, high thermal stability, non-flammability,  and  tunable  chemical  structures.  [15,16] These distinctive characteristics have led to increasing interest in ionic liquids across  diverse  applications,  [17] including  polymer  processing  and separation, e.g. the recycling of carpet waste, [2] energy storage elec trolytes, [18,19] designer solvents for chemical reactions, [20] and CO2 separation and capture. [21,22] However, despite increasing interest in solvent-based polymer recycling, the molecular-level mechanisms gov erning polymer dissolution remain insufficiently understood, particu larly the dynamics of polymer -solvent interactions during dissolution. Advanced analytical techniques are therefore required to probe poly mer -solvent interactions and elucidate the dissolution process.

text: Polypropylene is a highly non-polar polymer composed of saturated hydrocarbon chains, and its dissolution is therefore governed primarily by  dispersion  interactions.  The  long-branched  alkyl  chains  of  TEHA promote favourable hydrophobic interactions  with polyolefin chains, improving solvent compatibility with the polymer. Polypropylene is a highly non-polar polymer composed of saturated hydrocarbon chains, and its dissolution is therefore governed primarily by  dispersion  interactions.  The  long-branched  alkyl  chains  of  TEHA promote favourable hydrophobic interactions  with polyolefin chains, improving solvent compatibility with the polymer. In combination with DMBA, proton transfer generates an ammonium carboxylate ionic liquid containing  both  ionic  character  and  hydrophobic  alkyl  domains.  [2] Such solvent systems can promote polyolefin swelling and plasticisation, enabling solvent penetration into the polymer matrix and facilitating dissolution. In  addition, both  precursors exhibit low vapour pressure and high thermal stability, making them suitable for operation at the elevated temperatures required for polypropylene processing.

Using this solvent system, polypropylene was rapidly dissolved and recovered from non-woven materials, yielding a polymer with proper ties comparable to virgin polypropylene. The recovered polymer was characterised using FT-IR, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), differen tial  scanning  calorimetry  (DSC),  high-temperature  gel  permeation chromatography (HT-GPC), and nanoindentation. Proton nuclear mag netic resonance ( 1 H NMR) spectroscopy was used to confirm the for mation  and  stability  of  the  ionic  liquid,  while  quasi-elastic  neutron scattering (QENS) was employed to probe the molecular dynamics of the polymer -ionic liquid system and provide mechanistic insight into the dissolution process. These results demonstrate the potential of tailored ionic liquids as sustainable solvent systems for efficient polypropylene recycling.

text: To determine the degradation of TA-DA after the dissolution process, a Thermo Surveyor High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) system was used. This system consisted of a pump, an autosampler, and a  photodiode  array  (PDA)  detector,  all  coupled  to  a  Thermo  TSQ Quantum  mass  spectrometer.  A  range  of  sample  dilutions  were attempted to optimise peak shape and establish a linear range. Specif ically, dilutions ranged between 25 μ L mL 1 and 223 fL mL 1 . The in jection volume spanned from 5 to 25 μ L. Ultimately, an injection volume of 5.0 μ L was set, and the concentrations were between 22.7 nL mL 1 and 2.5 μ L mL 1 for acid precursor, and between 227 fL mL 1 and 2.27 nL mL 1 for the base precursor (note that the mass spectrometer is more sensitive to the base). For quantification, the peak area from a selected ion chromatogram at 354 m / z was used to assess the base. Additionally, the PDA peak area at a wavelength of 218 nm was used to quantify the acid. The samples were diluted in varying v /v proportions of IPA and H2O, ranging from 5:95 to 28:72 H2O:IPA. The chromatographic method for the base involved an ACE SuperC18 analytical column, measuring 150 mm in length and 3 mm in diameter, with 3 μ m particle size. The mobile phase was an isocratic mixture of 8:92 H2O:IPA, with a retention time of approximately 8 min. As for the acid, an ACE HILIC-B column of the same dimensions was used, with an isocratic mobile phase of 5:95 H2O:IPA and a retention time of about 11 min.

In this study, we explored a chemical recycling approach for poly propylene  (PP)  recovery  from  disposable  face  masks  using  an  ionic liquid (TA-DA) composed of tris(2-ethylhexyl)amine (TEHA) and 3,3dimethylbutyric  acid  (DMBA).  Proton  transfer  between  the  tertiary amine  (TEHA)  and  the  carboxylic  acid  (DMBA)  produces  a  tri alkylammonium carboxylate ionic liquid. These combined features  facilitate  efficient  dissolution  of  polypropylene  in  the  ionic liquid. The following sections discuss the characterisation of the nonwoven face masks, the dissolution and reprecipitation of PP, and the characterisation and stability of the ionic liquid used in this study.

3.1. Dissolution and reprecipitation of polypropylene

text:
Dissolution of non-polar polymers such as polypropylene typically requires elevated temperatures, and is conventionally achieved using aromatic hydrocarbons solvents, [28,29] which suffer from volatility, toxicity and suistainability profiles. Here, a low-volatility ionic liquid (TA-DA) is introduced as a viable alternative for selective polypropylene recovery from non-woven face masks materials. Temperaturedependent  studies  identified  160 °C  as  the  optimal  operating  condi tion, enabling rapid and efficient dissolution with high selectivity to wards PP.

To evaluate the performance of the proposed solvent system, a pre determined amount of the face mask material, cut into small sections, was introduced into the pre-heated solvent, resulting in rapid dissolu tion of polypropylene, with complete dissolution occurring in less than 1 min. The polymer was subsequently recovered by antisolvent induced reprecipitation using isopropanol (IPA) followed by membrane filtra tion. A schematic of the overall process is illustrated in Fig. 2 .

Using  this  approach,  a  recovery  rate  of  approximately  99%  was achieved for both the polypropylene introduced into the reactor and the ionic liquid solvent.

A solubility study was conducted to better understand the dissolution behaviour of polypropylene from face mask materials and to evaluate the effectiveness of the ionic liquid in the recovery process. Experiments were performed at three different temperatures: 140 °C, 150 °C, and 160 °C.

As shown in Fig. 3a, no measurable dissolution of PP was observed at 140 °C, indicating that significant dissolution occurs only at tempera tures above this threshold. At 150 °C, the maximum concentration of PP in TA-DA reached 9.12 wt/v%, while at 160 °C it increased to 14.28 wt/ v%,  corresponding  to  approximately  a  1.6-fold  increase  in  polymer solubility.  These  results  indicate  that  both  temperatures  can  support polymer  dissolution,  with  higher  temperatures  promoting  increased solubility and improved dissolution efficiency. The observed tempera ture  dependence  is  consistent  with  enhanced  polymer  mobility  and plasticisation effects, as later confirmed by the QENS analysis.

The  solubility  rate  results  shown  in  Fig.  3b  further  highlight  the strong influence of temperature on dissolution kinetics. Increasing the temperature from 150 °C to 160 °C resulted in an approximately 2.7-fold increase in the mean solubility rate and a nearly 3.8-fold increase in the maximum dissolution rate. The overall recovery of PP exceeded 98% at both temperatures. These findings indicate that elevated temperatures significantly enhance both the solubility and dissolution kinetics of PP in TA-DA. Consequently,  160 °C  was  selected  as  the  optimal  operating temperature for subsequent face mask recycling experiments.

3.2. Quasi-elastic neutron scattering

Molecular dynamics during the dissolution of PP in TA-DA has been studied utilising quasi-elastic neutron scattering (QENS). Figs. 4a-c show the QENS spectra of PP, TA-DA, and PP + TA-DA mixture respectively, with Fig. 4d showing the integration of the spectra around 0.0175 to 0.0175 meV, normalised against each sample at 125 °C.

The  integration  window  of ± 0.0175  meV  corresponds  to  the instrumental resolution of the spectrometer. Any dynamics occurring within this resolution window are too slow to be measured and represent elastic scattering, which can be approximated as atoms remaining static on the timescale probed by the instrument ( ≈ 40 ps). Consequently, the integrated elastic intensity provides a direct measure of the fraction of hydrogen atoms that appear immobile on the QENS timescale.

The TA-DA ionic liquid exhibits a single-stage process, showing a gradual and continuous decrease in normalised elastic intensity with increasing temperature. This monotonic decline is expected as the ionic liquid components (cations and anions) gain thermal energy, leading to increased molecular mobility and faster dynamics. The smooth transi tion reflects the intrinsic viscosity decrease and enhanced cation -anion motions with heating.

The  first  stage shows  a  gradual  decline  similar  to  the  individual  components  up  to approximately 140 °C. The second stage is characterised by a sharp drop centred at 140 °C, which indicates a substantial transfer of scattering weight from the elastic component into the quasi-elastic wings, signi fying that polymer segments become dynamically mobile on picosecond timescales. As this pronounced feature is absent in either component alone, it is attributed to polymer -ionic-liquid interactions leading to the onset of polypropylene dissolution at ≈ 140 °C. The sudden mobility increase corresponds to polymer chains or segments gaining sufficient freedom to move independently within the ionic-liquid matrix, marking the  dissolution  of  amorphous  PP  regions  and  the  penetration  of  IL molecules between polymer chains. The third stage occurs around 155 °C and is attributed to the melting of  the  solvated  PP.  In  contrast  to  the  sharp  drop  observed  to  the increased drop in neat PP, this stage involves a more gradual decline in elastic intensity. The decrease of the melting point and the attenuated transition indicate that TA-DA acts as a plasticiser, lowering the effective melting  temperature  of  the  crystalline  PP  domains.  [30,31] The  IL molecules that have already penetrated the polymer matrix disrupt the crystalline structure and reduce intermolecular forces between polymer chains.  [32] Consequently,  when  the  crystalline  regions  melt,  they transition  into  an  already-solvated,  mobile  environment  rather  than undergoing a distinct solid-to-melt transition as observed in neat PP. This plasticisation effect facilitates more  efficient dissolution  by reducing the energy barrier for melting and dissolution of crystalline domains.

This three-stage dissolution mechanism observed at the molecular level supports the solubility studies (Fig. 3), which showed that no PP was recovered at 140 °C as it only started to solvate at this temperature. Whilst the sharp increase in rate between 150 and 160 °C is attributed to the solvation, and plasticisation of the PP at 160 °C.

3.3. Characterisation of non-woven face masks

Disposable face masks typically consist of multilayers of non-woven fabric (see Fig. 6a). Although the exact composition can vary depending on the manufacturer, polypropylene (PP) is the dominant polymer due to its hydrophobic properties and suitability for filtration and protective applications. [33] ATR-FTIR was used to characterise the inner, middle, and  outer  layers  of  the  face  masks  used  in  this  study.  The  spectra exhibited characteristic PP absorption bands, including CH2  and CH3 bending  vibrations  at  1375  cm 1 (symmetric  CH3  deformation)  and 1456 cm 1 (CH2  deformation), as well as C -H stretching vibrations between 2839 and 2953 cm 1 . These spectral features were consistent with those observed for virgin PP, indicating that polypropylene is the primary polymer present in all layers (Fig. 6b). [34]

The thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) results for the different face mask layers and virgin PP are presented in Fig. 6c. All samples exhibit a major weight loss between 350 and 550 °C, corresponding to the ther mal degradation of polypropylene. The degradation profiles of the mask materials  closely  resemble  that  of  virgin  PP,  confirming  that  poly propylene is the dominant polymer in the non-woven fabric layers.

A slightly higher residual mass was observed for the mask materials compared with virgin PP. This residue is likely associated with inorganic additives such as pigments, dyes, or fillers incorporated during mask fabrication. The derivative thermogravimetric (DTG) curves (Fig. 6d) show a single dominant degradation peak occurring between 452.5 and 457.3 °C, which is consistent with the degradation temperature of virgin PP (457.7 °C). The similarity of the degradation temperatures further confirms that the polymer composition of the mask layers is predomi nantly polypropylene.

The  recovered  PP  obtained  from  the  dissolution -reprecipitation process initially exhibited a bluish colour, originating from pigments present in the outer mask layer (Fig. 7). To remove these colourants, an additional hot filtration step was introduced. After dissolution of PP in the  ionic  liquid,  the  solution  was  filtered  at  elevated  temperature through a membrane filter to remove insoluble additives. The filtered solution  was  subsequently  reprecipitated  using  isopropanol  (IPA), yielding colourless PP after a second filtration step, as shown in Fig. 7.

The FTIR spectra (Fig. 8a) of the recovered PP samples, both before and  after  filtration,  show  absorption  bands  consistent  with  those  of virgin polypropylene, indicating that the TA-DA recovery process does not alter the chemical structure of the polymer.

The DSC thermograms (Fig. 8b) show melting and crystallisation temperatures  in  the  ranges  of  158.8 -163.7 °C  and  119.1 -123.9 °C, respectively.  The  enthalpies  associated  with  these  phase  transitions were also comparable to those of virgin PP (Table 1), confirming that the dissolution -reprecipitation process preserves the thermal behaviour and crystallinity of the recovered polymer.

Having established the successful recovery of high-quality PP from face masks, we next examined the chemical stability of the ionic liquid under the applied processing conditions, an important factor in deter mining  the  overall  sustainability  of  our  process.  TA-DA  used  in  this study, along with its precursors (DMBA and TEHA), was analysed using UV -Vis  and  FTIR  spectroscopy  to  evaluate  any  changes  in  optical properties before and after ionic liquid formation (Fig. 9). [37] Addi tionally, solvent samples recovered after polypropylene dissolution at different  temperatures  were  analysed  to  assess  possible  chemical changes  during  recycling.  The  relative  concentrations  of  DMBA  and TEHA were further quantified using HPLC-MS, as shown in Fig. 10 .

The UV -Vis spectra (Fig. 9a -b) show that TEHA exhibits relatively weak absorption in the 275 -400 nm region compared to DMBA. The stronger absorption observed for DMBA arises from the C --O functional group of the carboxylic acid. The TA-DA ionic liquid displays increased absorption  intensity  within  this  region  due  to  the  presence  of  both components in the solvent mixture. Slight increases in absorbance were observed for the used TA-DA samples, which can be attributed to small variations in the acid concentration. This observation is supported by the HPLC-MS analysis described below.

Mass spectrometry identified four major signals at m / z 354( + ), 370 ( + ), 242( + ), and 116( ). The m/z 354( + ) signal corresponds to TEHA, while m/z 116( ) is associated with the DMBA anion. The additional peaks at m/z 370( + ) and 242( + ) correspond to minor impurities orig inating from the commercial amine precursor, namely tris(2-ethylhexyl) amine  N-oxide  and  bis(2-ethylhexyl)ammonium  ions,  respectively. To perform 1 H NMR analysis, solutions were mixed in 10% CDCl3: CHCl3, with recorded spectra shown in Fig. 11, with integrated values of shifts shown in Table 3. The 1 H NMR spectrum of TEHA in CDCl3  ex hibits the expected aliphatic resonances for its three branched 2-ethyl hexyl substituents. Two terminal methyl groups appear as triplets at 0.86 and 0.92 ppm, corresponding to the -CH3 groups at the ends of the alkyl chains. The methylene protons adjacent to the tertiary amine ni trogen  resonate  at  2.06  ppm,  while  the  remaining  methylene  and methine protons give rise to a broad multiplet centred at 1.29 ppm. [39] The integration ratios are consistent with the expected proton distri bution of TEHA (9:9:6:27 respectively).

The spectrum of DMBA displays a singlet at 2.24 ppm corresponding to the methylene group adjacent to the carboxylic acid and a singlet at 1.07 ppm assigned to the tert-butyl methyl groups (9H). A broad singlet at 10.7 ppm is observed for the carboxylic acid proton, characteristic of hydrogen-bonded carboxylic acid species in CDCl3.

The 1 H NMR spectrum of the recovered solvent (TA-DA 160 p-PP) retains the characteristic aliphatic resonances associated with the TEHA alkyl chains and the DMBA tert-butyl and methylene groups, confirming that  the  molecular  backbones  of  both  components  remain  intact following  high-temperature  polypropylene  dissolution.  Notably,  the resonance corresponding to the carboxylic acid proton (~10 -11 ppm) is absent in the recycled sample. Instead, a new broad signal appears at 6.37  ppm,  which  is  assigned  to  the  proton  of  a  trialkylammonium species (R3NH + ). [40] The disappearance of the -COOH signal together with  the  emergence  of  the  ammonium  resonance  is  consistent  with proton transfer and formation of a stable ammonium carboxylate ionic liquid.

Notably,  the resonance corresponding to the carboxylic acid proton (~10 -11 ppm) is absent in the recycled sample. Instead, a new broad signal appears at 6.37  ppm,  which  is  assigned  to  the  proton  of  a  trialkylammonium species (R3NH + ). [40] The disappearance of the -COOH signal together with  the  emergence  of  the  ammonium  resonance  is  consistent  with proton transfer and formation of a stable ammonium carboxylate ionic liquid.

4. Conclusions

text:
In this study, an efficient chemical recycling approach was developed for the recovery of polypropylene from non-woven waste using a hybrid ionic liquid composed of tris(2-ethylhexyl)amine (TEHA) and 3,3-dime thylbutyric  acid  (DMBA).  The  optimised  process  operates  at  160 °C under ambient pressure, achieving recovery rates of up to 99%, with complete dissolution occurring in less than one minute.

Quasi-elastic  neutron  scattering  (QENS)  provided  molecular-level insight  into  the  dissolution  process,  demonstrating  that  the  ionic liquid enhances polymer segmental mobility and plasticisation, thereby enabling rapid dissolution under the applied conditions. Coupled with an  integrated  hot  filtration  step,  the  process  enables  simultaneous polymer recovery and selective removal of additives within a simplified separation method.

The recovered polypropylene exhibits thermal, structural, and me chanical properties within the same order of magnitude as virgin ma terial, indicating preservation of polymer integrity. Spectroscopic and chromatographic analyses (UV -Vis, FTIR, HPLC-MS, and NMR) confirm that the ionic liquid remains chemically stable across the investigated temperature range while maintaining a consistent  DMBA -TEHA composition ratio, indicating its potential suitability for reuse.

text:
Overall, this work establishes a rapid and selective dis solution -reprecipitation strategy for polypropylene recovery enabled by a hybrid ionic liquid. The results show that solvent -polymer interactions govern polymer mobility and phase separation during dis solution -reprecipitation, providing a mechanistic basis for solvent se lection and process optimisation. This study defines a viable solventbased route for recovering polypropylene from complex waste streams and establishes  a  framework for extending such approaches to other polyolefin systems.

text:
Ever since fast fashion has attempted to satisfy the demands of a rapidly growing population(Hämmerle,2011), theglobal waste pollution has increased tremendously. Europe disposes 75% (4.3 million tons) of textiles waste annually due to the absence of viable recycling strategies. (Briga-Sá et al., 2013) Interwoven cotton polyester blendsrepresentoneofthemostprominentmixturesonthemarket, which are difficult to recycle because of their heterogeneity. Conventional fiber spinning processes can partly reuse pure cellulose waste (Shen and Patel, 2010), but they are unable to handle blended waste garments. Therefore, the recycling of cotton polyester blends has yet demanded either the depolymerization or dissolution of either component. The dissolution of polyester usually involves toxic solvents and elevated temperatures (DMSO), which can influence the properties of the cellulose component (Serad, 1993). Accordingly, polyester is preferably subjected to alcoholysis, hydrolysis, or glycolysis reactions ( 1992; Palme et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2013).

Ever since fast fashion has attempted to satisfy the demands of a rapidly growing population(Hämmerle,2011), theglobal waste pollution has increased tremendously. Europe disposes 75% (4.3 million tons) of textiles waste annually due to the absence of viable recycling strategies. (Briga-Sá et al., 2013) Interwoven cotton polyester blendsrepresentoneofthemostprominentmixturesonthemarket, which are difficult to recycle because of their heterogeneity. Conventional fiber spinning processes can partly reuse pure cellulose waste (Shen and Patel, 2010), but they are unable to handle blended waste garments. Therefore, the recycling of cotton polyester blends has yet demanded either the depolymerization or dissolution of either component. The dissolution of polyester usually involves toxic solvents and elevated temperatures (DMSO), which can influence the properties of the cellulose component (Serad, 1993). Accordingly, polyester is preferably subjected to alcoholysis, hydrolysis, or glycolysis reactions ( 1992; Palme et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2013).

text: Less destructive methods utilize ionic liquids (ILs) or NMMO to dissolve the cotton component. Negulescu et al. prepared a 1-2% cellulose solution from cotton polyester blends, and removed the polyester residue by filtration. Afterwards, the cellulose solution was further concentrated up to 15-17% using cotton material from an alternative feedstock (Negulescu et al., 1998). A recent patent further elaborates this approach. An amine oxide solvent such as NMMO is supposed to dissolve the cellulose component of various blended textile products to yield cellulose solutions of up to 35% (Brinks et al., 2013). Similarly, 1-allyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([AMIM] [Cl]) and 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium acetate ([BMIM] [OAc]) have been described to foster the recycling of blended textile waste. The process steps are comparable to NMMO. The ionic liquid dissolves the cellulose component, while filtration removes the polyester residue, and subsequent coagulation recovers the cellulose (de Silva et al., 2014). Although both NMMO and IL based approaches highlight the potential of the generated cellulose solutions to be used in a film or fiber spinning process, neither of them provides any relevant data that could serve as a proof of concept.

text: It is evident that there is a strong need to further develop recycling strategies for textile industry. A viable, ecofriendly concept for circular economy should allow quantitative and ''green' recycling of all material components without the generation of additional waste streams, or an increase in energy consumption resulting from complex processing steps. In many cases, the approaches discussed so far involve the degradation of either cotton or polyester, and therefore impede the simultaneous upcycling of both components within one process. Even more significantly, however, they fail to show the conversion of textile waste to new-value added products, i.e. to employ textile waste as a feedstock to spin new man-made cellulose fibers (MMCFs).

A viable, ecofriendly concept for circular economy should allow quantitative and ''green' recycling of all material components without the generation of additional waste streams, or an increase in energy consumption resulting from complex processing steps. In previous studies, we demonstrated the usage of [DBNH] [OAc] to convert cellulose based waste material such as cotton, cardboard, and paper to new high-tenacity Ioncell fibers (Asaadi et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2016). [DBNH] [OAc] does not require the addition of any stabilizers and allows to adjust the process conditions at temperatures 30 °C lower than for spinning solutions prepared from NMMO. In a current patent, we have also been able to show that this solvent enables the selective dissolution of cellulose in cotton polyester blends without any severe degradation of polyester, if adequate process conditions are applied (Haslinger et al., 2017). Utilizing this concept, the research disclosed herein aims to foster the creation of a circular economy for textile industry by transforming blended cellulosic waste material to new textile grade MMCFs. After filtration, the resulting cellulose solution could thus be used directly as a spinning dope for dry-jet wet spinning (Michud et al., 2015b; Parviainen et al., 2015; Sixta et al., 2015; Stepan et al., 2016) to obtain Lyocelltype fibers ranging from 0.7 to 3.0 dtex. The degradation of the recovered PET was studied dependent on treatment time and temperature. A detailed analysis on the further recyclability of PET such as in melt spinning was however beyond the scope of this study.

text:
2.1. Synthesis of [DBNH] [OAc]

The synthesis of [DBNH] [OAc] is a neutralization reaction of an equimolar amount of 1,5-diazabicyclo(4.3.0)non-5-ene (DBN) and glacial acetic acid. During the addition of acetic acid, permanent cooling is necessary because of the exothermic nature of the reaction. The resulting ionic liquid shows a melting point close to 65 °C and therefore requires stirring at elevated temperatures (80 °C, 1 h) in order to ensure a complete conversion.

2.2. Cotton polyester blend

text:
The cotton polyester blend was supplied by SOEX (Germany) consisting of white postconsumer textiles, which were shredded and blended to obtain a mixture with an overall concentration of 50 wt% cotton and 50 wt% polyester. The sample was pretreated by VTT (Finland) using an ozone based sequence Ew-disk refining-Z-P-A. The target of the alkaline washing stage (Ew) was to remove silicate, whereas ozone (Z) and hydrogen peroxide (P) were used to both adjust the viscosity (DP) and to bleach the material. Acid washing (A) aimed to decrease the metal content. Disk refining targeted to homogenize the sample mixture and to improve the reactivity for the following pretreatment and dissolution stages. The molar mass distributions (MMD) of both cellulose and the polyester fractions were determined by size exclusion chromatography, respectively, as described below. All samples were further disintegrated by the means of a Wiley Mill.

The MMD of the raw material and the spun fibers was determined by gel permeation chromatography (GPC) using a 5 column set up with one precolumn (PLgel Mixed-A, 7.5 -50 mm) and four analytical columns (4 -PLgel Mixed-A, 7.5 -300 mm) equipped with an RI-detector (Shodex RI-101). The samples were dissolved in a 90 g l � 1 LiCl/N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMAc) solution and diluted with pure DMAc in order to obtain a sample concentration of 1 mg ml � 1 in 9 g l � 1 LiCl/DMAc. 100 m l of the respective solution were injected at a flow rate of 0.750 ml min � 1 (9 g l � 1 LiCl/DMAc eluent) at 25 °C. The calibration was conducted with pullulan standards (Mw: 343-708,000 Da) based on a direct-standardcalibration model, in which the molar mass distribution was corrected according to the molar masses of cellulose equivalent pullulan standards (Berggren et al., 2003; Borrega et al., 2013; Michud et al., 2015a).

The limiting viscosity of the raw material before and after its pretreatment was determined according to the SCAN-CM 15:88 standard for viscosity in cupri-ethylenediamine solution.

text:
The cotton polyester blend was mixed with [DBNH] [OAc] (1 h, 80 °C) using a vertical kneader system (cf. experiments [S1], [S2], and [M2] in Table 1) to yield a cellulose solution of 6.5 w%. For [M1], [DBNH] [OAc] was prepared with an excess amount of HOAc in a ratio of 1:1.3 to reduce the degradation of PET. Subsequently, the undissolved polyester fraction was separated from the cellulose solution via hydraulic pressure filtration (70 °C, 1-8 MPa, metal filter mesh with 5-6 m m absolute fineness, Gebr. Kufferath AG, Germany). In experiment [M2], the filtered solution was transferred back to the kneader system and mixed with an additional amount of the cotton polyester blend (1 h, 80 °C) to obtain a final cellulose concentration of 10.5 wt% after filtration. Whereas the resulting cellulose solutions could be subjected to dry-jet wet spinning directly after solidification (storage at 8 °C for a couple of days), the recovered polyester fibers required further purification as they were still contaminated with residual cellulose. Therefore, the polyester residue was extracted with fresh ionic liquid (1 h, 80 °C, vertical kneader). Afterwards, the solvent was removed by filtration and subsequent washing with deionized water. This step was repeated for experiments [S2], [M1], and [M2].

The cotton polyester blend was mixed with [DBNH] [OAc] (1 h, 80 °C) using a vertical kneader system (cf. experiments [S1], [S2], and [M2] in Table 1) to yield a cellulose solution of 6.5 w%. For [M1], [DBNH] [OAc] was prepared with an excess amount of HOAc in a ratio of 1:1.3 to reduce the degradation of PET. Subsequently, the undissolved polyester fraction was separated from the cellulose solution via hydraulic pressure filtration (70 °C, 1-8 MPa, metal filter mesh with 5-6 m m absolute fineness, Gebr. Kufferath AG, Germany). In experiment [M2], the filtered solution was transferred back to the kneader system and mixed with an additional amount of the cotton polyester blend (1 h, 80 °C) to obtain a final cellulose concentration of 10.5 wt% after filtration. Whereas the resulting cellulose solutions could be subjected to dry-jet wet spinning directly after solidification (storage at 8 °C for a couple of days), the recovered polyester fibers required further purification as they were still contaminated with residual cellulose. Therefore, the polyester residue was extracted with fresh ionic liquid (1 h, 80 °C, vertical kneader). Afterwards, the solvent was removed by filtration and subsequent washing with deionized water. This step was repeated for experiments [S2], [M1], and [M2].

2.5. Dry-jet wet spinning

text:
The solidified cellulose solution was placed into a customized laboratory dry-jet wet piston spinning unit (Fourné Polymertechnik, Germany) and heated up according to its rheological properties. The melted spin dope was extruded through a multi hole spinneret (36 holes, 0.1 mm diameter, 0.02 mm capillary length) with a constant extrusion velocity of 1.6 cm 3 min � 1 . The resulting filaments were stretched in an 1 cm air gap by varying take up velocities to achieve draw ratios (DR) between 1-8.8 (DR = vtake-up/vextr) and coagulated in a water bath (10 °C).

2.6. Rheology of the spinning solution

The shear rheology of all spinning dopes was analyzed with an Anton Paar MCR 300 rheometer with a plate and plate geometry

(1 mm gap size, 25 mm plate diameter). Initial dynamic strain sweep tests were performed to define the linear-viscoelastic domain. A strain of 0.5% was chosen for the following frequency tests. All samples were subjected to a dynamic frequency sweep over an angular frequency ( x ) range of 0.01-100 s � 1 at relevant temperatures (40-100 °C). The complex viscosity ( N *) and dynamic moduli (G 0 , G 00 ) were recorded as a function of the shear rate. The zero shear viscosity ( ƞ 0*) was calculated using the cross model assuming that the Cox-Merz rule was valid (Sammons et al., 2008). The cross over points of storage and loss moduli were also determined.

2.7. Fiber properties and total orientation

Linear density (dtex), elongation at break (%), and tenacity (cN dtex � 1 ) of all spun fibers and of 3.3 dtex PET filaments were measured by a Vibroskop and Vibrodyn 400 set up (Lenzing Instrument, Austria) according to DIN 53816 standard (20 mm gauge length, 5.9 ± 1.2 mN/tex pretension, 20 mm/min test speed). The samples were conditioned prior to the measurement (20 °C, 65% humidity) and were tested in both dry and wet state (fiber count: 10). The young modulus (GPa) was calculated from the slope of the average stress strain curve based on the ASTM standard D2256/ D2256.

The total orientation of the spun fibers was determined by a polarized light microscope (Zeiss Axio Scope) with a 5 k Berek compensator. The birefringence ( D n) was calculated from the retardation of the polarized light divided by the fiber thickness assuming a density of 1.5 g cm � 3 for cellulose. In order to obtain the total orientation factor ft, D n was divided by the maximum birefringence value (0.062) of cellulose (Adusumalli et al., 2009).

2.8. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)

The cross sections of the spun fibers were observed on a Zeiss Sigma VP, Zeiss FE-SEM. An acceleration voltage of 1.5 kV was used and all samples were sputter coated with Au prior to the measurement.

2.11. 13 C CP-MAS NMR

The concentration of the residual cellulose in the recovered polyester fraction was estimated by 13 C CP-MAS NMR. All samples were analyzed on a Bruker AVANCE III spectrometer with a probe size of 4 mm employing an UltraShield Plus 400 MHz magnet running at 100.6 MHz. The spectra were recorded at a spinning speed of 8 kHz using a relaxation delay of 5 s and a CP contact time of 2 ms. 8000 scans with an acquisition time of 34 ms were measured. During contact time, a variable crosspolarization increasing from 50% to a maximum amplitude of 85 kHz was used. A SPINAL64 1 H decoupling aimed to decouple the protons during acquisition.

A sigmoidal calibration model was employed to quantify the cellulose content in the polyester residue. The ratios of the peak areas of C1 (cellulose) and C1-8 as well as C2-3-4-5-6 (polyester) were plotted as a function of the cellulose concentration (Haslinger et al., 2019).

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Cotton polyester based textile waste as a raw-material

In previous studies, we were able to demonstrate the conversion of pure cellulose waste to new MMCFs, if the material's properties classified it as spinnable (Ma et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2016). Any recycling concept relying on the dry-jet wet spinning of cellulose is challenged by heterogeneous substrates such as textile waste. Besides the removal of residual contaminants, i.e. synthetic fibers and metals, the cellulose fractions need to undergo certain pretreatments to achieve both an adequate average degree of polymerization ([ N ] ffi 450 ml g � 1 ) and a broad molar mass distribution (MMD) (Michud et al., 2015a). The properties of pre-consumer cotton waste are usually far beyond these criteria due to its high intrinsic viscosity and considerably narrow MMD, which makes pretreatments essential. In postconsumer textiles, laundering induces a certain degree of degradation, leading to an increased polydispersity index (PDI) and a lower intrinsic viscosity, thus allowing milder pretreatments (Palme et al., 2014).

text:
Consequently, the origin of the waste substrate governs the choice of the pretreatment. Whereas enzymes such as endoglucanase hydrolyze cellulose dependent on the amount of amorphous regions in the polymer, acids, e-beam radiation, and hydrogen peroxide cleave cellulose chains with a minor effect on the MMD (Pérez et al., 2002). Moreover, ozone and hydrogen peroxide also enable a bleaching of the waste substrate.

In this work, white postconsumer cotton polyester textiles were treated with an alkaline-disk refining-ozone-peroxide-acid sequence to decrease the intrinsic viscosity [ N ] of the cellulose fraction from 850 ± 50 ml g � 1 to 450 ± 50 ml g � 1 . Although the latter represent optimum conditions for dry-jet wet spinning, the effect of the pretreatment on PET should not be ignored.

Under standardized conditions, 13-15 wt% of cellulose is dissolved in [DBNH] [OAc] at 80 °C resulting in a highly viscous spinning dope. Even when prepared from pure cellulose streams, the solutions need to be filtered prior to their spinning due to certain impurities and undissolved residues. The filtration is demanding and usually requires special equipment (i.e. hydraulic press filtration units) to facilitate the purification of a solution in a highly viscous state (Asaadi et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2018, 2016; Michud et al., 2015b). These challenges increase in case of multicomponent materials, such as cotton polyester blends, and therefore demand adjusted processing conditions.

These obstacles have yet tried to be overcome by the choice of either ionic liquids with low viscosities, or considerably low concentrations of cellulose (Negulescu et al., 1998; de Silva et al., 2014). To compromise between facilitated processing and spinnability, we evaluated dope concentration of 6.5 wt% and 10.5 wt% cellulose implying that the same amount of PET remained undissolved in the ionic liquid solution. The concentration of a spinning solution correlates directly with the properties of the spun fibers. Higher concentrations usually lead to fibers with higher tensile strength, but also require higher draw ratios (DRs) to achieve filaments with titers low enough to be used in textiles (t < 3.0 dtex). This implies that a spin dope concentration of 6.5 wt% can already yield microfibers (t < 1.0) at a DR 8, while the same DR for a concentration of 10.5 wt% is just enough to reach a titer of about 2.0 dtex.

As stated before, the employed dissolution parameters mainly targeted to improve the processability of a blended waste substrate on a lab-scale, and to reduce the continuous degradation of PET throughout the process. We used shorter dissolution times for cellulose in [DBNH] [OAc] (1 h, 80 °C), and tried to add an excess amount of acetic acid (30%) to the ionic liquid (cf. [M1]) to prevent a possible degradation of PET (cf. PET section).

text: In this context, it is important to note that the spinning conditions are determined by the rheological properties of the solution. In principle, any fluid is spinnable as long as the formed filaments can withstand the applied deformation and surface forces (Ziabicki and Takserman-Krozer, 1964a, 1964b). During spinning, a certain DR (vtu/ve) is exerted on the extruded filaments in order to align the cellulose chains coaxially to obtain a higher fiber tenacity and a lower fiber diameter (Hauru et al., 2014; Sixta et al., 2015). A cellulose solution in [DBNH] [OAc] should thus display a N 0* of 20,00030,000 Pas and a COP of 2000-5000 Pa to yield optimum spinning conditions (Asaadi et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2018, 2016; Michud et al., 2015a, 2015b; Sixta et al., 2015). Besides varying concentration and MMD, these parameters can be reached through adjusting the spinning temperature. However, the melting point of [DBNH] [OAc] restricts the spinning window of cellulose solutions of lower concentrations and is evident in the values summarized in Table 3.

text: The spinnability under standardized conditions has been described as follows, DR < 2 non spinnable, 2-8 poor, 8-14 good, 14 < excellent (Asaadi et al., 2016). We redefined these criteria for cellulose solutions of lower concentrations to DR < 2 non spinnable, 2-4 poor, 4-8 good, 8 < excellent, as they require lower DRs to reach fibers with textile grade properties. All samples prepared from pure [DBNH] [OAc], i.e. [S1], [S2], and [M2], showed a good spinnability with maximum DRs of 8, 6, and 8.8, respectively. In case of [S1], the spinning at a DR of 8 led to fibers with a titer of 0.75 dtex, which classifies them as microfibers. The spinning of [M1] was accompanied by the formation of aggregates on the spinneret surface, which led to a maximum DR of 4. As mentioned before, the excess amount of acetic acid reduces the solvent power of the IL and therefore the solubility of cellulose therein, which is consequently reflected in the poor spinnability of [M1].

Besides additives, both the spin dope concentration and the draw ratio influence the tensile properties of dry-jet wet spun fibers. Due to shear forces, the cellulose molecules experience a pre-orientation in the spinneret during extrusion and are further aligned when stretched in the air-gap. As a result, the cohesive forces within the cellulose network increase, which eventually foster the formation of a dense fibrillar cellulose II structure (Fink et al., 2001). A raise in the cellulose content can improve this effect. The properties of the fibers presented in Fig. 2 confirm this principle.

3.3. The effect of [DBNH] [OAc] on PET

text:
In preliminary trials, we could observe a visible degradation of the recovered PET after its processing in [DBNH] [OAc] at 80 °C because of a change in color. PET is usually hydrolyzed under the presence of water and temperatures higher than 100 °C (Buxbaum, 1968). However, several imidazolium based ionic liquids, among them also [BMIM] [OAc], have been described to degrade and partly dissolve PET at elevated temperatures (Wang et al., 2009). These ionic liquids are supposed to catalyze the hydrolysis of PET, whose effectiveness is strongly influenced by the choice of their anion (Liu et al., 2009). Although reported in a number of publications (Brinks et al., 2013; Negulescu et al., 1998; de Silva et al., 2014), a separation of cotton and polyester without any degrading effect on the latter seems questionable.

text: The recyclability of PET fibers strongly depends on its degree of polymerization and purity. Only a high-grade PET substrate is suitable to be re-spun in a melt spinning process, fractions with a lower DP require alternative processing techniques (Venkatachalam et al., 2012). These circumstances inevitably denote the most substantial challenge in the recycling of PET. Any degradation occurring during a separation and recovery process is categorically unwanted. Nevertheless, a fact that yet has often been ignored is that virgin PET, which is converted into textile fibers, already loses its ability to be re-spun during its first melt spinning cycle. Various degradation reactions cause a decrease of the DP of PET before the spun fibers have even been worn once (Samperi et al., 2004). This makes it strictly speaking impossible to recycle PET based textile waste to new fibers without applying any chain extension (Awaja and Pavel, 2005) or depolymerization and repolymerization concepts (Sun et al., 2018a, 2018b). Alternative recycling strategies therefore suggest to separate the PET mechanically from the cellulose component in order to keep a further degradation as a low as possible (Sun et al., 2018b).

However, we still tried to avoid any unnecessary degradation of PET by keeping its treatment time in [DBNH] [OAc] as short as possible during the separation experiments. According to previous results, 1 h appeared effective enough to ensure a complete dissolution of the cotton fraction, and to prevent an extensive degradation of PET (Michud et al., 2015a). To remove any residual cellulose, the PET fraction was filtered off from the cellulose solution and washed with IL and water as described in the experimental section. Table 5 depicts the cellulose content in the recovered PET after the separation experiments. The respective NMR spectra can be found in Fig. S4 in the supporting information.

One washing step in [DBNH] [OAc] (1 h, 80 ° ) was sufficient to decrease the concentration of residual cellulose to 2.5 ± 0.5 wt% (cf. [S1]). The addition of one more washing step further lowered the amount of cellulose to 1.7 ± 0.4 wt% (cf. [S2]). The purity of PET is also confirmed by the TGA shown in Fig. 3c, and does not reveal a major change in the onset temperature To of the recovered fractions [S1] = 397 °C, [S2] = 398 °C, [M1] = 393 °C, and [M2] = 397 °C.

text: The heterogeneity of textile waste represents both a challenge and an opportunity. The different chemical nature of cotton and polyester enables them be separated efficiently, but also demands very specific processing conditions. [DBNH] [OAc] allows a selective dissolution of the cotton component, and a subsequent dry-jet wet spinning of cellulose to textile grade fibers. The spun fibers were found to have properties similar to Lyocell with linear densities between 0.75-2.95 dtex, breaking tenacities of 27-48 cN/tex, and elongations of 7-9%. The recovered PET fraction showed a very lowcellulose content (1.7-2.5 wt%), which could further be reduced onanindustrialscale by a multi-stage dissolution process. However, PET undergoes visible degradation once dispersed in [DBNH] [OAc], which becomes evident in a decrease of its MMD (<51%) and tensile properties (<52%). The presented data clearly demonstrate that cellulose based, blended textile waste has the potential to serve as a feedstock for conventional fiber spinning processes. Commercialization, nonetheless, requires the development of efficient, reliable techniques for sorting and material identification to be able to deal withaheterogeneoussubstratesuchastextilewaste.Moreover,further optimization of the process conditions, especially in terms of dissolution and filtration, might be necessary to limit the degradation of PET. Whereas a certain degradation of cotton is favorable to reduce the consumption of water and chemicals, a high DP of PET is essential to convert it to textile fibers. Therefore, a further possible pathway to recycle the recovered PET fraction might rather include the manufacture of composites or plastic based packaging materials (Joshi, 2001; Zou et al., 2011).

text: This article presents a novel approach for recycling polypropylene (PP) speci  cally derived from used carpets, with the potential for adaptation to other waste streams. The research conducted in this study holds signi  -cant promise for promoting sustainability and advancing circular economy principles. The article focuses on the development of a solventdriven process for the e ffi cient recovery of PP from waste carpets. The use of a solvent operating at mild temperatures minimizes the risks associated with traditional solvents like toluene, while optimizing the e ffi ciency of PP recovery. This innovative approach not only addresses environmental concerns but potentially can provide economic bene  ts by reducing the need for virgin PP production. One of the key highlights of this research is the achievement of a high recovery rate of recycled PP that exhibits qualities comparable to virgin polypropylene. This  nding holds immense value as it not only contributes to the circular economy by diverting waste from land  lls but also provides a sustainable alternative to the production of new plastic materials.

To address these issues, this study presents a novel approach for the recycling of PP speci  cally derived from waste carpets. The focus is on utilizing a proprietary protic ionic liquid (IL) (Fig. S1 † ) operating at a moderate temperature, minimizing the risks associated with more hazardous solvents and optimizing the e ffi ciency of PP recovery. text: The Korsmeyer -Peppas di ff usion parameter ( n ) indicates if the solvent transport or di ff usion is Fickian ( n # 0.5) or nonFickian ( n > 0.5). 19,20 The values for the present study revealed that the dissolution mechanism is Fickian ( n < 0.5), and the correlation coe ffi cient R 2 indicated a high consistency with the model. These results, together with those obtained with the pseudo- rst-order model, suggest that the dissolution of PP in the IL follows a regular di ff usion, but also, that there is a time dependency of the dissolution of PP in the solvent at 160 °C. This can be explained by the variable diameter of the PP  bres and their distinct morphology compared to pellets of virgin PP. This is consistent with the values of n ; the virgin PP with a more de  ned spherical shape of the pellets showed a higher value of the di ff usion parameter. This coe ffi cient is also a ff ected by the solvent thermodynamic characteristics, with the temperature of dissolution being within the melting point of PP. The higher value of R 2 for the dissolution of PP from carpet waste  bres is in correspondence with the faster dissolution compared to virgin PP, as demonstrated by the models analysed in this study.

A high-temperature GPC equipped with di ff erential refractive index (DRI), viscometry (VS) and dual angle light scatter (LS 90 + 15) detectors was used to analyse the molecular weight and molecular weight distribution of the PP from the samples. There is an evident di ff erence between the average molecular weight ( M w) values of carpet waste and virgin PP, being larger than their corresponding recycled specimens a  er the dissolution in the hot solvent (Fig. 5). Interestingly the polydispersity index (PDI) did not vary considerably a  er the recycling process, maintaining a similar broadness in the molecular weight distribution.

Fig. 6 displays a unimodal and broad (PDI $ 2.0) molecular weight distribution 21 in all cases, which is consistent with the explained behaviour. No changes were observed in the virgin PP and its recycled version, and the slight displacement observed in the PP recycled from carpet waste can be attributed to the fact that the carpet waste (raw material) did not fully dissolve during the HT-GPC analysis, so the presence of insoluble materials (such as  llers or pigments), with a very high M w or crosslinked would a ff ect this. Despite this raw material being thermomechanically pre-treated (sink- oat & drying), the additives used during manufacturing can still be present in the PP  bres.

DSC tests were performed to assess the melting temperature and enthalpy of the PP specimens. The results presented in Fig. 8a and b con  rmed the  ndings from the TGA analysis. The melting temperatures of the PP samples fall within the value reported for isotactic virgin PP, 160 -165 °C (Table S1 † and Fig. 8b), and the enthalpies of fusion were within the usual range values found in the literature 22,23 for polypropylene (60 -260 J g -1 ). 24,25

Conclusions

A new, single-step, eco-friendly polypropylene recovery process from carpet waste using a reusable protic ionic liquid as a selective dissolution environment was reported. High yields of polypropylene with similar qualities and properties to virgin PP were achieved. The process was successfully modelled by two di ff erent approaches. The process discussed is a promising candidate as an alternative in the polymer recycling sector.
