text: The XRD diffractogram of the cotton fabric exhibits the typical pattern of cellulose I, characterized by distinct peaks at approximately 14.87, 16.62, 22.78, and 34.52 ° , corresponding to crystallographic planes (010), (110), (220), and (004). On the other hand, the regenerated cellulose derived from the DES displays peaks at 12.02, 20.00, 21.7, and 34.52 ° , representing crystallographic planes (010), (110), (020), and (004), which are characteristic of cellulose II. 41,43 These findings suggest a transformation from cellulose I to cellulose II, accompanied by rapid dissociation and reformation of inter- and intramolecular hydrogen bonds among cellulose molecules during the process. Additionally, the reduced and borderline crystallinity peaks in the regenerated cellulose point toward a decrease in crystallinity, possibly due to unfavorable conditions for cellulose crystallization during the coagulation process.

text: The Fourier infrared spectrum of regenerated PET is very similar to that of original PET (Figure 3a), indicating the stability of the PET structure before and after component separation. Specifically, both samples display phenyl ring skeletal vibrations at the peak of 1410 cm -1 , characteristic group peaks of C  O at 1723 cm -1 , and characteristic group peaks of C -O at 1240 cm -1 . 44,45 Thermal weight loss is an important indicator of the thermal stability of materials. Compared to cellulose regenerated by dissolution, pure cotton textiles have better thermal stability, mainly due to changes in the crystalline structure of cellulose during the dissolution process. As can be seen from the TGA curves of the original PET and the PET after separation (Figure 3c), the ash residue rate (10.8%) of regenerated PET is very similar to that of the original PET (11.0%) under 800 °C, with a temperature difference of only 1.1 °C observed at the temperature of the maximum decomposition rate ( T max ). 44,46 However, the temperature at which 5% of PET decomposes ( T d at 5%) dropped from 400.2 °C (original PET) to 397.8 °C (regenerated PET), which is due to partial degradation of PET during the dissolution process.

This indicates that the solvent has not affected the polyester fibers during the dissolution process; thus, there has been no impact on its performance. Analysis of the curves shows that the glass-transition temperature is approximately 86 °C and the melting point is around 252 °C. 47 These results provide significant reference information for subsequent melt spinning or other processing conditions for the polyester fibers obtained after separation.

text: 3.2. Preparation of Spinning Solution for Separated Cellulose Component. We achieved the chemical separation of polyester/cotton-blended textiles by the directed dissolution of cellulose using a DES of metal salt hydrates. The green solvent laid the foundation for the green chemical recycling of blended textiles. In the wet-spinning process of cellulose, we employed a low-temperature coalkali green solvent system. First, the regenerated cellulose powder obtained after separation with a mass percentage of 6% was added into the prepared low-temperature coalkali solvent. The solution was stirred and dissolved by a high-speed shear dispersion machine to uniformly dissolve the cellulose and produce a viscous spinning solution, which was then wet-spun in a 10% H2SO4/ 15% Na2SO4 coagulation bath, as shown in Figure 4a. The spinning solution formed fibers after solvent exchange in the coagulation bath, as illustrated in Figure 4b. The relationship curve of the viscosity of the spinning solution with the change of shear rate shows that the solution viscosity remains unchanged at a lower shear rate for both solutions of pure cotton and recycled cellulose materials. With an increasing shear rate, the solution viscosity decreases significantly, displaying a typical shear-thinning phenomenon. Within the tested range of shear rates, the viscosity of the pure cotton polymer reduced from 220 to 80 Pa · s, while the viscosity of the recovered cellulose solution decreased from 100 to 30 Pa · s. The decline in the viscosity of the recovered cellulose solution is attributed to the various degrees of breakage in the cellulose molecular chains that occur during the dissolution recovery process, consequently reducing the level of entanglement action among the chains. The microstructure characterization of the regenerated cellulose fibers in Figure 4c shows that after the wet-spinning process, the fibers exhibit a relatively regular circular structure with irregular protrusions on the surface. This can be attributed to the differences in the solvent exchange rates during fiber formation. The regenerated fiber cross section is round and densely structured without any pore formation, indicating a homogeneous structure that was regenerated from the dissolved cellulose solution. The mechanical property curves in Figure 4e reveal that the regenerated cellulose fibers show a slight decline in mechanical performance compared to pure fibers after separation and regeneration. Specifically, the mechanical strength of the regenerated wet-spun fibers decreased from 158 to 135 MPa compared to the fibers directly obtained by dissolving pure cotton textiles, while the corresponding elongation at break also decreased from 11 to 8.9%. This is attributed to the various degrees of breakage in the cellulose molecular chains occurring in the DES of ZnCl2/H3PO4/H2O, which is consistent with the variation results in the viscosity of the spinning solution.

text: 3.3. Structure and Properties of the Regenerated Polyester Fibers. Through the trinary cosolvent of ZnCl2/ H3PO4/H2O, we can effectively achieve the separation of polyester and cellulose fibers. Furthermore, cellulose fibers can be regenerated through wet spinning, while the separated polyester fibers after blending and granulating can be regenerated through hot pressing or melt spinning, as shown in Figure 5a. Additionally, we have conducted a characterization of the rheological properties of the materials before and after recycling. As illustrated by the curve of the polyester fiber's melt viscosity versus shear rate at 240 °C in Figure 5b, the polyester fiber melt exhibits a typical shear-thinning feature. Moreover, the rheological properties of the polyester fibers before and after recycling did not present significant alterations. This further demonstrates that the dissolution and separation of cellulose materials by the DES of metal salt hydrates do not impact the structure and properties of polyester fibers.

text: Furthermore, we simulated the melt-spinning process using a capillary rheometer utilizing recycled polyester fibers. The manufactured regenerated polyester fibers are shown in Figure 5a5. Observations of the microstructure of these fibers by scanning electron microscopy, as seen in Figure 5c 1 -c4 , reveal a smooth surface and a circular shape for the regenerated polyester fibers. There are no visible grooves on the surface, and the cross section appears smooth and round in the presence of micropores. Upon analysis, it is likely that the formation of these pores occurred due to the presence of air during the spinning process. A comparative analysis of the mechanical properties of the polyester fibers before and after recovery and regeneration was conducted. As the recycled polyester fibers underwent two thermal processes: melt mixing and granulation and melt spinning, the polyester molecular chains became significantly fractured. This led to a reduction of over 50% in the mechanical strength and fracture elongation rate of the separated regenerated polyester fibers compared to pure polyester fibers. 47 Hence, it is evident that while melt spinning is commonly used in the recycling of polyester fibers, the initial processing of polyester fibers often involves the addition of various additives such as chain extenders, antistatic agents, and antioxidants. This may lead to severe degradation in the secondary melting process of polyester fibers, causing a decline in the material's performance. Although the separation process in this work of polyester/cotton-blended textiles does not impact the polyester fibers, the melt-spinning recycling scheme for polyester fibers still warrants further discussion and research.

text:
With the DES system based on ZnCl2/H3PO4/H2O demonstrating exceptional cellulose dissolution results and no reactivity with polyester fibers, the two components in polyester/cotton-blended textiles can be successfully separated. The most prominent advantage of the solvent system during the dissolution process lies in its selective dissolution of the cellulose part, with no reaction with the polyester fibers. Also, the system's eco-friendly nature results in separated products not requiring complex post-treatment. Comparative analyses are performed on mixed textiles, pure textiles, and separated components. Experimental results reveal that the solvent system thoroughly separates the polyester fibers and cellulose fibers with no damage to any properties of the polyester fibers. The cellulose solution obtained through the system separation, when treated, can be greenly wet-spun for regeneration. Similarly, the separated polyester fibers can go through hotpressing molding or melt spinning for regenerative recycling. All in all, the DES system based on ZnCl2/H3PO4/H2O not only accomplishes efficient cellulose dissolution but also holds considerable implications for the recycling and utilization of discarded polyester/cotton-blended products.

text:
Multilayer plastic films are widely used materials in the packaging industry [1] with global production exceeding 100 million tons each year. [2] Multilayer films are formed from several layers of common polymers, each of which is selected to contribute useful properties to the film. For example, polyethylene (PE) is chemically inert and serves as a good moisture barrier; ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) is a good gas barrier but a poor moisture barrier; polyvinyl chloride (PVC) has good cling behavior and puncture resistance but is oxygen permeable; and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is rigid and impact resistant but has poor alkali resistance. [3-5] The manufacture of multilayer films employs methods such as co-extrusion, layer-by-layer assembly, extrusion lamination, extrusion coating, adhesive lamination, and solvent casting to combine different polymers for various applications. [6,7] Unfortunately, the resulting materials are extremely challenging to recycle because of their complex compositions and the incompatibility of their different polymer components. text: Solvent-based polymer recycling processes are promising, near-term approaches that exploit differences in polymer solubility to recover polymer resins in pure form from carefully chosen solvent systems that dissolve only target polymers. A few solvent-based plastic recycling processes are being developed industrially. A German company, APK AG, developed a process called Newcycling to recycle low-density (LD)PE/polyaniline (PA) films. [14,15] A solvent-based PVC purification project, VinyLoop, was launched in Italy in 2002 but terminated in 2018 due to challenges in separating hazardous plasticizer additives. [16,17] Unilever and the Fraunhofer Institute launched a pilot project called CreaSolv that aims to recycle PE from packaging materials. [18,19] A Canadian startup called Polystyvert uses essential oils to recycle polystyrene (PS). [20] These examples demonstrate the industrial relevance and broad applicability of solvent-based polymer recycling technologies. However, limited information is available regarding the processing conditions and solvents used in these processes.

Solvent-based polymer recycling processes are promising, near-term approaches that exploit differences in polymer solubility to recover polymer resins in pure form from carefully chosen solvent systems that dissolve only target polymers. A few solvent-based plastic recycling processes are being developed industrially. A German company, APK AG, developed a process called Newcycling to recycle low-density (LD)PE/polyaniline (PA) films. [14,15] A solvent-based PVC purification project, VinyLoop, was launched in Italy in 2002 but terminated in 2018 due to challenges in separating hazardous plasticizer additives. [16,17] Unilever and the Fraunhofer Institute launched a pilot project called CreaSolv that aims to recycle PE from packaging materials. [18,19] A Canadian startup called Polystyvert uses essential oils to recycle polystyrene (PS). [20] These examples demonstrate the industrial relevance and broad applicability of solvent-based polymer recycling technologies. However, limited information is available regarding the processing conditions and solvents used in these processes.

text: Recently, we developed the solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP) process to recycle multiple polymer components from a multilayer plastic film. [8] The STRAP process selectively dissolves constituent polymers through a series of solvent washes, each designed to dissolve only a single polymer component. Pure resins are then precipitated from solution by changing the temperature and/or adding antisolvents. [21] We demonstrated that the STRAP process can successfully recover PE, EVOH, and PET resins from a post-industrial waste film using two solvent washes. [8] In the first solvent wash, toluene was used as a selective solvent and acetone as an antisolvent to recover PE. In the second solvent wash, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was used as a selective solvent and water as an antisolvent to recover EVOH. The remaining polymer component of the film was PET, which was recovered after removal of the other polymer components. The STRAP process highlights the feasibility of recycling multiple polymers from complex multilayer films.

text: There are several important design considerations underlying a solvent-based polymer recycling process like STRAP, including the selection of an appropriate solvent and antisolvent for each polymer component, the choice of temperature for dissolution and precipitation, and the selection of an optimal solvent/antisolvent ratio for precipitation. These considerations impact process design and corresponding process economics. The key information needed to quantify tradeoffs between different operating conditions and solvent systems is the temperature-dependent solubility of each polymer in a proposed solvent system. Experimental data on the solubility of common polymers in some solvents are readily available. For example, Bloch summarized solvents and non-solvents for a large library of polymers, [22] while Zhao et al. reviewed solventbased methods for waste plastics recycling [23] and listed solvents and nonsolvents for PS, polycarbonate (PC), PE, PP, PET, acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), and PVC with detailed experimental conditions. However, experimental collection of solubility data in the large number of possible solvents is prohibitively time-consuming, limiting the design of solvent systems for selective dissolution.

text:
To more rapidly screen potential solvent systems, various empirical solvent parameters are available to identify possible solvents/nonsolvents for a given polymer; examples include Hildebrand, [24] Hansen, [25] Kamlet-Taft, [26] Gutmann, [27] and Swain [28] parameters. Among these, Hansen solubility parameters (HSPs) are the most widely used for selecting solvents for polymer dissolution. Tabulated HSP values are available for most common polymers and solvents, and solvent screening based on HSPs has many successful applications. [29] Computational methods can also be utilized for solvent selection. For example, Chandrasekaran et al. trained a deep neural network for the binary classification of solvents/nonsolvents using over

4500 homopolymers and 24 common solvents with an accuracy of 93.8%. [30] In general, these various approaches focus on qualitatively distinguishing solvents and nonsolvents for a given polymer at room temperature and are most accurate for singlecomponent solvent systems. Quantitatively predicting temperature-dependent solubilities remains a challenge, which is the gap this research aims to fill.

text: Herein, we demonstrate a computational approach to quantitatively predict temperature-dependent polymer solubilities in different solvent systems. This approach improves upon the methodology that we previously employed to guide solvent design for the STRAP process, [8] which was suitable for qualitatively identifying potential solvent systems but overestimated polymer solubilities. Our approach employs classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and the conductor-like screening model for real solvents (COSMO-RS). We first model a polymer as a single oligomer molecule and simulate its motion in a dilute solution by MD simulation to obtain various conformations of the oligomer molecule. From this trajectory, we select representative conformations that span a range of structural parameters and use these as input to COSMO-RS for solubility calculations. We show that systematic variation of numerous simulation parameters leads to solubility predictions in good agreement with experimental solubility measurements for PE and EVOH in DMSO, water, tetrahydrofuran (THF), hexane, ethyl acetate, ethanol, acetone, toluene, and dimethylformamide (DMF). These predictions also outperform qualitative solubility predictions obtained from analysis with HSPs. We then demonstrate the applicability of the approach by screening a large library of 524 solvents at different temperatures to identify selective solvents for PE and EVOH dissolution. This computational approach thus can be used to screen solvents for solvent-based polymer recycling schemes and can be performed rapidly enough to guide process design.

A MD simulation of a single oligomer was performed in dilute solution to obtain a simulation trajectory of various oligomer conformations.

Molecular dynamics simulations

text: Atomistic MD simulations were performed in the isothermalisobaric ensemble using Gromacs 2016. [31] Each MD simulation contained 1 oligomer molecule (PE or EVOH) and 216 solvent molecules. PE was simulated in toluene and EVOH in water. All polymer and solvent molecules were parameterized using Antechamber and the Generalized AMBER force fields. [32,33] The simulation system was initialized with a cubic box containing a single polymer. The system was then solvated, energy minimized, and equilibrated for 2 ns in an NPT simulation at 300 K and 1 bar using a velocity-rescale thermostat and Berendsen barostat. A 10 ns NPT simulation was then performed at the same temperature and pressure using the Nose-Hoover thermostat and Parrinello-Rahman barostat. All simulations were performed using a leapfrog integrator with a 2-fs timestep. Verlet lists were generated using a 1.2 nm neighbor list cutoff. Van der Waals interactions were modeled with a shifted Lennard-Jones potential and Verlet cutoff-scheme that was smoothly shifted to zero at 1.2 nm. Electrostatic interactions were calculated using the smooth Particle Mesh Ewald method with a short-range cutoff of 1.2 nm, grid spacing of 0.14 nm, and 4th order interpolation. Bonds were constrained using the LINCS algorithm. All thermostats used a 2.0 ps time constant and all barostats used a 2.0 ps time constant with an isothermal compressibility of 3.0 × 10 5 bar 1 .

Conformational sampling and conformer selection

text: The MD trajectory of the oligomer molecule samples a large number of conformations as a function of simulation time. Since it is prohibitive to input all these conformers to COSMO-RS, we selected a set of representative conformers based on two structural parameters: the radius of gyration ( R g ) and the solvent-accessible surface area (SASA). We hypothesized that sampling conformers that capture a range of these parameters would provide reliable data to COSMO-RS for solubility predictions (see below). Figure 3 shows values in the two-dimensional R g-SASA space generated from the MD trajectory of an EVOH oligomer. R g and SASA values are normalized to a range from 0 to 1. Each blue dot corresponds to a conformer. We selected a set of conformers from this space by superimposing a square grid over the point cloud and selecting conformers closest to each grid intersection; sampled points are shown in red in Figure 3. The grid density can be tuned to control the number of conformer samples. Alternative methods for sampling conformers are discussed in the Supporting Information. In this work, 30 conformers of PE and 40 conformers of EVOH were studied.

Solubility prediction with COSMO-RS

text: COSMO files from the DFT calculations were input to COSMO-RS for property evaluation. COSMO-RS predicts the thermodynamic properties of multicomponent systems based on quantum mechanical calculations and statistical thermodynamics methods. [38,39] The chemical properties of each molecule are represented by the probability distribution of the screening charge densities (called the σ -profile) which arise at the molecular surface due to polarization within a virtual conductor environment. σ -profiles are obtained using DFT calculations as described in the preceding section. Once σ -profiles are known for all system components, the chemical potential of the solute is calculated based on molecular surface contacts and used to determine solubilities, solvent boiling points, and other thermodynamic properties. COSMO-RS was originally developed for liquid-liquid and liquid-vapor systems, and has been extended to solid compounds [40,41] and polymers. [42] We used σ -profiles of oligomer molecules with deactivated terminal groups to approximate the σ -profile of a polymer. [43] Since the screening charge density and resulting σ -profile depend on the specific molecular conformation, the MD simulation and conformational sampling steps described above were used to generate a set of oligomer conformations that span a range of possible σ -profiles. σ -Profiles for all selected conformers were then used to calculate the chemical potential of the polymer to enable predictions of polymer solubility via a solid-liquid equilibrium calculation [Eq. (1)]:

Experimental measurements of solubility

text: Experimental solubility measurements for PE and EVOH in DMSO, water, THF, hexane, ethyl acetate, ethanol, acetone, toluene, and DMF were performed to benchmark the computational predictions. The resins are LDPE and EVOH35 (molar ratio 35%:65% ethylene/ vinyl alcohol). These solvents were selected because they are commonly used in experiments, while the polymers are common components of flexible plastic packaging. The experimental set up consisted of a 250 mL round bottom flask connected to a reflux condenser with a cold-water supply line. The round bottom flask contained a specific solvent amount for the experiment ( � 30 g). In each experiment, the round bottom flask was partially submerged in a 1500 mL dish containing silicone oil as a heat transfer fluid. The system was heated to the desired polymer dissolution temperature with an electric heat plate equipped with a magnetic stir drive and the stirring rate was adjusted to have constant mixing. After the solvent reached the dissolution temperature, 1 wt% of polymer virgin pellets (with respect to the solvent) was added to the round bottom flask and mixed at a constant rate. If the polymer or part of the polymer was dissolved after 30 min, an additional 1 wt% of polymer pellets was added to the solvent. This procedure was repeated every 30 min. Once no further polymer could be dissolved, an additional 1 wt% was added to ensure an excess of undissolved polymer. After the final 30 min, the round bottom flask was removed from the oil. The liquid contents were poured into an antisolvent, either acetone or water, to precipitate the dissolved polymer. The precipitated material was filtered out of the solvent mixture, washed with water, and vacuum dried overnight. The undissolved solids remaining in the flask were also washed with water and vacuum dried overnight. The fractions were weighed after drying and the solubility was determined based on the amount of dissolved polymer with respect to the amount of solvent used. In some cases, the solubilities were regarded as a lower limit since there was a viscosity increase of the solvent (such cases are indicated below). The mass of the undissolved solids was included to complete the mass balance in each experiment.

Results and Discussion

Experimental solubility data

To develop a new workflow for quantitative polymer solubility prediction, we first present experimental measurements of PE and EVOH solubility in nine common solvents to provide benchmarks for comparison to COSMO-RS and HSP predictions. Table 1 shows experimental measurements of polymer solubility at elevated temperatures (close to the boiling point of each solvent).

HSP-based solvent screening

We first utilized HSPs to qualitatively identify good and poor solvents for PE and EVOH to compare against the measured solubility data. The HSP system assigns each compound (polymer and solvent) three parameters that account for dispersion ( δ D ), polar ( δ P), and hydrogen-bonding forces ( δ H ). text: Table 3 shows R a /R 0 values for the nine solvents tested experimentally for PE and for EVOH. Each value is formatted based on comparison to the experimental solubility data: values of R a /R 0 < 1 are bold if the experimental solubility is greater than 1 wt% and normal if the experimental solubility is less than 1 wt%, whereas values of R a /R 0 > 1 are bold if the experimental solubility is less than 1 wt% and normal if the experimental solubility is greater than 1 wt%. Excluding DMSO, the HSP values for EVOH generally were good predictors of experimental solubility data. The room-temperature DMSO value is also near the threshold and would likely be identified as a good solvent if temperature effects were included. However, different sets of HSPs for PE lead to different solvent screening results. Surprisingly, the HSPs of high-density (HD)PE resulted in a perfect match with the experiments, even though the polymer used experimentally was actually LDPE. The data for PE (1) and LDPE (2) correctly classify 8/9 solvents, but PE (2), LDPE (1), and LDPE (3) perform worse with only 5-6 correct classifications each. Moreover, the errors are generally due to HSP values identifying poor solvents as good (i.e., R a /R 0 values are erroneously low), which cannot be attributed to temperature effects. Since it can be unclear which of these values to select in advance, there are clear deficiencies with using HSP values for screening solvents for these polymers. Similarly, the solubilities of EVOH in DMSO and DMF are substantially higher than that of PE in toluene even though the ratio R a /R 0 for PE in toluene tends to be much lower, highlighting that HSPs cannot provide quantitative information on solubility predictions. These observations motivate the need for alternative methods for solubility predictions.

We sought to develop a quantitative solubility prediction workflow using COSMO-RS to improve upon the deficiencies of HSPs noted above. We first systematically compared the impact of several parameters by predicting solubilities for PE as a simple homopolymer for which HSPs were shown to be inaccurate. Since the computational modeling of a full-length polymer molecule is formidable, the polymers were modeled as oligomers. The oligomer chain length was thus the first parameter we considered: increasing the chain length will increase the computational cost of the DFT calculations (the most time-consuming step in the COMSO-RS workflow) but could increase prediction accuracy. Consequently, there is a potential tradeoff between prediction accuracy and computational time that must be quantified to guide the solubility prediction workflow.

To select a reasonable chain length, PE oligomers with 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, and 24 carbon atoms were selected. MD simulations were performed of each oligomer and 3 conformers of each length were randomly selected. Each conformer was then input separately to DFT and COSMO-RS solubility calculations, with the latter using literature values for the melting point and heat of fusion of PE. text: With the oligomer chain length determined, we next studied the impact of the number of conformers on the tradeoff between prediction accuracy and computational cost. Different chain conformations have different screening charge density profiles that can influence the solubility prediction results, with substantial differences possible given conformational flexibility of the oligomers. From the MD trajectory, we selected a set of 30 representative conformations that span a range of R g and SASA values for the 12-carbon PE oligomer using the grid sampling method. A series of subsets of different sizes (1, 3, 5, 10, and 20 conformers) were then generated by randomly selecting each number of conformers from the 30. 10 subsets were generated for each chosen subset size. Figure 5 shows the mean prediction error and DFT calculation CPU time as a function of the number of conformers (defined following the approach of Figure 4), with each point representing the average over all 10 subsets. The computational time required to generate a conformer set linearly scales with the set size. The mean prediction error decreases as more conformers are used and the error values tend to plateau as the number of conformers increases, again indicating that the COSMO-RS predictions can be systematically improved. Based on this comparison, the conformer number was selected to be 10 for the final solubility predictions.

With the oligomer chain length determined, we next studied the impact of the number of conformers on the tradeoff between prediction accuracy and computational cost. Different chain conformations have different screening charge density profiles that can influence the solubility prediction results, with substantial differences possible given conformational flexibility of the oligomers. From the MD trajectory, we selected a set of 30 representative conformations that span a range of R g and SASA values for the 12-carbon PE oligomer using the grid sampling method. A series of subsets of different sizes (1, 3, 5, 10, and 20 conformers) were then generated by randomly selecting each number of conformers from the 30. 10 subsets were generated for each chosen subset size. Figure 5 shows the mean prediction error and DFT calculation CPU time as a function of the number of conformers (defined following the approach of Figure 4), with each point representing the average over all 10 subsets. The computational time required to generate a conformer set linearly scales with the set size. The mean prediction error decreases as more conformers are used and the error values tend to plateau as the number of conformers increases, again indicating that the COSMO-RS predictions can be systematically improved. Based on this comparison, the conformer number was selected to be 10 for the final solubility predictions.

text: The 10-conformer set of the 12-carbon PE oligomer was used for final solubility predictions to compare to the experimental data. The solubility predictions in Figures 4 and 5 used the melting temperature and heat of fusion data of PE from literature sources, which leads to a relatively large error (Supporting Information). [45] However, the properties of PE resins could vary substantially between different samples, particularly since the heat of fusion will depend on polymer crystallinity. Therefore, we instead utilized the experimental solubility of PE in toluene at 110 °C as a reference value for the solid-liquid equilibrium calculation for all solvents. Table 4 shows corresponding predicted and experimental solubilities. As expected, the COSMO-RS protocol predicts near-zero solubilities for all solvents other than toluene in good agreement with the experimental measurements. Notably, several of these solvents are predicted by some sets of HSPs to be good solvents (e. g., hexane, THF, and ethyl acetate; see Table 3), indicating that the COSMO-RS approach qualitatively outperforms the HSP approach as well as providing quantitative solubility estimates. The COSMO-RS approach does slightly overestimate solubilities in nonsolvents, but these results are highly consistent with the experimental benchmarks if 2 wt% is used as a threshold to distinguish solvents and nonsolvents.

We performed a similar process to compare the influence of oligomer length and the number of conformers on solubility predictions for EVOH. Since EVOH is a copolymer, we utilized the block copolymer oligomer structure for predictions when varying these parameters (to ensure a consistent monomer sequence), then compared predictions using the block, alternating and random copolymer structures (Figure 2). Figure 6 shows the mean prediction error and computational cost as a function of oligomer chain lengths between 8 to 32 carbon atoms in increments of 6 carbon atoms. This increment corresponds to 3 monomer units to maintain the 1:2 ethylene/vinyl alcohol ratio. For each oligomer length there are 3 conformers randomly selected from the MD trajectories. Based on the tradeoff between prediction accuracy and computational cost shown in this figure, the 14-carbon EVOH oligomer was selected because of the relatively low error values in a short computational time. This oligomer has 2 ethylene units, 4 vinyl alcohol units, and 2 methyl end groups.

text: To further illustrate the effect of conformers on solubility predictions, Figure 8 shows the predicted EVOH solubility in DMSO as a function of temperature. Experimental data at four temperatures are included for reference. Predictions were based on either 1, 5, or 20 EVOH conformers, with 10 separate subsets of conformers used for predictions. Predicted solubilities with only a single conformer varied substantially and lie with the region indicated by the light blue color. The region bounding the solubility predictions decreased substantially for the 5conformer sets (light green region). For the 20-conformer sets, the solubility calculations are highly consistent leading to a deep blue region that nearly converges to a solid line such that variations are difficult to discern by eye. These results indicate that increasing the number of conformers both leads to a decrease in prediction accuracy (Figure 7) and decreases the variation between different subsets of conformers, suggesting more robust results. Moreover, all conformer sets exhibit reasonable agreement with experiments, with the final results (for 20 conformers) slightly overestimating the measured solubilities but exhibiting similar trends.

text: Unlike PE, EVOH is a copolymer that has two different monomer units. The arrangement of these units leads to different types of structures. As shown in Figure 2, three types of structures were compared using oligomers with 14-carbon chain lengths and 20 conformers per oligomer. For this comparison, the experimental solubility of EVOH in DMSO at 95 °C was used as the reference for the solid-liquid equilibrium calculation. Table 5 compares solubility predictions to the experimental data. Clearly, DMF was recognized as a good solvent in all three cases, but only the block structure result correctly identifies it as the best solvent in the list. Solubilities are somewhat overpredicted for experimentally identified nonsolvents, with ethanol being the most notable deviation. However, the values clearly differentiate solvents and nonsolvents, with a slightly higher threshold (3 wt%) required to distinguish these categories than is necessary for PE. With respect to quantitative predictions, the random structure has the lowest overall mean prediction error, which is consistent with the fact that EVOH is a random copolymer. [46]

text: To demonstrate the power of the proposed computational solubility prediction method, we applied the COSMO-RS protocol to identify selective solvents for PE and EVOH from a large library of 524 solvents. We note that the results in Tables 4 and 5 (and corresponding experiments) indicate that DMSO and DMF are selective solvents for EVOH (by promoting high EVOH solubility and low PE solubility) whereas toluene is a selective solvent for PE; the screening procedure thus seeks to identify additional selective solvents beyond these examples. As above, a 10-conformer set of 12-carbon PE oligomers and a 20conformer set of 14-carbon EVOH oligomers were used. The solubilities were computed at room temperature and 1 °C below the boiling points of the respective solvents. For this screening procedure, we define selective solvents as solvents with a solubility greater than 10 wt% for one polymer and lower than 1 wt% for the other. Table 6 shows some selected examples of identified selective solvents; full solubility prediction results are available in the Supporting Information. At room temperature, the PE solubility was < 1 wt% in all solvents considered, so no PE-selective solvents were found in this condition. PE-selective solvents were identified when temperatures were increased near the solvents' boiling points. EVOH-selective solvents were found at both room temperature and elevated temperatures. The calculations for this large-scale solvent screening were completed within 2 h since no new MD or DFT calculations were required, demonstrating the efficiency of this computational approach.

text: The computational efficiency of this solvent screening approach enables its application to the selection of solvents for solvent-mediated plastic recycling processes, such as the STRAP process described in our previous work. In our first STRAP process, pure DMSO was used to dissolve EVOH from a multilayer plastic film, and then water was added as an antisolvent to precipitate the polymer. [8] The computational approach presented in this work is more accurate than the prior approach due to the newly developed methods for conformational screening and oligomer length selection, suggesting that it can be applied to improve the recovery of polymers in revised STRAP processes. For example, our prior work selected solvents for STRAP based primarily on solubility considerations; technoeconomic analysis was then performed to evaluate the minimum selling price of the recovered materials necessary for economic feasibility. The computational screening approach could instead be applied to identify solvents that both selectively dissolve target polymers and reduce downstream costs associated with polymer recovery and solvent recycling, leveraging the computational efficiency and improved accuracy described in this work. The computational approach could also be utilized to identify temperature-controlled polymer dissolution and precipitation at fixed solvent compositions to reduce the use of antisolvent and improve process economics. [21] Another example application would be to search for green solvents (quantified by metrics such as energy demand and greenhouse gas emissions in solvent production or environmental health and safety rankings [47,48] ) as potential replacements for common industrial solvents, permitting quantification of tradeoffs between greenness and solubility behavior of the solvents. There are thus multiple opportunities to apply the computational protocol developed in this work to efficiently identify solvent systems that improve selective dissolution processes for plastic recycling.

The computational screening approach could instead be applied to identify solvents that both selectively dissolve target polymers and reduce downstream costs associated with polymer recovery and solvent recycling, leveraging the computational efficiency and improved accuracy described in this work. The computational approach could also be utilized to identify temperature-controlled polymer dissolution and precipitation at fixed solvent compositions to reduce the use of antisolvent and improve process economics. [21] Another example application would be to search for green solvents (quantified by metrics such as energy demand and greenhouse gas emissions in solvent production or environmental health and safety rankings [47,48] ) as potential replacements for common industrial solvents, permitting quantification of tradeoffs between greenness and solubility behavior of the solvents. There are thus multiple opportunities to apply the computational protocol developed in this work to efficiently identify solvent systems that improve selective dissolution processes for plastic recycling.

Conclusions

text: In this work, we present a computational approach to quantitatively predict temperature-dependent polymer solubilities in various solvents. Our approach employs molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and conductor-like screening model for real solvents (COSMO-RS) calculations. The MD simulation models a polymer as an oligomer and simulates its motion in a dilute solution to generate various chain conformations. Representative oligomer conformers that span a range of radius of gyration ( R g ) and solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) values are then used as input structures to COSMO-RS solubility calculations. We note that while this work uses COSMO-RS, we expect that alternative COSMO-based models (e. g., COSMOSAC) may also be suitable for this approach. [49] We studied the effects of oligomer length, conformer numbers, and copolymer structures on the accuracy of solubility predictions. We show that increasing the oligomer length and number of conformers can systematically improve prediction accuracy, albeit with increased computational cost. By selecting a reasonable oligomer length and number of conformers, the proposed approach leads to solubility predictions in good agreement with experimental measurements for polyethylene (PE) and ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) in DMSO, water, THF, hexane, ethyl acetate, ethanol, acetone, toluene and DMF. These predictions outperform qualitative Hansen solubility parameter (HSP)-based solubility predictions while also enabling predictions of temperature-dependent behavior, and lead to more accurate predictions than the protocol employed in our past work. [8] We demonstrated the applicability and efficiency of the new computational approach by screening 524 solvents to identify selective solvents for the dissolution of PE and EVOH at two temperatures. Future work will apply this protocol to additional polymers, including both industrially relevant polymers and biopolymers (e. g., lignin) that must be solubilized prior to depolymerization. A current limitation of the method is the need for a single experimental solubility measurement in a good solvent as input to account for sample-specific parameter. While a suitable reference good solvent could be identified by initial qualitative screening using HSP values, future work will aim to reduce the amount of needed experimental input by incorporating explicit consideration of polymer molecular weight and crystallinity.

A B S T R A C T

text: Plastics are widely used materials composed of polymers and various additives to achieve specific properties. Their composition is often highly complex, particularly in post-consumer plastic waste. As mechanical recycling faces increasing limitations, chemistry-driven strategies are attracting growing interest to improve plastic re covery. Among these, dissolution recycling offers the possibility of selectively recovering pure polymers free from additives and contaminants. However, the absence of efficient methods to separate and analyze the different components of plastics remains a major bottleneck to evaluate recycling processes effiency. Here, we report the first application of Centrifugal Partition Chromatography (CPC) to address this challenge using polyvinyl chlo ride (PVC) as a model material. A biphasic solvent system based on heptane, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and 3pentanone (DEK) (25/45/30 w/w/w) was developed, guided by Hansen solubility parameters. CPC enabled the separation of the polymer from organic additives and contaminants, as well as the fractionation of additives into distinct groups, facilitating their subsequent identification and potential quantification. Moreover, CPC allows the recovery of sufficient amounts of purified polymer, enabling detailed spectroscopic characterization to assess its  structural integrity and purity. After fractionation, additives were identified by reverse phase liquid chro matography coupled with tandem high resolution mass spectrometry (RPLC -HRMS/MS), while the recovered polymer was analyzed using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). Overall, these results demonstrate that CPC is a promising tool to fractionate complex plastic matrices, offering  new  opportunities  for  advanced  material  characterization  and  supporting  the  development  of  more efficient recycling processes.

text: Today, methods to characterize plastic waste, including their aging, are limited due to the complexity of the matrix. The two parts of plastics (polymer  and  additives)  are  characterized  differently  and  by  conse quence, their separation is required. In literature, different solid/liquid extraction methods exist, as microwave assisted extraction, accelerated solvent extraction, ultrasonic assisted extraction, soxhlet, etc [6]. The dissolution-precipitation method is also well known as a purification method and continue to be developed [7]. However, this method pre sents limits as capture of additives during reprecipitation or degradation of polymer with high temperature involved [8]. In particular, multiple steps are required to fully recover additives with dissolution-precipitation and obtain a purified polymer. For instance, one  study  demonstrated  that  at  least  seven  purification  steps  are necessary to separate DEHP from PVC resin [9]. text: Centrifugal  partition  chromatography  (CPC)  is  a  well-established method for purifying natural materials. It can also be used to purify macromolecules such as proteins or to fractionate some complex mix tures such as lignocellulosic hydrolysates [24 -27]. This type of chro matography involves two immiscible liquid phases, similar to liquid-liquid  extraction:  one  serves  as  the  stationary  phase  and  the other as the mobile phase. The compounds in the sample are distributed between the two phases according to their affinity for each. Their sep aration depends on their partition coefficients, defined as the ratio of solute concentrations in the stationary and mobile phases. A low parti tion  coefficient  indicates  a  high  affinity  of  the  solute  for  the  mobile phase. During CPC, the mobile phase flows through the stationary phase, which is retained in the CPC cells by centrifugal force. Compounds with higher affinity for the mobile phase elute more quickly, corresponding to higher partition coefficients. One major advantage of CPC is its versa tility:  a  tailored  biphasic  solvent  system  can  be  designed  to  match  a specific  sample  matrix,  provided  the  two  phases  remain  immiscible. Moreover,  both  the  mobile  and  stationary  phases  can  be  recovered, enabling complete recovery of the sample without loss.

text: This study presents the first application of CPC on plastic materials. It purposes a methodology to separate additives and polymers from plastic without degrading them, focusing on PVC -based materials. Inspired by the  use  of  CPC  as  a  purification  technique  for  natural  products,  the methodology aims to extract and purify molecules of interest -specif ically  additives  such  as  phthalates -and  the  polymer  itself  from  a complex matrix. The main advantages of CPC, as previously discussed, include  its  versatility,  complete  sample  recovery,  and  suitability  for preparative-scale applications. In the context of plastic characterization, separating additives from the polymer is essential to facilitate accurate analysis. CPC is therefore employed to recover all organic additives in one phase while the polymer remains in the other, enabling its total purification  and  recovery.  The  initial  step  consisted  of  identifying  a biphasic solvent system adapted to the PVC matrix, using Hansen solu bility parameters and refining it through the UNIFAC method to ensure stability. The CPC method was then developed using a model feedstock containing a plasticizer from a regulated family (phthalates), and the additive fractions were characterized by liquid chromatography coupled with electrospray ionization high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-ESIHRMS) to confirm complete additive removal. The polymer resin was finally characterized by SEC and FTIR to assess its purity and potential degradation.

The chromatographic system was hyphenated to a trapped ion mobility quadrupole-time-of-flight mass spectrometer (timsTOF, Bruker Daltonics, Germany) through an electrospray ionization (ESI) interface (Apollo II, Bruker Daltonics, Germany) for analyte detection.

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Optimization of CPC operational parameters

This study presents a method for separating a polymer from additives using a model formulation. The objective is to identify a solvent system that retains the polymer in one phase while extracting and recovering the additives in the other. To achieve this, the system must satisfy four key criteria:

 both the polymer and the additives must be soluble in the solvent system  without  any  precipitation,  to  avoid  damaging  the  CPC equipment and to enable their separation.

 the solvent system must form two immiscible liquid phases.

 effective  separation  in  CPC  requires  the  additives  to  partition between the two phases, while the polymer remains exclusively in one (Figure S2). This behavior is reflected in the polymer ' s partition  coefficient,  which  should  ideally  approach  infinity, indicating  complete  retention  in  a  single  phase -unlike  the additives.

3.1.1. Selection of biphasic solvent systems

The key to selecting an effective solvent system lies in its ability to solubilize compounds and separate them without causing precipitation.

In  CPC,  three  commonly  used  biphasic  solvent  systems  are:  the ARIZONA system (heptane, ethyl acetate, methanol, water), the OKA system (hexane, ethyl acetate, n-butanol, methanol and water) and the acetone  scale  (heptane,  toluene,  acetone  and  water)  which  together cover most cases in natural product purification [24]. When these sol vents are incompatible with the samples -resulting in precipitation -alternative approaches using ' good ' solvents can be considered [29]. This is referred to as the good solvent approach for CPC solvent system selection,  which  has  been  described  in  the  literature  when  standard systems  are  ineffective  [25,30,31].  In  this  study,  the ' good ' solvent approach is applied using HSPs as a guiding tool.

text:
HSPs are used to characterize the solubility of a polymer in a solvent. They are three parameters: δ D  (quantify the strength of dispersion in teractions), δ P (quantify the dipole-dipole interactions) and δ H (quantify the hydrogen bonding interactions). Theses parameters are determined theoretically  or  experimentally  for  a  solvent  or  a  solute  and  can  be represented on a 3D diagram with the three parameters as coordinates.

For polymers, an additional parameter is introduced, represented by a sphere centered at the point corresponding to the polymer ' s Hansen Solubility Parameters (HSPs) in the three-dimensional HSP space. The radius of this sphere (R ₀ ) defines the boundary for ' good ' solvents. The geometric distance (Ra) between a solvent and the polymer in the 3D HSP space indicates how compatible they are. If the ratio R ₀ /Ra is greater than  one  -  meaning  the  solvent  lies  within  the  polymer ' s  solubility sphere - the solvent is considered ' good ' [10].

The same goes for additives, the geometric distance Ra can be used to determine which solvent is the most likely compatible with them. The smaller Ra is, the more compatible they are:

Ra² = 4 ( δ D 1 δ D 2 ) ² + ( δ P 1 δ P 2 ) ² + ( δ H 1 δ H 2 ) ²

text:
The first step involves selecting the most suitable solvent for dis solving PVC. DEK was chosen for this purpose, with Ra values (distance in  Hansen space) of 2.4 MPa 1/2 from PVC and 3 MPa 1/2 from DIDP, indicating it is likely a good solvent for both the polymer and the plas ticizer. Next, heptane was selected for its ability to dissolve the phthalate (Ra = 7.2 MPa 1/2 ) while being a poorer solvent for PVC. This is reflected by its location at the edge of the PVC solubility sphere in the HSP dia gram, suggesting limited compatibility with the polymer. Finally, DMSO was chosen as a third solvent to establish a biphasic system. In the HSP space, it is positioned opposite to heptane, promoting phase separation. However, DMSO still lies within the PVC solubility sphere (Ra = 9.6 MPa 1/2 ),  ensuring  that  the  polymer  remains  dissolved  and  does  not precipitate. (Table 2)

To create a stable bi-phasic system for CPC separation, the ratio of solvent was determined with a ternary diagram (Fig. 2). This diagram was built with the software ASPEN V11 and based on UNIFAC theory [34].

Finally, DMSO was chosen as a third solvent to establish a biphasic system. In the HSP space, it is positioned opposite to heptane, promoting phase separation. However, DMSO still lies within the PVC solubility sphere (Ra = 9.6 MPa 1/2 ),  ensuring  that  the  polymer  remains  dissolved  and  does  not precipitate. (Table 2)

To create a stable bi-phasic system for CPC separation, the ratio of solvent was determined with a ternary diagram (Fig. 2). This diagram was built with the software ASPEN V11 and based on UNIFAC theory [34].

text:
The solvent ratios were selected to ensure compatibility with both the polymer and the additive. PVC should not be exposed to excessive amounts of heptane (e.g., 50 %), as this may lead to precipitation of the resin. Conversely, the phthalate additive (DIDP) should not be in contact with high concentrations of DMSO (e.g., 50 %) to avoid immiscibility issues. As previously mentioned DEK is not considered a limiting sol vent, due to its good compatibility with both components. In this study, a heptane/DMSO/DEK (w/w/w) ratio of 0.25/0.45/0.30 was used. This solvent system proved to be stable, with a phase separation time (also called demixing) of less than 30 s after shaking. The upper phase con sisted of 62.0 % (w) heptane, 7.8 % (w) DMSO, and 30.2 % (w) DEK, while  the  lower  phase  consisted  of  7.7  %  (w)  heptane,  61.4  %  (w) DMSO, and 30.9 % (w) DEK.

The sharing of components between phases is represented by parti tion coefficients, as compiled in Table 4. These partition coefficients are initially  estimated using HSPs and then confirmed experimentally by SEC analysis of each phase. For the HSP estimation, the lower the Ra value, the higher the affinity of the solute for the phase. This estimation helps  determine  whether  the  CPC  method,  along  with  the  identified solvent  system,  can  effectively  separate  plasticizers  from  the  PVC polymer.

In the end, the four prerequisites for developing a suitable solvent system were validated: the organic fraction of the plastic (polymer and organic additives) is totally soluble, the system is biphasic and stable, the polymer remains in the lower phase and the additives of interest are shared between the 2 phases.

3.2. CPC method development: elution-extrusion

The CPC method is divided in two parts: the elution and the extru sion. After the equilibration of the two phases in the CPC cells at a given flow, the solute is injected. The mobile phase flows through the sta tionary phase and is recovered during the elution part. The stationary phase  is  then  extruded  (pushed  out)  from  cells,  it  corresponds  to extrusion part.

The choice of the solvent system leads to the polymer being present in the lower phase, while the additives are distributed between both phases. The mobile and stationary phases are then selected to promote the partitioning of the different sample components according to the separation objectives. To enable the separation of the additives from each other and from the polymer, the upper phase is selected as the mobile phase. Since the polymer is expected to elute with the extrusion fractions, it should preferentially remain in the stationary phase.

text:
To  characterize  the  elution  fractions  with  potential  additives,  a RPLC -HRMS method is used. The RPLC provides another dimension of separation while HRMS enables a supervised screening. The Fig. 4 shows the two-dimensional separation obtained, with the CPC separation as a function  of  the  LC  separation.  This  cartography  was  built  from  the Extract Ion Chromatograms ( ± 0.005 Da). Principal organic components present in the PVC model sample were annotated according to mass accuracy  ( < 2  ppm)  and  isotopic  pattern  accuracy.  Specifically,  the phthalate DIDP and its isomers were found in the fractions 11 and 13 between 17.4 and 18 min. ESO, chemically corresponding to epoxidized triglycerides, was found in different fractions (10 to 40) and the wax, identified as oxidized polyethylene, was found in fractions 10, 11, 12, 16, 17 and 18.

This cartography allows for conclusions about the recovery of each soluble organic additive from soft PVC in the CPC elution fractions, with these  additives  being  separated  into  distinct  elution  fractions.  This separation is driven by the interactions of each component with the two phases, governed by HSPs, including dipole-dipole interactions, hydrogen bonding, and dispersion forces. In this study, the objective was to separate the polymer from its organic additives, and CPC successfully facilitated this separation.

3.4. Extrusion fractions: recovery of PVC resin

At  the  end  of  the  previous  additive  separation  and  their  total recovering,  the  extrusion  step  is  done.  The  extrusion  fractions  are combined. They contained the polymer dissolved in a solvent incom patible with subsequent analyses. Then to recover polymer, 500 mL of MeOH are added to  the  300  mL  collected  during  CPC  extrusion  for polymer  precipitation.  The  solution  was  filtered  on  Büchner  with cellulose filter. The powder was recovered and dried at 70 °C in oven for 4 h. SEC analysis was then performed to characterize the resin fraction recovered after CPC separation. This analysis yields multiple pieces of information: the refractive index (RI) signal allows quantification of the PVC resin  using  the  appropriate dn/dc value,  while  molar  mass  and intrinsic  viscosity  measurements,  obtained  via  universal  calibration, provide insights into potential polymer degradation [36]. A quantitative analysis by weight confirms the total recovery of the resin.

To  compare  results  with  current  literature:  S.  Wagner  and  M. Schlummer employed the dissolution-precipitation method -currently considered  the  reference  technique  for  PVC  resin  purification -to remove phthalate-type plasticizers from post-consumer flooring mate rials [9]. The authors report a reduction in DEHP concentration from 100,000 ppm to 60 ppm. However, the dissolution-precipitation process, as currently described in the literature, focuses primarily on the removal of  phthalate  plasticizers,  with  a  particular  emphasis  on  DEHP,  while other additives such as stabilizers are not addressed. In contrast, the CPC-based  approach  enables  the  removal  of  all  organic  additives regardless of their chemical nature or functional role. Furthermore, CPC allows for the recovery of pure PVC resin in a single step, compared to the seven purification steps required for dissolution-precipitation.

4. Conclusion

text: The lack of techniques for separating polymers from all additives and recovering them for characterization remains a major obstacle to the development of physical  recycling  processes.  CPC,  typically  used  for purifying natural products, is applied here for the first time to plastics fractionation. The selection of the two-phase solvent system is critical to the performance of this technique and often requires numerous labo ratory tests. In this study, a more theoretical approach based on HSPs is proposed. This approach facilitates solvent selection with fewer exper imental tests by providing insights into the parameters governing the solubility  of  both  the  polymer  and  representative  additives,  such  as phthalates.

For  a  soft  PVC  the  DMSO/heptane/DEK  system  proved  effective, enabling the complete recovery of the polymer while removing all sol uble organic additives and offering a first dimension of additive sepa ration. These results were validated using RPLC -HRMS analysis of the additive fractions, and FTIR and SEC analyses of the polymer fractions. Importantly, the recovered polymer was pure and remained structurally unaffected by the CPC fractionation process. This method demonstrates its  effectiveness  in  simplifying  complex  plastic  formulations  by  fully isolating soluble organic additives, making it a valuable tool for char acterizing materials such as PVC.

CPC can also be used as a quality assessment method during recy cling, allowing the characterization of plastics through the detection of polymer degradation and the quantification of regulated additives (such as phthalates) and impurities prior to processing. The flexibility of the technique supports its application across a wide range of thermoplastics and polymer-based materials. Moreover, by adjusting the solvent system ratios, CPC can be adapted to achieve tailored separations according to specific objectives -whether focused on time efficiency, solvent usage, or targeting compounds for removal. This adaptability highlights CPC ' s strong potential for broad applications in plastic analysis and recycling.

1. Introduction

text:
Plastics are an essential part of the world economy and are used in different market sectors. In 2021, 390.7 Mt of plastics were produced globally, of which 90.2% were fossil-based, 8.3% were produced from post-consumer recycled plastics and 1.5% were bio-based plastics. The biggest annual producer in 2021 was China (32% of the total produc tion),  followed  by  the  free  trade  zone  of  'United  States,  Canada  and Mexico ' and Europe, accounting respectively for 18% and 15% of the total  amount [1].  Within the wide range of polymers in the market, polystyrene (PS) represents 5.3% (~21 Mt) of the total plastic produc tion worldwide and 6% (3.5 Mt) of the total production in Europe [1].

A B S T R A C T

text: Polystyrene (PS) is a versatile polymer typically used in applications such as yogurt cups, packaging trays, disk cases and toys. To increase recycling rates of PS, dissolution recycling is being investigated, which involves the liquefication of the polymer in a suitable solvent, allowing deep cleaning of the polymer from impurities. Quite specific to PS is that polystyrene waste contains both general-purpose polystyrene and high-impact polystyrene (HIPS), which is composed of free PS and polystyrene-grafted polybutadiene particles. In this work the potential of filtration and centrifugation is analyzed with the aim of cleaning the polymer from both, insoluble PB-PS particles and pigments (TiO2, Cr/Sb/Ti oxide and carbon black). The dead-end lab scale filtration were per formed at room temperature and at pressures between 1.5 and 30 bar. The pigments were successfully removed, yet, filtration of HIPS solutions results in low fluxes due to extreme membrane fouling caused by the PB-PS particles, which was confirmed by the application of pore-blockage filtration models. Alternatively, centrifu gation at 14,052 G-force has shown to be a promising alternative to separate the particles from HIPS, resulting in 100% turbidity reduction. Equally, the separation of pigments was successful, highlighting that TiO2 and Cr/Sb/ Ti oxide have shorter sedimentation times compared to carbon black. Finally, the two separation processes are tested on a PS rigid packaging waste sample coming from a sorting line and the results show that centrifugation allows a high turbidity reduction and that a two-step separation process starting with centrifugation for PB-PS particles removal can facilitate further downstream cleaning.

text: Polystyrene has versatile and tunable properties, making it suitable for applications in several sectors, such as packaging (e.g. yogurt cups, fish boxes),  electric  and  electronics  (e.g.  refrigerator),  building  and  con struction  (e.g.  insulation  foams),  and  automotive  (e.g.  bumper),  and many other applications (e.g. toys, disk and cosmetic cases) [1]. Current installed recycling input capacity for polystyrene is of approx. 0.10 Mt in Europe [2]. Thus, there are still quite some milestones to be achieved towards closing the loop for polystyrene.

text: Recycling options for polystyrene-based materials include mechan ical  recycling,  chemical  and  dissolution-based  (also  called  solventbased)  recycling  [3].  Yet,  polystyrene-based  materials  differ  in  their composition  and  physical  structures,  resulting  in  challenges  for  the different recycling techniques (Table 1). General-purpose polystyrene (GPPS) is a resin of atactic PS with transparent properties and good ri gidity, moldability and processability but low impact resistance, being mostly used as blend component together with high-impact polystyrene (HIPS)  for  food  packaging  or  as  pure  GPPS  in  disk  and  jewel  cases. Mechanical  recycling  of  GPPS  is  limited  by  the  quality  of  the  input material  and  presence  of  contaminants  that  reduce  the  quality  and properties of the recycled plastic [4]. HIPS is reinforced with grafted polybutadiene (PB) rubber particles that increase the impact resistance properties of PS, making it suitable for applications such as household appliances or more resistant food packaging. Next, acryloni trile -butadiene -styrene  (ABS)  is  a  copolymer  containing  rubber  in different  amounts  compared  to  HIPS  as  well  as  acrylonitrile,  which makes this polymer suitable for applications that require high impact, chemical and heat resistance. These rubber-containing polymers can be subject to some thermo-oxidative degradation during processing, with the double bond of polybutadiene being the main site of oxidation of HIPS and ABS [5 -7]. Multiple recycling loops with high thermal stress therefore might affect the quality of the recycled HIPS and ABS conse quently the types of applications it can be used for [5].

HIPS is reinforced with grafted polybutadiene (PB) rubber particles that increase the impact resistance properties of PS, making it suitable for applications such as household appliances or more resistant food packaging. text: Collected rigid PS-based waste contains both HIPS and GPPS, which have the same recycling code number 6. HIPS is composed of 12 -30 wt % PB-PS particles (or 6 -12 wt% PB), which are formed by PB rubber dispersed in the form of particles into a polystyrene matrix (Fig. 1) [7,8]. The dispersed rubber particles are grafted by PS chains and contain PS inclusions (Fig. 1). The higher the degree of grafting, i.e. the higher the number of grafted chains, the better the dispersion of the rubber parti cles  in  the  matrix  [9].  Choi  et  al.  (2000)  [9]  observed  that  with increasing degree of grafting, PS occlusion in the particles increases in size and is not enclosed well by the rubber layers. The size of the par ticles can vary between 0.5 and 9 μ m [10].

text: Apart from the rubber particles, PS-based waste typically contain colorants that are added during the manufacturing processes in plastics mostly for aesthetic purposes. These can lower the market price of the recyclate when not removed, since it limits the recoloration options of the  recyclate  [18,19].  Within  colorants,  dyes  and  pigments  can  be distinguished [20]. Dyes are organic molecules that are soluble and are retained in the polymer matrix as a result of an affinity between indi vidual dye molecules and the polymer molecules [21]. On the other hand, pigments are not soluble and are incorporated in the polymer while  it  is  in  a  liquid  phase  and  after  solidification,  the  dispersed pigment particles are retained physically in the polymer matrix [21]. Pigments can be subdivided into organic (e.g. Cu-phthalocyanine, azosalts) and  inorganic pigments  (e.g. TiO2, Cr2O3,  Fe2O3) [3,18]. Compared  to  dyes,  pigments  have  better  migration  resistance  and inorganic pigments can be preferred over organic pigments since these can offer better heat, light, and weathering resistance [21]. Inorganic pigments are added as a colorant to the plastic in a concentration range between 0.01 to 5 wt% and particle sizes varies in general between 0.1 to 1 μ m [3]. Pigments present in the polymer waste will result in greyish polymer recyclates which also poses a limitation towards closed-loop recycling of plastics. Recycling techniques, being able to remove rub ber  particles  and  pigments  (together  with  other  impurities),  should allow a wider use of post-consumer waste in closed loop recycling.

text: Dissolution  recycling  (or  solvent-based  recycling)  is  a  promising complementary route to conventional mechanical and chemical recy cling, as it avoids the energy costs typically involved in thermal based recycling methods where the polymer chains are broken down, like in thermal depolymerization or pyrolysis (including subsequent purifica tion of co-boiling by-products), but still allows the removal of contam inants and additives [3]. The so-called dissolution-precipitation technique follows 4 steps: (1) dissolution of the polymer with a suitable solvent; (2) solid -liquid separation process for the removal of undis solved contaminants; (3) precipitation of the polymer by the addition of an antisolvent to the solution; (4) recovery of the polymer by filtration and drying steps [3]. When in contact with solvents, HIPS forms turbid suspensions with undissolved PB-PS particles [22], which are in a gel phase whilst free dissolved PS in the liquid phase [23]. Thus, the par ticles  can  be  removed  with  a  solid -liquid  separation  step.  To  our knowledge,  few  publications  can  be  found  on  the  removal  of  PB-PS particles from HIPS. Da ǧ li et al. (1995) [23] have made an attempt to separate PB-PS from HIPS with microfiltration as sample preparation for particle size analysis with different membrane pore sizes between 10 and  1 μ m.  Whilst  reporting  clogging  issues,  the  effect  of  different filtration conditions such as pressure and stirring are not mentioned or tested. Da ǧ li et al. (1995) [23] has then used centrifugation (300 rpm, 2 h, toluene) to separate the particles (gel phase) from the free PS and redispersed the gel phase in toluene to obtain a specimen for the particle size analysis. Keskkula and Turley (1969) [24] used a mixture of MEK and acetone (50/50 by volume) and centrifuged (47000 g, 19500 rpm, 10 °C) to separate the PB-PS particles from free PS as sample preparation for particle size analysis.

text: Related to dyes and pigments, Mu and Yang (2022) [25] successfully removed dyes from textiles, i.e. CI Disperse Blue 56 from poly(ethylene terephthalate), CI Acid Blue 40 from nylon 6,6 and CI Direct RED 72 from cotton. The removal of dyes was achieved by minimization of fiber density using solvents and temperatures, which results in disruption of dye-polymer interactions and leaching of dyes from the fiber, without dissolving the polymer. Ferreira et al. (2021) [26] successfully removed the organic pigments Cu-phthalocyanine (PB15) and Cromophtal ® Or ange (PO64, benzimidazolone pigment family) from high density poly ethylene (HDPE) by solvent extraction with biosolvents (T > 110 °C, S/L ratio  of  0.02).  In  their  process,  HDPE  is  dissolved  and  antisolvent  is added to precipitate the polymer. The organic pigments remain in liquid phase,  i.e.  antisolvent/solvent  mixture.  Dissolution  in  limonene  has shown the best results for the removal of both PB15 (~90% removal with 1,4 -butanediol as antisolvent) and PO64 (100% removal with 1,2,3- propanetriol and 1,2,4- butanediol as antisolvent). Arends et al. (2012) [19] removed inorganic pigments (TiO2, Cr2O3 and Fe2O3) from ABS by filtration and centrifugation after preparing an ABS solutions in acetone  and  CreaSolv ® solutions.  However,  a  systematic  study  of filtration and centrifugation engineering and solvent effects on free PS recovery and pigment/grafted particles removal is currently lacking.

This  paper  evaluates  filtration  and  centrifugation  parameters  to wards optimizing the cleaning of undissolved particles, with focus on PB-PS  particles  and  pigments,  in  the  dissolution-based  recycling  of polystyrene-based waste. For this, solutions of 5 wt% polymer in xylene and limonene were prepared for filtration and centrifugation. Two HIPS samples with different PB-PS particles  concentrations  were  used  and three common inorganic pigments with different particle size distribu tions were chosen: TiO2 (white color), Cr/Sb/Ti oxide (yellow color) and carbon black (black color). Lastly, the most promising process for the recycling of PS is proposed and tested on a real PS rigid waste sample.

The waste sample ( ' waste PS ' ) consists of PS rigid packaging and comes from the P + MD (kerbside collected packaging) sorting line from Vanheede  in  Rumbeke  (Belgium).  The  waste  PS  was  inserted  in  the shredder (Piovan type RSP15/30) as real-size items without any sample preparation and was shredded first using a sieve diameter of 8.0 mm. Next, a sieve shaker (Endecotts LTD) was used to obtain particles with a narrower size distribution between 2.0 and 5.6 mm. The sample was further  pulverized  (Fritsch,  pulverisette  19)  into  particles  with  size smaller than 1.0 mm to ensure homogeneity upon preparation of solu tions (Fig. S1). To help the pulverization, liquid nitrogen was added to the 2.0 -5.6 mm pieces. Polymer solutions of 5 wt% concentration were prepared in the different solvents in closed vials, with stirring and at room temperature. In a 5 wt% polymer solution, this corresponds to a polymer content of 4.99 wt% for the compounded polymer solution and for the waste sample (Fig. S1).

text: A microscope setup was also built to analyze the PB-PS particles in the HIPS samples and calculate their sizes based on captured video re cords (Fig. 2). The optical axis of the setup is horizontally oriented, the holder is designed to support a test tube or a calibration slide, and is attached to a vertically oriented linear table with a positioning accuracy of 0.01 mm. Another linear table is used to adjust the position of the microscope in two perpendicular horizontal directions: for focusing and transversal alignment with an object. A 50X metallurgical microscope objective with a working distance (WD) of 7 mm was chosen (Fig. S2). To  record  videos,  a  camera  module,  12.3-megapixel  Sony  IMX477 sensor, connected to the Raspberry PI 4 model B through an I 2 C interface was  used.  The  video  was  captured  with  Raspivid,  a  command  line capturing application from RaspiCam package written for Raspberry PI single board computers. The resulting files with a 1080p resolution at 30 frames per second (FPS) were further processed on a personal computer with an open-source software: Python V3.9 [29] and OpenCV computer vision and machine learning library [30]. To define the relative scale of the  image,  a  calibration  slide  was  used.  Details  can  be  found  in  the Supporting Information.

A  dynamic  light  scattering  (DLS)  equipment,  Zetasizer  ZS  from Malvern (T = 20 °C, angle of measurement = 173) was used to qualify the presence of smaller carbon black particles ( < 0.1 μ m) in the permeate and supernatant of black PS.

The mass concentration of the PB-PS particles in HIPS, cparticles,HIPS , was calculated using equation (1). The mass fraction of free PS in HIPS was obtained by measuring the mass fraction of polymer in the clear supernatant with TGA, which is free of PB-PS particles [23]. To know if the supernatant was clear, its turbidity was compared with the turbidity of a reference, which was a 5 wt% pure PS solution in the respective solvent  (see  Section  2.3.  and  Eq.  (3)).  For  HIPS  E/xylene,  HIPS  R/ limonene, HIPS E/limonene, a clear supernatant was obtained with a 1hour centrifugation. For HIPS R in xylene, 100% turbidity reduction was not achieved after 2-hour centrifugation time, and therefore a 6-hour duration centrifugation was performed to ensure that all PB-PS parti cles have sedimented. The centrifugations were performed at 20 °C and with a G-force of 14052, see Section 2.5.

Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was conducted to quantify con centration of polymer in the permeate and supernatant [27]. The mea surements were carried out in a Netsch TG 209 F3 Tarsus thermogravimeter under a constant flow of dry nitrogen at a rate of 20 mL ⋅ min 1 . The temperature profile was as follows: dynamic step from 35 to 250 °C at 15 °C ⋅ min 1 , followed by an isothermal at 250 °C for 15 min, dynamic step up to 600 °C at 100 °C ⋅ min 1 , followed by a dynamic step at 20 °C ⋅ min 1 until 700 °C. The mean absolute error associated with TGA measurement is of 0.09 wt% and the standard deviation of 0.08 wt%, which were obtained by performing five measurements of a solution with a known concentration of 5 wt%.

The  supernatant  of  waste  PS  was  analyzed  with  a  UV -Vis  spec trometer (Hach Lange, DR 6000) to check for the presence of dissolved organic colorants.

Dispersion of particles in suspensions prior to measurements were ensured  by  immersion  of  the  solutions  in  an  ultrasonic  bath  (Ultra schallprozessor UP 400 s, Hielsher GmbH) with an amplitude of 60 % and 0.5 cycles for a minimum of 2 min.

text: Filtration  experiments  were  performed  using  a  high-pressure  cell (HP4750X Stirred Cell) from Sterlichtech (membrane diameter of 47 mm) with a dead-end filtration configuration and magnetic stirring (500 rpm). The experiments were conducted under constant pressure at room temperature. Different pressures between 1.5 and 30 bar were applied and three microfiltration commercial membranes with different pore sizes  were  tested:  0.1 μ m (Durapore ® ,  PVDF),  0.45 μ m (Durapore ® , Gridded PVDF), 1 μ m (Whatman TM , PTFE supported). The volumetric flux was calculated by measuring the volume collected over time with a graduated cylinder. The retained mass on the membrane was left to dry in the oven at 60 °C for 1 week. A successful microfiltration would be achieved when the pigments and PB-PS particles are retained on the membrane  whilst  clean  dissolved  polystyrene  passes  through  the membrane and can be recovered with further downstream processes [3].
