text: According to Fig. 4.1, the assessment of the solid-liquid extraction and the dissolution-precipitation processes have different conclusions in terms of potential economic profit. In the bestcase scenario which is at 100% extraction efficiency with � 100 € /ton plastic waste, the solid-liquid extraction process has economic benefits even without solvent recovery, whereas the dissolution-precipitation process needs to recover at least 70% of the solvent. In the worst-case scenario which is at 50% extraction efficiency with 400 € /ton plastic waste, the Soxhlet extraction process requires almost 100% solvent recovery, while dissolutionprecipitation cannot become economically feasible. In fact, it is important to note that the plastics should be equally clean after both treatments in order to make a proper comparison. This basic assessment shows that the dissolution-precipitation can only become competitive if it is highly efficient in recovery of polymer (and eventually also the additives) and also if proper medium recovery processes are developed. This is not unlikely, however, it seems that there is a long way to go for this process. On the other hand, this analysis, within all its limitations and assumptions, shows that the solid-liquid extraction process has a promising economic potential despite of the limitations from a technical perspective. These limitations were especially related to highmolecular-weight components, but optimizing process parameters such as particle size and swelling conditions for the polymer might solve such diffusion limitations.

4.3. Life cycle assessment

The removal of additives from plastic waste is an important step towards closed-loop recycling in a sustainable circular economy. Therefore, a suitable extraction method should preferably not only be profitable from an economic perspective but also be beneficial from environmental perspective. For this reason, a screening life cycle assessment (LCA) using the OpenLCA software is performed (with the Recipe Endpoint (H) methodology) for both the solidliquid extraction and the dissolution-precipitation case studies. The Environmental Benefit is calculated similarly to the cost of the process as seen in Eq. (4.2), but in this case the impact is expressed in ecopoints per ton plastic treatment (points/ton). Data for the calculations were obtained from the Ecoinvent Database v3. Also in this case, we not only applied the ''zero burden assumption', meaning that we did not allocate environmental impact to the waste stream, but we also excluded factors such as logistics, other pretreatments, etc. Again, this is thus a very best-case scenario.

The Environmental Benefit is calculated similarly to the cost of the process as seen in Eq. (4.2), but in this case the impact is expressed in ecopoints per ton plastic treatment (points/ton). Data for the calculations were obtained from the Ecoinvent Database v3. Also in this case, we not only applied the ''zero burden assumption', meaning that we did not allocate environmental impact to the waste stream, but we also excluded factors such as logistics, other pretreatments, etc. Again, this is thus a very best-case scenario.

text:
Solvent-based extraction techniques show a great potential towards upgrading the plastics waste and making them suitable towards closed-loop recycling. In order to design a proper solvent-based polishing technique, solubility and diffusivity are key to predict the extraction performance. Also, it is essential to make a clear classification of additives based on their physical properties. Furthermore, the extraction conditions such as the type of solvent, temperature and pressure, among others play an important role to design these processes. Therefore, in addition to conventional solid-liquid extraction methods, specific variations of these technologies working with supercritical solvents, microwaves, assisted by pressure, etc. are also being considered. Each of these processes have their specific strengths and weaknesses.

For example, the popular SFE technique does not result in high extraction yields for highly polar additives such as for phenolic antioxidants due to the low polarity of scCO2, yet this might be solved by adding a more polar solvent as a modifier. In MAE, a polar/apolar solvent mixture is needed to be effective to allow microwave heating in the polar phase and polymer swelling in the apolar phase.

text: Beside the selection of a potential process in terms of extraction efficiency, economic feasibility and environmental impact are crucial to move to higher TRL's. Therefore, two case studies were explored towards their economic and environmental sustainability. According to our screening, solid-liquid extraction case study has economic advantages compared to dissolution-precipitation, even without solvent recovery and for the most expensive plastic waste streams (400 € /ton). Similarly, in terms of environmental impact, solid-liquid extraction has a lower environmental impact compared to dissolution-precipitation in which high amount of solvents with higher environmental impact are used. Solvent choice should thus be based on applicability, e.g. in order to swell the plastics efficiently, as well as on their recoverability, e.g. by distillation, and their net environmental impact during virgin production.

text:
Extraction methods should be specifically tuned based on type of additives and plastics. Although obtaining high extraction yields is theoretically possible and much of the current research has focused on the solvent-polymer-additive interactions, there is a significant lack of process optimization to make these techniques potentially environmentally and economically feasible in the circular economy. For example, regarding plastic industry solid-liquid extraction processes are less frequently used in pilot-scale applications compared to dissolution-precipitation, but based on our assessment they have a higher chance to become competitive if diffusion limitations are overcome. On the other hand, dissolution-precipitation is a widely used technique, but it is not feasible in terms of environmental and economic aspects. It is thus important to note that unless the process allows a highly efficient extraction of additives by using low amounts and relatively cheap solvents at moderate conditions, the process might not be applicable, even in the long term. Concluding, we suggest to perform more research on process optimization and upscaling of solvent-based techniques, including medium recovery, reactor design, search for new and greener solvents, etc. to increase their potential to further unlock the circular economy for plastics.

text: In general, scientific literature regarding this recycling process focuses on the quality of the recovered polymer and/or the energy consumption of the process, [7,8,17 -22] yet another important aspect would be the polymer dissolution kinetics. The dissolution of a polymer involves two main steps: solvent diffusion and chain disentanglement, [10,23] as is depicted in Figure 1 . When a rubbery, amorphous, and uncrosslinked polymer, such as plasticized poly(vinyl chloride) ( P -PVC), comes into contact with a compatible solvent, the solvent will diffuse into the polymer, causing the polymer to swell. The solvent has a plasticizing effect and forms a gel-like layer with the polymer. This layer, depicted in Figure 1, consists of polymer chains that are increasingly surrounded by solvent molecules and is situated between the polymer chains untouched by the solvent and the external boundary layer. Depending on the prevailing local solvent concentration, the gel layer can be subdivided into different regions where the degree of gelation differs, [10] this subdivision, however, is omitted in this article. A measurement of the local solvent and/or polymer concentration in the gel phase is difficult to obtain since this involves a tiny region that changes geometrically as time progresses. Koenig et al. [10,24 -26] demonstrated that a semiquantification with Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR)-microscopy is possible and concluded that the solvent does not dissolve the polymer uniformly at the polymer -solvent interface. This causes cracking and roughening of the polymer edges, making interface concentrations difficult to measure. [24] FTIR-microscopy can also depict in a semiquantitative manner how the solvent diffuses into the polymer matrix, which causes the polymer -solvent interface to move. [25] The local concentrations could also be obtained using thermodynamic theories such as the Flory -Huggins polymer solution theory, which involves calculating the equilibrium between the solvent and polymer-rich phases.

The polymer chains in the gel layer possess a higher mobility and start to disentangle, after which they can diffuse into the bulk of the solution through the external boundary layer. Once in the bulk phase, the polymer chains are surrounded by solvent molecules and are thus dissolved. An additional step is required in the dissolution process if the polymer is in the glassy state, namely, the presence of the solvent also initiates a glass transition that occurs before the polymer chains can disentangle. text: One of the first contributions describing polymer dissolution behavior was Ueberreiter et al. [29 -31] who investigated the temperature and molecular weight dependency of the dissolution process as well as surface layer effects. They defined a dissolution rate and expressed the temperature and molecular weight dependence as an Arrhenius relationship and power law, respectively. The thickness of the gel layer was also found to obey the same temperature and molecular weight dependencies. Over the years, a variety of authors have built upon the preliminary results of Ueberreiter and Asmussen [30,31] and have proposed different mathematical models describing the polymer dissolution kinetics. [10,32,33] They can be classified according to five categories: 1) phenomenological models based on Fickian equations, [34 -38] 2) models with external mass transfer as the controlling resistance to dissolution; [39,40] 3) stress-relaxation models; [41,42] 4) anomalous-transport models [43 -45] and 5) continuum-framework models. [23,46]

The thickness of the gel layer was also found to obey the same temperature and molecular weight dependencies. Over the years, a variety of authors have built upon the preliminary results of Ueberreiter and Asmussen [30,31] and have proposed different mathematical models describing the polymer dissolution kinetics. [10,32,33] They can be classified according to five categories: 1) phenomenological models based on Fickian equations, [34 -38] 2) models with external mass transfer as the controlling resistance to dissolution; [39,40] 3) stress-relaxation models; [41,42] 4) anomalous-transport models [43 -45] and 5) continuum-framework models. [23,46]

text: The first category of models, 1) describes the polymer dissolution behavior in a phenomenological manner based on Fickian diffusion equations. These models show a high degree of complexity and already take into account important polymer dissolution phenomena like solvent diffusion, chain disentanglement, external mass transfer, etc. Tsampanakis and White [47] noted that the proposed models still possess some gaps when it comes to the physical origin of some parameters, which are also difficult, if not impossible, to obtain experimentally. Despite these shortcomings, these models, which are intuitively based on fundamental equations like Fick ' s laws, have good agreement with experimental data and thus have shown great use in the engineering community. [47] The second category, 2), essentially treats the polymer dissolution as one of a nonpolymeric material by considering that the external mass transfer is the kinetically limiting step. However, models solely based on external mass transfer have proven to be incomplete, as experiments have shown that the polymer dissolution rate does not depend on external mass transfer alone. [32] As mentioned earlier, phenomena like solvent diffusion and chain disentanglement are proven to have a greater impact on the overall dissolution kinetics. [10] Stress relaxation models 3) do describe solvent penetration and actual polymer dissolution. However, they involve parameters that can only be measured experimentally, and many assumptions are necessary to describe the process, making these models undesirable. [47] Models describing anomalous transport 4) were the first to describe the idea of chain disentanglement by deriving scaling laws for the chain disentanglement rate. These models show a higher complexity than the phenomenological models, which is a result of taking into account glassy polymers and the induced stresses within them during dissolution. Even though this method was a great leap forward in understanding polymer dissolution, it still failed to take into account the viscoelastic effects of the polymer. [32] The most up-to-date models for dissolving polymers in a solvent are the continuumframework models. 5) Most of the phenomena that were lacking in previous models are accounted for; however, this leads to an even higher degree of complexity as well as a potentially higher risk of overfitting. The model complexity makes subsequent implementation in process simulation software, like Aspen Plus, more challenging, which can diminish the model ' s success. In general, difficulties also arise when dealing with plastic waste, which contains a multitude of different additives and other contaminants. text: Experimentally, polymer dissolution is often studied by measuring dependencies on material properties (such as molecular weight, detailed particle geometry, solubility parameters, etc.) as well as reactor and process parameters (such as stirring speed, reactor geometry, etc.). [48,49] An important material property that can influence the kinetics is the molecular weight of the polymer chains. Theoretically, the molecular weight dependence can be predicted based on reptation theory, as was outlined by Brochard and De Gennes. [41] This theory inherently assumes that the dissolution of the polymer is kinetically limited to the relaxation of the polymer chains. Subsequently, the dissolution time can be related to the reptation time, which in itself is proportional to the molar mass to the power of 3. Experimentally, the power was found to be 3.4, indicating a strong dependence on the molar mass. [50] However, in contrast to these theoretical predictions, a different dependency of the dissolution time on the molecular weight was found by Valois et al. in their recent study. [48] They investigated the molecular weight dependency by considering the dissolution of polyethylene oxide and found that the reptation mechanism is not a kinetically limiting process for dissolution. Instead, the argument was made that chain contraction in the Doi -Edwards tube, to relieve the stresses induced by swelling, leads to the disentanglement and thus dissolution of the polymer chains. Thus, it was shown from dissolution experiments that the dissolution time as a function of polymer molar mass can be fitted to a power law with exponent 2/3.

text: Valois et al. also investigated the dependence of the dissolution time on the stirring rate in their study. [48] By using scaling law arguments, a theoretical power law dependency was derived with exponent � 1. Experimental fitting of the dissolution data gave a power law exponent of � 1.2, of which the difference from the theoretical value is attributed to the nonlaminar flow in the experimental set-up. Subsequently, in a more practical study, Kol et al. [49] investigated the stirring regime in order to lower the dissolution time for polystyrene (PS) waste. To this end, they considered a more optimized reactor design by introducing baffles and two types of stirrer shafts, namely a Rushton turbine shaft and a 3-bladed propeller shaft. With these additions, they were able to reduce the dissolution time from 40 to 7 min, which can be attributed to the increase in turbulence provided by the stirrers and baffles. Furthermore, it was observed that an increase in stirring rate between 750 rpm and 1000 rpm of the Rushton turbine had a negligible effect on the dissolution time, whilst some effect was still observed for the 3-bladed propeller, going from 750 rpm to 875 rpm.

text: The aim of this article is to gain an understanding of the dissolution process and kinetics of plasticized PVC ( P -PVC) waste, including the polymer, but also additives such as plasticizers. The presence of such additives may alter the dissolution mechanism, leading to deviated kinetics compared to the pure polymer. To that end, dissolution kinetic experiments were conducted on unused consumer flexible PVC tubing, to represent a PVC waste fraction containing plasticizers, in this case bis(7-methyloctyl) cyclohexane-1,2-dicarboxylate (DINCH). DINCH is used in high volumes as one of the more popular alternatives to the traditional phthalate plasticizers like bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) and diisononyl phthalate (DINP). [51 -53] A permanent ban has been imposed in the European Union on the use of these phthalate plasticizers. [54] This type of plastic was chosen because a relatively large portion of PVC in Europe is used in applications where plasticizers are used, e.g., vinyl flooring (7%), electric cables (7%), and PVC films (7%). [2] First, the dissolution profile of the plasticizer and PVC was analyzed separately, which, to the best of the authors ' knowledge, has not yet been done before. To verify the generality of these findings, the same analysis was also performed with DEHP as the plasticizer. Next, experiments were carried out according to a 3 2 4 1 full factorial design (FFD) where the temperature and particle size were varied. This was done in four different solvents: methyl ethyl ketone (MEK), cyclohexanone, N-methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP), and 2-MeTHF.

text: The plasticizer content in the P -PVC sample, in this case DINCH, was determined using gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (GC/MS). The DINCH extraction and analysis method from ISO 16 181-1:2021 standard was used; slight modifications were made to the GC/MS temperature profile as described next. To perform the analysis, an Agilent Technologies 6890 N Network GC System with 5973 Network Mass Selective Detector and Gerstel MPS2 autosampler was used. As described by the standard, a HP-5ms column ((5%-phenyl)methyl polysiloxane phase) with a length of 30 m, an interior diameter of 0.25 mm, and a film thickness of 0.25 μ m. The helium flow was kept constant at 1 mL/min. The inlet temperature was set to 320 °C, and a volume of 1.0 μ L was injected with a split ratio of 10:1, the MS source temperature was 230 °C. The oven temperature was first held at 200 °C for two minutes, followed by a ramp to 325 °C at 15 °C min � 1 and then held for 3 min at that final temperature. To quantify DINCH, the 155 m/z ion was used. A calibration curve was constructed in a volumetric mixture of 2:1 n-hexane:THF, ranging from 5 to 100 ppm (Section 3 of Supporting Information). The helium flow was kept constant at 1 mL/min. The inlet temperature was set to 320 °C, and a volume of 1.0 μ L was injected with a split ratio of 10:1, the MS source temperature was 230 °C. text: Second, to assess the amount of PVC dissolved, the samples were analyzed using pyrolysis-GC/MS (Py-GC/MS), in which the release of HCl during the pyrolysis can be quantified. [59] Linearity of the response was ensured by analyzing different amounts of pure PVC dissolved in cyclohexanone at a concentration of 2.9 wt%. By varying the amount of solution in the microvial, the PVC content was varied between 0.060 and 0.162 mg, see section 2 in Supporting Information. Next, as a reference, the response of a 10 wt% solution of the P -PVC sample in cyclohexanone was analyzed, and the accompanying release of HCl was calculated. Subsequently, all measured samples could be expressed as a fraction of the expected response of this 10 wt% P -PVC solution (the end concentration of all preformed kinetic experiments). For the analyzes, a Shimadzu Nexis GC-2030 was used in conjunction with an OPTIC-4Pyro GC Pyrolizer, AOC-6000 Plus autosampler, and GCMS-QP2020 NX mass spectrometer. Samples were added to a micro-vial (conditioned DMI Sample Inserts 30 μ L (2406 -1010)) and placed in a liner (GL Sciences Fritted Liner 5 -81 mm (2414 -1001) with GL Sciences OPTIC Nonstick O -ring Viton (2406 -1018)). The installed column was an HP-5 ms ((5%-phenyl)-methyl polysiloxane phase) with a length of 30 m, an interior diameter of 0.25 mm, and a film thickness of 0.25 μ m. The pyro inlet temperatures were based on thermogravimetric analysis-FTIR screening tests, which are detailed in section 2 of the Supporting Information. The initial inlet temperature was set to 160 °C for 10 min, to evaporate the solvent from the sample and avoid column overload during the analysis of the HCl (cf. solvent delay in Liquid injection GC-MS). Next, the inlet temperature was increased to 400 °C to pyrolyze the PVC and evaporate the resulting compounds. The settings timeline for the pyrolysis unit, column, and split ratio are provided in Table 2 . To quantify the HCl release, the 36 m/z ion was used, qualitatively verified with the 35 m/z ion. At the end of each run, a cleaning program was conducted comprising a helium backflush (Trajan Scientific and Medical with Shimadzu SilFlow Tubing 0.5 m -150 μ m -363 μ m, P/N 980 -10 599) for 9.2 min at an oven temperature of 325 °C.

This disentanglement rate k d is said to be a parameter that is difficult to estimate a priori, so this was often treated as a model parameter by earlier authors. [36,38,62,63] Narasimhan and Peppas [64] attempted to obtain an expression based on molecular arguments and proposed that the disentanglement rate can be defined as the ratio between the radius of gyration of the polymer and the reptation time. For more details on concepts such as the reptation time within reptation theory and the derived scaling laws, the reader is referred to works by De Gennes [41,43,65] and Doi and Edwards. [66] Making use of these concepts, a subsequent derivation was made by Narasimhan and Peppas [23] and a semiempirical correlation was obtained. [47] It was found that the disentanglement rate was linearly proportional to temperature T ½ K  and inversely proportional to the solvent viscosity η 1 ½ Pas  .

3.2. First Order Diffusion Model

text:
Based on an earlier model by Martini et al., [61] the second model that is proposed considers first-order mass transfer kinetics for the entire dissolution process. This approach implies a drastic simplification of the prevailing phenomena discussed above, as it does not directly model solvent diffusion or chain disentanglement. This model can, however, be used for dissolution processes where transient effects (such as concentration changes in the boundary layer) occur at very short timescales compared to the dissolution time. [61] In this case, no induction time is observed, meaning that there is no time-lag between the start of the experiment and the first measured dissolved polymer concentration, which is the case for the executed dissolution experiments. Therefore, this model is valid at higher times, i.e., times where solvent diffusion and chain disentanglement take place and can thus be considered as a first approximation of a polymer dissolution process. [61] In spite of its abstractions and shortcomings, it is still used when modeling dissolution profiles. [49,69] The model equation is given by Equation (7). [49]

With D 0 ½ m 2 s � 1,  the pre-exponential factor. This model is also a simplified phenomenological model, where the diffusion coefficient describes the diffusion of the polymer chains out of the solid particle into a dissolved state. A contentious parameter in the disentanglement model, as well as the first-order diffusion model, is the equilibrium value of the mass fraction of polymer ω 2, eq . If the solvent is able to dissolve all of the polymer added to the system at the start of the dissolution process, this value can be set equal to the initially added polymer weight fraction. As was described in section 2.2.2.2, this value was always set at 10 wt% in the experiments that were carried out. The value of ω 2, eq is, however, different if the polymer -solvent system displays a solubility limit below 10 wt%. In this case, not all of the initially added polymer is dissolved, and a different equilibrium value is reached. Since the solubility limit of different polymer -solvent systems is very difficult to predict a priori, it is not possible to prescribe a value to ω 2, eq beforehand. Hence, the value of ω 2, eq will be set at the equilibrium value obtained when the dissolution process is completed, as was mentioned before.

3.3. Parameter Regression and Statistics

text:
For each solvent separately, both models have been fit to the experimental dissolution kinetic data in function of temperature and particle size, as outlined in Table 1. This was done in R, [71] using the flexible modeling environment (FME) package [72,73] with the Levenberg -Marquardt algorithm. Different statistical parameters have been used to compare and validate the results of the different model: sum of squared errors, coefficient of determination (R 2 ), hybrid fractional error function, Theil ' s inequality coefficient (TIC), the mean relative error (MRE) and the 95% confidence interval (95% CI). For a model to be considered as an accurate description of the experimental data, the TIC value should be smaller than 0.3. The MRE is a measure of the overall error of the model, where a smaller value is indicative of an overall smaller error between the model and the experimental data.

4.2. DINCH, PVC, and P-PVC Dissolution Profiles

text: First, it was analyzed whether the additive (DINCH) is released at a rate equal to the dissolution of the polymer (PVC) itself. This was done in cyclohexanone at 30 °C and with 2190 μ m particles. All results in Figure 3 are normalized according to their concentration in the P -PVC sample and are thus presented as a fraction of the expected response of the completely dissolved P -PVC. If both analyzed components in the P -PVC dissolve simultaneously at the ratio of their presence in the P -PVC tubing, then all measurements should follow the exact same profile. From Figure 3, it can be concluded that for most of the experimental measurements, except for the experiments at 2 and 15 min, the profile of both measured components indeed follows the same trend as the refractive index (RI) method, within the range of the standard error of the respective methods. This means that both the plasticizer and the polymer dissolve at the same rate. This was confirmed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) tests, where no significant (p > 0.05) difference was observed between the measured averages of the three tested methods at 5, 30, 60, and 120 min (see Section 3 of Supporting Information). This leads to the conclusion that other methods, like refractometry, that cannot differentiate between an increase in RI due to the dissolution of PVC or DINCH, could be used as a faster alternative to measure the dissolved sample concentration, at least in this case. For the calibration curves, the increase in RI is thus representative of the total dissolved sample, so both the PVC and DINCH. text: These results further indicate that on a molecular level, the dissolution of P -PVC is largely similar to that of pure PVC. Intuitively, one would expect that the plasticizer would dissolve faster than the PVC, since it has a lower molecular weight and experiences less steric hindrance in comparison to a polymer chain. The data shows, however, that this does not occur. Therefore, it is conjectured that simultaneous dissolution is observed because the diffusion of the plasticizer through a polymer matrix is a rather slow process. The plasticizer is not chemically bonded to the polymer chains, so in principle could be released when there are sufficiently large gaps between the polymer chains. The simultaneous dissolution of the plasticizer and the polymer indicates that these gaps do not reach the necessary size to allow fast diffusion from the polymer core to the solvent bulk. Instead, chain disentanglement and subsequent polymer dissolution go faster. This hypothesis is backed up by the extraction data of typical plasticizers under similar experimental conditions. For instance, Messori et al. [74] investigated the release of DEHP from uncoated PVC samples in a hexane solution at room temperature and under mechanical stirring and found that after an extraction time of 10 h, the amount of leached DEHP amounted to 55 wt% of the total DEHP content.

For both the model based on chain disentanglement and the first-order model, the parameters, resulting from the regression of the model on the experimental data, are provided in Table 3 . and 2-MeTHF. The confidence intervals of the model parameters underpin this observation, as the percentage error is smaller for these solvents. text: In the following section, the resulting dissolution profiles of the different models will only be presented for NMP and 2-MeTHF. The profiles of MEK and cyclohexanone can be found in section 5 of the Supporting Information. Comparing both models for NMP with the experimental data, as shown in Figure 8 , leads to the conclusion that the chain disentanglement model is generally a better representation for this solvent. This is also confirmed when looking at the TIC and MRE of the chain disentanglement model, which are 0.024 and 5.5% respectively, compared to the first-order model, where the TIC is 0.040 and the MRE is 7.6%. Additionally, Figure 8 reveals that the first-order model mostly overestimates the dissolution time for 2190 and 2990 μ m particles, while underestimating for the smaller 1090 μ m particle sizes. The reason for this could be found by comparing the particle size dependency of both models, where the first-order diffusion model only accounts for the initial particle size, r0, while the chain disentanglement model accounts for the change in the particle size over time.

text: When looking at 2-MeTHF ( Figure 9 ), having a TIC of 0.024 and MRE of 6.9%, the first-order model provides a better fit for all performed experiments, independent of temperature or particle size, compared to the chain disentanglement model with a TIC of 0.037 and MRE of 9.3%. text: Finally, a spider diagram is provided in Figure 10 , where the MRE of both models is plotted, individually for every experiment. This also confirms the previous statements, where it is clear that the first-order kinetics provides an all-round better description of the dissolution profiles for MEK and 2-MeTHF, while it does not for NMP. This leads to the conclusion that the chain disentanglement model, within this experimental design, seems to be more suitable for the description of good to very good PVC solvents like NMP and cyclohexanone. The chain disentanglement model for NMP is considerably better at describing the dissolution profile at temperatures around or below the glass transition temperature of the polymer sample. This difference was less pronounced at higher temperatures. It would be interesting to see if the conclusions of this research hold true when moving toward even higher dissolution temperatures (e.g., 100 -150 °C) as well as larger particle sizes, e.g., 10 -50 mm.

text: A full factorial experimental design was conducted on a plasticized PVC sample, containing DINCH, with a varying average particle size (1090, 2190, and 2990 μ m) and temperature (30, 45, and 60 °C). In every experiment, 10 wt% solutions of the sample in one of the following four solvents were prepared: NMP, cyclohexanone, MEK, and 2-MeTHF. Using a combination of GC/MS to measure the plasticizer in solution and Py-GC/MS to measure the amount of PVC in solution, it was found that overall, both the plasticizer and the polymer dissolved at the same rate. These findings were backed up by analyzing a different P -PVC sample where the plasticizer was DEHP. This could indicate that the overall dissolution behavior of P -PVC is governed by the disentanglement of the PVC matrix. Concerning the kinetic dissolution experiments, it was found that in general, the order from fastest to slowest solvents for PVC dissolution was NMP, cyclohexanone, MEK, and 2-MeTHF. It was also noticed that both MEK and 2-MeTHF could not completely dissolve the sample at temperatures around or below the glass transition temperature of the P -PVC sample. Furthermore, as expected, reducing the particle size of the sample as well as increasing the temperature, positively affected the dissolution speed regardless of the solvent used. It was found that the dissolution times for the prepared 10 wt% P -PVC solutions were at most around 120 min. This was the case for both 2-MeTHF and MEK at 30 °C and with 2990 μ m particles. In contrast, the fastest dissolution time was 5 min in NMP at 60 °C and with 1090 μ m particles.

text: Next, two models are proposed to describe the dissolution profile: a chain disentanglement-based model and a first-order diffusion model. It can be concluded that both models are capable of describing the dissolution profile of a real P -PVC sample, with an MRE of 12.1% or less. It appears that the chain disentanglement model is generally more accurate in describing the dissolution profile of good solvents, like NMP, whilst the firstorder model excels at describing the dissolution profile of slower solvents like MEK and 2-MeTHF. It would be interesting to expand the dissolution experiments to more solvents, higher temperatures, and a wider range in particle sizes, in order to further calibrate both models. Further efforts should also be made in developing a theoretically based formula for the disentanglement rate with respect to macroscopic parameters. This includes material properties (such as molecular weight, detailed particle geometry, solubility parameters, etc.) as well as reactor and process parameters (such as stirring speed, reactor geometry, etc.). In essence, a more advanced understanding of the specific process of chain disentanglement in a practical context. Finally, the simplicity of both models could allow for easy integration into process simulation software, such as Aspen Plus, for example, to perform energy optimization studies. Additionally, understanding the dissolution behavior of polymer waste can aid the industry toward an increase in the dissolution rate, which could, for example, allow for the use of smaller reactors. These vital improvements can pave the way for a viable dissolution-based PVC recycling process in the future.

text: Solvent-based recycling approaches are receiving industrial and academic interest for their ability to produce high-quality plastic resins from a variety of plastic waste sources without breaking the polymer chains. Here we highlight the development of solvent-based technologies, focusing on the underlying principles, techno-economic and life-cycle analyses, and commercialization. The basic steps in solvent-based recycling include plastic size reduction, plastic dissolution, filtration or centrifugation, and optional additional cleaning steps such as adsorption, precipitation and solvent removal. Impurities that build up in the solvent must also be removed. The goal of solvent-based technologies is to produce a high-quality resin without plastic contaminants or other added substances. Disadvantages of these solvent-based technologies are their physicochemical complexity and the difficulty in scaling up to achieve continuous operations with high polymer and solvent yields and throughputs. Chemical engineering is thus critical in bringing solvent-based recycling technologies to market.

text: Global annual plastic production reached 413.8 million metric tons in 2023, while the recycling rate was only 9.6% (ref. 1). Globally, most plastic waste is either landfilled or disposed of in open pit dumps. It is estimated that 2-5% of all plastic produced ends up in the ocean 2 . Mechanical recycling is the main current approach to recycle plastics 3 . In mechanical recycling, plastics undergo sorting, separation, grinding, cleaning by (friction) washing, sink-float separation (to separate heavier polymers such as polyethylene terephthalate (PET) from polyolefins), drying and then re-extrusion. Although some color sorting is possible before mechanical recycling, the recycling process does not remove colors or other common additives, nor is it capable of eliminating many other impurities such as adhesives. Beyond mechanical recycling, several chemical recycling technologies, such as plastic pyrolysis and polyester methanolysis 4,5 , are being developed and commercialized. These technologies are typically integrated with existing petrochemical infrastructure, such as steam-cracking or PET polymerization 6 . Researchers have discussed various plastic waste recycling technologies and their implications. For instance, Tiwari et al. provided a comprehensive analysis of mechanical and chemical recycling methods of plastic waste, highlighting the challenges in plastic sorting and segregation 7 ; Zhang et al. covered the technological mechanisms and development status of mechanical and chemical recycling technologies 8 ; additionally, Li et al. provided a comprehensive review of plastic recycling, detailing the chemistry, engineering and technological aspects of various plastic recycling methods 9 .

text:
Flexible packaging plastic is a complicated waste stream to recycle because moisture, dirt, other polymer layers, adhesives and inks build up during the mechanical recycling process 10,11 . For example, multilayer flexible packaging is composed of multiple polymer and adhesive layers, each with varying chemical compositions and properties. These complex combinations can make it challenging to recycle films and to produce high-quality products via mechanical or chemical recycling methods 12 . Solvent-based recycling, also called dissolution-based recycling, is a promising solution that separates individual polymers from multipolymer streams and simultaneously allows deep cleaning of the dissolved polymers. In addition to films, this approach is well suited to other combinations of materials such as mixed plastic bales 13 , electronic 14,15 and automotive waste 16 , and multicomponent flooring 17 . Dissolution-based recycling can also be applied to monomaterial waste streams to perform deeper removal of impurities, while keeping the polymer chains intact.

Dissolution-based plastic recycling has several advantages compared with mechanical recycling. The process produces a high-quality virgin-like resin where impurities, other polymers and other unintentionally added substances (such as color bodies, often referred to as 'non-intentionally added substances') can be removed. Although dissolution-based recycling is often still classified under 'mechanical' recycling because it does not break the polymer chains, traditional mechanical recycling cannot achieve the same level of impurity removal. Therefore, dissolution-based recycling is categorized as 'physical' recycling 18 . This approach recovers high-quality polymers, leaving polymer chains intact. In this Review, we discuss current academic research, industrial processes and future research needs of dissolution-based recycling technologies. There are variations in the technology, but in general dissolution-based recycling of waste polymers involves several fundamental steps: (1) preprocessing (such as shredding/downsizing, densification, metal removal, washing and drying), (2) dissolution of targeted polymer, (3) separation of the dissolved polymer from the remaining non-dissolved material, (4) precipitation of the dissolved polymer, (5) separation of the precipitated polymer from the solvent, (6) drying and solvent purification from the nondissolved polymer and precipitated polymer and (7) resin production. Additionally, solvents have been used for the removal of colorants, adhesives, plastic additives and odor 21-25 . While the technology needs time to mature and expand, dissolution-based recycling will likely fill a role in processing complex but low-variability waste streams, such as many of those listed in Table 1, that allow simplification of the preprocessing steps.

text:
Preprocessing of plastic waste involves the following steps: (1) collection and transportation, (2) sorting and separation, (3) size reduction (typically to less than 2 mm) 26 , (4) cleaning, (5) drying and (6) additional processing (such as decontamination, densification, microperforation and thermal conditioning). Quality control is critical to ensure that the undesired components are removed. The collection and sorting of the waste feedstock is one of the most challenging steps in this process. It plays a pivotal role in the whole recycling process to determine the solvent type and operating conditions. Most material recovery facilities use a series of sorting processes including optical methods such as near-infrared spectroscopy, which typically have accuracies of above 90% at object level (an object can consist of different polymers) 27 . Dissolution-based recycling plants can process sorted bales, and even shredded and washed waste, or undertake some of these steps in house 9 .

Dissolution

text: The shredded plastics are mixed with a potentially heated solvent in a dissolution vessel. Solvent choice and temperature depend on the target polymer. Ideally, only the targeted polymer is dissolved, without dissolving other polymers and small additives including pigments, which facilitates their separation. The viscosity of the solution, an important parameter for the whole process, can be influenced by concentration, temperature, pressure and polymer-solvent interactions 28 . Generally, for dissolution-based plastic recycling, the recommended polymer concentration is 5-20 wt% (ref. 28). A concentration above 10 wt% often results in a very viscous solution, depending on the polymer type, molecular weight and operating conditions. For example, at 155 °C and 20 MPa, the viscosity of the PE solution (1 wt%, weightaveraged molecular mass of 2,150 g mol -1 ) is approximately 0.125 mPa s, and it increases to 0.15 mPa s when the pressure is raised to 40 MPa (ref. 28); for the combination of PS/ o -xylene at room temperature (RT), the entanglement concentration is 13.9 wt%, and the viscosity is noticeably increased at this concentration, reaching ~0.9 Pa s (ref. 29). High viscosity of the polymer solution often leads to difficulties in material flow, separation and post-process cleaning. Polymer solutions are typically categorized as either Newtonian or non-Newtonian fluids on the basis of how the fluid viscosity changes upon the application of shear stress. Researchers have proposed the Carreau and Yasuda-Armstrong-Cohen model to describe both Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids 28 . These model parameters require modification for each polymer-solvent combination, as the complexity of the polymer solution viscosity requires further study 28 .

text:
Separation of dissolved polymer from undissolved material

The undissolved material needs to be separated from the viscous polymer solution. Equipment such as centrifuges, strainers, centrifugal sifters and candle filters can be used for this step. For example, centrifugal filters with a rotary knife/brush with fixed screens can be used in this step. In such equipment, material is fed into the chamber, where the rotating knife/brush pushes the material against the screen. Solvent and finer particles pass through the screen to the next step, while larger undissolved particles are pushed out 30 . As an alternative to centrifugation, filtration is often applied to remove undissolved particles. Filter media must be carefully selected to avoid clogging, often consisting of multiple steps aimed at removing increasingly smaller particles. A common filtration method is candle filters, which use cartridges to filter fluid and trap impurities and particles. These candle filters can often remove smaller-sized impurities (down to a nominal size of 0.5 μm) from the fluid 31 .

Post-cleaning dissolved substances

text:
Additional cleaning steps may be necessary to remove contaminants that are not removed by filtration. Such contaminants often include dissolved dyes, organic and inorganic pigments, residue pigments and other undissolved particles that have passed through the previous filter size. Currently, adsorption is the predominant method to achieve this step. For example, Procter and Gamble has reported using adsorbents selected from metal oxides, covalent organic frameworks, metal-organic frameworks and zeolitic imidazolate frameworks to remove contaminants from the polymer solution 32 . Other adsorbents that can be used include activated carbon, Fuller's earth and/ or quartz sand to remove the colorants and other dissolved additives from the polymer solution 33 . Another approach for post-cleaning is ion exchange; however, it is not yet widely adopted, with rather limited information available 34 .

Precipitation of dissolved polymer and solvent separation

text: The cleaned polymer is then precipitated from the solution by one of three different approaches: (1) adding antisolvent, (2) changing the temperature or pressure of the solvent or (3) evaporation of the solvent. The selection of the appropriate method in this step depends on the types of polymer and solvent used in the process. If possible, antisolvents should be avoided because they introduce the need for costly separation steps, such as distillation, to separate solvent from antisolvent. The second method is useful if the polymer-solvent interaction is highly dependent on temperature or pressure, and the third option is often preferred when the solvent has a low boiling point. More information on the methods used for various polymer-solvent systems is included in Tables 1 and 2. During this stage, a notable challenge is the gelation of polymers (a process where the precipitated polymer and solvent form a single gel-like phase instead of distinct liquid and solid phases) during precipitation, which leads to complications in subsequent separation of precipitates from the solvent 35 . After precipitation, the precipitated polymer will be separated from the solvent. Researchers have used methods such as decantation 32 and filtration to remove the solvent 36 . Even in complex mixed plastic wastes that contain ten different plastics, laboratory-scale experiments recovered 89 wt% or higher for each polymer 37 .

text:
Solvent recovery and purification

After the separation steps, the undissolved material and precipitated polymer contain certain amounts of solvent. These remaining solvents must be recovered for safety, environmental and economic reasons. Solvents are removed from the solid materials by further drying, often with a vacuum followed by condensing the vapors; however, quantitative studies on this aspect are still lacking. In addition, impurities in the solvent after dissolution can include organic or very fine inorganic color bodies, phthalates, rubbers/gels and smaller fragments of the plastics. Low levels of impurities (less than 0.5 wt%) can be removed by adsorption 32 . The solvent often needs to be purified before reuse to remove the impurities or any antisolvent used in the process. In this case, a distillation step is required to separate the solvent from the antisolvent. In the case of precipitation without antisolvent, the solvent might be recovered by a simpler evaporation step. Although solvent purification technologies have undergone extensive studies, integration of these methodologies into recycling processes presents challenges due to the diverse spectrum of contaminants produced during the process.

text: The final purified and extruded resins need to be qualified in the downstream application to make sure the products meet consumer needs. The quality (for example, purity and resulting mechanical and thermal properties) of the recovered resin can be assessed across various categories such as Fourier transform infrared spectra, melt flow index, crystallinity and thermomechanical properties (for example, tensile strength and thermal stability). Studies have shown that the crystallinity 38 and mechanical properties 39 of solvent-extracted polymers are affected by the process. Limited studies on the purity of solventrecovered polymers have been carried out. Recently, Deng et al. used dimethyl isosorbide to extract PET from a PET-PS-PVC-PE-PLA blend. No characteristic peaks associated with additives were observed in the 1 H NMR spectra of the recovered PET, showing the high purity of the recovered polymer 40 . Property changes of the recovered polymers can be attributed to the minor degradation of the polymer chains during the dissolution/precipitation stage, the presence of mixtures of polymer architectures in the input material 41 or the removal/degradation of some additives during the process 42 . Thermodynamics of polymer solubility

Understanding solvent-polymer thermodynamic properties allows for the selection of a suitable solvent and operation conditions for dissolution and precipitation. While some solvents and antisolvents have been identified and tabulated for common polymers 9 , identifying solvents that enable the selective dissolution of a single polymer component from a multicomponent mixture of plastic waste remains a challenge. Thermodynamics of polymer solubility

Understanding solvent-polymer thermodynamic properties allows for the selection of a suitable solvent and operation conditions for dissolution and precipitation. While some solvents and antisolvents have been identified and tabulated for common polymers 9 , identifying solvents that enable the selective dissolution of a single polymer component from a multicomponent mixture of plastic waste remains a challenge. Figure 2 summarizes four broad categories of theories and computational models that can efficiently guide solvent selection by predicting polymer solubility.

In equation (1), R is the ideal gas constant, T is the temperature, component 1 is the solvent, component 2 is the polymer, ni is the number of moles of component i and ϕ i is the volume fraction of component i . The first two terms account for the combinatorial entropy contribution to Δ S mix , while the third term uses the parameter χ 12 to account for polymer-solvent interactions that contribute to Δ H mix . Solubility parameters are another powerful tool to predict polymer dissolution. Most solubility parameter systems adopt the 'like dissolves like' concept and postulate that materials with similar parameter values will be miscible 56 . Notable examples include the Hildebrand parameter and HSPs 60 . The Hildebrand solubility parameter is derived from a material's cohesive energy density and has reasonable predictive accuracy for non-polar systems, but is limited when there are strong polar or specific interactions such as hydrogen bonds. HSPs extend this concept to three parameters that assess the chemical similarity between a polymer and a solvent on the basis of dispersion ( δ D ), polar ( δ P ) and hydrogen-bonding ( δ H ) interactions. Polymer-solvent interactions are quantified by their virtual distance R a as shown in equation (2).

R 2 a = 4 ( δ solvent D -δ polymer D ) 2 +( δ solvent P -δ polymer P ) 2 +( δ solvent H -δ polymer H ) 2 . ŷ2Ÿ

Polymer solution theories and solubility parameters have laid the foundation for polymer dissolution behaviors and solubility predictions (Box 1). Phase diagrams based on Flory-Huggins theory have provided physical insight into the key contributions to the free energy associated with polymer-solvent mixing, Δ G mix , at different temperatures and compositions. However, Flory-Huggins theory is a highly simplified physical model and cannot capture all features of a polymer solution, such as the volume change of mixing, the energetically favorable arrangements of molecule segments, or the composition dependence of the interaction parameter 43 . Hansen solubility parameters (HSPs) are more frequently used to guide solvent selection. HSPs have been tabulated for a wide range of polymers and solvents and are a benchmark method for screening solvents to dissolve polymers 44 . While parameter systems such as HSPs have many successful applications, they only qualitatively predict whether a polymer should dissolve in a target solvent, and generally are less accurate at temperatures other than RT.

text: Recent studies have applied modern molecular models and computational methods to evaluate polymer solubility in various solvent systems. For example, Zhou et al. 45 developed a computational approach to predict temperature-dependent polymer solubilities using molecular-scale models. This approach employs molecular dynamics simulations, conformational sampling techniques and the conductor-like screening model for real solvents (COSMO-RS) 46 . COSMO-RS is a statistical thermodynamics model that can perform solid-liquid and liquid-liquid equilibrium calculations to calculate polymer solubilities. This approach can rapidly predict quantitative polymer solubilities at different temperatures and in both single- and multicomponent solvent systems. Results using this approach have been tabulated as part of a computational polymer solubility database that includes over 10 polymers and 1,000 solvents at multiple temperatures. The database has paved the way to new studies that integrate solvent screening, TEA, LCA and process optimization 35,43,47 and has successfully been used to guide the design of multistep processes for polymer dissolution and separation in complex mixtures 37 . Following a similar approach to identify new green solvents, Soyemi and Szilvási 48 established a solvent library that contains over 9,000 glycerol derivatives and predicted their physicochemical properties using quantum chemical methods, COSMO-RS and machine learning models. The predicted properties included densities, dipole moments, water solubilities, octanol-water partition coefficients, melting points and HSP values. Potential solvent candidates and dissolution strategies for six common polymers were identified on the basis of the predicted data.

text: Most recently, machine learning methods have been developed to predict properties relevant to polymer dissolution. Chandrasekaran et al. 49 introduced a solvent/antisolvent classification model using a deep neural network, which Aoki et al. 50 extended to predict temperature-dependent Flory-Huggins interaction parameters. Ethier et al. 51 combined Flory-Huggins theory with neural networks to improve model interpretability and accuracy. Sanchez-Lengeling et al. 52 introduced the Gaussian process HSP, a Bayesian method for HSP determination. Kurotani et al. 53 used an in-phase deep neural network to predict solubility parameters. Kern et al. 54 proposed fingerprints of polymers and solvents for room-temperature solubility prediction. These studies largely focus on qualitatively classifying solvents and antisolvents for target polymers or predicting solubility parameters, but a research gap remains in developing machine learning models to quantitatively predict polymer solubilities. Training these models also requires large-scale and high-quality data on polymer solubility, requiring the development of standardized, high-throughput experimental solubility measurement approaches 55 .

text: This previous discussion has largely focused on polymer solubility at ambient pressure. Another important factor that influences both the enthalpy of mixing (Δ H mix ) and the entropy of mixing (Δ S mix ) is solvent density 56,57 . In a homogeneous solution, the contribution of pairwise interactions to Δ H mix is roughly proportional to the density, which approximately determines the number of interactions per volume. Increasing solvent density for a system with favorable polymer-solvent interactions can thus increase polymer solubility 57 . However, if there are large differences in the densities of the solvent and polymer, the corresponding change in volume upon mixing also contributes to Δ S mix (ref. 56). Unlike the combinatorial entropy, which always promotes mixing, the non-combinatorial contribution to Δ S mix due to this density difference disfavors mixing by reducing the entropy of the lower-density (typically solvent) component. This behavior leads to phase separation at temperatures above the lower critical solution temperature 56 ; at high temperatures, the solvent density decreases to a much greater degree than the polymer density and the non-combinatorial entropy is highly unfavorable. The impact of solvent density on polymer solubility has motivated interest in supercritical fluids as solvents for polymer dissolution 58 . Unlike typical solvents, which are nearly incompressible, the density of a supercritical fluid can be varied from gas-like to liquid-like by manipulating the pressure. Increasing the pressure of a supercritical fluid such that its density approaches that of a target polymer will drive dissolution by reducing the unfavorable non-combinatorial entropy 57 . Pressure variations can also lead to differences in solubility for polymers with similar chemical properties but distinct densities (for example, low-density PE (LDPE) versus high-density PE (HDPE)) 59 . The addition of pressure as a 'knob' to tune the properties of supercritical fluids has motivated the use of solvents with low critical temperatures and pressures, such as carbon dioxide, ethylene propane and butane, to dissolve and purify polymers; one such example is the PureCycle process (discussed below).

text: Together, the exciting developments in physics-based and datadriven predictions of polymer solubility support the ability of modern computational methods to screen large sets of solvents, including new solvents for which experimental data may not be available. Ongoing challenges include treating variations in polymer solubility associated with molecular weight, crystallinity 60 and the presence of small-molecule components, such as common additives, pigments or contaminants in plastic waste 61 . Predictive methods for solubility are also less established for supercritical fluids than for typical solvents. Current methods rely on equation-of-state models, such as the perturbed chain-statistical associating fluid theory equation of state 62 , and some recent methods have developed machine learning methods or extended COSMO-RS models appropriate for predicting solubility in supercritical carbon dioxide 63 , but more generalizable methods are needed. Other challenges include predicting solution properties other than solubility, such as viscosity, that will influence the design of solvent-mediated recycling methods 28 . For example, thermodynamic models to understand solubility are also useful for understanding the thermodynamics of precipitation as a method to recover dissolved polymer resins from solution. However, polymer crystallization during precipitation depends upon the thermodynamics of nucleation, which remains challenging to predict 64 . The kinetics of polymer crystallization during precipitation can likewise greatly affect the properties of the recycled materials. For example, crystallization temperature, cooling rate and the application of high shear strain are typical factors to control the crystal structure and morphology of polymers 64 . Therefore, while polymer solubility is a critical factor in solvent selection, both thermodynamic and kinetic factors need to be considered in process design. Because the thermodynamic properties of solvents, polymers and impurities strongly influence the operating conditions of the recycling process and its overall economic and environmental performance, another important challenge is the co-design of solvents and of the recycling process (particularly when diverse polymers and impurities are present in the input waste feedstock) 65 .

CreaSolv

CreaSolv is a plastic recycling process developed by the Fraunhofer Institute for Process Engineering and Packaging IVV 66,67 . According to their official website, the process involves solvent selection, targeted polymer dissolution, removal of contaminants from the solution, precipitation of the polymer, drying and final product processing 68 . text:
APK Newcycling operates an 8,000-ton-per-year plant in Merseburg, Germany, that has been in operation since June 2018 70 . Their process extracts PE and PAs from post-industrial multilayer plastic wastes. According to one of the patents published in 2022, the process involves the shredding and categorization of feedstock, washing and separation through density differences, dissolution of targeted polymer, solid and liquid separation using a centrifuge, cross-flow filtration with a membrane for purification, flash evaporation and devolatilization for polymer extraction, and extrusion to produce final product (see Fig. 1b) 71 . The company has partnered with Coperion to incorporate ZSK twin-screw extruder technology into its process, ensuring efficient polymer devolatilization and extrusion 72 .

APK Newcycling operates an 8,000-ton-per-year plant in Merseburg, Germany, that has been in operation since June 2018 70 . Their process extracts PE and PAs from post-industrial multilayer plastic wastes. According to one of the patents published in 2022, the process involves the shredding and categorization of feedstock, washing and separation through density differences, dissolution of targeted polymer, solid and liquid separation using a centrifuge, cross-flow filtration with a membrane for purification, flash evaporation and devolatilization for polymer extraction, and extrusion to produce final product (see Fig. 1b) 71 . The company has partnered with Coperion to incorporate ZSK twin-screw extruder technology into its process, ensuring efficient polymer devolatilization and extrusion 72 .

text:
Polystyvert has demonstrated a 600-ton-per-year plant since August 2018 in Montreal, Canada, focusing on the recovery of PS 73 . According to a patent published in 2023, the process uses PS waste, such as foam packaging, as feedstock 74 .The material is dissolved in p -cymene, followed by filtration and precipitation using a non-polar antisolvent such as heptane or hexane. The precipitated PS undergoes several washing and separation steps to remove impurities, after which it is dried and extruded. The process flow diagram can be found in Fig. 1c. One of the key innovations lies in its solubilization stage, where the solvent is also able to dissolve various non-polar additives such as hexabromocyclododecane and silicone oils. The dissolution equipment utilizes a metallic grid to help push the expanded PS into the solvent, which further reduces the dissolution time 75 . To advance the commercial scale-up of this technology, Polystyvert partnered with INEOS Styrolution in 2021 74 .

text: PureCycle Technologies is commercializing a proprietary process developed by Procter and Gamble that uses supercritical butane to recycle PP plastic waste into high-quality resin. The company worked with KraussMaffei, a company that specializes in degassing extruders, to upscale its process 76 . A simplified process flow diagram is shown in Fig. 1d ref. 32. The process begins with preprocessing feedstock. According to a report published by Leidos, the preprocessing for high-purity PP wastes involves feedstock de-baling, shredding, metal removal, granulating and agglomeration 77 . After preprocessing, the feedstock is fed into an extruder to melt the material and remove solid impurities. The melted PP is then fed into a light extraction column, to extract and remove light, soluble impurities. The solvent is then directed to a flash tank for separation. The remaining PP-solvent mixture enters a mixing column to fully dissolve the PP. Subsequently, the mixture moves into a settler, and the heavy phase is conveyed out of the settler for scrap storage. Additionally, the PP-solvent mixture from the settler passes through candle filters to remove insoluble solid impurities, after which adsorption columns are utilized to remove remaining impurities. The PP solution is then reheated to further remove the solvent. The PP undergoes further pelletization for storage or reprocessing as needed.

STRAP is building a 200-ton-per-year pilot system, which can process mixed plastic wastes including multilayer plastic to extract highquality resin, in the United States 30 . Figure 1e shows the simplified process flow diagram of STRAP. After the feedstock is preprocessed, it is selectively dissolved and undergoes hot filtration. The undissolved material is discharged and dried to recover solvent, while the solution undergoes hot adsorption to remove small-sized impurities. The solution is then cooled to allow precipitation, after which the precipitated polymer is separated and dried for resin production and the solvent is purified to be reused in the process. text: recycling processes can produce high-quality polymers, and additional attributes to characterize include tensile strength, flexural strength, impact strength, membrane performance and polymer solution characterization (density, refractive index, viscosity) 25 . The materials recovered via dissolution-based processes can have potential applications in packaging films, membranes, glues, paint additives, natural/fiber composites and textiles, depending on the recovered material and its properties. Therefore, dissolution-based processes can help produce high-quality products from diverse feedstocks that are hard to recycle (Table 2) and be used as a separation technology for multicomponent complex waste. Some limitations include separating mixtures with specific polymers that are challenging to dissolve (for example, PET and nylons). Previous approaches have overcome this issue by leaving the challenging component (for example, PET) at the end of the separation sequence and recovering it as a residual solid without being dissolved 25 . Two other challenges are the separation of different grades of the same polymer and the removal of impurities such as dyes, which impact the color and final use of the recycled materials. Often, in the case of these more challenging separations, costly process steps such as elevated temperatures, pressures or added separation steps are required to achieve high-quality resins 13,82-85 . More research is needed to outline the tradeoffs between product quality and process costs. Demonstrating the food safety of polymers recovered from dissolution recycling also needs further research. Nevertheless, at least on a theoretical basis, dissolution-based recycling has the potential to overcome these challenges and produce virgin-like resins.

Economic analysis

Academic and industry reports have shown that the economic feasibility of dissolution-based processes depends strongly on the precipitation method, feedstock type, recovered polymers, economies of scale (plant capacity) and solvents (type and recycling rate) 13,82,84,85 . Table 3 summarizes key variables for different processes in various stages of development. The processes were differentiated by name and precipitation method including antisolvent (A), cooling (C) or other (O), which comprise a combination of methods. These data are primarily based on laboratory studies, rather than on commercial data, which are difficult to obtain. While estimates of economic and environmental impacts from laboratory data can have limited accuracy, comparing different processes and studies helps identify the main impact drivers and general trends.

text: Table 3 presents the capital costs for different processes at different plant capacities. These costs are heavily dependent on the required type of equipment. A trend of similar costs in processes with equal capacities and assumptions can be seen (for example, antisolvent-PET and cooling-PET) 86 . However, the technology that uses antisolvent as a precipitation technique results in higher capital costs. The same trend can be observed comparing STRAP-A, which uses antisolvent, and STRAP-B, which uses cooling 87 . These studies have reported that the need for distillation steps to separate the solvent/antisolvent mixture and the required process utilities lead to higher capital and operating costs. In addition, it has been reported that the solvent/polymer ratio and non-feedstock inputs (mainly solvent) are large contributors to process economics 87 . Therefore, high polymer concentrations with high solvent recycling rates are typically necessary to achieve profitability.

text:
Feedstock type and composition are also key economic drivers; some processes may have to purchase feedstock with prices depending on the quality and availability, while others may receive a tipping fee for accepting waste 86 . To date, there is no clear trend between feedstock quality and cost. Some companies, such as PureCycle, have invested in sorting technologies to source ideal feedstocks, but this does not mean that high-quality low-cost feedstocks such as post-industrial waste are not available 88 .

Feedstock composition plays a key role because prices of recovered materials can vary (for instance, HDPE may sell for US$1 kg -1 and EVOH may sell for US$8 kg -1 ) 89,90 . These differences can drive process profitability and design (number of solvent washes to recover all polymers or only the most valuable components). It is also important to highlight that certain polymers require higher energy inputs to dissolve (due to unfavorable thermodynamics), and contaminated feedstocks may need prewashing and other purification steps 91 . Solvent choice impacts energy requirements for solvent removal and affects product use (for example, only some solvents may be suitable for food contact applications).

text: Many studies report that dissolution-based recycling can produce high-quality recycled resins at prices competitive with those of virgin polymers (using the minimum selling price (MSP) as a metric) 86,87,91 . The recovered resins are typically cleaner than mechanically recycled resins and more valuable than the oils or monomers produced by chemical recycling, offering a competitive advantage over other recycling methods 84 . This suggests that dissolution-based recycling can be profitable despite initial capital expenditures, if there is sufficient volume to achieve favorable economies of scale. The larger commercial processes aim to recycle at 20,000-50,000 metric tons per year 70,77 ; this is the current best indicator for necessary scale, but operational data sre lacking. It is important to note the significant uncertainty in current academic and industrial preliminary estimations, which require more detailed studies in pilot systems.

text:
Feedstock selection can have a large impact on capital costs for dissolution recycling plants and should be carefully considered during the commercialization of this new technology. Cleaner feedstocks such as post-industrial multilayer waste require fewer preprocessing and contaminant removal steps, which can considerably lower capital expenses. Similarly, colorless plastic waste may require fewer treatment steps and save costs. If available, plastic waste containing only two polymers presents an opportunity for plants to recover two products with a single solvent, improving the plant's economic efficiency. If possible, early commercial solvent-based recycling plants should focus on 'ideal' feedstocks first, moving to more complicated waste streams as the technology is better tested and understood.

text: The environmental impacts of dissolution-based processes have been quantified by various LCA methodologies. Most studies only report the climate change impact or equivalent greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of the process 82,92 . However, other environmental metrics, such as resource use, water use, land use, toxicity, material circularity and others, can also be relevant, as the single metric of climate change is likely insufficient in determining all environmental impacts of a process 9 . For instance, modern engineered landfills are the most used plastic waste management process, and generate minimal GHG emissions, although their environmental impacts related to soil and groundwater pollution are substantial 9 . Additionally, current LCA approaches have not standardized the selection of system boundaries 93 . This lack of consistency hinders the comparison between approaches and can result in inconsistent or misleading conclusions 94 .

text: Table 3 provides a summary of the climate change impact and key drivers reported by different references. Most studies use a cradle-togate approach, and depending on the type of waste (post-industrial or post-consumer) some approaches include pretreatment 9,86 . A common environmental impact driver in the processes that use antisolvent is steam, which is required to separate the solvent-antisolvent mixture via distillation. The climate change impacts reported with the virgin production alternative are compared in Fig. 3. It is important to note that these studies may use different assumptions, and reported values may become outdated with updates to technology or LCA methodology. It can be found that, in general, the processes with a higher environmental impact than the virgin alternative use antisolvent as a precipitation method. The specific increase in GHG emissions appears in Fig. 3 as a positive percentage highlighted in red. This impact is a direct result of the energy required to separate the solvent and antisolvent and to recycle them. On the other hand, the processes that use cooling or other methods have a lower climate change impact than virgin polymer production because of lower energy requirements. These methods also include solvent recovery and recycling, but the energy demand is lower because there are no solvent mixtures (see the above discussion for more details on solvent recovery). These results again highlight the need to identify solvents that lead to favorable process designs and operating conditions. The lowest emissions were reported by the company Polystyvert, followed by Solvent-based PLA and STRAP-PP I. Some important characteristics of the Polystyvert-commercial process are the use of low operating temperatures, an essential oil as solvent and the removal of the flame retardant hexabromocyclododecane 95 . However, there are no publications available that outline their LCA assumptions and methodology. The other processes with low reported impacts recover only one component and do not use antisolvents for the precipitation. Previous studies reported the solid/liquid ratio and process energy consumption as the main contributors to GHG impacts and identified that high solvent recycling rates are essential to reduce emissions 9 . Furthermore, the environmental benefits of the different dissolutionbased processes are a function of the material that is treated and the number of recovered polymers 42,48 . All commercial processes report a reduction in climate change impact and use multicomponent waste as feedstock 67,77 .

text: As shown in Fig. 3, reported dissolution processes without antisolvents have a GHG impact of approximately 1-2 kg CO 2 -equivalent per kg plastic produced, roughly 50% lower than virgin resin production. text:
Almost all chemical processes have economic and environmental trade-offs; however, the evaluated dissolution-based recycling processes agree on common drivers for cost and GHG emissions. For instance, the need for high solvent recycling rates and cooling as a precipitation method has been consistently shown to lead to economic and environmental benefits (mainly focusing on GHG emissions). Of course, solvent consumption is also related to the polymer concentration used in the system. While reducing solvent use lowers environmental impact, it also increases solution viscosity, and maintaining a viable working viscosity takes precedence over minimizing solvent consumption. There is still significant uncertainty in current TEA and LCA approaches; therefore, these conclusions may change as dissolution-based technologies evolve and other environmental metrics are evaluated.

Challenges for commercialization

text: It is unknown if commercial dissolution-based technologies are operating at full capacity. Several of the facilities have been reported to have operational challenges, which are to be expected for pioneer process plants. For instance, a PVC recycling plant in Europe that was designed to recycle 10,000 ton yr -1 of PVC ceased to operate in 2018 68 . Publicly available information indicated that this closure was partly due to the new legislation that identified the phthalates used in their process being hazardous 99 . Another 49,000-ton-per-year plant built in North America is currently operating at lower than its design capacity 100 . It is thus clear that dissolution-based recycling still has several challenges, often related to chemical engineering. First, a solvent must be chosen that only dissolves the targeted polymer and only minimally dissolves any of the other polymers, the pigments or any additives. The undissolved solids are then removed by filtration or centrifugation from a viscous polymer solution without clogging. Depending on the polymer, the dissolution temperature can also be relatively high (for example, >130 °C for polymers such as PP and PET) 45,101 , which means that the processes, equipment, tubing and so on need to withstand high-temperature solvent environments, while every cold spot can induce polymer precipitation and clogging. After the solid-liquid separation, the dissolved impurities should be removed, for example by an adsorption bed. However, adsorption from mostly apolar solvents of additives is not well studied 61 , compared with, for example, adsorption in wastewater treatment, in which the process starts from a polar matrix (water). Afterwards, the polymer must be precipitated from the solution, which could cause gel formation if not well operated 35 . Avoiding gel formation and forming good polymer precipitates is a challenge in dissolution-based recycling. Limiting solvent entrapped in the precipitates reduces the need to remove high amounts of solvent from the resulting gel. The polymer has to be dried to the appropriate level (typically in the ppm range). Dissolution-based recycling thus requires a completely different plant design compared with traditional mechanical recycling plants, as dissolution plants could deal with volatile/ flammable solvents 102 . Therefore, correct safety/hazard engineering controls need to be built into any system. Further details regarding the chemical engineering challenges associated with the commercialization of dissolution-based plastic recycling are summarized in Supplementary Table 1.
