text:
Key recommendations for the future

Dissolution-based plastic recycling technologies have shown considerable potential in producing high-quality resins from diverse plastic waste streams. The thermodynamics of pure polymer-solvent interactions are well documented, and TEA and LCA data indicate that these methods are potentially cost-effective and environmentally sustainable, with several companies now developing industrial plants.

However, several challenges must be addressed to advance this technology. (1) Preprocessing and sorting: enhanced techniques for sorting plastic waste are crucial to optimize the recycling process. (2) Additives in plastics: research is needed to better understand what happens to additives during dissolution and how to remove additives if desired. (3) Polymer solution properties: improved predictions and management of polymer solution properties, such as viscosity, are essential for optimizing the dissolution and precipitation stage of the process. (4) Solvent reuse and impurity accumulation: investigating the impact of impurity build-up in reused solvents and develop methods to mitigate their effects is vital. (5) Recovered-resin properties: further study is required to understand and enhance the properties of recovered resins for various applications.

text:
Some of the above challenges can be addressed in part by policy. For example, improved sorting practices can be required, or dangerous additives can be outlawed. However, many of the challenges related to dissolution recycling are chemical engineering challenges. By addressing these challenges through targeted research and development, dissolution-based plastic recycling technologies can be optimized and integrated into the broader plastic recycling landscape, providing a sustainable solution for managing plastic waste, and making them a key solution for sustainable plastic waste management.

text:
Abstract There is substantial economic and environmental incentive to remove the ink (deink) from heavily printed plastic films so that the plastic can be reused to produce clear films. In this study, polyethylene films printed with solvent-based ink were deinked using surfactants under a variety of conditions. Water without surfactant does not deink the solvent-based ink from plastic films over a pH range of 3 to 12. In common with earlier studies of water-based inks, it is found that solutions of cationic surfactants are the most effective for deinking of solvent-based ink but a pH of at least

11 is required. Presoaking of plastic film in aqueous solution of cationic surfactant increases the level of deinking. Limited studies performed with a pilot-size paper deinking apparatus on solvent-based ink removal indicates that the deinking of plastic film using surfactant solutions is technically feasible.

In-plant, plastic film recycling is successful if the source is known and the scrap plastic is clean; however, most scrap films are heavily printed. Polymers produced from recycled printed film are not as valuable as virgin polymers because the residual ink colors repelletize resins and changes the physical properties of plastic. Solventbased deinking techniques such as the NOREC process have been developed and used in Europe [7]. However, these techniques are expensive, complicated, and produce hazardous waste at the end. For this study, we investigated the use of aqueous surfactant solutions for plastic film deinking since surfactants are more environmentally compatible [5, 6].

Polymers used for films include low-density polyethylene (LDPE), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), polyethylene terephthalate, ethylene vinyl acetate, poly(vinyl chloride), and polypropylene. Most plastic packaging is made of either LDPE, HDPE, or a mixture of LDPE and HDPE [8, 9,10].

text: The plastic film surface is almost always treated using one of several alternative surface treatment processes before printing to increase the surface energy of the plastic surface and enhance ink wettability. These surface treatments are flame treatment, corona discharge, plasma treatment, and UV treatment. Treatment with corona discharge is common and involves application of a high voltage (about 10,000 V) to an electrode which is positioned a short distance from the plastic film. The air between the electrode and the plastic is ionized, and this corona of ionized air oxidizes the surface [11].

text: Water-based or solvent-based ink is used for printing the plastic film surface with flexographic or gravure printing processes. The main ingredients of the inks are pigments, binders, carriers (vehicles), and additives. Organic and inorganic pigments give color and opacity to the ink and influence its fluidity. Binders, which are mostly low-molecular-weight polymeric resins, disperse the pigments and retain them on the plastic film surface after printing. The carrier (or vehicle) is a liquid, which provides fluidity for the ink and transfers the ink from the printing system to the substrate. Solvent-based ink uses solvent, solvent mixtures, or water-miscible solvent as the carrier [12]. Water-based ink uses water as the carrier, but might contain up to 20% alcohol. After application, the carrier should evaporate quickly and completely. Additives in the ink include waxes, surfactants, drying agents, and antioxidizing agents. Hence, the ink on a plastic film surface is a combination of pigments, binders, and additives. Water-based inks occupy a large and increasing fraction of plastic film inks since environmental regulations are restricting the percentage of volatile organic compounds from printing press emissions [13, 14, 15, 16]. However, more energy is required to dry water-based ink. Water-based ink also requires a higher surface energy of the film for good wet out and produces lower quality printing compared to solvent-based ink.

Water-based ink also requires a higher surface energy of the film for good wet out and produces lower quality printing compared to solvent-based ink.

In our previous study, surfactants were determined to be effective in the removal of water-based ink from polyethylene film [5, 6]. Deinking, which involves the removal of various colors and layers of ink from the plastic film, can be considered as a laundering process. This process requires the detachment of the soils (ink), which adhere to the surface by VAN der Waals, electrical, and mechanical forces, and the dispersion of soil in a washing bath. Mechanical action, process chemistry, pH, time, and temperature are important in both plastic deinking and laundering of textiles [5, 6, 17].

In this paper, a discussion is given of the use of surfactants to deink solvent-based ink printing from both commercial plastic packaging film and from plastic films printed with one color (yellow, pink, red, green, gold, black, or violet). Removal of ink from solventbased ink printed plastic films has been studied as a function of surfactant type, surfactant concentration, pH, agitation time, and presoaking. Scaling up of this solvent-based ink removal was conducted using a paper deinking apparatus.

Acommercial plastic film (packaging of Kleenex UltraSoft) and plastic films printed with either yellow, pink, red, green, gold, black, or violet were supplied by Kimberly-Clark. These plastic films were composed of 70% LDPE and 30% HDPE. They were reverse printed with solvent-based ink by the flexographic printing process after surface treatment with corona discharge. The printed surface was then coated with white ink (overcoat) to give an opaque appearance and to protect the ink layers. Printed and clear parts of the plastic film were segregated for this study, and the clear part was used as a standard for comparison with deinked plastic film.

Methods

A backscatter image of the surface containing both clear and printed parts of the plastic film was taken by a scanning electron microscope (SEM, model JEOL JSM-880). A representative sample was mounted on a copper sample holder with double-sided carbon tape and coated with 60/40 gold/palladium in a Hummer VI sputtering system in order to make the sample surface conductive. After coating, a small dot of silver paint was placed on the edge of the sample to ensure conductivity. The same sample was also analyzed with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer attached to the SEM in the spot mode.

text: All glassware was cleaned with a regular laboratory detergent and then acid-washed with Nochromix solution (Godax Laboratories) for at least 1 h. The surfactant solution was always prepared fresh with double deionized water for each of the experiments, and the pH level of the aqueous surfactant solution was adjusted immediately with Fisher-brand certified sodium hydroxide or hydrochloric acid before the deinking experiment was conducted. A representative sample (2.5 cm · 2.5 cm) was cut from the printed part of the plastic film and soaked in a 20 mL solution (water or surfactant solution) with 20 irregularly shaped porcelain beads in 30-mL glass vials. The glass vial was then placed on a reciprocating-action Eberbach shaker for the desired period of agitation at high speed. After agitation, plastic film samples were taken out of the washing bath, rinsed with deionized water, and air dried. In addition, the deinking was scaled up to 2 L by using a Denver Laboratory model D-12 flotation machine with the attrition scrubber kit (Denver Equipment) [6]. After draining the washing bath, deinked plastic film strips were rinsed several times with water and dried in a vacuum oven overnight. Thirty plastic film strips (about 4 wt% of the deinked samples) were randomly picked up from the batch to analyze the level of deinking. All experiments were performed at room temperature and each experiment was performed at least twice.

text:
Each deinked plastic sample was first evaluated visually and was then analyzed using a Hunterlab UltraScan Ô spectrocolorimeter system (Hunter Associates Laboratory) in regular transmission mode. The Hunterlab UltraScan Ô spectrocolorimeter system consists of an UltraScan optical sensor (SN-7834) with a sensor interface unit and an IBM computer that includes dataevaluation software. In the regular transmittance mode, the intensity of the light passing directly through the plastic film was measured wavelength by wavelength. The total color difference (DE*) between the standard (clear plastic film) and the sample (printed plastic film before and after deinking) was determined at the chosen standard illuminant (D65, representing daylight with a correlated color temperature of 6,500 K) and observer (10 0 standard observer). An average value from six measurements for each sample is reported. The lower the value of DE*, the better the deinking. More details about this procedure are given in Ref. [5].

text:
Deinking involves the removal of overcoat (white ink) and colored ink layers from plastic film. In Fig. 1, the backscatter images of the commercial plastic film taken by the SEM show the clear plastic film, ink layer, and overcoat. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectrograms of clear plastic film, colored ink, and overcoat from commercial plastic film are presented in Fig. 2. Energy-dispersive Xray spectrograms of seven individual color printings, overcoat on these printings, and a clear part of the plastic film were also taken (not shown here). In these spectrograms, the detected copper is from the sample holder, while gold and palladium are from the sputter coat. Silicon was detected in all samples because silicon additives are used as flow-control agents, slip aids, defoamer, and hammer finish additives in ink formulations. Aluminum exists in the white overcoat and the gold ink layer, while titanium is only present in the overcoat layer. TiO2 is a common pigment for white ink. Chlorine was detected in all ink layers except pink, black, and overcoat. Most of the organic pigments are halogenated. Calcium exists only in the pink ink layer.

text:
The cationic surfactant CTAB removes the solventbased ink from the plastic film at pH 11, 11.5, and 12 (Fig. 3). The nonionic surfactants AO-DMSi (600) at pH 11.5 and 12, and AEO5 at pH 12 (Fig. 4) partially remove the printing. Although the use of DDAO and AMEO5 does not result in a significant change (Fig. 5), decolorization of the pink color on the plastic film at various levels was observed with the amphoteric surfactants DDAO and AMEO5 at pH 12. The nonionic surfactant AEO5 at pH 11.5 and the cationic surfactant CTAB at pH 10 also decolorized the pink color. The use of SDS, SDOSS, and SDS with Ca ions removes neither overcoat nor ink layers (Fig. 6). Sodium hydroxide is hypothesized to break up the print particle network by hydrolyzing the ester groups in the ink binder [18]. However, surfactants may be necessary to reduce the surface or interfacial tension at the air/water, ink/water, and plastic/water interface, and this can increase the wettability of the solution and allow alkali to penetrate between the ink particle and the plastic film.

text: The deinking with CTAB (1 wt%) of plastic films printed with single colors at pH 12 with 15 min of agitation with and without 2 h of presoaking is shown in Fig. 8. Without presoaking, visual evaluation of the samples indicated that the white overcoat from all the samples except those with pink ink was totally removed, and a small portion of the ink stayed on the plastic film. However, the pink color was completely extracted in CTAB solutions. With presoaking, all colors except red and black are completely removed from the plastic film surface. Even increasing the agitation time to 30 min does not change the level of deinking for the red and black colors (Figs. 9, 10). However, as seen in Fig. 9, addition of 0.2 wt% SS into 1 wt% CTAB solution results in almost complete removal of red ink from the plastic film (DE*=0.22). It has been suggested that silicate acts as a dispersing agent and creates a stable environment for peroxide in the paper deinking processes [19, 20]. On the other hand, the presence of SS in the surfactant solution does not improve the removal of black ink from the plastic film. The addition of AEO5 (0.5 wt%) in CTAB (0.5 wt%) solution enhances the deinking of black ink (Fig. 10). These experiments show that the removal of black ink (which is carbon black) poses the greatest challenge in deinking. Our deinking studies with water-based ink printed plastic film also indicated that the level of deinking depends on the process parameters: pH, agitation time, agitation speed, presoaking, and temperature [5, 6].

text:
Cationic surfactant is the most effective surfactant for the removal of solvent-based ink from plastic film. The process pH is required to be adjusted to 11 or above for complete deinking. All colors except red and black inks can be completely removed from the plastic film by presoaking in a 1 wt% cationic surfactant solution at room temperature at pH 12. The addition of SS to the cationic surfactant completely removes red ink. Substantial, but not complete deinking of carbon black from plastic film was observed when plastic film was deinked with a mixture of nonionic and cationic surfactants.

In general, deinking of solvent-based inks using aqueous solutions of surfactants requires severe conditions

text:
Abstract: Polyamides (PAs, nylons) are a ubiquitous class of high-performance plastics used extensively in a wide range of applications. Their high resistance to many common solvents and tendency to hydrolyze in strong acids or bases creates a major hurdle to low-emissions material recycling (i.e., resource separation and recovery). In the present study, the first detailed investigation into the molecular mechanisms of polyamide dissolution, we show that introducing a weakly hydrogen-bonding cosolvent into formic acid can effectively tune the solvent-solvent and solvent-polymer interactions, drastically accelerates the room-temperature dissolution kinetics of common (short-chain) polyamides such as PA6 and PA66, as well as long-chain and semi-aromatic varieties. The recovered polymers show no change in their chemical structures or properties, and sufficient selectivity allows for fillers such as short and long fibers, inorganic nanoparticles, metals, and other mixed polymer phases to be recovered at high efficiency ( > 95%) along with recirculation of all solvents ( > 98%). This cosolvent-enabled approach has the potential to make polyamide recycling more sustainable and economical by reducing the energy input and CO2 emissions required to separate and recover the various constituent materials from automotive and electrical components, textiles, and beyond.

Introduction

text:

text: The majority of research studies and patented technologies regarding PA dissolution-mostly electrospinning, but some recycling-employ either formic acid (FA) or polar solvents (e.g., benzyl alcohol), which vary widely in their agreement with HSP predictions (Figure S1). [17-24] While FA can dissolve PA6 and other short-chain PAs at room temperature, the slow kinetics can make complete dissolution take up to 24 hr depending on the recyclate geometry. Other polar solvents require high temperatures (140 °C200 °C) and long dissolution times (4-24 hr), [1,17-24] which is comparable to chemical recycling conditions in terms of carbon footprint (Figure 1b). Furthermore, long-chain PAs (e.g., PA12 and bio-based PA11) only dissolve in pure FA at elevated temperatures ( -80 °C) and require long dissolution times (4-24 hr). [30,31] High-performance semiaromatic polyphthalamides (PPAs) are even more resistant to these solvents and do not dissolve even under harsh conditions. By contrast, fluorinated alcohols and acids such as hexafluoroisopropanol (HFIP) and trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) can easily dissolve a range of PAs (short- and long-chain) at ambient conditions, [32] but they are too expensive to be used in an economically viable scaled-up recycling process. There is an urgent need for a versatile and cost-effective recycling method that can recover valuable resources from a range of polyamide-containing waste with minimal carbon emissions. [33-35]

It is well known that short-chain PAs dissolve in FA at room temperature (RT), but it can take up to 12 h for complete dissolution. As shown in Figure 2a, PA6 formed a slightly cloudy solution after 4 hr in pure FA (RT, no agitation), whereas PA66 became completely clear (Figure S2). After screening various solvents (see Supporting Information), a measurable positive effect on the dissolution rate of PA6 was only observed for chlorinated hydrocarbons like dichloromethane (DCM), chloroform (CHCl3), and dichloroethane (DCE); they have characteristic low polarity and the ability to form weak H-bonds and effectively solvate hydrocarbons. [36] Ethyl acetate (EtOAc), MEK, and THF are similar to DCM in terms of, e.g. viscosity and HSPs, but they had the opposite effect of decreasing overall solubility. H-bond titration of PA6 solutions revealed that FA is more sensitive than PA to the cosolvent and that solubility shows strong negative correlation with the cosolvent's donor number (DN) (Figure S3). This means it must act as a weak H-bond donor (HBD)

and poor H-bond acceptor (HBA) to promote polyamide dissolution. This characteristic has been demonstrated for fluorinated polar solvents such as HFIP, [37] suggesting that chlorinated hydrocarbons combined with formic acid can serve the same role.

text: DCM was selected as the primary cosolvent for our study due to its compatibility with FA, relatively low cost, and low boiling point. PAs do not dissolve in pure DCM at RT (Figure 2a), contrary to predictions by HSP theory and implicit solvation models which do not account for explicit H-bonding (Figure S1). PA6 dissolution in FA/DCM mixtures is accelerated by varying degrees depending on the cosolvent ratio, reaching a maximum at 1:1 w/w (i.e., DCM fraction of f DCM = 0.5) and reversing to a slower rate at f DCM = 0.7 (Figure 2b). When f DCM > 0.7, only swelling with limited dissolution is observed. Viscosity measurements of PA6 solutions at different solids concentrations and cosolvent ratios, shown in Figure 2c normalized to the molar ratio of FA to amide units, made it clear that higher f DCM correlates to lower solution viscosity with the lowest value obtained when f DCM = 0.7, which tells us that dissolution rate is not necessarily affected by viscosity of the bulk solvent or solution (Figure S2).

text: DFT calculations of binding energies ( Delta1 E bind) at the M062X/def2-TZVP level [40,41] for dimers of pure FA and DCM and FA/DCM are shown in Figure 3a (see Supporting Information for details). FA in bulk solvent form is assumed to consist primarily of so-called 'open' dimers (FF o ) [42-48] with moderately large Delta1 E bind dominated by H-bonding, while the mildly polar DCM dimer has a smaller Delta1 E bind dominated by van der Waals (vdW) interactions. [49-51] Combining them into the solvent-cosolvent dimer (FC) yields smaller Delta1 E bind and longer H-bond lengths than pure FA (Figures 3a and S5), with FA and DCM acting as the HBA and HBD, respectively. FTIR spectroscopy of the cosolvent system revealed a blue-shift in the C ═ O region of FA with increasing f DCM (Figures 3b-d) which was reproduced by DFT (Figure S5). We attribute this shift to the transition from FF clusters to FC and (albeit rare) F monomers. [42-51] These results imply the presence of weak hydrogen bonds between FA and DCM, with the largest shift occurring between 0.5 < f DCM < 0.7. Replacing DCM with EtOAc, which negatively affected PA6 solubility, gives a FC dimer with larger Delta1 E bind than FF (Figure S5), supporting our assertion that weak H-bonds play a major role in dissolution kinetics. We next examined the solvent-polymer interactions using DFT and FTIR. The PA6 oligomer used in our DFT study is the α -phase crystal configuration (PA6α ) [52-54] depicted in Figure 3e, with possible solvent interaction sites identified as the amide group (-CONH) and methylene groups (-CH2) that act through HBA/HBD or vdW-dominant interactions, respectively. The individual binding energies of FA and DCM monomers with PA6 at these sites are compared in Figure 3f. Figure 3g shows steady growth of the so-called solvation energy ( Delta1 G solv) of PA6α , which we take as the binding energy between an explicit solvent cluster and polymer oligomers, with increasing cosolvent fraction up to f DCM = 0.9 (see Supporting Information for details). Final solvated structures for 0 ≤ f DCM < 0.7 show full breakage of H-bonds and conformational change of the alkyl segment, whereas H-bonds are partially and fully intact at f DCM = 0.7 and 0.9, respectively (Figure S6). Using the binding energies of individual solvent-polymer interactions to decompose Delta1 G solv into approximate H-bond and vdW components, we see that poor affinity of FA toward methylene units in PA6 results in a large endergonic vdW component, but the strong H-bond component is large enough to create a net exergonic interaction that exceeds the Delta1 E bind of PA6α ; this explains why short-chain PAs dissolve in pure FA at room temperature. As f DCM increases, the two components approach each other while the total Delta1 G solv continues to grow larger until f DCM = 0.9, at which point the H-bond component grows smaller than the pure PA6α binding energy (Figure S7, Table S3).

text: In particular, polyamides are semi-crystalline polymers typically exhibiting a highly stable α -phase crystal formed by H-bonding; this must be overcome for decrystallization occur, followed by conventional dissolution mechanisms (i.e., disentanglement and diffusion). [56] DFT calculations of PA6α (H-bonded oligomers) and solvated PA6 chains in explicit solvent clusters indicated that the N ─ H and C ═ O bonds do not significantly change when going from crystal to solution, as the corresponding HBA/HBD simply changes from PA to FAwith similar binding energies (Figures 3 and S8). However, our calculations show that the carbonyl C ─ N (CONH) bond is sensitive to the HBA/HBD species, and experimental and theoretical studies have demonstrated that -CONH exhibits distinctly different IR absorption bands (850-1100 cm -1 ) depending on the crystal structure. [52-54] By monitoring this band for a thin PA6 film exposed to FA/DCM (1:1 w/w) using transmission-mode FTIR, we found an exponential-type decrease over time that indicates rapid decrystallization in the early stages of solvent contact (Figure S8).

The question becomes, at what point does the cosolvent negatively affect dissolution kinetics despite more favorable Delta1 G solv? Considering the role of cosolvent described above, we contend that the beneficial effect of cosolvent on dissolution kinetics reaches a maximum when the solvent-cosolvent interactions (FC) are nearly balanced by the solvent-polymer interactions (SP). text: The unprecedented dissolution kinetics achieved by the present cosolvent strategy can be utilized to establish a room-temperature protocol for dissolution-based recycling of PA-containing waste with an ultra-small carbon footprint. Figure 5a illustrates the general scheme for polyamidetargeted rapid dissolution with photos of some specific conditions for separating and recovering PAs as well as secondary materials (SMs). After precipitating the polymer in acetone (PA6: 99.2% yield), we completely separated and recovered all three solvents by sequential rotary evaporation with high yield (FA: 99.5%, DCM: 98.5%, acetone: 98.2%). The evaporation rate of the cosolvent system is considerably lower than that expected for a linear mixture, suggesting that DCM is stabilized by interactions with FA and thus solvent loss by evaporation is subdued (Figure S9). Residual solvents in recycled PA6 and PA66 after just one washing cycle were examined by headspace gas chromatography (HS-GC) and revealed minor and trace amounts of FA (200-300 ppm) and DCM (1 ppm), respectively (Table S4). There are no universal limits for residual solvent in recycled plastics in general, as different plastic types and applications (e.g., food packaging versus electrical components) all have different purity requirements, but the levels in our study are well below the strict limits set for pharmaceuticals, for example (FA: < 5000 ppm, DCM: < 600 ppm). [60]

By comparison, conventional dissolution methods using polar solvents [1,24] produce fewer carbon emissions than depolymerization, but energy demand for the high temperatures necessary for dissolution is still considerably large. A hypothetical case of pure FA as solvent reduces the GWP substantially, but the slow dissolution kinetics influences output rate and ultimately results in large energy demand. Our cosolvent strategy for accelerating PA dissolution kinetics at RT without agitation can potentially reduce the GWP of any aliphatic-containing PA down to 0.8 kg CO2-eq with a PED of just 16 MJ kg -1 ; this is over 50% lower than depolymerization or conventional dissolution, and roughly 80% lower than virgin material.

Since a variety of SMs can also be recovered in pristine condition, we also considered the recovery of valuable resources such as glass fibers (GF), which are used in high volume, and carbon fibers (CF), which carry a large carbon footprint and high cost (Figure 6c). If our cosolvent-based approach was used to recovery only the fibers (i.e., ignoring the plastic) in model compounds containing 30 wt% short fibers, allocating the full GWP and PED to the fiber fraction alone would still yield drastically reduced emissions compared to virgin fibers.

text: Finally, we extend our approach to upcycle real PA waste into valuable composite materials. Figure 7a shows a facile process in which used fishing nets (containing PA6, PE, and Pb) are rapidly dissolved in the FA/DCM system and separated (see Movie S1), after which carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are mixed into the PA6 to produce functional nanocomposites (Figure S14). The tensile properties and thermal conductivity (Figures 7b-e) are competitive with similar nanocomposites produced using pristine materials as reported in the literature (see Supporting Information for details). Similarly, PA6 was extracted from used textile waste (containing PA6, PU elastomer, and dyes) by first removing the acid dye and elastomer in DMSO before rapidly dissolving the PA in FA/DCM(see Movie S2) and laminating with recycled carbon fiber cloth (rCF) that was previously recovered by dissolution (Figure 7f). The tensile properties of the recovered neat PA (rPA6) were lower than virgin PA6 (Figure 7g), likely to a difference in grades, but the mechanical performance of the rPA6/rCF laminates exceeded 85% of the virgin equivalent and thus could be used in structural applications. LCA/TEA calculations summarized in Figure 7i of the GWP, PED, and MSP of these two upcycled composite materials show reductions of up to 90% compared to similar virgin materials. This demonstrates that rapid, dissolution-based room-temperature recycling processes with minimal carbon emissions can achieve a good balance between material performance, carbon footprint, and cost. Our cosolvent strategy for drastically enhancing RT dissolution kinetics is one promising approach to accomplish this.

text:
Conclusion

Closing the loop for polyamides remains difficult due to the high energy demand and carbon emissions associated with current dissolution-based recycling methods, despite showing great promise for efficient separation of valuable materials in mixed polyamide waste. In this work, we have demonstrated that formic acid, a relatively cheap and environmentally benign solvent known to dissolve short-chain PAs, can be used for rapid, room-temperature recycling of all varieties of PAs when a weak hydrogen-bonding cosolvent is added. Through a combination of experiments and DFT calculations, we showed that: 1) polyamides dissolve when the interactions with H-bonding solvents (having both HBA and HBD characteristics) are more favorable than polymer-polymer interactions, and 2) the cosolvent can tune the solvation behavior of FA toward PA with drastically accelerated dissolution rates by regulating both solvent-solvent and solventpolymer interactions. While DCM (or another chlorinated solvent) was used as a model cosolvent, the major value of this work is the improved understanding of how cosolvent systems interact with polyamides at the molecular level, providing a foundation for future work on cosolvent design.

Conclusion

Closing the loop for polyamides remains difficult due to the high energy demand and carbon emissions associated with current dissolution-based recycling methods, despite showing great promise for efficient separation of valuable materials in mixed polyamide waste. In this work, we have demonstrated that formic acid, a relatively cheap and environmentally benign solvent known to dissolve short-chain PAs, can be used for rapid, room-temperature recycling of all varieties of PAs when a weak hydrogen-bonding cosolvent is added. Through a combination of experiments and DFT calculations, we showed that: 1) polyamides dissolve when the interactions with H-bonding solvents (having both HBA and HBD characteristics) are more favorable than polymer-polymer interactions, and 2) the cosolvent can tune the solvation behavior of FA toward PA with drastically accelerated dissolution rates by regulating both solvent-solvent and solventpolymer interactions. While DCM (or another chlorinated solvent) was used as a model cosolvent, the major value of this work is the improved understanding of how cosolvent systems interact with polyamides at the molecular level, providing a foundation for future work on cosolvent design.

Green foundation

This work proposes computational methods to identify solvents that can remove hazardous contaminants from plastic waste, thereby facilitating the design of sustainable recycling processes that minimize plastic pollution in the environment.

The computational methods developed in this work quantify contaminant partitioning into di ff erent solvents based on thermodynamically well-defined partition coe ffi cients. The integration of these calculations with previous methods to predict polymer solubility enable contaminant removal from plastic waste, as demonstrated in multiple case studies.

This work could be extended to a broader range of harmful contaminants by integrating the thermodynamic methods with machine learning methods, which could also permit analysis of solvent greenness.

Solvent-mediated contaminant removal from plastic waste using thermodynamic modeling

Panzheng Zhou, † a Ugochukwu M. Ikegwu, † a Elizaveta Radkevich, a Euncheol Ra, a Hadeia Liburd, b George W. Huber, a Victor M. Zavala a and Reid C. Van Lehn * a,c

text: Plastics recycling is hindered by the compositional complexity of plastic waste, which can include numerous polymer components as well as low concentrations of additives and non-intentionally added substances. These latter small-molecule species, which we collectively refer to as contaminants, can harm human health and will build up in recycled plastic causing environmental and downstream processing challenges if not removed. In this work, we present molecular modeling approaches using the COnductor-like Screening MOdel for Real Solvents (COSMO-RS) to guide the selection of solvents that are capable of removing targeted contaminants from plastic waste. By considering the thermodynamic partitioning of contaminant species between a solvent phase and polymer phase, we identify guidelines for solvent selection to promote either the low-temperature extraction of contaminants from plastic waste or the removal of contaminants as part of a dissolution-based plastics recycling process. We present four case studies to illustrate the application of the computational approach to the removal of brominated fl ame retardants, phthalates, and selected per fl uoroalkyl substances, and compare to both literature and newly collected experimental data to illustrate model prediction accuracy. The case studies highlight the capability of the modeling approach to help design recycling processes that explicitly account for contaminant removal, thereby increasing product purity during dissolution-based recycling or facilitating chemical recycling of contaminant-free plastics.

text: Despite their benefits, some additives raise concerns due to their persistence in the environment and potential health impacts, which have led to regulatory restrictions on their usage. 18 The presence of additives can also pose a challenge for plastics recycling processes due to their potential to be unintentionally present in recycling streams, particularly for post-consumer plastics that are mixed with a wide range of di ff erent plastic products and other types of waste. 19,20 Postconsumer waste plastics can also include non-intentionally added substances (NIAS) that migrate into plastic products from the environment or other waste materials. 21 NIAS also include substances that are present in plastics without intentionally imparting a technical function to the plastic. As such, NIAS include impurities found in starting materials such as monomers, processing aids, colorants and printing inks, cross-linking agents, as well as by-products or intermediates from polymerization reactions. 10 The most common plastics recycling technology, mechanical recycling, does not remove additives or NIAS without specific preprocessing steps, such as washing in surfactant solutions, 22,23 which can lead to these molecules persisting into the final recycled product raising regulatory and health concerns. 24 -27 Similarly, additives or NIAS can impact the e ffi ciency or products of chemical recycling processes. 28 Consequently, we collectively refer to additives and NIAS as ' contaminants ' for the remainder of this work due to their undesirable presence in recycling streams and need for removal.

text: Because contaminants in plastic waste streams pose a substantial hindrance to plastics recycling due to industrial standards regulating the maximum concentration of these chemicals in pure polymers, processes are required to remove potential contaminants prior to or during plastics recycling. Example processes for contaminant removal include washing in water or surfactant solutions or solvent extraction in organic solvents. 22,23 These processes rely on the selection of solvent or processing conditions to preferentially remove contaminants from the polymer matrix or surface prior to recycling and are often incorporated as pre-processing steps that are applied to waste prior to mechanical or chemical recycling. Alternatively, solvent-based recycling methods that involve the dissolution of polymer resins may also lead to the dissolution of contaminants in the solvent phase, where they can be removed by adsorption. 4,29 For example, Solvent-Targeted Recovery and Precipitation (STRAP ™ ) is a solvent-mediated process in which target polymer resins are recovered from multicomponent plastic waste via selective dissolution and precipitation. 30,31 STRAP has been applied to a variety of complex feedstocks 31 -37 and can also lead to the removal of inks which would otherwise be contaminants in the recovered resins. 32,33 There is thus the potential to combine solventmediated contaminant removal steps with polymer recovery steps, thereby intensifying solvent-based plastics recycling processes while improving product quality. Designing any of these solvent-mediated contaminant removal processes is challenging, however, because each category of contaminant encompasses a large family of hundreds of di ff erent chemical compounds and compounds can be present in low concentrations, which can hinder the rational selection of solvent and operating conditions.

text: To address this problem, in this work we develop computational modeling methods to screen solvents for selectively removing contaminants from plastic waste. Our approach builds upon our prior computational screening methods for polymer solubility to identify solvents capable of extracting classes of di ff erent contaminants without dissolving the target polymer based on thermodynamic calculations. 38 -41 We focus on three categories of contaminants that have recently gained increasing attention due to issues related to toxicity: brominated flame retardants (BFRs), phthalates, and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). We present strategies for contaminant removal from plastic waste by leveraging computational predictions of contaminant partitioning across a broad range of solvents, supported by experimental validation using real-world applications involving these representative contaminants. Comparison to experiments reveals that thermodynamic modeling is suitable for identifying solvents capable of removing target contaminants through leaching or in combination with STRAP, although kinetic e ff ects may also impact the e ffi cacy of these processes. These advances pave the way for the development of sustainable plastics recycling methods like STRAP that can produce high-quality, contaminant-free plastics, thereby diverting plastic materials from landfills for reuse in place of petroleum-derived virgin plastics.

text: material. STRAP contaminant removal refers to the incorporation of contaminant removal steps into a dissolution-based plastic recycling process. In the STRAP process, a target polymer is first dissolved in a selective solvent that does not dissolve other polymer components of the waste. The target polymer is then precipitated by decreasing the temperature or adding a nonsolvent to the solution. Therefore, if properly designed, STRAP can be directly used for contaminant removal by dissolving both a target polymer and contaminants then selectively precipitating the polymer without precipitating the dissolved contaminants. The recycling of pure polymer resins and contaminant removal would be achieved in a STRAP process simultaneously. Fig. 1 illustrates both processes for a single contaminant. Our goal is to develop methods that would permit the simultaneous removal of multiple contaminants using either of the two processes shown in Fig. 1.

Here, c refers to a specific contaminant, the superscript s indicates the solvent, the superscript p indicates the polymer, [c] s and [c] p refer to the concentration of contaminant c in the solvent and polymer, respectively, μ i j is the infinite-dilution chemical potential of component i in pure liquid phase j , and V j is the molar volume of liquid phase j . A positive partition coe ffi cient (log P > 0) indicates that at equilibrium the contaminant is more likely to partition to the solvent phase, while a negative value (log P < 0) indicates that the contaminant prefers to remain in the polymer matrix. In the context of contaminant removal from plastics, we thus hypothesize that calculating log P can predict the e ffi ciency of contaminant removal to determine the selection of appropriate solvents to remove one or more targeted contaminants from a given polymer. We note that this approach is based on equilibrium thermodynamics, without consideration of kinetic factors that may substantially impact low-temperature leaching. 43 Consequently, log P values determine the maximum theoretical removal capacity to guide solvent selection, whereas practical contaminant removal rates could be governed by mass transfer kinetics that are not considered here.

text: The conductor-like screening model for real solvents (COSMO-RS) is used to predict thermodynamic properties that are relevant to contaminant removal, including polymer solubilities, solvent miscibility with contaminants, and contaminant log P values. 44 COSMO-RS is well-suited for this study because it can predict thermodynamic behavior while requiring only input density functional theory calculations (DFT), without requiring new experimental data, which is advantageous for considering the properties of chemically diverse contaminants. Several studies have shown COSMO-RS to predict organic compound solubility and partitioning in liquid phases in strong agreement with experimental measurements, with performance comparable to or more accurate than alternative equation-of-state or continuum-solvation methods. 45 -49 Finally, this approach enables the use of our previous methodology 38,39 to represent the physicochemical properties of polymers using DFT calculations of representative oligomers, as detailed in the SI, to predict contaminant removal.

text: Examples of the molecular structures are shown in Fig. 2a for an example polymer (PVC), solvent (tetrahydropyran, THP), and contaminant (2,4,4 ′ -tribromodiphenyl ether, Tri-PDBE). This step includes a geometry optimization in implicit water using the conductor-like polarizable continuum model and a single-point calculation in the infinite dielectric constant limit, and is performed with Gaussian 16 at the BVP86/TZVP/ DGA1 level of theory. 50 Examples of the resulting screening charge densities and corresponding σ -profiles for the polymers, solvents, and contaminants from this step are also depicted in Fig. 2a. Screening charge densities for polymers and solvents were obtained from our prior work, 38,39 whereas screening charge densities for contaminants were newly computed using a single energy-minimizing conformer per contaminant molecule. A summary of our previously developed method for obtaining screening charge densities for polymers 38,39 is presented in the ' polymer and solvent modeling ' section of the SI, and a complete list of the 32 solvents considered in this work is included as part of Table S1. Second, COSMO-RS statistical thermodynamics calculations use the screening charge density to calculate the chemical potentials of the compounds. Polymer solubilities, solvent miscibility, and contaminant partition coe ffi cients are then calculated via solid -liquid and liquid -liquid equilibrium calculations. 51,52 In this study, a contaminant is considered miscible in a solvent if the predicted liquid -liquid solubility at a given temperature exceeds 15%. Given that most contaminants exhibited high solubility values (approaching 100%) across multiple solvents, miscibility was treated as a binary property: ' yes ' for solubility values greater than 15% and ' no ' otherwise, with this threshold chosen as a conservative value to account for any potential simulation error. All COSMO-RS calculations were performed using the COSMOtherm19 software with the BP_TZVP_19 parameterization, 53 although the BP_TZVP_FINE_19 parameterization was used when predicting partition coe ffi cients in solvent mixtures for better accuracy. 49 Fig. 2b shows an example of the temperature-dependent solubility curve of polyethylene in three di ff erent solvents obtained from COSMO-RS. Similarly, Fig. 2c shows an example of the free energy of mixing of an example contaminant (tri-PDBE) in two solvents at room temperature to illustrate characteristic curves for a solvent in which the contaminant is fully miscible (DMSO) and immiscible (water). We similarly compute log P values using COSMO-RS, 54,55 although these are not shown in Fig. 2.

text: Experiments were carried out for the phthalate removal case study. Benzyln -butyl phthalate (BBP) was selected for it due to its characteristic peak appearance in gas chromatograms. It appears as one clear peak while some other phthalates have multiple peaks. BBP was physically blended with polyvinyl chloride (PVC, Sigma Aldrich average M w ∼ 80 000 and average M n ∼ 47 000) at a ratio of 1 : 2.5 by mass, respectively, to a total mass of 100 g, then melt-compounded in a twin-screw extruder at 150 °C and a screw speed of 30 rpm under mild conditions to minimize thermal degradation. The produced cylindrical filament was 2 -2.2 mm in diameter which was cut into 4.8 -6 mm long pieces. Three consecutive solvent washes were performed in each solvent at each temperature. Xylenes (Aqua Solutions, Reagent ACS Grade) and dodecane (ThermoFisher Scientific, mixture of isomers) were selected as solvents to assess BBP removal e ff ectiveness at room temperature and at 130 °C. The starting polymer mixture mass was 1.0 g and solvent mass was 75 g. Experiments were conducted in glass pressure tubes to avoid solvent evaporation. The solution and polymer were allowed to stir for 1 hour per wash. After each wash, the polymer was recovered, dried for three hours at 100 °C in a vacuum oven and transferred to the next wash with 75 g of new solvent. For experiments at 130 °C, glass tubes were quenched in ice for 5 minutes prior to solvent recovery. Prior to analysis, all samples were filtered using 0.22 μ mfilters to ensure no PVC was retained in the injected samples. Recovered solvents were analyzed through gas chromatography (Shimadzu GC-2010) with a Phenomenex ZB-5HT Inferno ™ column and N2 as the carrier gas. A calibration curve was used for determining the concentration in samples. The concentrations were converted into mass and compared to phthalate mass in the added polymer mixture to calculate the percent recovery. For experiments at 130 °C, some PVC dissolved (as expected; vide infra ) and precipitated during quenching. The solution was filtered using a 100 -200 μ m wire mesh to separate the solution and the PVC. Precipitated PVC was collected from the mesh while any remaining dissolved PVC and BBP was retained in solution. The collected PVC was then dried and transferred to the next wash.

Results and discussion

Solvent selection criteria for contaminant removal

For a given set of contaminants, we propose di ff erent solvent selection criteria based on the characteristics of the two contaminant removal processes in Fig. 1. These selection criteria depend upon contaminant miscibility, the contaminant partition coe ffi cient, and polymer solubilities in the possible solvents.

The selection criteria for leaching are:

The target contaminants must be miscible in the selected solvent ( i.e. , the solvent can dissolve the contaminants).

Contaminants should have positive partition coe ffi cients (log P > 0); higher values are preferred to limit retention within the polymer.

Ideal solvent candidates will swell but not dissolve the polymer.

These criteria are designed to ensure the preferential retention of the contaminants within the chosen solvent without dissolving the polymer itself. Swelling of the polymer is desired to maximize solvent contact with contaminants within the polymer matrix and to enable e ffi cient mass transport into the solvent phase.

The selection criteria for the STRAP contaminant removal process are:

The solvent can dissolve both the polymer and target contaminants.

The solvent does not dissolve non-target compounds, such as other polymers in the plastic waste.

The polymer can be precipitated from solution either by decreasing the temperature (or by adding an antisolvent).

Contaminants should have positive partition coe ffi cients (log P > 0); higher values are preferred.

The contaminants do not precipitate ( i.e. , they remain miscible in the solvent) under the conditions in (4) that induce polymer precipitation.

These criteria are designed to ensure that target contaminants dissolve along with the target polymer and then preferentially remain in the solvent phase when the polymer precipitates. In this work, we assume that precipitation is induced by a decrease in temperature, as opposed to adding an antisolvent, due to more favorable environmental and economic impacts associated with temperature-dependent precipitation. 56 Following our past work, we set a threshold of 1 wt% as the maximum computationally predicted solubility to achieve precipitation, although in practice lower solubilities are observed experimentally. 31,32,38 -40 Dissolved contaminants removed during this process can be potentially removed from the solvent via additional methods not explicitly discussed here, such as by adsorption. 33

text: It is computationally expensive to perform property predictions for every exact chemical structure because contaminants in plastic waste (including both BIAS and additives intentionally included in plastic products) are often mixtures of similar chemical compounds. Most of these chemical families include a wide range of di ff erent substances. 10 To conduct feasible property calculations suitable for satisfying the above criteria, we first need to select a set of representative chemicals, then use their molecular structures to perform predictions of interest. In this work, we propose multiple case studies in which we select representative chemical structures for di ff erent classes of contaminants based on common compounds reported in literature. Specifically, given the large number of contaminants classified within each ' priority group of chemicals ' identified by Monclús and co-workers due to their significant risks to human health, safety, and the environment, 10 a representative subset was selected for detailed investigation. This subset comprised of four BFRs, eight phthalates, and twenty-six PFAS. The rationale for selecting these compounds is provided within the corresponding case studies presented in the following sections. Their structures are then input to COSMO-RS to predict miscibility, solubility, and partition coe ffi cients as detailed in the Methods to identify solvents suitable for contaminant removal via leaching or STRAP. Fig. 3 shows the chemical structures of polymers, example common solvents, and example contaminants studied below. The full list and chemical structures of contaminants studied in the work are included in the SI.

text: Case study 1: BFR leaching from plastic products. As a first case study, we consider solvent selection for the leaching of brominated flame retardants (BFRs) from common polymers including polystyrene (PS), polypropylene (PP), polyethylene (PE), and polyethylene terephthalate (PET). We compare computational predictions to known literature data and identify solvent candidates for BFR removal. BFRs are synthetic chemicals widely used as additives in plastic materials to reduce product flammability. 13,57 Furthermore, BFRs are incorporated as flame-retardant additives into consumer products, particularly electrical and electronic equipment, many of which are predominantly composed of PS. 10 However, they are persistent organic pollutants with bio-accumulative properties. 58 They have been reported at hazardous concentrations in aquatic environments and soils where they can accumulate on PP, PE, and PET microplastics which constitute a significant fraction of microplastics detected in terrestrial and aquatic environment. 59 Exposure to BFRs has been associated with serious health concerns, including cancer, neurobehavioral disorders, and reproductive issues. 57 Common end-of-life plastic management processes, such as mechanical recycling or incineration, are not able to separate BFRs from the target polymer resins, thus posing significant environmental and health risks by releasing hazardous halogenated compounds. 60 Conversely, recent work has indicated the feasibility of solvent-based methods for removing BFRs from waste plastics obtained from electrical and electronic equipment. 61

text: Fig. 4 shows selected common BFRs and their chemical structures, along with COSMO-RS σ -profiles to illustrate the distinct chemical properties for these molecules. These BFRs were selected due to the availability of literature experimental data reporting the solvent extraction of BFRs from common polymers. 62,63 These literature references provide the opportunity to perform computational screening to select solvents according to the leaching process in Fig. 1, then compare computational predictions to literature results. Hexabromocyclododecane (HBCD), decabromodiphenyl ether (DECA), and 2,4,4 ′ -tribromodiphenyl ether (Tri-PBDE) are designated as ' chemicals of concern ' in the PlastChem database, reflecting their persistence, bioaccumulation potential, carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, and reproductive toxicity. 10 In addition, polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs) form a major class of BFRs and have been detected at extreme concentration levels in waste plastics, particularly ocean plastics. 63 Based on the BFRs and polymers reported in the literature, we thus first performed computational predictions of log P values for BFRs, polymer solubilities, and BFR miscibility to qualitatively compare with experimental observations in the literature.

text: Table 1 presents data on the experimental solvent extraction of the four BFRs introduced in Fig. 4 from di ff erent polymers 62,63 and compared to our computational predictions. HBCD, DECA, and TBBPA-bis-2,3-dibromopropylether (TBBPAdbp) were extracted from PS obtained from discarded television and personal computer housings at 60 °C using di ff erent solvents while tri-PBDE that first adsorbed to PET, PE, PS, and PP polymers from aqueous solution (to represent contaminated environmental plastics) was extracted at room temperature. Experimental procedures used by Singla et al. 63 and Altwaiq et al. 62 for these samples are summarized in the SI. In both experimental studies, the extraction e ffi ciency for each contaminant was calculated as the percentage of the contaminant mass recovered in the organic extract from the plastic relative to the total amount of contaminant introduced onto the plastics. This was quantified using GC/MS or HPLC/UV. Based on our framework for extracting contaminants via leaching, we expect that a target BFR will be extracted if log P > 0 in the selected solvent, the target BFR is miscible in the selected solvent, and the solubility of the polymer in the selected solvent is low, thus fitting the criteria for process 1 in Fig. 1.

text: Given the strong agreement between literature data and our computational predictions, we subsequently screened 32 common solvents to identify those capable of simultaneously removing all four selected BFRs from the polymers listed in Table 1 (PS, PET, PE, and PP) at room temperature. The objective was to identify solvents that satisfy the established screening criteria while enabling the removal of all four BFRs rather than optimizing for a single compound. The predicted log P values, BFR -solvent miscibility, and polymer solubilities across di ff erent solvents are summarized in Tables S1 -S4. The results reveal that, even if several solvents have the potential to extract all four BFRs, distinct trade-o ff s are evident. Specifically, solvents demonstrating high e ffi cacy for one BFR often perform sub-optimally for others. Representative examples of these trade-o ff s for BFR removal from polystyrene using five selected solvents are illustrated in Fig. 5. While all five solvents meet the BFR miscibility criteria, variations arise in their ability to satisfy the log P requirements across all BFRs. For instance, N , N -dimethylformamide (DMF) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) exhibit favorable partitioning for HBCD and TBBPA-dbp but are less e ff ective for DECA, as reflected by its low log P value. Conversely, tetrahydropyran (THP) demonstrates favorable partitioning for Tri-PBDE, HBCD, and TBBPA-dbp, but not for DECA, which displays a negative log P value. This example highlights that selecting solvents for BFR removal by maximizing the partitioning of a single compound may not be optimal for removing all possible BFRs. In contrast, even they do not lead to the highest log P values for any individual BFR, benzene and diphenyl ether exhibit consistently favorable partitioning across all four BFRs, suggesting that these solvents are preferred for more broadly removing a wider range of BFRs; selection between these solvents may ultimately depend on economic, availability, environmental, and safety considerations. 40

text: Case study 2: phthalate removal from PVC. The first case study established that computational predictions align qualitatively with experimental literature results for the leaching of BFRs from varied polymers at temperatures close to, or somewhat above, room temperature. In the second case study, we extended the computational screening protocol to identify suitable solvents for removing phthalates from PVC resins. Phthalates are a family of synthetic chemical compounds used in plastics, solvents, and personal care products. In plastic products, phthalates are widely used as plasticizers in the production of flexible and durable plastic materials, particularly PVC. 64,65 Phthalates are often physically integrated into plastics rather than chemically bound, which means they can migrate out of products through wear, heating, or contact with liquids. 66 Short-chain phthalates, such as dimethyl phthalate (DMP), are more volatile and can evaporate into the air, whereas longer-chain phthalates, like di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP), tend to leach from plastics into surrounding environments over time. 64,67 Phthalates are also endocrine-disrupting substances associated with numerous adverse health consequences, including elevated risks of cancer, and consequently have been subjected to increased regulation for recycled plastics, motivating their removal. 68,69 Since there are hundreds of di ff erent phthalate compounds, selecting a representative set of structures is essential for practical analysis and computational modeling. Table S5 presents the eight selected phthalates for this study and their common applications in commercial products. 67,69 These representative phthalates were chosen based on their prevalence in commercial applications, structural diversity, and relevance to environmental and health concerns. 67 By focusing on a subset of commonly used phthalates, we can e ff ectively predict their properties and interactions with plastic resins and in the meantime maintain the generalizability of the findings. The chemical structures and σ -profiles showing the chemical diversity of the eight representative phthalates are presented in Fig. S1 and S2 of the SI.

text: In this second case study, we sought to perform both computational predictions and experiments to evaluate both distinct processes (leaching and STRAP contaminant removal) presented in Fig. 1. The primary di ff erence between these processes is that STRAP contaminant removal involves a hightemperature polymer dissolution step followed by low-temperature polymer precipitation, whereas leaching is performed a single temperature and does not involve polymer dissolution or precipitation. We note that STRAP also requires considering only the selective dissolution of a target polymer when multiple polymer components are present, although that consideration is omitted for this case study (but is included as part of Case study 4, vide infra ). To identify suitable solvents that facilitate phthalate removal via both processes, we used COSMO-RS to compute log P values (relative to PVC), phthalate miscibility in each solvent, and PVC solubility at multiple temperatures. A library of 32 common solvents was considered. Table 2 presents computational prediction results for a subset of solvent candidates; additional log P data are presented in Table S6. We placed an upper bound of 130 °C on the screening temperature for polymer solubility because higher temperatures may lead to degradation of some plastics.

text: We sought to identify a solvent capable of performing both leaching at room temperature and STRAP contaminant removal at a high temperature to compare contaminant removal e ffi ciencies with both processes. According to our solvent selection criteria for both leaching and STRAP, the ideal solvent should be miscible with all eight phthalate compounds considered and should promote positive log P values (with higher values preferred) at room temperature. Additionally, we also require a low PVC solubility at room temperature in the solvent, with a high solubility at elevated temperatures to enable polymer dissolution as part of STRAP. Based on past studies, 31,32,38 -40 we defined the low temperature solubility threshold as <1 wt% and the high temperature solubility threshold as >15 wt%. From the COSMO-RS calculations, nine solvents meet the log P > 0 and miscibility requirements: chloroform, tetrahydrofuran, tetrahydropyran, 2,3-dihydropyran, acetone, toluene, ethyl acetate, o -xylene, and diphenyl ether. These solvents (the first nine listed in Table 2) are thus expected to be suitable for leaching. In addition to having positive mean log P values, these solvents have positive log P values for each individual phthalate, suggesting that these solvents are capable of extracting all eight representative phthalates. This result is consistent with the structural resemblance among the eight phthalates, as illustrated by their molecular structures and σ -profiles in Fig. S1 and S2. However, not all solvents with positive mean log P values have positive log P values for all phthalates; DMSO and triethylamine are notable counterexamples, indicating the need to evaluate log P for all possible contaminants, not just individual contaminants, to ensure a high probability of removal.

Among the evaluated solvents, only one solvent -ortho -xylene ( o -xylene) - satisfies the PVC solubility requirements at both high and low temperatures. Toluene meets the low-temperature solubility threshold and is also very close to meeting the high-temperature solubility threshold with a predicted PVC solubility of 14.8 wt%, while diphenyl ether also meets the low-temperature solubility threshold and has a moderate PVC solubility of 11.5 wt% at a high temperature. These solvents are thus likely to be suitable for both leaching and STRAP contaminant removal. Of the solvents considered, o -xylene was chosen as a suitable solvent for experimental evaluation of both STRAP contaminant removal and leaching, since it exhibits a favorable mean log P value of 0.61 at room temperature, has the highest predicted PVC solubility of the three potential STRAP solvents at the maximum temperature of 130 °C, and has minimal predicted PVC solubility at room temperature.

We conducted two sets of experiments on a sample of PVC and phthalate to verify the ability of o -xylene to remove phthalates from PVC resins. The sample is a physical mixture of PVC powder and liquid butyl benzyl phthalate (BBP) with a mass ratio of 2.5 : 1. This ratio was determined based on the typical concentration of phthalate additives in industrial PVC materials. 70 The mixture was extruded as filaments and cut into short pieces (Fig. 6a). Experiments used a mixture of xylene isomers (xylenes) due to their availability and the expectation that they would behave similarly to o -xylene alone for the proposed contaminant removal processes. The first set of experiments used xylenes to remove BBP from the PVC sample based on the criteria described above. The second set of experiments used dodecane as a solvent to compare to xylenes

We employed dodecane as a negative control solvent to test our computational predictions. Three experimental wash steps were adopted. The first wash step (wash step 1) involved immersing the sample in fresh solvent for 1 hour, after which further analysis quantified the fraction of BBP that was removed. Next, the sample after wash step 1 was dried and then immersed in a fresh solvent for another 1 hour after which the fraction of removed BBP was quantified. text: Fig. 6 shows the experimental measurements of phthalate mass recovered from the PVC removal experiments at room temperature and at 130 °C as well as an image of the sample after BBP removal. At room temperature, an average of 63.0 ± 5.2% (with the average and standard deviation computed across three replicate experiments) of the phthalates was removed in the 3-hour experiment ( i.e. , after the three wash steps), with decreasing percentages recovered after each wash step. We note that the predicted log P value for o -xylene is modest (with a mean value < 1 and value for BBP of 0.28; see Table S6). As shown in Table 1, similar predicted log P values led to modest extraction e ffi ciency of BFRs at room temperature ( e.g. , acetonitrile had a log P value of 0.4 and led to 71.8% extraction e ffi ciency for leaching tri-PBDE from PET). Fig. 6c shows that performing the high-temperature STRAP experiments significantly improved BBP extraction e ffi ciency to an average of 113.9 ± 6.4%, with nearly all of the contaminant removed in the first wash step. In contrast, dodecane was ine ff ective for phthalate removal as expected. At room temperature, dodecane was completely unable to extract BBP from PVC in agreement with our computational predictions, while at 130 °C the average extraction e ffi ciency of BBP from PVC was 16.7 ± 1.6%, indicating a substantially lower extraction e ffi ciency compared to o -xylene. Table 2 also indicates that at the elevated temperature BBP is miscible in dodecane, yet was still not readily removed, highlighting the utility of log P values for predicting contaminant removal. The slightly higher fraction of BBP that was removed at the high temperature is likely due to the slight dissolution of the polymer, but the low removal indicates that dissolved BBP preferentially precipitates with the PVC in dodecane.

text: Overall, the increased extraction e ffi ciency at 130 °C suggests that polymer dissolution as part of STRAP generally leads to higher contaminant removal than leaching. These results validate the ability of xylenes to remove phthalates from PVC resins, and more broadly serve as proof-of-concept for the computational methodology. However, Fig. 6c also shows continuous removal of BBP after each 1 hour solvent wash at room temperature, whereas the predicted room temperature log P value of 0.6 should indicate an ∼ 4× preference of BBP for the solvent vs. the polymer. Given the large amount of solvent compared to the amount of polymer sample (75 g solvent, 1 g polymer), these experimental observations indicate a lower extraction e ffi ciency than would be expected based on the predicted log P value, which is likely due to mass transfer kinetics governing contaminant migration from the polymer phase into the solvent phase. 43 Such kinetic e ff ects would be expected to be prominent at lower temperatures and in the absence of polymer dissolution and will depend on process variables such as contact time, temperature, and concentration gradients, which are not captured within the current equilibrium-based modeling approach. Therefore, we expect that operating conditions such as time and temperature could be further investigated to improve the e ffi ciency of the process for actual deployment in more realistic scenarios.

text: Case study 3: STRAP with PFAS removal from LDPE. Case studies 1 and 2 established that predicted log P values can be used to guide solvent selection for contaminant removal via leaching processes, with solvents exhibiting high log P values removing contaminants in experiments as expected. These promising results motivate additional case studies that integrate contaminant removal with STRAP to enable the simultaneous recovery and purification of target polymers during a recycling process. As an additional example of integrating STRAP with contaminant removal for a larger category of contaminants, we use computational predictions to assist the design of a process for removing PFAS from plastic waste. PFAS are a diverse group of synthetic fluorinated compounds known for their remarkable stability, water and oil repellency, and resistance to heat and chemical degradation. 71 These properties have made PFAS essential in applications such as nonstick cookware, waterproof fabrics, grease-resistant food packaging, and firefighting foams. 72 However, their environmental persistence and bioaccumulation pose significant health risks, including links to cancer, liver toxicity, and immune system disruption. 72 Common PFAS, including perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), both containing eight carbon atoms, as well as shorter chain perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAAs) and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSAs), have been detected in aquatic systems, soils, and other environmental ecosystems. 73,74 Although the use of PFAS as additives in plastic manufacturing has been increasingly regulated over the past two decades, their environmental ubiquity has led to their detection in commercial products. 75 This observation suggests that these compounds can migrate into plastic waste streams from surrounding environments through pathways such as aquatic systems, landfills, material recovery facilities, municipal waste collection systems, and open dumps. Recent studies have further confirmed the presence of PFAS in postconsumer recycled polyolefins used in food-contact applications. 21 Consequently, PFAS must be removed during recycling processes to avoid their reintroduction into the plastic packaging industry, particularly via post-consumer recycled resins. 76

Although thousands of PFAS have been identified by the US EPA, 77 their detection via experimental approaches have been limited. However, the FDA have been successful at detecting 26 PFAS concentration levels in food samples purchased at grocery stores in the US. 78,79 Therefore, in this work, we apply our contaminant removal strategy to this set of PFAS. Table S7 and Fig. S3 and S4 of the SI show the PFAS compounds and chemical structures, and their σ -profiles, grouped based on their structures and primary functional groups. All 26 PFAS considered are small molecules representative of non-intentionally added substances that might be found in post-consumer waste; however, we note that fluorinated polymers such as polytetrafluoroethylene are also incorporated into plastic products as processing aids 80 as well as anti-drip additives, particularly in polycarbonates (PC) and PC/acrylonitrile butadiene styrene blends 81,82 and may potentially be removed by similar solvents selected to remove the 26 target PFAS.

We considered the same library of 32 common solvents used in previous case studies for removing PFAS from lowdensity polyethylene (LDPE) as a reference polymer. As shown in Fig. S3 of the SI, some PFAS exist as ionized compounds.

text: Therefore, in the case of PFAS, distribution coe ffi cients (log D values) which account for multiple ionization states are determined using COSMO-RS and used in place of their partition coe ffi cient (log P ); these quantities have similar interpretations during solvent selection. 83 We performed COSMO-RS predictions of the distribution coe ffi cients of all 26 PFAS in each solvent relative to LDPE, determined the miscibility of PFAS and each solvent, and computed LDPE solubility at multiple temperatures in the solvents. For STRAP contaminant removal, we require a high LDPE solubility at the elevated temperature and low LDPE solubility at room temperature to achieve temperature-based precipitation, with a mean log D value that is high at both temperatures to ensure preferential partitioning into the solvent of as much PFAS as possible.

text: We divided the 26 PFAS compounds into three di ff erent groups based on structural similarity (Fig. S3): PFAS within each group had similar chemical structures and consequently σ -profiles (Fig. S4), suggesting that they would be removed from LDPE resins using similar solvents. Fig. 7 presents the average σ -profiles and representative structures for each group, showing how the key functional groups in each PFAS group contribute to slight di ff erences in σ -profiles. For example, group 2 is distinguished by the presence of sulfonic acid groups that contribute to a unique shoulder in the average σ -profile as a distinguishing feature of this group. Table 3 shows solvent screening and property calculation results for each group. THP is identified as the best solvent to remove PFAS in groups 1 and 2 as it has excellent mean log D values while leading to low LDPE solubility at room temperatures. Toluene is the best choice for group 3, since it satisfies positive log D requirements and has a strong temperature dependence of LDPE solubility ( i.e. , able to dissolve LDPE at an elevated temperature and precipitate at room temperature), which is beneficial for STRAP.

text: In practice, the set of PFAS present in any given plastic waste may be unknown, so ideally single solvents capable of removing all PFAS would be identified. THP, toluene, and cyclohexanol were identified as e ff ective solvents capable of removing all 26 PFAS by satisfying all the solvent screening criteria via the STRAP approach. THP exhibited consistently positive log D across all PFAS with an average of 5.1, satisfied the miscibility criteria for all PFAS, and showed low (0.1 wt%) and high (7.3 wt%) LDPE solubility at room and high temperatures, respectively. Similarly, toluene exhibited consistently positive log D across all PFAS with an average of 0.7, satisfied the miscibility criteria for all PFAS, and showed low (0.1 wt%) and high (22.6 wt%) LDPE solubility at room and high temperatures, respectively. Lastly, cyclohexanol exhibited consistently positive log D across all PFAS with an average of 3.8, satisfying the miscibility criteria for all PFAS, and showed low (0.0 wt%) and high (22.1 wt%) LDPE solubility at room and high temperatures, respectively. Owing to its high average log D value and pronounced temperature-dependent solubility behavior, cyclohexanol is identified as the preferred solvent for e ff ectively removing all 26 PFAS from LDPE. These findings further support the potential for identifying a single solvent capable of extracting groups of structurally similar contaminants. The detailed predicted miscibility and log D values of all 26 PFAS considered in this work are presented in the SI. These results can further guide the experiment of PFAS removal from LDPE resins.

text: Case study 4: STRAP with BFR, phthalates, and PFAS removal from mixed plastic waste. Having studied the removal of three di ff erent classes of contaminants in di ff erent polymer systems, in this final case study we apply the computational framework to understand the potential removal of contaminants during the separation of multicomponent plastics via STRAP. Specifically, we analyze two previously developed, experimentally tested STRAP processes for multicomponent plastic waste recycling by Sánchez-Rivera and colleagues. 31,32 The first process involved the separation of a 4-component multilayer plastic film containing LDPE, ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH), PET, and ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA). In the first step of this process, toluene was used to selectively dissolve PE from the remaining polymers at 110 °C. The dissolved PE was then cooled to 35 °C to aid its precipitation. The second process involved the separation of the same multilayer film composition with the addition of a polyurethane (PU)-based ink component. The first step of this process used dodecane instead of toluene to selectively dissolve PE at 95 °C while avoiding the dissolution of the PU-based ink, which was removed in a further processing step. The PE was then recovered by precipitation at 35 °C. Neither of these studies explicitly considered the potential for contaminants (other than the ink) to be dissolved and removed during STRAP. Therefore, in this case study, we aim to identify the contaminants that would have been removed from the first STRAP step in both processes (toluene and dodecane) based on the sets of contaminants (BFRs, phthalates, and PFAS) studied in the previous case studies.

text: step using either toluene or dodecane, since the same polymer resin was removed first in both processes. Based on these values, and miscibility criteria, toluene is expected to remove all contaminants considered from PE during STRAP. This result suggests that during the recycling of the multilayer plastic via STRAP studied by Sánchez-Rivera and colleagues, 31 all four BFRs, eight phthalates, and 26 FDA-identified PFAS would have been removed, producing a recycled LDPE film with little to no traces of the studied contaminants. On the contrary, dodecane is less e ffi cient in removing any of the contaminant considered in this study, as also discussed in the negative control experiments conducted for phthalates in PVC in Case study 2. A summary of these findings, showing the flow of polymers and the extraction of these contaminants via the STRAP process using these two solvents based on an ideal, equilibrium process as predicted by our thermodynamic modeling approach is presented in Fig. 8. Since toluene was replaced by dodecane to avoid the co-dissolution of PU-based inks during the recycling of multilayer plastic film containing PU-inks, 32 this suggests that dodecane can be first used to recover PU-based ink-free LDPE and subsequently toluene can be used to further remove all the contaminants listed in this study from the residual solids if desired.
