text: In experimentally validated STRAP processes, the target polymer typically remains swollen with solvent after precipitation ( i.e. , to form a polymer gel), which is not considered in the calculations above or Fig. 8. Retained solvent could impact the partitioning of contaminants between the solvent and (swollen) polymer by making these two phases more chemically similar, such that multiple wash steps would be required to remove this residual contaminant. Indeed, similar behavior was observed by Wagner and coworkers during the recycling of PVC waste containing phthalates via a multistep solvent-based process. 84 To assess the impact of retained solvent, we performed additional log P (or log D for PFAS) calculations to predict the room-temperature partitioning of contaminants between the solvent phase and a model swollen polymer phase. Similar to the data in Table 4, we chose two representative contaminants from each class (Tri-PBDE/HBCD as BFRs, BBP/DiNP as phthalates, and PFOA/PFOS as PFAS) and computed log P or log D in toluene and dodecane relative to a ' swollen ' PE phase. To represent the ' swollen ' PE, we note that prior STRAP studies have reported that the precipitated polymer gel retained between 70 -80 wt% solvent after separ- PE -polyethylene, Tri-PBDE -2,4,4 ′ -tribromodiphenyl ether, DECA -decabromodiphenylether, BBP -butyl benzyl phthalate, DiNP -di-isononyl phthalate, PFOA -perfluorooctanoic acid, PFOS -perfluorooctanesulfonic acid.

text: Table 5 shows that, as expected, predicted log P (or log D ) values substantially change for all contaminants investigated. While the signs of all values remain the same, indicating no qualitative change in partitioning preference, all values are closer to zero when compared to values computed for partitioning from a pure polymer phase. These di ff erences indicate that the presence of retained solvent would cause contaminants to distribute more evenly between the swollen PE and the solvent compared to the assumption of a dry polymer with minimal retained solvent. Consequently, in Fig. 8, retained solvent would lead to some contaminants remaining with the PE in the case of STRAP with toluene and some contaminants dissolving with the PE in the case of STRAP with dodecane. From a practical standpoint, this behavior implies that multiple washing steps following precipitation are likely required to obtain near contaminant-free PE after the STRAP process. Alternatively, additional processing steps could reduce the amount of retained solvent. For example, Yan et al. found that using a piston to mechanical compress the polymer during filtration substantially decreased the amount of retained solvent, which also reduced the amount of contaminant pigment species in agreement with this work. 33 These considerations highlight the potential of utilizing this contaminant removal framework to inform STRAP process design when considering the recovery of plastics from mixed plastic waste.

text:
Conclusions

The removal of contaminants from plastic waste is a critical challenge for improving recycling e ffi ciency and ensuring the safety of recycled materials. We have developed computational approaches for guiding solvent selection to facilitate contaminant removal. By leveraging molecular models, it is possible to identify suitable solvents that selectively remove target smallmolecule contaminants and recover high-quality target polymer resins. We specifically consider the design of two contaminant removal methods based on leaching or on the integration of contaminant removal considerations during dissolution-based plastics recycling with the goal of achieving higher-purity recovered polymers. Two case studies leveraging either previously reported or newly collected experimental data validate the framework for the removal of brominated flame retardants and phthalates from common polymer resins. Two additional case studies then apply the computational tools to identify solvents for the removal of a broad range of PFAS from LDPE and to determine the likely contaminant removal e ffi ciency of steps in previously published plastics recycling processes.

Conclusions

The removal of contaminants from plastic waste is a critical challenge for improving recycling e ffi ciency and ensuring the safety of recycled materials. We have developed computational approaches for guiding solvent selection to facilitate contaminant removal. By leveraging molecular models, it is possible to identify suitable solvents that selectively remove target smallmolecule contaminants and recover high-quality target polymer resins. We specifically consider the design of two contaminant removal methods based on leaching or on the integration of contaminant removal considerations during dissolution-based plastics recycling with the goal of achieving higher-purity recovered polymers. Two case studies leveraging either previously reported or newly collected experimental data validate the framework for the removal of brominated flame retardants and phthalates from common polymer resins. Two additional case studies then apply the computational tools to identify solvents for the removal of a broad range of PFAS from LDPE and to determine the likely contaminant removal e ffi ciency of steps in previously published plastics recycling processes.

text: Moving forward, further integration of computational modeling with experimental validation will enhance the predictive accuracy of solubility models and expand their applicability to a wider range of plastic waste streams. Other additive compounds in plastic products (such as stabilizers, plasticizers, modifiers, pigments, fillers, and processing aids) can also be taken into consideration with a similar approach. We note that the current methodology utilizes thermodynamic models to predict polymer solubility and contaminant removal at equilibrium and therefore neglects practical considerations, such as the kinetics of contaminant mass transfer, 43 which will be important to consider explicitly in future work. Because STRAP involves polymer-rich phases, contaminant partitioning may di ff er from the dilutepolymer limit modeled here. Our predictions therefore represent upper-bound removal e ffi ciencies; future work will incorporate polymer-rich phase behavior and experimental validation. Similarly, we found that solvent retained within polymers recovered after STRAP would a ff ect contaminant removal e ffi cacy. The case studies on STRAP presented in this work use a single solvent for contaminant removal, with the same solvent leading to both polymer dissolution and precipitation depending on the temperature. However, polymer precipitation can alternatively be induced through the addition of an antisolvent, 4,31 which then would lead to a solvent mixture that could further be used to tune contaminant removal strategies in future STRAP process designs. The computational approach also treats the partitioning of each contaminant separately, whereas interactions between contaminants may a ff ect partitioning behavior. While preliminary analysis (described in the SI) indicates minimal such interference e ff ects, further investigation of interactions between contaminants will be a subject of future work. Finally, we envision combining these methods with new computational tools, such as machine learning models, to aid in the selection of representative contaminant models in order to expand the scope of possible target contaminants considered during process design.

text: Achieving circularity in the plastic economy predominantly depends on sourcing higher quality recyclates. Packaging plastic poses a significant challenge as it is often not prioritised for collection or recycling initiatives. The presence of additives, such as printing ink, impedes the quality of recyclates. Considering the volume of packaging plastics and the importance of branding (aesthetics and consumer information), ink removal is a critical pre-treatment step. However, the literature is limited, with only 14 studies exploring de-inking processes. Drawing parallels with the detergent laundering process, surfactants have been widely investigated in plastic deinking, with cationic surfactants proving the most effective with a de-inking efficiency of up to 100%. However, concerns exist regarding the toxic and hazardous nature of the surfactants and chemicals. The average hazard quotient (AHQ) was developed, which compares de-inking chemicals as one of the key findings. text: Since the early 1900s, the annual plastic production has grown 230fold to reach 460 million tonnes in 2019 [1]. Two-thirds of the plastic waste generated in 2060 will be from ephemeral applications such as packaging, consumer products and textiles [2]. Packaging plastic accounts for 44% of polymer consumption [3] and 46% of plastic waste generation [4]. By 2060, the sector is projected to double in size, more specifically, the use of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and polyethylene (PE) [1]. The growth is primarily from the versatile use of PE as short-lived packaging plastic in flexible packaging applications [5]. Even with a high recycling potential, an effective recycling strategy for flexible packaging waste is lacking. This can be attributed to material properties and additives, lack of technology readiness, and inadequate material recovery strategies [6,7]. Due to this, 95% of the packaging material, valued between USD 80 -120 billion, is lost from the economy annually, and the resultant additional recoupment cost to society per annum is USD 40 billion [8].

Since the early 1900s, the annual plastic production has grown 230fold to reach 460 million tonnes in 2019 [1]. Two-thirds of the plastic waste generated in 2060 will be from ephemeral applications such as packaging, consumer products and textiles [2]. Packaging plastic accounts for 44% of polymer consumption [3] and 46% of plastic waste generation [4]. By 2060, the sector is projected to double in size, more specifically, the use of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and polyethylene (PE) [1]. The growth is primarily from the versatile use of PE as short-lived packaging plastic in flexible packaging applications [5]. Even with a high recycling potential, an effective recycling strategy for flexible packaging waste is lacking. This can be attributed to material properties and additives, lack of technology readiness, and inadequate material recovery strategies [6,7]. Due to this, 95% of the packaging material, valued between USD 80 -120 billion, is lost from the economy annually, and the resultant additional recoupment cost to society per annum is USD 40 billion [8].

text:
Packaging plastics are often printed with inks as part of branding or to convey necessary consumer information. On average, 2 -4% of the total weight of packaging plastic is printed ink [9]. While these inks are essential, they are also the source of significant contamination in plastic recycling [10,11]. Printing inks are mainly composed of pigments that impart colour, binders that provide adhesion, carriers (also referred to as solvents) that hold the suspension and additives for additional characteristics (Table 1).

Based on the carrier, inks are classified as water-based, solvent-based or UV-based (Table 1) [12]. The carriers evaporate during ink drying processes (i.e. manufacturing stage) and are insignificant during recycling [13]. However different binders are used, based on the carrier type, which is problematic in packaging plastic recycling. Solvent-based inks are compatible with most surfaces on which to print. In contrast, water-based inks have limited application as water evaporates slower than solvent, making the drying process energy-intensive. These inks are preferably used in papers and boards, which promote absorption capabilities. Finally, UV-based inks use reactive resins such as acrylates that can be activated by UV irradiation [14,15].

text:
Realising a circular plastics economy will significantly depend on advancements in the recycling infrastructure, especially closed-loop recycling strategies. In such cases, removing additives and contaminants becomes imperative to producing higher-quality recyclates [20]. De-inking is a critical yet undermined pre-treatment step in recycling printed plastic waste. In the past decade, a renewed focus has been on de-inking research. Studies have explored the potential of various de-inking media, specifically surfactants. The effect of surfactant concentration, pH, temperature, ink pigment composition, and other parameters in de-inking have also been experimented with. However, there is a lack of streamlined information on how the research area has developed over time and the status quo of plastic de-inking. Thus, a systematic literature survey will be conducted to collate and critically analyse the packing plastic de-inking literature. In addition, the surfactants and chemicals employed in previous de-inking studies have not been assessed for their toxic and hazardous nature. Thus, as another niche aspect, a chemical selection tool based on the average hazard quotient (AHQ) will be formulated, and it will offer new avenues for sustainable de-inking surfactant and chemical development in the future.

Plastic waste can be managed through closed-loop or open-loop recycling (Fig. 1). In closed-loop recycling, plastic waste is recycled back into plastic products in the same product category, though openloop recycling produces a recyclate employed in different applications.

2.1. Mechanical recycling

Mechanical recycling (cascade recycling) is the most prevalent method employed at a large scale. This is further classified into primary and secondary recycling based on the source of waste [21]. Mechanical recycling is affected by the quality of the waste stream, as different types of plastic respond differently to treatment based on their physio-thermo-chemical properties [22,23].

text:
Primary recycling sources plastic waste from post-industrial applications, which are of higher quality. The collected waste is often recycled back into production after shredding and blending with virgin plastic. Secondary recycling handles the post-consumer plastic waste mixed with different plastic types (i.e. lower quality feed) [24]. The key steps involve washing, shredding, melting and remoulding. In secondary recycling, the quality of the recyclates is inferior, resulting in downgraded applications. Other interferences, such as organic contaminants, labels, inks, fillers, and additives, significantly deteriorate the material and optical properties of the recycled product [25,26]. Thus, secondary recycling is not favourable for a circular plastic economy in the long run.

The collected waste is often recycled back into production after shredding and blending with virgin plastic. Secondary recycling handles the post-consumer plastic waste mixed with different plastic types (i.e. lower quality feed) [24]. The key steps involve washing, shredding, melting and remoulding. In secondary recycling, the quality of the recyclates is inferior, resulting in downgraded applications. Other interferences, such as organic contaminants, labels, inks, fillers, and additives, significantly deteriorate the material and optical properties of the recycled product [25,26]. Thus, secondary recycling is not favourable for a circular plastic economy in the long run.

2.2. Waste-to-energy recycling

text:
In this open-loop recycling process, the heat from incinerating plastic waste generates superheated steam for electricity production [27]. The lower heating values (LHVs) of PE (42.8 MJ kg 1 ) and polypropylene (PP) (46.5 MJ kg 1 ) are closely comparable to that of petroleum (42.3 MJ kg 1 ) and kerosene (46.5 MJ kg 1 ) [28]. However, post-consumer plastic waste (mixed, low-quality) is 40% less efficient, which can be improved upon segregation. It has been shown that the best fuel efficiency is obtained from the purest waste streams [27]. A comparative study by the Waste & Resources Action Programme (WRAP) showed that recycling was better than incineration, considering greenhouse gas emissions and energy balances [29]. In contrast, incineration performed better when a significant volume of recycled plastics could not be incorporated back into virgin plastic production or when there was a high washing requirement [29]. Even if waste-to-energy is prioritised higher than landfilling in the waste hierarchy, its preference is debated. This is because waste-to-energy provides an incentive to avoid other recycling strategies where the materials could be retained in use for longer life. Hence, it contradicts the principles of the circular economy.

2.3. Chemical recycling

text: The chemical recycling method comprises various strategies to convert plastic waste into reusable monomers or to produce fuels and feedstock for subsequent processes [21]. 'Chemical recycling ' and 'feedstock recycling ' are often used interchangeably. In reality, chemical recycling can be considered an umbrella term including both open-loop thermolysis and closed-loop solvolysis. Thermolysis, also known as 'feedstock recycling ' , produces chemicals for other purposes, including fuels, syngas or naphtha. Whereas solvolysis produces monomers that can be used in polymer production [30]. Chemical recycling is limited by economic viability, feedstock availability and feedstock quality. Often, it is hard for the recycling process (including pre-treatment and purification steps) to compete with the costs of virgin material production. Heterogenous plastic waste from post-consumer sources, contaminated with additives, colourants, impurities, moisture and dirt, severely impacts the feedstock quality. Nevertheless, extensive research is focused on chemical recycling due to the potential to recover high-quality recyclates and remove contaminants, such as halogenated flame retardants [27]. It was also found that supplementing mechanical and chemical recycling can improve the overall recycling rates [27]. Holistically, advancements in chemical recycling are needed to maximise material utilisation and further circularity in the plastic economy.

3.4. Development of AHQ model

text:
The surfactants currently used in de-inking are toxic and hazardous. However, there may be instances where such surfactants are unavoidable. The previous de-inking studies did not quantify the surfactants ' physical, environmental and health hazards. Furthermore, no specific toxicity tests were performed using standards, such as the Globally Harmonised System (GHS) and the Registration, Evaluation, Authorization and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 December 2006 (EC No 1907/2006) [33].

Traditionally, the methods of hazard classification follow a qualitative or semi-quantitative approach, which provides the necessary information but can be complex to interpret and compare chemicals directly. This presented the need for a mathematical model to categorise and rank the chemicals employed in de-inking based on their potential hazards. As such, the AHQ was introduced to simplify comparisons and decision-making on surfactant and chemical selection.

The surfactants currently used in de-inking are toxic and hazardous. However, there may be instances where such surfactants are unavoidable. The previous de-inking studies did not quantify the surfactants ' physical, environmental and health hazards. Furthermore, no specific toxicity tests were performed using standards, such as the Globally Harmonised System (GHS) and the Registration, Evaluation, Authorization and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 December 2006 (EC No 1907/2006) [33].

Traditionally, the methods of hazard classification follow a qualitative or semi-quantitative approach, which provides the necessary information but can be complex to interpret and compare chemicals directly. This presented the need for a mathematical model to categorise and rank the chemicals employed in de-inking based on their potential hazards. As such, the AHQ was introduced to simplify comparisons and decision-making on surfactant and chemical selection.

The GHS hazard classification provides baseline data to model the AHQ in this work. As of June 2023, twenty-one countries have fully adopted the GHS classifications, including Australia and Malaysia [34]. Several countries have adopted part of it as required, as well. The GHS classifications are presented as part of material safety data sheets (MSDS) or safety data sheets (SDS) for chemicals. They offer a standardised approach to presenting hazard classification and necessary precautions. However, GHS only provides qualitative data on hazards by broadly classifying them into three classes: physical, health, and environmental. There are 16 physical hazards, 10 health hazards and 2 environmental hazard classes. Based on the severity, each hazard is categorised from 1 to N (where N = 2, 3, 4, etc.) or A to G. In each case, 1 or A presents a more severe hazard, and severity reduces as the value increases. Furthermore, every SDS has a signal word, such as ' danger ' , ' warning ' , or ' nothing ' . It was observed that the signal word ' danger ' was used whenever a category 1 or 2 hazard was present in any of the classes.

This work employed the given classifications and qualitative descriptions to model the AHQ (Eq. 1). A sample AHQ calculation using SDS data for cyclohexane is shown in Appendix B.

AHQ = ∑ α r α [ 1 N α × ∑ n i = 1 1 H f i ] (1)

4.1. De-inking methodology

Based on the literature, a generalised de-inking procedure can be summarised as follows:

Sample preparation: Commercial PE films [32,35], uni-coloured PE films [36], PP films [11], rigid high-density polyethylene (HDPE) [37,38], low-density polyethylene (LDPE) films [13], and multilayer plastic films [39] were used in previous studies. Surfactant preparation: The required amount of surfactant is determined based on the surfactant-specific CMC and the test condition (above, below or at CMC). The surfactant solution is freshly prepared by mixing the required surfactant with either de-ionised or distilled water. The pH level of the surfactant solution is immediately adjusted using either sodium hydroxide or hydrochloric acid solutions.

Experiment: The cut plastic pieces are soaked in water for the specified duration to analyse the effects of pre-soaking. The samples are then transferred to the surfactant solution in a beaker in a temperature-controlled water bath or magnetic stirrer. The experiment is allowed to run for four hours on average. Once the experiment is completed the samples are thoroughly washed and air-dried. Some researchers have employed control experiments in de-inking, for example, using water [13,32]. However, those did not result in any significant de-inking.

Image analysis and de-inking efficiency: Using CIELAB, flake sorting or scanning and pixel reading methods detailed in Appendix C, the samples are analysed before and after the experiment. The respective equations are then utilised to calculate the de-inking efficiency in each case.

text:
(which is hydrophobic) and the positively charged areas on the ink surface. This tail-in arrangement is made possible by Van der Waal ' s force of interactions and results in a monolayer (hemimicelle) of surfactant molecules. A head-in tail-out arrangement of surfactant molecules is observed for the negatively charged areas on the ink surface. Progressively, this will result in a bilayer (admicelle) formation, with a second layer of surfactant molecules getting attached in a tail-in headout arrangement over the previous layer. Complete wetting is achieved when the contact angle becomes 0 ° . However, it is difficult to differentiate between hemimicelle and admicelle formations, resulting in reduced contact angle and increased zeta-potential.

Step 2: Solubilisation of binder in micelles. This is hypothesised to be due to three factors: (i) the hydrophobic components of the ink being incorporated into the micelle core, (ii) electrostatic binding of the negatively charged carboxylate groups on the binder and the positively charged surfactant head groups on the micellar surface, (iii) the iondipole interactions between π -electrons of aromatic rings and hydrophilic surfactant head groups. Step (ii) is the most dominant de-inking mechanism, especially in cases where the surfactant concentration is above its CMC [13], and it happens simultaneously with Steps (i) and (iii).

Step 3: Detachment of ink from the plastic surface. This is hypothesised due to the electrostatic repulsion between the surfactant head groups. As the edge of the ink surface detaches, more surfactant molecules can be adsorbed to the newly uncovered areas on both the ink and plastic surfaces. It increases the electrostatic repulsion, resulting in further ink detaching.

Step 4: Stabilisation and dispersion of the detached ink particles. As more surfactant molecules are adsorbed to the detached ink particles and plastic surface, electrostatic stabilisation is achieved. Further, the electrostatic repulsion between the surfactant head groups on the plastic surface and detached ink prevents the redeposition of ink.

It can be noted that plastic de-inking is a surface reaction, which means the contact between ink on the plastic surface and the surfactant is vital to facilitate de-inking. This has been validated by Sánchez-Rivera et al. [39], who used a multi-layered printed plastic film and observed no significant de-inking compared to single-layer LDPE/HDPE films employed by several authors, including Gecol et al. [32], Songsiri et al. [38] and Chotipong et al. [40]. Despite varying surfactant concentrations, reaction temperatures and pH were tested, including using a pressurised system, de-inking efficiency was poor with multi-layered printed plastic films.

text:
Binder systems can be classified into two based on the bonding mechanisms -(i) resulting in only Van der Waal ' s forces and hydrogen bonds due to polar groups in binders and the activated plastic surface from corona treatment, (ii) resulting in covalent bonds in addition to Van der Waal ' s forces and hydrogen bonds due to the presence of a reactive cross-linked system [13]. The latter enhances the bonding between the binder and the plastic surface, making it harder for ink removal. In such cases, a surfactant alone cannot cleave covalent bonds. In contrast, the surfactant hinders de-inking as it forms a protective layer over the ink surface when the hydrophilic-lipophilic balance (HLB) value is too low. Furthermore, alkaline hydrolysis can be an effective de-inking mechanism, as shown in Figure D.1 in Appendix D.

Based on the above discussion, a modified de-inking mechanism was proposed by Guo et al. [13], including (i) surfactant adsorption, (ii) breaking of hydrogen bonds via solubilisation and covalent bonds via chemical reaction, (iii) detachment of ink from the plastic surface through micelle solubilisation (for non-cross-linked binders) and mechanical peel off (for cross-linked binders), and (iv) stabilisation and dispersion of pigment particles.

text: Cationic surfactants are characterised by nitrogen-containing functional groups, such as amines, quaternary ammonium, imidazolium and pyridinium [41]. As the amine-based surfactants can only be protonated (activated) at acidic pH, their applications are limited to this pH range. Whereas quaternary ammonium-based surfactants ('quats ' ) are not pH sensitive [42]. Cationic surfactants find major applications where surface adsorption is required (Fig. 7a), as most surfaces (including plastics) at neutral pH have a negative charge [43]. Thus, cationic surfactants are most explored for packaging plastic de-inking, even though they are the third by size in surfactant application. The various cationic surfactants employed in plastic de-inking are summarised in Table 2.

Cationic surfactants were effective in plastic de-inking above its CMC over a broad range of pH values. As cationic surfactants showed the most de-inking potential in early studies, the effect of various process parameters was explored in detail over time. Pre-soaking and mixing the samples via mechanical agitation improved de-inking efficiencies [38]. However, the design conditions are to be determined based on economic optimisations. More than 90% de-inking can be obtained with 5 h of pre-soaking and 2 h of mixing with hexadecyl trimethylammonium bromide at CMC. Conversely, if the pre-soaking time is reduced to 2 h, the mixing time increases to 4 h to obtain the same de-inking efficiency.

Cationic surfactants were effective in plastic de-inking above its CMC over a broad range of pH values. As cationic surfactants showed the most de-inking potential in early studies, the effect of various process parameters was explored in detail over time. Pre-soaking and mixing the samples via mechanical agitation improved de-inking efficiencies [38]. However, the design conditions are to be determined based on economic optimisations. More than 90% de-inking can be obtained with 5 h of pre-soaking and 2 h of mixing with hexadecyl trimethylammonium bromide at CMC. Conversely, if the pre-soaking time is reduced to 2 h, the mixing time increases to 4 h to obtain the same de-inking efficiency.

Increasing the lengths of alkyl chains was found to favour de-inking, as longer hydrophobes improved the adsorption rates [44]. The longer alkyl chains produced stronger Van der Waal ' s forces between the surfactant and ink particles [37]. Significantly high to complete de-inking can be achieved at highly alkaline pH. This is hypothesised due to the opening of epoxide rings (carrying negative charges) within the epoxy resins in inks, providing additional adsorption sites for the positively charged cationic head groups [37]. On the other hand, calcium ion addition was found to impede de-inking performance due to competitive adsorption (Fig. 7b).

5.2. Anionic surfactants

Anionics are the largest surfactant class used worldwide, accounting for roughly 70% of overall consumption [46]. This popularity is attributed to the ease and low cost of manufacturing. They are characterised by carboxylate, sulfonate, sulfate or phosphate functional groups [47] and are widely employed in detergent formulations and paper de-inking processes [48]. Anionics possess the highest cleansing power and good wetting properties. Table 3 summarises the anionic surfactants used in packaging plastic de-inking.

A few early studies in plastic de-inking explored the potential of using anionic surfactants. Observations show that they are barely better than de-inking using water at respective pH. A possible explanation is the electrostatic repulsion between the negatively charged ink particles and the hydrophilic head of the surfactant, hindering adsorption (Fig. 7c). This is probably why recent studies have opted out of exploring anionic surfactants. However, adding calcium ions improved the deinking capacity by providing additional sites for co-adsorption (Fig. 7d) [44]. Nevertheless, it was only found to be practical above the CMC of the surfactant in alkaline conditions.

5.3. Non-ionic surfactants

Non-ionics are the second largest class of surfactants used worldwide [41]. They are preferred due to the ease of production, readily available and inexpensive feedstock, and wide-ranging applications. This category is characterised by either polyether or polyhydroxyl functional groups [42]. A list of non-ionic surfactants used in packaging plastic de-inking is given in Table 4.

Early studies on non-ionic surfactants were conducted as they were less expensive and more biodegradable than amphoteric and cationic surfactants [49]. Generally, non-ionic surfactants are effective in plastic de-inking above its CMC in alkaline conditions. The exception is ethoxylated amines, which is a non-ionic. Despite that, it behaves like cationic in acidic conditions with low ethylene oxide levels [50]. Consequently, ethoxylated amines exhibit similar de-inking behaviour to cationic surfactants at acidic, neutral and basic pH, which is favourable. However, Guo et al. [12] observed no notable influence from pH values on de-inking efficiencies for non-ionic surfactants.

Temperature promotes de-inking monotonically until the cloud point is passed, after which the efficiency reduces. In the cases of ethoxylated amines and ethoxylated alcohols, a lower cloud point resulted in higher de-inking efficiencies. Similarly, longer carbon chains in ethoxylated alcohols increased de-inking [49]. The addition of calcium ions was found to lower the de-inking efficiencies [44]. In the case of ethoxylated amines, this is explained by the fact that they behave as cationic surfactants at lower pH, creating a competition for adsorption sites on the ink particle.

In an amphoteric surfactant, the three states exist in equilibrium, depending on the pH range. Under acidic conditions, the molecules will be protonated to form cations, whereas in an alkaline condition, they will be deprotonated to form anions. text: Gecol et al. [32], the earliest work on packaging plastic de-inking, explored the potential of various surfactants (amphoteric, anionic, cationic, and non-ionic) in removing water-based inks from commercial plastic films. A control test was also designed using water to de-ink plastic films by varying the pH at room temperature. Results showed no significant de-inking until pH 10. At pH values 11 and 12, partial de-inking of 30% and 60% was observed. Several characterisation tests were conducted to understand the effect of inks on re-extruded plastic and how it impacts recycling. It was observed that there were significant colour changes, including the clear films turning beige and the printed films turning reddish brown. The decomposition of inks during re-extrusion released gases that caused crack points and holes across the cross-section. Ink aggregates were found to act as stress concentration points, reducing the strength of the material (e.g. modulus, ultimate strength and elongation at break are reduced). It was concluded that cationic surfactants are the most effective choice functional across various CMC and pH levels. Conversely, anionic surfactants were the least effective.

text:
Following this, extended studies were conducted to understand various facets of de-inking. Exploring potential non-ionic surfactants, it was seen that nonylphenol polyethoxylate and ethoxylated alcohols exhibited good de-inking capacity at pH 10. In contrast, ethoxylated amines (which are amphoteric and classified as non-ionic but behave as cationic in acidic media) showed de-inking capacity at acidic, neutral, and basic pH [49]. Cationic surfactants, such as n-hexadecyl trimethyl ammonium bromide, exhibited de-inking capacity only above its CMC (complete de-inking at 5 times CMC) and high pH levels above 11.75.

In recent years, more systematic and non-conventional approaches to packaging plastic de-inking have been observed. Guo et al. [12], explored the possibility of using a new type of non-ionic surfactant oxirane, methyl-, polymer (commercial name: TEGO Surten W111) to de-ink LDPE film samples from post-consumer waste. In addition to the conventional CIELAB method for de-inking performance evaluation (Appendix C), a flake sorting method (Appendix C) is also considered to account for the heterogeneity of post-consumer plastic waste.

text:
Guo et al. [13] explored the effects of various binders, pigments, over-print varnishes (OPV), cross-linkages in binders or OPVs and the materials ' layering. Five detergents and four test conditions were included to analyse various possible scenarios. NC binder-based inks exhibited high de-inkability, and crosslinked binder systems can impede de-inking. Based on the above, it was concluded that breaking the Van der Waals forces, hydrogen bonds, and covalent bonds between inks and the plastic surface are critical steps in de-inking.

Ügdüler et al. [11] conducted an interesting study to understand the effect of seven different de-inking media in liquefying and solubilising 14 chemically different polymer resins in printing inks. The basic cost assessment also determined that the price of the de-inking agent and its required volume played a crucial role in the economic feasibility of the de-inking process.

text: Only four studies attempted sustainably sourced solvents in plastic de-inking by utilising biomass-derived or valorised waste materials in surfactant production. El-Sherbiny et al. [45] developed novel cationic surfactants from recycled PET waste (GT-pyr-Br and GD-pyr-Br -Table 6), which were achieved by depolymerising PET followed by esterification and quaternization. Gd-pyr-Br resulted in a maximum de-inking efficiency of 96% at CMC. Ferreira et al. [51] performed solvent extraction using the dissolution-precipitation technique to remove blue and orange pigments from HDPE using a range of bio-solvents. 94% and 100% de-inking were observed for blue and orange pigments, respectively. In this method, a solvent is initially used to solubilise HDPE and then an anti-solvent is used to selectively precipitate the polymer. Both the solvent and anti-solvents could be recovered and reused, ensuring economic and environmental sustainability. Ye et al. [35] explored the potential of quarternary ammonium-modified waste cooking oil (soybean oil) in de-inking. This was prepared by ring-open esterification and quaternary amination reactions. De-inking efficiency of around 70% was observed through this method. Sánchez-Rivera et al. [39] reported a solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP) strategy to de-ink a multilayer plastic film from post-industrial sources. It was seen that biomass-derived gamma-valerolactone (GVL) was able to de-ink all the studied colours. The techno-economic analysis also showed that the STRAP process could be economically viable for a processing capacity of 6000 tonnes per year. This shows the efficacy of bio-based and waste-based surfactants, and the de-inking efficiencies are comparable to those of synthetic ones.

In this method, a solvent is initially used to solubilise HDPE and then an anti-solvent is used to selectively precipitate the polymer. Both the solvent and anti-solvents could be recovered and reused, ensuring economic and environmental sustainability. Ye et al. [35] explored the potential of quarternary ammonium-modified waste cooking oil (soybean oil) in de-inking. This was prepared by ring-open esterification and quaternary amination reactions. De-inking efficiency of around 70% was observed through this method. Sánchez-Rivera et al. [39] reported a solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP) strategy to de-ink a multilayer plastic film from post-industrial sources. It was seen that biomass-derived gamma-valerolactone (GVL) was able to de-ink all the studied colours. The techno-economic analysis also showed that the STRAP process could be economically viable for a processing capacity of 6000 tonnes per year. This shows the efficacy of bio-based and waste-based surfactants, and the de-inking efficiencies are comparable to those of synthetic ones.

7. Impacts of conventional de-inking surfactants

Drawing parallels with the detergent laundry processes, surfactants are predominantly used in packaging plastic de-inking. However, the use of surfactants poses several ecotoxicological and health hazards (Fig. 8). Anionic surfactants, such as linear alkylbenzene sulfonates (LAS), cause pathological, biochemical, and physiological impacts on terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. It also interferes with marine biota ' s environmental stress, reproduction, and growth. Surfactants facilitate eutrophication by increasing the solubility of contaminants in water bodies (Fig. 8). Their toxicity increased proportionally with increasing hydrophobic properties [58].

Even wastewater treatment plants cannot properly manage the surfactants, which are incompletely degraded and discharged into water bodies. Surfactant concentrations above 0.1 mg/L in water bodies cause huge, persistent foams that prevent oxygen adsorption [59]. It also impacts the hydrological cycle by impeding evaporation. When the surfactant concentration increases beyond the CMC, higher concentrations of soluble and insoluble pollutants in the water are observed [59].

text:
Surfactants also interfere with soil properties, primarily by reducing the capillary pressure at the air-water interface [60]. This causes an altered air and water distribution in the soil ' s pore system and reduces water retention and infiltration (Fig. 8). Irrigating soil with surfactant-rich water increased the soil salinity, electrical conductivity, sorptivity and pH, while hydraulic conductivity was reduced [61]. It was also studied that surfactants retarded microbial growth and increased microbial mutation and mortality [62].

Fig. 8. Potential environmental and human health hazards from surfactant use.

In humans, when ingested, surfactants react with proteins in the liver and serum, causing long-term metabolic effects and disrupting the endocrine system [63]. It was reported to cause skin burning, eye irritation and respiratory problems. Nonylphenol ethoxylates were studied to have estrogenic effects in mammals, Pisces, and amphibians [64] (Fig. 8). Surfactants, such as LAS, can change the cell membrane structure and impair the transpiration and translocation of water and essential nutrients [58]. Sodium dodecyl sulfate inhibits ATPase activity, damages membrane structures and initiates oxidative stress [65].

In an attempt to reduce the impacts of plastic waste, it is vital not to unintentionally cause secondary impacts through the use of hazardous and toxic chemicals and surfactants. Thus, the surfactant selection in packaging plastic de-inking applications is paramount.

8. Modelled AHQ values for chemical selection

Calculated AHQ values based on the GHS can be used for one-to-one comparison of chemical hazards (Table 8). Based on the current dataset, cyclohexane would be the most hazardous chemical (check the note in Appendix B). Cationic surfactants (e.g. hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide, cetyltrimethylammonium chloride, dodecyltrimethylammonium bromide, hexadecylpyridinium chloride) have been extensively studied for de-inking, though possess the maximum environmental AHQ. Hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide, explored in 9 studies, has a concerning total AHQ of 1.43 out of the maximum possible 3. In this way, informed decisions can be made when selecting appropriate solvents for de-inking purposes.

All chemicals with a total AHQ less than 0.5 in this work match with the signal words ' warning ' or ' nothing ' in the SDS. The only exception is polydisperse nonylphenol polyethoxylate with the signal word ' warning ' , though the calculated AHQ is 1.0. In short, the consistent method employed in work to ascertain AHQ values is satisfactory, though improvements can be made based on the significance level of hazard classes (Eq. 1 and check the note in Appendix B).

Appropriate chemical selection tools, such as AHQ, should be utilised to minimise potential hazards and toxicities from plastic waste recycling. While AHQ is a preliminary chemical assessment tool, local sociotechno-economic factors, such as low chemical cost, desirable chemical action, low carbon footprint and local availability, should also be considered to improve the quantitative assessment of chemical and surfactant selection.

9. Future directions

Material characterisation tests should be conducted to address the conflict of opinion on whether de-inking improves recyclate quality.

Only Guo et al. [13] explored the impacts of ink pigments, binders, OPVs and cross-linking in de-inking. Future studies can characterise the most common ink types, categorise them based on application (food contact materials and others) and identify whether a specific de-inking solution is required for each application.

text:
With 175 nations agreeing to develop a legally binding Global Plastics Treaty by 2024, all the aspects of plastic recycling should be thoroughly explored. Obtaining the highest quality of recyclates will be paramount in moving towards a circular plastics economy. While advancements have been made across various fronts in plastic recycling, de-inking was found to be an undermined pre-treatment step. This study provided a critical understanding of plastic de-inking ' s state of the art. While surfactants are conventionally utilised in de-inking owing to similarities with laundering processes, a general caution needs to be exercised regarding potential hazards and toxicities. The proposed AHQ model could be an effective chemical rating and selection tool. Advancements in plastic de-inking will contribute towards the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, such as Industry, innovation, and infrastructure (Goal 9), Responsible consumption and production (Goal 12), and Climate Action (Goal 13).

In a thematic map, the Cartesian coordinates characterise the research topics based on centrality and density. This helps to classify the topics into motor themes, niche themes, emerging or declining themes and basic themes. Motor themes possess high density and centrality and act as the driving force of the research field. In this case, as seen in Figure A.2, the overlap between the critical topics, such as 'ink ' and 'polyethylene ' , which are commonly used in packaging plastic applications, are the driving forces. On the other hand, with low centrality and low density, emerging or declining themes represent marginal or underdeveloped fields. CMC, pH effects and adsorption fall into the basic themes, with high centrality and low density. This reflects cross-cutting topics that are well connected to the rest yet poorly developed themselves. Finally, niche themes, including plastic packaging, dissolution and environmental impact, with high density and low centrality, have been explored thoroughly. Yet they are poorly connected with the rest of the field.

Figure A.2. Thematic map for packaging plastic de-inking studies.

C. Methods used in de-inking performance evaluation

C.1. CIELAB method (by the International Commission on Illumination)

text:
Eight of the fourteen studies in de-inking literature have employed a standardised evaluation, the CIELAB method. It was first devised by the International Commission on Illumination in 1976 based on the tristimulus values of a colour. It quantifies the red, green, and blue light required to produce that colour [66]. A spectrophotometer or a colorimeter is used to evaluate the CIELAB values (L*, a*, b*) (Figure C.1).

Figure C.1. Schematic of the three-dimensional CIELAB colour model (adapted and redrawn from [67]).

Once the averaged values for L* , a* and b* are obtained, the de-inking efficiency can be calculated as follows:

DE * = ̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅ Δ L 2 sample blank + Δ a 2 sample blank + Δ b 2 sample blank 2 √ DE * blank (C.1)

where, DE* - De-inking efficiency. DE * blank - De-inking efficiency for reference material. Δ L , Δ a , Δ b -Differences in CIELAB values between the sample and reference materials.

C.2. Flake sorting method

text:
To account for the heterogeneity of post-consumer plastic waste, Guo et al. [12] implemented a modified approach to analysing the de-inking efficiency. The de-inked samples were manually sorted into -fully transparent, partially transparent, and opaque (non-de-inked). The weight of each of these sample groups is measured, and the de-inking efficiency is then calculated as follows:

.

DE * = ( mct + mpt × 0 . 5 ) msample (C.2)

where, DE* - De-inking efficiency. mct -The mass of fully transparent flakes (in grams). mpt -The mass of partially transparent flakes (in grams). msample -The mass of the entire selected sample (in grams).

Guo et al. [12] showed significant variations between the CIELAB and the flake sorting methods. It was determined that the CIELAB method displayed a high standard deviation (11% to 76%) and was suggested not to be the optimal choice for evaluating post-consumer plastic waste. However, CIELAB is still the most suitable method for a homogenous sample.

C.3. Scanning and pixel reading

text:
Another approach observed in the literature is scanning the plastic specimen directly or sticking it to a white paper using transparent glue [40,37, 38]. The scanned copies were then analysed using software, such as Adobe Photoshop, to count the number of pixels (in proportion to the amount of ink) on the plastic surface. The de-inking efficiency is then calculated as follows:

DE * = ( Pixelsbefore de inking Pixelsafter de inking ) Pixelsbefore de inking × 100 (C.3)

Meanwhile, Guo et al. [13] developed a Python code to read the pixels from the scanned files and generate the L* , a* , and b* values as per the CIELAB standards. The output from running the Python can then be used in Equation C.3 to calculate the deinking efficiency. Another Python code was developed by Ügdüler et al. [11] using the Open-Source Computer Vision (OpenCV) Library. The scanned images were first grey-scaled and processed to obtain arrays with values ranging between 0 (black) to 255 (white). This represented the shades of grey and corresponded to the amount of ink remaining on the plastic film. The de-inking efficiency can then be calculated as follows:

DE * = ( dsample d min ) ( d max d min ) × 100 (C.4)

Where, dsample -the average grey value of the sample. d max -the average grey value of the fully printed plastic film. d min -the average grey value of the transparent plastic film.

text:
Plastic pollution is a pervasive and growing global problem 1-4 . Chemicals in plastics are often not sufficiently considered in the overall strategy to prevent and mitigate the impacts of plastics on human health, the environment and circular economy 5-7 . Here we present an inventory of 16,325 known plastic chemicals with a focus on their properties, presence in plastic and hazards. We find that diverse chemical structures serve a small set of functions, including 5,776 additives, 3,498 processing aids, 1,975 starting substances and 1,788 non-intentionally added substances. Using a hazard-based approach, we identify more than 4,200 chemicals of concern, which are persistent, bioaccumulative, mobile or toxic. We also determine 15 priority groups of chemicals, for which more than 40% of their members are of concern. Finally, we examine data gaps regarding the basic properties, hazards, uses and exposure potential of plastic chemicals. Our work maps the chemical landscape of plastics and contributes to setting the baseline for a transition towards safer and more sustainable materials and products. We propose that removing known chemicals of concern, disclosing the chemical composition and simplifying the formulation of plastics can provide pathways towards this goal.

Plastic pollution is a pervasive and growing global problem affecting all dimensions of the triple planetary crisis 8-10 . Awareness of this issue has grown in recent years, and all United Nations member states committed to creating an international legally binding instrument to end plastic pollution in 2022 (ref. 5). Achieving this ambitious goal not only requires a holistic approach that addresses the entire life cycle of plastics but also encapsulates a vision to make plastics safer and more sustainable. Indeed, chemical safety is key to both, yet it is often neglected in these transition processes, creating a critical gap in the overall strategy to prevent and mitigate the impacts of plastics on human health and the environment globally.

safer plastics and a sustainable plastics economy, therefore, requires a better understanding of the chemicals involved, including their properties, functions, hazards, prevalence and releases.

text: Plastics contain complex mixtures of chemicals, including the polymer backbone and additives as well as unreacted starting substances, residual processing aids and non-intentionally added substances (NIASs), such as impurities and reaction by-products 11-13 . These chemicals can be released throughout the entire plastic life cycle, from feedstock extraction and production to use and waste 7,14-19 . Specific end-of-life treatments, such as uncontrolled landfilling or incineration, can further exacerbate chemical releases 20,21 . This leads to widespread human and environmental exposures that can result in health impacts, with strong epidemiological evidence linking certain plastic chemicals to reproductive, neurodevelopmental, immune and metabolic disorders 3 .

text: Plastic chemicals may also impede the transition to a circular economy, including technological solutions to plastic pollution 6 . For instance, increasing the reuse of plastic products can increase the release of chemicals 22,23 , and uncontrolled recycling can further perpetuate the spread of hazardous chemicals in products with high exposure potential, such as food packaging and toys 24,25 . Chemicals in plastics can also hinder sorting and recycling and thereby impede the production of high-quality secondary materials 6,26,27 . Transitioning to At present, crucial information on plastic chemicals remains scattered across the public domain or restricted within the private sector. Previous efforts to compile an overview of the chemical diversity of plastics 26-29 have jointly identified more than 13,000 known plastic chemicals 30 . However, these studies are domain specific (for example, food contact plastics and plastic toys), lack a comprehensive assessment of hazards and other relevant properties, or focus on intentionally added chemicals. To address these gaps and equip the scientific community with the evidence needed to design safer plastics, we provide a comprehensive and consistent global inventory of known plastic chemicals, including relevant information on their properties, presence in plastics and regulation.

text:
Taking this one step further, we identify chemicals of concern in plastics. We develop a hazard-based approach to classify chemicals as of concern if they are persistent, bioaccumulative, mobile or toxic. We also introduce a new approach to identify groups of chemicals of concern on the basis of their structure. The combination of these components creates a robust framework that addresses existing challenges in making plastics safer (Methods, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Text 1) and can be translated to other domains, such as industrial sectors and materials. Finally, we outline pathways towards creating safer plastics by removing chemicals of concern, improving transparency and chemical simplification.

text: Building on the inventory, we identify 4,219 chemicals of concern, representing one-quarter of all known plastic chemicals. We classify a chemical as of concern according to four broad hazard criteria, namely its persistence (P), bioaccumulation (B), mobility (M) and toxicity (T; Fig. 2a, Methods and Supplementary Text 4). The identification of chemicals of concern is based on information originating from 15 regulatory sources with high reliability (Methods and Supplementary Tables 4 and 5), either through robust assessments by government authorities, or through industry self-reporting, which tends towards under-reporting 33 . More than half of the chemicals of concern (2,388) are classified as hazardous by at least two sources (Supplementary Table 6). The approach can be considered conservative as we do not include hazard information from the scientific literature. Considering that 10,726 plastic chemicals (66%) lack official hazard classifications by regulatory agencies or industry, it stands to reason that there could be more chemicals of concern in plastics than the ones identified here.

Data availability varies with polymer type, with most information being available for PET and polypropylene (PP; Extended Data Fig. 5). The fraction of chemicals of concern that are associated with a specific polymer type ranges from 31% in PET to 62% in polyurethane (PUR), with the highest prevalence in PUR, PVC (48%) and PP (45%). State of governance of plastic chemicals

text: To better understand the state of play of the global governance, we assess which plastic chemicals are covered by Multilateral Environmental Agreements (Methods, Supplementary Text 6 and Supplementary Table 7). We find that only 6% of all plastic chemicals (980) are regulated under the Basel, Stockholm and Minamata Conventions, and the Montreal Protocol. These regulations address specific chemical classes (for example, persistent organic pollutants and mercury-containing substances), and some of them regulate chemicals only in certain stages of the life cycle (that is, waste in the Basel Convention). Of the 4,219 chemicals of concern identified, 568 are regulated under these Multilateral Environmental Agreements (Fig. 2a). However, most chemicals of concern (3,651) remain unregulated globally, despite plastic chemicals, materials, products and waste being globally traded. National regulations cover an additional 1,021 chemicals, although implementation and oversight vary widely across regions. This implies that a substantial governance gap exists regarding chemicals of concern in plastics.

Grouping to address chemicals of concern

Given the vast number and diversity of plastic chemicals, along with the many unknowns and data gaps, managing them individually is both challenging and inefficient. As a pragmatic solution, we group chemicals on the basis of structural similarities. Grouping also helps prevent regrettable substitutions, specifically in cases of 'drop-in' substitution, in which a known chemical of concern is replaced by a structurally similar chemical with similar hazard properties 38,39 . Grouping of chemicals also has regulatory precedent, for instance, in the Montreal Protocol, Stockholm Convention and European REACH regulation 38 .

text: We group more than 10,000 plastic chemicals (Methods, Supplementary Text 7 and Supplementary Table 8), resulting in 28 groups with clear structural similarities and containing at least 10 members each. The largest groups are alkenes (802 chemicals), silanes, siloxanes and silicones (443) and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs; 440), and parabens (10) is the smallest group. We prioritize 15 groups of chemicals of concern, with each group consisting of at least 40% of known chemicals of concern or having strong evidence for the entire group to be hazardous (for example, PFASs 40,41 , chlorinated paraffins 42 ; Fig. 4 and Supplementary Tables 9 and 10). Among these 15 groups, aromatic amines, aralkyl aldehydes and alkylphenols are made up of more than 75% of chemicals of concern. Grouping plastic chemicals can support an efficient management and redesign of plastics by eliminating the need to fill data gaps and preventing regrettable substitutions. However, the grouping process also has some technical challenges, primarily due to the lack of a single automated tool for categorizing a large number of substances. Instead, various techniques are necessary. For instance, an algorithm helped identify homologue series covering more than 2,000 chemicals, but further expert evaluation is needed to refine these groups (see Methods for further details). To address these issues, better structural identifiers and automated grouping tools are needed.

Pathways towards safer plastics

Our study shows that the universe of chemicals in plastics is vast, with more than 16,000 known plastic chemicals, including in excess of 4,200 chemicals of concern. This poses two major challenges for the safety, sustainability and circularity of plastics. First, the sheer number of plastic chemicals exceeds the capacity of manufacturers and governments to ensure their safety, with more than 10,000 chemicals remaining to be tested and assessed. Second, we present robust evidence for the presence of numerous, well-established chemicals of concern, based on regulatory data and including their commercial use and detection in plastics. This suggests that plastic products on the global market can contain and release substances known to harm human health or the environment, across all major polymer types. Collectively, this raises the question of how the safety of plastics can be improved.

Removing known chemicals of concern, whether voluntarily or through regulatory measures, is a crucial first step in making plastics safer. This can be guided by the essential use concept, which involves three key considerations 43-45 . First, chemicals of concern that are not necessary for the performance of a material, product or service can be removed. Second, chemicals of concern essential for health, safety or critical societal functions should be replaced with safer alternatives. Our results point towards the availability of alternatives as we find that many substances serve the same technical function (Fig. 1b). Finally, if one or more uses of a chemical of concern cannot be removed or replaced for the moment, innovative solutions, including new product design, should be fostered to substitute such uses. However, the major challenge in this process is the lack of suitable alternatives as indicated by the few non-hazardous chemicals we identify (Fig. 2a) and the high proportion of chemicals of concern in certain functions (for example, heat and light stabilizers; Extended Data Fig. 6). This emphasizes the need to develop safer plastic chemicals and create incentives for their adoption. Removing known chemicals of concern, whether voluntarily or through regulatory measures, is a crucial first step in making plastics safer. This can be guided by the essential use concept, which involves three key considerations 43-45 . First, chemicals of concern that are not necessary for the performance of a material, product or service can be removed. Second, chemicals of concern essential for health, safety or critical societal functions should be replaced with safer alternatives. Our results point towards the availability of alternatives as we find that many substances serve the same technical function (Fig. 1b). Finally, if one or more uses of a chemical of concern cannot be removed or replaced for the moment, innovative solutions, including new product design, should be fostered to substitute such uses. However, the major challenge in this process is the lack of suitable alternatives as indicated by the few non-hazardous chemicals we identify (Fig. 2a) and the high proportion of chemicals of concern in certain functions (for example, heat and light stabilizers; Extended Data Fig. 6). This emphasizes the need to develop safer plastic chemicals and create incentives for their adoption. Achieving this goal relies on suitable frameworks to guide chemical design, such as the 'safe and sustainable

text:
by design' framework 46 as well as robust tools to evaluate the safety of alternatives.

We also identify many data gaps that prevent understanding the complete scope of plastic chemicals and their impacts on human health and the environment. For instance, 9% of chemicals in the inventory lack basic structural information, 25% lack chemical property data, more than 50% miss details on their functions or presence in plastics, and 66% have no hazard information (Extended Data Fig. 7). By logic, the safety of these chemicals cannot be ascertained, and our assessment of chemicals of concern remains incomplete. This has multiple reasons, including the limitations of using CAS RNs for tracking information (for example, use of multiple CAS RNs per chemical, or the same CAS RN for multiple chemicals 32,47 ). However, major uncertainties in our work originate from the lack of transparency, as manufacturers do not publicly disclose the chemical composition of their materials and products 23 . Accordingly, the PlastChem inventory may not reflect the dynamic changes in the plastics and chemical market. Removing existing barriers to information and creating more transparency within supply chains and the public domain 48 is key for resolving these issues.

text: Redesigning plastic materials and products towards safety and sustainability is essential to enable a transition towards a non-toxic circular economy 46 . Removing known chemicals of concern and improving transparency are necessary but not sufficient to address the chemical complexity of plastics. It is improbable that regulators and scientists can determine the impacts of 16,000 plastic chemicals on human health and the environment in a timely manner, particularly as new ones continue to proliferate. Therefore, a simplification of plastics is needed 49 . This includes minimizing the number and molecular complexity of chemicals intentionally used in plastics as well as optimizing production processes to mitigate the introduction and generation of NIASs (for instance, by using additives with higher purity). The aforementioned redesign should start with critically assessing the true needs for specific chemical functionalities in specific plastic applications. This requires engaging with all relevant stakeholders, in particular plastic manufacturers 48 .

text:
Our work sets the baseline for the transition to a safer, more sustainable and circular plastics economy by mapping the chemical complexity of plastics consistently and comprehensively. It also provides scientists and other stakeholders working towards such transition with consolidated information on plastic chemicals, their hazards and regulation, their uses and functions, and their detection in polymer types. A dedicated list of chemicals of concern and the associated chemical groups will further help to avoid problematic chemistries in the design and manufacture of plastics.

We built a comprehensive and globally applicable inventory of all known plastics chemicals and developed an innovative framework combining hazard and grouping components with the aim to facilitate a transition towards safer plastics. We define plastic chemicals as all chemicals that can be present in plastic materials and products, including the polymer backbone, intentionally added substances (that is, starting substances, processing aids and additives) and NIASs (for example, impurities, unreacted intermediates, reaction by-products and degradation products). The fact that some plastic chemicals may have additional uses in non-plastic applications has no bearing on their inclusion. Contaminants sorbing to plastics during use or end-of-life are not considered plastic chemicals. See complete definitions in Supplementary Text 1.

text: To identify chemicals of concern in plastics, we developed and applied a hazard-based approach. In brief, we classified a plastic chemical as of concern on the basis of the criteria of persistence, bioaccumulation, mobility and toxicity. The rationale for taking this approach is threefold. First, we argue that plastics should not contain hazardous chemicals, to protect human health and the environment. Although this approach might be considered conservative, it enables scientists and businesses to improve the safety of plastics and proactively prevent potential harm in a timely and efficient manner. Second, we posit that exposure to most plastic chemicals is probable given that most are not covalently bound to the polymer. This is backed by empirical evidence showing that 83% of the 1,788 chemicals tested for release from plastic food contact materials indeed migrate into foodstuff 17,25 . Third, we reason that an alternative risk-based approach is neither efficient nor effective-and often infeasible-to identify chemicals of concern owing to numerous practical challenges, blind spots and high implementation costs that would unduly delay a transition to safer plastics.

First, we argue that plastics should not contain hazardous chemicals, to protect human health and the environment. Although this approach might be considered conservative, it enables scientists and businesses to improve the safety of plastics and proactively prevent potential harm in a timely and efficient manner. Second, we posit that exposure to most plastic chemicals is probable given that most are not covalently bound to the polymer. This is backed by empirical evidence showing that 83% of the 1,788 chemicals tested for release from plastic food contact materials indeed migrate into foodstuff 17,25 . Third, we reason that an alternative risk-based approach is neither efficient nor effective-and often infeasible-to identify chemicals of concern owing to numerous practical challenges, blind spots and high implementation costs that would unduly delay a transition to safer plastics.

text:
Apart from the identification of chemicals of concern, we collected additional evidence on the use, presence and release of plastic chemicals. We use this information to link chemicals to specific polymer types, shed light on which compounds are intentionally added to plastics (commercial use) and infer their exposure potential. Although the last of these is only qualitative, it suggests that human and environmental exposures to these chemicals are probable, given that scientific studies demonstrate their migration or volatilization into foodstuff or environmental media.

We grouped plastic chemicals on the basis of their structure to efficiently address chemicals of concern as well as regrettable 'drop-in' substitutions (that is, replacing a chemical of concern with a structurally very similar compound). We assumed a chemical without hazard data is 'guilty by association' if it is part of a group that consists of many known chemicals of concern. This is supported by ample evidence available for certain groups, such as bisphenols 50 , as well as the fact that the structure of a chemical determines its hazards. In combination with the hazard-based approach, such chemical grouping offers a robust framework to improve the chemical safety of plastics in a timely and efficient manner.

text:
We built the PlastChem inventory by: compiling and harmonizing information from seven prior databases; retrieving additional and updated information on hazard classifications and regulatory status from 15 authoritative sources (latest update August 2023) to identify chemicals of concern; integrating data on the use, detection and release of chemicals in and from plastics; and grouping the chemicals on the basis of their structure (Extended Data Fig. 1). All data engineering work was performed using R (R Consortium, 2023) and Microsoft Excel (see Data and Code availability).

text:
To identify chemical structures, compile data from various sources and assemble the inventory, we used CAS RNs or chemical names (when CAS RNs were invalid or unavailable) with the automatic Application Programming Interface services of PubChem. The information retrieved included the PubChem Compound Identification (CID), molecular formula, molecular weight, canonical SMILES, isomeric SMILES, InChI, InChIKey, IUPAC name, predicted octanol/water partition coefficient (XLogP), exact mass, monoisotopic mass, topological polar surface area, complexity and charge. CAS RNs were validated according to CAS guidelines 51 . Further details are available in Supplementary Text 2.

Despite thorough quality assurance and control, some uncertainties may remain in the inventory (Supplementary Text 2). For example, 400 duplicates were identified, originating from the use of multiple names for the same chemical or from non-unique CAS RNs that correspond to multiple substances. These duplicates are shown in an additional file in the inventory. Of these, 188 chemicals were manually selected by expert judgement for inclusion in the main inventory, as they were deemed the most likely matches for the corresponding CAS RNs. Although we validated and curated the CAS RNs to reduce duplication, additional duplicates may still exist.

To identify chemical structures, compile data from various sources and assemble the inventory, we used CAS RNs or chemical names (when CAS RNs were invalid or unavailable) with the automatic Application Programming Interface services of PubChem. The information retrieved included the PubChem Compound Identification (CID), molecular formula, molecular weight, canonical SMILES, isomeric SMILES, InChI, InChIKey, IUPAC name, predicted octanol/water partition coefficient (XLogP), exact mass, monoisotopic mass, topological polar surface area, complexity and charge. CAS RNs were validated according to CAS guidelines 51 . Further details are available in Supplementary Text 2.

Despite thorough quality assurance and control, some uncertainties may remain in the inventory (Supplementary Text 2). For example, 400 duplicates were identified, originating from the use of multiple names for the same chemical or from non-unique CAS RNs that correspond to multiple substances. These duplicates are shown in an additional file in the inventory. Of these, 188 chemicals were manually selected by expert judgement for inclusion in the main inventory, as they were deemed the most likely matches for the corresponding CAS RNs. Although we validated and curated the CAS RNs to reduce duplication, additional duplicates may still exist.

Information on functions and regulation

text:
Additional information on the known functions of plastic chemicals and their regulatory status is also included in the PlastChem inventory. Briefly, the functions were gathered from ref. 27, CPPdb 28 and PlasticMAP 26 , aligned to a common terminology and assigned larger functional classes (starting substances, additives, processing aids and NIASs). See further details in Supplementary Text 3.

To integrate regulatory information, we compiled information from the Basel, Stockholm and Minamata Conventions, along with the Montreal Protocol, to identify the chemicals globally regulated under Multilateral Environmental Agreements at present. In addition, we also included regional and national lists of chemicals that were easily accessible, including chemicals regulated in the EU, Japan, the Republic of Korea and the USA, along with those substances regulated under the Rotterdam Convention. See further details in Supplementary Text 6.

Hazard information was collected from 15 regulatory sources, some of which aligned with the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling (Supplementary Table 4). This information is consistent with the principles outlined in the EU Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability 52 and the updated Classification, Labelling and Packaging of Substances and Mixtures regulation 36 . text: We applied a stepwise process to harmonize the compiled hazard information and translate it into a single hazard score per chemical. First, chemicals with hazard data for a specific trait (for example, carcinogenicity) were assigned a score ranging from 0 to 2, with 0 indicating non-hazardous, 0.5 indicating less hazardous, 1 indicating hazardous, and 2 indicating very hazardous (Supplementary Table 5). Chemicals with hazard evaluations under development, postponed or pending received a score of 0.25 to reflect that these are undergoing assessment but have not been classified yet. A blank indicates that no information is available. In cases of multiple classifications per source, we used the highest scores for each trait, with regulatory information taking precedence over industry data. As a second step, we aggregated the individual scores per trait into a single score for each hazard criterion (P, B, M and T) using the highest score whenever multiple traits within a criterion had information, retaining the 0-2 scoring system as described above. Finally, the maximum score across the P, B, M and T criteria resulted in a unique hazard score for each chemical that we used to identify chemicals of concern when the score was ≥1, indicating that a chemical of concern fulfils at least one hazard criterion. Additionally, we calculated the sum of hazard scores across the P, B, M and T criteria, ranging from 0 to 8, and provide an evidence score reflecting the number of sources that classify a chemical as hazardous for the same criterion, ranging from 0 to 31. Further details are available in Supplementary Text 4.

Use, presence and release information

We compiled and harmonized data on the use, presence and release of chemicals in plastic polymers from FCCmigex 17 , PlasticMAP 26 and LitChemPlast 25 . Presence data were derived from studies performing extraction experiments (for example, with solvents); release data came from studies performing migration experiments (for example, with food simulants). Chemicals with release data were assigned a score of 2, and those with only presence data received a score of 1. Data on the commercial use of plastic chemicals were sourced from PlasticMAP and given lower priority (score of 0.5 if no presence or release data are available). Chemicals with inconclusive information were scored 0.25, and substances that were analysed but not detected in experimental studies were scored 0. Finally, chemicals without data received a blank. See Supplementary Text 5 for further details.

text: Plastic chemicals were grouped on the basis of their structures following two approaches (details in Supplementary Text 7). In brief, the first approach consisted of searching a predefined set of keys in the chemical names to identify inorganic compounds, organometallics and metalorganics, UVCBs, polymers and mixtures. This was followed by searching the name and chemical symbol of respective elements in the chemical names and SMILES to identify organohalogens, organophosphates, organosilicons and various chemicals containing certain metal(loid) elements. The second approach consisted of matching chemicals in the PlastChem inventory with existing lists of chemical groups (list in Supplementary Text 7). In addition, we applied expert judgement to identify PFASs from all organofluorine chemicals, as well as those PFASs and chlorinated paraffins regulated under the Stockholm Convention.

Plastic chemicals were grouped on the basis of their structures following two approaches (details in Supplementary Text 7). In brief, the first approach consisted of searching a predefined set of keys in the chemical names to identify inorganic compounds, organometallics and metalorganics, UVCBs, polymers and mixtures. This was followed by searching the name and chemical symbol of respective elements in the chemical names and SMILES to identify organohalogens, organophosphates, organosilicons and various chemicals containing certain metal(loid) elements.
