In addition, we applied expert judgement to identify PFASs from all organofluorine chemicals, as well as those PFASs and chlorinated paraffins regulated under the Stockholm Convention.

text: Groups of plastic chemicals were prioritized on the basis of the number of chemicals of concern they contain. As some groups of chemicals lack hazard data, our prioritization considers only groups with sufficient information. Starting with more than 100 initial groups, we isolated relevant groups by excluding groups that were too large and unspecific (for example, mixtures), groups that are regulated internationally, and groups with too few members. The final selection of prioritized groups was ranked on the basis of the proportion of known chemicals of concern they contain. This follows the rationale that groups consisting of many hazardous chemicals have more evidence for being concerning. Priority was assigned to groups for which ≥40% of the members are chemicals of concern or if additional scientific considerations pointed towards group-specific hazards (details in Supplementary Text 6 and Supplementary Table 9).

text:
During the grouping, we also identified some technical challenges. Notably, no single automated tool is available to consistently group large numbers of chemicals. Instead, a combination of various techniques is required. For example, we used an algorithm 53 to identify homologue series containing repeating units of -CH 2 -, -CF 2 -, -CF 2 O- or -CF 2 CF2O-, covering more than 2,000 substances. Additionally, it is possible to identify UVCBs, polymers and other mixtures using predefined keyword searches 47 . However, in both cases, the subsequent assignment into more specific groups (for example, PFASs) requires manual inspection and expert judgement. This is due to a lack of machine-processable structural identifiers for these substances. Therefore, the manual curation of grouping and certain entries may have introduced some inconsistencies in our inventory. More work is needed to improve the availability of unique structural identifiers for chemicals on the global market, and to develop cheminformatics tools for grouping.

text:
ABSTRACT: A variety of chemical substances used in plastic production may be released throughout the entire life cycle of the plastic, posing risks to human health, the environment, and recycling systems. Only a limited number of these substances have been widely studied. We systematically investigate plastic monomers, additives, and processing aids on the global market based on a review of 63 industrial, scienti fi c, and regulatory data sources. In total, we identify more than 10'000 relevant substances and categorize them based on substance types, use patterns, and hazard classi fi cations wherever possible. Over 2'400 substances are identi fi ed as substances of potential concern as they meet one or more of the persistence, bioaccumulation, and toxicity criteria in the European Union. Many of these substances are hardly studied

*

Supporting Information

according to SciFinder (266 substances), are not adequately regulated in many parts of the world (1'327 substances), or are even approved for use in food-contact plastics in some jurisdictions (901 substances). Substantial information gaps exist in the public domain, particularly on substance properties and use patterns. To transition to a sustainable circular plastic economy that avoids the use of hazardous chemicals, concerted e ff orts by all stakeholders are needed, starting by increasing information accessibility.

1. INTRODUCTION

Plastics are widely used in various industrial sectors including packaging, construction, automotive, electronics, textiles, household items, and toys, with the current global production reaching over 350 million tonnes per year (t/yr). 1 These synthetic materials can be molded or shaped and are made of an organic polymer matrix and chemical additives. In their production and processing, a variety of chemical substances are used. 2 -5 The basis of plastics, organic polymers, is made from repeating monomer units. 4 Additives help to maintain, enhance, and impart speci fi c properties (e.g., antioxidants for maintaining the polymer matrix against oxidative conditions, plasticizers for enhancing fl exibility, and fl ame retardants for imparting fi re resistance). 6,7 Processing aids enable or ease the production or processing of plastics (e.g., polymerization catalysts, solvents, or lubricants). 8,9 In addition to these intentionally used chemicals, many nonintentionally added substances (NIASs) can also be present in plastics, including byproducts, breakdown products, and contaminants. 10,11

text:
This study was conducted in four steps: (1) identi fi cation of relevant data sources, (2) inclusion of relevant substances and information, (3) categorization of substance types and use patterns, and (4) identi fi cation of substances of potential concern (Figure 1). Individual steps are summarized in the following subsections, and additional details are provided in the Supporting Information fi les, Supporting Information S1 and Supporting Information S2.

2.1. Identi fi cation of Relevant Data Sources. Relevant data sources were identi fi ed from (1) target scienti fi c literature, 13,43,44 (2) a bibliographic search of the keywords ' plastic additives ' , ' plastic ' , and ' polymer ' in the Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar, and (3) a search of manufacturers ' , distributors ' , and regulators ' websites and databases. In the bibliographic search, books and review articles were manually selected, and individual research articles were excluded due to time and resource constraints. Sources were excluded that deal solely with polymers but are irrelevant for plastics; similarly, sources that deal exclusively with NIASs were excluded, as this study deals with substances intentionally added to plastics. The internet search focused on sources that include explicit use information.

text:
In total, 190 relevant sources were identi fi ed and categorized based on information content, data accessibility, and source type (i.e., regulatory, scienti fi c, and industrial), see Sheet S1 in Supporting Information S1. Among them, 63 sources provided readily accessible information and were further processed; the rest were not used, as they referred only to general groups of substances (e.g., phenolic antioxidants and fatty acid esters) or were not machine-processable (e.g., information embedded in unstructured texts; only in print versions). Data treatment and retrieval processes varied for the 63 sources; for details, see Sheet S1 in Supporting Information S1.

2.2. Inclusion of Relevant Substances and Information. Plastic monomers, additives, or processing aids were identi fi ed by searching for plastic-related keywords in the respective use descriptions of individual substances (for details, see Sheet S1 in Supporting Information S1). Some NIASs may also be included where the keywords appeared in their use descriptions, but no speci fi c e ff orts were made to distinguish them. Only substances for which the assigned Chemical Abstract Service Registry Numbers (CASRNs) were provided in the sources were included for further analysis, and the rest were excluded, due to the high workload and uncertainties associated with fi nding their corresponding CASRNs.

Regulatory status in speci fi c regions was assessed by checking the presence of identi fi ed substances on various regulatory lists (Sheet S2 in Supporting Information S1). These include lists of chemicals regulated under the Stockholm Convention, the Montreal Protocol, and the Rotterdam Convention, as well as the regulatory lists in the EU, Japan, Republic of Korea, and the US (Figure S7 in Supporting Information S2). Also, the regulatory positive lists of substances allowed in food-contact plastics in the EU, US, and Japan were included. In some cases, groups of chemicals [for example, per fl uorooctanoic acid (PFOA), its salts, and related compounds; cadmium compounds] are regulated without explicit referencing all relevant substances; such cases required manual searches for relevant substance names, SMILES, or molecular formulas.

Categorization of Substance Types and Use Patterns. Using keyword searches, identi fi ed substances were categorized according to their substance types (e.g., organometallic or organohalogen compounds) and use patterns. These included functions (e.g., colorants and fi llers), compatible polymer types (e.g., polyethylene or PE, polyvinyl chloride or PVC), and industrial sectors of use (e.g., automotive, packaging, and food-contact plastics).

(a) Initial categories and associated keywords were de fi ned for functions (using de fi nitions in industrial handbooks), 6,8,9,63 compatible polymer types, and industrial sectors of use (based on recent plastic material fl ow analyses). 1,64,65 Keywords included synonyms (e.g., ' HDPE ' for high-density polyethylene), hyponyms (e.g., ' fridge ' for electronics and ' milk bottle ' for food packaging), and hypernyms [for example, ' polyole fi n ' for (highand low-density) polyethylene]. (b) The categorization was conducted by carrying out regular expression searches for keywords in the use descriptions of identi fi ed substances.

(c) A random selection of the categorization results was manually checked for errors (Sheet S7 in Supporting Information S1). 2.4. Identi fi cation of Substances of Potential Concern. Substances of potential concern were identi fi ed and assigned a level of potential concern using a simpli fi ed two-step approach, based on hazard classi fi cations and production volumes as surrogate re fl ecting potentials for causing adverse e ff ects and exposure, respectively.

In the fi rst step, substances that ful fi ll one or more of the following hazard criteria under EU REACH were identi fi ed as substances of potential concern: PBT/very persistent and very bioaccumulative (vPvB), carcinogenicity (C), mutagenicity (M), reproductive toxicity (R), endocrine disruption (ED), speci fi c target organ toxicity upon repeated exposure ( STOT-RE), and chronic aquatic toxicity (AqTox). Detailed criteria for the di ff erent hazard classi fi cations can be found in Table S5 in Supporting Information S2. Substances with insu ffi cient hazard information or without any information at all in the considered regulatory databases were categorized as ' unknown ' , whereas those with full hazard information but that did not meet any of the considered hazard criteria were categorized as the ' low level of concern ' . In the second step, depending on production volumes, identi fi ed substances of potential concern were either considered the ' medium level of concern ' (<1'000 t/yr) or ' high level of concern ' (>1'000 t/yr).

2.5. Quality Assurance and Quality Control. As stated above, data quality was assured using several procedures. For substance identi fi cation, quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC) included assigning con fi dence scores to the sources and substances (Sheet S1 in Supporting Information S1), verifying the check digit of CASRNs, 45 and checking the CASRN status in SciFinder (Section 2.2). For substance type and use pattern categorization, QA/QC included iterative keyword optimization (Section 2.3) and assigning con fi dence scores to each categorization. For the identi fi cation of substances of potential concern, QA/QC included a hazard data consistency check (Figure S6 in Supporting Information S2) and manually double-checking the regulatory status. The remaining uncertainties are mostly due to misreported or missing information and are qualitatively discussed in Section 4.

text:
3.1. Overview of Plastic Monomers, Additives, and Processing Aids. In total, substances with 10'547 unique active CASRNs are identi fi ed, mostly with high con fi dence in their use as plastic monomers, additives, and processing aids (Figure 2A, Sheet S8 in Supporting Information S1). These active CASRNs are associated with another 24'901 deleted CASRNs (i.e., replaced by the active CASRNs) and 22 alternate CASRNs (i.e., CASRNs in parallel use to the active ones). A number of these deleted or alternate CASRNs are still being used in di ff erent information sources.

All source types (scienti fi c, regulatory, and industrial) are important for substance identi fi cation (Figure 2A). A total of 4'280 CASRNs have been reported in more than one type of source, whereas over 6'267 CASRNs have only been reported in one type of source (note that they can occur in several sources, but all of these belong to the same source type).

More than 25% of the substances (2'703 CASRNs) are UVCBs, mixtures, and polymers, whereas almost all the rest (7'561) are individual compounds (Figure 2A). The majority of individual compounds are organic ones (6'513), including 232 organosilicons, 228 organophosphorus, 418 organosulfurs, 1'189 organohalogens, and 1'268 organic metal(loid) salts, metalorganics, or organometallics. For 2.5% of the identi fi ed substances (283), their substance types are currently uncategorizable (Figures 2A, 3  data availability) because they are registered by their trade or trivial names [for example, Ixol M 125 (CASRN 86675-46-9), C.I. 3.2. Overview of the Use Patterns. Functions are identi fi ed for a majority of the substances (7'265 CASRNs, 69%), in comparison to the much lower identi fi cation of information on compatible polymer types (3'002 CASRNs, 28%) and industrial sectors of use (4'383 CASRNs, 42%). Typically, substances can ful fi ll several functions (on average, two to three functions), be used in multiple polymer types (particularly in similar polymer types such as polyole fi ns), and be used in multiple industrial sectors (Figure 3). A total of 2'263 CASRNs are reported for use in the following applications with high exposure potential: 2'109 in food-contact applications, 522 in toys, and 247 in medical items including masks (Sheet S8 in Supporting Information S1 under the ' industrial_sector ' ).

Based on the production volumes reported in the EU, the US, and the Nordic countries and the OECD HPVC list, about 4'000 substances are HPVCs (i.e., >1'000 t/yr; Figure 3); however, these represent their total production volumes for all uses and not just the fractions used in plastics. If production volumes in other regions were available, more substances might be identi fi ed as HPVCs. Furthermore, the production volumes of many substances have been reported as ' con fi dential ' ; their share was the largest for antioxidants (10%), fl ame retardants (11%), and uncategorizable substances (12%).

3.3. Substances of Potential Concern and Their Regulatory Status. In total, reported hazard classi fi cations are available for about 6'400 substances (61%), whereas about 4'100 substances (39%) lack any reported hazard classi fi cations in the considered regulatory databases (unknown level of concern). In total, 3'950 substances (37%) do not meet any of the considered hazard criteria, while their hazard classi fi cations are available; these are designated as substances of a low level of concern. Another 2'486 substances (24%) meet one or more of the hazard criteria considered and are identi fi ed as substances of potential concern; among them, 1'254 substances (12%) are also HPVCsandthus of a high level of concern. The remaining 1'232 substances (12%) are of a medium level of concern.

text: national/regional chemical inventories provide limited help on this matter, due to (1) limited public accessibility of production and use information (e.g., only three of the 21 investigated inventories made use information public; much of the information reported in these three inventories is claimed to be ' con fi dential business information ' ) and (2) incompleteness (e.g., reduced reporting requirements for low production volume or ' non-hazardous ' chemicals 62 ). text: II Not all data in the public domain are readily machineaccessible and processable; in this study, substances for which the assigned CASRNs are not provided are excluded from the analysis, including ions for ionizable substances or structural isomers (see Section 2.2). This is largely due to a combination of the following reasons: (1) the wide use of nonmachine-readable data formats; (2) current limitations in reporting all relevant substances, including the common use of ambiguous trivial names and group names such as phenolic antioxidants without specifying relevant substances, the wide use of di ff erent names for the same substances, the underuse of unique identi fi ers such as assigned CASRNs, SMILES, and InChI(Key), 62 and common mixed reporting of neutral, ionized substances, isotopologues, and other isomers using the same identi fi ers such as CASRNs and chemical names; and (3) a lack of standardized terminology for use patterns across jurisdictions. Concerted e ff orts to address these problems are necessary to improve, harmonize, and foster nonambiguous reporting of substance identities and use patterns by all stakeholders across the world, building on existing initiatives. 3,73 -76 In addition, advances in information technologies (such as optical character recognition, natural language processing, and cheminformatics tools) to unambiguously recognize di ff erent types of chemical identi fi ers in the text and convert between them may help collect information that currently requires manual processing. 77 -81

text: The screening of regulations in this study reveals some gaps and inconsistencies; this e ff ort is not comprehensive. This is partially due to (1) a lack of easy information access to regulations in many parts of the world, (2) a common listing of groups of substances using generic descriptions without specifying individual substances, and (3) general challenges in identifying all relevant substances by manual list curation or manual search. An example of (2) is that the listing of PFOArelated compounds under the Stockholm Convention refers to ' any substances that degrade to PFOA, including any substances (including salts and polymers) having a linear or branched per fl uoroheptyl group with the moiety (C7F15)C as one of the structural elements ' ; the recognition of individual substances such as ' alkyl iodides, C 10 -12 , γ , ω -per fl uoro ' (CASRN 6839033-0) as PFOA-related compounds currently requires expert knowledge. Therefore, facilitating information access to regulations around the world, for example, through a global virtual knowledge base and further developing cheminformatics tools that help identify whether a substance is listed based on its molecular structure can be highly useful. Speci fi cally, data engines that are capable of identifying all related CASRNs, chemical names, and structures and of indexing them based on InChI(Keys) could prove to be bene fi cial in this work.

5. POSSIBLE WAYS FORWARD

This study identi fi es over 10'000 plastic-related substances and details several critical knowledge and data gaps, particularly in terms of substance- and use-speci fi c information. This scale of chemicals to be addressed may be much greater than previously expected according to previously published assessments. Here, we highlight the following overarching areas that warrant concerted international e ff orts, in order to address these chemicals e ffi ciently and e ff ectively. This study can also serve as a starting point of immediate action, for example, by prioritizing substances of potential concern and the critical knowledge and data gaps identi fi ed above. Furthermore, while this study focuses on plastic monomers, additives, and processing aids, many of the lessons learned may also be used to enhance the general sound management of chemicals.

text: 5.1. Establishing a Centralized Knowledge Base. Information on chemicals is scattered throughout the public domain, resulting in numerous di ffi culties in understanding the presence of chemicals in plastics and other products and their properties and risks, as illustrated above. It may be worthwhile to consider establishing an open and transparent centralized knowledge base of chemicals in products with inputs and support from all relevant stakeholders along the supply chains (e.g., chemical and material producers, product designers, retailers, and waste managers). It can contribute to a better overview of relevant chemicals and related information and thus provide a basis for prioritization of future work, for example, based on production volumes and/or hazardous properties.

text: Such a knowledge base could build on this work and other existing public databases (e.g., PubChem, SciFinder, OECD eChemPortal, CAS Common Chemistry, and USEPA CompTox Chemicals Dashboard) and industrial transparency initiatives [for example, Global Automotive Declarable Substance List (GADSL), the HolyGrail project led by P&G]. 70 The costs of establishing and maintaining such a large database can be perceived an impediment, as well as questions around data ownership (e.g., CASRNs are intellectual properties of the Chemical Abstracts Service and may require licensing for publication). 101 Options to navigate these barriers to access may include cofunding such an initiative through public -private partnerships, as a part of companies ' corporate social responsibility and commitments to the human right to science, and harmonizing information exchange standards across the existing major databases to allow easy retrieval and compilation of information at one central place. 102 -104 Regardless, transparency, independence, and open accessibility are crucial for such a knowledge base, and strong leadership through national and/or international governmental organizations (e.g., United Nations Environment Programme, OECD, ECHA) is needed for setting it up.

Such a knowledge base could build on this work and other existing public databases (e.g., PubChem, SciFinder, OECD eChemPortal, CAS Common Chemistry, and USEPA CompTox Chemicals Dashboard) and industrial transparency initiatives [for example, Global Automotive Declarable Substance List (GADSL), the HolyGrail project led by P&G]. 70 The costs of establishing and maintaining such a large database can be perceived an impediment, as well as questions around data ownership (e.g., CASRNs are intellectual properties of the Chemical Abstracts Service and may require licensing for publication). 101 Options to navigate these barriers to access may include cofunding such an initiative through public -private partnerships, as a part of companies ' corporate social responsibility and commitments to the human right to science, and harmonizing information exchange standards across the existing major databases to allow easy retrieval and compilation of information at one central place. 102 -104 Regardless, transparency, independence, and open accessibility are crucial for such a knowledge base, and strong leadership through national and/or international governmental organizations (e.g., United Nations Environment Programme, OECD, ECHA) is needed for setting it up.

text: 5.2. Ensuring Transition to a Safe and Sustainable Circular Plastic Economy. A vast number of diverse substances are potentially used in the manufacture of plastics, with over 20% being substances of potential concern. Meanwhile, current regulations, scienti fi c and regulatory monitoring e ff orts, and industry initiatives lag far behind the introduction of these substances to the market, to ensure clean, safe, and highquality virgin and recycled plastics. For example, the current European chemicals regulations mostly focus on single substances and/or certain industrial sectors (e.g., plastics for food-contact purposes, in toys, in electrical and electronic equipment, and in automotive applications). 105 -107 Similarly, current industrial circular economy initiatives focus primarily on the material level (e.g., using the same polymer for multilayer plastics to increase recyclability), with limited attention paid to the chemicals therein. 108 -113

text:
To ensure the transition toward a safe and sustainable circular plastic economy, concerted e ff orts by all stakeholders are needed in at least the following areas: 114 developing standardized approaches to assessing the sustainable circularity of plastics and chemicals therein; avoiding hazardous substances and embedding sustainable circularity in the design phase of plastic polymers, additives, processing aids, and value chains; fostering greater transparency throughout value chains including waste management and broadening monitoring e ff orts; developing and sharing knowledge on creating sustainable circularity of plastics and chemicals therein; and fostering innovative and chemical management enabling business models and practices.

The information compiled in this study may help initial screenings of safer alternatives in speci fi c applications, followed by more detailed alternative assessments. 115 Note that the indispensability or ' essential ' use of a substance for a speci fi c function/performance (in a speci fi c application) may also be evaluated fi rst to phase out those uses that are nonessential and thus reduce the numbers of existing chemicals on the market and their uses to be assessed and transitioned. 114 -118

text: 5.3. Expanding and Harmonizing Regulatory E ff orts. Current chemical regulation does not ensure global sustainable management of chemicals for several reasons: (a) not all substances of potential concern are listed under relevant international or regional regulations (Section 3.3); (b) substance-by-substance regulations may not protect against regrettable substitutions; 119,120 (c) regional regulations might lead to shifting chemical pollution elsewhere; 121 and (d) negative externalities (e.g., monitoring costs, potential cleanup costs, public health damages, and impaired ecosystem services) of chemicals throughout their life cyles are not fully addressed by current regulations. 122,123 Potential ways forward include (a) increasing the number of substances under regulatory scrutiny to cover all substances of potential concern; 124 (b) focusing on group- or class-based regulatory approaches to avoid substituting one hazardous substance with another hazardous one in the same group or class; 125,126 (c) fostering cooperation among regulators from di ff erent fi elds 96,127 and regions 128,129 to ensure consistent measures and avoid shifting pollution to countries with less stringent regulations; and (d) complementing current regulation with market-based policy instruments to internalize externalities and incentivize true innovation and pioneers. 114 Examples of market-based policy instruments include tradable use permits or a Pigouvian tax, where the raised governmental revenue is used to fi nance cleanup or chemical-related public health costs and helps to create fi nancial incentives for avoiding the use of hazardous or unnecessary chemicals. 122,123 Overall, concerted e ff orts from industry, civil society organizations, the scienti fi c community, regulatory agencies, and other policymakers are urgently needed to ensure sustainable chemicals management in the future.

text: Several technologies for de-inking plastics have been developed, yet, most face a similar problem, namely colorant staining. This means the ink may be removed, but some colorant re-adsorbs to the plastic resulting in recyclates with a slightly colored shine after extrusion. This re-adsorption or staining of colorants occurs as they become  available  in  the  medium  during  de-inking  by  dissolution  or  solubilization,  followed  by  dynamic adsorption -desorption of the dissolved and solubilized pigments between the medium and the plastic surfaces. In this paper, staining was analyzed, and methods for reducing staining are proposed. First, it was confirmed that staining is a reversible adsorption-desorption process. Next, kinetic models were established to describe the deinking, dissolution-solubilization, and adsorption-desorption for a yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) and red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) in caustic soda with detergent. First-order models were able to describe these processes, and were implemented in Aspen Plus to examine the effect of residence time, ink load, wastewater treatment efficiency, and flow pattern. It was shown that colorant adsorption increases with residence time, and that an increase in ink load or decrease in wastewater treatment efficiency also results in an increased adsorption. Next, it was shown that crossflow results in negligible adsorption of colorants ( < 0.5 ppm), and counter-current also results in reduced adsorption (up to 85 %) compared to single reactor de-inking (around 200 ppm and higher). Washing  with  fresh  media  enables  colorant  desorption  when  its  driving  force  exceeds  that  of  adsorption. Regardless, it can be argued that it is industrially unfeasible to completely counteract staining by merely altering the process flow, and more advanced techniques are needed to prevent staining.

This is due to the complexity of this waste stream, which is very  heterogeneous  and  contaminated. text: Several techniques have been developed to de-ink plastic waste, but not all are equally effective for the wide variety of inks. The first is the patented Nordenia Extraction and Cleaning (Norec ® ) process (DE19651571A1), performing solvent-based extraction to remove inks using  hot  ethyl  acetate  [11,12].  Furthermore,  extensive  research  has been performed on the use of surfactants as de-inking agents, such as Sodium  dodecyl  sulfate  (SDS),  Cetrimonium  bromide  (CTAB)  or Dimethyl  dodecyl  amine  oxide  (DDAO).  Research  by  Gecol  et  al. [13 -15] has shown that cationic surfactants in alkaline environments, at elevated temperatures, yield the best removal rates for both water and solvent-based  inks.  Besides,  Chotipong  et  al.  [16]  has  shown  that surfactant-based  de-inking  comprises  4  steps:  (1)  adsorption  of  the surfactant on the plastic surface, (2) solubilization of the binder in the micelles, (3) detachment of the ink particles from the surface and (4) stabilization of the free ink particles. The CADEL, or nowadays named KEYCYCLE process, is a patented surfactant-based technique originating from the University of Alicante (EP2832459B1), making use of a waterbased caustic soda solution containing detergent, and is already proven at semi-industrial scale (1200 kg.h 1 ) [17 -19]. Furthermore, mechani cal cleaning is also applied to remove surface printed inks. The ECO CLEAN process, developed by Gamma Meccanica, removes inks from the plastic surface by friction using mechanical brushes. Consequently, this process  can  only  de-ink  surface  printed  plastics  [11,20].  Another patented  process  (EP1419829A1)  makes  use  of  rotating  brushes  in combination with organic solvents and nonionic surfactants. However, the medium results in a remarkable decrease in the physicochemical properties of plastics. Consequently, this process is less known and en counters problems in upscaling [7,11,21].

text: All these technologies face an issue that is hardly described in the scientific  or  open  literature,  namely  the  staining  or  discoloration  of plastics during the de-inking of plastic waste in liquid media. In the past, this staining was not really noticed in a research context as most ex periments were conducted at laboratory scale or relatively low solidliquid (S/L) ratios, or the de-inked flakes were not re-extruded as the color becomes only, or at least more, visible after the extrusion to a thicker shape. However, upon scaling up these de-inking technologies, it was  observed  that  this  often  resulted  in  stained/shady  plastics.  This effect is enhanced in industrial plants that operate medium circulation and might have accumulation of colorants. Consequently, the value of these recyclates becomes substantially lower, as these colored plastics have a reduced applicability for high-value applications [22]. It was found that the staining was often attributable to the colors blue, yellow, and red, caused by organic pigments such as Pigment Blue (PB) 15:4, Pigment Yellow (PY) 13, and Pigment Red (PR) 57:1. This staining was not observed for non-dissolving or non-solubilizing colorants such as carbon black (PBk 7) or TiO2. It is thus clear that organic pigments are the main cause of this staining in water-based de-inking media. When organic pigments enter the de-inking medium because the ink binder has been  removed,  the  pigments  will  undergo  an  interplay  between  the solubilization by the aid of surfactants used in the de-inking medium or already  present  on  the  pigment,  broader  dispersion,  or  true  partial dissolution of the molecule. Indeed, pigments comprise a wide variety of molecular structures to which substances are added to stabilize/disperse them in the ink medium and in the binder of the inks. It can thus be hypothesized that depending on the properties of the pigment itself, as well  as  the  substances  added  to  stabilize  it  in  the  binder,  their  in teractions  with  the  de-inking  medium  may  vary.  Regardless  of  these exact mechanisms, the pigments are 'stabilized ' in the liquid. Although not encompassing all potential phenomena, we propose in this paper to consider this as the 'dissolution and solubilization ' of the pigments. After this, the color molecules can adsorb on the plastic and cause 'staining ' . It should be noted that the term staining was preferred because it is a phenomenon different from bleeding. Bleeding refers to the inability to remove colorants, like especially soluble dyes, from the wash medium by available (wastewater) treatment technologies, whereas staining is the uptake of colorants from the wash medium onto the plastics.

text: Since staining has currently been observed for organic pigments, it can be presumed that this phenomenon is similar to the re-adsorption of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) during the washing of plastic waste. In previous research, it was highlighted that non-polar VOCs favor the rather  non-polar  polymer  matrix  over  the  aqueous  wash  medium [23 -26].  Consequently,  re-adsorption  of  these  VOCs  occurs  when  a contaminated polar wash medium comes in contact with relatively clean plastics [23 -25]. In addition, a more direct link can also be made to the disperse dyeing of textiles. Here, the poorly water-soluble dyes are sol ubilized using dispersing agents, being surfactants, where they contribute to the breakdown of aggregated dye particles and dispersion of the dye in the liquid [27]. In this process, the surfactants direct their nonpolar groups toward the center of the dye in the micelle and the polar group outward, stabilizing the dyes, resulting in higher apparent solubility of the dye in the polar medium [27 -29]. In this process, an equilibrium is established between the undissolved dyes, the solubilized dyes present in the micelles, and partially dissolved dyes. The dissolved and solubilized dyes are consequently readily available in the medium and are able to adsorb onto the textile fibers, resulting in a new equi librium between the dyes present in the medium and those adsorbed onto the textile fibers. Consequently, a dynamic equilibrium is estab lished  where  the  adsorption  of  dyes  is  a  reversible  process,  and desorption of the dyes can occur depending on the prevailing conditions [27,28,30].

Since staining has currently been observed for organic pigments, it can be presumed that this phenomenon is similar to the re-adsorption of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) during the washing of plastic waste. In previous research, it was highlighted that non-polar VOCs favor the rather  non-polar  polymer  matrix  over  the  aqueous  wash  medium [23 -26].  Consequently,  re-adsorption  of  these  VOCs  occurs  when  a contaminated polar wash medium comes in contact with relatively clean plastics [23 -25]. In addition, a more direct link can also be made to the disperse dyeing of textiles. Here, the poorly water-soluble dyes are sol ubilized using dispersing agents, being surfactants, where they contribute to the breakdown of aggregated dye particles and dispersion of the dye in the liquid [27]. In this process, the surfactants direct their nonpolar groups toward the center of the dye in the micelle and the polar group outward, stabilizing the dyes, resulting in higher apparent solubility of the dye in the polar medium [27 -29]. In this process, an equilibrium is established between the undissolved dyes, the solubilized dyes present in the micelles, and partially dissolved dyes. The dissolved and solubilized dyes are consequently readily available in the medium and are able to adsorb onto the textile fibers, resulting in a new equi librium between the dyes present in the medium and those adsorbed onto the textile fibers. Consequently, a dynamic equilibrium is estab lished  where  the  adsorption  of  dyes  is  a  reversible  process,  and desorption of the dyes can occur depending on the prevailing conditions [27,28,30].

text: It is hypothesized that a similar phenomenon occurs during the deinking  of  plastics,  as  shown  in  Fig.  1,  where  the  inks  are  removed from the surface, the colorants dissolve and solubilize in the de-inking medium and then, depending on the affinity, tend to adsorb on to the polymer structure. Consequently, it is presumed that this adsorption of colorants  is  a  reversible  process.  As  with  disperse  dyeing  and  the removal of VOCs, it can be presumed that the actual rate of staining depends on a wide variety of factors, including the dispersing agents or surfactants  present,  physiochemical  properties  of  the  polymers,  pH, temperature, S/L ratio, contamination of the medium, residence time and potential interdependent effects [23 -25,27].

This research aimed to gain insight into the mechanism and kinetics of the staining of plastic films during de-inking in water-based media, and to assess different process configurations by means of simulations to better  control  this  phenomenon.  For  this  purpose,  an  experimental screening was performed to assess the adsorption-desorption hypothesis described  above.  Next,  the  kinetics  of  the  various  processes,  the  deinking,  dissolution  and  solubilization,  and  adsorption-desorption  of colorants, were determined and described by commonly used kinetic models. These models were implemented in Aspen Plus to assess the effect of residence time, the amount of ink present on the plastics or socalled  ink  load,  wastewater  treatment  (WWT)  efficiency  and  flow pattern on the de-inking and potential uptake of colorants. Finally, these findings were used to assess the potential to reduce staining by means of proper  process  design  and  media  management,  Design  for  Recycling guidelines and fine-tuning of the washing medium composition.

The LDPE films had a thickness of 47 μ m and  were  also  provided  by  Siegwerk  Druckfarben  AG & Co.KGaA (Siegburg,  Germany). The samples were then dried for 2 days at room temperature, in open air, before being cut into 1 cm × 1 cm particles.

text: The dissolved and solubilized concentrations of colorant in the media were determined by UV -VIS spectrophotometry measurements, using a Shimadzu  UV-1280  UV-VIS  spectrophotometer  with  a  scan  range  of 190 -1100 nm, a resolution  of ± 1  nm,  utilizing  a  semi-micro  quartz cuvette (Hellma Analytics) with an outer cell dimension of 12.5 mm × 12.5 mm × 45 mm and an optical pathlength of 10 mm. First, the op timum absorbance wavelength was determined for each colorant in the de-inking medium by a full-wavelength scan in scan mode. The optimum wavelength was considered to be the wavelength at which a distinct peak in absorbance could be observed. The output of these wavelength scans is shown in Fig. 1 of the Supplementary Materials. Thereby, it was decided to measure the absorbances for the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) at 453 nm and the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) at 489 nm. Calibration lines were established for each colorant; these are shown in Fig. 2 of the Supplementary Materials. In this process, the calibration lines for both colorants were established such that the maximum con centration was limited so that the absorbance did not exceed a value of 2.5. Hence, calibration lines were established in the range of 5 to 70 ppm for PR 57:1, and 4 to 58 ppm for PY 13. If the absorbance was higher than  the  maximum  absorbance  included  in  the  calibration  line,  the aliquot was diluted with fresh de-inking medium and measured again. At all times, the calibration lines and samples were measured at room temperature.

text: ICP-OES  was  utilized  to  determine  the  amount  of  red  azo  lake pigment (PR 57:1) on the one-side full-tone coated samples. Since PR 57:1 can be traced based on Ca 2 + , it was possible to determine the ink load  on  the  plastics  by  determining  the  Ca 2 + concentration  after destruction of the sample. Hence, microwave destruction was performed in  an  Anton  Paar  Multiwave  5000,  utilizing  Teflon  bombs  (Pressure Vessel SVT50). Therefore, 0.1 g of sample was weighed into the bombs, using an analytical balance, and 2 mL of double distilled water and 8 mL of HNO3 (65 %) were added. Similarly, a blank was prepared with un coated  plastics  to  determine  the  amount  of  Ca 2 + pre-existing  in  the plastics.  The  destructions  were  performed  by  heating  the  samples  to 200 °C, at a constant rate of 5 °C.min 1 for 40 min, maintaining the temperature for 20 min. After cooling, the samples were transferred into 25  mL  volumetric  flasks,  diluted  with  double  distilled  water,  and homogenized.

2.3.1. De-inking conditions

All experiments were performed in a 2 wt% caustic soda aqueous solution  containing  9.2  mmol.L 1 ( = 10  CMC)  CTAB  in  tap  water, heated to 80 °C. This study focused on the staining of flexible plastic films during the de-inking process, and thus, for simplicity, only surfacecoated samples were considered. LDPE films of approximately 1 cm × 1 cm were used throughout this study, with particle size kept constant. As demonstrated by De Somer et al. [25], particle sizes within this range have a negligible effect on VOC adsorption -desorption for plastic films. This is attributed to the inherently low thickness of films, which limits the influence of particle size on the specific surface area. In contrast, rigid plastics, due to their greater thickness, exhibit a higher sensitivity to  particle  size,  resulting  in  a  more  pronounced  impact  on  adsorp tion -desorption phenomena. Consequently, since adsorp tion -desorption phenomena are governed by specific surface area, the assumption is that staining is minimally affected in the range of indus trially relevant particle sizes of plastic films.

2.3.2. Experimental assessment of the adsorption-desorption mechanism

text:
First, a screening was performed to verify the hypothesis that the staining of plastics is due to an adsorption-desorption mechanism. For this purpose, 5 g of coated plastics was weighed and brought into contact with 150 mL of de-inking media. The media and plastics were heated up to 80 °C in a round-bottom flask equipped with reflux cooler and mixed at 500 revolutions per minute (rpm) using an overhead stirrer, equipped with a half-moon impeller. After at least 2 days, the plastics and deinking medium were separated with a sieve, and an aliquot was taken using a syringe (10 mL) with needle (Length = 120 mm, Diameter = 0.80 mm). Next, the plastics were rinsed three times with 250 mL of water to remove residual de-inking medium from the plastics. The above procedure was then repeated with the same plastics that were already washed in the previous cycle, using fresh de-inking medium. This was repeated five times, each time collecting an aliquot of the medium after washing. The aliquots were kept in vials, wrapped in aluminum foil to avoid  UV  degradation,  and  stored  at  room  temperature.  Finally,  the dissolved and solubilized concentration of colorant in the aliquots was analyzed by UV -VIS.

For each of these steps, a separate parameter regression was per formed by nonlinear regression, utilizing the FME package in R. The ModFit function was used to minimize the Sum of Square of Errors (SSE) by  means  of  the  Levenberg-Marquardt  algorithm.  During  parameter regression of the dissolution and solubilization kinetics, the maximal dissolved and solubilized concentration [cD & S]max  was also considered as regression parameter. Since the de-inking kinetics were experimen tally determined in terms of the dissolved and solubilized concentration of colorant (cD & S) as a function of time, it was necessary first to decide on the dissolution and solubilization, and adsorption-desorption kinetics. Hence, during the parameter regression of the de-inking kinetics, these dissolution and solubilization, as well as adsorption-desorption kinetics, were taken into account to describe the dissolved and solubilized con centration of colorants. Finally, the models were validated based on the Theil ' s Inequality Coefficient (TIC), Mean Relative Error (MRE), Stan dard Error of regression (SE) and R 2 to indicate their accuracy.

text: The resulting  kinetic  models  were  implemented  in  Aspen  Plus  as described  using  the  Gujer  matrix,  shown  in  Table 1 .  This  made  it possible  to  assess  the  effect  of  several  process  parameters  and  flow patterns on the adsorption-desorption of the colorants during de-inking, assuming  equal  reactor  design  and  hydrodynamics.  The  Aspen  Plus simulations  serve  the  goal  to  validate  seven  hypotheses  which  are formulated in Table 2. The simulations were not intended to serve as a detailed design for washing installations. The underlying models were calibrated and validated using experimental data on mass transfer and equilibria at consistent temperature and mixing. The stirring speed was consistently maintained at 500 rpm, as this provided effective mixing without  causing  adhesion  of  the  plastic  films  to  the  glassware.  The simulations assume an idealized scenario, excluding influence and het erogeneity of temperature and mixing, as well as dead zones. While this simplification  is  deemed  suitable  for  the  hypothesis  testing  and  first insight generation aimed in this paper, in future work detailed design and hydrodynamics of washing processes for plastic waste should be included. Further investigation is warranted into the effects of temper ature  and  mixing  on  both  the  de-inking  efficiency  and  the  staining behavior of plastics. With regard to mixing, attention should not only be given to the stirring speed, but also to the type and dimensions of the impeller, as these factors may significantly influence the process out comes. Additionally, scale-up phenomena such as plastic film agglom eration  and  curling  were  not  yet  examined  and  should  be  carefully evaluated during pilot testing. Further investigation into these effects is essential  to  enable  accurate,  simulation-based  process  design.  Conse quently,  validation  at  pilot  or  industrial  scale  is  recommended  for practical implementation.

text: The first  three  hypotheses  are  that  a  longer  residence  time  (H1), higher ink load (H2), and worse water treatment efficiency (H3) have a positive effect on colorant adsorption, meaning more staining. For these three  hypotheses,  simulations  with  a  single  continuous  stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) are performed. All simulations were consistently per formed for both the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) and the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) in order to gain insight into the extent to which the colorant affects the degree of adsorption and desorption. Next, the influence of the flow pattern and resulting contact time between col orants and plastics on potential adsorption and desorption was assessed. This involved the simulation and comparison of different configurations, consisting of co-, counter-current, and crossflow multi-stage processes of CSTRs. In addition, based on the crossflow configuration, the extent to which a high degree of media refreshment is conducive to counteracting the  staining  of  plastics  was  investigated  (H4 -5).  For  more  details regarding  the  several  flow  patterns,  reference  is  made  to  literature [44,45]. Besides, the extent to which de-inking kinetics are crucial in process configurations with a high degree of media refreshment with respect to adsorption and potential desorption of colorants (H6) was also examined. Finally, it was also verified if applying a stand-alone second wash with de-inking media could result in the desorption of the previ ously adsorbed colorants (H7). For this purpose, a two-step wash was considered, each reactor having a separate media cycle including media treatment. A schematic representation of the several configurations is given in Fig. 2 and an overview of the main settings for the various scenarios applied during the simulations is given in Table 3.

text: The colorants were specified multiple times as conventional com ponents in the property section of Aspen Plus to describe their concen trations  in  the  different  phases,  being  colorant  present  in  ink  (QInk), undissolved colorant in the medium (CUndissolved), dissolved and solu bilized colorant (cD & S) in the medium and adsorbed colorant (qadsorbed) on the plastics. The properties and relevant parameters of the compo nents were obtained by enabling all databases integrated in Aspen Plus, and any missing parameters were determined by means of the built-in estimation  tool,  using  group-contribution  methods.  For  this  purpose, the molecular structure of the molecules was specified in the properties section. The non-random two-liquid model (NRTL) property method was applied during these simulations. The kinetic models previously estab lished in Section 2.4 were applied for the conversion from one phase to another. These equations are elaborated for each phase in the Supple mentary  Materials  (S1-S4).  The  parameters  used,  determined  by parameter regression as described in Section 2.4, are shown in Table 4. The reactions were specified in the simulation environment of Aspen Plus as General type reactions, utilizing Custom terms. In this process, the reversible first-order model to describe the adsorption - desorption was  rederived  into  the  separate  first-order  models  to  describe  the adsorption  and  desorption.  As  shown  in  the  Gujer  matrix  (Table 1 ), CUndissolved  is not included in the equations, and one might expect these reactions to continue to be calculated resulting in negative concentra tions. However, this is not the case because the solver of Aspen Plus does not continue to calculate reactions once the reagent is no longer avail able. Consequently, no negative concentrations for the different forms of the colorants can be obtained during the simulations.

text: The  one-side  full-tone  coated  samples  were  considered  reference scenarios during the simulations. The simulations were performed for a capacity of 1000 kg.h 1 of plastics at a S/L-ratio of 42 kg plastic.m 3 deinking media, considering the 2 wt% caustic soda + detergent solution at 80 °C as de-inking medium. A S/L ratio of 42 kg/m 3 was adopted as this study was conducted as part of the CIRCULAR FoodPack project (European Union ' s Horizon 2020 research and innovation program), in which tests were performed at this S/L ratio. Furthermore, this is within the common range of 10 to 50 kg/m 3 that is typically applied in washing processes for recycling plastic film waste. Here the S/L ratio is preferably as high as possible, in order to achieve a higher capacity on a single washing line. However, the (bulk) density and the size of the shredded plastics often lowers the actual achievable capacity on a washing line for plastics [23,46 -48].

However, the (bulk) density and the size of the shredded plastics often lowers the actual achievable capacity on a washing line for plastics [23,46 -48].

text: A  residual  moisture  content  of  11.5  wt%  on  the  plastics  was considered after mechanical separation [49]. The resulting loss of the de-inking medium was compensated via a make-up flow, added to the recirculated  de-inking  medium  after  the  wastewater  treatment.  The mechanical separations were simulated using a USER2 block coupled with  an  external  Excel  script  to  separate  the  de-inking  medium, including  the  undissolved  (CUndissolved)  and  dissolved  and  solubilized colorants (cD & S), from the plastics, including the colorants in ink (QInk) and adsorbed (qadsorbed) colorants. For this purpose, the USER2 block was combined with a split and mixer block to reintroduce the residual moisture content (11.5 wt%) to the plastics and to send the remaining de-inking medium to the wastewater treatment. The standard settings of the USER2 block were retained, and the Stream Flash calculations based on temperature and pressure were activated for the outgoing streams. Since no dedicated studies were published on the wastewater treatment of such a de-inking medium, the wastewater treatment was considered a black  box  with a certain efficiency. This efficiency was  varied throughout the sensitivity analyzes to examine the effect of the waste water treatment on the process. The wastewater treatment was simu lated  similarly  to  the  mechanical  separation.  Here,  the  undissolved (CUndissolved), and dissolved and solubilized (cD & S) colorants were sepa rated from the medium by a USER2 block and then removed using a split block according to a certain defined wastewater treatment efficiency. An equal degree of removal was assumed for the undissolved, and dissolved and solubilized colorants. The remaining fraction of undissolved, and dissolved  and  solubilized  colorants  was  then  reintroduced  into  the recirculating  de-inking  medium  via  a  mixer  block.  The  recirculation flow of the washing medium was closed by implementing a Transfer block, in which all properties of the obtained flow after the WWT were transferred to the input stream of the washing process, supplemented with  fresh  medium  to  compensate  losses.  A  design  specification  was applied to regulate this compensation stream in order to maintain the S/ L ratio at 42 kg/m 3 throughout the simulations. The above methodology is demonstrated in the process scheme shown in Fig. 10 of the Supple mentary Materials.

Several  multi-stage  process  simula tions of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, and 10 reactors were performed, each simulating the medium ' s co- and counter-current profiles relative to the plastics. Next, for the multi-stage processes consisting of 4 CSTRs, the WWT efficiency was varied between 20 and 90 %, in increments of 10 %, to get insight on the difference in effect of the WWT efficiency on the adsorption of colorants in the case of co-current and counter-current configuration. text: 2.5.3.2. Crossflow. A crossflow scenario was simulated consisting of a multi-stage process of 30 reactors, each with a residence time of 1 min and a S/L-ratio of 42 kg.m 3 , considering a 100 % wastewater treatment efficiency. Consequently, the plastics were repeatedly washed with un contaminated de-inking medium. Only the 11.5 wt% residual moisture content after mechanical separation and the colorants present as ink (QInk), and these already adsorbed on the plastics (qAdsorbed) were cotransferred  to  the  subsequent  reactor.  This  made  it  possible  to  gain insight into the effect of short contact times and high levels of media refreshment on the adsorption and if it is possible to desorb the adsorbed colorants by contacting the plastics with uncontaminated media. Also, the de-inking rate constant was varied during these simulations with ratios of 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, and 1/32 relative to the experimentally determined de-inking rate constant to obtain some understanding of the effect  of  de-inking  kinetics  on  the  uptake  of  colorants.  A  schematic representation of the simulated crossflow process is shown in Fig. 2(d).

text: As shown in Fig. 3, it can be observed that after de-inking of both, the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) and red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1), a concentration of 194 mg.L 1 and 319 mg.L 1 of dissolved and solubi lized  colorant  (cD & S)  was  present  in  the  medium,  respectively.  The higher  red  azo  lake  pigment  concentration  in  the  medium  can  be assigned to the higher concentration of PR 57:1 in the ink. For subse quent cycles with fresh de-inking media, logically, the dissolved and solubilized concentration was the highest after the second cycle. Still, somehow surprisingly, it became more or less constant from the third wash onwards. A One-Sample t -test was performed to confirm that for both  screening  experiments  with  PY  13  and  PR  57:1,  the  measured concentration  of  colorant  in  the  medium  at  the  second  cycle  was significantly different from subsequent cycles. Here, the null hypothesis, stating that the average concentration in the medium in the third and subsequent wash cycles was equal to the concentration in the medium obtained after the second cycle, was rejected for both colorants with a p -value ( α = 0.05) of 1.53*10 5 and 4.64*10 2 for PY 13 and PR 57:1, respectively. It can be observed that in the fifth wash cycle, both PY 13 and  PR  57:1  exhibit  lower  values  compared  to  the  preceding  and following cycles.  However, these measurements fall below the lower limit of the calibration curves. Therefore, this deviation is not consid ered  substantial  and  does  not  impact  the  overall  findings  of  this screening. This indicates that the majority of colorants were released during the second cycle, being the first post-wash. Thereby, it can also be noted that the release of colorants to the medium in this first post-wash was considerably lower in the case of PR 57:1 (1 mg.L 1 ) compared to PY 13 (6 mg.L 1 ), which can be related to the lower uptake of colorant and  corresponding  staining  during  the  de-inking  process.  This  lower degree  of  staining  can  be  observed  in  the  images  in  Table  2  of  the Supplementary Materials. In the case of the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13), the plastics had a yellow appearance after de-inking, and there was a noticeable release of colorants during the first post-wash. This resulted in the disappearance of the yellow staining of the plastics.

Furthermore,  cross-sectional  images  of  the  stained  LDPE  films, initially coated on one side with PY 13 and PR 57:1 inks, were obtained using microscopy, as shown in Fig. 4. A 20 μ m cross-section was pre pared using a Leica RM 2155 microtome and subsequently visualized with a Nicolet ™ iN10 infrared microscope via Omnic Picta software. Imaging was performed in transmission mode under cooled conditions (liquid nitrogen), with a collection time of 3 s. Here, it can be observed that the colorants are adsorbed to the surface of the LDPE films, indi cating that these are not able to diffuse into the polymer structure in the applied water-based de-inking medium. Similar observations were ob tained when examining cross sections of virgin, unprinted plastic films that were added to the de-inking media to confirm the occurrence of staining and no residual ink was observed. These observations, com bined  with  the  preceding  discussion  in  the  introduction  on  the adsorption-desorption of VOCs during the washing of plastic waste and the disperse dyeing of textiles, support the hypothesis that the staining of plastics is due to the reversible adsorption-desorption of the colorants released during the de-inking process.

text: Thereby, the TIC values are consistently lower than the threshold value of 0.3, indicating that the models are capable of accurately describing the various steps [50]. This is also represented by the MRE and R 2 values for the models. It may be noted that the description of these steps for the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) is systematically better compared to the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13). Still, nevertheless, it is confirmed that the models are able to accurately describe the kinetics for both color ants. It should be noted, however, that at present no extensive testing and validation of the model has been conducted, as this is a first model that  does  not  yet  include  detailed  effects.  Therefore,  subsequent research should focus on further developing the model based on the insights  gained  to  include  several  effects,  such  as  ink  and  media composition, and process parameters, such as temperature and stirring rate,  on  the  staining  of  plastics  during  de-inking,  and  subsequent exhaustive  testing  of  the  applicability  and  validation  of  the  model should be conducted. However, it can be asserted that current models enable the description of the observed phenomena, thereby facilitating the  acquisition  of  insights,  through  subsequent  simulations,  into  the influence of the considered process parameters and flow configurations on the staining of plastics. It should be noted that the exact values of the regression  parameters  will  vary  depending  on  the  specific  process applied. Moreover, these values are also influenced by factors such as the  composition of the ink and the type of plastic. It can further be estimated that these factors may exert a more substantial influence on the regression parameters. As a result, minor errors in parameter esti mation obtained through regression are unlikely to have a significant impact on the conclusions drawn from the simulations.

text: As shown in Fig. 5(a), it can be observed that the rate of adsorption of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) is substantially lower compared to the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13). This is also reflected by the rate constants for adsorption shown in Table 4, here the rate constant for adsorption of PY 13 is about 5 times higher than for PR 57:1. For the yellow diarylide pigment, the adsorption-desorption equilibrium of the colorant  in  the  medium  relative  to  the  plastic  was  reached  rather quickly. Here, over the last 4 measurements (180 -330 min), an adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) of 44 ± 3 mg.kg 1 was determined at a dis solved  and  solubilized  concentration  (cD & S)  of  16.6 ± 0.1  mg.L 1 . However, in the case of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1), this equi librium was not yet observed after the intended run time of the exper iment. Hence, it was decided to continue the experiment overnight. In doing so, there was a further increase in adsorbed concentration from 28 mg.kg 1 to 76 mg.kg 1 , with the dissolved and solubilized concen tration  in  the  medium  decreasing  from  16  mg.L 1 to  14  mg.L 1 .  As shown in the zoom of Fig. 5(a), a more or less linear decrease in the dissolved and solubilized concentration of the red azo lake pigment was observed  in  the  first  stage.  However,  based  on  the  extra  data  point overnight and with the aid of the reversible first-order model, it can be estimated that these sorption kinetics tend to level off and approach an equilibrium.

text: On the other hand, as shown in Fig. 5(b), it can be observed that the rate of dissolution and solubilization of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) is substantially faster, and this is with higher maximal dissolved and solubilized concentration compared to the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13), being 1921 ± 52 mg.L 1 and 663 ± 26 mg.L 1 , respectively. The lower extent of adsorption combined with faster dissolution and solubilization kinetics,  and higher maximal dissolved and solubilized concentration indicates a higher affinity of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) for the de-inking medium, making it less likely to adsorb on the polymer. This was also observed during the screening experiments. This can be attributed to the chemical structure of both colorants, shown in Figs.  4  and  5  of  the  Supplementary  Materials.  The  yellow  diarylide pigment is a symmetric molecule, resulting in a more non-polar nature, while the red azo lake pigment will be ionized and is, therefore, a more polar molecule. The above is supported based on the Hansen solubility parameter distance [51], Dipole Moment and LogP values of PY 13 and PR 57:1, being 43.30 MPa 0.5 ,  1.29 Debye and 1.8, and 42.86 MPa 0.5 , 3.75 Debye and 0.7, respectively. This is also reflected in the red azo lake pigment ' s  dissolution  and  solubilization  rate  constant,  which  is  1.7 times higher than the yellow diarylide pigment. The dipole moments were extracted from calculations based on the density functional theory (DFT)  performed  with  Gaussian  16  [52].  The  calculations  used  the B3LYP hybrid functional [53], along with the 6 -311 ++ G(d,p) basis set, which has a proven record for organic molecules [54]. text: In addition to molecular structure, several other factors such as the presence  of  coatings,  dispersants,  as  well  as  the  particle  size  of  the pigments can affect the staining of plastics. Based on input from the ink producer, it can be assessed that the coatings and dispersants present on the pigments used in solvent-based inks will not affect the staining of plastics in water-based de-inking media. Maleic resin and gum resin are used  as  coatings  for  PY  13  and  PR  57:1,  respectively.  Both  coatings dissolve in the alkaline de-inking medium and consequently will not affect the adsorption-desorption of the colorants. Also, it can be assumed that the dispersants introduced on the pigments will not substantially affect  the  staining  process.  Since  solvent-based  inks  were  used,  the pigments contain dispersants which are insoluble in water. Hence, it can be assumed that staining will be more pronounced when water-based inks  are  introduced  into  water-based  de-inking  media,  as  the  disper sants in these inks are designed to stabilize the pigments in aqueous media,  contributing  to  the  availability  of  the  pigments  [55,56].  In addition,  it  can  be  assumed  that  the  effect  of  particle  size  is  rather limited as this is typically around 75 -200 nm for most of the pigments, including PY 13 and PR 57:1 [33,57 -59]. This particle size is consis tently employed as it yields optimal ink properties, given that both light scattering and absorption by pigments are strongly dependent on par ticle size, and that the total ink layer is only a few μ m thick [60]. Here, the smaller particle size will favor the dissolution-solubilization kinetics due to the larger specific surface area. An exception is PW 6 or TiO2 where this is around 500 nm, which can be considered non-dissolving in the considered de-inking medium, consequently not staining the plas tics. Nevertheless, the use of commercially available particle sizes, as presented in this study, is considered most representative of real-world industrial  practice.  Therefore,  it  was  deemed  of  limited  relevance  to explicitly incorporate particle size effects into the models.

text: Furthermore,  the  washing  medium  also  substantially  affects  the dissolution-solubilization of the colorants. This has been demonstrated by a screening in which PY 13 and PR 57:1 were dissolved in bi-distilled water, a 10 CMC CTAB solution, 2 wt% NaOH solution and a 2 wt% NaOH + 10 CMC CTAB solution. The results obtained for PY 13 and PR 57:1  are  shown  in  Figs.  6  and  7  of  the  Supplementary  Materials, respectively. In the case of PY 13, it can be observed that it does not solubilize in water and the NaOH solution, while adding CTAB, whether in the presence of NaOH or not, results in an increase in color intensity. Here, CTAB will act as a dispersant in the aqueous de-inking medium and thus induce the solubilization of the pigments. On the other hand, for PR 57:1, a slight color was already observed in water, attributable to the  dissociation  of  the  colorant.  Moreover,  the  addition  of  NaOH resulted in a substantial further increase in color intensity of the solu tion. Indeed, PR 57:1 is a laking pigment, made by the addition of acids, thereby  shifting  from  a  molecule  behaving  as  a  dye  to  a  pigment. Consequently, the addition of NaOH will result in the opposite effect, resulting in an increase in solubility of PR 57:1. Furthermore, a further increase in color intensity was observed with PR 57:1 by the addition of CTAB, which again acted as a stabilizer, promoting the solubilization of the pigment in the de-inking medium. Additionally, by measuring the absorbance of the liquids before and after filtering with syringe filters with pore sizes of 0.1 and 0.7 μ m, it was shown that both medium and colorant affect the particle size of colorants in the media. The decrease in absorbance for PY 13 and PR 57:1 in the several media is shown in Figs. 8 and 9 of the Supplementary Materials, respectively. Likewise, this can be visually observed in Figs. 6 and 7 of the Supplementary Materials, where the first vial is the initial solution, the second is the solution after filtering with a 0.7 μ m syringe filter and the third vial is this one after filtering with a 0.1 μ m syringe filter. Here it can be observed that the very  limited  color  present  in  water  of  both  colorants  is  almost completely removed by filtering with a pore size of 0.7 μ m, indicating poor dispersion of the colorants in water. On the other hand, it was found that the removal of PR 57:1 is considerably lower by adding CTAB and/or NaOH to the medium, indicating the formation of better dis persions with small particle sizes or dissolution of the colorant as dis cussed earlier. In the case of PY 13, it can be observed that the removal with the 0.1 μ m filter is about 20 % lower with the addition of NaOH compared to the CTAB solution, indicating better dispersion and thus lower particle size or better dissolution of the colorant in the medium.

text: Consequently, it can be postulated that the de-inking medium has a substantial influence on the dissolution and solubilization of the pig ments, and hence the degree of staining of the plastics. This will result in synergistic and antagonistic effects between the properties of the pig ments,  binder,  plastics,  de-inking  medium  and  potentially  also  the process  parameters.  It  is  essential  that  future  research  focuses  on acquiring  more  fundamental  insights  into  the  staining  of  plastics, particularly regarding the influence of surface characteristics of poly mers such as zeta potential and hydrophobicity/wettability, as well as investigating more types of pigment and the role of pigment properties and the washing medium. Preliminary findings from ongoing research suggest  that  pigment  solubilization  in  aqueous  media  is  a  timedependent process, characterized by a gradual decrease in particle size distribution (PSD). Accordingly, this explains the observed lag phase between the de-inking and staining. More in-depth research is needed to identify  and  examine  these  effects  and  to  incorporate  these  into  the model to describe the de-inking and staining of plastics. Acquiring this knowledge  will  contribute  to  a  more  detailed  understanding  of  the staining mechanisms and support the development of effective strategies to mitigate staining in recycled plastics.

text: First, the effect of residence time (H1) and the wastewater treatment efficiency (H3) on the adsorption of colorants was examined; these re sults are shown in Fig. 6. For both colorants, a de-inking of about 99.5 % was obtained at a residence time of 25 min. As mentioned above, the comparable degree of de-inking of both colorants can be attributed to the similar ink composition. Fig. 6(a) represents the adsorption of the yellow  diarylide  pigment  (PY  13)  against  the  residence  time  in  the reactor. It can be noticed that the degree of adsorption starts to level off once the residence time exceeds 60 min, but it continues to increase slightly, and no equilibrium is reached within 2 h of residence time. For example, at a WWT efficiency of 90 %, 494 mg.kg 1 the yellow diarylide pigment is adsorbed at a residence time of one hour, while it further increases to 662 mg.kg 1 when the residence time is extended to 2 h. This leveling off can be assigned to the relative decrease in the domi nance  of  adsorption  over  desorption,  attributable  to  the  increasing driving force for desorption due to the increase of adsorbed colorant (qadsorbed) in the plastics. Nevertheless, the first hypothesis, which states that  increasing  residence  time  results  in  higher  adsorption,  can  be considered valid.

text: The adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) with respect to the residence time is shown in Fig. 6(b). In contrast to the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13), no distinct leveling off in an increase in adsorbed concentration can be observed with an in crease in residence time. This can be attributed to the rate constants for adsorption  and  desorption  being  substantially  lower  for  PR  57:1 compared to PY 13, resulting in lower adsorption kinetics and a slower increase in driving force for desorption. A similar trend, as discussed for the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13), is observed with respect to the influence of the wastewater treatment efficiency. Yet, no overlap of the curves  is  observed  with  a  decrease  in  WWT  efficiency.  This  can  be attributed to the higher maximal dissolved and solubilized concentration of the red azo lake pigment (1921 mg.L 1 ) compared to the yellow diarylide pigment (663 mg.L 1 ), as shown in Fig. 6(c and d). Consequently,  due  to  the  higher  Qink combined  with  the  higher maximum solubility, a higher driving force for adsorption can be ach ieved in the case of PR 57:1. However, the rate of adsorption of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) is consistently lower than for the yellow diarylide  pigment  (PY  13),  attributable  to  the  lower  adsorption  rate constant.  For  example,  at  a  WWT  efficiency  of  90  %,  the  adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) of PY 13 is about 494 mg.kg 1 at a residence time of 60 min, whereas this is only 227 mg.kg 1 in the case of PR 57:1. Moreover, at a WWT efficiency of 30 %, the dissolved and solubilized concentration (cD & S) PR 57:1 increases to 1881 mg.L 1 , while the cD & S of PY 13 is limited by the [cD & S]max and will be about 660 mg.L 1 . Even in this situation, the adsorbed concentration of PY 13 at a residence time of  60  min  is  higher,  being  799  mg.kg 1 ,  compared  to  the  adsorbed concentration PR 57:1 of 732 mg.kg 1 .

text: As  stated  in  the  second  hypothesis,  the  adsorbed  concentration (qAdsorbed) increases as the degree of printing of the plastics increases. As more ink is present on plastics, more colorant will be available in the medium, resulting in a higher driving force for adsorption. For example, at a WWT efficiency of 90 %, the adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) of PY 13 increases from 116 mg.kg 1 at a relative ink load of 0.5 to 328 mg. kg 1 at  a  relative  ink  load  of  1,  being  the  full-tone  coated  plastics, attributable to an increase in dissolved and solubilized concentration (cD & S) from 216 mg.L 1 to 439 mg.L 1 . This effect continues to increase as the ink load increases to the point where the maximal dissolved and solubilized concentration is reached. Once achieved, there is no further increase in dissolved and solubilized amount of colorant in the reactor, and consequently, the driving force for adsorption will be constant. A similar pattern can be observed for both colorants. However, it is more pronounced in the case of the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13) due to its lower  maximal  dissolved  and  solubilized  concentration  and  stronger adsorption compared to the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1).

text: 3.3.3.1. Effect  of  contact  time  and  media  refreshment. First,  several multi-stage process simulations were performed with 2 to 10 CSTRs in co- and counter-current configuration, each with a total residence time of 30 min equally distributed among the reactors, as 30 min is a typical residence time in existing washing plants (including float-sinking, etc.). In first instance, the WWT efficiency was maintained at 90 %, and the number of CSTRs in the co- and counter-current multi-stage processes was varied. The output of these simulations is shown in Fig. 8 (a). As in previous simulations, the uptake of the red azo lake pigment (PR 57:1) is systematically lower than the yellow diarylide pigment (PY 13), but a similar pattern is noticed for both. It was observed that a counter-current multi-stage process results in a lower uptake compared to single CSTR de-inking. This can be explained by the shorter contact time between the plastics and colorants released during de-inking. This shorter contact time can be attributed to the total residence time distributed over the multiple reactors, with the medium flowing through the system in the opposite  direction,  taking  the  released  colorants  with  it.  Here  the maximum contact time depends on the number of CSTRs that must be passed through before complete de-inking is obtained. Thereby, there was a 43 % decrease in adsorbed concentration (qAdsorbed) of the yellow diarylide  pigment  when  switching  from  a  single  CSTR  to  a  countercurrent  configuration  consisting  of  2  CSTRs,  and  an  85  %  reduction when applying a counter-current consisting of 10 CSTRs. A similar trend could be observed for PR 57:1, with a 42 % decrease when applying a counter-current  configuration  comprised  of  2  CSTRs,  and  an  80  % decrease when using a counter-current consisting of 10 CSTRs.
