John F. Scamehorn holds the Asahi Glass Chair in Chemical Engineering and is Director of the Institute for Applied Surfactant Research at the University of Oklahoma. He received his B.S. and M.S. at the University of Nebraska and his Ph.D. at the University of Texas, all in chemical engineering. Dr. Scamehorn has worked for Shell, Conoco, and DuPont and has been on a number of editorial boards for journals in the area of surfactants and of separation science. He has coedited four books and coauthored over 150 technical papers. His research interests include surfactant properties important in consumer product formulation and surfactant-based separation processes.

Sherril D. Christian (1931-2000) was the George Lynn Cross Professor in Chemistry, University of Oklahoma (1956-2000). His major research interests were in the fields of surface and colloid chemistry, molecular complex chemistry, and solution thermodynamics. He was director of the Institute for Applied Surfactant Research, University of Oklahoma, from 1987 until 2000. He served as chairman of the department of chemistry, assistant dean of the College of Arts and Sciences, and chair of the Faculty Senate. He was elected as a foreign member to the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters in 1988. He was the winner of the Oklahoma Chemist of the Year (1986) and the Burlington Northern Faculty Teaching Award (1989).

Abstract

text: Direct reuse of plastic film with printing results in a colored polymer, which is less stiff and weaker than the original plastic upon re-extrusion. There is substantial economical and environmental incentive to remove the ink (deink) from heavily printed plastic film so that it can be reused to produce clear films. In this study, a commercial polyethylene film with water-based ink printing was deinked using different surfactants under a variety of conditions. At a pH of 12, water (containing no surfactant) can achieve about 90% deinking, but less basic solutions are less effective; at a pH 10 and below, insignificant-deinking occurs. Solutions of cationic surfactant are the most effective at deinking, showing high efficiency at surfactant concentrations both above and below the critical micelle concentration (CMC) over a pH range of 5-12. Amphoteric surfactant is effective above the CMC over a wide pH range. Both anionic and nonionic surfactants are only effective at deinking above the CMC at very basic conditions, with anionic surfactant being only slightly better than just water even at these high pH levels. The cationic surfactant is most effective and the anionic surfactant is least effective, possibly because the binder is an acidic acrylate with a negative charge. © 2001 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.

The United States generated 207 million tons of municipal solid waste annually in 1993 of which 9.3% is plastic [1]. Only about 3.5% of this plastic is recycled [2]. This recovery rate is so low because of limitations on the technology for sorting, cleaning, and reformulating the recyclate. Since the source is better defined, in-plant plastic recycling is more successful, totaling 4 billion pounds annually in 1993 [2].

Since the source is better defined, in-plant plastic recycling is more successful, totaling 4 billion pounds annually in 1993 [2].

text:
Plastic film packaging, totaling an estimated 12.4 billion pounds annually in 1998 in the United States, is expected to grow at an annual rate of 3.1% [3]. The fraction of plastic film in total sorted plastic in the US is 21-57% [4]. However, most research on plastic recycling has focused on rigid containers. Polymers used for films include low density polyethylene (LDPE), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), polyethylene terephthalate, ethylene vinyl acetate, polyvinyl chloride, and polypropylene. The highest volume resin used is LDPE due to toughness, sealability, inertness and action as a moisture barrier. LDPE has greater clarity and flexibility than HDPE, making it particularly valuable for clear films.

Scrap printed plastic packaging is primarily used to make low value colored products such as trash cans, pipes, and signposts. Repelletized colored resins can crack, as gases associated with ink decomposition are released [5,6]. Effective film deinking technology could permit reuse of the polymer to produce clear films, reducing solid waste for landfills, reducing raw material demand for polymer production, and aiding process economics. Possible alternatives for deinking of plastic film are using either organic solvents or surfactants.

2. Background

Printing of films is important in the packaging industry because the printing describes the product to help the customer make a purchasing decision. Ink on a film must not change the character of the film and print must not be destroyed in packing the goods or when consumers purchase the product.

text:
Ink is a dispersion of pigments or dyes in a fluid carrier (vehicle). Commercially, there are two types of printing inks available: ultraviolet curing printing inks and conventional inks. Ultraviolet curing printing inks are used for plastic containers and closures (tapered pots, cups, tubes, lids) but not for plastic films due to the high cost and technological difficulties [7]. Conventional inks are used in either a flexographic or a gravure printing process to print plastic films [7-9]. The main ingredients of the conventional inks are pigments, binders, carriers (vehicles) and additives. Organic and inorganic pigments give color and opacity to the ink and influence its fluidity. Binders, which are mostly low molecular weight polymeric resins, disperse the pigments and retain them on the plastic film surface after printing. The carrier (or vehicle) is a liquid, which provides fluidity for the ink and transfers the ink from the printing system to the substrate. After application, the carrier should evaporate quickly and completely. Additives in the ink include waxes, surfactants, drying agents, and antioxidizing agents.

text: [8]. Water-based ink uses water as carrier, but might contain up to 20% alcohol. Pigment particle sizes for water-based ink are smaller than that for oil-based ink. Binders for water-based ink are acidic resins that dissolve or disperse in water when neutralized by organic bases such as amines [7,10]. Acrylics are often used in water-based ink formulations because of their superior properties such as nonfoaming characteristics, faster drying, better dispersion, heat resistance, gloss levels, and longer shelf stability. Water-based ink is nonflammable, produces less objectionable vapors in the workplace, and does not contaminate packaged products. However, more energy is required to dry water-based ink. Water-based ink also requires a higher surface energy of the film for good wet out and produces lower quality printing compared with solvent-based ink. However, water-based inks occupy a large and increasing fraction of plastic film inks since environmental regulations restrict the amount of volatile organic compounds (VOC) from flexographic and gravure press emissions [7,10,11].

During printing, inks need to wet the surface of the film in order to uniformly cover and bond to the surface. There are several film treatment processes applied just before printing which increase the surface energy of the plastic surface and enhance ink wettability. These surface treatments are chemical treatment, flame treatment, corona discharge, plasma treatment, and ultraviolet treatment. The corona discharge treatment involves application of high voltage ( p2 10 000 V) by using electrodes positioned a short distance from the film. The air in the gap between the electrodes is ionized, and this corona of ionized air oxidizes the surface [12].

The plastic film was composed of 70% low density and 30% high density polyethylene, and was reverse printed with various colors waterbased ink (black, white, purple, pink and orange) by the flexographic printing press after surface treatment with corona discharge. The printed surface was then coated with white ink to give an opaque appearance and to protect the ink layers. This film was commercial plastic packaging supplied by Kimberly-Clark Corporation. Printed and clear parts of the plastic film were segregated for this study, and the clear part was used as a standard for comparison with deinked printed plastic film.

3.2. Methods

A back-scatter image of the surface containing both clear and printed parts of the plastic film was taken by scanning electron microscope (SEM, model number JOEL JSM-880). A representative sample was mounted on a copper sample holder with double sided carbon tape and coated with 60 / 40 gold / palladium in a Hummer VI sputtering system in order to make the sample surface conductive. After coating, a small dot of silver paint was placed on the edge of sample to ensure conductivity. The same sample was also analyzed with an energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy attached to the SEM in the spot mode.

The clear and printed part of the plastic packaging were separated, shredded and then extruded either as a pellets or as a film with a Killion Extruder KL-100 at approximately 232°C. The extrusion temperature is suggested as 160-240°C for LDPE and 200-280°C for HDPE [13]. Cross sectional areas of the re-extruded pellets were analyzed with Transmittance Electron Microscope (TEM, JEOL 2000 FX). Samples for the TEM were prepared with MF-6000 Ultramicrotomy attached with FS-100 Cryosectioning at -120°C and picked up with 200 mesh nickel folding grids.

Fig. 11. The total color difference (DE*) between the plastic film treated with CPC and the clear plastic film as a function of pH.

For stress-strain property measurements, reextruded film strips were first pressed with a Carver M Press including a Carver 2101 heating plate at approximately 150°C in order to achieve uniform thickness and then cut with an ASTM standard D-1708 die [14]. The samples were stretched with an Instron TT-C-L tensile tester having a computerized data acquisition system at a rate of 0.51 cm min -1 at room temperature. Measurements were repeated four times for reextruded clear or printed film.

All of the glassware was cleaned with a regular lab detergent, after which, it was acid washed with nochromix solution (Godax Laboratories Inc.) for at least an hour. The surfactant solution was always prepared fresh with double deionized water for each the experiments, and the pH level of the aqueous surfactant solution was adjusted immediately with sodium hydroxide or hydrochloric acid before the deinking experiment was conducted. A representative sample (2.5 × 2.5 cm) printed with each of the colors white, black, orange, purple and pink was cut from the printed area of the plastic and soaked in a 20 ml solution (water or surfactant solution) with or without 20 irregular shaped porcelain beads. The 30 ml glass sample tube was then placed on a reciprocating Eberbach shaker for 4 h. After 4 h of agitation, plastic samples were taken out of the washing bath, rinsed with deionized water and air dried. All experiments were performed at room temperature and each experiment was repeated at least twice.

Each deinked plastic sample was first visually evaluated and then analyzed using a Hunterlab UltraScan™ Spectrocolorimeter system (SN 7834, diffused d8 / sphere with 8° viewing area)

The CIELAB (L*, a*, b*) color scale was chosen to specify the sample colors. This method has been recognized for color stimulus evaluation by the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) and it gives measurements of color in units of approximate visual uniformity throughout the colored solid. Thus, the L* measures the lightness and varies from 100 for perfect white to zero for black. The a* measures redness when it is positive, gray when it is zero and greenness when it is negative. Similarly, the b* measures yellowness when it is positive, gray when it is zero and blueness when it is negative. The total color difference between standard (clear film) and sample (printed or deinked film) can be quantified by a single parameter (DE*) at the chosen standard illuminant and observer to indicate the degree of deinking. The illuminant chosen was D65, representing daylight with a correlated color temperature of 6500 K, with a 10° standard observer for this work. The DE* is calculated as:

DE * = [(DL*) 2 + (Da*) 2 + (Db*) 2 ] 1 / 2

4. Results and discussion

4.1. Physical properties of re -extruded plastic films

Deinking involves the removal of multiple ink layers from the plastic film. In Fig. 1, the back scatter image of the plastic film taken by SEM shows these layers. Energy dispersive x-ray spectrograms of clear plastic film, ink layer and white overcoat layers are presented in Fig. 2. In these spectrograms, detected copper is the sample holder while gold and palladium are the coating produced with the sputtering system. As seen in Fig. 2, silicon was detected in all samples. However, the ink layer has more silicon than clear plastic and the single layer print overcoat. Aluminum was found in both the ink layer and the white overcoat layer while titanium is only present in the overcoat layer (TiO 2 is commonly used as a pigment for white ink).

Clear film had a beige appearance upon re-extrusion into pellets while re-extruded printed film was reddish brown. Crack points and holes were also observed on the cross sectional area of the pellets produced from printed film because gases associated with ink decomposition were released. As shown in Fig. 3, TEM micrographs clearly indicate ink aggregates of approximately 2-5 p109 m in size in the re-extruded printed film.

During measurement of stress-strain properties, stress-induced crystallinity was observed for both clear and printed plastic film samples. Tensile stress-strain curves for these polymeric films are shown in Fig. 4. Young's modulus, yield stress, tensile strength, and elongation at break for each film were determined with a 90% confidence interval from stress-strain curves of four measurements and tabulated in Table 1. Ink contamination makes the plastic less stiff (modulus is decreased) and weaker (ultimate strength and elongation at break are decreased). Particle agglomeration reduces the strength of a material because agglomerates act as stress concentration points [15]. Therefore, plastic contaminated with heavy printing is not a suitable raw material for clear plastic film production due to reduced and variable physical properties, pellet cracking, and color from residual ink.

text: Printed plastic samples were treated with deionized water containing only acid or base (pH of 3-12) at room temperature and the resulting DE* values are presented in Fig. 5. The value of DE* should be as close to zero as possible, for it to exhibit complete deinking. As seen in Fig. 5, printing was not significantly removed by water at pH values of 3-10 with or without the presence of abrasives (abrasives only scrubbed a trace amount of ink from the surface at pH levels of 9 and 10) but the plastic samples treated with water at pH of 11 (30% ink removal) and 12 (60% ink removal) were partially deinked. Transmittance of these partially deinked films is also presented and compared with the transmittance of clear and printed films in Fig. 6. For complete deinking, the transmittance of deinked samples should be as close as possible to the transmittance of clear film. High pH was partially successful in removing water-based ink because the binders have carboxylic acid groups which deprotonate to form anionic carboxylates under basic conditions [10]. Hence, the binder has a higher solubility at high pH. Adding abrasives to the water increases the deinking level by approximately a factor of three (refer to Fig. 5 and Fig. 6) at a pH of 11 or 12, so mechanical force provided by the shaking action with abrasives aids in dispersing the ink in the washing bath after being loosened at high pH.

4.3. Deinking with surfactant solutions

Deinking of plastic packaging is consistent with a laundering process: detachment of soil (inks) from the substrate (plastic packaging) by a chemical mechanism, and separation of the detached soil from the substrate and dispersion of soil in a washing bath by mechanical action. In order to detach the inks from plastic film, four groups of surfactants with the presence of abrasives were studied, anionic SDS, nonionic NP(EO)10, amphoteric DDAO, and cationics CPC and CTAB. Nonionic and anionic surfactants are widely used in detergent formulations [16] and in paper deinking processes [17-19]. Some characteristics of these surfactants are given in Table 2.

The surfactant concentration used was either below or above the critical micelle concentration (CMC) as shown in Table 3. The total color differences (DE*) between deinked plastic and clear plastic as a function of pH levels are presented and compared with DE* values obtained from experiments with only water (with the presence of abrasives) in Figs. 7-11. Due to the above mentioned nature of water-based ink resins, ink solubilization and partial deinking were expected at pH values of 11 and 12 for all solutions. On the other hand, deinking at pH levels other than 11 or 12 indicates the effectiveness of surfactants in the deinking process.

Only partial deinking was observed at pH of 10, 11 and 12 with the anionic surfactant SDS below its CMC (4 mM) as seen in Fig. 7. Increasing the concentration of SDS to above its CMC (25 mM) also yields partial deinking at a pH of 8 and 9. Increasing SDS concentration from below to above its CMC at basic pH levels and increasing the pH levels from 8 to 12 increases deinking. However, SDS deinks the plastic film only slightly better than water.

The nonionic surfactant NP(EO)10, as seen in Fig. 8 does not cause sufficient deinking at any pH level below its CMC (0.025 mM) but increasing the concentration above the CMC of the surfactant (25 mM) produces deinking at pH of 8-12 and demonstrates almost complete deinking at a pH of 10. At pH 11 and 12, NP(EO) 10 above its CMC increases the deinking level compared with water.

Amphoteric surfactant DDAO is almost completely cationic at low pH values ( p2 2), and is almost completely nonionic at high pH values ( p2 8 or greater) [20]. At intermediate pH values, both the cationic and nonionic DDAO molecules are present at equilibrium. Therefore, the CMC of DDAO is a function of pH as shown in Table 2. Below the CMC (0.2 mM), DDAO partially deinks the plastic film at pH 7 and 10 (Fig. 9) and increases the deinking level at pH 11 and 12 compared with water. Increasing the concentration of DDAO to above the CMC (25 mM) results in improved deinking. No clear trend is observed in deinking as a function of pH at this DDAO concentration.

Deinking at varied levels as seen in Fig. 10 was observed at pH of 5-12 with the cationic surfactant CTAB below its CMC (0.5 mM). Increasing the CTAB concentration to above its CMC (25 mM) enhances deinking at all pH levels except pH 3. CTAB above its CMC is very effective at slightly acidic, neutral and low basic pH levels for the deinking of water-based ink printed plastic film. The experiment with cationic CPC (Fig. 11) confirms the effectiveness of cationic surfactant in the deinking of plastic film below and above its CMC and at pH levels from 4 to 12. However, we observed that CPC degrades to shorter chain chemicals at high pH levels.

Amphoteric surfactant DDAO is almost completely cationic at low pH values ( p2 2), and is almost completely nonionic at high pH values ( p2 8 or greater) [20]. At intermediate pH values, both the cationic and nonionic DDAO molecules are present at equilibrium. Therefore, the CMC of DDAO is a function of pH as shown in Table 2. Below the CMC (0.2 mM), DDAO partially deinks the plastic film at pH 7 and 10 (Fig. 9) and increases the deinking level at pH 11 and 12 compared with water. Increasing the concentration of DDAO to above the CMC (25 mM) results in improved deinking. No clear trend is observed in deinking as a function of pH at this DDAO concentration.

Deinking at varied levels as seen in Fig. 10 was observed at pH of 5-12 with the cationic surfactant CTAB below its CMC (0.5 mM). Increasing the CTAB concentration to above its CMC (25 mM) enhances deinking at all pH levels except pH 3. CTAB above its CMC is very effective at slightly acidic, neutral and low basic pH levels for the deinking of water-based ink printed plastic film. The experiment with cationic CPC (Fig. 11) confirms the effectiveness of cationic surfactant in the deinking of plastic film below and above its CMC and at pH levels from 4 to 12. However, we observed that CPC degrades to shorter chain chemicals at high pH levels.

To summarize the effect of surfactants, shown in Figs. 7-11, cationic surfactants are the only effective surfactants either below or above their CMC and at acidic, neutral, and basic pH levels. Amphoteric surfactant is effective at deinking above the CMC over a wide pH range. Nonionic surfactant is only effective at deinking above the CMC at a pH of 10. However, anionic surfactant above the CMC is slightly better than water even at high pH levels. The cationic surfactant is the most effective and the anionic surfactant is the least effective, possibly because the binder in water-based ink formulations is an acidic acrylate.

text: Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) is a high utility engineering thermoplastic, abundantly present in waste electronic and electrical goods. The demand for this plastic resin increases continuously with rapid industrial growth across the world. During the recycling of e-waste plastics, it is a common occurrence to find brominated flame retardants, such as Tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) in the plastic. These flame retardants are intentionally added to the plastics as additives. Three processes were investigated to find the optimum solvent/antisolvent combinations, process parameters for the efficient recovery of TBBPA free plastics: microwave assisted extraction (MAE), ultrasound assisted extraction (UAE), and dissolution reprecipitation (DR). Rigorous solvent screening was carried out for both TBBPA and ABS using Hansen Solubility Parameters (HSP), and their interactions with the solvents were investigated with a molecular based Conductor like Screening Model for Realistic Solvents (COSMO-RS) software platform. A 4:1 (v/v) solvent mixture of 1-propanol and heptane was found to be ideal for the solid -liquid extraction process. The optimal extraction conditions (Temperature = 110 -130 °C, time = 60 to 70  min  solid/liquid  ratio  of  0.025)  in  MAE  were  predicted  using  machine  learning  based  Support  Vector Regression (SVR) technique. MAE was found to be superior to UAE and DR processes in terms of quantity and quality of recovered plastics. The maximum extraction efficiencies for TBBPA removal were achieved with MAE, UAE, and DR processes at 95.81%, 93.92%, and 98.15%, respectively. However, the DR process had a relatively lower plastic recovery.

TBBPA and its derivatives were identified as pri ority substances for screening assessment under the Canadian Environ mental  Protection  Act,  1999  due  to  their  persistence  and  inherent toxicity to non-human organisms [9]. This is because available plastic sorting technologies are unable to differentiate between restricted and non-restricted BFRs. An operational threshold of 2,000 ppm total bromine has been set to aid in the separation of plastics containing BFRs[11]. Heat plays a vital role in various production processes, including injection  molding,  extrusion,  3D  printing,  and  others.  However,  the presence of BFR in the plastic during heating can result in the emission of toxic fumes, posing a serious health hazard to individuals in the vi cinity[28].  Furthermore,  dumping  of  such  plastics  can  lead  to  the leaching of brominated components into the environment [29,30]. Sun, et al. [31] have argued that there is even a subtle diffusion of the BFRs from the plastic to the air through molecular matrix, and this diffusion can be significantly enhanced by abrasion tear and pulverisation of the plastics. Hence, it is essential to remove the excess BFR from the plastics before recycling.

Sun, et al. [31], Wan, et al. [32] reported the mass transfer kinetics involved in the release of BFRs such as PBDEs, TBBPA-bis-(2,3-dibromo2-methylpropyl ether) from plastics, respectively. Which implies that the interaction between the polymer, the additive, and the solvent is an important  consideration  in  the  solvent  extraction  of  additives  from plastics [33]. For efficient extraction, the solvent must diffuse into the polymer matrix by swelling/softening the polymer, followed by disso lution of the TBBPA (BFR), and diffusion back into the solvent phase with minimal loss to the polymer [34,35].

text: In this study, solvent-based green recycling of ABS impregnated with TBBPA from e-waste stream was performed using suitable solvents and solvent mixtures by extraction. The solvents were screened using Han sen Solubility Parameter (HSP) calculation to achieve optimal extraction efficiency. The recovery of pure polymers from contaminated plastics is important to reduce the production of virgin plastics from petroleum sources, hence decrease the carbon footprint and also fulfill the circular economic  goal  [36].  Statistically,  the  recycling  of  such  plastics  is significantly  low  due  to  process  complexity,  polymer  contamination, and limited profitability. Prior to 2020, only 10% of all plastic waste generated  had  been  recycled,  the  rest  was  either  incinerated  or  dis carded [37]. Hence, a sustainable and economical recycling of plastic will greatly reduce CO2 emissions, plastic accumulation in landfills, and environmental hazards associated with plastic.  It  was  estimated  that 30% of e-waste plastics are ABS [38,39]. ABS Plastics are made from acrylonitrile,  butadiene,  and  styrene  by  emulsion  polymerization. Acrylonitrile  is  a  synthetic  monomer  made  from  propylene  and ammonia. Butadiene is a product of hydrocracking petroleum, and sty rene is produced by dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene. All these pro cesses are highly energy intensive and carbon negative. ABS is one of the most  important  plastic  components,  used  primarily  in  electronics, electrical  equipment,  and  automotive  parts  due  to  its  high  impact strength and flexibility. The global production of ABS plastic reached 11.38 million metric tons in 2020 [40]. The cost of ABS plastic has risen sharply recently, reaching $3,305/ton (injection molding grade) in the USA[41].  Recycling  of  pristine  ABS  from  e-waste  will  increase  the availability of these plastics.

Bhaskar, et al. [49] carried out the microwave irradiation of BFR laden HIPS using aqueous organic solvents with triethylene glycol and achieved a Br removal efficiency of 85 % (w/w) at 250 °C and 30 min run time. Past studies concentrated on the separation of the BFR from the plastic, but little attention was paid to the quality of the recovered plastic. A detailed mechanism of the solvent and polymer/BFR interaction was lacking. Hence, this study focuses on the screening of appropriate solvents to improve extraction using mi crowaves  or  ultrasound  and  also  investigates  the  plausibility  of  the dissolution  and  re-precipitation  method.  Here,  we  have  reported  a computationally  guided  approach  to  rationally  select  solvents  using Hansen solubility parameters (HSPs), and demonstrated the mechanism of interaction between the solvent and the polymer/BFR [50]. This was performed using the platform combining quantum chemical and statis tical software called ' conductor-like screening model for realistic sol vents ' (COSMO-RS).  Solvent properties, including solubility and polarity, significantly impact the recovery of plastics and the extraction of specific additives during solvent extraction processes. These proper ties  are  crucial  for  determining  the  effectiveness  of  the  extraction method.  The  optimal  process  conditions  were  determined  using  the machine learning  based  Support  Vector  Regression  (SVR)  technique. The  post-process  recovered  polymers  were  analysed  intensively  and comparisons were made for all the process outcomes in terms of effi ciency and polymer recovery. The findings of this study will significantly contribute to the e-waste (plastic) recycling industry.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Sample selection and preparation

Three  real  ABS  plastic  samples  from  real  e-waste  sources  and  a customized  sample  (CS)  with  a  known  concentration  of  BFR  (Tetra bromobisphenol-A) were chosen for this study (Table 1). The prepara tion process of the real sample is explained in Text 1S in the supporting information file. The CS in granular form was obtained from Shandong Tianyi Chemical Company, China. The standard TBBPA, pure ABS as 3D printing filament (ABS3D), and all the organic solvents (Purity > 99.5%) for the screening were procured from Sigma Aldrich Singapore. The Br concentration was measured by X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (Text 2S).

2.2. Calculation of the solubility score (Si) for solvent screening

0.1 g of the solid samples (ABS3D, TBBPA) was mixed with 10 ml of the  solvent  at  40 °C  and  kept  under  ultrasound  (Qsonica  sonicator, Q125, 125 W, 20 kHz) for 30 min. Solubility was observed visually (Fig. 2S) and assigned solubility scores ( Si ) of 0, 1, and 2 for no disso lution,  partial  dissolution,  and  fully  dissolved  solutions,  respectively. The solubility score was used for the calculation of the Hansen solubility parameters  (HSP).  The  HSP  calculation  method  is  explained  in  the supporting information (Text 3S).

2.3. Extraction processes

Following  the  solvent  screening,  microwave  assisted  extraction (MAE)  was  performed,  and  the parameters were  optimized for maximum  efficiency.  Initial  trial  experiments  were  conducted  at  a temperature ( T ) of 110 °C; for time ( t ) up to 90 mins; and a solid to liquid ratio ( s/l ) of 0.025 g/ml based on past studies [51]. The Br extraction efficiency (%) and the recovered plastics (%) were calculated based on the Eq. (1) and Eq. (2), respectively. The parameter limits are listed in Table 2. Parameters were selected based on preliminary experiments, and the maximum temperature was limited to 130 °C, considering en ergy  efficiency  and  thermal  stability  of  the  polymer. Details of the MAE process can be found in Text 4S in the supporting information file.

text: The σ -profiles reflect the polarity comparison between the solute and the solvent. There are three regions in the sigma profile: the values of σ between 0.01 to + 0.01 e/Å 2 , ∞ to 0.01 e/Å 2 and + 0.01 to + ∞ e/ Å 2 , as the nonpolar region, hydrogen bond (H-bond) donor region and H-bond  acceptor  region,  respectively[54].  The σ -profile  peaks ' in tensities  beyond σ = -0.01  e/Å 2 and + 0.01  e/Å 2 correspond to the strength of the H-bond donor and the acceptor region on the surface. A larger peak beyond ± 0.01 e/Å 2 increases the probability of H-bond interaction, and the further the peak is from the center, the stronger the H-bond interaction. The peaks of the nonpolar segments of the surfaces are visible in the range near σ = 0 e/Å 2 . An asymmetric σ -profile can be seen for ABS and TBBPA (Fig. 3(b)). Indeed, in the case of ABS, a narrow peak beyond -0.01 and -0.02 e/Å 2 of the σ -region and the peak shifting slightly away from the center generally corresponds to the presence of H-bond donor sites. However, a slightly broad peak at 0.01 e/Å 2 rep resents  the  influence  of π -electrons  of  the C ≡ N group of the ABS molecule,  represented  by  the  slightly  red  colored σ -region  (H-bond acceptor) (Fig. 3(a)). The σ -potential ( μ ( σ )) of the ABS shows a distinct shape (Fig. 3(c)). The negative side of the σ -region ( σ > 0.01 e/Å 2 ) has more  negative  value,  indicating  its  affinity  to  interact  with  H-bond donor surfaces. On the other hand, the positive value of μ ( σ ) in the re gion ( σ > + 0.01 e/Å 2 ) reflects that ABS lacks the H-bond donor surface and has the affinity to attract H-bond acceptor surfaces. The σ -profile of the TBBPA is dominating in the non-polar region ( σ ~ 0 e/Å 2 ) with a narrow cusp near 0.01 e/Å 2 representing the π -electrons of the ring, and a small bump in the region of the σ = -0.01/Å 2 representing the elec tronegativity  around  the  oxygen  atom.  However,  the μ ( σ )  values  of TBBPA have positive values in the region of σ > -0.01 e/Å 2 and negative values in a wider range in the region σ > + 0.01 e/Å 2 , which signifies the availability  of  H-bond  acceptor  surfaces  on  the  molecule. text: The microwave heat is transferred to the sample via a dual mecha nism of dipole rotation of the solvent and the sample, as well as ionic conduction [35,56,57]. Experimental outcomes of the MAE are shown in Fig. 4 for the solvent mixture 1P / Hp performed at initial experimental conditions. Fig. 4(a) and 4(b) show the % Br extraction efficiency and the plastic recovery for three mixing ratios and for all four samples, respectively. Using a 4:1 mixing ratio of 1P to Hp solvents, the maximum extraction rates were achieved for all four samples, as depicted in Fig. 4 (a).  Specifically,  the  extraction  rates  for  CS,  ReBRS1,  ReBRS2,  and ReBRS3 samples were 91.25%, 94.02%, 95.81%, and 91.03%, respec tively.  Correspondingly,  the  plastic  recovery  percentages  for  these samples  when  using  the  4:1  1P  and  Hp  solvent  mix  were  88.29%, 84.66%,  80.24%,  and  84.4%,  respectively.  Recovery  of  plastic  was consistent across all conditions, and > 80% of clean ABS plastics were recovered in each run (Fig. 4(b)). Mass loss occurred due to BFR and additive  dissolution  and  experimental  losses  during  collection.  Small particle  size  leads  to  better  extraction  efficiency  (Fig.  4(c)).  Earlier studies  have  reported  extraction  efficiencies < 85%  [42,48,49].  MAE with a suitable solvent can be a viable option for the recovery of clean plastics. High-capacity microwave ovens are used in the food, paper, timber and textile industries primarily for drying [58], with some design modifications.  A  high-capacity  microwave  oven  has  the  potential  to serve as a viable technique for the extraction of TBBPA from ABS plastic, particularly in the context of recycling e-waste plastics [59].

text: After MAE, a comparative evaluation of UAE and DR techniques was conducted. A 4:1 (v/v%) mixing ratio of 1P and Hp was used for UAE. Table 3 presents the Br extraction efficiencies (%) and the corresponding plastic recoveries (%) obtained from all three processes experimentally. The results obtained from the UAE technique were found to be like those obtained through MAE, though a minor decrease in plastic recoveries was observed, possibly attributed to high agitation leading to polymer dissolution.  In  contrast,  the  DR  method  resulted  in  almost  complete elimination of BFR, albeit at the expense of a substantial reduction in the amount of recovered uncontaminated plastics (Fig. 5(b)). The solution may contain a considerable amount of plastic material, particularly low molecular weight ABS, that may remain dissolved [60]. Low extraction efficiency (50 -60%) for TBBPA from HIPS was reported by Vilaplana, et al. [51] using UAE. Guo, et al. [61] used d-limonene as solvent and npropanol  as  precipitant  (anti-solvent)  to  recover  HIPS  from  e-waste plastic  sample  with  decaBDE as  BFR  and  achieved only ~  88% BFR removal efficiency in the DR process. Table 4 showcases several previ ously documented results pertaining to the extraction of bromine (Br)/ BFR  from  e-waste  plastics.  However,  most  of  these  studies  lack comprehensive data regarding plastic recovery. In contrast, the results obtained from the present study demonstrate high Br extraction effi ciency  over  the  reported  finding  and  yield  a  substantial  quantity  of recyclable ABS plastics.

The thermal degrada tion characteristics of the plastics recovered after microwave-assisted extraction (MAE) demonstrated a comparable peak degradation tem perature  to  that  of  the  reference  ABS  plastics,  with  a  temperature proximity of 440 °C observed under non-isothermal heating conditions of 20 °C/min for all samples (Fig. 5(d))[68]. Therefore, the disappear ance of the peak associated with TBBPA in the DTG analysis following MAE did not significantly alter the properties of the polymer. In sum mary, all  the  properties  of  ABS,  which  was  treated  with  MAE,  were consistent with those of the reference polymer.

The characterization results of the recovered polymers after UAE and DR  processes  are  shown  in  Fig.  8S  and  Fig.  9S,  respectively.  The chemical structure of the polymer, as shown by the FTIR-ATR spectra and Tg from DSC, appears to be consistent with pure ABS. No significant changes appeared in the TGA/DTG plot of the samples recovered from UAE.

text: A  slight  distortion  in  the  DTG  profile  can  however  be  seen  in recovered samples of the DR process (Fig. 9S(c)). Changes in the peak degradation  temperature  can  be  seen,  particularly  for  the  ReBRS2, which changes from 436 °C to 465 °C. This could be due to the removal of the stabilizing additives during the dissolution process. The GCMS peaks  from  the  MAE  and  DR  processes  are  shown  in  Fig.  10S  and Fig. 11S, respectively, along with the likely components discovered by searching the Mass spectral library. TBBPA appeared in all the solutions. In addition to that, traces of phenolic compounds, aromatic compounds (isoquinols), and organic acids were also present in the solutions, which could be attributed to the various additives, such as dyes, antifungals, antioxidants, and anti-aging compounds mixed within the plastics. The presence of Butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) in the solvents from the DR process can be attributed to the usage of THF for dissolution, as BHT is a stabilizer commonly found in THF solvents. Among the two solid -liquid extraction processes, MAE appeared to be better than UAE in terms of plastic  recovery  yields.  However,  both  processes  have  challenges  in terms of scale-up and implementation. UAE requires external heating, while MAE uses microwaves to heat the system. Management of heat and pressure is simpler in MAE compared to UAE because heat can be delivered to the target material via microwave without contact. On the other hand, the DR process can restore the purity of the polymer by reprecipitation  from  the  liquid  phase,  with  reduced  polymer yield  and abated polymer properties. A DR-like process (CreaSolv ® ) was devel oped by Unilever/Fraunhofer Institute for the separation of polymers from a mixed polymer stream of plastics (from different sources)[69,70]. Walker, et al. [71] developed a similar process called solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP) process to deconstruct multilayer films  and  recover  the  pure  resin  by  performing  rigorous  solvent screening using HSP and COSMO-RS calculations. Peng, et al. [43] used supercritical CO2 as an antisolvent for the separation of Deca-BDE (BFR) from HIPS obtained from e-waste. Our results show that MAE can be an excellent  method  for  removing  BFR  from  plastics  without  affecting plastic properties.

4. Conclusions and perspectives

text: This study reports the optimal combination of solvents that can be applied to remove the tightly bound BFR additive (TBBPA) from ABS plastics recovered from e-waste[31]. We adopted a rigorous methodol ogy  to  screen  suitable  solvent/solvent  mixtures  that  would  allow maximum extraction and minimum loss of plastic. The mixture of 1propanol and heptane was found to be suitable for the extraction of TBBPA from ABS plastics. Non-polar solvents, such as heptane mixed with alcohol, improved the extraction efficiency more significantly than their individual counterparts. COSMO-RS Calculations showed that both TBBPA and ABS have polar and nonpolar properties on their molecular surfaces  that  influence  the  extraction.  The  targeted  solvent-based extraction  for  recovery  of  BFR  (TBBPA)-free  plastics  from  contami nated e-waste ABS plastics was improved by heating with microwave/ ultrasound.  In  terms  of  extraction  rates,  MAE  was  superior  under optimal process conditions as it also preserved/improved the polymer properties of the ABS. The recovery of ABS plastics from the DR process was low compared to MAE /UAE with high extraction efficiency. Such processes could provide a common framework for developing solvent based processes for debromination of BFR laden e-waste plastics. The implementation of a selective and targeted approach is better suited for the recovery of clean plastics and achieving a closed-loop system for recycling e-waste plastics.

We adopted a rigorous methodol ogy  to  screen  suitable  solvent/solvent  mixtures  that  would  allow maximum extraction and minimum loss of plastic. The recovery of ABS plastics from the DR process was low compared to MAE /UAE with high extraction efficiency. Such processes could provide a common framework for developing solvent based processes for debromination of BFR laden e-waste plastics. Polyolefins, produced from olefin (alkene) monomers, are the most widely used commercial polymers [1]. Ethylene-based polyolefins can be  classified  as  low-density  polyethylene  (LDPE),  linear  low-density polyethylene (LLDPE), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), ultrahigh-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE), and ultralow-density polyethylene (ULDPE). Polyolefins are widely used due to their unique properties, such as durability, barrier performance, op tical  clarity,  versatility,  processability,  and  cost-effectiveness  [2,3]. LDPE and LLDPE are utilized in the manufacture of reusable bags, trays and  containers,  agricultural  films,  industrial  wrappings,  and  food packaging films. A B S T R A C T

text: Increased use of plastics and corresponding generation of plastic waste leads to growing pressure for recycling technologies that are both economically viable and environmentally sound. For plastic films, widely used in packaging  and  comprising  mostly  polyolefins,  mechanical  recycling  is  not  practical,  hence  the  interest  in chemical recycling. Dissolution/precipitation recycling can recover polyolefins for re-use, with energy needs and emissions much lower than pyrolysis. The dissolution of polyolefins is key to this recycling process, however, the underlying phenomena which govern the dissolution of semicrystalline polymers are little studied. To address this  gap  in  knowledge,  the  swelling  and  dissolution  kinetics  of  high-density  polyethylene  (HDPE)  films  are investigated here. Experiments are designed to obtain the time evolution of HDPE dissolved mass and degree of crystallinity.  A  mathematical  model  is  developed  to  describe  the  swelling  and  dissolution  of  semicrystalline HDPE based on the transport phenomena and thermodynamics governing the process. Experimental data are used to validate the model and to obtain values for the two key fitted parameters, decrystallization constant and disentanglement rate. The detailed information provided by the model, spatial and temporal composition and solvent diffusion, reveals the molecular mechanism of HDPE dissolution. A parametric analysis is performed using the validated model to simulate dissolution phenomena at varying conditions, including initial degree of crystallinity and film thickness. These insights on polyethylene dissolution facilitate the design of more energy efficient and environment-friendly dissolution-precipitation recycling processes. The model can be extended to probe the dissolution of other semicrystalline polymers.

Global  plastic  production  grew  at  a  compound  annual  growth  rate (CAGR) of 8.3%, increasing from 1.7 Mt in 1950 to 348 Mt in 2017 [4]. From 2017 to 2023, growth slowed to ~2.9% CAGR, reaching 413.8 Mt in 2023 [6]. Polyethylene (PE) is the largest single contributor to this output, accounting for 26.2% of total global plastic production in 2023 [6]. In 2017, over three-quarters of end-of-life plastic in the US was sent to landfill [7]. It has been reported that PE accounts for more than 33% of microplastics in landfill leachate [8]. According to a 2019 Department of Energy (DOE) study, the US landfilled 82% of HDPE, while only 10% was recycled [9], highlighting that much remains to be done to improve HDPE recycling. Mechanical recycling alone is insufficient for PE due to a  range  of  material  and  process  limitations  [10,11].  Many  PE-based products, particularly in packaging, are multilayer films that incorpo rate  incompatible  polymers,  and  even  metal  layers  (e.g.,  in  aseptic packaging).  These  material  combinations  compromise  the  recycled output [12 -14]. Additionally, PE waste is often contaminated with food residues,  labels,  inks,  pigments,  and  odors  that  are  difficult  to  fully remove through  mechanical  processes,  further  degrading  the  quality and usability of the recycled product [15,16]. Addition of compatibil izers could help improve mechanical recycling rates [17,18], but their application  remains  limited  due  to  high  costs.  In  general,  PE-based products, especially packaging, tend to be difficult to recycle through primary and secondary (mechanical) recycling methods [13,15].

text: A solution for managing such plastic waste is tertiary recycling, also known  as  advanced  or  chemical  recycling,  which  converts  polymer chains into feedstock for the production of fuels [19], chemical building blocks [20], or specialty chemicals [5,19], through depolymerization [19],  pyrolysis  [19],  hydrocracking  [21],  or  gasification  [22].  These methods  involve  high  energy  consumption  and  CO2  and  toxic  gases emissions,  and  limited  sustainability  [23].  Consequently,  chemical recycling is viewed as an environmental health risk and attracts negative publicity [23]. In addition, the presence of additives in plastic waste complicates  chemical  recycling  processes  [24].  Some  of  these  disad vantages  can  be  mitigated  using  dissolution-precipitation  recycling [25 -28].  In  dissolution-precipitation  recycling,  plastic  waste  is  first processed in a selective solvent to dissolve the target polymer. Immis cible solids are then removed via filtration. The target polymer is next precipitated from its solution using an anti-solvent, temperature drop, or both [29]. This method can unlock the potential for utilizing polyolefins that are currently landfilled or incinerated. Compared to other chemical recycling methods, dissolution-precipitation can be considered as true recycling,  as  it  recovers  polymers,  and  involves  lower  energy  re quirements and CO2 emissions [30]. The potential of dissolution-precipitation  for  recycling  PE  in  an  industrial  scale  is demonstrated by APK ' s Newcycling facility in Merseburg, Germany that recovers  primarily  PE,  and  in  some  cases  polypropylene  (PP),  from multilayer  film  waste  [31,32].  This  platform  is  being  scaled  under LyondellBasell ' s new  ownership, signaling continued commercial development  [33,34].  In  addition,  through  pilot  and  demonstration plants [31], such as a Unilever project in Indonesia and a unit at L ¨ OMI in Germany,  the  Fraunhofer  Institute  IVV ' s  CreaSolv  process  recovers quality PE from multilayer flexible packaging [35,36].

text: Central to dissolution-precipitation recycling of polyethylene is its dissolution. Despite PE being produced in high volumes for decades, there is  no  published information on PE dissolution kinetics and the underlying mechanisms. Few solvents are capable of dissolving poly ethylene, typically at high temperatures and low polymer concentra tions.  No  experimental  studies  of  PE  dissolution  are  available,  and relevant reports that focus on PP date from the 1970s [37]. Models of semicrystalline-polymer dissolution efforts are also scarce; the earliest study from 1997 was for poly(vinyl alcohol) in water [38]. In a more recent study, a phenomenological model was developed to analyze the dissolution of micrometer-sized semicrystalline cellulose fibers in ionic liquids [39 -41].

text: This  study  addresses  the  following  open  questions:  What  are  the underlying  phenomena  governing  the  dissolution  of  semicrystalline polyethylene? What are the key parameters governing the dissolution kinetics of semicrystalline polyethylene, and how do variations in these parameters influence the overall dissolution behavior? An integrated experimental and modeling effort was deployed to this end. Two types of time-resolved experimental data were generated in this work, crystal linity  of  undissolved  polymer  and  mass  loss  due  to  dissolution.  A comprehensive mathematical model, incorporating relevant transport phenomena  and  thermodynamic  principles,  described  the  coupled swelling and dissolution behavior of polyethylene. Experimental data were used to validate the model and extract key fitted parameters that carry  physical  meaning.  The  validated  model  was  used  to  perform parametric analyses across a range of conditions, enabling assessment of how key parameters influence dissolution behavior.

The novelty of this work includes: (i) integration of experiments and modeling to understand the mechanism underlying the dissolution of semicrystalline polyethylene; (ii) model-predicted information at experimental conditions that are difficult or expensive to access exper imentally;  and  (iii)  parametric  analysis  on  dissolution  kinetics  that benefit large-scale recycling applications. The experimentally-validated dissolution model developed here provides a predictive basis for largescale processing and reveals operating windows for the efficient disso lution  and  recovery  of  polyethylene  and  other  polyolefins  during dissolution-precipitation recycling.

High density polyethylene copolymer 1-butene with density of 0.94 0.97 g/cm 3 , melting range 125 - 140 °C, and auto-ignition temperature 350 °C, produced by Braskem S.A. and supplied by Braskem America, Inc. (Philadelphia, PA), is used in this study. The solvent used for dis solving HDPE is p -xylene (99 + %, extra pure, Fisher Scientific Company LLC, Boston, MA), with 0.8660 g/mL density, 106.17 g/mol molecular weight, 13.0 °C melting point, and 138.0 °C boiling point. Dissolution experiments  were carried  out  at  101 °C  and  104 °C  with  temperature fluctuation within 0.5 °C. These temperatures were selected based on the dissolution temperatures of low weight fractions (0.0149 to 0.42) HDPE in xylene at 1 bar, reported in the range 97 °C - 107 °C [42]. The selected temperatures were below both the p -xylene boiling point and the HDPE melting temperature.

text: HDPE films were prepared by placing approximately 60 HDPE pellets into  two  custom-made  brass  ring  molds.  Two  mold  geometries  were used: one with a thickness of 0.1 mm and an inner diameter of 5 mm, and the other with a thickness of 0.6 mm and an inner diameter of 2.5 mm, each of which was wrapped in a Teflon PTFE film (McMaster-Carr, P/N: 8569K36). The sample mold was then transferred to a pre-heated hy draulic press (Carver Inc.) set to 180 °C. A force of 4000 pounds was applied for 5 min to produce HDPE films with uniform thicknesses of 0.1 mm and 0.6 mm. Electronic calipers (McMaster-Carr, P/N: 4996A51, increment: 0.01 mm) were used to confirm the thickness of the polymer films. Individual samples were cut using a scalpel from the bulk mold to achieve the desired dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 0.1 mm and 10 mm × 10 mm × 0.6 mm, respectively. A cage-shaped holder made of 304 stainless steel wire mesh (1 mm square holes, 0.4 mm wire diam eter) was used to contain the polymer fully surrounded by solvent and avoid contact with the container.

First,  10  mL  solvent  was  poured  into  a  pre-weighed  30  mL  glass container. The container was then placed in a preheated silicone oil bath (Sigma-Aldrich),  with  temperature  controlled  by  a  hotplate-stirrer (VWR). The system was left for approximately 30 min to equilibrate with the oil bath temperature. Then the pre-weighed wire mesh con taining the polymer sample whose weight is known was put in the sol vent. At certain time intervals, the dissolution process was stopped by pulling out the wire mesh and putting it in a pre-weighed 20 mL vial. Immediately after that,  the  glass  containing  the  solvent  and  the  dis solved polymer was removed from the oil bath, and the outer wall of the glass was cleaned completely from oil droplets using tissue paper.

Afterward, the vial containing wire mesh with undissolved polymer was placed in an oven at 60 °C for 12 h to completely evaporate the solvent. The glass containing the dissolved polymer was dried at 130 °C for  12  h.  The  amounts  of  undissolved  and  dissolved  polymer  were determined by weighing the dried vial (including wire mesh and un dissolved polymer) and the glass (containing dissolved polymer), and subtracting their respective initial weights. At each time interval, the reported  results  and  corresponding  error  bars  are  obtained  by  mean average of at least five experimental data sets.

Since the FT-IR liquid flow cell is limited to rather thin films ( ≤ 0.05 mm), visual inspection was used to determine the time for full decrys tallization of thicker (0.6 mm) HDPE films. To initiate the decrystalli zation process, HDPE films (10 mm × 10 mm × 0.6 mm) were placed inside a stainless steel wire mesh that was then fully immersed in a 10 mL vial containing solvent at the target temperature. The progress of decrystallization was monitored visually, with the film ' s transition to complete transparency serving as the indicator of complete decrystallization.

2.3. Modeling of semicrystalline polyolefin film dissolution kinetics

text:
Although the mechanism of semicrystalline polymer dissolution is still under investigation [39,44,45], previous studies have proposed a multi-step process involving solvent diffusion into the polymer struc ture,  disruption  of  crystalline  domains  (decrystallization),  polymer swelling due to solvent, disentanglement of polymer chains, and even tual diffusion of these disentangled chains into the surrounding solvent [46]. In this study, a model for dissolution of semicrystalline polymer fiber [39] was modified to describe the swelling and dissolution of a semi-infinite semicrystalline slab. A key modification was to account for temperature-  and  composition-dependent  variations  of  the  solvent diffusion coefficient in the polymer, through the incorporation of free volume theory.

The  model  captures  each  step  of  polyolefin  dissolution  using appropriate  transport  phenomena  and  thermodynamics  equations,  as depicted in Fig. 2: solvent diffusion into the polymer, specimen swelling coupled with decrystallization of crystalline domains, chain disentan glement, and diffusion of disentangled chains into a gel-like boundary layer, followed by gradual specimen shrinkage as the dissolution pro gresses. In the following, the governing equations used to model the dissolution kinetics of polyolefin films are presented.

2.3.3. Diffusion of disentangled polymer chains to the boundary layer

text:
In semicrystalline polymers, after solvent diffuses into the polymer, it may take some time to unfold the crystalline domains [39,49 -51]. The period  during  which  the  polymer -solvent  interface  becomes  fully amorphous is defined as the induction time (tind). Chain disentangle ment and dissolution may proceed only after this interfacial decrystal lization is complete. At this point, disentangled polymer chains diffuse into the surrounding solvent through a thin, gel-like boundary layer; defined  as  the  interface  between  the  polymer  and  solvent;  with  a thickness ( δ ), assumed to be 5% of the initial film thickness, i.e., δ = 0.05 × L(t = 0) [39,52]. The exact value of δ does not affect the model out comes, since the fitting parameters are independent of δ . δ influences the amorphous polymer volume fraction within the gel-like boundary layer. The diffusion of amorphous polymer into the gel-like boundary layer (solvent) is modeled using Eq. 4:

2.3.5. Diffusion coefficient of solvent in the bulk polymer

text:
Recent  studies  have  highlighted  the  importance  of  selecting  an appropriate relationship for solvent diffusivity in the polymer [53 -55], considering factors such as polymer morphology, solvent-polymer in teractions, and temperature effects. As more solvent diffuses into the polymer,  solvent  diffusivity  increases  accordingly  [39,46,55].  The Vrentas-Duda  free  volume  theory,  which  has  demonstrated  strong capability in capturing changes in solvent diffusivity, 94 is used in this study to determine the solvent diffusion coefficient Ds in semicrystalline high-density polyethylene.

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Polyethylene decrystallization and dissolution kinetics: Experimental data

text:
Experimental data on decrystallization and dissolution kinetics of HDPE films in p -xylene are discussed here, with a focus on the effects of film thickness and temperature. Dissolution progresses approximately linearly with time for both 0.1 mm and 0.6 mm HDPE films, indicating a steady dissolution rate once the process begins (Fig. 3). This is consistent with  observations  in  semicrystalline  polymer  systems  such  as  poly ( α -methylstyrene) (PAMS) films dissolving in binary solvents [58], and poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) crystals dissolving in various solvents [45].

The polymer crystallinity drops rapidly upon solvent contact, with the film becoming fully amorphous before dissolution is completed. The shorter  decrystallization  time  compared  to  the  total  dissolution  time confirms  that  chain  disentanglement  and  diffusion  out  of  the  solid polymer film are the slower, rate-limiting processes [39]. This separa tion of timescales supports the model ' s assumption that decrystalliza tion precedes dissolution. In all cases, a short, initial delay is observed

To  validate  the  dissolution  model,  its  predictions  were  fitted  to experimental data on HDPE decrystallization and dissolution kinetics. Fig. 3 shows the model fits well experimental results for both the un dissolved polymer fraction and crystallinity time evolution for two film thicknesses at 101 °C, while the corresponding agreement at 104 °C is provided in the Supplementary document (Figure S4). This validates the molecular-level  mechanisms  described  in  the  model,  and  provides values for key fitting parameters and insights regarding  HDPE dissolution.

text:
The key fitting parameters, disentanglement rate (rdis) and decrys tallization constant (Kdec), were determined from the fits to the validated model: rdis = 2.2 × 10 8 m/s ( ± 6.89%) and Kdec = 12.8 × 10 3 1/s ( ± 6.0%) at 101 °C, and as rdis = 2.4 × 10 8 m/s ( ± 2.8%) and Kdec = 33.5 × 10 3 1/s ( ± 7.13%) at 104 °C. As expected, both Kdec and rdis were found to be independent of film thickness. The increase in Kdec  with temper ature (~161%) is substantially greater than that of rdis  (~9%). This is consistent with findings on cellulose decrystallization [40], and with kinetic theory indicating that structural transformations of crystalline domains are governed by temperature-dependent rate constants [38,39, 60 -62]. Indeed, polymer melting and crystallization kinetics in semi crystalline polymers often follow Arrhenius-type behavior [63], indicating  that  even  modest  temperature  increases  can  substantially enhance  crystalline domain  mobility  [64], and, correspondingly, accelerate structural disruption (decrystallization).

The induction time (tind) for both 0.1 mm and 0.6 mm thick HDPE films is approximately 48 seconds at 101 °C, decreasing to 30 seconds at 104 °C in p -xylene. This reduction is attributed to enhanced molecular mobility  at  elevated  temperatures,  which  accelerates  the  start  of dissolution.

In  thicker  films  (0.6  mm),  longer  diffusion  paths  lead  to  steeper solvent concentration gradient and lower ∅ s values (Fig. 5b) compared to the 0.1 mm films (Fig. 5a), resulting in reduced polymer swelling in thicker film (Fig. 4). This observation is consistent with prior studies showing that polymer film thickness significantly influences temperature-dependent swelling [65].

text: A 3 °C temperature increase reduces swelling in the 0.1 mm films but enhances it in the 0.6 mm films (Fig. 4). This behavior arises from the competition between solvent-induced swelling and chain disentanglement-driven  dissolution.  In  the  0.1  mm  films,  the  higher temperature  accelerates  dissolution,  allowing  less  time  for  polymer swelling to develop. In contrast, in the 0.6 mm films, the same tem perature  rise  slightly  increases ∅ s within  the  inner  half  of  the  film (Fig. 5b), resulting in a modest increase in swelling before the dissolu tion becomes dominant. Additionally, the higher temperature leads to a reduction in ∅ p,c across  the  film  thickness.  This  trend  highlights  the temperature  sensitivity  of  crystalline  domain  conversion,  as ∅ p,c is directly governed by the decrystallization rate constant, Kdec  (Eq. 3), which is itself strongly temperature-dependent [40,63].

text: While  typical  commercial  HDPE  exhibits  high  crystallinity,  pro cessing modifications such as copolymerization or rapid quenching can reduce crystallinity to 30% in order to tailor mechanical properties. The degree of crystallinity of the solid HDPE specimen significantly affects its  dissolution behavior. Fig. 6 illustrates how varying initial crystal linity (in the range 30% to 70%) influences the time-dependent behavior of a 0.1 mm thick HDPE film in p -xylene at 104 °C. The Kdec  and rdis values used in these simulations are specific to this temperature. High initial crystallinity results in a modest reduction (~10%) in the degree of swelling (Fig. 6a), which in the model is reflected by a lower solvent volume fraction within the film (Fig. 6c). Fig. 6d further highlights that higher  initial  crystallinity  (70%)  sustains  a  larger  crystalline  volume fraction deeper within the film compared to lower crystallinity (30%), thereby delaying decrystallization and dissolution. However, as shown in Fig. 6c, the film approaches solvent saturation in the intermediate to late stages of dissolution. This suggests that the initial polymer crystal linity  primarily  affects  the  early-stage  dissolution,  with  its  influence diminishing over time, and having little impact on the overall dissolu tion time or late-stage solvent diffusion in the film. We note that this relatively  minor  effect  of  initial  crystallinity  on  the  time  for  full decrystallization and dissolution is applicable to the experimental con ditions where Kdec = 33.5 × 10 3 1/s (reported in Fig. 6). However, a sensitivity  analysis  revealed  that  the  effect  of  initial  crystallinity  is strongly modulated by the value of Kdec. 3.4.2. Effect of film thickness

text: The dissolution kinetics of semicrystalline polymers such as poly olefins are not only of fundamental scientific interest but also critically important  in  practical  applications  such  as  plastics  processing  and recycling [46,66]. A key parameter influencing dissolution kinetics is the thickness of the polymer material, such as plastic films. Film thick ness  affects  durability,  mechanical  strength,  and  protective  perfor mance, and is commonly expressed in ' mil ' , where 1 mil = 0.001 inch = 0.0254 mm. Plastic films are produced in a wide range of thicknesses, from lightweight protective covers (~1-2 mil or 0.025-0.05 mm) and retail shopping bags (~3 mil or 0.08 mm), to heavy-duty construction barriers (6-20 mil or 0.15-0.5 mm) and robust containment liners used in agriculture and landfilling (20-40 + mil or 0.5-1 + mm) [67,68]. This wide range of applications highlights the need for a fundamental un derstanding of  how  film thickness influences processes such as dissolution.

To address this, the impact of thickness, in the range from 0.03 mm ( ≈ 1.18 mil) to 3 mm ( ≈ 118 mil), on the dissolution kinetics of HDPE films in p -xylene at 104 °C was investigated. This range spans commer cially  relevant  thin  films  to  thick  structural  sheets.  The  simulations across this range used the Kdec = 33.5 × 10 3 1/s and rdis = 2.4 × 10 8 m/s values obtained from experimental results for HDPE dissolution at the same solvent and temperature. We note that the film thickness re ported here corresponds to the full, initial thickness (in the model, the initial film thickness equals 2L0).

Both  full  decrystallization  time  and  complete  dissolution  time increase with film thickness, but their scaling behaviors differ (Fig. 7). Time for complete dissolution increases linearly with thickness, while time  for  full  decrystallization  shows  a  weaker  dependence  on  film thickness, as it is primarily controlled by solvent disrupting the crys talline order. Dissolution involves the additional, slower step of polymer chain disentanglement and diffusion out of the solvent-swollen polymer matrix, which becomes the dominant rate-limiting step in thicker films.

For thin films (0.03-0.1 mm), short diffusion pathways enable rapid solvent diffusion, leading to swift decrystallization throughout the film (Fig. 8b, and 8d). Consequently, a large fraction of polymer chains is simultaneously disentangled and dissolved, allowing complete dissolu tion within minutes (Fig. 8a). In contrast, for thicker films (0.6-3 mm), significantly  longer  diffusion  paths  create  a  pronounced  solvent  con centration gradient, leading to the observed reduction in the polymer swelling  degree  (Fig.  8c)  and  delayed  decrystallization  of  the  film ' s center.  Thus,  the  dissolution  process  in  thicker  films  proceeds  more gradually,  becoming  sequentially  limited  by  solvent  diffusion  -> decrystallization -> chain disentanglement.

text: The decrystallization rate constant (Kdec) significantly influences the overall dissolution kinetics of semicrystalline HDPE films. Fig. 9 illus trates the impact of Kdec  on the time-dependent behavior of a 0.1 mm thick HDPE film exposed to p -xylene at 104 °C. The 5 × 10 3 to 1 × 10 1 1/s  Kdec  range  was  chosen  based  on  values  obtained  through  model fitting to experimental data (Kdec = 12.8 × 10 3 1/s at 101 °C and 33.5 × 10 3 1/s at 104 °C). This Kdec  range captures decrystallization kinetics both slower and faster relative to the experimentally derived values, enabling the model to explore conditions that are physically plausible and relevant across a broader range of processing scenarios. Addition ally, values outside this range were found to either produce negligible changes in dissolution behavior (due to other rate-limiting steps such as disentanglement, for example, the results for 1 × 10 1 1/s are nearly identical to those at 5 × 10 2 1/s), or to yield physically unrealistic results, even though the model remained numerically stable. Therefore, the  chosen  Kdec  interval  keeps  the  parametric  analysis  reported  here grounded in experimentally-validated behavior, while capturing effec tively the system ' s sensitivity to variations in Kdec.

text: As  Kdec increases,  the  time  required  for  complete  dissolution  de creases due to faster unfolding of crystalline domains, allowing for faster dissolution. However, beyond Kdec = 3 × 10 2 1/s, increasing Kdec  has little additional impact, as the rate of disentanglement (rdis) becomes the controlling factor. In fact, the dissolution of semicrystalline polymers depends  on  both  decrystallization  and  chain  disentanglement;  the slower of the two ultimately governs the overall process. An increase in Kdec  also shortens the induction time (tind) and reduces the degree of swelling (Fig. 9a and 9b), due to faster unfolding of crystalline domains. The plateau in dimensionless thickness at lower Kdec  values (Fig. 9a) indicates a delay in the conversion of crystalline to amorphous domains. During this period, the polymer may become saturated with solvent, limiting  further  solvent  diffusion.  Fig.  9c  shows  that  increasing  Kdec accelerates  the  conversion  of  crystalline  domains  at  any  given  time, consistent with the direct relationship described in Eq. 3. In Fig. 9d, solvent diffusion toward the center of the slab ( ξ 1 = 0) decreases with increasing Kdec up to approximately 2 × 10 2 1/s. Beyond this point, the polymer  dissolves  more  rapidly,  so  the  time  corresponding  to  20% progress toward full dissolution occurs earlier in the process, resulting in a higher solvent volume fraction in the polymer at that stage.

text: The disentanglement rate (rdis) directly affects polymer dissolution kinetics by controlling the availability of disentangled polymer chains to diffuse into the solvent. The selected range for rdis, 1 × 10 10 m/s to 5 × 10 8 m/s,  was  informed  by  values  derived  through  model  fitting  to experimental data (rdis = 2.2 × 10 8 m/s at 101 °C and 2.4 × 10 8 m/s at 104 °C). These fitted values fall near the upper end of the rdis range, but rdis values  were  also  considered  to  capture  conditions  where  chain disentanglement becomes the primary limiting factor. rdis values above 5 × 10 8 m/s were found to have minimal influence on dissolution ki netics  due  to  the  increasing  dominance  of  decrystallization  as  ratecontrolling  mechanism.  The  1 × 10 10 m/s  -  5 × 10 8 m/s  range therefore enables the model to capture both kinetically restricted and transport-limited regimes, while remaining consistent with experimen tally observed behavior. Fig. 10 illustrates the effect of the rdis  on the dissolution process of a 0.1 mm thick HDPE film in p -xylene at 104 °C. Increasing rdis reduces the time required for full dissolution and results in more dissolved polymer at any given time. This is because a higher rdis value leads to more disentangled polymer chains available to diffuse into the solvent. text: HDPE  is  used  in  diverse  products  and  accounted  for  12%  (~51 million tons) of global plastic production in 2023. Less than 10% of HDPE waste is recycled in the United States, and over 80% is landfilled, underscoring  the  need  for  expanded  recycling  options.  Pyrolysis  can handle  HDPE  waste  that  cannot  be  mechanically  recycled,  however, pyrolysis is associated with high energy demands and CO2  emissions, and concerns about circularity, as pyrolysis products typically become fuel and not polymers. Dissolution/precipitation is capable of producing high-quality  recovered  HDPE,  as  it  involves  physical  processes  that retain polymer chains intact. Dissolution/precipitation recycling main tains the embodied energy of HDPE, hence it is energy efficient, and can recover HDPE from mixtures, blends or multilayer films, purified from additives or fillers. Polymer dissolution is key to dissolution/precipita tion  recycling.  Notably,  despite  HDPE  being  a  commodity  polymer produced in high volumes for decades, there is no published information on HDPE dissolution kinetics and the underlying mechanisms.

text: To address this knowledge gap, we pursued an integrated experi mental and modeling approach to investigate the dissolution of semi crystalline polyethylene. The crystallinity of undissolved polymer was tracked via in situ FT-IR spectroscopy over the time course of dissolu tion, while the mass of dissolved/undissolved polymer was quantified gravimetrically. The swelling and dissolution of a semi-infinite semi crystalline  slab  were  captured  using  a  phenomenological  model  that incorporated  solvent  diffusion  into  the  polymer,  decrystallization  ki netics,  polymer  chain  disentanglement,  and  the  diffusion  of  polymer chains  into  the  solvent.  The  fitted  parameters,  decrystallization  rate constant (Kdec), which characterizes the conversion of crystalline do mains into amorphous ones, and disentanglement rate (rdis), which re flects  the  rate  at  which  amorphous  chains  disengage  and  become available to diffuse into the solvent, quantify the kinetics of these key steps in the dissolution process. The model fits well experimental results for  HDPE  dissolution  in  xylene,  confirming  that  the  incorporated mechanisms  capture  the  key  physical  processes.  Consequently,  the model can reliably provide information, e.g., compositions, that is not obtained experimentally, and predict system behavior under conditions beyond those tested experimentally.

text:
Film thickness strongly influences dissolution kinetics. Total disso lution time increases nearly linearly with thickness, while full decrys tallization  time  increases  more  gradually.  Thin  HDPE  films  dissolve within minutes due to short diffusion paths that enable rapid solvent diffusion,  decrystallization,  and  chain  disentanglement.  In  contrast, thick films develop steep solvent gradients, swell less, and experience delayed decrystallization at the center. In thin films, higher temperature accelerates  disentanglement  and  reduces  swelling,  whereas  in  thick films, the same temperature rise increases the solvent volume fraction within the film and promotes swelling.

The initial degree of crystallinity affects primarily the early stages of HDPE dissolution. Higher crystallinity reduces swelling modestly and sustains crystalline domains longer, delaying decrystallization. Howev er, under the experimental conditions studied, the influence of the initial degree of crystallinity on total dissolution time is minimal. Sensitivity analysis reveals that the impact of initial crystallinity becomes more pronounced  when  Kdec  is  lower,  underscoring  the  coupled  roles  of crystallinity and temperature-dependent kinetics in governing dissolution.

text: This is the first integrated experimental + modeling framework link ing real-time measurements of HDPE crystallinity and mass loss with a comprehensive  model  of  semicrystalline  polymer  dissolution.  The framework  advances  fundamental  understanding  of  semicrystalline polymers dissolution and provides a predictive tool for tailoring polymer dissolution under diverse conditions, with applications in recycling and other  processes  where  controlling  polymer  dissolution  kinetics  is critical.  The  dissolution  model  developed  here  for  semicrystalline polyethylene can be extended to study other polymers, whether semi crystalline or amorphous, of various shapes, as well as multilayer films composed  of  different  polymers,  under  diverse  solvents  and  experi mental conditions [69]. The insights gained from this project can help optimize the recycling process by identifying ideal conditions, such as temperature,  solvent  type,  and  time,  thereby  reducing  energy  con sumption and improving overall efficiency. Beyond dissolution-precipitation recycling, the model and mechanistic insights developed in this work may also inform related fields such as drug de livery and biomedical applications -for example, by enabling prediction of  polymer  matrix  dissolution  and  controlled  release  profiles -and polymer  processing,  through  the  informed  selection  of  solvents  and conditions.

1. Introduction

The demand for unwanted plastic toy disposal has increased in recent years, as many households find themselves stuck with collections of toys that their children have outgrown. Unfortunately, plastic toys typically are not accepted by municipal recycling programs. As a result, many toy manufacturers and retailers have instituted take-back programs. How ever,  the  collection  of  post-consumer  toys  results  in  plastic  mixture waste, which becomes a problem for disposal of plastics. Therefore, it is crucial to develop a reliable recycling process for plastic separation and material  recovery.  The  study  on  material  recycling  of  ABS  from  toy waste  can  be  potentially  extended  to  post-consumer  and/or  postindustrial  ABS  waste  from  consumer  goods,  automotive,  electronics and appliances.

text: Toy waste is an issue for municipal plastic recycling programs. In particular, toy waste typically is composed of different plastics and some metals. Separation of different parts of toy waste is necessary before recycling. In this study, a dissolution-precipitation process coupled with density separation was developed to extract acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) from toy waste using safer solvents and antisolvents. The polymer solubility of ABS was measured using Hansen solubility parameters, which were then used to down-select proper safer solvents and antisolvents. The acetone-water with a volumetric ratio of 3:1 was determined to be the most effective safer solvents and antisolvents for extracting 81 wt.% of ABS at room temperature. The recovered ABS has comparable mechanical behavior to the feedstock material with a similar glass transition temperature and molecular weight distribution. Compared to producing virgin ABS material, the dissolution-precipitation process reduces embodied energy by 58%.
