text: Solvent extraction is proven to be an efficient way for recovering and purifying  plastics  (Anderson  et  al.,  2022;  Chen  et  al.,  2019;  Layman et  al.,  2017).  The  general  principle  of  solvent  extraction  is  selective dissolution, referring to the dissolution of a target polymer or all other polymers except a target one (Chen et al., 2019; Layman et al., 2017). Solvents have been used to dissolve and reclaim polymer structures back from rigid plastics, packaging materials (Achilias et al., 2009), electronic waste  (Anderson  et  al.,  2022;  Weeden  et  al.,  2015),  and  recently multilayered films (Cervantes-Reyes et al., 2015; Mumladze et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2020). Hazardous solvents such as toluene (for recovering polyolefins) and dichloromethane (DCM, for reclaiming polycarbonate (PC) and polystyrene (PS)-based plastics) were mostly used to recover plastics in literature (Chandrasekaran et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019; Weeden et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2017). For example, a room-temperature sequential extraction process using a solvent blend of DCM/acetone for computer housing waste containing several types of plastics has been developed (Weeden et al., 2015). A high yield ( > 95%) of PC was recovered with high purity. A significant decrease in cost and energy  requirements  were  also  reported  for  recovering  PC  using DCM/acetone.  Similarly,  N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone/methanol  has  been used  as  the  solvent/antisolvent  to  recover  PC  from  a  mixture  of PC/polyamide, the compositions of cellphone plastics (Chandrasekaran et al., 2018). In this study, the reused solvent obtained from the second run (with 79% purity) can still recover 90% of PC, suggesting promising potential to reuse solvents by simple distillation. However, the volatile organic  compounds  of  these  solvents  accumulated  in  working  areas could be hazardous to human health with long term exposure. There fore, safer solvents with less toxicity or the use of proper personal pro tective equipment are recommended.

text: It is often found that it would not be economically feasible to use solvents to recycle horribly mixed plastics (Anderson et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2019). However, guided by selective dissolution, single plastic extraction can be further modified into a sequential extraction process for multiple polymers by multi-dissolution steps. Basically, the polymer mixture extraction is achieved by the solubility difference in selected solvents assisted with sequential separation techniques such as centri fugation and filtration. For example, a dissolution-precipitation process was developed to recover and separate nearly 100% of polyethylene (PE), ethylene vinyl alcohol, and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) in multilayer  films  using  toluene  and  dimethyl  sulfoxide  sequentially. Likewise, mixed solvent extraction was developed to recover PC, PS, ABS, and styrene acrylonitrile (SAN) in electronic waste (Zhao et al., 2017). The extraction performed at room temperature yielded accept able recovery rates of PC, PS, ABS and SAN in 64%, 86%, 127% and 143%, respectively. Notably, solvents resided in ABS and SAN not only led to an over-estimated polymer recovery yield, but also contaminated recovered polymers and initiated polymer degradation in some cases.

text: Additionally,  emerging  solvent  systems  like  switchable  hydrophi licity  solvents  have  been  recently  used  to  recover  polymer  films (Mumladze  et  al.,  2018).  Despite  the  high  polymer  recovery  yield ( > 90%) and easiness to be recovered, switchable hydrophilicity solvents are  expensive  to  manufacture  (Jessop  et  al.,  2011).  Some  of  the switchable hydrophilicity solvents also have health and safety concerns (Vanderveen  et  al.,  2014).  On  the  other  hand,  supercritical  fluid extraction has also been explored in plastics separation and decontam ination.  A  near-critical  solubilization  using  n-pentane  and  n-heptane was developed to selectively dissolve polypropylene (PP) from PP/PS blends (Martini et al., 2006). Supercritical extraction using carbon di oxide (CO2) at 300 bar and 80 ⁰ C was conducted to extract hydrocarbon oils and lubricants in oil-adhesive high-density polyethylene containers (Alassali et al., 2020). Some efforts have also been made by industries to develop supercritical fluid extraction process. For instance, Purecycle has recently adopted supercritical propane and butane to purify and reclaim  post-consumer  and  post-industrial  PP  (Layman  et  al.,  2017). However, few studies have focused on using safer solvents to recover real-world waste, which is a knowledge gap in realizing the full potential of dissolution-precipitation technologies.

text:
This  study  aims  to  develop  a  dissolution-precipitation  process  to recover ABS from the post-consumer plastic toys using safer solvents at ambient conditions. Acetone and water, selected as a solvent-antisolvent system, were determined in accordance with the solubility, safety con cerns and cost. The solvent to antisolvent ratio was further optimized in the gram scale dissolution-precipitation test. To understand the effect of the recycling process on the chemical and mechanical properties of the recycled ABS, thermal transition behavior, molecular weight distribu tions, chemical compositions, and tensile properties of the precipitated ABS were compared to the feedstock material. Finally, energy analysis was carried out with the optimized dissolution-precipitation process to evaluate their energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions and how they compared to virgin ABS polymer and mechanical recycling.

2.1. Materials

The toy blasters were commercially available and donated by a local industrial  partner  (Hasbro  Inc.,  Pawtucket,  RI).  A  toy  contains  ABS (84.5%), polyoxymethylene (POM, 8.0%), thermoplastic rubber (2.6%), PP (0.9%), polyethylene foam (1.0%) and metals (2.9%), provided by the manufacturer.

2.1. Materials

The toy blasters were commercially available and donated by a local industrial  partner  (Hasbro  Inc.,  Pawtucket,  RI).  A  toy  contains  ABS (84.5%), polyoxymethylene (POM, 8.0%), thermoplastic rubber (2.6%), PP (0.9%), polyethylene foam (1.0%) and metals (2.9%), provided by the manufacturer.

2.2. Density separation of plastic mixture

text:
The toys were manually disassembled first, and all the metal parts were removed. After disassembling, the ABS parts were manually sorted out from the toy waste. As ABS accounts for the most materials of the toy blaster, ABS was the focus of this study. The disassembled ABS plastics were ground into particles with a dimension of 1 -3 mm using a grinder (TF  68,  Cincinnati  Milacron,  Batavia,  OH).  Based  on  the  component information provided by the manufacturer, the main impurity present in ABS, which may affect the following solvent dissolution-precipitation process, is POM. Hence, a laboratory float/sink-based density separa tion was conducted on the ABS parts before dissolution-precipitation. The density of ABS used in the products is 1.04 g/cm 3 (confirmed by the manufacturer) and the typical density of POM is about 1.40 g/cm 3 (according to the literature) (Gent et al., 2009). Thus, a salt solution with a density of 1.2 g/cm 3 ( i.e., 26 wt.% sodium chloride in deionized water) was used to separate ABS from POM. The ground ABS/POM mixture was fed into the solution and stirred with a glass rod for 2 min. The floated particles (expected to be ABS), which accounted for 96 ± 2% ( n = 3), were collected and dried at room temperature over night before solvent dissolution.

text: The key to achieving an efficient solvent extraction of target polymer is  the  selection  of  solvent  system.  In  this  study,  an  efficient  solvent screening tool, Hansen Solubility Parameters (HSP), was used. In prin ciple, HSP defined the solubility into three parameters: dipole-dipole interactions  ( δ D),  polar  forces  ( δ P)  and  hydrogen  bonding  force  ( δ H) (Abbott et al., 2015). The solvents are considered to have absolute HSPs estimated based on enthalpies of vaporization (Walker et al., 2020). The application  of  HSP  on  a  polymer  is  to  construct  a  sphere  in  the three-dimensional Hansen space. The center point of the sphere repre sents the solubility parameters of the polymer while the radius defines the solubility range. Theoretically, good solvents that likely dissolve the polymer fall  within  the  sphere  whereas  solvents  that  would  perform poorly and thus should be avoided are excluded from the sphere (Díaz de los Ríos and Hernández Ramos, 2020; Weeden et al., 2015).

text:
The solubility parameters are affected largely by material grades, measurement  methods  and  dissolution  status  decided  by  the  re searchers. Thus, a dissolution test was performed to characterize the HSP values of ABS using 30 solvents, following a protocol modified from our previous studies (Anderson et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2021). First, about 0.5 g of particles were immersed in 10 ml of solvents for 2 h without agitation at ambient temperature. The test solvents were classified as good (which led to a complete dissolution) or bad solvents (which end up having incomplete dissolution), determined by the dissolution status of ABS after 2 h. Subsequently, the assessment of solvents was used to establish the best-fit polymer sphere using multi-response optimization algorithms (Lu et al., 2021). Solvent candidates can thus be selected based on the distance to the sphere center. Further solvent optimization included safety concerns, cost and actual polymer dissolution efficiency. Once the solvent was decided, the selection of antisolvents was deter mined by the miscibility of solvents and antisolvents, safety concerns and cost of antisolvents (Walker et al., 2020).

text:
To  evaluate  the  property  of  the  recovered  ABS  polymer,  several physicochemical characterizations were performed for the ABS products reclaimed by the dissolution-precipitation process and compared to the original  ABS  in  the  toy  blaster.  The  glass  transition  temperatures  of precipitated ABS and feedstock ABS were analyzed using a differential scanning calorimeter (RES-02 -002-B, TA Instruments, New Castle, DE). A heat-cool-heat cycle was applied using the following protocol: about 5 mg of ABS was heated from 50 °C to 200 °C at 20 ⁰ C/min and cooled down to 50 °C at 20 ⁰ C/min, followed by a second heating to 200 °C at 20 °C/min.  The  first heating is to erase thermal  history during manufacturing, so the glass transition temperatures were determined from the second heating cycle.

The thermal degradation behavior of ABS was characterized by a thermogravimetric analyzer (Discovery RES-02 -001-A, TA Instruments, New Castle, DE) from 50 to 550 °C at 20 °C/min with 25 ml/min N2. Duplicate analyses were performed using an elemental analyzer (Exeter Analytical,  Inc.,  North  Chelmsford,  MA)  to  measure  the  carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen content of ABS.

Gel permeation chromatography (GPC) was used to determine the molecular weight of the precipitated and feedstock ABS with a Waters Alliance 2695 HPLC system equipped with PDA detector and refractive index detector. Waters Styragel HR columns were used for molecular weight determination of up to 600 kDa. The system used 100% tetra hydrofuran (THF) as the mobile phase at a flow rate of 0.9 mL/min. Each sample  was  dissolved  in  100%  THF  over  night  before  being  filtered through a 0.45-micron nylon or PTFE filter and analyzed at an injection rate of 10 -20 mg/mL. Polystyrene standards from molecular weight of 500 Da -400 kDa were used to create the calibration curve.

The additives and other volatile compounds in ABS were character ized using pyrolysis-gas chromatography mass spectrometry (Py-GCMS) by the mean of thermal desorption analysis (K ¨ appler et al., 2018). A furnace type pyrolyzer (AS-1020E, Frontier, Tokyo, Japan) was heated from 40 °C to 300 °C at 20 °C/min for 0.7 mg sample. The collected gas was carried by helium into Agilent 7890B gas chromatography (Agilent, Santa Clara, CA) with a UA-5 column (Frontier, Tokyo, Japan) linked to the mass spectrometer in m/z 30 -800 scan range. The gas chromatog raphy was set at 40 °C for 1 min and then ramped at 20 °C/min to 320 °C with another 5 min hold time (K ¨ appler et al., 2018). The target com pounds were identified based on the similarity of the mass spectrum of library results and targets using NIST 17 library. Only the match with the highest quality ( > 90%) would be assigned to the identified compound.

The precipitated ABS was ground again into smaller particles before micro-injection molding. Micro-injection molding was carried out in an injection molder (IM12, Xplore, Netherlands) to make tensile bars. The injection unit was pre-heated to 200 °C and then filled with 9 g of ABS particles. The mold temperature was set at 40 °C. After a 10 min preheating period, the materials were injected into the mold by 15-bar in jection pressure followed by 12-bar pack pressure for 15 s.

text:
The HSPs of ABS were determined according to the dissolution test results  using  a  two-hour  dwell  time,  following  literature  measuring solubility parameters for polymeric coatings (Lu et al., 2021). In total, 31 solvents were tested ( Table S1 ). According to the dissolution results presented in Table S1 ,  a  3D  Hansen solubility sphere of ABS can be constructed. The 3D sphere plot was then converted into a 2D ternary diagram for better visualization (Fig. 2 a ). Based on the relative distance to the sphere center, cyclohexanone and acetone were selected as po tential solvents with the considerations of toxicity and cost as mentioned above.  In  the  later  dissolution  efficiency  test,  acetone  was  able  to dissolve 0.5 g ABS within 30 min while the dissolution time for cyclo hexanone was 2 h. As a result, acetone was selected for dissolution-precipitation process and for screening antisolvent in this study.

text: It was found that water was the most distant solvent from the center of  ABS  and  thus  was  selected  as  an  antisolvent.  Moreover,  water  is miscible with acetone, inexpensive, widely available and safe. HSP also can be used as a guide to optimize the solvent to antisolvent ratio. In principle, the higher amount of antisolvent added to the solution, the more efficient the precipitation would be. This is because that the HSPs of the solvent blend ( i.e., the mixture of solvent and antisolvent) are moving further from the center of ABS (Fig. 2 b ) (Abbott et al., 2015). By adjusting  the  ratio  between  solvent  and  antisolvent,  the  amount  of antisolvent can be minimized while effectively precipitating ABS in this study. For example, as shown in Fig. 2 b , using the solvent blend with a 7:1 or 3:1 acetone to water volumetric ratio can precipitate 81 wt.% of ABS in 0.5 g ABS precipitation test. However, the solvent blend with a 7:1 ratio only worked well for a small scale of dissolution-precipitation test ( i.e., 0.5 g ABS), and took longer to precipitate ABS than a 3:1 ratio (note: the precipitation yield obtained with a 7:1 ratio was low within 10 min; typically, an effective precipitation should take place momen tarily).  In  fact,  the  solvent  blend  with  a  3:1  acetone  to  water  ratio precipitated 15 g ABS effectively within 5 min, and thus was used to scale up the dissolution-precipitation processes in the following sections.

3.2. Comparison of characteristics between feedstock and precipitated ABS

Several physicochemical characterizations were conducted to assess the  properties  of  the  reclaimed  ABS  polymer  obtained  through  the dissolution-precipitation  process.  A  comparative  analysis  was  carried out between the ABS products recovered and the original ABS in the toy blaster.  First,  the  possible  chemical  structure  change  affected  by  the dissolution-precipitation  process  was  analyzed  by  FT-IR.  As  Fig.  3

% Transmittance

Fig. 3. FT-IR spectra of precipitated ABS and feedstock ABS.

shows, similar spectra were obtained for precipitated and feedstock ABS, indicating no significant contamination happened during the dissolution-precipitation  process.  However,  the  carbonyl  groups  at 1720 cm 1 and C -O stretching at 1248 cm 1 are clearly seen in the precipitated ABS. The appearance of the two oxygenated groups is likely due  to  oxidative  degradations  in  ABS  after  precipitation,  probably during the extensive drying process. As reported in literature, oxidation of ABS took place easily in the butadiene phase, especially in the carbon double bonds, resulting in the production of carbonyl groups (Arostegui et  al.,  2006).  Accordingly,  the  obtained  FTIR  spectra  (Fig.  3)  also implied the loss of antioxidants in the precipitated ABS.

text: To further understand the changes in the additives and other low molecular  portions,  thermal  desorption  analysis  was  used  to  charac terize the compounds released below 300 °C ( Figure S1 and Table S3-S4 in Supplementary Data ). Interestingly, fluorine-containing chemicals were detected in the feedstock ABS, apart from alkene hydrocarbons as an  ABS  derivative  from  polybutadiene.  The  fluoro  chemicals  were speculated as additives in coating materials or within ABS. On the other hand, various oxygenated compounds originated from chain hydrocar bons were observed in precipitated ABS, indicating that oxygen prob ably accounted for the majority of the impurity present in precipitated ABS  ( Table  S4 ),  The  presence  of  these  oxygenated  compounds  also suggests oxidation of ABS. This is in agreement with the FT-IR results and the finding in the previous study, which reported that butadiene was more susceptible to oxygen after precipitation (Arostegui et al., 2006). Somewhat  differently,  oxidation  could  also  happen  in  styrene  and acrylonitrile to form phenolic compounds and oxazole. The absence of fluorine-containing chemicals in the precipitated ABS could be contributed by the dissolution of fluorine-containing compounds in the solvent-antisolvent solution. As reported in the literature, dissolution-precipitation process could also be used to remove additives from a polymer based on their solubility differences  (Ügdüler et  al., 2020). The additives typically are more readily dissolved in solvents and would remain in the solution while polymers would be precipitated and recovered  as  solids.  In  addition,  aromatic  compounds  derived  from polystyrene were largely found, and more compounds were detected in a short  retention  time  (with  a  correspondingly  lower  temperature), probably due to an inferior thermal stability of the precipitated ABS to the feedstock ABS ( Figure S1 and Table S4 ).

To further understand the changes in the additives and other low molecular  portions,  thermal  desorption  analysis  was  used  to  charac terize the compounds released below 300 °C ( Figure S1 and Table S3-S4 in Supplementary Data ). Interestingly, fluorine-containing chemicals were detected in the feedstock ABS, apart from alkene hydrocarbons as an  ABS  derivative  from  polybutadiene.  The  fluoro  chemicals  were speculated as additives in coating materials or within ABS. On the other hand, various oxygenated compounds originated from chain hydrocar bons were observed in precipitated ABS, indicating that oxygen prob ably accounted for the majority of the impurity present in precipitated ABS  ( Table  S4 ),  The  presence  of  these  oxygenated  compounds  also suggests oxidation of ABS. This is in agreement with the FT-IR results and the finding in the previous study, which reported that butadiene was more susceptible to oxygen after precipitation (Arostegui et al., 2006). Somewhat  differently,  oxidation  could  also  happen  in  styrene  and acrylonitrile to form phenolic compounds and oxazole. The absence of fluorine-containing chemicals in the precipitated ABS could be contributed by the dissolution of fluorine-containing compounds in the solvent-antisolvent solution. As reported in the literature, dissolution-precipitation process could also be used to remove additives from a polymer based on their solubility differences  (Ügdüler et  al., 2020). The additives typically are more readily dissolved in solvents and would remain in the solution while polymers would be precipitated and recovered  as  solids.  In  addition,  aromatic  compounds  derived  from polystyrene were largely found, and more compounds were detected in a short  retention  time  (with  a  correspondingly  lower  temperature), probably due to an inferior thermal stability of the precipitated ABS to the feedstock ABS ( Figure S1 and Table S4 ).

text: Having demonstrated the unchanged polymer structure and similar thermal degradation behavior,  the  precipitated  ABS  was  expected  to retain  most  properties  and  be  ready  for  remanufacturing.  The  glass transition temperature (Tg) and the molecular weight distributions were measured using DSC and GPC respectively to assess the any signs of degradation during the dissolution-precipitation process (note: the raw date  obtained  from  DSC  and  GPC  are  available  as Figure  S3 and Figure S4 in the Supplementary Data). As displayed in Table 1, there is no significant difference in the molecular weights and polydispersity. The Tg  of precipitated ABS is slightly higher than that of the feedstock ABS. The higher Tg of the precipitated ABS is possibly due to the loss of the plasticizers. As widely reported with various polymers in literature, plasticizers are typically added to plastic toys during polymer processing to enable plasticization, increasing the flexibility, toughness and pro cessability of plastics (Babich et al., 2020; Immergut and Mark, 1965). The addition of plasticizers increases chain flexibility by lowering Tg, allowing  the  movement  of  chains  at  lower  temperatures  (Yoo  et  al., 2018). On the contrary, a rigid polymer can have higher Tg  without plasticization.

text: Tensile stress-strain curves of feedstock ABS and precipitated ABS were available in the Supplementary Data ( Figure S5 ). Both modulus and yield stress of precipitated ABS (Fig. 5) decreased slightly, while the yield  strain  increased.  The  precipitated  ABS  after  injection  molding seems to have better flexibility with sacrificing rigidity. Similar trends were also reported by Arostegui et al., while the decrease in yield stress was speculated to result from the molecular weight reduction and the entanglement density reduction (Arostegui et al., 2006). However, in this  study,  the  molecular  weight  of  the  precipitated  ABS  was  nearly unchanged (confirmed by GPC). It is probably because the absence of additives in ABS could further promote degradation when the precipi tated ABS was subjected to high temperature and shear stress in the microinjection  molding  process,  resulting  in  a  decreased  material strength.

In summary, based on the comparison of chemical structures, ther mal transition behavior, and elemental compositions of the recovered ABS, it is generally believed that no notable impurity was present in the recovered ABS. In other words, the analyses performed suggest that the recovered ABS is expected to be near 100% and did not contain any other polymers such as POM or PP, which has different polymer solu bility, chemical structures, thermal transition behavior, and elemental compositions from ABS. Similar findings were also reported in literature (Chandrasekaran  et  al.,  2018;  Weeden  et  al.,  2015).  For  instance, Weeden et al. used solvent-based recycling to reclaim polycarbonate (PC) from e-waste and reported a purity of 95% or higher (Weeden et al., 2015). From the present study, it is also learned that low molecular additives  could  be  removed  during  dissolution-precipitation  process without causing serious degradation in polymer chains. New additives such as antioxidants or stabilizers should be added in the compounding process to improve the mechanical properties of ABS recovered from the dissolution-precipitation process, as the absence of additives decreased the  stability  of  the  polymer  and  induces  oxidation,  thus  decreasing material properties of the precipitated ABS.

3.3. Environmental implications

The energy required to recover ABS from toy waste was estimated on the basis of 1 kg ultimate recovered product using the REMADE calcu lator,  which  is  publicly  available  (https://remadeinstitute.org/projec t-impact-calculator).  The  embodied  energy  and  the  equivalent  CO2 (CO2e) emission of recycled ABS were estimated following the stepwise calculations through all procedures within the solvent recycling process (note: detailed calculations were available in the Online Supplementary File).  The  procedures considered include collection, sorting, prepara tion, solvent-based recycling and extrusion. As a result, the total process energy to produce pellets from current waste stream is 39.3 MJ/kg and the estimated CO2e emission is 2.0 kg per kg of recovered ABS (Fig. 6).

text: As mentioned above, dissolution-precipitation did not cause signifi cant degradation in polymers but only removed additives, which purifies waste plastics. On this account, an appropriate compounding process with  required  additives  following  solvent  recovery  is  suggested  to improve material properties of the solvent-recycled polymer. In short, the presented solvent-based recycling process demonstrates great po tential to enable the use of recycled polymer as original products, which provides another application other than downcycling and blending with virgin polymer. Notably, even for virgin polymer, additives are required and incorporated by extrusion during manufacturing. Considering the 58%  energy  reduction  by  dissolution-precipitation  in  comparison  to producing  virgin  ABS,  there  would  be  sufficient  margins  in  energy consumption to include additional compounding processes for incor porating  additives.  As  a  result,  solvent-based  recycling  would  be  an important recycling method in parallel to the mechanical recycling as it has advantages in polymer separation, purification ( e.g., removing un wanted additives like flame retardants, inks, or colorants), and energy savings  (Anderson  et  al.,  2022;  Ferreira  et  al.,  2022;  Ügdüler  et  al., 2023). Overall, the solvent-based dissolution-precipitation methodology established in this study can recover targeted material ( i.e., ABS) from a plastic mixture ( i.e., toy waste). Similar processes can be applied to other types of toy waste.

3.4. Technoeconomic feasibility discussion

Despite that solvent-based recycling shows competitiveness in en ergy use and greenhouse gas emissions compared to virgin material in this study and other similar studies, dissolution may not always have better economic performances than mechanical recycling (Uekert et al., 2023). From an economic standpoint, considering market dynamics in the  recycling  of  PE,  PP,  and  PET,  mechanical  recycling  consistently outperformed  solvent-based  recycling  with  minimum  selling  prices being 38 -49% lower (Uekert et al., 2023). This can be attributed pri marily to the lower operational and capital costs associated with me chanical  recycling,  along  with  its  well-established  maturity  in  the industry. As dissolution is advantageous in separation and purification, the  large  capacity  unit  operations  ( e.g.,  fi ltration)  required  in  the refinement stage account for the most to the overall process cost (Lehr et al., 2022). On the other hand, mechanical recycling typically led to downcycling,  while  dissolution  is  appreciated  for  its  high  material retention and quality.

text:
In contrast to commodity plastics recycling mentioned above that typically  needs  higher  dissolution  temperatures  ( e.g., boiling  toluene used in dissolving PE), solvent-based recycling of ABS requires lower dissolution temperature and energy consumption in recovering solvents because of lower boiling points of the solvents used ( e.g., acetone used in this study). This feature could reduce the cost of solvent-based recycling. However, more studies are needed to evaluate the feasibility of 1) using safer solvents to recover ABS with higher contamination levels and 2) achieving higher solvent recovery rate. In particular, solvent recovery efficiency plays a key role in operational profits. For example, it was found that the solvent recovery rate must be over 90% to make profits in using DCM and methanol to dissolve and precipitate plastics present in e-waste (Anderson et al., 2022). Similar perspectives regarding the ne cessities to minimize the consumption of solvents and energy were also discussed in literature (Uekert et al., 2023).

In contrast to commodity plastics recycling mentioned above that typically  needs  higher  dissolution  temperatures  ( e.g., boiling  toluene used in dissolving PE), solvent-based recycling of ABS requires lower dissolution temperature and energy consumption in recovering solvents because of lower boiling points of the solvents used ( e.g., acetone used in this study). This feature could reduce the cost of solvent-based recycling. However, more studies are needed to evaluate the feasibility of 1) using safer solvents to recover ABS with higher contamination levels and 2) achieving higher solvent recovery rate. In particular, solvent recovery efficiency plays a key role in operational profits. For example, it was found that the solvent recovery rate must be over 90% to make profits in using DCM and methanol to dissolve and precipitate plastics present in e-waste (Anderson et al., 2022). Similar perspectives regarding the ne cessities to minimize the consumption of solvents and energy were also discussed in literature (Uekert et al., 2023).

4. Conclusion

text:
This study developed a recycling process including density separa tion and dissolution-precipitation to recover ABS from toy waste. The solvent-antisolvent  system  of  acetone-water  with  a  ratio  of  3:1  was selected  and  determined  using  Hansen  solubility  parameters  and  the solubility test. This study shows that the solvent-based dissolution-pre cipitation is capable for recovering ABS with comparable mechanical behavior  to  feedstock  ABS  without  changing  its  molecular  weight significantly. Meanwhile, the additives were found to be removed dur ing  the  dissolution-precipitation  process.  A  higher  weight  loss  of  the precipitated ABS below 300 °C was found, suggesting a reduced thermal stability of ABS. Chemical characterizations revealed that oxidation took place in the solvent-recycled ABS, probably due to the absence of ad ditives. The recovered ABS can be readily used for plastic reprocessing, while proper additives are suggested to improve the thermal stability and mechanical performance. Compared to producing virgin ABS, the dissolution-precipitation process was estimated to save 58% energy and 48% CO2  emission, suggesting solvent-based recycling as a promising method for recycling post-consumer ABS.

The global production of plastics has increased tremendously in the last decades  resulting  in a  concurrent  increase  in  plastic  waste (European  Parliament,  2021;  PlasticsEurope,  2024).  From  the  413.8 million  tons  (Mt)  produced  in  2023,  only  8.9  %  and  0.5  %  can  be attributed  to  post-consumer  recycled  and  bio-based  plastics,  respec tively (PlasticsEurope, 2024). Hence, more than 90 % of the produced plastics are still made from virgin and fossil-based polymers, stressing the need of a proper end-of-life waste management. In Europe, only 32 % of plastic waste is recycled, whereby the remaining is either incin erated (43 %) or landfilled (25 %), causing harm to the environment (European Parliament, 2021). Consequently, there is increasing regu latory pressure on recycling targets and recyclability. Several initiatives have been launched to tackle plastic pollution and accelerate the tran sition to a circular and resource-efficient plastics economy. The Euro pean Plastics Strategy, part of the EU ' s Circular Economy Action plan, seeks to revolutionize the way plastic products are designed, produced, used and recycled within the EU (European Commission, 2018). Available online 19 April 2025

A B S T R A C T

For  the  first  time,  rigid  polyvinyl  chloride  (PVC)  waste  has  been  successfully  recycled  using  a  dissolutionprecipitation  approach  with  biobased  solvents.  Hansen  Solubility  Parameter,  HSP,  predictions  guided  the  sys tematic selection of solvents, while a modified HSP approach was developed to estimate the required non-solvent amounts for efficient polymer precipitation. Among the tested biobased solvents cyrene, γ -valerolactone (GVL) and 2-methyltetrahydrofuran demonstrated excellent dissolution performance, with water, methanol or isopropanol serving as effective non-solvents. The GVL-water system was the most efficient, requiring less than 10% non-solvent to achieve nearly complete separation and recovery of both the polymer and inorganic fraction without inducing polymer degradation. This optimized system was applied to a commercial PVC formulation for window frames, an end-of-life  PVC  window frame and a rigid PVC tube, achieving over 95% polymer recovery. Additionally, the process  successfully  removed  more  than  99%  of  inorganic  fillers,  enabling  the  selective  purification  and  covalorization of CaCO3  or the valuable TiO2.

instance, Vinylplus has set a goal to incorporate 1 Mt of recycled PVC waste  in  new  products  by  2030  (Vinylplus,  2020).  To  achieve  these recyclability commitments, new efficient plastic recycling methods and measures to stimulate the market for recycled plastic are key.

With a consumption volume of more than 50 Mt worldwide, PVC is one  of  the  most  extensively  utilized  plastics  in  the  world  (Statista, 2023a). Its widespread application in e.g. construction, electronic and healthcare applications, can be attributed to its good physical, chemical and weathering properties  combined with low cost  and various  pro cessing possibilities (Titow, 1990). Even if the mechanical recycling of PVC is well established (Plinke, 2000; Schyns and Shaver, 2021), only 24.3  %  of  all  PVC  waste  generated  in  2023  in  Europe  was  recycled (VinylPlus, 2024). PVC recycling remains highly challenging due to the versatility of the waste streams and the presence of multiple and varying amounts of additives (e.g. plasticizers, heat stabilizers, pigments) (AitTouchente  et  al.,  2024;  Ragaert  et  al.,  2017;  Ügduler  et  al.,  2020). Moreover, partial degradation of the PVC during reprocessing can in fluence the applicability and economic value of the recyclate (Hoff and Jacobsson, 1981; Lase et al., 2022).

text: To address these limitations, chemical recycling has gained signifi cant popularity in recent years (Klotz et al., 2024). In this process the polymer  is  converted  at  higher  temperatures  into  lower  molecular weight substances that can be reused as building blocks for the pro duction of chemicals, polymers or fuels (Parida et al., 2024). Various chemical recycling technologies for PVC and its derivatives have been extensively reviewed by Lu et al. (Lu et al., 2023). However, the high chlorine content of PVC, which constitutes at least 57 wt% of its mass, presents significant challenges, as it can lead to the formation of highly corrosive hydrogen  chloride  and  chlorinated  organic  compounds (Rahimi and García, 2017). In this sense, the dissolution-precipitation process, or physical recycling, is a promising alternative in which plas tic waste is dissolved in a selective solvent and subsequently precipitated using a low-solvating non-solvent (Li et al., 2022; Ügduler et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2018a). This methodology is an interesting intermediate solution for PVC as it operates at mild conditions, limiting dechlorina tion and allowing to recover intact polymer (Sherwood, 2020; Ügduler et al., 2020). It has also successfully been applied in the past to recycle soft  PVC  at  pilot  scale,  i.e.,  in  the  VinyLoop ® plant  in  Ferrara-Italy (Vandenhende,  2001;  VinylPlus,  2017).  Nevertheless,  this  plant  was closed due to changing sustainability regulations that hampered eco nomic viability, stressing the need of continued innovations to maximize sustainability and economic feasibility.

text: Currently, the physical recycling process still relies heavily on con ventional  organic  solvents  (Zhao  et  al.,  2018b).  For  PVC  it  concerns solvents such as dichloromethane, tetrahydrofuran (THF), toluene and xylene, which are hazardous for the environment, limiting their appli cation at industrial level. (Achilias et al., 2009; Kampouris et al., 1986; Sánchez-Rivera  et  al.,  2025;  Sperber  and  Rosen,  1976)  Also,  the VinyLoop ® process used a solvent mixture based on methyl ethyl ketone (MEK) with a low life cycle score (Vandenhende, 2001). To increase the overall sustainability of the process, it remains thus key to identify new powerful  green  solvent  systems.  Especially  solvents  that  can  be  pro duced from renewable sources, i.e., biobased solvents, are of particular interest. Very recently, solvents such as d -limonene, α -pinene and GVL were successfully applied for the dissolution-based recycling of poly styrene (Kazuyuki, 2015; Kol et al., 2023; Mangalara and Varughese, 2016),  high-density  polyethylene  (Aparício  et  al.,  2024)  and  poly ethylene  terephthalate  (Chen  et  al.,  2021).  Yet,  to  date,  no  suitable biobased solvents have been identified for the physical recycling of PVC.

text: Aside from being green, also the solvent ' s functional efficiency is of utmost importance. Especially in the case of the non-solvent, a high excess is applied to precipitate the polymer, which is undesirable from a sustainability perspective given the high energy demand associated with its  recovery  (Zhao  et  al.,  2018b).  The  Hansen  Solubility  Parameters (HSP) have demonstrated their utility as a guiding tool for solvents, but have been seldomly applied for the selection of non-solvents. In these studies, the non-solvents are chosen based on only their HSP neglecting the  influence  of  the  initial  solvent  on  the  precipitation  at  low  nonsolvent  excess  (Gorre  and  Tumolva,  2020;  Hansen,  2012;  Lu  and Chen, 2023; Venkatram et al., 2019). To overcome this limitation, very recently, an adapted approach has been proposed using the HSP of the solvent:non-solvent  mixture  instead.  This  approach  was  successfully applied to recycle acrylonitrile butadiene styrene, but its validation on other polymeric systems is still missing (Lu and Chen, 2023).

text: Beyond optimizing solvent use, the overall sustainability and eco nomic feasibility of recycling can be further improved by maximizing material utilization, such as through the co-valorization of additives. Rigid PVC contains significant amounts of calcium carbonate (CaCO3) and titanium dioxide (TiO2) to improve rigidity, thermal stability or as a pigment.  Given  its  market  price  of  approximately  3 € /kg  (Statista, 2023b), especially the co-valorization of TiO2 can allow to improve the economic feasibility of the recycling process. text:
The objectives of this research are: [i] to introduce a novel approach to the physical recycling of rigid PVC using bio-based solvents; [ii] to enable the co-valorization of CaCO3 and TiO2; and [iii] to demonstrate the effectiveness of Hansen Solubility Parameters (HSP) as a practical tool  for  selecting  suitable  bio-based  solvents  and  non-solvents.  The recycling process was first optimized with virgin PVC, and the estab lished  conditions  were  successfully  extended  to  commercial  formula tions  and end-of-life rigid PVC materials. Furthermore, the inorganic fraction  was  selectively  purified  to  recover  TiO2  or  CaCO3,  and  the recycled  PVC  was  characterized  to  evaluate  its  purity  and  structural integrity. This work highlights a sustainable, dual-recovery strategy that enhances  both  material  circularity  and  resource  efficiency  in  PVC recycling.

2. Experimental

2.1. Materials

Virgin PVC powder without additives was received from Centexbel, commercial PVC flakes designed for window profiles and a shredded end-of-life  mixture  were  obtained  from  a  window  producer,  and  a commercially produced rigid PVC tube was sourced from a construction site.  The PVC tube was cryogenically ground using a Pulvurisette 14 equipped with a 1 mm sieve before use. The remaining materials were used as received.

text: PVC Molecular weight was determined by SEC, using a Waters sys tem with an HR5E column connected to an RI and UV detector. The instrument was calibrated with polystyrene internal standards (1920 -1500000 g ⋅ mol 1 ) and eluted with THF. Ash content analysis was performed in triplicate for each sample in a Thermo Fisher Scientific Thermolyne muffle furnace. Approximately 100 mg of the dried material was added into a pre-weighed aluminum cup. The samples were placed in the muffle furnace and following heating profile was used: heating to 250 °C at 5 °C/min, isothermal for 5 min, heating until 550 °C at 5 °C/ min, isothermal for 4 h, cooling to 105 °C. Afterwards the sample was cooled to room temperature and weighed to determine the ash content. Determination of the CaCO3, TiO2 and Zn content was done by ICP-AES using a Thermo Fisher Scientific iCAP Pro XP system. 50 mg of polymer was weighed in a Teflon recipient of 18 mL. 1.5 mL nitric acid Pico-Pure Plus and 1.5 mL hydrofluoric acid were added to the sample. The sample was digested in an Anton Paar Multiwave 7000 microwave digestor, by heating it at 250 °C for 3 h. After cooling down to room temperature, the sample was transferred to a test tube and neutralized with 16 mL of a 4 % boric acid solution. The sample was diluted to a total of 50 mL using ultrapure water and measured. Elemental quantities of calcium (Ca), titanium (Ti), and zinc (Zn) measured by ICP-AES were converted into the amounts of their respective target compounds, such as CaCO3 TiO2 using the stochiometric information. The limit of quantification (LOQ) was 10 mg/kg for Ca and Zn and 5 mg/kg for Ti, and a limit of detection (LOD) being half of LOQ.

text:
Supercritical CO2 extraction was used to completely dry the recycled PVC before compounding. This was performed using a laboratory scale JASCO SFE system from JASCO Isogen Life Science using a flow-through extraction cell (Elst et al., 2018). The cell was filled with 4 to 4.5 g of dried and ground PVC sandwiched between two layers of glass wool. The extraction was performed during 3 h using pure CO2, a flow rate of 1 mL ⋅ min 1 , temperature of 50 °C and pressure of 35 Mpa. Afterwards, the polymer was collected and analyzed for solvent content. The system was rinsed using IPA.

2.2.6. Compounding PVC into dog bone tensile bars

Minicompounding to tensile dog bones was done using a Thermo Fisher ™ HAAKE ™ miniCTW equipped with a Force Feeder system to guarantee  continuous  flow  of  the  material  and  an  air-cooled  screw feeder to avoid clogging of the system. The MiniCTW is combined with the MiniJet injection moulder to shape the dog bones. PVC dog bones were  compounded  using  the  co-rotating  configuration  with  direct extrusion at 190 °C with a screw speed of 80 rpm. The PVC was directly extruded to the MiniJet cylinder heated to 200 °C and to be injected into an ISO 5A mold at 95 °C. The injection was performed with a pressure of 950 bars within 10 s and a post pressure of 10 s at 700 bars was applied.

text:
The inorganic fractions were purified using a thermal treatment to remove  the  remaining  organic  residues  followed  by  a  double  acid treatment to recover TiO2. The thermal treatment was performed using the previously described ashing conditions (see 2.2.1). The residues with high TiO2 content were suspended 1 M HCl solution (1 g in 10 mL) and stirred  at  room  temperature  for  3  h.  The  resulting  suspension  was centrifuged at 4500 RCF for 45 min to separate TiO2 from the dissolved CaCl2. The TiO2  was washed with deionized water and centrifuged an additional three times. The purified TiO2  was then dried in a vacuum oven at 105 °C overnight. Those steps were repeated with 30 mL HCl solution. ICP-AES was employed to assess the final purity. In the case of the PVC tube, the TiO2 content was very low, and instead the recovery of CaCO3 was targeted by applying solely the thermal treatment.

text: Recent studies have explored the use of biobased solvents for the physical recycling of various plastics. Various terpenes and terpenoids were evaluated for their ability to recycle polystyrene based plastics whereby d -limonene was proven to be successful for both expanded and high impact polystyrene (Kazuyuki, 2015; Kol et al., 2023; Mangalara and Varughese, 2016). Similarly, d-Limonene was investigated for the recycling of high-density polyethylene achieving approximately 78 % polymer and 57 % solvent recovery. For this material, however, the highest recovery was obtained with α -pinene also allowing to keep the structural integrity of the recycled polymer intact (Aparício et al., 2024). Another biobased solvent, GVL, was applied successfully for the physical recycling of polyethylene terephthalate (Chen et al., 2021). However, to the  best  of  our  knowledge,  no  suitable  biobased  solvents  have  been identified for PVC yet. In this study, the theoretical solvent selection for the dissolution of PVC was performed using HSP. HSPiP software was used for the solvent selection (see supporting information), with the following parameters for PVC: δ d = 18.8, δ p = 9.2 and δ h = 6.3. Fig. 1 shows the HSP sphere for PVC with R0 equal to 8.0. A list of conventional organic solvents and commercially available biobased solvents such as cyrene, diethyl carbonate, GVL, p-cymene, methyl oleate, d-limonene, 1butanol, m-THF, EtOAc and EtOH were included in the study and their A. text:
3.1.2. Non-solvents

The theoretical selection of non-solvents for the precipitation of PVC was  also  performed  using  the  HSP.  In  the  previously  reported  ap proaches, the prime criteria for selection non-solvents is that their RED as compared to the polymer is larger than one (Venkatram et al., 2019). While this approach is effective at the typical large non-solvent excess, it faces  limitations  when  lower  non-solvent  dosages  are  targeted  to enhance the sustainability. Under these conditions, the initial solubili zation  solvent  remains  at  relatively  high  concentrations,  which  can interfere  with  precipitation  performance.  Therefore,  in  this  study,  a novel approach was applied based on the HSP of the solvent:non-solvent mixture to assess the non-solvent behavior. A good solvent:non-solvent pair was defined as the combination of a good solvent with a non-solvent that allows to increase the RED of the mixture above one over a small concentration span. Water, MeOH, EtOH, IPA, hexane, toluene, EtOAc and acetone were evaluated as potential non-solvent candidates in the presence  of  the  selected  biobased  solvents  cyrene,  GVL  and  m-THF. Hexane  was  not  evaluated  in  the  system  with  GVL  because  of  its immiscibility.

3.1.2. Non-solvents

The theoretical selection of non-solvents for the precipitation of PVC was  also  performed  using  the  HSP.  In  the  previously  reported  ap proaches, the prime criteria for selection non-solvents is that their RED as compared to the polymer is larger than one (Venkatram et al., 2019). While this approach is effective at the typical large non-solvent excess, it faces  limitations  when  lower  non-solvent  dosages  are  targeted  to enhance the sustainability. Under these conditions, the initial solubili zation  solvent  remains  at  relatively  high  concentrations,  which  can interfere  with  precipitation  performance.  Therefore,  in  this  study,  a novel approach was applied based on the HSP of the solvent:non-solvent mixture to assess the non-solvent behavior. A good solvent:non-solvent pair was defined as the combination of a good solvent with a non-solvent that allows to increase the RED of the mixture above one over a small concentration span. Water, MeOH, EtOH, IPA, hexane, toluene, EtOAc and acetone were evaluated as potential non-solvent candidates in the presence  of  the  selected  biobased  solvents  cyrene,  GVL  and  m-THF. Hexane  was  not  evaluated  in  the  system  with  GVL  because  of  its immiscibility.

text: In  Fig.  2,  the  HSP  distance  (Ra)  between  the  solvent:non-solvent mixtures and PVC at different solvent:non-solvent ratios is illustrated. In this way, the best non-solvent candidates and their required amounts for PVC precipitation were identified. According to the R a  values be tween solvent:non-solvent mixtures and PVC, water could be considered to be the best non-solvent to precipitate PVC in combination with cyrene and GVL as solvent. In both cases, a water concentration of maximum 20 wt% (ratio 80:20, solvent:non-solvent) was theoretically sufficient for the precipitation of PVC, which is significantly better compared to the typical 300 % of non-solvent used for polymer precipitations (Achilias et  al.,  2009).  A  sharp  increase  of  the R a  values  was  observed  with increasing  water  content,  which  can  be  explained  by  the  elevated hydrogen bond and polarity parameters of water as compared to PVC and  the  selected  biobased  solvents.  Unfortunately,  the  miscibility  of water and m-THF is limited and hence water could not be considered as a good non-solvent for the precipitation of PVC from a solution in mTHF.

text: Solvents  inside  and  outside  of  the  solubility  sphere  of  PVC  were experimentally tested to evaluate the accuracy of the HSP predictions for this system. A temperature interval of 40 -100 °C was selected for the dissolution experiments unless the boiling point of the solvent was lower than the desired temperature. Pressurized conditions were avoided and hence, the temperature was kept below the boiling point. Dissolution experiments started at 40 °C for  30  min  in  a  thermal  shaker,  and  if visually incomplete dissolution of PVC was reached, the temperature was increased 5 °C for 30 extra minutes. This process was repeated until PVC was visually completely dissolved. The effect of polymer concen tration  (5 -25  wt%)  on  the  dissolution  was  investigated  for  selected solvents  and  the  results  are  represented  in  Fig.  3.  The  individual experimental data are shown in Table S2 (see supplementary informa tion),  where  the  solvents  were  ranked  in  descending  order  for  HSP predicted affinity to PVC. The results demonstrate that solvents with theoretically high PVC-dissolving capabilities, including cyclohexanone, cyrene, GVL, anisole, THF, MEK, and m-THF, successfully dissolved the polymer at concentrations ranging from 5 wt% to 15 wt%. Among these, THF  and  cyclohexanone  were  specifically  observed  in  literature  to effectively separate PVC from PET (Grause et al., 2017). In the case of cyclohexanone and GVL, complete dissolution of PVC was reached at even higher polymer concentrations up to 20 and 25 wt%. A general trend was observed, where an increased PVC concentration led to more viscous solutions and higher dissolution temperatures. Solvents such as acetone,  CPME,  and  EtOAc,  were  unable  to  dissolve  PVC  under  the investigated conditions, despite being within the HSP solubility sphere of PVC. Although these solvents are poor at dissolving the polymer, they can  still  induce  PVC  swelling,  enabling  the  extraction  of  additives (Kumar  et  al.,  2020).  Additionally,  as  predicted  using  HSP,  solvents located  outside  the  PVC  solubility  sphere,  such  as  d-limonene,  pcymene, and diethyl carbonate, were unable to completely dissolve PVC at any of the investigated conditions.

Those selected cases were further investigated to identify the optimal conditions for the precipitation of  PVC and the results are shown in Fig. 4 (see also supplementary information Table S4 and Fig. S1). This figure presents the yield of recovered PVC (Equation (1) as a function of non-solvent concentration for the systems with cyrene, GVL and m-THF as well as the SEC chromatograms of the polymer clearly proving that there  is  no  PVC  degradation  after  the  purification  via  dissolutionprecipitation (Fig. 4d). The utilization of water as non-solvent in com bination with cyrene or GVL as solvent led to maximal PVC recovery using less than 10 % (9:1 solvent:non-solvent) of water. When using MeOH  as  non-solvent,  the  maximum  yield  of  PVC  precipitate  was reached at MeOH concentrations of at least 25 wt% (3:1 solvent:nonsolvent) and 30 wt% (7:3 solvent:non-solvent) for systems with cyrene and GVL, respectively. As observed during the screenings, the precipi tation of PVC from m-THF was less effective, resulting in maximal re covery using at least 50 wt% MeOH and IPA (1:1 solvent:non-solvent). However, this is still lower than the traditionally applied 1:3 ratio of solvent:non-solvent  for  the  precipitation  of  polymers  (Achilias  et  al., 2009; Chen et al., 2021; Kampouris et al., 1986). text: The most promising combinations, being GVL or cyrene and water as the solvent:non-solvent combination was applied to commercial PVC and end-of-life materials. Three materials were selected for the recycling of the  PVC  using  the  optimal  solubilization-precipitation  procedure:  a commercial PVC formulation to produce window frames as a reference, a PVC window frame and an end-of-life rigid PVC tube (Fig. 5a-c). Those materials were analyzed for inorganic content and ICP-AES was used to identify  elements  and  quantify  various  inorganic  additives,  including TiO2, CaCO3 (Fig. 5d and e). An inorganic content of 13.2 %, 9.8 % and 9.1 % was obtained for the commercial PVC, the window frame and the tube, respectively. The ICP-AES results (Fig. 5e) clearly showed that sig nificant amounts of Ti and Ca were detected, originating primarily from the TiO2 and CaCO3 that are present in the material. This is in in-line with expectations since those additives are mainly added as a pigment or to tune  the  material ' s  properties  and  increase  strength  and  durability. Additionally, small amounts of Zn ( < 0.2 %) were observed, likely linked to  Ca/Zn-stearates  that  are  commonly  added  as  a  stabilizer.  The  Ca amount that can originate from this stabilizer was estimated to be at most 0.5 %, which is negligible as compared to the total Ca amount, supporting the hypothesis that the Ca originates primarily from the CaCO3.

text: Additionally,  ash  content  analysis  was  performed  to  confirm  suc cessful separation of the organic and the inorganic fraction of the PVC materials. The ash content of both the polymeric (P) and inorganic (I) phase were determined and compared. Fig. 6c and 6d clearly demon strate that the dissolution-precipitation process, using GVL and water as a solvent system, effectively removed nearly all inorganic components from  the  polymer  phase.  ICP-AES  was  employed  to  analyze  the composition of the inorganics. In case of the PVC tube, a small residual amount of CaCO3 (0.6 %) was detected in the polymer phase, whereas for both the PVC and window frame samples, less than 0.1 % remained. The inorganic fractions were predominantly composed of CaCO3  and TiO2, with a relatively low Zn content from the thermal stabilizer, as anticipated.  The  inorganic  components  closely  matched  the  starting materials, confirming successful separation of the polymer from inor ganic fillers through the GVL-water system. The significant TiO2 content in the treated samples suggest developing a purification method for TiO2 to enhance the economic viability of the process. The inorganic fraction, mainly CaCO3 and TiO2, underwent a thermal and acidic treatment to eliminate  residual  organics  and  CaCO3  (Fig.  6e).  Thermal  treatment eliminated organics, producing CaCO3  with a purity higher than 92 %

The tensile curves of all samples are similar overall. The slight dif ferences  in  ultimate  tensile  strength  and  elongation  at  break  in  the mixed samples compared to virgin PVC could be the result from residual organic additives enhancing mechanical properties. The purified mate rials from different resources exhibit consistent stiffness with a Young ' s modulus of ~ 1.7 GPa. However, end-of-life materials display slightly lower elongation at break than the commercial PVC window (V-PVC + PVC), likely due to soluble organic contaminants reducing mechanical performance (Yarahmadi et al., 2003). Similarly the decrease in ultimate tensile  strength  when  comparing  the  window  formulation  (V-PVC + PVC)  with  the  end-of-life  window  frame  (V-PVC + PVC window) is possibly caused by contaminants in the real PVC waste.

However, end-of-life materials display slightly lower elongation at break than the commercial PVC window (V-PVC + PVC), likely due to soluble organic contaminants reducing mechanical performance (Yarahmadi et al., 2003). Similarly the decrease in ultimate tensile  strength  when  comparing  the  window  formulation  (V-PVC + PVC)  with  the  end-of-life  window  frame  (V-PVC + PVC window) is possibly caused by contaminants in the real PVC waste.

4. Conclusions

text: This  study  demonstrates  that  while  HSP  do  not  provide  direct quantitative predictions of solubility, it serves as a powerful and prac tical tool for selecting solvents to efficiently dissolve PVC and optimize solvent:non-solvent  combinations  for  selective  polymer  precipitation. Using HSP predictions combined with experimental verification, GVL and  water  was  identified  as  the  optimal  solvent  system  for  the dissolution-precipitation purification of rigid PVC and CaCO3 and TiO2. We achieved a recovery of over 95 % of the material with a minimal nonsolvent  addition  of  less  than  10  %,  while  preserving  the  structural integrity of the polymer. Furthermore, the developed method proved to be highly effective across three distinct types of PVC, including end-oflife materials such as a PVC window frame and a tube, achieving over 99 % removal of inorganic fillers. The purified PVC exhibited properties comparable to virgin PVC, with only minor deviations, demonstrating the  potential  for  high-quality  material  recovery.  Additionally,  we established a viable route for the selective recovery of inorganic com ponents: CaCO3 was successfully extracted from PVC tubes via thermal treatment, while TiO2 was efficiently recovered through a combination of  thermal  treatment  and  acidified  water  washing.  These  findings highlight  the  potential  of  solvent-based  recycling  as  a  scalable  and sustainable approach for rigid PVC recovery, contributing to improved material  circularity  and  resource  efficiency.  However,  although  real end-of-life materials were used in this study, implementing this tech nology for mixed waste streams requires further investigation into the effects of various materials and additives. Additionally, since the purity of end-of-life materials depends on the efficiency of pre-sorting tech nologies, their role in ensuring process effectiveness across diverse and complex waste compositions must be carefully considered.

Elizaveta Radkevich a , Charles Granger a , Kevin Nelson b , Kevin Guigley b , Steve Grey b , Daniel Miller b , Ezra Bar-Ziv c , Styliani Avraamidou a , George W. Huber a,*

A B S T R A C T

text:
The solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP ™ ) process separates polymers from contaminants present in the feedstock. In this work, we demonstrate the recyclability of a post-consumer waste (PCW) shrink wrap that contains inks, adhesives, and paper using STRAP. We produced a clear rPE cast film from the PCW shrink wrap with no visual contamination from paper or inks. STRAP decreased the ash content from 0.96 wt% to 0.24 wt%. A techno-economic analysis (TEA) shows that a STRAP plant processing 50,000 metric tons annually of shrink wrap waste (purchased at $0.25/kg) containing 85 wt% PE can achieve an IRR of 16.2% when selling rPE at $1.30/kg, an IRR of 10.7% with an rPE price of $1.00/kg, or an IRR of 3.79% with an rPE price of $0.70/kg. The life cycle assessment (LCA) shows a 64% reduction in global warming potential (kg CO2 equivalent) when compared to the production of virgin LDPE. This work shows how feedstocks with insoluble impurities can be recycled using STRAP on a large scale.

text: Approximately 40% of plastic waste comes from packaging (Plastics Europe,  2021). These plastics are often  discarded with landfilling or incineration  being  the  most  common  form  of  disposal  (Geyer  et  al., 2017).  Packaging  can  be  rigid  or  flexible  films  that  are  often  coprocessed  with  multiple  polymers  (Food  and  Beverage  Packaging Technology, 2011). Shrink wrap is a type of mostly monolayer flexible packaging material. Several polymers including oriented polystyrene, polyvinyl chloride (PVC), poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), or poly ethylene (PE) can be used depending on the application (Roberge, 2019; Sutaria,  2023;  Recycle  Ann  Arbor,  2024;  Recycle  Ann  Arbor).  Poly ethylene shrink wrap is often used to bundle packages, and PS or PET are commonly used to form safety sleeves on items such as bottles. Most of the current shrink film is a blend of low-density PE (LDPE) and linearlow  density  PE  (LLDPE)  as  PVC  has  been  phased  out  for  environ mental reasons (Roberge, 2019). High-density polyethylene (HDPE) can also  be used in shrink films (Polyflex, 2023). LLDPE is cheaper than LDPE due to milder operating pressure during synthesis and LLDPE is the most flexible with the highest resistance to tears providing strength and durability (Dalai, 2025; LDPE Price Index; LLDPE Price Index). This  recycling approach allows for producing virgin-like recycled polymers. Dissolu tion  recycling  without  anti-solvent  also  has  lower  greenhouse  gas emissions and fossil energy input than production of the virgin resins while solvent based recycling with antisolvent results  in a 2.5  times increase  in  CO2  emissions  compared  to  virgin  production  (MunguíaLópez  et  al.,  2023).  Solvent  targeted  recovery  and  precipitation (STRAP ™ ) is a solvent based technology that enables the recycling of multilayer films (Walker et al., 2020). text: LDPE and LLDPE films are not commonly sorted at material recovery facilities  (MRF)  as  they  clog  sorting  equipment  (Recycle  Ann  Arbor, 2024; Recycle Ann Arbor). Some films are collected at drop-off locations at grocery or retail stores (Laville, 2024). Films accepted at such loca tions in the US include grocery bags, produce bags, appliance wraps, bubble wrap, case wrap, shipping air pillows, mailer bags, pallet wrap, stretch film, and more (Plastic Film Recycling Home Page; NexTrex ® Plastic Bag & Film Recycling). Currently, some downcycling applica tions are available including transforming PE films into outdoor com posite decking, e.g., Trex Company, Inc. and incorporation of PE into asphalt formulations for road pavement applications (NexTrex ® Plastic Bag & Film  Recycling;  Yaghoubi  et  al.,  2017).  For  outdoor  decking, reclaimed sawdust is combined with plastic films to produce the panels that can last to up to 50 years and require low maintenance (Trex ® Composite Decking). In asphalt incorporation, the addition of plastic content does not have a significant change to the geotechnical quality of the  recycled  concrete  aggregate  (Yaghoubi  et  al.,  2017).  Polyolefin shrink wrap films are perfect candidates for dissolution recycling due to their  large  available  quantities  and  low  recycling  rates.  Dissolution recycling  can  also  conserve  the  quality  of  shrink  wrap  by  removing contaminants  that  cannot  be  easily  removed  in  standard  recycling practices.

In this work, we aim to demonstrate how STRAP can purify a mixture of PCW LDPE and LLDPE shrink wrap and remove inks and paper labels. We show successful paper removal along with minimal ash content in the resulting recycled polymer. The plastic ' s volatile content also de creases as part of the process.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Materials

The feedstock material was acquired from a MRF facility in Chicago. The material was then forwarded to a shredder at Michigan Techno logical University and shredded to an average particle size of 2 -4 mm. The  shredded  material  mainly  contained  plastic  material  with  paper labels and traces of debris.

The solvents used in the dissolution process include xylenes (VWR), dodecane (mixture of isomers, Thermo Scientific), and heptane (labo ratory reagent, VWR). PCR (Post-consumer recyclate) pellets (Ravago Ravapura ® 10002), virgin LDPE pellets (Westlake EG 412 AA), virgin LLDPE pellets (ExxonMobil Exceed ® 1018 Series),  and virgin LLDPE pellets (Nova Novapol ® PF-0118 Series) were provided by Amcor. Vir gin HDPE Dowlex ® IP40 was used as a reference for HDPE.

text: The  shrink  wrap  feed  was  shredded  using  a  cross-cut  shredder (Allegheny 16-75CX) at Michigan Technological University. The mate rial was shredded to 2 -4 mm size. The selected size reflects a trade-off between dissolution efficiency and energy consumption: smaller parti cles  enhance  solvent-polymer  mass  transfer  and  dissolution  kinetics, while  further  size  reduction  would  require  disproportionately  higher shredding  energy  and  associated  processing  costs.  Mechanical  size reducing preprocessing aids in feedstock transport and  material composition  consistency  (Saha  et  al.,  2023).  No  other  pretreatments were performed in this study.

text: For solvent ratio experiments, the minimum ratio was selected so that all material was covered by solvent. This was done to ensure liquid and solid contact for better mass transfer. The dissolution on a small scale  was performed in a round bottom flask (2 or 3 neck, 250 mL) heated with silicone oil (heat transfer fluid) bath, shown in Fig. 1A. A thermometer was placed inside the flask for accurate temperature con trol. A reflux attachment was used to prohibit the solvent from evapo rating  and  maintain  constant  temperature.  The  solvent  solution  was heated to 65, 80, or 95 °C. Polymer solubility is a function of temperature with higher solubility observe at elevated temperatures. To keep tem peratures constant among solvents, 95 °C was chosen as the higher limit due  to  heptane  boiling  point  while  65 °C  and  80 °C  were  chosen  as comparison points. Dissolution continued for 60, 90, or 180 min. Later, the hot mixture was filtered through a stainless-steel wire metal mesh (500 µ m) to separate undissolved particles from solution. The solution was allowed to precipitate and cool to room temperature. The solvent was then removed using a Buchner funnel and a vacuum flask with 1 µ m paper filter. The polymer cake was then dried under vacuum at 100 °C.

text:
The dissolution on a larger scale was performed in an, 8 L, contin uously stirred, jacketed vessel, shown in Fig. 1B. Silicone heating oil flows through the jacket to provide heat. The mixer was set to 400 rpm. Xylenes were heated to 95-100 °C then shredded shrink wrap was added and allowed to dissolve for 2 h. After the 2 h, the solution was drained passing  through  2  filter  disks,  500  and  100 µ m.  The  solution  was precipitated and cooled to room temperature. The solvent was removed using a Buchner funnel and a vacuum flask with 1 µ m paper filter. The polymer cake was then dried under vacuum at 100 °C.

Compressed films were made using a Carver Press 3970. The mass of post  STRAP  cake  was  1.0  g.  Samples  were  heated  at  190 °C  without pressure  (minimal  contact)  for  1  min,  followed  by  3  metric  tons  of pressure for 1 min also at 190 °C. The sample was placed between two Teflon laminated cloths. The Teflon sheets were placed between two thin metal plates. Films were allowed to cool to room temperature after being removed from the press.

The  dried  post  STRAP  PE  was  ground,  extruded,  pelletized,  and extruded into cast film, as shown in Fig. 1C. Virgin LDPE Westlake EG 412 AA pellets and LDPE PCR pellets were acquired through Amcor. STRAP  material  was  ground  using  Thomas  Scientific  grinder  model 1188Y51 to  3  mm.  The  ground  material  was  then  extruded  using  a Leistritz  twin-screw  extruder  with  8  heated  sections  (167 °C,  174 °C, 179 °C, 184 °C, 189 °C, 192 °C, 192 °C, 192 °C) and a 40-rpm screw speed. The extruded material was pelletized with a strand pelletizer. The pellets were processed into cast films at Amcor using a Labtech Engineering extruder with an average barrel and melt temperature of 205 °C.

2.3.1. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR)

FTIR aided polymer characterization. The data was collected using a ThermoScientific Nicolet iS50 (ATR-FTIR) with SMART-iTX attachment and diamond standard crystal. Each FTIR sample was averaged from 16 scans  with  4  cm 1 resolution.  On  average,  20  FTIR  samples  were analyzed per polymer sample.

Cellulose hydrolysis experiments were performed using a modified procedure  from  National  Renewable  Energy  Laboratory  (NREL). Initial analysis with Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was performed to understand the polymers present in the shrink wrap. As seen in Fig. 2G, the main polymer present is polyethylene. The specific type of PE is determined using DSC. From comparison of several types including LDPE, LLDPE, and HDPE and different grades, the shrink wrap film is most likely LLDPE, possibly blended with a minor portion of LDPE and HDPE. As shown in Fig. 2H, the curve of the PCW shrink wrap and post-STRAP material matches astandard LLDPE, e.g.,Novapol PF-0118 Series, the most. The red and green curve both have a slight peak at 98 -99 °C  (crystallization)  indicative  of  potential  LDPE  presence  (Tc 99 °C). The broad composition of the PCW film makes DSC interpretation difficult. Since the shrink wrap consists of paper labels with visible ink and LLDPE polymer, we define LLDPE being our target to be recovered, but ultimately this is a mix of LLDPE, LDPE and HDPE. The FTIR of our sample also shows an increased absorbance at 1375 cm 1 (C -H bend) which  indicates  increased  terminal  CH3  groups  commonly  found  in LLDPE (Mohrig et al., 2014). text:
The ash content of the PCW shrink wrap is 0.96 ± 0.076 wt%. This ash is due to paper contamination and dirt or other debris that collect in the shrink wrap. Paper contains 55.7 -87.4 wt% cellulose and 5 -30 wt% fillers often calcium carbonate and clay (Guerfali et al., 2015; Hubbe and Gill, 2016). This paper in the PCW shrink warp includes printed labels with adhesives. These labels can differ between facilities that use shrink wrap. Labels can also be laminated, increasing the variability in the estimate. We estimated the paper content through cellulose hydrolysis as 1.9 -2.3 wt%. Paper is the most prevalent contaminant in the shrink warp. Paper can clog filters and other equipment in a continuous recy cling  process.  Unremoved  paper  also  decomposed  during  extrusion, creating a brown discoloration.

text:
We have previously used alkanes (heptane and dodecane) and aro matics (xylenes and toluene) to separate polyolefins with the STRAP process (Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2023; Walker et al., 2020; Sánchez-Riv era et al., 2021). Pigments have a higher solubility in toluene and xy lenes compared to dodecane (Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2025). Particularly, yellow and orange pigments have been shown to have higher solubility in toluene (Yan et al., 2025). There may be yellow and  black  printed  inks  which  may  cause  discoloration  of  the  final product with the use of xylene. In the case of the shrink wrap material, heptane, dodecane, and xylene were studied in the dissolution process. Dodecane and xylene have previously been identified as effective sol vents at temperatures of 95 °C and 130 °C (Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2023).

Heptane has been most effective near its boiling of 98 °C. Previous results have predicted lower PE solubility in heptane compared to dodecane (Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2023).

text: Table  1 compares the effects  of  solvents,  temperature  dissolution time, and solvent to plastic ratio on the recovered yield in 250 ml roundbottom flask. Over 82% of the PE could be recovered when xylene was used as a solvent at 95 °C. In heptane at 80 °C, only 18.7 wt% of the polymer could be recovered. This demonstrates that temperatures above 95 °C  are  required  to  dissolve  the  polymer  efficiently.  Increasing  the heptane to plastic ratio from 15:1 to 17.5:1, increased the recovered polymer from 44 to 51.6 wt%. The recovered polymer and undissolved residual are included in the mass balance and the remaining is lost in the experimental process. Further increasing the heptane to plastic ratio to 20:1 and 25:1 or dissolution time from 90 min to 120 min had minimal effect  on  the  recovered  polymer.  Comparing  xylene,  dodecane,  and heptane at 15:1 solvent ratio and 90 min dissolution time showed xylene to be the most effective at dissolving shrink wrap, followed by dodecane. Besides  increased  yield  in  xylenes,  it  provided  other  advantages including lower solvent and drying costs. The price of industrial grades of mixed xylene isomers varies between $0.60 and $1.30 per kilogram, while dodecane prices vary between $2 and $10 per kilogram (MetaXylene Price Index; Para-Xylene Price Index; Ortho-Xylene Price Index). The heat of vaporization for xylenes is about 42 kJ/mol while the heat of vaporization of dodecane is about 61 kJ/mol (NIST; NIST; Dodecane). Therefore,  we  proceeded  with  xylene  as  the  solvent  in  the  scale-up process.

Table  1 compares the effects  of  solvents,  temperature  dissolution time, and solvent to plastic ratio on the recovered yield in 250 ml roundbottom flask. Over 82% of the PE could be recovered when xylene was used as a solvent at 95 °C. In heptane at 80 °C, only 18.7 wt% of the polymer could be recovered. This demonstrates that temperatures above 95 °C  are  required  to  dissolve  the  polymer  efficiently.  Increasing  the heptane to plastic ratio from 15:1 to 17.5:1, increased the recovered polymer from 44 to 51.6 wt%. The recovered polymer and undissolved residual are included in the mass balance and the remaining is lost in the experimental process. Further increasing the heptane to plastic ratio to 20:1 and 25:1 or dissolution time from 90 min to 120 min had minimal effect  on  the  recovered  polymer.  Comparing  xylene,  dodecane,  and heptane at 15:1 solvent ratio and 90 min dissolution time showed xylene to be the most effective at dissolving shrink wrap, followed by dodecane. Besides  increased  yield  in  xylenes,  it  provided  other  advantages including lower solvent and drying costs. The price of industrial grades of mixed xylene isomers varies between $0.60 and $1.30 per kilogram, while dodecane prices vary between $2 and $10 per kilogram (MetaXylene Price Index; Para-Xylene Price Index; Ortho-Xylene Price Index). The heat of vaporization for xylenes is about 42 kJ/mol while the heat of vaporization of dodecane is about 61 kJ/mol (NIST; NIST; Dodecane). Therefore,  we  proceeded  with  xylene  as  the  solvent  in  the  scale-up process.

text: Compressed films were made from the dried post-STRAP recycled PE (rPE) and a PCR pellet which was sourced from Amcor. A color analysis was performed on the compressed films. In  this  analysis,  we  aim  to compare  the  color  quality  of  material  after  STRAP  to  the  currently available PCR PE pellet film quality. Companies aim to have clear films without any colorants, especially in food applications. Based on optical parameters, virgin LLDPE and the post STRAP PE have similar optical properties, as shown in Table 2. The films used in this study are com pressed films and cast films. Looking at the compressed films in Fig. 3, we observe that STRAP can remove paper content from the PCW shrink wrap and does not appear to have significant color issues in the post STRAP  PE. text: Mechanical properties are somewhat dependent on the processing condition of the polymer, as well as the specific ratios of PE types that comprise the films. Since the shrink film recovered from the MRF un doubtedly was produced by multiple manufacturers, the actual composition  was  compositionally  broad.  These  properties  can  be compared  between  materials  if  both  materials  undergo  similar  pro cessing conditions. We compared a virgin LLDPE/LDPE blend cast film to a post STRAP shrink wrap LLDPE cast film and PCR pellet cast film. We find the post STRAP cast film to have lower force at break, stress at break, and elongation at break compared to the virgin film and PCR film while the stress at yield and the Young ' s modulus are higher. As shown in Table 3, the thickness is between 72 and 84 µ m for all samples. The force at break is similar in the machine and transverse direction for the virgin blend cast film while the post STRAP PE and PCR cast films have a lower force at break in the transverse direction than in the machine direction. The force at break of the post STRAP PE is 42.1 N which is significantly lower than the virgin blend and PCR cast films at 57.5 N and 52.2 N, respectively in the machine direction. The stress at break follows a similar trend in the machine versus transverse direction and between the post STRAP PE, virgin blend, and PCR samples. The largest variation between the post STRAP PE and virgin blend and PCR is the elongation at break. The elongation at break of post STRAP PE is 151% and  635%  in  the  machine  and  transverse  direction,  respectively, compared to 547% and 838% in virgin blend cast film and 661% and 752% in PCR cast film, respectively. The stress at yield increases in the machine direction from undetectable in the virgin blend, to 12.4 MPa in E. Radkevich et al.
