text: The  virgin  blend  exhibits  the  most  desirable  properties,  showing greater elongation and higher force and stress at break, along with a lower  Young ' s  modulus.  Among  the  materials  tested,  virgin  LLDPE/ LDPE  shows  the  best  mechanical  performance,  followed  by  PCR  PE pellet and STRAP PE. However, all films have good mechanical prop erties that they can be used in a wide variety of film applications. The uncertainty of composition of the PCR PE and STRAP PE can provide an explanation to these trends. The virgin LLDPE/LDPE blend was created in an attempt to mimic the commercial shrink wrap film and to serve as a benchmark for comparison, although the actual composition of the postconsumer film was unknown. Both PCR PE and STRAP PE materials have PCR content, yet the full contents of PCR PE are not known. It may be a blend  of  virgin  and  PCR  material  resulting  in  improved  properties compared to 100% PCR (STRAP PE) but not quite as good as virgin which can explain why it is often found in the middle of the trend. Since the production origin of the shrink wrap used in this study is not known, it is possible that it already contains PCR content with varying LDPE and LLDPE molecular weights and grades. The increased number of recycles can cause polymer chain degradation further weakening the material ' s flexibility  and  increasing  its  stiffness  (Estela-García  et  al.,  2025). Moreover,  additives  may  play  an  additional  role  in  the  mechanical properties, if any are present. Mechanical recycling often cannot remove these additives while dissolution recycling may remove them. Therefore, the lack of additives may cause embrittlement. Additionally, STRAP PE may show diminished properties due to potentially modified molecular weight distribution. Some short PE chains may remain dissolved in the solvent upon precipitation at room temperature. The recovered STRAP PE  would  result  in  a  more  narrowed  molecular  weight  distribution which can be linked to embrittlement as well.

For  practical  film  application,  STRAP  PE ' s  mechanical  properties may be modified through blending and reformulation to achieve virginlike properties. Shrink wrap mainly relies on its abilities to be stretched and shrunk to prevent damage of its contents which would require the addition of some virgin LLDPE/LDPE to decrease the Young ' s modulus and allow for greater elongation.

Besides  film  appearance,  inorganic  content  in  the  polymer  is important. The amount of ash content in our product material can be compared with other dissolution post-consumer recycling processes, like APK AG Newcycling ® ,  to  estimate  the  success of  STRAP with shrink wrap material. This helps compare the quality of PCR materials avail able  on  the  market  currently  and  other  emerging  technologies  like STRAP. The APK product Mersalen ® LDPE NCY01 has an ash content of less than 0.4 wt% while the post STRAP shrink wrap material has an ash content of 0.24 wt%, compared to the 0.96 wt% in the PCW shrink wrap prior to treatment (APK). The PCR PE pellet has an ash content of 0.93 wt%.

text: Volatile impurities in the STRAP cast film are determined using gas chromatography  (GC)  headspace  analysis.  The  total  volatile  organic content  (TVOC)  of  the  feed  material  was  2.5  ppm  and  5.4  ppm  for boiling  points  below  100 °C and below 200 °C,  respectively.  The  post STRAP shrink wrap cast film has a TVOC of 0.0 and 3.4 for boiling points below 100 °C and below 200 °C, respectively. A product specific migra tion test would be needed to confirm suitability for use in consumer products, but the low levels of residual VOCs indicate STRAP plastic is likely suitable to replace virgin materials (Food and Drug Administra tion).  Moreover,  STRAP  continues  to  show  potential  in  contaminant removal as the TVOC decreased from 5.4 mg/kg in the feed material to 3.4 mg/kg in the STRAP cast film. The volatile impurities in the film are all from the xylenes solvent including ethylbenzene (7.39%), p-xylene (49.91%), o-xylene (34.18%), and 2,2,4,6,6-pentamethylheptane (8.52%) calculated by relative peak area during gas chromatography.

text: Although the material has very low VOC content, odor influences the usability of the material. The cast film has a strong odor whose source is explained through volatile chemical analysis and human odor percep tion. The human nose can detect 0.058 ppm of p-xylene in air, 0.041 ppm of m-xylene in air, and 0.67 ppm of n-heptane in air (Yoshio and Nagata,  2003).  Since  the  xylene  content  exceeds  the  human  xylene sensitivity  threshold,  we  are  able  to  smell  the  volatile  compounds released by the film. The smell is not desirable as it can prevent potential customers from using the material. After several months of storage in a foiled storage bag, the film odor subsided and was not as noticeable. Aeration is performed in industry to devolatilize materials and remove smells (Roosen et al., 2022; Erema). Pellets can also be flushed with hot air for several hours to remove volatile compounds (Strangl et al., 2019). However, most of these techniques are done to remove multiple classes of chemicals and require long contact times (Kol et al., 2022). In addi tion to the drying and devolatilization units, an aeration unit may need to be applied to pellets from the STRAP process to decrease the odors in a larger scale process. STRAP itself can be capable of entrapping some chemicals in the solvent during the dissolution as solvent washes can be employed to remove odor (Roosen et al., 2022). In a commercial pro cess, several solvent removing units should be used including mechan ical  separation,  vacuum  drying,  and  devolatilization  extrusion.  It  is important to consider that lab drying via vacuum drying is not how the drying would be done in a commercial STRAP operation.

text:
3.4. Economic and environmental impact analysis

3.4.1. Technoeconomic analysis

The  following  analysis  looks  at  a  commercial-scale  STRAP  plant processing mixed-grades A and B shrink wrap and pallet wrap assumed to  cost  $0.25/kg  to  produce  recycled  PE  (rPE)  (recyclingmarkets.net staff; Association of Plastic Recyclers, 2024; Association of Plastic Re cyclers, 2024). The feedstock is assumed to be 85 wt% PE. Feedstock preprocessing includes 3-stage shredding and metal removal; no densi fication or prewashing is performed. The solid waste leaving the process is composed of labels, non-PE polymers, and other waste residues; and it is incinerated for energy in an on-site combined heat and power unit. The dissolved contaminants, including inks and adhesives, are removed in an adsorption column that is used to clean the solvent before it is recycled within the process. In this specific analysis, the spent adsorbent is landfilled after use.

text: Process economics are highly dependent on the purchase price of the feedstock and the sale price of the product. Assuming the rPE from this process can be sold at virgin resin prices, an analysis based on a range of PE prices was performed. The average price of mixed virgin LLDPE and LDPE from 2018 to 2025 is approximately $1,000 per metric ton in the US. However, markets have seen this price drop as low as $700 or as high as $2010 in the last 7 years (LDPE Price Index; LLDPE Price Index). Fig. 4A shows the impact of product sale price by comparing internal rate of return (IRR) with processing capacity for three rPE sale prices. Also shown in Fig. 4B is the minimum selling price (MSP) of STRAP resin vs plant feedstock capacity, where MSP is defined as the product selling price necessary to break even (cumulative NPV = 0) with all plant costs over a 20-year plant lifetime including a 15% IRR. For each plant ca pacity on the x-axis, MSP was calculated 500 times using a Monte Carlo simulation that randomly sampled all variables from Table S1 within their specified bounds. Fig. 4C shows the most impactful variables and their relative impact on STRAP MSP.

Process economics are highly dependent on the purchase price of the feedstock and the sale price of the product. Assuming the rPE from this process can be sold at virgin resin prices, an analysis based on a range of PE prices was performed. The average price of mixed virgin LLDPE and LDPE from 2018 to 2025 is approximately $1,000 per metric ton in the US. However, markets have seen this price drop as low as $700 or as high as $2010 in the last 7 years (LDPE Price Index; LLDPE Price Index). Fig. 4A shows the impact of product sale price by comparing internal rate of return (IRR) with processing capacity for three rPE sale prices. Also shown in Fig. 4B is the minimum selling price (MSP) of STRAP resin vs plant feedstock capacity, where MSP is defined as the product selling price necessary to break even (cumulative NPV = 0) with all plant costs over a 20-year plant lifetime including a 15% IRR. For each plant ca pacity on the x-axis, MSP was calculated 500 times using a Monte Carlo simulation that randomly sampled all variables from Table S1 within their specified bounds. Fig. 4C shows the most impactful variables and their relative impact on STRAP MSP.

text: As shown in Fig. 4B, a STRAP plant that processes 50 kton of waste per year has a total capital investment (TCI) of 166 million USD. Holding all other variables constant, this plant would achieve an IRR of 16.2% when selling rPE at $1.30/kg, an IRR of 10.7% with an rPE price of $1.00/kg, or an IRR of 3.79% with an rPE price of $0.70/kg, as shown in Fig. 4A. While a STRAP plant can be profitable selling rPE at virgin PE prices, the ability to sell the rPE at a premium price would allow for increased  profitability  or  economic  viability  at  smaller  scale.  For example, a plant selling rPE at a roughly 50% premium or $1.50/kg could achieve a 15% IRR by processing 25.6 kton per year with a TCI of 106 million USD.

text:
A 50 kton/year plant processing an 85 wt% PE feedstock was sub jected to a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment to directly compare a range of environmental impacts of the STRAP process to virgin resin production. The modeled plant incinerates all its waste on site to pro duce electricity and steam. Natural gas is used to fulfill the additional energy needs that are not met by the process waste. Additionally, it is assumed  that  any  fugitive  solvent  emissions  from  the  process  are collected in a vapor trap through the ventilation system and burned. Recycled pellet aeration was not considered in this analysis, because the differences in lab scale and commercial scale VOC removal are not clear. Aeration is a common practice for resin producers, and the same tech nology would likely be used if required for STRAP plastic (Roosen et al., 2022; Erema). Fig. 5 shows the global warming potential (GWP) impact of producing the rPE resin for a plant processing 50 kton/year of PE wrap waste.

text: The STRAP resins have a GWP 64% lower than that of virgin PE production. Emissions from the on-site boiler are the largest contributor to the process GWP (direct non-biogenic emissions). If the undissolved waste is sent to landfill instead of being incinerated for energy, the GWP of the STRAP PE increases to 0.887 kg CO2 eq. The main reason for this increase is the switch to grid electricity which emits more GHG. How ever, this is not consistent trend and depends highly on the source of grid electricity and the ratio of plastic to natural gas being used in the boiler The GWP impact was also analyzed with single-point sensitivity analysis (Figure SI 2). The 3 most influential variables in order are target polymer mass fraction, solvent loss, and feedstock transportation distance. Sol vent loss is often cited as a make-or-break variable for dissolution-based plastic recycling, but a 10X increase in solvent loss only leads to an 18% increase in GWP while process utilities contribute to 92% of GWP.

3.4.3. Market outlook

text:
The combined shrink and stretch wrap markets produce roughly 7.2 million tons of plastic wrap annually, with approximately 70% of market share  coming  from  PE  (Standout  Insight  into  the  Global  Stretch  and Shrink Film Market Found in New Report, 2024; Sutaria, 2025). Other polymers and formulations of these films are often more expensive than PE, meaning that 70% of 7.2 million tons or 5.04 million tons of PE plastic wrap produced per year is likely a conservative estimate. The US has roughly 20% of global market share in the shrink and stretch wrap industry, leading to an estimate of just over 1 million tons of PE plastic wrap consumed in the US each year (Grand View Horizon; Bagekari, 2025). This means that a 50,000 ton STRAP plant would process 5.0% of all PE plastic wrap produced in the US each year. To collect and recycle such a significant portion of the US plastic wrap market would require a well-designed feedstock supply chain and highlights the importance of site  selection  for  future  recycling  plants.  The  ability  of  dissolution recycling to accept mixed plastic feeds would allow for PE-containing waste other than plastic wrap to be processed at the same plant, but the importance of a well-designed supply chain remains.

text: In  this  work,  we  show  the  possibility  of  applying  dissolution recycling technologies like STRAP to post consumer films. LLDPE films are often not recycled using conventional mechanical recycling tech nologies and are rarely accepted at MRFs. STRAP enables the recycling of  these  films,  specifically  shrink  wrap.  The  novelty  of  this  work  is demonstrating the circularity of contaminated waste films that are often considered difficult to recycle. We remove paper, adhesives, and inks from  the  polymeric  content  of  shrink  wrap  such  that  the  recovered polymer can be used to produce plastic articles with quality comparable to those made from virgin PE. No paper or inks are visible in the post STRAP  product  and  the  produced  films  appear  visually  clear.  We decrease the ash content from 0.96 wt% to 0.24 wt% which is a signif icant  improvement  from  the  ash  content  of  PCR  pellets  currently available (0.93 wt%). The TVOC of the post STRAP rPE is below 3.4 ppm. The CIELAB color parameters L, a, b, and YI of the post STRAP rPE cast film are 94.10, 1.53, 5.81, 9.89, respectively, which are com parable to 95.04, 1.77, 6.68, and 11.25, respectively, of the virgin LDPE/LLDPE  blend  cast  film.  TEA  indicates  that  a  plant  processing 20,000 metric tons annually of shrink wrap waste containing 85 wt% PE per year should be profitable. A STRAP plant processing 50,000 metric tons annually of shrink wrap waste (purchased at $0.25/kg) containing 85 wt% PE can achieve an IRR of 16.2% when selling rPE at $1.30/kg, an IRR of 10.7% with an rPE price of $1.00/kg, or an IRR of 3.79% with an rPE price of $0.70/kg. LCA shows a 64% reduction in global warming potential  (kg  CO2  equivalent)  when  compared  to  the  production  of virgin LDPE. The commercialization of shrink wrap circularity is highly possible yet faces some technological and economic challenges. A con stant supply chain for feed materials needs to be established. The STRAP process  needs  to  be  technically  capable  of  reducing  contaminants including odor causing residues.

ScienceDirect

Review

Computational methods in solution-based plastics purification

Ali Altamimi 1 and Reid C Van Lehn 1,2

Plastic waste can be recycled into resins with near-virgin properties by solution-based purification processes that selectively dissolve polymers, remove contaminants, or detach printing residues. In this review, we examine computational methods for predicting the behavior governing solution-based plastic purification, motivated by the vast polymer-solvent-contaminant compositional space. We discuss thermodynamic and machine learning methods for predicting polymer-solvent and polymer-contaminant interaction and review physics-based molecular dynamics simulations that resolve molecular-scale phenomena within polymer matrices inaccessible to screening methods. We highlight how these methods have informed experimental design for dissolution-based recycling and solvent-based contaminant removal. Finally, we discuss the prospective role of agentic AI in integrating these computational tools with real-time sorting data to adapt purification conditions to the compositional variability of real post-consumer feedstocks. This review charts a path toward computationally guided solutionbased purification workflows that can respond to the complexity

inherent in plastic waste streams.

Introduction

text: Recycling post-consumer plastic waste to produce polymer  resins  with  properties  comparable  to  virgin materials remains a challenge that is essential to achieving circularity in the plastics industry [1-4]. The underlying difficulty stems  from  the complexity  of plastic waste streams, which include numerous polymers and  difficult-to-remove  components  introduced  during manufacturing  and  end  use.  For  example,  multilayer films  present a  compatibility  issue upon  remelting that degrades the mechanical properties of recyclates, while printing  residues,  which  contain  polymer  binders  and pigments, compromise both the mechanical and optical properties  of  the  final  recyclate  [2,5].  Plastic  waste  can also  contain  intentionally  and  non-intentionally  added substances (which we refer to as contaminants) that are persistent, bioaccumulative, or toxic, restricting the use of  contaminated recyclates in applications such as food packaging [6,7].

The underlying difficulty stems  from  the complexity  of plastic waste streams, which include numerous polymers and  difficult-to-remove  components  introduced  during manufacturing  and  end  use.  For  example,  multilayer films  present a  compatibility  issue upon  remelting that degrades the mechanical properties of recyclates, while printing  residues,  which  contain  polymer  binders  and pigments, compromise both the mechanical and optical properties  of  the  final  recyclate  [2,5].  Plastic  waste  can also  contain  intentionally  and  non-intentionally  added substances (which we refer to as contaminants) that are persistent, bioaccumulative, or toxic, restricting the use of  contaminated recyclates in applications such as food packaging [6,7].

text: Addressing these limitations has motivated the develop ment of solution-based purification approaches, in which plastic  waste  is  contacted  with  a  liquid  medium  to  se lectively remove or recover target components (Figure 1) [4,5,8-10]. Solvent-based washing, exemplified by Norec ® ,  can  remove  inks  and  leach  non-volatile  con taminants from a swollen polymer matrix [8,9]. Aqueous surfactant  washing,  employed  by  companies  like  Cadel Deinking (now KEYCYCLE) and Sorema, targets printing  residue  removal  [8-10].  Dissolution-based  re cycling recovers purified polymer resins without chemical degradation and can separate the individual polymers in multilayer  films,  as  demonstrated  by  processes  such  as CreaSolv ® ,  Newcycling ® ,  PureCycle ® ,  and  Solvent-Tar geted Recovery and Precipitation (STRAP™) [4,11]. The feasibility,  selectivity,  and  scalability  of  these  processes are  governed  by  molecular-scale  interactions  between plastics, contaminants, and the liquid medium [4]. Iden tifying  optimal  process  conditions,  however,  is  challen ging due to the vast polymer-solvent-contaminant compositional  space,  the  inherent  complexity  of  poly meric  materials,  and  the  variability  of  real  feedstocks, motivating the development of computational methods to navigate this design space.

Computational methods for predicting polymer dissolution

A  first  challenge  in  a  solution-based  plastic  purification process is solvent selection, which requires the prediction of polymer-solvent interactions. Polymers present unique thermodynamic complexities arising from their high mo lecular  weights,  polydispersity,  chain  connectivity,  and conformational flexibility, which complicate the definition of representative molecular structures for thermodynamic calculations [12,13]. For semicrystalline polymers, an ad ditional solid-state reference contribution to the dissolu tion free energy, requiring knowledge of melting temperature and enthalpy of fusion,  must  be  accounted for, which can vary depending on resin type [14].

Computational methods for predicting polymer dissolution

A  first  challenge  in  a  solution-based  plastic  purification process is solvent selection, which requires the prediction of polymer-solvent interactions. Polymers present unique thermodynamic complexities arising from their high mo lecular  weights,  polydispersity,  chain  connectivity,  and conformational flexibility, which complicate the definition of representative molecular structures for thermodynamic calculations [12,13]. text: Semi-empirical  approaches,  including  Hildebrand  and Hansen  solubility  parameter  models  and  Flory-Huggins theory, have traditionally been used to quantify polymersolvent  compatibility  using  a  small  set  of  descriptors [15-18]. While simple and widely used, with parameters available in established databases, these methods achieve only moderate predictive accuracy; for example, a recent study  found  that  Hansen  solubility  parameters  correctly identify good and nonsolvents in 67% and 76% of cases, respectively [18]. Equation of state (EOS) models, parti cularly perturbed-chain statistical associating fluid theory (PC-SAFT),  offer  improved  treatment  of  temperatureand pressure-dependent polymer-solvent thermo dynamics,  but  require  experimentally  fitted  parameters that  must  be  refit  for  novel  systems  or  chemically  com plex mixtures [19]. COSMO-RS (Conductor-like Screening  Model  for  Real  Solvents)  addresses  this  lim itation by leveraging quantum-chemically derived charge densities  to  calculate  activity  coefficients,  from  which solubility,  miscibility,  and  partition  coefficients  can  be obtained [20]. Recent approaches have used COSMO-RS to  predict  the  solubilities  of  polymers,  biopolymers,  and biomass  materials  [21,22].  For  example,  Zhou  et  al.  de veloped a temperature-dependent solubility database by combining  conformational  sampling  based  on  all-atom (AA)  MD  simulations  with  COSMO-RS  calculations using  experimental  thermal  data  to  approximate  the  fu sion free energy of the polymer resin [11,14,23]. COSMORS polymer predictions were found to accurately predict activity  coefficients  across  a  range  of  molecular  weights, provided that MD-sourced conformers having undergone DFT  optimization  with  a  small  basis  set  are  used  to generate  realistic σ -profiles  that  accurately  capture  the residual  chemical  potential  and  that  the  combinatorial contribution,  a  separate  additive  term  derived  from  mo lecular volume, is included [12].

text: ML models offer the ability to screen polymer-solvent interactions across large chemical spaces at low compu tational cost once trained on sufficient data. ML efforts have been reviewed [17] and span a range of prediction targets from Hildebrand solubility parameters [18,24,25] to  binary  good  solvent/non-solvent  classification  using deep  learning  [26,27] and  large  language  models  [28]. While  these  approaches  are  useful  for  many  screening applications,  they  may  not  be  suitable  for  applications requiring  more  detailed  thermodynamic  information, such  as  temperature-dependent  solubility.  Other  pre dictions  have  pushed  toward  more  experimentally  re levant outputs like cloud-point temperatures [13], weight-based  infinite  dilution  activity  coefficients  [29], and PC-SAFT EOS parameters that enable full polymer-solvent  phase  equilibria  calculations  [19].  Ad ditionally,  efforts  have  standardized  polymer  solubility experiments  and  tested  multiple  concentrations  to  en able classification of soluble, insoluble, and partially so luble polymer-solvent combinations [30].

text: Recently,  these  computational  methods  have  been  ap plied to choose solvents for dissolution-based plastics re cycling. Hansen solubility parameters (HSPs) have guided  solvent  selection  for  polyethylene  (PE),  poly propylene (PP), polystyrene (PS), acrylonitrile butadiene styrene  (ABS),  polyethylene  terephthalate  (PET),  poly vinyl  chloride  (PVC),  and  ethylene-vinyl  acetate  (EVA) solvent-based  recycling  processes  [31-33].  For  example, in single-polymer dissolution-precipitation recycling, HSPs were used to identify an acetone-water system for ABS recovery  from  toy  waste  and  biobased  solvents  for rigid  PVC  recycling  [32,33].  Similarly,  COSMO-RS  has been applied to screen candidate solvents for dissolutionbased recycling of PET, PS, PVC, ABS, and high density polyethylene (HDPE), including virtual screening of over 9000  ionic  liquids  for  PET  dissolution,  identification  of selective  solvents  for  PVC  removal  from  mixed  waste streams, and optimization of dissolution-precipitation processes for PS and ABS recovery from e-waste [34-36]. This  approach  has  been  applied  extensively  for  the STRAP  process,  where  COSMO-RS  enabled  selective sequential dissolution of  PE, ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH),  and  PET  from  one  another  in  commercial multilayer  films  with  near-complete  material  recovery [11].  An  expanded polymer solubility database was sub sequently applied to printed films containing poly urethane inks, biopharmaceutical bags,  postconsumer shrink-wrap, and post-industrial mixed plastic waste containing up to ten polymers [14,23,37-39].

text: Several  critical  gaps  remain  to  broaden  the  utility  of computational  methods  for  solvent  selection.  From  a thermodynamic perspective, many current models treat the effect of molecular weight on polymer-solvent thermodynamics  using  simplified  or  monodisperse  re presentations,  limiting  their  accuracy  for  polydisperse industrial  polymers  whose  molecular  weight  distribu tions  can  span  orders  of  magnitude  [12,13].  Extending these  models  to  solvent  mixtures,  where  phenomena such as preferential solvation and cosolvency effects in troduce  complexity,  and  to  polymer  mixtures,  where dissolved  polymers  alter  solvent  quality,  could  also  in crease  opportunities  to  tune  selectivity,  reduce  cost,  or enable  greener  solvent  systems  [40-42].  Beyond  ther modynamics, computational studies should continue to address kinetic factors, such as dissolution rates and so lution viscosity, as well as precipitation phenomena like crystallization and physical gel formation [31,40,43-45]. Addressing these challenges will require closer integration  of  molecular  and  process  models,  ML  ap proaches that leverage computational descriptors to generalize  beyond  limited  experimental  datasets,  and systematic experimental data collection performed with predictive modeling in mind.

text: Whereas dissolution-based processes remove a con taminant  polymer  by  selectively  dissolving  it  from  the target resin, purification also requires removing nonpolymer  contaminants  such  as  additives,  plasticizers,  and printing  residues.  Similar  computational  methods  have been applied to guide solvent-based washing processes for contaminant removal, in which the solvent swells but does not  dissolve  the  polymer,  allowing  contaminants  to  leach into the solvent phase [8,36,46]. This process is governed by  solubility  and  diffusivity:  the  partitioning  of  the  con taminant  into  the  solvent  should  be  thermodynamically favorable,  and  the  migration  of  the  contaminant  through the swollen polymer matrix must proceed at a practical rate [36,46].  HSPs  have  been  applied  to  guide  solvent  selec tion, with the Relative Energy Difference (RED), defined as the Hansen distance (Ra) normalized by the interaction radius R0 (RED=Ra/R0), used to predict partitioning; sol vents  whose  parameters  fall  close  to  those  of  the  target contaminant  are  expected  to  yield  higher  extraction  effi ciency,  while  the  solvent's  RED  with  respect  to  the polymer  is  kept  above  1  so  that  it  does  not  dissolve [35,36,46].  A  combined  computational  approach  was  de veloped  for  the  removal  of  brominated  flame  retardants (BFRs)  from  ABS  plastic,  which  used  HSPs  to  identify candidate solvents that dissolve the BFR while leaving the polymer intact [36].  Similarly,  Zhou  et  al.  extended  their COSMO-RS-based  screening  framework  to  predict  con taminant  partition  coefficients  (LogP)  between  a  solvent phase and a polymer phase, enabling solvent selection for both  contaminant  leaching  and  contaminant  removal  in tegrated into the STRAP process [46].

text: These  limited  studies  highlight  potential  opportunities for  computational  methods  to  predict  contaminant  re moval,  but  several  challenges  point  to  important  oppor tunities  for  future  work.  First,  the  chemical  space  of potential  contaminants  is  vast;  the  PlastChem  database catalogs over 16 000 chemicals associated with plastics, of which over 4000 are hazardous, highlighting the need to combine  thermodynamic  methods  with  ML  approaches capable of rapidly screening conditions that better control the removal of families of contaminants [6]. Second, while these  methods  focus  on  the  thermodynamics  of  con taminant removal, contaminant removal is also governed by kinetic factors such as diffusion through polymer ma trices  [47,48].  Empirical  diffusivity  models  have  been used to estimate migration of contaminants in food con tact applications, demonstrating that diffusion coefficients decrease  with  increasing  migrant  molecular  weight,  in crease  exponentially  with  temperature,  and  depend  on polymer  chain  flexibility  [8,49].  However,  studies  ap plying these techniques to plastic contaminants are lim ited.  Third,  larger  contaminants  such  as  TiO2 pigment particles  are  not  well  described  by  thermodynamic  fra meworks  that  do  not  account  for  colloidal  interactions [32,50]. Fourth, these methods do not capture interfacial phenomena,  such  as  the  detachment  of  contaminants from polymer surfaces, which are central to processes like ink  removal  and  delamination  [10].  These  limitations motivate  the  use  of  particle-based  simulation  methods, which can provide mechanistic insight into contaminant removal  while  also  informing  process  optimization  stra tegies, such as surfactant selection for aqueous de-inking.

Molecular methods for mechanistic insights

text: Physics-based  MD  simulations  complement  thermo dynamic and ML-based approaches by directly resolving the molecular-scale structural and dynamic phenomena governing  processes  such  as  solvent  penetration,  con taminant  diffusion,  and  other  interfacial  interactions [51,52].  In  AA  MD  simulations,  every  atom  is  re presented explicitly with its own interaction parameters defined by a force field [53], which makes certain solu tion-based  recycling  phenomena  computationally  in feasible to model. For example, it has been established that molecular simulations are limited in their ability to capture dissolution kinetics due to the length and time scales  of  atomistic  models;  the  physics  of  polymer  dis solution has been reviewed in detail elsewhere [51,54]. AA MD simulations have been applied to more tractable phenomena in solution-based plastics purification, such as the penetration of polymers by solvents, a process that precedes  polymer  dissolution  [55].  Studies  have  also used  molecular  simulations  to  predict  the  leaching  of additives  and  plasticizers  from  polymers  [56].  While contaminant removal is dictated by solvent penetration and  additive  leaching,  MD  has  seen  limited  use  in guiding  solvent  selection  for  this  application;  recent work  has  compared  candidate  solvents  for  separating additives  from  PVC  [57],  but  capturing  these  relation ships  across  the  broad  range  of  relevant  polymers  and contaminants continues to present modeling challenges.

text: Coarse-grained  (CG)  MD  simulations  group  atoms  into effective  'beads'  to  access  longer  timescales  and  larger length scales while retaining a semi-quantitative level of accuracy. For example, the MARTINI CG model maps groups  of ∼ 4  heavy  atoms  onto  beads  and  has  enabled systematic  CG  modeling  of  a  broad  range  of  polymer systems  [58].  CG  simulations  have  been  valuable  for studying  slow  transport  and  interfacial  phenomena,  in cluding  plasticizer  migration  in  PVC  [59],  solvent  diffu sion  in  PS  dissolution  [52],  solvent  swelling  of  polymer brushes  [60],  and  solvent  evaporation  from  polymercontaining  systems  [61],  where  the  extended  timescales accessible at the CG level are essential to capturing the underlying  physics.  The  behavior  of  contaminants  as medium-sized molecules embedded in polymer matrices has  also  been  investigated  [62,63],  including  leaching dynamics  that  are  relevant  to  contaminant  removal  in recycling  contexts  [64].  Beyond  transport  phenomena, CG simulations  have  been  coupled  with  the  PC-SAFT EOS to better describe complex phase behavior [65], and have  been  used  to  characterize  polymer-solvent  inter facial  structure  [66].  CG  approaches  have  recently  been extended  to  surfactant-mediated  de-inking,  a  pretreat ment  process  in  which  ground  plastics  are  washed  in surfactant solutions to remove printing inks from singlelayer  films  and  rigid  materials  [10].  Altamimi  et  al.  le veraged  CG  MD  simulations  to  quantify  binder  deso rption free energies in the presence  of a range of surfactants,  demonstrating  that  charged  surfactants  re duce the energy barrier for binder desorption to achieve increased  experimental  de-inking  efficiency  [67].  These results  provide  molecular-level  guidance  for  surfactant selection and motivate future studies to consider pigment dispersibility  in  surfactant  micelles,  corona  treatment  of polymer surfaces, and a broader range of binder types.

text: In the preceding sections, we highlighted computational methods  that  can  screen  large  libraries  of  polymers, solvents, and contaminants and demonstrated their use in informing process design. A potential opportunity for future development is the integration of these methods with  AI  to  process  real-world  feedstocks.  Agentic  AI systems, in which autonomous AI agents plan and exe cute multi-step tasks with minimal human intervention, are  well-suited  for  these  challenges  [71,72].  Such  sys tems can orchestrate the computational tools discussed in  this  review  alongside  real-time  sensor  data  and  ex ternal regulatory information, enabling process re commendations that adapt to variable feedstock compositions and evolving contaminant regulations. To illustrate  this  vision,  we  consider how agentic AI could be  integrated  across  the  plastics  recycling  process,  in cluding sorting at advanced materials recycling facilities (MRFs), pretreatment, and reprocessing (Figure 2).

text: MRFs separate commingled recyclables and sort plastics into commodity bales [73]. Advances in near-IR imaging, AI-assisted  robotic  sorting,  and  complementary  spectro scopic  methods  now  enable  near-real-time  identification of polymer type and, increasingly, chemical contaminants in waste streams [74-76]. These techniques are well es tablished  for  single-layer  plastics,  while  identification  of multilayer  materials  is  more  challenging  and  remains  an area of active development [77]. Coupling these detection capabilities  with  the  thermodynamic  and  ML  tools  dis cussed above could help assess whether a contaminated feedstock  requires  additional  purification,  thereby  in tegrating upstream contaminant identification with downstream process selection. For example, detection of regulated  contaminants  could  flag  a  feedstock  for  a  tar geted solvent-based leaching step, heavily printed plastics could  be  routed  to  aqueous  washing,  while  relatively clean  feedstocks  proceed  with  venting-only  mechanical recycling.  Complementary  modeling  of  chemical  migra tion through food contact materials could further inform pretreatment  by  predicting  migration  rates  through  dif ferent  polymers  [78].  More  broadly,  the  rich  material characterization data generated by these sensing systems creates  an  opportunity  for  agentic  frameworks that  relay feedstock  information  downstream  and  adaptively  re commend process adjustments to recycling and purifica tion conditions in response to material variability.

MRFs separate commingled recyclables and sort plastics into commodity bales [73]. Advances in near-IR imaging, AI-assisted  robotic  sorting,  and  complementary  spectro scopic  methods  now  enable  near-real-time  identification of polymer type and, increasingly, chemical contaminants in waste streams [74-76]. These techniques are well es tablished  for  single-layer  plastics,  while  identification  of multilayer  materials  is  more  challenging  and  remains  an area of active development [77]. Coupling these detection capabilities  with  the  thermodynamic  and  ML  tools  dis cussed above could help assess whether a contaminated feedstock  requires  additional  purification,  thereby  in tegrating upstream contaminant identification with downstream process selection. For example, detection of regulated  contaminants  could  flag  a  feedstock  for  a  tar geted solvent-based leaching step, heavily printed plastics could  be  routed  to  aqueous  washing,  while  relatively clean  feedstocks  proceed  with  venting-only  mechanical recycling.  Complementary  modeling  of  chemical  migra tion through food contact materials could further inform pretreatment  by  predicting  migration  rates  through  dif ferent  polymers  [78].  More  broadly,  the  rich  material characterization data generated by these sensing systems creates  an  opportunity  for  agentic  frameworks that  relay feedstock  information  downstream  and  adaptively  re commend process adjustments to recycling and purifica tion conditions in response to material variability.

text: Downstream of  automated  sorting  and  contaminant  iden tification,  adaptive  process  control  could  guide  decisionmaking  across  recycling  approaches,  though  its  feasibility varies substantially with process complexity. This has been pursued  in  mechanical  recycling  through  real-time  spec troscopic  analysis  and  in-line  melt  rheometry  to  adjust processing parameters in response to feedstock varia bility  [79,80];  however,  such  control  is  constrained  to  a narrow  range  of  process  parameters.  In  dissolution-based recycling, adaptive approaches are a more challenging pro spect due to cost and safety constraints, but agentic process design with human oversight could align solvent selection, temperature,  and  processing  time  with  incoming  polymer composition and contamination state. For contaminant re moval, thermodynamic frameworks could be integrated into agentic  workflows  that  autonomously  screen  new  con taminant  chemistries  and  recommend  process  conditions for adaptive, feedstock-aware purification.

text: Solution-based  plastics  purification  encompasses  a  broad and interconnected set of challenges, ranging from selec tive  dissolution  for  separating  polymers  in  multilayer  and mixed-plastic  waste,  to  solvent-  and  aqueous-based  con taminant  removal,  that  benefit  from  a  combination  of computational approaches to accurately guide process de sign.  Thermodynamic  approaches  such  as  COSMO-RS provide  accurate  predictions  of  polymer-contaminant-sol vent  interactions,  molecular  simulations  reveal  the  me chanistic detail of interfacial and transport phenomena that screening-level  methods  cannot  access,  and  ML  models offer  the  throughput  needed  to  navigate  vast  chemical spaces when adequate training data is available. Refining these methods, however, requires broader standardization of  condition-resolved  experimental  datasets,  molecularweight-dependent  solubility  predictions  for  polydisperse industrial  polymers,  more  broadly  applicable  contaminant leaching models for swollen polymer matrices, and higherthroughput,  physically  realistic  simulation  frameworks  to guide the rational design of surfactant formulations. Looking  forward,  integrating  upstream  sensing,  thermo dynamic  screening,  and  agentic  AI  frameworks  into  uni fied, feedstock-adaptive workflows, with appropriate human oversight,  offers  a  promising  path  toward  compu tational  guidance  that  can  better  accommodate  the  varia bility inherent in real post-consumer plastic waste streams.

Solution-based  plastics  purification  encompasses  a  broad and interconnected set of challenges, ranging from selec tive  dissolution  for  separating  polymers  in  multilayer  and mixed-plastic  waste,  to  solvent-  and  aqueous-based  con taminant  removal,  that  benefit  from  a  combination  of computational approaches to accurately guide process de sign.  Thermodynamic  approaches  such  as  COSMO-RS provide  accurate  predictions  of  polymer-contaminant-sol vent  interactions,  molecular  simulations  reveal  the  me chanistic detail of interfacial and transport phenomena that screening-level  methods  cannot  access,  and  ML  models offer  the  throughput  needed  to  navigate  vast  chemical spaces when adequate training data is available. Refining these methods, however, requires broader standardization of  condition-resolved  experimental  datasets,  molecularweight-dependent  solubility  predictions  for  polydisperse industrial  polymers,  more  broadly  applicable  contaminant leaching models for swollen polymer matrices, and higherthroughput,  physically  realistic  simulation  frameworks  to guide the rational design of surfactant formulations. Looking  forward,  integrating  upstream  sensing,  thermo dynamic  screening,  and  agentic  AI  frameworks  into  uni fied, feedstock-adaptive workflows, with appropriate human oversight,  offers  a  promising  path  toward  compu tational  guidance  that  can  better  accommodate  the  varia bility inherent in real post-consumer plastic waste streams.

In ∼ 0.25 M surfactant solutions, up to a 52% reduction in the free energy barrier is computed, with trends in good agreement ( R 2 = 0.92, Pearson ' s r = -0.96, Spearman ' s ρ = -0.83) with experimental de-inking e ffi ciencies. text: Global plastic production is expected to rise to 884 million tons by 2050, yet less than 10% of plastics are currently recycled, and many recycled materials have reduced value due to altered physical properties. 1 -3 Mechanical recycling, a process in which plastics are rinsed and re-molded via extrusion, is the most prevalent approach for recycling plastics. 4 A major challenge for mechanical recycling is that it cannot remove embedded or strongly adsorbed contaminants. For example, roughly 70% of plastic fi lm waste is printed with inks, which need to be removed to reintegrate printed plastics into manufacturing streams. 5,6 Incomplete removal of printed inks from plastic substrates can alter the color and transparency of the recycled plastics, create defects that impact the mechanical properties of the recycled fi lms, and introduce odorous or migratable degraded ink species. 7,8

text: Some technologies have emerged for recycling printed postindustrial plastic waste. One approach involves fi ltration, homogenization, and degassing of the hot melt during extrusion. 13,14 This process has been patented by EREMA and is e ff ective for low ink loads, but the products of this process are generally still downcycled into lower grade products. 13 Other approaches rely on exposing the plastics to organic solvents in which the inks are soluble; however, this is mainly oriented towards multilayer fi lms and is less desirable due to the cost and potential residues of organic solvents. 15,16 These considerations have motivated the development and implementation of de-inking processes for highly printed single-layer fi lms and rigid plastic materials (i.e., rigids) that rely on washing the ground plastics in a caustic aqueous solution with surfactants before drying, pelletizing, and extruding them into clear fi lms.

Some technologies have emerged for recycling printed postindustrial plastic waste. One approach involves fi ltration, homogenization, and degassing of the hot melt during extrusion. 13,14 This process has been patented by EREMA and is e ff ective for low ink loads, but the products of this process are generally still downcycled into lower grade products. 13 Other approaches rely on exposing the plastics to organic solvents in which the inks are soluble; however, this is mainly oriented towards multilayer fi lms and is less desirable due to the cost and potential residues of organic solvents. 15,16 These considerations have motivated the development and implementation of de-inking processes for highly printed single-layer fi lms and rigid plastic materials (i.e., rigids) that rely on washing the ground plastics in a caustic aqueous solution with surfactants before drying, pelletizing, and extruding them into clear fi lms.

text: Scamehorn et al. explored the e ffi ciency of surfactants for de-inking in a series of papers. 6,17 -21 This work found that surfactant type (cationic, anionic, amphoteric, or nonionic) and concentration, ink type (solvent or water-based), solution pH, experiment duration, and mechanical agitation all impacted de-inking of plastic fi lms and rigids. Surfactant-mediated deinking was demonstrated at the semi-industrial scale in the Cadel Deinking plant (now KEYCYCLE, an EREMA group subsidiary) using 0.1 -5% by weight cetrimonium bromide (CTAB), dodecyltrimethylammonium bromide (DTAB), or dodecyl sulfate (SDS) surfactant solutions between pH 11 and 13. 22 Another patented process from Duchenaud Uni fl exo used nonionic surfactants, including alkoxylated alcohols (AEOs) or alkyl polyglycosides (APGs), along with an organic solvent and an alkaline aqueous solution to achieve high deinking e ffi ciency. 22 The Italian companies Sorema and Gamma Meccanica use a similar approach with the former commercializing a batch de-inking line and the latter o ff ering ECO CLEAN with detergent formulations for fl exible printed fi lms. 22,23 Recently, surfactant-based de-inking mechanisms have been tested in advanced plastics recycling technologies. Ügdüler et al. reported that the addition of cationic surfactants improved the removal of cellulosic and acrylic inks, 24 although Sánchez-Rivera et al. found that surfactant-based de-inking was less e ff ective for color removal with multi-layered reverseprinted plastic fi lms. 25 In a related application, aqueous surfactant solutions with small amounts of a good solvent for the ink have been used for the removal of hydrophobic polymer coatings from artistic surfaces. 26,27 While there is signi fi cant interest in surfactant-based de-inking, the mechanism of the process remain poorly understood, limiting the ability to rationally optimize surfactant formulations and other process parameters.

text: De-inking above the surfactant critical micelle concentration (CMC) is hypothesized to proceed by a process similar to textile laundering that consists of three steps: surface wetting, solubilization, and ink detachment and dispersion. 6 Good wetting of the plastic surface through the formation of a surfactant monolayer is expected, which reduces the ink-water and plastic-water surface tensions. 19 Next, hydrophobic segments of the binder are solubilized into surfactant micelles while larger binder fragments are stabilized by surfactant adsorption onto their surfaces, as has been discussed for cross-linked binders. 6 Additional stabilization may arise through electrostatic interactions for charged binders or ion-dipole interactions for binders with π -electron rich aromatic rings. 6 Once detached, inksurfactant complexes are dispersed and prevented from readsorbing to the surface by electrostatic repulsion with the surfactant-wetted surface. 6 As in typical laundering, surfactants that e ffi ciently solubilize hydrophobic compounds and stabilize detached particles are preferred. For example, previous work reported complete de-inking using CTAB at a concentration 4 × the CMC, tetradecyltrimethylammonium bromide (TTAB) at 8 × the CMC, and DTAB at 24 × the CMC for a solvent-based epoxy ink screen-printed on high-density polyethylene. 19 Cationic surfactants are generally preferred for deinking because binders like nitrocellulose and acrylates become negatively charged through alkaline hydrolysis, leading to strong electrostatic interactions. 6,28 However, anionic, amphoteric, and nonionic surfactants have also been tested with varying results under di ff erent conditions. 6,20,21 Despite continued interest in surfactant-based de-inking, it is not clear how molecular-scale surfactant organization impacts the underlying interfacial phenomena of surface wetting and binder solubilization and detachment. This knowledge gap, along with continued uncertainty regarding molecular mechanisms of de-inking, motivates mechanistic investigation of surfactant-mediated de-inking through molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, which have provided useful insights for a range of related phenomena. 29 -34

In this work, we used all atom (AA) and coarse-grained (CG) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations alongside alkaline surfactant washing experiments to investigate the interactions between CTAB, TTAB, DTAB, STS, SDS, DOSS, DDAO and AEO5 surfactants and a high molecular weight polyether urethane (PEU) binder in solution and on a polyethylene (PE) surface. To model appropriately large system sizes while retaining molecular-scale chemical details, we develop a CG PEU model and show through desorption free energy calculations that charged surfactants favor de-inking while neutral surfactants only slightly promote de-inking relative to water. Experimental alkaline surfactant washing trials show the same rank-ordering of surfactant de-inking e ffi ciency, providing experimental support to corroborate that simulated desorption free energies for the simpli fi ed simulation systems can predict de-inking. Based on these fi ndings, we propose three regimes of de-inking (good, moderate, and poor) which are related to the packing e ffi ciency of surfactants around the binder as is demonstrated by the coverage levels and morphology of the binder in di ff erent surfactants throughout the desorption process. Together, these results provide quantitative insights into the thermodynamics of surfactant-mediated de-inking and elucidate di ff erent aspects of the mechanism of this process.

Based on these fi ndings, we propose three regimes of de-inking (good, moderate, and poor) which are related to the packing e ffi ciency of surfactants around the binder as is demonstrated by the coverage levels and morphology of the binder in di ff erent surfactants throughout the desorption process. Together, these results provide quantitative insights into the thermodynamics of surfactant-mediated de-inking and elucidate di ff erent aspects of the mechanism of this process.

Surfactants were selected based on a wide range of de-inking studies 6,17 -21 and were all modeled at concentrations above their CMC to re fl ect our experimental conditions (Figure 1; see fi gure for surfactant names and acronyms). Quaternary ammonium surfactants are widely used in detergent formulations and have demonstrated good de-inking, so we selected surfactants with variations in alkyl tail length. Similarly, we selected anionic surfactants with varying tail length (STS and SDS) and morphology (DOSS) that have been tested in de-inking experiments. Amphoteric (DDAO) and non-ionic surfactants (AEO, AMEOs, etc.) have been tested in de-inking experiments as well so we selected a representative non-ionic AEO 5 surfactant for comparison to the charged surfactants.

The samples were then recovered, fi ltered, and dried in a vacuum oven overnight at 60 °C prior to scanning.

Plastic samples before and after surfactant treatment were scanned using a Canon LiTE 400 scanner at 600 dpi resolution. The resulting images were analyzed using ImageJ software to quantify ink removal. A threshold value was applied to each scanned image to identify and count the remaining ink pixels after treatment. De-inking e ffi ciency was calculated by comparing the pixel count of treated samples to the initial untreated sample, allowing for quantitative assessment of ink removal performance across di ff erent surfactant formulations.

All-Atom Molecular Dynamics Simulation Parameters

For AA MD simulations, all system components were parameterized using the Generalized Amber Force Field (GAFF). 37 GAFF has been widely validated for reproducing experimental surfactant interfacial properties, including interfacial and surface tensions of ionic and nonionic surfactants, surface excess concentration at the CMC, and selfassembled morphologies with reasonable accuracy. 38 -41 Water was modeled using the TIP3P force fi eld. MD simulations were performed using a leapfrog integrator with a 2 fs timestep using Gromacs

text: For CG MD simulations, all system components were parameterized using the MARTINI 3 force fi eld. 44 MARTINI employs a parameterization strategy in which nonbonded interactions are calibrated against experimental partitioning free energies while bonded interactions are derived from reference AA simulations. 44 As such, CG models parameterized against AA (GAFF) reference data are expected to inherit the reasonable experimental agreement demonstrated by the underlying AA force fi eld. 44 For surfactants, bead types were chosen based on literature precedents for CTAB, TTAB, DTAB, 45 and AEO5 46 (Figure 2d). Polymer bead types were based on mapping schemes previously described for other systems using the MARTINI 3 forcefi eld. 44,47,48 The bead types of polar functional groups were iteratively updated until the computed SASA and radius of gyration (R g ), de fi ned as the mass-weighted root-mean-square distance of all atoms from the center of mass of the molecule (illustrated in SI Figure S2b), 49 for the CG system in representative ' good ' and ' poor ' solvents showed good agreement with an AA system of the same size. For example, increasing the attractiveness of the carbamate functional group in the urethane bond (P3 to P6) and increasing the repulsiveness of the ether bond in the soft segment of PEU (SN3 to SN1) resulted in good agreement between AA and CG models for PEU in water (discussed in more detail in the Results). Bonded interactions for the CG models were initialized by de fi ning bonds and angles with generic force constants. These parameters were then iteratively updated for both surfactants and a PEU trimer using Swarm-CG, which employs a particle swarm optimization algorithm to minimize the di ff erence between CG and mapped AA bond/angle distributions (SI Figures S3 -10). 50

text: The trimer parameters served as inputs for a custom polyply fi le, which builds the polymer chain by repeating the central repeat unit of the trimer while preserving the terminal units to capture endgroup e ff ects. We constructed a 24,282 g/mol CG PEU binder topology, though this approach is generalizable to PEU chains of arbitrary lengths. The fully extended contour length ( L c ≈ 118 nm) was estimated by summing the equilibrium bond lengths along the shortest backbone path through the CG topology, providing a reference scale for interpreting desorption distances. This molecular weight was chosen to balance approximating physical binder molecular weights (10,000 + g/mol) with practical simulation system size constraints.

The trimer parameters served as inputs for a custom polyply fi le, which builds the polymer chain by repeating the central repeat unit of the trimer while preserving the terminal units to capture endgroup e ff ects. We constructed a 24,282 g/mol CG PEU binder topology, though this approach is generalizable to PEU chains of arbitrary lengths. The fully extended contour length ( L c ≈ 118 nm) was estimated by summing the equilibrium bond lengths along the shortest backbone path through the CG topology, providing a reference scale for interpreting desorption distances. This molecular weight was chosen to balance approximating physical binder molecular weights (10,000 + g/mol) with practical simulation system size constraints.

text: The thin fi lm system was constructed by generating a PE layer with 85 chains, each containing 200 CG beads (representing 400 ethylene repeat units) yielding a 1.1 g/cm 3 slab spanning 6 nm in the z direction and 17 nm in the x and y directions using polyply (Figure 2c). 51 A 13,583 nm 3 water box (100,000 CG water molecules) with dimensions of 17 × 17 × 47 nm 3 was added at the edge of the PE fi lm to ensure adequate room for desorption of PEU. The system underwent steepest descent energy minimization and was equilibrated for 5 ns in the NPT ensemble using a semi-isotropic barostat. The binder was then added in solution (replacing solvent molecules) and the system was equilibrated in the NVT ensemble for 3 ns. To generate a PE-adsorbed initial con fi guration, the binder was pulled toward the PE surface in the z -direction over 2 ns using a moving harmonic restraint with a force constant of 1000 kJ/mol · nm 2 and a pull rate of 0.008 nm/ps. This pulling step was used solely for system preparation; the pulling restraint was then removed, and the adsorbed system was equilibrated for 1.2 μ s in the NVT ensemble, allowing for complete spreading of PEU on the PE surface as veri fi ed by convergence of the PEU R g and end-toend distance (SI Figure S11). Restraints were added to PE in the presence of PEU and in subsequent simulations to avoid intercalation of the PEU into PE or distortion of the thin fi lm structure. Surfactants were then added to the system using random coordinates between 8 and 40 nm in the z direction and spanning the xy plane to ensure no initial contact between the surfactants and PE surface. All surfactant systems were simulated at a concentration of 0.25 M except AEO 5 , which was simulated at ∼ 0.18 M due to instability during NPT equilibration at higher concentrations arising from its lower aqueous solubility. Additionally, DDAO systems were simulated at 315 K (42 °C) rather than 300 K (27 °C) to suppress an arti fi cial water freezing artifact associated with the MARTINI 3 force fi eld in systems containing solid surfaces and charged species, as discussed further in the Results. Although our de-inking experiments are performed at ∼ 80 °C, our primary simulations were carried out at 27 °C (300 K). This is done to establish our methodology under conditions where MARTINI 3 is best benchmarked, as the force fi eld is parameterized against experimental partitioning free energies at 298 K and may exhibit temperature transferability limitations away from this reference. 52 -54 Additional simulations performed at 0.15 M and at 27/80 °C verify that trends in desorption free energies are robust to concentration and temperature; these are discussed in the Results and Supporting Information. Simulations performed at 0.25 M and 27 °C with additional 0.25 M NaCl further verify robustness to salinity and approximate the ionic strength of the experimental 2 wt % NaOH de-inking solution. Di ff erent random coordinates were used for each independent simulation replica. Each system then underwent energy minimization, 5 ns of semi-isotropic NPT equilibration, and 3 ns of NVT equilibration.

All CG MD simulations were performed using a leapfrog integrator with a 20 fs timestep using Gromacs 2021.5. 42 Verlet lists were generated using a 1.1 nm neighbor list cuto ff . Van der Waals interactions were modeled with a shifted Lennard-Jones potential. Electrostatic interactions were calculated using the reaction- fi eld method with a cuto ff of 1.1 nm and a dielectric constant of 15. Temperature coupling was controlled with the velocity-rescale thermostat at 300 K with a relaxation time of 1 ps. The Berendsen barostat was used with a 4 ps time constant and an isothermal compressibility of 3 × 10 -4 bar -1 . Position restraints were applied to PE atoms with a force constant of 400 kJ/mol · nm 2 . Initial velocities were generated from a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at 300 K.

text: CG umbrella sampling (US) simulations were performed to compute the free energy for desorbing the PEU binder from PE. Dz was de fi ned as the collective variable for US and quanti fi es the distance, projected onto the z -axis, between the center of mass of PEU and the center of mass of PE. Dz is reported in units of nm and was calculated in GROMACS. The ratio Dz / L c serves as a measure of chain anchoring to the surface: small Dz / L c indicates more favorable detachment of adsorbed segments, while large Dz / L c re fl ects persistent polymersurface contacts (trains) that must be sequentially peeled before full desorption. 33,55 All US simulations used an umbrella potential between the reference groups with a force constant of 1000 kJ/mol · nm 2 . US was performed using independent simulation windows restrained to values of Dz from 3.0 to 18.0 nm (or until desorption) in 0.25 nm increments. US windows were simulated sequentially in increasing increments of Dz , with the fi nal con fi guration of each window used as the initial con fi guration for the next window corresponding to an increased value Dz . This approach ensured that surfactants remained in contact with PEU throughout all windows during the desorption process. All windows starting at 3.25 nm were simulated for 50 ns, except for a 2 μ s equilibration that was performed for Dz = 4.75 nm. This distance corresponds to the transition of PEU from a spread to droplet con fi guration on the PE surface, at which surfactants were found to aggregate on the protruded PEU polymer (SI Figure S11). Additional equilibration for this window maximized PEU-surfactant interactions during desorption and led to lower free energy and more consistent replicate results. Potentials of mean force (PMFs) were calculated using the Weighted Histogram Analysis Method (WHAM). 56 Convergence was assessed by varying beginning cuto ff times as well as varying the segments of beginning and end times (SI Figures S12 and S13). To analyze the US trajectories, the SASA and R g for the complete trajectories were calculated.

■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Experimental De-Inking Reveals Distinct Performance Di ff erences

To establish a baseline understanding of surfactant performance in polymer de-inking, we fi rst conducted experimental de-inking trials on materials that our computational models were designed to represent. We selected eight surfactants spanning cationic, anionic, zwitterionic, and nonionic surfactants with CMCs ranging from 0.76 to 16 mM (Figure 1). These choices were intended to probe how surfactant headgroup chemistry, chain length, and self-assembly behavior in fl uence de-inking e ffi ciency.

■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Experimental De-Inking Reveals Distinct Performance Di ff erences

To establish a baseline understanding of surfactant performance in polymer de-inking, we fi rst conducted experimental de-inking trials on materials that our computational models were designed to represent. We selected eight surfactants spanning cationic, anionic, zwitterionic, and nonionic surfactants with CMCs ranging from 0.76 to 16 mM (Figure 1). These choices were intended to probe how surfactant headgroup chemistry, chain length, and self-assembly behavior in fl uence de-inking e ffi ciency.

text: Figure 3 summarizes measured de-inking e ffi ciencies. CTAB demonstrated the best de-inking e ffi ciency with 95.4% ( ± 2%) color removal compared to all other surfactants. The shorterchain quaternary ammonium surfactants DTAB (88.9% ± 3%) and TTAB (89.4% ± 4%), along with the anionic STS (87.9% ± 5%), exhibited comparable de-inking e ffi ciencies, forming a second group of comparable performance. SDS (72.1% ± 13%) and DDAO (71.3% ± 18%) showed moderate de-inking capability but with notably higher variability between replicates. The nonionic surfactant AEO5 (23.8% ± 15%) and the branched surfactant DOSS (7.2% ± 8%) were the poorest performers, achieving minimal ink removal from the plastic substrates. These results indicate that there is no simple relationship between de-inking and surfactant properties like the CMC, headgroup charge, or tail group length, motivating computational analysis to investigate the origin of the observed de-inking trends.

Ink removal percentages show that CTAB achieves the best performance ( > 95%) while DTAB, TTAB, and STS achieve good performance ( ∼ 89% removal), SDS and DDAO demonstrate moderate performance ( ∼ 72%), and DOSS and AEO 5 exhibit poor de-inking performance ( < 25%). Representative photographs of washed plastic fi lm samples (bottom) illustrate the contrast between high ink removal (left) and low ink removal (right) conditions.

Surfactant Charge Leads to Di ff erences in Solution-State Binder Coverage

Our experimental results suggest that increasing the alkyl tail length of ionic surfactants improves de-inking while introducing branched or zwitterionic/nonionic surfactants inhibits deinking. As a fi rst step toward understanding the molecularscale interactions governing these trends, we performed unbiased, all-atom MD simulations to quantify surfactant interactions with the PEU binder in aqueous solution. Based on previous reports that surfactants with longer tails favor deinking due to increased adsorption of the tail to hydrophobic parts of the binder, 17 we hypothesized that the bestperforming surfactants from our experiments would have the greatest binder coverage in our simulations.

Our experimental results suggest that increasing the alkyl tail length of ionic surfactants improves de-inking while introducing branched or zwitterionic/nonionic surfactants inhibits deinking. As a fi rst step toward understanding the molecularscale interactions governing these trends, we performed unbiased, all-atom MD simulations to quantify surfactant interactions with the PEU binder in aqueous solution. Based on previous reports that surfactants with longer tails favor deinking due to increased adsorption of the tail to hydrophobic parts of the binder, 17 we hypothesized that the bestperforming surfactants from our experiments would have the greatest binder coverage in our simulations.

text: We fi rst simulated the PEU binder in water in the absence of any surfactant, which led to the collapse of the polymer into a single, nearly spherical globule whose SASA is shown in Figure 4. This conformation is consistent with the behavior of polymers in poor solvents and the hydrophobic nature of the binder. Coverage of the binder surface by surfactants would thus be expected to decrease the SASA, thereby increasing binder stability in solution which could correlate with improved de-inking. We observe surfactant coverage of the binder that is generally consistent with experimental de-inking trends, with longer alkyl tail lengths producing greater coverage based on analysis of the SASA (Figure 4). Among the cationic surfactants, CTAB exhibited the greatest coverage (lowest SASA), followed by TTAB and then DTAB as the tail length decreased. A similar trend was observed for the anionic surfactants, with STS exhibiting greater coverage than SDS. However, DOSS exhibited very high coverage with a SASA near zero despite its poor deinking e ffi ciency (Figure 3), indicating that binder coverage alone does not fully explain the de-inking trends. Unlike most charged surfactants, the zwitterionic and uncharged surfactants DDAO and AEO5 tended to form a single aggregate with the binder, leading to low SASA and few surfactants remaining in solution. These simulations were also repeated with a 30,173 g/mol PEU binder with a larger polyol unit, which yielded consistent surfactant coverage trends, with the exception that DTAB exhibited the greatest coverage among the cationic surfactants (SI Figure S1). These results motivated further investigation of the de-inking ability of di ff erent surfactants as binder coverage alone does not align with the de-inking results in Figure 3 or prior experimental reports of the best surfactants for de-inking. 6,17 -21

Because surfactant coverage of PEU in solution was insu ffi cient to explain trends in de-inking e ffi ciency, we next sought to model a more complete process of surfactant-mediated desorption of PEU from a PE thin fi lm. Such simulations are too computationally expensive to perform at AA resolution, motivating the development of a CG simulation representation of the PEU and surfactant systems. As detailed in the Methods, we parameterized PEU and the surfactants using the MARTINI 3 CG force fi eld, 44 with CG bead types (which de fi ne nonbonded interactions) summarized in Figure 2. PEU bonded parameters were obtained based on a CG PEU trimer input to polyply and these generally agreed well with the AA bonded parameters (SI Figure S3).

text: Accurate parameterization of the solution properties of the CG PEU model was con fi rmed by comparing the structural properties of PEU (13,200 g/mol, 32 repeat units) in water (a ' poor ' solvent) and dimethylacetamide (DMAc; a ' good ' solvent) using both AA and CG simulations (Figure 5a). Good agreement was obtained in water with SASA and R g values of 56.3 nm 2 and 1.3 nm for the AA model and 49.3 nm 2 and 1.2 nm for the CG model (Figure 5b). In DMAc, higher SASA and R g values of 165.3 nm 2 and 2.8 nm were obtained for the AA model compared to 92.5 nm 2 and 1.9 nm for the CG model. Since we are primarily concerned with the solution behavior of PEU in water, and the CG model does correctly predict larger SASA and R g values in DMAc compared to water, the larger deviation between AA and CG structural parameters in DMAc was considered acceptable. Close agreement between the AA and CG SASA values for a single surfactant in water with one counterion were also obtained for all surfactants (Figure 5C) after adopting literature mapping schemes and parametrizing bonded parameters using SwarmCG (SI Figures S4 -S10). 50 We further computed the water contact angle on the CG PE surface using a sessile drop method, as detailed in the Supporting Information (SI Figure S14). The water contact angle was computed to be 100.2 ° , which agrees well with experimental values of 96 -103 ° for virgin LDPE. 12,57 Overall, these comparisons indicate that the MARTINI 3 CG parameters can reliably reproduce AA or experimental values for the custom components of our system.

text: To model PEU desorption, US was performed using a sequential approach as described in the Methods. Potentials of mean force (PMFs) associated with desorption in pure water (HOH) or in a 0.15 M CTAB solution at 27 °C are compared in Figure 6A; results at 0.25 M are presented below. Although our de-inking experiments are performed at 80 °C to accelerate de-inking kinetics, 24 our primary simulations were performed at 27 °C, where the MARTINI 3 force fi eld is most reliable. 52 -54 Since both experiments and simulations are performed well above the CMC of each surfactant, this temperature di ff erence is not expected to alter the underlying driving forces captured by our PMFs. Additional simulations at 80 °C were also performed to con fi rm the robustness of this approach, as discussed below. Similarly, experiments were performed in 2% NaOH but all simulations were performed without added electrolyte because the MARTINI 3 force fi eld models a weakly screened environment by setting a system-wide dielectric constant of 15 and using a short-range electrostatic potential. Prior experimental studies of the e ff ect of salinity on de-inking using charged surfactants suggest that salt contributes to de-inking predominantly through reducing the surfactant CMC, 18 but as all simulations are performed at concentrations substantially higher than the CMC added salt is not expected to in fl uence the simulation results, as con fi rmed by additional simulations described below.

text: Two PMFs are computed for both systems, initiated from independent initial con fi gurations, to quantify uncertainty. Both sets of PMFs show well-de fi ned global minima for Dz = 3.5 nm, indicating a thermodynamic preference for the PEU to adsorb to the PE surface as expected. The PMF then increases with D z until plateauing for large values of Dz , corresponding to the PEU fully desorbing into the surrounding solution. Since the PMF can be interpreted as the variation in the free energy as a function of Dz , we thus associate the di ff erence in the PMF between its global minimum value (arbitrarily set to a value of zero) and its plateau value as the magnitude of the desorption free energy. Smaller values of the desorption free energy indicate that desorption can more readily occur, which we would associate with increased de-inking in experiments. Figure 6A shows that, as expected, the two PMFs for desorption in CTAB correspond to substantially lower desorption free energies (330 and 510 kJ/mol) than the two PMFs for desorption in pure water (830 and 890 kJ/mol), representing a reduction of up to 500 kJ/mol (discussed further below). These data indicate that surfactant molecules can reduce free energy barriers for desorption, in agreement with our core hypothesis that desorption thermodynamics in fl uences de-inking e ffi cacy.

Surfactants A ff ect PEU Structure During Desorption

text: Figure 6A shows simulation snapshots that illustrate key structural changes in the PEU binder during desorption. These metrics, namely SASA and R g , are further quanti fi ed in Figure 6B. We additionally computed the relative shape anisotropy κ 2 , a dimensionless descriptor derived from the eigenvalues of the gyration tensor that is bounded between 0 (for a spherical mass distribution) and 1 (for a fully linear, extended mass distribution), to distinguish isotropic from anisotropic changes in chain conformation during desorption (SI Figure S16). 59,60 PEU fi rst adopts a con fi guration that can favorably interact with the surfactant micelles present in solution. The structural change in PEU during this onset of desorption is marked by a decrease in R g at Dz = 4.75 nm. The PEU SASA decreases substantially at this value of Dz for the CTAB solution, signifying interactions between the PEU and surfactants in solution (Figure 6B). For the plateau region of Dz , the PEU is completely desorbed from the surface and collapses into a globule in pure water, leading to decreased SASA and R g values. These structural changes accompany the gradual rise in the PMF between the global minimum and the plateau and re fl ect the sequential detachment of adsorbed polymer segments from the PE surface. text: Based on our analysis, we delineate three mechanistic steps in the surfactant-mediated desorption process, each associated with characteristic D z values during US and illustrated by representative simulation snapshots in Figure 6A. (I) Dissociation : the binder is dislodged from its equilibrium spread con fi guration on the PE surface, reaching an R g minimum at Dz = 4.5 nm that is characterized by a droplet-like con fi guration that facilitates interactions with surfactants. (II) Stabilization : Surfactant micelles subsequently stabilize the partially detached binder to maintain its low R g and SASA values. Di ff erences in the PMF slopes emerge between Dz = 4.5 nm (e.g., water vs CTAB) and arise through 7.5 nm (e.g., fi rst and second water replicates). (III) Desorption : the binder is completely removed from the PE surface, which occurs for values of Dz as small as 8.5 nm ( ∼ 7% of the fully extended contour length, L c ≈ 118 nm) in the presence of CTAB or as large as 20 nm ( ∼ 17% of L c ) in the presence of neutral surfactants (see below). Comparing the PMFs indicates that larger desorption free energies are correlated with higher SASA and R g values. High SASA values indicate less surfactant coverage of the binder during desorption and high R g values indicate stronger binder anchoring to the PE surface, which leads to the binder adopting unfavorable extended conformations as it continues to be pulled.

text: To further quantify the reduction of the free energy barrier for binder desorption and investigate di ff erences owing to surfactant morphology, we performed umbrella sampling simulations for the additional surfactants listed in Figure 1. In pure water at 27 °C, the mean free energy of PEU desorption for two replicates is 895 kJ/mol (Figure 6b) or 7.73 kT/nm 2 (SI Figure S17). This is a substantial energy barrier that is addressed in industrial de-inking processes by employing a combination of elevated temperatures, mechanical agitation, extended residence times ( ∼ 0.5 -1 h), and controlled addition of feedstock and surfactants. 61 Due to the long timescales associated with desorption in our umbrella sampling approach, our simulations were performed at high concentrations ( ∼ 0.15 and 0.25 M) compared to prior de-inking experiments ( ∼ 0.05 M or 0.1 -5% by weight) 61 as this increases the likelihood of surfactant interactions with the binder during the simulations. Figure 7a compares corresponding desorption PMFs. In ∼ 0.25 M surfactant solutions at 27 °C, the CTAB system had the lowest desorption free energy of 430 kJ/mol or 3.7 kT/ nm 2 , which is a ∼ 52% reduction in the energy barrier for desorption relative to water. The TTAB (550 kJ/mol), DTAB (570 kJ/mol), STS (510 kJ/mol) and SDS (590 kJ/mol) systems all had similar desorption free energies between 500 and 600 kJ/mol (4.4 -5.1 kT/nm 2 ). The DDAO system was simulated at a slightly elevated temperature of 42 °C due to freezing of the system at room temperature after 1 -2 μ s of total simulation time (an issue which has been reported in MARTINI 3), 54
