Furthermore, γ i S and p i,IG vap are the activity coe ffi cient of solute i in solvent S and the pure compound vapor pressure of i assuming ideal gas behavior. In the following, the experimental vapor pressures have been used, in combination with the COSMO therm computed activity coe ffi cients. To estimate vapor pressures for small gases with critical temperatures below 298 K, an extrapolation via Wagner coe ffi cients has been done. If those coe ffi cients were not available, for example, for cases where the critical temperature was below room temperature, an extrapolation on the basis of COSMO therm has been carried out using an experimental starting point for the vapor pressure. Such an extrapolation beyond the critical temperature is a common approximation for the determination of Henry ' s law constants 47 and, as long as the gas will behave almost ideally at the (vapor) pressures under consideration, is expected to give reasonable results. Please note that most of the experimental gas solubilities of the Pauly data set have been measured indirectly, i.e. by measuring the permeability P and the di ff usivity D , according to S = P / D , which is possibly less reliable than a direct measurement of S . 48

text: Concerning PET, separate experimental data for the amorphous and the semicrystalline polymer were given. Figure 5 shows that there are some outliers at either end of the solubility spectrum due to H 2 and to H2O. The strong outliers for H2 in PTFE and LDPE, which have been corrected for semicrystallinity, could be due to the fact that hydrogen as opposite to the other larger solutes is partially soluble also in the crystalline regions of those polymers. A possible explanation for the overestimation of the solubility of water is the fact that the constraints resulting from the polymer structure are suppressing the local structure formation required for the e ffi cient solvation of a water molecule with its four strong interaction sites. Indeed, the polymers for which the solubility of water is overestimated have glass transitions above room temperature (PEMA, PVC, PODP, ethylcellulose), except for nitrocellulose, where the overestimation is smallest, and which has a glass transition below room temperature. 45 Interestingly, apart from this issue, no signi fi cant di ff erence in predictive accuracy is found within this data set irrespective of whether the pure polymer systems are above or below their respective glass transition. This may be explained by the comparatively high liquid solubility of most compounds within the polymers of this study. This may also be the reason why taking into account the free volume e ff ect does not in fl uence the gas solubility results signi fi cantly. The high liquid solubility within the polymers of this study results in a free volume fraction φ i fv close to one. Furthermore, the computed log10( S ) values have a signi fi cant contribution originating from the compound vapor pressure (eq 7), mitigating any modi fi cations made to ln( γ ) and hence the liquid phase.

text: Another data set containing polymer -water partition coe ffi cients has been extracted from the work of Gasslander et al. 50 They have investigated the partition of molecules covering a broad range of polarity for the polymers polyethylene, polypropylene and polyethyleneco -butyl acrylate (17 wt % butyl acrylate). Unfortunately, neither a density nor crystalline fraction of those polymers are speci fi ed in the paper. Thus, the crystalline fraction α had to be treated as a fi tting constant ( α , fi t in Table 3), which basically lowers the computed logP values by a constant shift, see eq 9. The polymer -water partition coe ffi cients in ref 50 have been determined indirectly via linear regression from liquid chromatographic retention times using acetonitrile, ethanol and isopropyl alcohol. Accordingly, no dissociation correction for acidic molecules in the water phase had to be taken into account.

text:
Interestingly, as summarized in Table 3, the regression slope of the predictions versus the experimental data is for all three polymers signi fi cantly below unity. This is partially due to the experimental data points belonging to the rather nonpolar compounds, octadecyl 3-(3,5-ditert -butyl-4-hydroxyphenyl)propanoate and bis(2-ethylhexyl)phthalate, having very high log K values, which are possibly out of range of what is reliably measurable. However, even excluding the two most extreme data points (see Table 3) the regression slope remains still somewhat low. Experimental and predicted values for the three systems are shown in Table S5 in the SI.

However, its position seems to be at least surprising if not questionable if this solute ' s predicted and experimental log K values for example in EBA having a similar polarity are considered.

Furthermore, the results of Table 3 clearly show that more consistent results are obtained if the free volume combinatorial term is included. The crystalline fraction, which has been treated as a fi tting constant, corresponds roughly to what can be expected from experience. The regression slope is somewhat higher with the free volume term, though still not unity, leading to a better coincidence with the experimental data and consequently a lower root mean squared error (RMSE).

text:
In summary, it is feasible to make quantitative predictions using COSMO-RS theory for vapor/gas -liquid data and partition coe ffi cients on systems containing polymers. In many cases consideration of free volume e ff ects seems to improve the results as compared to the omission of the combinatorial term. However, this requires some additional information to be taken into account, i.e. the density of polymer and solute, the molecular weight and the crystallinity of the polymer. For the examined data it was su ffi cient to estimate the free volume simply based on the computed COSMO volumes and experimental densities. Sometimes, the study of polymer systems is hampered by the fact that experimental conditions are not speci fi ed with su ffi cient accuracy. Then, those missing parameters have to be fi tted using the remaining experimental information.

Most of the investigated polymer systems were of a rather simple chemical structure. Furthermore, cross-linking and polymer swelling e ff ects were not examined so far. It remains to be shown whether such e ff ects, which will play an important role in many practical applications, can be incorporated into COSMO-RS calculations.

Abstract

text:
TheeffectsofpH,temperature,andsalinityontheremovalofsolvent-basedinkfromhigh-densitypolyethylene(HDPE)surfaceswereinvestigated using three alkyltrimethylammonium bromides (i.e., dodecyl-, tetradecyl-, and hexadecyl-trimethylammonium bromide or DTAB, TTAB, and CTAB, respectively). Ink removal increases with increasing concentration, increasing pH, decreasing temperature, and increasing salinity of the CnTAB solutions. The zeta potential of ink becomes more positively charged with increasing pH as well as concentration and alkyl chain length of CnTAB, indicating that adsorption of CnTAB on ink pigment occurred more readily with an increase in any of those parameters. The solubilization of epoxy ink binder was found to increase with increasing surfactant concentration, decreasing temperature, and increasing salinity of the CnTAB solutions. Adsorption of cationic surfactant onto the ink pigment particles and solubilization of ink binder molecules into surfactant micelles are important mechanisms causing ink removal from the plastic surface. © 2006 Elsevier B.V. 1. Introduction

text:
Steady growth of demand in plastics leads to increasing demand for natural gas and petroleum as the raw materials for plastic production. An increase in the utilization of plastics translates into a steady growth of plastic wastes as a consequence. A means for dealing with such a problem is through recycling, but it has been reported that recycled plastics often bear poor physical and mechanical properties in comparison with those of virgin polymers [1,2]. For printed plastics, the presence of residual inks can be a primary cause of the deterioration of polymer properties. Previous work, for example, reported the deterioration effect of residual ink on physical properties of re-extruded polyethylene [3]. Therefore, removal of ink from the plastic surface prior to recycling is a prerequisite. Generally, ink can be removed by either physical [4] or chemical [3,5-7] means.

Chemically, ink can be removed by organic solvents, but, due to their toxicity, alternative deinking media are desirable. Due to their biodegradability, non-toxicity, and non-volatility, aqueous solutions of surfactants are considered good alternatives for such a task.

text:
Previous studies on surfactant-based deinking process have been carried out on surfaces of either plastic films [3,5,7] or rigid plastics [6] in order to remove either water-based [3,5] or solvent-based [6,7] ink using an anionic surfactant [3], nonionic surfactants [3,5,7], an amphoteric surfactant [3,7], or cationic surfactants [3,6,7]. For either water- or solvent-based ink, cationic surfactants were the most effective in ink removal at concentrations well above their critical micelle concentration (CMC) and at high pH levels (generally greater than or equal to 11) [3,6,7]. Furthermore, increased temperature during deinking, increased pre-soaking time in the surfactant solutions prior to mechanical agitation, and increased shaking time helped increase deinking efficiency [5-7]. The cationic surfactants which have been previously investigated were hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB;

C16H33 + N(CH3)3Br -) [3,6,7] and hexadecylpyridinium chloride (CPC; C16H33 + N(C5H5)Cl -) [3], but CPC was found to degrade at high pH levels.

text: In the first paper of this series [8], we reported the use of three alkyltrimethylammonium bromides (i.e., dodecyl-, tetradecyl-, and hexadecyl-trimethylammonium bromide or DTAB, TTAB, and CTAB, respectively) to remove blue solvent-based ink from a printed surface of high-density polyethylene (HDPE) bottles. All studies were carried out at a fixed temperature and pH of 30 °C and 12, respectively. Both the increase in the alkyl chain length and the surfactant concentration increased the deinking efficiency. Complete deinking was achieved at concentrations of about3,8,and24timesoftheCMCofCTAB,TTAB,andDTAB, respectively. For CTAB, ink removal began at a concentration close to its CMC and increased significantly at concentrations greater than its CMC, while, for TTAB and DTAB, significant deinking was only observed at concentrations much greater than their CMCs. Both the wettability of the surfactant on the ink surface and the solubilization of ink binder in the surfactant micelles increased with an increase in both the alkyl chain length and the surfactant concentration. Finally, we proposed a mechanism for the removal of a solvent-based ink from the HDPE surfaces as consisting of four main steps: (1) surfactant adsorption on both printed and unprinted HDPE surfaces; (2) solubilization of ink binder in micelles; (3) detachment of ink pigment from HDPE surfaces; (4) stabilization and dispersion of the detached ink particles.

In the present contribution, the effect of pH, temperature and addition of a simple salt, sodium chloride, on deinking for this same system using DTAB, TTAB and CTAB was studied. The effect of their concentration on zeta potential of ink particles and solubilization of ink binder pigment particles was investigated under different deinking conditions (i.e., pH 11-12; temperature = 30, 35, 40, and 45 °C; and addition of 0.1 M sodium chloride salt (NaCl)) from that performed in our previous work [8] (i.e., pH 12 and temperature = 30 °C).

2. Experimental details

2.1. Materials

High-density polyethylene (HDPE) sheet samples were obtained from commercial drinking water blow-molded bottles produced by SVB Drinking Water Company (Thailand). Printing of these bottles was done at CK-Plastic Company (Thailand). Prior to printing, the HDPE bottles were flame-treated. A blue solvent-based ink formulation (UPE-B4009/2) from Uni Ink Company (Thailand) was screen-printed on the treated HDPE surfaces. The printed parts of the bottles were then cut into 8 mm × 40 mm sheets.

N -dodecyltrimethylammonium bromide (DTAB) (99% purity; powder) and n -tetradecyltrimethylammonium bromide (TTAB) (98% purity; powder) were purchased from Aldrich (USA), while n -hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) (98% purity; powder) was purchased from Fluka (Switzerland). Sodium chloride (NaCl) was purchased from Aldrich (USA). Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) (98% purity), purchased from EKA Noble (Sweden), and hydrochloric acid (HCl) (AR grade), purchased from BHD (Germany), were used for pH adjustment. All of these chemicals were used as-received.

Ink powder was prepared by mixing the as-received ink with an appropriate solvent and the mixture was evenly pasted onto a 15 in. × 10 in. glass plate. The layer of ink was made as thin as possible to hasten the drying. The painted glass was later dried in an oven at 60 °Cover night, after which time the ink was scraped off from the glass surface, ground in a mortar, and finally sieved into powder of about 100 mesh or less (i.e., <150 𝛍 m). The asprepared ink powder was kept in a desiccator prior to further use. The chemical composition of the ink powder was investigated by a Fourier-transformed infrared spectrometer (FT-IR; Bruker Vector 3.0), operating at a resolution of 4 cm -1 and a frequency range of 4000-400 cm -1 .

text:
Averysmallamountoftheas-preparedinkpowderwasadded into a CnTAB solution. The pH level of the mixture was adjusted to either 11 or 12 and the mixture was stirred for 24 h. The temperature of the mixture was equilibrated at 30 ± 1 °C. The as-prepared mixture was then transferred to an electrophoretic cell of a zeta meter (Zeta Meter, 3+), equipped with a microscope module. After applying a suitable voltage according to the solution conductivity, the time for any visible ink particle to move for a certain distance was measured. For a given data set, at least 20 ink particles were monitored, from which the average time was calculated. The average time was then used to calculate the average zeta potential value for that particular data set.

2.3. Deinking experiments

text:
Toinvestigate the effects of alkyl chain length, surfactant concentration, pH, temperature, and salinity on deinking efficiency, DTAB, TTAB, and CTAB solutions were prepared at different concentrations, pH levels (i.e., between 11 and 12), temperatures (i.e., between 30 and 45 °C), and salinity (i.e., with or without 0.1 M NaCl). The as-prepared printed HDPE specimens were first pre-soaked (without shaking) in a 15 mL surfactant solution for 2 h and further soaked while being shaken at 200 cycles/min for another 2 h in a shaking water bath. Then, the specimens were washed with deionized water and later dried in open air at room temperature overnight. The amount of ink on the plastic before and after deinking was measured using the optical scanning method [6]. In this method, each plastic specimen was carefully positioned on and scanned by a HP ScanJet 4C optical scanner using the factory settings. The scanned files were analyzed by a copy of Adobe Photoshop 5.5 by counting the number of pixels (proportional to the amount of ink present) on the plastic surface. The amount of ink removed (%) was then calculated based on the following relationship [6]:

ink removed (%) = [ pixelsbefore deinking -pixelsafter deinking pixelsbefore deinking ]

2.4. Critical micelle concentration measurement

text:
At 30 ± 1 °C, the critical micelle concentration (CMC) of pure DTAB, TTAB, and CTAB solutions was determined based onconductivity, using a conductivity meter (Orion, 125). Surface tension values, used to determine the CMC of the CnTAB solutions in the presence of 0.1 M NaCl, were measured by a drop shape analyzer (KR ¨ USS, DSA10-Mk2). The temperature was maintained at 30 ± 1 °C. For both surface tension and conductivity, the CMC is the surfactant concentration at which there is an abrupt change in the slope of the property values as a function of the surfactant concentration.

text:
Theconcentration of solubilized ink in CnTAB solutions with or without the presence of 0.1 M NaCl was indicated by first mixing 10 mg of the as-prepared ink powder in a 15 mL CnTAB solution at pH 12 in a 50 mL Erlenmeyer flask. The flask was then placed in a shaking water bath with the temperature of the water being varied between 30 and 45 °C and the shaking frequency of the sample stage being set at 200 cycles/min for 4 h. The solution was later filtered to remove undissolved ink particles using filter paper (Whatman no. 7402-001; average pore size = 0.2 𝛍 m). The UV absorbance of the filtrate was measured by a UV-visible spectrophotometer (Shimadzu, UV-2550) at a wavelength of 273.8 nm. The absorbance for accurate measurement is in the range of 0.1-0.8. If the sample solution showed an absorbance greater than this range, it was further diluted. The absorbance versus the concentration of CnTAB solutions is a qualitative measure for ink binder solubilization in the CnTAB solutions as increased absorbance corresponds to increased solubility of the binder in the surfactant solutions due to increased solubilization in micelles.

3.1. Zeta potential of ink

text: The effects of initial concentration and pH on zeta potential of ink in CnTAB solutions are shown in Fig. 1. For a given type of CnTAB solution, the zeta potential of ink pigment particle at pH 12 is consistently greater than that at pH 11 over the entire concentration range investigated. For a given pH, an increase in the initial concentration of the CnTAB solutions increases the zeta potential of ink pigment particles due mainly to the adsorption of the positively charged head groups of the CnTAB monomers onto the initially negatively charged ink pigment surfaces. This was possible because the point of zero charge (PZC) of the ink particles in water was observed at a pH of about 3.3 [8], which means that the ink particles exhibit a positive charge at pH < 3.3, while they are negatively charged when pH > 3.3. The particles became more negatively charged with increasing pH. As a result, the absorption of CnTAB monomers on the ink particles could occur much better at pH 12 than at pH 11, causing the particles to become more positively charged at pH 12. This 'charge reversal' effect is commonly observed when ionic surfactants adsorb onto oppositely charged solid surfaces. In the presence of cationic surfactants, the zeta potential reaches a plateau at approximately the CMC because surfactant adsorption onto solids levels off above the CMC due to the surfactant monomer concentration (and therefore thermodynamic activity) becoming constant when micelles form at or above the CMC.

Fig. 2 shows the effects of alkyl chain length and pH on the zeta potential of ink pigment particles in CnTAB solutions. For a given initial concentration and pH of CnTAB solutions, the zeta potential of pigment increased with increasing alkyl chain length both below and above the CMC. The longer the alkyl chain length, the stronger the van der Waal interaction of the tail groups with the pigment surface [8], which, in turn, helps render more CnTAB monomers to adsorb onto the particles.

Fig. 2 shows the effects of alkyl chain length and pH on the zeta potential of ink pigment particles in CnTAB solutions. For a given initial concentration and pH of CnTAB solutions, the zeta potential of pigment increased with increasing alkyl chain length both below and above the CMC. The longer the alkyl chain length, the stronger the van der Waal interaction of the tail groups with the pigment surface [8], which, in turn, helps render more CnTAB monomers to adsorb onto the particles.

text: Fig. 3 shows the FT-IR spectrum of the solvent-based ink used in this study. A typical composition of screen-printing ink for HDPE bottles usually comprises 5% organic pigment, 11% titanium dioxide pigment, 82% epoxy resin, and 2% napthenate catalyst [9]. Since the majority of the ink formulation contains epoxy resin as the binder, it is expected that chemical fingerprints obtained in the FT-IR spectrum should belong to those of the epoxy resin. Normally, the epoxide group exhibits a weak C-H stretching peak around 3050-2990 cm -1 , while aromatic rings show absorption peaks over the wave number range of about 870-670 cm -1 [10]. According to Fig. 3, the absorption peak at about 3026 cm -1 and the absorption peaks at about 870-670 cm -1 were evident. Under the strongly basic condition of the deinking process, the cationic head groups of the CnTAB monomers can associate with the negative moieties of the epoxy molecules (due to the opening of the epoxide rings) via electrostatic interactions, thus enhancing the adsorption of CnTAB monomers on the ink surfaces [8], although the epoxy molecules are simultaneously being solubilized into micelles as will later be discussed, making the deinking process quite complex.

The adsorption of CnTAB monomers on the ink pigment surfaces is driven by both electrostatic and van der Waal forces. Since the possibility for the formation of negatively-charged moieties of the epoxy binder and on the pigment (e.g., TiO2) surfaces themselves is greater at a higher pH, increasing the pH value also renders greater adsorption of CnTAB monomers onto the ink pigment surfaces. On the other hand, pH does not affect the van der Waal interactions between the tail groups of the adsorbed CnTABmonomersandthehydrophobicpartofthepigment surfaces greatly. In addition, the van der Waal interactions should increase with the length of the hydrophobic part of the CnTAB molecules. We cannot, however, differentiate between the adsorption of CTAB onto the pigment particles themselves or onto epoxy molecules attached to the pigment surface.

Plots of the CMC values of CnTAB solutions over a temperature range of 25-50 °C are illustrated in Fig. 4. The CMC of these CnTAB solutions increased very slightly with increasing temperature. Specifically, the CMC values increased from about 0.93 mM at 25 °C to about 1.28 mM at 50 °C for CTAB, from about 3.67 mM at 25 °C to about 4.06 mM at 50 °C for TTAB, and from about 16.1 mM at 25 °Cto about 17.8 mM at 50 °Cfor DTAB. This mild effect of temperature on CMC of ionic surfactants is commonly observed [11] and necessary to know in this work to interpret the temperature dependence of deinking.

3.2.2. Effect of salinity

TheCMCsofCnTABwithandwithout0.1MNaClareshown in Table 1. There is good agreement between the two methods of measurement except in one case where we will use the conductivity values in the absence of added NaCl since the change in the slope of the curve used to obtain the CMC is sharper in that case. The CMCs of CnTAB without NaCl addition were 0.96, 3.75 and 16.29 mM, for CTAB, TTAB and DTAB, respectively, whereas, in CnTAB solutions with 0.1 M NaCl, the CMCs were reduced to 0.04, 0.74 and 12.77 mM for CTAB, TTAB and DTAB, respectively. The reduction in the CMC with increasing alkyl chain length and the added electrolyte is well known for a cationic surfactant and the values shown here are quite in line with a similar system [11].

text: In our previous work [8], solubilization studies were carried out at pH 12 and 30 °C. We found that the solubilization of ink binder in CnTAB micelles increased with an increase in both the alkyl chain length and the concentration of CnTAB. In this work, the temperature was varied between 30 and 45 °C. Apparently, for any given CnTAB concentration, the solubilization of ink binder within the micelles decreases with increasing temperature. Interestingly, the effect of temperature on the decrease in the solubilization of ink binder in CTAB micelles was more pronouncedathigher concentrations. The results could be explained based on the effect of temperature on the CMC values and the aggregation numbers of CnTAB. As mentioned earlier, a slight increase in the CMC values with increasing temperature is evident (see Fig. 5) and this leads to a smaller fraction of surfactant being in micelle form, however, this factor will have a small effect on solubilization capacity at the surfactant concentrations used here. An increase in the temperature causes the aggregation number to decrease [12,13]. The decreased aggregation number translates into less micellar volume that can accommodate solubilized ink binder [14].

Among the three surfactants investigated, the effect of temperature on solubilization of ink binder in TTAB solutions is more pronounced than for DTAB or CTAB. It is possible that the effect of the particular alkyl chain length of TTAB monomers affects the size of micelles more than CTAB and DTAB. The decrease in the size of TTAB micelles with increasing temperature is relatively more important than those of CTAB and DTAB, as evidenced by greater temperature dependence of solubilization in TTAB.

text:
The effect of NaCl addition on the solubilization of ink in CnTAB solutions is illustrated in Fig. 6. The experiments were carried out at pH 12 and 30 °C. For all surfactants, the addition of NaCl significantly improved the solubilization of ink binder. The difference in the solubilization of ink binder in CnTAB in comparison with that with NaCl salt addition was found to be more pronounced at higher CnTAB concentrations, except for DTAB. The addition of NaCl contributes two main effects regarding to the solubilization capacity of ink binder. First, it lowers the CMC, which results in the improvement in the solubilization capacity of ink binder at low surfactant concentrations. Second, the aggregation number is increased when NaCl is added.

3.4. Deinking

3.4.1. Effect of pH

text: Fig. 7 shows the ink removal as a function of pH for different values of normalized CnTAB concentration (i.e., CnTAB concentration divided by corresponding CMC value). These measurements were carried out at a fixed temperature of 30 °C. Evidently, deinking is not possible in surfactant-free basic solutions. For a given type and concentration of CnTAB solutions, the amountofinkremovalincreasedmonotonicallywithincreasing pH of the solutions. For any given CnTAB concentration, the lowest pH value at which deinking began is about <11.0, <11.5, and 11.5 for CTAB, TTAB, and DTAB solutions, respectively. Significant deinking (i.e., at least 40% of ink removal) was observed at about 2 × CMC and pH of about 11.5 for CTAB, 6 × CMC and pH of about 11.8 for TTAB, and 16.5 × CMC and pH of about 11.7 for DTAB, respectively. Evidently, for a given pH, the amount of ink removal increased monotonically with increasing alkyl chain length of CnTAB. Fig. 7 also shows that complete deinking was observed at concentrations of about 4, 8, and 24 × CMC for CTAB, TTAB, and DTAB solutions, respectively [8]. Clearly, the effect of pH on deinking is less pronounced with CnTAB having a longer alkyl chain length. As previously mentioned, longer alkyl chain length helps promote the adsorption of CnTAB monomers onto the ink pigment surfaces (as evidenced from the observed increase in the zeta potential of ink particles with increasing alkyl chain length of CnTAB; see Fig. 2) and adsorption of surfactant on both printed and unprinted HDPE surfaces is the first step in the deinking process of solvent-based ink from HDPE surfaces [8].

Fig. 7 shows the ink removal as a function of pH for different values of normalized CnTAB concentration (i.e., CnTAB concentration divided by corresponding CMC value). These measurements were carried out at a fixed temperature of 30 °C. Evidently, deinking is not possible in surfactant-free basic solutions. For a given type and concentration of CnTAB solutions, the amountofinkremovalincreasedmonotonicallywithincreasing pH of the solutions. For any given CnTAB concentration, the lowest pH value at which deinking began is about <11.0, <11.5, and 11.5 for CTAB, TTAB, and DTAB solutions, respectively. Significant deinking (i.e., at least 40% of ink removal) was observed at about 2 × CMC and pH of about 11.5 for CTAB, 6 × CMC and pH of about 11.8 for TTAB, and 16.5 × CMC and pH of about 11.7 for DTAB, respectively. Evidently, for a given pH, the amount of ink removal increased monotonically with increasing alkyl chain length of CnTAB. Fig. 7 also shows that complete deinking was observed at concentrations of about 4, 8, and 24 × CMC for CTAB, TTAB, and DTAB solutions, respectively [8]. Clearly, the effect of pH on deinking is less pronounced with CnTAB having a longer alkyl chain length. As previously mentioned, longer alkyl chain length helps promote the adsorption of CnTAB monomers onto the ink pigment surfaces (as evidenced from the observed increase in the zeta potential of ink particles with increasing alkyl chain length of CnTAB; see Fig. 2) and adsorption of surfactant on both printed and unprinted HDPE surfaces is the first step in the deinking process of solvent-based ink from HDPE surfaces [8].

3.4.2. Effect of temperature

Fig. 8 shows the ink removal as a function of temperature for different values of normalized CnTAB concentration. These measurements were carried at a fixed pH of 12. Deinking is not significant in surfactant-free basic solutions at any temperature. The amount of ink removal decreases monotonically with increasing temperature for all surfactants and concentrations. ForCTAB,significantdeinking(i.e., at least 40% of ink removal) was observed at concentrations greater than about 1 × CMC when the temperature is 30 °C. At 35 °C, significant deinking is only observed at 5 × CMC. For TTAB, significant deinking is only observed at 30 °C, provided that the concentrations are greater than about 5 × CMC. For DTAB, at 30 °C, significant deinking is observed at all concentration ranges investigated. However, at 35 °C, significant deinking is only observed at a concentration of 22 × CMC or greater.

The significant improvement in the deinking performance of TTAB with salt addition over those of CTAB and DTAB can be explained based on the results from the solubilization studies (see Fig. 6), where the presence of NaCl increased the solubilization capacity of ink binder in the TTAB solutions in a much greater extent than it did with the CTAB and DTAB counterparts. For examples, at the concentration where CTAB solutions with added salt showed complete deinking (i.e., 1.5 mM), the solubilization capacity for that particular concentration was not very different from that when no salt was present (see Fig. 6a). On the other hand, for TTAB, at the concentration where complete deinking was observed in the presence of salt (i.e., 8.2 mM), the solubilization capacity for that particular concentration was far greater than that when no salt was added (see Fig. 6b). Based on these observations, the observed significant improvement in the deinking efficiency of TTAB solutions in comparison with the other two surfactants is reasonable.

text: The present contribution investigates the effects of pH, temperature, and salinity on the removal of solvent-based ink from high-density polyethylene (HDPE) surfaces based on the use of three alkyltrimethylammonium bromides (i.e., dodecyl-, tetradecyl-, and hexadecyl-trimethylammonium bromide or DTAB, TTAB, and CTAB, respectively). The critical micelle concentration (CMC) values of these surfactant solutions was found to increase very slightly with increasing temperature and decreased significantly with the addition of 0.1 M NaCl. Ink removal was found to increase with increasing concentration, increasing pH, decreasing temperature, and increasing salinity of the CnTAB solutions. The zeta potential of ink became more positively charged with increasing pH as well as concentration and alkyl chain length of CnTAB, suggesting that the adsorption of CnTAB molecules on ink pigment occurred more readily with an increase in any of those parameters. The solubilization of epoxy ink binder was found to increase with increasing surfactant concentration, decreasing temperature, and increasing salinity of the CnTAB solutions. Without the NaCl salt addition, complete deinking was observed at a concentration equivalent to about 3, 8, and 23.5 × CMC for CTAB, TTAB, and DTAB, respectively, while, with the salt addition, it was observed at about 40, 11, and 23.5 × CMC for CTAB, TTAB and DTAB, respectively.

The present contribution investigates the effects of pH, temperature, and salinity on the removal of solvent-based ink from high-density polyethylene (HDPE) surfaces based on the use of three alkyltrimethylammonium bromides (i.e., dodecyl-, tetradecyl-, and hexadecyl-trimethylammonium bromide or DTAB, TTAB, and CTAB, respectively). The critical micelle concentration (CMC) values of these surfactant solutions was found to increase very slightly with increasing temperature and decreased significantly with the addition of 0.1 M NaCl. Ink removal was found to increase with increasing concentration, increasing pH, decreasing temperature, and increasing salinity of the CnTAB solutions. The zeta potential of ink became more positively charged with increasing pH as well as concentration and alkyl chain length of CnTAB, suggesting that the adsorption of CnTAB molecules on ink pigment occurred more readily with an increase in any of those parameters. The solubilization of epoxy ink binder was found to increase with increasing surfactant concentration, decreasing temperature, and increasing salinity of the CnTAB solutions. Without the NaCl salt addition, complete deinking was observed at a concentration equivalent to about 3, 8, and 23.5 × CMC for CTAB, TTAB, and DTAB, respectively, while, with the salt addition, it was observed at about 40, 11, and 23.5 × CMC for CTAB, TTAB and DTAB, respectively.

text: Laminated plastic films, especially mono-material multilayer polyethylene-based (MM-PE) films, have attracted strong interest within the packaging industry over the past decade. Towards closing the material loop, MM-PE films should be recycled in a film-to-film mechanical recycling process, while preserving their desired perfor mance. However, MM-PE laminates typically contain polyurethane (PUR) adhesives between PE film layers, which can affect their recyclability. Herein, three MM-PE films containing different PUR adhesives were studied to assess the effect of the PUR characteristics on the films ' recyclability. The processability of MM-PE laminated films produced via film-blowing extrusion was evaluated, followed by structural, rheological, mechanical, and optical characterization of the recycled films. The composition of the PUR adhesive substantially affects the closed-loop recyclability of the films, and even a small PUR content (2 wt%) can hinder the recycling process. Overall, PUR adhesives reduce the zero-shear viscosity and increase the heterogeneity of the recycled laminates, reducing toughness and increasing haziness. By assessing the morphology and the physicochemical character istics of the PUR adhesives, it is possible to estimate the impact of these materials on the recyclability of MMPE laminates. PURs presenting a higher degree of mixing between hard and soft phases, as indicated by a lower content of hydrogen-bonded groups among hard segments, are preferred for improving the recyclability of MMPE laminates.

text: Depending on the packaging requirements, multilayer flexible films are  produced  through  co-extrusion  or  lamination  [6].  Since  the  pro duction processes for MDOPE and LDPE layers differ, the MM-PE films are  produced  using  a  lamination  process,  and  PUR  adhesives  are commonly  used  as  a  binder  in  the  final  laminate  structure  of  the multilayer flexible film [17]. PUR is synthesized from the reaction of isocyanates and polyols. Isocyanate ( -NCO) groups undergo addition reactions  with  hydrogen-containing  nucleophiles,  such  as  hydroxyl ( -OH), amino ( -NH2), or carboxyl ( -COOH) groups [18]. PUR adhesives are generally formed from the reaction of an NCO-terminated prepol ymer with a polyester- or polyetherpolyol [19 -23]. Common monomers for polyester synthesis include terephthalic acid (TPA), isophthalic acid (m-phthalic acid), adipic acid, diethylene glycol, neopentyl glycol, and ethylene glycol [24]. Among polyethers, polypropylene glycol (PPG) is one of the most widely used polyols for adhesive formulations [25].

text:
Both aromatic and aliphatic diisocyanates are employed in the PUR adhesive synthesis. Typical aromatic isocyanates include toluene diiso cyanate (TDI) and 4,4 ′ -diphenylmethane diisocyanate (MDI) [26], while widely used aliphatic options are hexamethylene diisocyanate (HDI), isophorone diisocyanate (IPDI), and xylylene diisocyanate (XDI) [27, 28]. The isocyanate index, defined as the molar ratio of NCO to OH groups, is commonly in the range of 1.5 -2 to achieve an optimal balance between reactivity, properties, and processing requirements, and results in a crosslinked PUR adhesive [19,21].

The choice of polyol backbone, the type of the diisocyanate, and the isocyanate  index  represent  the  key  parameters  affecting  the  perfor mance  of  PUR  laminating  adhesives,  including  flexibility,  adhesion strength,  chemical resistance, heat stability,  and retortability  [18,19, 28]. The final structure and morphology of PUR adhesives depend on the chemical structure and molecular weight of the raw materials, the vol ume fraction of the hard and soft segments, and the extent of intra- and inter-molecular interactions in each segment and between hard and soft segments, especially hydrogen bond formation [29 -34]. Additionally, the  content  of  PUR adhesive  used during  film  lamination affects the performance of the adhesive [35,36].

text: In general, the processability and performance of a final film-blown product are highly dependent on the macromolecular architecture of PE, particularly its molecular weight, molecular weight distribution, and the content and distribution of short-chain branches [42]. However, MM-PE films typically contain PUR adhesives, and due to the presence of polar chemical groups in PUR, such as urethane and ester/ether functional ities, there is an inherent incompatibility of PUR with the non-polar PE matrix during the melt blending stage of mechanical recycling [43,44]. It has been previously found that contaminations will drastically reduce the processing window and the quality of the final film [45]. Conse quently,  it  is  essential  to  investigate  the  influence  of  the  chemical structure of PUR adhesive on the processability and final performance of the  recycled  films  within  the  closed-loop  mechanical  recycling  of MM-PE.

The present study systematically evaluates the recyclability of MM- PE laminated films. Herein, the impact of three different types of PUR adhesives on the processability, mechanical, and optical performance of MM-PE laminates is evaluated in a closed-loop film-to-film mechanical recycling  process.  To  the  best  of  our  knowledge,  no  comprehensive study currently exists for evaluating the recyclability of MM-PE lami nates containing PUR adhesives. This study aims to identify the main effects of PUR adhesives on the film-blowing processability and prop erties of recycled MM-PE films.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Mono-material multilayer polyethylene-based (MM-PE) laminates

Three commercial MM-PE laminates, each one containing a different PUR adhesive (PU1, PU2, and PU3) were evaluated. The composition of the  layers  in  all  the  laminates  was  consistent,  comprising  a  50 μ m MDOPE layer, a 2 g/m 2 PUR adhesive, and a 50 μ m LDPE film as a sealant layer. A film consisting of MDOPE/LDPE without PUR adhesive (PU0) was used as a control.

Herein, the impact of three different types of PUR adhesives on the processability, mechanical, and optical performance of MM-PE laminates is evaluated in a closed-loop film-to-film mechanical recycling  process.  To  the  best  of  our  knowledge,  no  comprehensive study currently exists for evaluating the recyclability of MM-PE lami nates containing PUR adhesives. This study aims to identify the main effects of PUR adhesives on the film-blowing processability and prop erties of recycled MM-PE films.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Mono-material multilayer polyethylene-based (MM-PE) laminates

Three commercial MM-PE laminates, each one containing a different PUR adhesive (PU1, PU2, and PU3) were evaluated. The composition of the  layers  in  all  the  laminates  was  consistent,  comprising  a  50 μ m MDOPE layer, a 2 g/m 2 PUR adhesive, and a 50 μ m LDPE film as a sealant layer. A film consisting of MDOPE/LDPE without PUR adhesive (PU0) was used as a control.

2.2. Closed-loop mechanical recycling

text: In this study, closed-loop mechanical film to film recycling refers to the process of converting MMPE laminated films into new films through a shredding, compounding and film-blowing process. At the first step, the laminates were comminuted in a shredder with a 6 mm diameter sieve (Hellweg MDS 340/150). Before the compounding and granulation steps, the shredded flakes were dried for 24 h at 60 °C. The dried flakes were fed into a co-rotating twin screw extruder compounder (KraussMaffei ZE 25R52D) at temperatures ranging from 30 to 230 °C (feeding zone to the die), using both vacuum and atmospheric degassing. The screw rotation speed was maintained at 270 rpm. The resulting pellets were dried again (1 h at 60 °C) before proceeding to the film-blowing step.

text:
The film-blowing process was conducted using a Brabender singlescrew extruder (screw diameter 30 mm; length-to-diameter, L/D = 25) equipped with a melt pressure sensor and a screen changer (100 mesh). The channel depth of the screw in the metering section was 1.66 mm. The film-blowing die had a diameter of 40 mm and a die gap of 1 mm. The barrel temperature was set in the range of 190 -220 °C, and the die head was maintained at 220 °C. Two different screw speeds, 25 and 40 rpm, were set during the production of the film. The cooling fan rate was adjusted for all samples to keep the frost line height (FLH) at 12.5 cm. The blow-up ratio (BUR) and draw-down ratio (DDR) were calculated using Equations (1) and (2), respectively:

BUR = DB DD (1)

BDR = h t × BUR (2)

Where DB is the bubble diameter, DD the die diameter, h the die gap, and t is the film thickness.

The processing for each sample was conducted at two different film thicknesses (25 and 55 μ m), corresponding to two different DDRs. A 25 μ m thickness setup was selected as the critical benchmark for evaluating processability, as thinner films present more challenges in maintaining a stable bubble.

2.3. Characterization of the PE film layers, PUR, and recycled MM-PE after compounding

Differential  scanning  calorimetry  (DSC),  melt  flow  rate  (MFR), density, and rheological analysis of the laminate layers were performed on  compression-molded  sheets,  which  were  prepared  directly  from discarded shredded films. The compression molding was carried out at 220 °C for 5 min.

2.3.1. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC)

Prior to the DSC analysis of PUR adhesives, a reflux technique was employed to dissolve the PE layers of the laminates. For this extraction, approximately 10 g of MM-PE films were placed in a 500 mL roundbottom flask containing 200 mL of p-xylene at 150 °C and kept under reflux for 15 min. After cooling to room-temperature, the sample was filtered to separate the PUR adhesive from the PE solution. The recov ered PUR was further washed with fresh p-xylene to remove residual PE, and subsequently dried under 10 mbar vacuum at 40 °C for 48h. DSC measurements of the extracted PUR adhesives were conducted on a DSC Q2000 (TA Instruments). All DSC measurements were performed under nitrogen atmosphere, using samples of ca. 8 mg. The heating and cooling rates were set to 30 °C/min. The PUR samples were heated from 60 to 120 °C, kept at 120 °C for 3 min, cooled down to 60 °C, and then reheated to 120 °C.

The density of  PE  layers  and  the  control  sample  was  determined using the density method in accordance with ISO 1183 -1:2025 (Method A). MFR strands were first weighed in air using an analytical balance (Mettler Toledo XSE105). Subsequently, the specimens were immersed in ethanol of known density at room temperature, and their apparent weight in the liquid was recorded with a density determination kit.

2.3.4. Attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR)

Infrared spectroscopy analyses were conducted using a PerkinElmer Spotlight 400 FT-IR Spectrometer equipped with a Golden Gate diamond single attenuated total reflectance (ATR) cell. The MDOPE/LDPE films were delaminated and ATR-FTIR measurements were performed on the surface of the PUR layer. The spectra were recorded at a resolution of 2 cm 1 .  Subsequently,  the  spectra  underwent  baseline  correction  and were normalized according to the maximum absorbance observed in the range 1760 - 1700 cm 1 .

text:
A thermogravimetric analyzer (TA Instruments Q500) was used to investigate the mass loss profiles of the compounded samples (7 -8 mg). The samples were analyses in titanium crucibles using three successive dynamic steps: 10 °C/min from 25 to 180 °C; 2 °C/min from 180 to 420 °C; and 10 °C/min from 420 to 550 °C under a nitrogen atmosphere (60 mL/min). The heating rate was set at 2 °C/min in the temperature range of PURs mass loss (180 -420 °C) to increase the resolution of the analysis, accessing the PUR segments degradation steps, given the low concentration of PUR in the films (2 g/m 2 ).

2.3.6. Rheological measurements

For the rheological analysis, the  compounded  samples  were compression-molded into rectangular sheets with thicknesses of (1.0 ± 0.1) mm. Two layers were placed on top of each other to ensure suffi cient material without voids. Any excess material was trimmed prior to measurement.  Zero-shear  viscosity  values  were  calculated  using  the modified rheological model from Carreau (Equation (5)):

η = η 0 [ 1 +( λ ˙ γ ) m ] n 1 m (5)

Where ( η 0 ) represents the zero-shear viscosity, ˙ γ stands for shear rate, and λ , m , and n are the constants of this model [47].

Tensile tests of the recycled films were performed according to the ISO 527 standard, using a Zwick Roell Z020 testing machine equipped with a 100 N static load cell and a video extensometer. Test specimens (ISO 527 type 2) were cut from the films in both machine direction (MD) and transverse direction (TD), using a manual press (Ray-Ran) equipped with a cutting die. During the tensile tests, an initial pre-load of 0.1 N was applied, following a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min up to a strain of 1 % to determine the elastic modulus. Afterward, the test continued at 50 mm/min until the failure occurred. The tear force of the recycled films  was  measured  according  to  the  ISO  6383-1  standard  using  an Instron 5566 tensile test machine at a crosshead speed of 200 mm/min. The impact resistance of the films was measured according to the freefalling  dart  method  (ASTM  D  1709, method  A)  in  an  RDM  FD-1709 falling dart impact tester.

2.3.8. Optical properties

The total light transmission, yellowing index (YI), and haze of the recycled films were measured according to the ASTM E1164 standard, using  a  HunterLab  UltraScan  VIS  spectrophotometer  in  the  trans mittance mode.

A polarized optical microscope (Olympus DP27) equipped with a Linkam hot stage device was employed to assess the morphology of the PUR particles dispersed in PE. The reported number of gels corresponds to an equal surface area of 1 cm 2 for all samples.

3.2. PUR characterization

3.2.1. ATR-FTIR

The FTIR spectra (400 -4000 cm 1 ) of the samples (PU0 -PU3 in Figure A.9) indicates that PU1 is a polyether-based PUR, with a strong band at 1098 cm 1 , referring to the C-O stretching mode vibration in ethers. PU2 and PU3 most likely consist of polyester-based PUs since they do not present absorption peaks associated with ether bands [55]. Fig. 3a presents the ATR-FTIR spectra of the PU0-PU3 sample in the region related to the carbonyl region (1620 -1780 cm 1 ), emphasizing their different compositions and hydrogen-bonding (H-bond) characteristics.

text: The development of hydrogen bonding networks within the hard segments or between hard and soft segments, and the microphase sep aration between hard and soft phases determine the morphology and properties of PURs [33,60]. Analyzing the FTIR spectra of the samples, it is shown that PU3 exhibits a distinct absorption pattern compared to PU1 and PU2. PU3 shows three strong absorption peaks corresponding to two H-bonded peaks at 1662 and 1684 cm 1 (present in the ordered phase in hard segments and disordered phase within hard-soft segment, respectively)  and  free,  non-H  bonded  urethane  carbonyl  groups.  In contrast, PU1 and PU2 show a single peak in the range of free urethane carbonyl,  while  only  a  shoulder  towards  the  disordered  H-bonded carbonyl groups region between soft and hard segments is observed. The ordered H-bonded carbonyl groups in the hard phase of PU3, as indi cated by the peak 1662 cm 1 , suggest that some of the hard segments are incorporated into the hard phase and developed H-bond with other hard segments [31,61], leading to phase separation between the hard and soft microphases [57]. A small shoulder in the range of 1706 -1712 cm 1 for PU1 and PU2 indicates the presence of weakly H-bonded hard segments [61].  Considering  these  peaks  for  PU1  and  PU2,  it  is  shown  that  a fraction of hard segments is dispersed within the soft segments, resulting in a lower level of phase separation for these samples [57]. The proposed morphology model of PU1 and PU2 is shown in Fig. 4a, and that of PU3 is  depicted  in  4b.  For  simplicity,  the  isocyanate  functionality,  polyol molecular weight, and isocyanate index are assumed to be equal for all three  PURs.  The  HBI  values  indicate  that  PU2  has  a  higher  ratio  of H-bonded urethane carbonyls compared to PU1. However, PU3 presents the lowest ratio of H-bonded urethane carbonyls, while the hard seg ments in PU3 show ordered hydrogen bonds compared to PU1 and PU2, indicating a morphology consisting of packed and phase-separated hard segments  for  PU3,  as  evidenced  by  the  strong  absorption  related  to H-bonded  urethane  carbonyls  at  lower  wavenumbers.  The  type  and symmetry of the isocyanate, the type and molecular weight of the pol yol, and the ratio between these PURs constituents (isocyanate index) are important factors affecting the H-bond network in the final PUR structure. The linear and planar isocyanates enable more H-bonds and higher  ordering  of  the  hard  segments  in  the  hard  domains  [57,61].

The ordered H-bonded carbonyl groups in the hard phase of PU3, as indi cated by the peak 1662 cm 1 , suggest that some of the hard segments are incorporated into the hard phase and developed H-bond with other hard segments [31,61], leading to phase separation between the hard and soft microphases [57]. A small shoulder in the range of 1706 -1712 cm 1 for PU1 and PU2 indicates the presence of weakly H-bonded hard segments [61].  Considering  these  peaks  for  PU1  and  PU2,  it  is  shown  that  a fraction of hard segments is dispersed within the soft segments, resulting in a lower level of phase separation for these samples [57]. The proposed morphology model of PU1 and PU2 is shown in Fig. 4a, and that of PU3 is  depicted  in  4b.  For  simplicity,  the  isocyanate  functionality,  polyol molecular weight, and isocyanate index are assumed to be equal for all three  PURs.  The  HBI  values  indicate  that  PU2  has  a  higher  ratio  of H-bonded urethane carbonyls compared to PU1. However, PU3 presents the lowest ratio of H-bonded urethane carbonyls, while the hard seg ments in PU3 show ordered hydrogen bonds compared to PU1 and PU2, indicating a morphology consisting of packed and phase-separated hard segments  for  PU3,  as  evidenced  by  the  strong  absorption  related  to H-bonded  urethane  carbonyls  at  lower  wavenumbers.  The  type  and symmetry of the isocyanate, the type and molecular weight of the pol yol, and the ratio between these PURs constituents (isocyanate index) are important factors affecting the H-bond network in the final PUR structure. The linear and planar isocyanates enable more H-bonds and higher  ordering  of  the  hard  segments  in  the  hard  domains  [57,61].

PURs presenting high miscibility between the hard and soft segments typically exhibit a single  glass  transition  temperature  ( Tg ),  positioned  between  the Tg values  of  the  hard  and  soft  segments  [67,68].  Among  the  samples studied,  only  PU3  displayed  a  well-defined  glass  transition  at Tg = 9.9 °C, as highlighted by the peak observed in the first derivative of heat flow of this sample. In contrast, PU1 and PU2 exhibited Tg in a broad range of temperature, with estimated average Tg values lower than that of PU3. The broad transition temperatures observed for PU1 and PU2 is attributed to the extensive degree of mixing between the hard and soft segments, being consistent with the FTIR results shown in Fig. 3a [69, 70].

Figure A.11 presents the TGA thermograms (mass versus temperature) of PU0-PU3 of samples from 25 to 550 °C, while Fig. 4c depicts the first derivative (DTG) of the mass change as a function of the temperature curves during the initial stage of mass loss (from 190 to 390 °C) for PU0 PU3 samples.

text: Under a nitrogen atmosphere, PU0 (PE) shows a single step of mass loss  starting  at  350 °C [71], as observed in Fig. 4c. For the samples containing PUR adhesives (PU1-PU3), the mass loss occurs in two or three steps, starting around 200 °C [30]. The thermal degradation of PUR initiates  with  the  breakdown  of  urethane  bonds  from  the  hard segment, and the onset temperature and magnitude of this stage depend on the type of isocyanate and polyol, as well as their ratio. A higher content of the soft segment decreases the rate and intensity of the mass loss observed during this first degradation step [34]. In addition, ure thane groups presenting low amount of hydrogen bonds are less stable and degrade faster [32]. The second and third DTG peaks are related to the decomposition of soft segments which occur at a slower rate than the first step [30]. PU3, presenting a higher content of ordered hard seg ments shows mass loss at higher temperatures [30,72]. PU1 and PU2 show  a  similar  first  DTG  peak,  starting  at  around  195 °C  with  a maximum mass loss rate at 250 °C. However, PU1 shows a higher rate of mass  loss,  indicating  a  possible  higher  content  of  hard  segments. Conversely, PU3 demonstrates a diverse thermal decomposition behavior, starting at a higher temperature compared to PU1 and PU2, and showing the first DTG peak as a shoulder beginning at 210 °C and the second DTG peak with a maximum at around 311 °C. These results suggest that PU3 presents more stable hard domains, such as urethane formed from alkyl-isocyanate and alkyl-polyols instead of aryl-isocyanate  and  aryl-polyol  [32].  Furthermore,  increasing  the crosslinking density or the isocyanate index improves the PURs thermal stability since more energy is required to breakdown the PUR network [30].

text: The dynamic intersection of storage and loss moduli curves, and the dynamic intersection frequency values of the samples can be seen in Fig. 6a. A higher value of the dynamic intersection or an increase in the crossover  frequency  indicates  a  less  homogenous  system  [76,77].  As such, PU3 shows the lowest degree of homogeneity among the samples, while PU1 demonstrates the highest level of homogeneity among sam ples containing PUR adhesive and its homogeneity level is similar to PU0 (Control sample). PU2 is positioned between PU1 and PU3 based on intersection frequency. The homogeneity of these systems is related to the chemical structure of the PUR adhesives. For instance, polyether polyol-based PUR is expected to have a better affinity with PE. This may result in a more regular morphology for the PUR dispersed phase than polyester polyol-based PUR [78]. From this result it is expected that PU1 presents molecular segments with lower surface energy, thus showing better  affinity  with  PE  chains.  In  contrast,  PU3  contains  more  polar groups, and it is less compatible with the non-polar PE chains. As pre viously described, PU1 is based on a polyether polyol and PU3 is based on a polyester polyol. Also, PU3 showed a higher proportion of hydrogen bonds within the hard phase, which makes PU3 more heterogeneous in the recycled laminate leading to a higher number of instabilities during the film-blowing process. The shift of crossover frequencies to higher values  corroborates  with  the  poor  processability  of  PU3  during  the film-blowing, as it leads to more bubble rupturing [79].

For instance, polyether polyol-based PUR is expected to have a better affinity with PE. This may result in a more regular morphology for the PUR dispersed phase than polyester polyol-based PUR [78]. From this result it is expected that PU1 presents molecular segments with lower surface energy, thus showing better  affinity  with  PE  chains.  In  contrast,  PU3  contains  more  polar groups, and it is less compatible with the non-polar PE chains. As pre viously described, PU1 is based on a polyether polyol and PU3 is based on a polyester polyol. Also, PU3 showed a higher proportion of hydrogen bonds within the hard phase, which makes PU3 more heterogeneous in the recycled laminate leading to a higher number of instabilities during the film-blowing process. The shift of crossover frequencies to higher values  corroborates  with  the  poor  processability  of  PU3  during  the film-blowing, as it leads to more bubble rupturing [79].

text: The average tensile modulus of PU2 in the MD is slightly higher than that of PU0, while it is lower for PU1 and PU3. This may be attributed to the  presence  of  stiffer  PUR  particles  in  PU2,  which  have  a  stronger interface with the PE matrix and act as reinforcing agents within it [90, 91]. In the TD, the tensile modulus follows a similar trend as the MD. However, the absolute TD values are higher, due to the strong orienta tion of PE chains in the MD at high DDR values [92]. At high DDR, the PE melt  undergoes  strong  stretching  in  the  MD  and  is  subsequently quenched immediately after exiting  the  die.  This  rapid  solidification preserves the chain orientation in the MD, while the crystalline lamellae tend  to  stack  preferentially  perpendicular  to  this  direction  [92 -94]. Such a microstructural arrangement reduces stiffness along the MD but enhances  resistance  to  deformation  in  the  TD,  resulting  in  a  higher modulus  in  the  latter  [92 -94].  In  the  TD,  the  films  behave  as  an iso-strain system, where  the crystalline regions, showing  higher modulus  than  the  amorphous  phase,  dominate  the  overall  tensile response [92]. Therefore, the increase in modulus for PU2 is less pro nounced in the TD compared to the MD, as the TD already exhibits a higher initial modulus. In the case of PU3, the decrease in modulus is more significant in the TD than in the MD, likely due to poor stress transfer between the PE and PUR phases [95]. Since the crystalline re gions with higher modulus dominate the tensile behavior in the TD, the material experiences higher stress and its microstructure becomes more sensitive to defects. Finally, PU1 shows a reduction in modulus in the TD similar to that observed in the MD.

4. Conclusion

In this study, the effect of PUR adhesives on the recyclability of MMPE laminated films was assessed during a closed-loop film-to-film me chanical recycling process. It is shown that the type of PUR adhesive will affect the recyclability of MM-PE films, leading to higher melt pressure build-up and more instabilities during the film-blowing process. Rheo logical investigation of recycled MM-PE laminates containing PUR ad hesives proved to be an effective method to evaluate their processability and large number of instabilities during the film-blowing process.

This  study  highlights  how  existing  Design  for  Recycling  (DfR) guidelines for PE-based flexibles could be further refined down to the level of the chemistry used in adhesives for MM-PE. Overall, maximizing recycling efficiency requires a holistic approach in which all compo nents, especially those present in minor quantities, such as labels, ad hesives, lacquers, inks, and pigments, are carefully selected and assessed for compatibility with the intended recycling process and each other. Only through such comprehensive material design can true circularity in flexible packaging be achieved.

ABSTRACT

text: Polyolefins are widely employed as external skins for flexible packaging, yet their nonpolar, hydrophobic surfaces present challenges for high- resolution, wear- resistant printing. Converters have traditionally relied on surface treatments, such as corona treatment, to increase surface free energy (SFE) and promote compatibility with solvent- based inks. While water- based inks offer sustainability advantages and reduced volatile organic compound exposure over solvent- based inks, their adhesion to polymer substrates is inconsistent and generally not robust. Industry guidelines suggest SFE differentials between ink and substrate are the only factor influencing adhesion; however, this factor may not completely describe the ink- substrate interactions. The adhesion performance of water- based inks was evaluated on polyethylene, ethylene acrylic acid copolymer, ethylene vinyl alcohol copolymer, and polyamide. Polymer films were examined pre-  and post- corona treatment to assess changes in surface energy, chemistry, and topography on ink printability and durability. To achieve acceptable print durability, these polymers all required corona treatment, leading to chemical and morphological modifications to the film surface. Results demonstrated that surface chemistry and topography are stronger indicators of water- based ink adhesion than SFE alone. These findings establish a framework for optimizing the durability of water- based inks on polyolefins and related substrates through targeted surface treatment strategies.

1   |   Introduction

The surface printing of flexible polymer packaging is crucial for  aesthetic  and  informational  reasons.  Enhancing  a  product's attractiveness and functionality to consumers is a significant factor in the supply chain processes involved in finished goods  production.  Flexible  packaging  articles  are  typically produced with polyolefins (e.g., polyethylene) as external skin layers  due  to  their  abuse  resistance,  durability,  flexibility, and  corrosion  resistance  properties,  in  addition  to  low  cost and ease of processing. However, due to polyolefins' chemical structure  and  their  resulting  low  surface  free  energy  (SFE), these polymers cannot form strong bonds with ink, overprint varnish, or lacquer coatings [1]. To overcome adhesion issues common with  low  SFE  materials,  packaging  producers  (referred to in the industry as converters) apply a combination of  surface  treatment  and  organic  solvent- based  ink  systems to enable surface printing of these materials. text: Interactions  between  inks  and  substrates  are  critical  during printing. The adhesion of the ink to the outer layer of the packaging film is hypothesized to be determined by the interactions between polar and nonpolar (dispersive) components of the inks and the polymer films. The greater the similarity between the polar and dispersive components of inks and substrates, the better the wetting and adhesion on the surface of the printing substrate. Increasing the surface density of polar functional groups and the resulting increase in SFE can overcome poor wetting and adhesion on polymer surfaces. A guideline commonly used in  industry  is  that  the  SFE  of  the  printing  substrate  typically needs to be 15-20 dynes/cm higher than the ink's surface tension to achieve proper adhesive bonding. To the authors' knowledge, no comprehensive study has critically assessed the overarching applicability  and  limitations  of  this  industrial  guideline.  This study evaluates this widely used industry guideline on surface energy differences, specifically studying SFE and other physical and chemical factors that may contribute to ink adhesion and durability.

text: There  are  several  methods  that  converters  can  use  to  modify polymer  film  surfaces  prior  to  printing,  promoting  ink  adhesion,  including  corona  treatment,  flame  treatment,  plasma treatment, and chemical treatment [7, 8]. Generally, these surface  treatments  are  designed  to  increase  the  SFE  of  the  film by ~15-20 dynes/cm compared to the neat film by introducing reactive  groups  that  bond  with  the  ink  on  the  surface  [9-13]. A  typical  water- based  ink  has  a  surface  tension  in  the  range of  25-30 dynes/cm. Using the industry guideline that the substrate surface tension should be 15-20 dynes/cm higher than the ink, the target surface energy of the print substrate should be 40-50 dynes/cm to achieve acceptable adhesion [3].

text: Methods such as corona treatment are widely used in industry to promote surface oxidation that can increase the adhesion between solvent- based  inks  and  polyolefin  surfaces  [9].  When  a film  is  subjected  to  corona  treatment,  the  treatment  produces polar  and  hydrophilic  functional  groups  on  the  surface,  such as  hydroxyl  ( OH),  carboxyl  (R COOH),  carbonyl  (C O), or  ester  (R CO OR) groups [10,  13].  Introducing  these  polar groups on the film surface increases the SFE and subsequently improves the wettability and adhesion properties between the liquid  ink  and  the  polymer  film  [13].  A  drawback  of  corona treatment is that the treatment effects decrease over time as non- functionalized polymer chains diffuse from the bulk to the surface. As a result, films often need to be retreated if they are not printed immediately [14, 15]. While these surface treatments are commonly used in typical packaging polyolefins, they are not always available (capital expense), may not produce adequate oxidation to increase the surface energy of these films and have the limitation of needing to print very soon after treatment. Another consideration is that different polymers have varied responses to these surface treatments, resulting in variable levels of oxidation and, in some cases, detrimental responses to treatment, such as chain scission [10].

A wide variety of polymers are used in packaging films, each exhibiting  a  range  of  surface  and  bulk  properties.  This  study focuses on a group of polymers extensively utilized in packaging films to explore how their surface characteristics influence printability and print stability. Polyethylene is used as a model nonpolar polymer for comparison with the other selected polymers. The selected polymers in this study that possess inherent latent  functionality  include  ethylene  acrylic  acid  copolymer (EAA),  ethylene  vinyl  alcohol  block  copolymer  (EVOH),  and polyamide (PA) (Figure 1).

Polyethylene  (PE)  is  the  most  commonly  used  polymer  in flexible packaging [9]. PE has the least complex structure in polymers, with only methylene (CH 2 ) repeat units, which are nonpolar and relatively inert. PE and other nonpolar polymer films are difficult to print on due to their nonpolar and hydrophobic  nature,  as  indicated  above.  Without  any  hydrophilic functional groups, PE must be surface- treated to create functional groups that can provide favorable interactions with the inks to improve printing.

text:
EAA copolymers are used in the packaging industry to adhere to polar substrates or act as interlayer adhesion layers between coextruded  multilayer  polymer  films  [16].  Occasionally,  EAA has also been used on external surfaces where increased adhesion is desired for the surface. The carboxylic acid groups from the acrylic acid content [10] in EAA can serve as reactive functional groups and orient to the surface, and this polar surface functionality promotes adhesion with polar inks.

EVOH was selected as one of the polymers due to its surface energy value of 41-45 dynes/cm [17], which is comparable to corona- treated PE. EVOH is a random copolymer of PE and poly  (vinyl  alcohol)  (PVA).  PVA  contains  an  aliphatic  C C backbone and pendant OH groups, and these polar groups render  the  copolymer  hydrophilic  [17].  EVOH  is  commonly used in packaging as a barrier layer to protect the contents due to its performance as a barrier to various gases. The selection of EVOH for this study is based on its hydrophilic nature, desirable SFE values, and functional groups available for interactions with ink.

text:
PA also has a higher native surface energy that falls in the typical range of 48-51 dynes/cm [18] and has available amide functional  groups  ( CONH 2 ).  Commercial  polyamide  comes  in  a variety of grades based on monomer structure (e.g., PA6, PA66, copolymer PA6/66). PA6/66 is often used in packaging for film strength, barrier properties, and improved processing compared to PA6 and PA66 grades, and can be used throughout multilayer structures, including as an exterior skin layer. Due to its prevalent use in commercial applications, the copolymer PA6/66 is the form of PA selected for this study.

Most of  the  literature  data  targeting  improved  adhesion  between water- based ink and polymer film surfaces has focused on  the  ink  composition  [19,  20].  Limited  research  has  been performed that modifies the polymers and their surface characteristics  while  maintaining  the  constant  ink  composition. Also,  how  the  surface  treatment  alters  the  surface  topography and correspondingly changes the ink adhesion behavior is not well understood. This study aims to provide a new understanding of the critical surface characteristics of polymer films to achieve acceptable ink adhesion and durability in digital print applications.

The  test  samples  used  in  this  study  are  multilayer  polymer films  produced  on  a  commercial  coextrusion  line  at  Sealed Air Corporation. The bulk layers were produced similarly for all  films  used  in  the  study,  and  only  the  external  skin  layer (5-10 μm layer thickness) was modified. The commercial polymers used for this study include the polyethylene grade linear low- density (LLDPE) octene copolymer PE ExxonMobil Exact 3024,  SK  Primacor  1410  EAA,  BASF  Ultramid  C33  PA6/66 polyamide copolymer, and the Kuraray EVAL E171B, a 44 mol% grade EVOH.

2.1.2 | Printing

text:
The films were printed using a water- based polyurethane ink system  prepared  by  Sealed  Air  Corporation.  The  ink  consists of  the  following  components:  pigment,  polymer,  co- solvent, humectant,  surfactant,  and  water,  with  an  approximate  total solids  content  of  less  than  20 wt%  and  an  initial  surface  tension  of  less  than  ~50  dynes  per  centimeter  upon  application. The printing involves a piezoelectric four- color CMYK process. The  ink  and  the  printing  process  are  described  in  US  Patent Applications US20230118001A1 [21], US 2024/0327662A1 [22], US  2024/0010019A1  [23],  and  US  Patent  US11008478B2  [24]. The films were corona- treated in line with a treatment setting of  1  W/ft 2 (10.76 W/m 2 )  where  applicable.  Films  were  printed on the exterior  layer  only.  All  bulk  layers  remained  the  same throughout the study, and only the surface layer was modified, as illustrated in Figure 2.

2.1.3 | Contact Angle

text:
SFE was evaluated using contact angle measurements collected using a Krüss MSA One- Click SFE surface analyzer. Sessile drop experiments  were  conducted  using  water  (deionized  UHPLC water, Sigma Aldrich, CAS 7732- 18- 5) as the polar probe liquid and diiodomethane (ReagentPlus, 99%, Sigma Aldrich, CAS 75- 11- 6) as the dispersive probe liquid, with a 2 μL drop volume. The Kruss ADVANCE software was used to estimate the contact angle values from the captured images using the Young- Laplace fitting method. The surface free energies for the films were calculated using the OWRK (Owens, Wendt, Rabel, and Kaelble) method [25].

2.1.4 | Ink Adhesion and Durability

text:
Ink durability testing was completed immediately after printing  using  the  ASTM  F2252- 03  tape  adhesion  test  method [26].  A  piece  of  ¾"  3 M  #600  clear  pressure- sensitive  tape was applied across the entire printed surface. The tape was then pulled with a steady, smooth motion at a 45° angle. The tape was then assessed for ink transfer, and a score was assigned based on the amount of ink present on the tape. Rub testing was conducted using a Testing Machines Inc. Digital Ink Rub Tester 10- 20 using ASTM D5264 [27], where samples are  mounted to a sled with the printed side in contact with Kraft paper. The unit then oscillates the sled back and forth for the desired cycle time. For this study, the oscillation cycles were 2 min long, with 100 cycles/min for 200 cycles. The characteristic adhesion and durability tests selected for this study are  based  on  the  commercial  usage  conditions,  specifically printed  ink  resistance  to  scuffing  due  to  repeated  external stressors, such as rubbing contact with other materials during packaging and transport. In this case, the rub testing method provides a representative evaluation of the ink's contact durability in packaging applications.

text:
The  surface  topographies  and  phase  contrast  imaging  of the  film  samples  were  investigated  using  a  Dimension  Icon AFM (Bruker). A silicon NCHV probe with 42 N/m of spring constant  and  320 kHz  of  frequency  was  used  in  all  experiments, and the film sample was mounted on glass slides with double- sided tape. AFM height and phase scans (5 × 5 μm 2  and 50 × 50 μm 2 ) were collected using tapping mode under ambient air conditions.

2.1.6 | Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR)

The samples were characterized using FTIR in attenuated total reflectance (ATR) mode to examine the functional groups present within the film surface. The equipment was a Nicolet iS20 FTIR spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, USA) equipped with a SMART iTX ATR accessory (Thermo Scientific, USA) and a diamond crystal. All spectra were analyzed using OMNIC (Thermo Scientific, USA) software. Each sample was run with 32 scans, with a spectral range of 1500-600 cm -1 and a spectral resolution of 0.25 cm -1 .

text:
XPS  analysis  was  performed  using  a  Physical  Electronics PHI VersaProbe 5000 station XPS to obtain survey and high- resolution  (HRES)  spectra  of  the  neat  and  corona- treated polymer films. The XPS instrument is equipped with a monochromated  25.0 W  Al  1486.6 eV  source.  To  assess  elemental composition, survey spectra were collected at a pass energy of 117.4 eV and a resolution of ±0.5 eV. For all elements observed in the survey scan, HRES spectra were collected at a pass energy of 23.5 eV and a resolution of ±0.2 eV. All XPS data were analyzed using CasaXPS software (version 2.3.23PR1.0). Atomic percentages were determined from the survey spectra after processing each elemental region with Shirley backgrounds and applying the Physical Electronics instrument relative sensitivity factors (RSF), which are instrument dependent. All HRES spectra were charge- corrected  by  pinning  the  C1s  aliphatic  (C C/C H) band to  285 eV  and  were  processed  with  Shirley  backgrounds and CasaXPS 's  LA  line  shapes,  which  combine  Gaussian  and Lorentzian peak shape contributions that are typical for polymers [28].

XPS  analysis  was  performed  using  a  Physical  Electronics PHI VersaProbe 5000 station XPS to obtain survey and high- resolution  (HRES)  spectra  of  the  neat  and  corona- treated polymer films. The XPS instrument is equipped with a monochromated  25.0 W  Al  1486.6 eV  source.  To  assess  elemental composition, survey spectra were collected at a pass energy of 117.4 eV and a resolution of ±0.5 eV. For all elements observed in the survey scan, HRES spectra were collected at a pass energy of 23.5 eV and a resolution of ±0.2 eV. All XPS data were analyzed using CasaXPS software (version 2.3.23PR1.0). Atomic percentages were determined from the survey spectra after processing each elemental region with Shirley backgrounds and applying the Physical Electronics instrument relative sensitivity factors (RSF), which are instrument dependent. All HRES spectra were charge- corrected  by  pinning  the  C1s  aliphatic  (C C/C H) band to  285 eV  and  were  processed  with  Shirley  backgrounds and CasaXPS 's  LA  line  shapes,  which  combine  Gaussian  and Lorentzian peak shape contributions that are typical for polymers [28].

text: As the printing process depends on the surface characteristics, the film samples were characterized by FTIR and contact angle measurements (and subsequent calculations of SFE) before and after corona treatment. FTIR spectra for all untreated polymer samples  are  shown  in  Figure  3.  For  neat  PE  (control),  peaks at ~2850 and 2920 cm -1 are  attributed to C H stretching, and peaks at 1460 and 720 cm -1 are  associated with C H bending and rocking modes, respectively [29, 30]. For EAA, the peak at ~1700 cm -1  is the identifying peak for this material, which corresponds to the carbonyl stretch of carboxylic acid [29, 30]. For PA, the peaks of interest are 1635 and 1537 cm -1 ,  which correspond to N H bending in amines [28-31]. EVOH is a copolymer of PE and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA). A strong peak at 3307 cm -1 indicates OH stretching, which is characteristic of PVA in the EVOH copolymer [30, 31]. Additionally, a peak at 1430 cm -1 is associated with the C H bending mode in PE in the EVOH copolymer [30, 31].

text: Corona  treatment  directs  a  high- frequency  discharge  at  the polymer surface, leading to surface oxidation and the generation of polar functional groups such as carbonyl groups, among others previously mentioned [10, 13, 32]. These generated polar groups lead to higher surface energy compared to untreated PE and improve the likelihood of adhesion between the liquid and the polymer film. The presence of polar groups such as hydroxyls or carbonyls is desired at the surface and can contribute to increased ink durability performance.
