text: FTIR characterization was conducted after corona treatment for each sample type (Figure 3). Distinct changes in the FTIR spectral peaks due to the corona treatment process were expected. Still, they were not distinctly discernible in this case, as no additional peaks or shifts in peaks were detected (see Figure S1, ESI). The corona treatment settings used in this study were a quick- treat,  or  in- line  corona  treatment  unit  on  the  printing  press. Correspondingly, the specimens were exposed to corona treatment for a short time (< 1 s). Due to the short treatment times, the  corona  treatment  was  expected  to  lead  to  chemical  functionalization over a very thin surface layer. FTIR measurements cannot capture the surface layer exclusively, and the responses from the bulk are dominant in the FTIR spectra obtained here. Instances of marked changes in FTIR spectra are reported in the literature where polymer films were subjected to corona treatment for an extended period of time, with some studies reporting treatment times of seconds-as low as 5 s [33]-and others up to 50 h [34], which are not representative of industrial in- line corona treatment processes (Figure 3). Studies with treatment times similar to this study (~1s) have also been reported in the literature, where treated samples did not display any significant changes in spectral patterns [12].

text:
Neat and corona- treated polymer films were analyzed by XPS. Both survey and high- resolution (HRES) spectra were collected to assess the atomic composition and chemical bonding changes in the polymer films due to the corona treatment. Comparison of the HRES spectra for C 1s and O 1s regions, as well as the ratio of O 1s/C 1s atomic percentages, indicates a change in chemical bonding and an increase in oxygen content for the PE, EVOH, and  PA  films,  while  changes  in  the  monolayer  EAA  film  are ambiguous.

As summarized in Table 2, the oxygen content increased after the samples were corona- treated, which was expected. For example,  the  PE  oxygen  content  of  the  PE  sample  after  corona treatment was 18.25%, compared with 1.49% before corona treatment. Also, the carbon content decreased from 98.50% before the corona treatment to 74.47% after the corona treatment. This is expected due to the known functional groups introduced by corona treatment (C O, OH, OOH, and COOH) [10, 13, 32], which explains the increase in the oxygen content as the pre- treatment surface contained only CH 2 functional groups.

For PE, the C1s and O 1s HRES spectra indicated an increase in peak intensities for CO (eV) and C O/COOH (eV) functional groups, and a broadening of the overall C1s peak was observed after corona treatment. text: AFM was used to examine the changes in surface topography of the film samples before and after corona treatment and how the surface topography relates to the ink adhesion behavior of the polymer films. AFM height and phase images are shown in Figures  6  and  7,  respectively.  Untreated  samples,  specifically PE,  display  fibrous  features,  which  have  also  been  reported previously  in  the  literature  [35-39].  This  has  been  attributed to crystallites present in PE, affected by the orientation of the polymer chains during processing and subsequent quenching. After corona treatment, the PE, EAA, and EVOH films exhibit a  distinct  change  in  surface  topography,  where  the  surface  of the  film  appears  to  have  globule- like  structures,  or  'globular mounds'.  These  were  not  present  before  treatment  but  have been reported in the literature for  polypropylene  after  corona treatment [35-39]. These mounds have been hypothesized to be low molecular weight oxidized material (LMWOM) [35-39] and have also been found to be water- soluble through several characterization  methods.  The  similarities  in  appearance  between the results presented by Strobel et al. [35] for PP and the samples in this study are notable. Given the similarities in structures between the PE and PP, the presence of LMWOM on the surface of  the  samples in this study could be assumed; however, with water- based ink, the treatment effects would be expected to contradict an improvement in ink adhesion.

In the case of PA, the film may have needed a longer exposure to corona treatment to have an adequate effect to demonstrate observable changes in film surface morphology and chemistry. This is beyond the scope of the work of this study.

text: The  ASTM  tape  standard  test  defines  both  slow  and  fast  tape pulls  to  determine  ink  adhesion  on  a  printed  surface  [26].  The test  method  is  described  in  more  detail  in  the  materials  and methods section. In summary, after an image is printed onto a surface (Figure 8A), a piece of tape is applied to the printed surface smoothly and then pulled off either slowly or quickly according to which test is being conducted. This test method is a measure to assess the strength of adhesion between the ink and the print surface. The amount of ink that is on the tape after it is removed is an indication of the ink's adhesion to the surface. Figure 8B-E are images of the tape after slow and fast tape pulls. If there is a high percentage of ink on the tape and little ink left on the film, as shown on the untreated images in Figure 8 (left side; untreated PE [B] and untreated PA [D]), the ink adhesion is poor. An indication of good ink adhesion would result in little to no ink on the tape after it is pulled off the printed area, as seen in Figure 8C, where the tape test results of treated PE are depicted. Tape test results of treated PA are shown in Figure 8E. After the tapes were pulled, the amount of ink on the tape was evaluated and scored according PE Films Printed image before tape tests to the Durability Rating Scale shown in Table 3. A summary of the results of tape testing and rub evaluations by polymer type and corona treatment level is also available in Table 3.

The results above suggest that the oxygen content, and more importantly, the reactive groups present on the surface along with surface topography, are more influential for ink adhesion and durability than factors such as high native SFE. While it can be observed that all four polymer types studied were affected by the corona treatment, it can be justifiably concluded that polymer types have varied responses to corona treatments, resulting in varied surface topographies, surface chemistries, and ink adhesion and durability capacity. The types of functional groups, surface density of the functional groups, and reactivity of the functional groups, combined with surface topography, directly influence the level of ink adhesion and durability of the polymer surfaces, signifying that the degree of ink adhesion and durability is more complex than SFE guidelines used in industry. While PE was the most promising substrate for printing in this study, future investigations would be necessary to understand the effects of comonomer content, molecular weight, branching, and other physical attributes of PE grades.

text: Industry guidelines for acceptable ink adhesion and durability currently reference SFE differentials as the primary factor in predicting successful printability. Based on this guideline, the SFE of a print substrate should be in the range of 40-50 dynes/ cm to generate successful ink adhesion with a representative water- based ink. The initial hypothesis of this work was that polymer films having native SFE values that are in the same range as those achieved by corona treatment of polyethylene, ca. 41-46 dynes/cm, will have significantly higher ink adhesion and rub- resistance durability compared to a standard polyethylene, with typical SFE values of 28-33 dynes/cm. However, the findings from this study show that polymers with native SFE in the range of 41-46 dynes/cm, due to their chemical composition and surface functional groups, did not demonstrate improved ink adhesion or durability. All polymers tested required corona treatment to demonstrate any notable improvement in ink adhesion and durability. The analysis methods, including ATR- FTIR, contact angle goniometry with resulting SFE calculations, AFM, XPS, and ink adhesion and durability testing, established  baseline  information  for  untreated  samples  and demonstrated surface functionality changes that were expected in  the  corona- treated  samples,  confirming  the  surfaces  were adequately treated and prepared for printing. Combining the results  of  ink  adhesion  and  durability  testing  with  other  analytical  data,  it  was  determined  that  the  influence  of  corona treatment through oxidation, production of surface- active functional groups present at the surface, and topographical modifications  are  more  significant  factors  for  predicting  acceptable ink adhesion and durability than the SFE differences between the ink and the polymer substrates. Polymers with high native SFE values in the range of corona- treated PE (ca. 41-46 dynes/ cm) (i.e., PA, EVOH) did not demonstrate better or improved ink adhesion or durability versus polymers with lower native SFE values (i.e., PE, EAA, ca. 28-33 dynes/cm) either pre-  or post- corona treatment. The observed changes in corona- treated PE and EAA, including oxidation and changes in surface topography, in combination with a higher SFE, led to higher ink adhesion and durability performance in comparison to PA and EVOH. From these  results,  it  can  be  concluded  that  surface chemistry and surface topography combined are more influential factors than SFE alone as a means of achieving improved ink  adhesion  and  durability.  These  observations  and  corresponding  conclusions  provide  updated  guidance  for  flexible packaging converters, as the industry's rule of thumb for using ink and substrate SFE differentials to predict acceptable ink adhesion is not adequate.

Based on this guideline, the SFE of a print substrate should be in the range of 40-50 dynes/ cm to generate successful ink adhesion with a representative water- based ink. The initial hypothesis of this work was that polymer films having native SFE values that are in the same range as those achieved by corona treatment of polyethylene, ca. 41-46 dynes/cm, will have significantly higher ink adhesion and rub- resistance durability compared to a standard polyethylene, with typical SFE values of 28-33 dynes/cm. However, the findings from this study show that polymers with native SFE in the range of 41-46 dynes/cm, due to their chemical composition and surface functional groups, did not demonstrate improved ink adhesion or durability. All polymers tested required corona treatment to demonstrate any notable improvement in ink adhesion and durability. The analysis methods, including ATR- FTIR, contact angle goniometry with resulting SFE calculations, AFM, XPS, and ink adhesion and durability testing, established  baseline  information  for  untreated  samples  and demonstrated surface functionality changes that were expected in  the  corona- treated  samples,  confirming  the  surfaces  were adequately treated and prepared for printing. Combining the results  of  ink  adhesion  and  durability  testing  with  other  analytical  data,  it  was  determined  that  the  influence  of  corona treatment through oxidation, production of surface- active functional groups present at the surface, and topographical modifications  are  more  significant  factors  for  predicting  acceptable ink adhesion and durability than the SFE differences between the ink and the polymer substrates. Polymers with high native SFE values in the range of corona- treated PE (ca. 41-46 dynes/ cm) (i.e., PA, EVOH) did not demonstrate better or improved ink adhesion or durability versus polymers with lower native SFE values (i.e., PE, EAA, ca. 28-33 dynes/cm) either pre-  or post- corona treatment. The observed changes in corona- treated PE and EAA, including oxidation and changes in surface topography, in combination with a higher SFE, led to higher ink adhesion and durability performance in comparison to PA and EVOH. From these  results,  it  can  be  concluded  that  surface chemistry and surface topography combined are more influential factors than SFE alone as a means of achieving improved ink  adhesion  and  durability.  These  observations  and  corresponding  conclusions  provide  updated  guidance  for  flexible packaging converters, as the industry's rule of thumb for using ink and substrate SFE differentials to predict acceptable ink adhesion is not adequate.
